headline: Meet The Press for September 18, 2022, NBC
story_text: [09:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) CHUCK TODD, NBC HOST MEET THE PRESS: This Sunday Poll Vault. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) PRESIDENT JOE BIDEN : People are back to work. (END VIDEO CLIP0 TODD: Our new NBC News Poll shows a jump in President Biden`s approval ratings. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) PRESIDENT JOE BIDEN : We`re making progress. We`re getting places done as well. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: And signs that Democrat standing may be improving ahead of November. One explanation the overturning of Roe v. Wade. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNKNOWN: We`re moving backwards. We`re taking one step forward, three steps back. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: Another the high profile presence of former President Trump. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: We may have to do it again. Stay tuned everybody. Stay tuned. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: My guest this morning, the number two Democrat in the Senate, Dick Durbin of Illinois and Republican Senate candidate Joe O`Dea running to flip a Colorado seat. Plus, the Senate will look into charges by a former U.S. attorney that Mr. Trump tried to use the Justice Department to punish his enemies and protect his friends. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GEOFFREY BERMAN , FORMER U.S. ATTORNEY: Pissing off the president is not a Federal crime. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: Geoffrey Berman joins me this morning. Also, border wars amid a surge at the southern border. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNKNOWN: Some of them have been through, really horrific things. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: Florida Governor Ron DeSantis ships four dozen unsuspecting Venezuelan migrants from Texas to Martha`s Vineyard in Massachusetts. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GOVERNOR RON DESANTIS (R-FL): Every community in America should be sharing in the burdens. It shouldn`t all fall on a handful of red states. UNKNOWN: (Inaudible) is so cruel, so depraved that someone would do that. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: Joining me for inside and analysis are New York Times Chief White House Correspondent Peter Baker, former Obama White House Senior Advisor Stephanie Cutter, Republican Strategist Al Cardenas and Leanne Caldwell of the Washington Post . Welcome to Sunday. It`s Meet the Press. ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest running show in television history this is Meet the Press with Chuck Todd. TODD: Good Sunday morning. President Biden is finally getting his polling bump. A spade of news from anger over the overturning of Roe v. Wade to falling gas prices, has helped push the president`s poll numbers to their highest point in almost a year, and it`s thanks mostly to Democrats coming home. In fact, among all registered voters Mr. Biden`s job approval in our new NBC News Poll is sitting at 45 percent, 52 disapproving. The big jump really was from Democrats, particularly younger ones, happy about the passage of the agenda, perhaps student loans as well, but those are hardly robust numbers and they`re a jump from last months 42-55 split. And the race for control of Congress is dead even, 46 percent for Democrats, 46 percent for Republicans. The remarkable thing about Mr. Biden`s numbers is how he even manages to get to 45 percent. On issue after issue, his approval ratings are actually consistently below 45 on foreign policy, it`s just 42 percent. The economy even lower 40, border lower than that 36 and on cost of living even lower at a paltry 30 percent. So what`s happening? One is, of course, the Dobbs decision. It`s clearly energizing voters and not just Democrats. Only 37 percent approve of the Supreme Court`s decision to overturn Roe. Sixty-one percent disapprove of that decision, but just as important to President Biden is getting a lift from simply Donald Trump`s presence. The high-profile investigations, all of it, is preventing Republicans from turning the mid-terms into a referendum on Mr. Biden, and he loves to say judging by the alternative not the almighty and he may be benefiting from that right now. Voter feelings towards Mr. Trump are just 34 percent positive, 54 percent negative, 20 points underwater. It`s lowest point in a year and a half. Compare that to President Biden`s current personal ratings, 42 percent positive, 47 percent negative. Not great, but that`s only five points underwater. So where are we? The bottom line is this, less than two months from the mid-terms each political party is running the campaign they want to run. Republicans on crime, economy and immigration and they`re winning with that battle with the voters. Democrats are running on Mr. Trump and abortion rights and they`re winning that battle with the voters. So, what`s going to happen? Joining me now is the number two Democrat in the Senate Dick Durbin of Illinois. Senator Durbin, welcome back to Meet the Press. SEN. DICK DURBIN (D-IL): Good to be with you Chuck. TODD: So I`m going to start with the -- the stunt I guess is the best way to call it that Governor DeSantis did when trying to fund the flight of migrants in Texas, that he claimed might have been coming to Florida. He - - you know and sent them to Massachusetts. Here was his rational for it and then I want to ask you more on the other side. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GOV. RON DESANTIS (R-FL): We are not a sanctuary state and it`s better to be able to go to a sanctuary jurisdiction. [09:05:00] And yes, we will help facilitate that transport for you. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: All right, do you think these bus, whether it`s these bus tickets to the Naval Observatory, New York, D.C. or Martha`s Vineyard, do you think the Federal government should stop them and prevent them from happening? DURBIN: Well I can tell you this. I`ve been to the Salvation Army Rescue Center in Chicago and I met with the people that came off the buses. I sat down with one of the families and they told me the story. It is pathetic that these governors are taking advantage of these helpless people, making promises to them to get on the bus and life is just going to be fine, and off they go to places far removed from where they`re supposed to be appearing under the requirements of our law in a matter of weeks and months. So he`s jeopardizing their stay in the United States when they make -- each governor makes this decision, and the second part I want to raise is this Chuck. Why is it when the Republicans want to enforce their immigration theories? It`s always the kids that end up being the victims. We saw it with kids in cages. We saw it with a forcible removal of children from their parents, some who`ve never been reunited with their families and now once again, it`s the kids and families that are put on these buses and transported for political purposes across the United States. TODD: Do you believe laws were broken here by Governor DeSantis? DURBIN: I don`t know if the laws were specifically broken but it broken -- they have broken every basic standard of decency when it comes to dealing with children and families. These people are at the moment legally in the United States. Some of them, one family I met, it`s been five months coming up from Venezuela, literally walking to our border. They went through every possible outrage that you could imagine from theft, stealing their cellphones, pushing them into a jungle for a period of time with this man didn`t think he could survive, and they finally made it to the United States only to be exploited by the governor of Texas in -- in their case. I just don`t think -- when you get down to the basic rules of politics, this passes the smell test. TODD: All right. Senator, let`s talk about the actual issue at the border. We`re getting upwards an average, I think, 8,000 folks a day. We`re already over 2 million for the year. Right now, I do not believe the Federal government has the authority that ICE or DHS has the funding authority to, you know, help move -- move these folks to other parts of the country. Do you think they should have that authority? DURBIN: We put a dramatic investment into our -- our border operations and President Biden has called for that and we have supported it on a bipartisan basis. But I want to tell you the bottom line and it`s a clich \'20\'1A about our broken immigration system is the truth, unless and until we come together in a bipartisan fashion in the Senate particularly, and once again entertain the comprehensive immigration bill we are just inviting trouble. Across my state of Illinois and virtually every other state, there is a desperate need for workers. Our birth rate is not keeping up with our demands for workers and -- and every walk of -- of life that you can imagine, we need more people. And there are those who want to serve this country, but we need an orderly process at the border -- TODD: Right. DURBIN: To do that we need Congress to do its part on a bipartisan basis, Republicans complain about the situation and it -- it needs to be changed dramatically, but they won`t engage in helping us reach a -- a -- any kind of solution. TODD: I want to play for you what the vice-president told me about her take on the border and get your comments. Take a look. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) VICE-PRESIDENT KAMALA HARRIS: The border is secure but we also have a broken immigration system, in particular over the last four years before we came in and it needs to be fixed. TODD: We`re going to have 2 million people cross this border for the first time ever. You`re confident this border is secure. HARRIS: We have a secure border in that is a priority for any nation including ours and our administration, but there are still a lot of problems that we are trying to fix given the deterioration that happened over the last four years. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: You know Senator, I -- I understand your comment about the Republicans here and I think there`s a lot of evidence and many of them want -- would prefer the issue for the -- for the ballot box than a solution. But Democrats don`t look like their anxious to do something, you`re an exception. You`re -- you`re one of the few people that wants to talk about this issue and try to solve it, but you know there`s a lot of Democrats that would prefer to ignore it and hope that, hey, we`ll -- we`ll deal with it, maybe, at another time. How do you fix that mindset? DURBIN: There`s political danger, don`t get me wrong but we faced that eight years ago when we set down with our gang of eight with John McCain , myself and Schumer and even Senator Graham and came up with a comprehensive plan that was embraced by business and labor and groups across the board. We passed it in the Senate Chuck, you`ll remember that. Fourteen Republicans voted for it. [09:10:00] DURBIN: Five of them are still around today and then sent it over to the House where it died unfortunately. The Republican leadership refused to take it up. It can be done. We can make the border safe and have a system of legal entry into the United States to work, put -- put these people on the books, have them pay taxes, make sure we`ve done a background check. All of these things can be done. Are they controversial? You bet. Some of them are very controversial but we know we need to do it. The United States is a nation of immigrants. I`m proud to be a son of an -- TODD: Right. DURBIN: -- immigrant who came to this country but -- but I will tell you, if we`re going to do it in this era we can`t wait another 30 years to get around to the solution. TODD: I want to pivot to a couple other things that you -- that are under your umbrella as Senate Judiciary Chair in particular. If Democrats hold the Senate but Republicans take the House, are you prepared as Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee , they essentially take over the January 6th investigation? DURBIN: Well I can tell you this. This is a remarkable investigation. I know they`re going to have at least one more hearing before the end of the year. I don`t know if they`ve concluded their remarks, concluded their investigation say or -- or more has to be done, but that was a seminal event in American history. I was there and many members of both chambers were there when this insurrection, this mob stormed the Capital. TODD: Yes. DURBIN: Five people died, 149 law enforcement were injured and sadly most Republicans, the overwhelmingly majority of Republicans in Congress want to ignore it, not even ask the question. It has to be asked and it has to be part of our history. So I want the January 6th Committee to do its work in the House and if there`s more work to be done and I`m in a position to call for it, you bet I will. TODD: I was just going to say during the lame duck, if there`s -- if the Republicans don`t want to continue the January 6th but the committee, you`re prepared to essentially take over the investigation if that`s what`s necessary to get, you know, to protect whatever materials could be -- could be threatened if this investigation isn`t over. Because it`s my understanding, they`re not going to finish by the end of the year. DURBIN: But there`s one key difference, in the Senate Judiciary Committee , in order to issue a subpoena you need bipartisan agreement to do it. That`s not the case I understand in the House. TODD: Right. DURBIN: So, if -- if the Republicans want to resist this it`s going to be difficult to continue the investigation. I hope the House gets it done. TODD: Finally, really quickly, on same-sex marriage, are you all concerned that if Republicans win the Senate that in the lame duck, you won`t get the votes to codify same-sex marriage? DURBIN: I am worried about that but my north star in this issue is Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin. TODD: Right. DURBIN: She has led the bipartisan effort and she believes this is the right way to deal with it. I defer to her, but this is a serious issue just like the Dobbs decision. Clarence Thomas made it clear that he`s going to move toward Oberfeld the Supreme Court case related to gay rights in this country. We better take him seriously. TODD: Senator Dick Durbin, number two in Senate leadership, also Chairman of the Judiciary Committee. Thanks for coming on, sharing your perspective. DURBIN: Thanks Chuck. TODD: One reason Democrats are hopeful about holding the Senate is because Republican primary voters have nominated numerous candidates in Trump`s image, who just may be too controversial to win over swing voters. THOMPSON: Would there be a place for same sex couples? WILSON: Well, you mean legally? THOMPSON: Yes. WILSON: You mean like marriage? THOMPSON: Uh-huh. WILSON: No. No marriage. But there`d be same sex couples-- THOMPSON: No marriage, even though it`s the law of the land in the United States? WILSON: Just like Roe used to be, right? THOMPSON (voice-over): Reverend Dr. Elizabeth Stevens leads the Unitarian Universalist Church of the Palouse. REVEREND DR. ELIZABETH STEVENS, UNITARIAN UNIVERSALIS CHURCH OF THE PALOUSE: In the public square, I don`t see them representing Christianity. I don`t see them representing the values that I find in the Bible. I see them representing patriarchy. I see them fighting the culture war. WILSON: You can`t have a naval warfare without ships. And you can`t have tank warfare without tanks. And as I tell Christians all around the country, you can`t have culture war unless you have a culture. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: You can see the full episode of "Meet the Press Reports" on Peacock, YouTube , Roku or anywhere you get NBC News videos. New episodes first air on NBC News Now on Thursdays at 10:30 p.m. Eastern. So let me bring the panel back. Peter, this is not sort of disaggregated from the world of Trump. In many ways, it`s fused with Trumpism. In fact, let me put a mash together of some candidates that Trump has endorsed who are all sort of preaching this, there`s no wall between church and state. Take a look. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) REP. LAUREN BOEBERT (R-CO): And I`m tired of this separation of church and state junk. DOUG MASTRIANO (R), PENNSYLVANIA GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: In November, we`re going to take our state back. My God, we`ll make it so. We will. REP. MARJORIE TAYLOR GREENE (R-GA): We need to be the party of nationalism. And I`m a Christian and I say it proudly. We should be Christian nationalists. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: Now, Donald Trump has embraced this. Evangelicals embraced Trump. It was sort of a grand bargain, right? They seemed to get what they want, and it has fused into something else here. In your reporting on Trump, how does he view this sort of Christian nationalism that is attaching itself to Trumpism? BAKER: Well, he`s very opportunistic, of course. Obviously, it`s not saying anything surprising to say that Donald Trump is not exactly the most religious person in the world. Certainly his values are not particularly Christian. But he recognized in 2016 something important, which is these Christian conservatives were important to his victory, right? That was something therefore he needed to pay attention to. [09:55:01] He once told in fact, Lindsey Graham , and you played that clip from him earlier. He once told Lindsey Graham about these pastors who called him to tell him they were praying for him in the middle of impeachment. He says, those F`ing Christians just love me. I mean, he`s very opportunistic and kind of cynical about it, but he recognizes that it`s important to his political success. And they have recognized it`s the important -- that his success is important to them because he gave them a lot of what they wanted, in terms of judges, in terms of policies. He was the most overtly anti-abortion president and arguably the one most responsible for the overturning of Roe v. Wade. TODD: You know, look, some of this is reactionary, Leigh Ann. I want to put up this statistic. Are you a member of a church, synagogue, or mosque? Membership over the decades. So in 1940, 73 percent of Americans were a member of a church, synagogue, or a mosque. Look where we are in 2020. We`re down to 47 percent. So, it does -- how much of this rise of Christian nationalism is almost sort of like a reaction to the fact that we`re becoming more secular as a country? CALDWELL: Yeah, that`s a huge problem for some of these people. They don`t want that to happen. They don`t like these trends. But they are also a very powerful minority in this country. I mean, you look at the abortion movement. They have -- they organized 50 years ago after Roe v. Wade was decided, and they got the result that they wanted. And so, there is some political belief among this group that they can continue to move the country, even though they are in a minority, in the direction that they want. TODD: You know, Stephanie, there`s like -- we`ve noticed in our show for the most part there is one voting group in the Democratic coalition that does want to see, you know, religious texts sometimes be fused with public politics, and that`s churchgoing African Americans in particular. But Democrats in general are becoming more secular as a party. Do you ever worry about that sort of uncomfortable partnership there? CUTTER: Uncomfortable partnership with? TODD: Just on religious stuff. CUTTER: No, I don`t worry about it. You`ve got, you know, a Catholic president who very much believed in people having their own beliefs. And, you know, there are plenty of opportunities for Democratic politicians or electeds to show their faith. Look at what`s happening in Pennsylvania with Josh Shapiro. He`s Jewish, but he is not ceding churches to Mastriano, who is very much a Christian nationalist. And he`s going and he`s very comfortable preaching from the pulpit about why he`s running for office, how his faith informs what he believes politically. And that`s exactly what Democrats need to keep doing because we should not cede the faith issue to Republicans. TODD: You know, Al, the Republican Party over the last 30 years was very much tied to many churchgoers-- CARDENAS: Ronald Reagan became a -- TODD: Is this going to become a liability? CARDENAS: Probably. You know, I`m saddened by the fact that America is becoming more secular just from a spiritual point of view. I also am saddened by the fact that my Catholic Church and the non-Evangelical Protestants have weakened themselves to the point where they`re not as relevant. And so the most relevant political group in the religious movement right now are Evangelicals. And they have always had a different perspective than my Catholic Church or non-Evangelical Protestants. And I think these guys are talking to Evangelicals, not the rest of us. TODD: No, I think you`re absolutely right. Well, I hope you catch the episode if you get a chance. That`s all we have for today. Thank you for watching. We`ll be back next week because if it`s Sunday, it`s "Meet the Press". Thank you, John. headline: Katie Couric`s Message On The Importance Of Those Yearly Mammograms As She Reveals Her Own Breast Cancer Diagnosis
story_text: [07:41:32] CRAIG MELVIN: We are back. It is 7:41. We`re back with In-Depth Today. And this morning, an important story that`s really close to our hearts. HODA KOTB: Yes, every two minutes, a woman in this country is diagnosed with breast cancer and yesterday, our friend and our former colleague Katie Couric revealed she is now one of them. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE: And of course Katie has been on the frontlines of cancer awareness for decades, she lost her husband to cancer. And she`s using her story now to urge all women to get checked and to advocate for themselves. Sheinelle is here with more on that. Hi, good morning. SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. As she battles breast cancer, Katie is turning her story into a cautionary tale in hopes of saving lives. She wants to educate women not only on the importance of screening but also about something called dense breast tissue. It affects nearly half of women in this country including Katie. And doctors say knowing you have it and how to ask for proper screenings could be lifesaving. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JONES (voice-over): Former today anchor Katie Couric has revealed that for the past several months, she has been privately battling cancer. COURIC: Thank you all for your support. JONES (voice-over): In an essay titled "Why Not Me?" the 65-year-old journalist says she was stunned by a stage one breast cancer diagnosis in June after missing her annual mammogram. I`m normally vigilant, bordering on neurotic, about taking care of my health. COURIC: I want to make sure that you all don`t put off your mammograms. JONES (voice-over): Katie is among nearly half of women over 40 in the U.S. who have dense breast tissue, which makes it more difficult to detect abnormalities on a mammogram and also increases your risk of breast cancer. Armed with this knowledge, her mammogram was followed by additional screening using an ultrasound, doctors biopsied a mass. The next day, Katie received the shocking results. It`s cancer. You`re going to be fine, but we need to make a plan. I felt sick and the room started to spin. What does this mean? What will the next weeks, months, even years look like? This isn`t the first time cancer has touched her life. Katie has long been an advocate for cancer awareness and screenings ever since her husband, Jay, was diagnosed with colon cancer and died of the disease at the age of 42. COURIC: Words of course will never describe how devastating this loss has been. JONES (voice-over): She famously underwent an on air colonoscopy on Today to encourage others to get checked. As a result, screenings went up by 20 percent, some dubbing it the Couric effect. COURIC: I have a pretty little colon. JONES (voice-over): She also lost her sister, Emily, to pancreatic cancer and 2001. The deaths of her loved ones prompting Katie to co found Stand Up to Cancer. COURIC: And I just realized I had to do something about this. JONES (voice-over): But with no family history of breast cancer, her own diagnosis came as a particular shock. Katie`s surgeon Dr. Lisa Newman. DR. LISA NEWMAN, KATIE COURIC`S SURGEON: More than three quarters of the breast cancers that we diagnose occur in women that do not have any established risk factors for breast cancer. JONES (voice-over): Katie`s cancer was caught early. She underwent a lumpectomy along with radiation and says she`ll need to take medication for the next five years. NEWMAN: It is wonderful that Katie has gone public with her experience and early detection of breast cancers will save millions of lives. JONES (voice-over): Now as she`s done before, Katie is determined to shine a light once again, on the importance of screening for cancer. Please get your annual mammogram. I was six months late this time. I shudder to think what might have happened if I had put it off longer. (END VIDEOTAPE) [07:45:08] JONES: Just six months late, here`s what we know for sure. When we do stories like this, our hope is that a woman watching or maybe a family member, that we give you a little nudge to go ahead and get that checkup. That`s what`s most important. KOTB: Six months is nothing, I mean especially with COVID and people not going in for a checkups. GUTHRIE: Yes, and you know, you kind of think, when I feel something -- KOTB: I did that. She thought she did it. She`s like, oh, it`s been that long. GUTHRIE: Really, for a mammogram or any of those screening, I actually made an appointment yesterday for a yearly physical I need. And it`s like because you remember, like, oh, yes, you know what, I`m going to do it. I`m not going to put it off another day. JONES: These kinds of stories save lives. MELVIN: We`re going to hear from Katie too, right? GUTHRIE: Yes, she`s going to join us on Monday. It`ll be her first live interview since sharing her diagnosis. It`ll be good to see Katie and give her a hug. And obviously she`s got a really important message to share. KOTB: We look forward to that. We`re going to get another check of the weather from Bill Karins. He`s in for Al. And some people have been wondering during the storm, where is Al, Al happen to test positive for COVID. We`re happy to say he`s feeling fine, just mild symptoms. He`s home. KARINS: He`s been sending us notes like he`s, you know, he wants to be here, he feels well. I can only imagine a step count in his house just like going back before, just like, you know, it`s like, yes. GUTHRIE: Disengage. KARINS: But Al has help us build an incredible weather team here at NBC News. And, you know, we`re getting you through this storm. And Al we`ll see you back here very soon. So concerns for today, the one thing I`m going to be watching is the storm surge. We have a storm surge warning still in effect for areas of northeast Florida. We`re not done yet. Irma really surprised us with the storm surge in the Jacksonville area. And here`s what we`re going to watch, the St. Johns River is one of the few rivers in our country that actually flows from south to north so that water that`s now falling in Orlando is going to trickle northwards up through the river at the same time. We`re going to see the storm surge coming in this afternoon at high tide about noon. This is all going to meet near Jacksonville. So we`re going to watch that area closely for the possibility of the four to six feet of storm surge. Right now they`ve already got a surge of about two feet. That`s look at your national weather. Now here`s a look at the weather outside your window. (LOCAL NEWS) KARINS: And that`s your Thursday forecast. MELVIN: All right. Thank you, Bill. Up next, he did it. Homerun history overnight, and we`re going to hear from Yankee`s superstar Aaron Judge after belting that 61st of the season to officially join baseball royalty. But first, these messages. headline: Today for September 29, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Hi everybody. It`s Thursday. Millions in Florida waking up to catastrophic damage from Ian. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes, the full impact being revealed as the sunrises this morning. It is September 29th. This is Today. Path of destruction, massive flooding and power outages as Ian barrels across Florida crashing ashore as one of the strongest hurricanes to ever hit the state. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: All the sudden I felt something and then heard like a train coming right to the house. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Nearly 3 million people in the dark, the devastating storm surge leaving entire neighborhoods underwater, homes and cars floating down streets. This hospital swapped from above and below, losing part of its roof, its ground floor flooded, crews still carrying out emergency rescues on land and at sea. We`re live across the state with complete coverage and what millions need to know as the threat moves up the East Coast. Get out, the urgent security alert for all Americans in Russia to leave the country immediately. And the new warning that anyone there with dual citizenship couldn`t be drafted into the Ukraine war, we`ll have the very latest. Breast cancer battle, well wishes pouring in for Katie Couric this morning after she revealed her diagnosis. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) KATIE COURIC, AMERICAN JOURNALIST: Thank you all for your support. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Just ahead, her decision to speak out and what she wants all women to know. Those stories, plus, historic blast. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Judge keep the left field. This could be it. See you. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Yankee`s superstar Aaron Judge crushes his record tying 61st homerun of the season, cementing his place among baseball royalty. Today, Thursday, September 29th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Good Thursday morning. So happy you`re joining us today. Good to see you. GUTHRIE: Yes. The sun is coming up in Florida and we`re getting a closer look now at the widespread devastation left behind by Ian. KOTB: Yes, there are two major concerns right now there, the flooding of course and the power outages. Nearly 3 million people across the state woke up this morning and could not turn the lights on, no electricity. GUTHRIE: Ian made landfall yesterday as a major category four packing 150 mile an hour winds and causing massive storm surges across Florida`s Gulf Coast. KOTB: So right now, Ian is making its way east toward the eastern side of Florida. We have a live look at some of the conditions going on. This is Orlando. And while the storm did weakened overnight, it still remains a serious threat. GUTHRIE: Yes, it`s a rain story there. And then once Ian heads away from Florida, it is expected to then curve back toward the Georgia, South Carolina coastlines impacting millions across the South in the coming days. KOTB: Yes, we got it all covered for you this morning. We`re going to start off with NBC`s Sam Brock. He is in Venice, Florida. That`s just north of where Ian made landfall. Hi, Sam, what`s the assessment this morning? SAM BROCK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Yes, Hoda, Savannah, good morning. It is terrifying to think what we`re going to see in the light of day. I was just talking to a police officer here in Venice. They resume search and rescue operations at 2 o`clock this morning looking for critically injured people. But he said look, I got to warn you, block to block, there`s dead wire, there`s live wire. As you look behind me right now, you`ll see splintered signs and power lines down all through here. Now when East Naples guys, there were 30 rescue missions yesterday as the urgent efforts right now are underway to find those imperiled by Ian. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BROCK (voice-over): It`s devastation that was predicted with the grim reality of this storm`s warped power defies imagination. Ian now with tropical storm hit the coast as a fierce hurricane shredding homes apart and Placida, Florida, tearing off roofs and splintering trees. While in the Tampa area, extremely causing this tree to crash through a home. In one of the hardest hit areas, Fort Myers, there were storm surges nearly seven feet high, nearly double the previous record more than 20 years ago. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Oh my God. BROCK (voice-over): The massive surge of water leaving entire communities completely underwater. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Do you want me to come out? BROCK (voice-over): Roads looking more like the ocean for block after block. Ian packed catastrophic 150 mile an hour winds knocking out power to more than 2 million customers. GOV. RON DESANTIS (R-FL): We have seen life threatening storm surge as was predicted. We`ve also seen major flooding, but that`s going to rank as one of the top five hurricanes to ever hit the Florida peninsula. BROCK (voice-over): This team of emergency responders unable to respond, a massive wall of water swamping their fire truck. [07:05:06] UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Now we have a truck issue and the guys are pushing the truck out of the bay. BROCK (voice-over): In Port Charlotte, hospital staff working through the storm to protect patients. Other first responders struggling to help those in need, unable to start rescues until after life threatening conditions subsided. Despite repeated warnings to leave, some people did not or could not evacuate. They found themselves stranded by a 12 foot storm surge. Mark and Elizabeth living in an apartment in Venice Island, Florida but at the last minute, grab their air mattresses and hunker down in this Sarasota office when her boss offered it to them. (on camera): Here you are with air mattresses in an office space. Your home is 50 or 100 miles away. But you consider yourself lucky. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We are. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes. BROCK: Is that because you`re saved from the storm? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes, yes, because somebody helped us. BROCK (voice-over): Others stayed behind in the flood zone, trying to help those who were unable to leave. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I want to help the people in here because they`re good people here in paradise. BROCK (voice-over): This morning, the destruction left behind by this massive blow from Mother Nature is just starting to come into focus. (END VIDEOTAPE) KOTB: Well, hats off to those first responders, all those helpers out there, Sam. There were some viral images in Tampa that were just shocking. It was actually Tampa Bay, and it looked dry. It looked like you could walk on it. People were taking video and pictures of it. What`s the after effects there? BROCK: Yes, so here`s the deal, Hoda, you`re seeing all this water being really sucked out. It`s called negative storm surge. And the reason behind it, you have counterclockwise winds and hurricanes. So on the northern edge of the eye wall, the water was being pulled out of Tampa Bay, into the Gulf of Mexico. The problem with this, Hoda, is the fact that it can then refill when wind directionality change. And it can happen in a matter of minutes. So if you see this, it might be tempting to go out there on the sand and check it out. Don`t do it for your own safety. Hoda? KOTB: All right, Sam Brock for us there in Venice, Sam, thanks. GUTHRIE: Yes. These conditions can change in a split second, the water has finally stopped rising in Fort Myers. But this morning, the impact of the catastrophic flooding there is being felt across the city. And joining us now Fort Myers Mayor Kevin Anderson. Mr. Mayor, good morning. We`re glad to have you on the phone with us this morning. Have you been able to assess damage? I know it`s still early there. What`s your sense of how bad it was? MAYOR KEVIN ANDERSON, FORT MYERS, FL: We haven`t had a full assessment obviously with the sun just coming up, but it is pretty bad. I`m standing on a floating concrete dock. I`m down in the River District of downtown. The problem is the dock is in the middle of an intersection, a block, two blocks away from the water. This is about a piece of concrete that weighs a ton. And it was moved this far away. It shows you how powerful the waters were last night. KOTB: I know one of the things, that`s most concerning in a moment like this is what happened to the people who decided to stay or who were left behind. Have you guys been able to conduct rescues? Do you know how many people are still out there and in need of your help? ANDERSON: We would estimate several dozen people who stayed behind were in need of some assistance. Our teams have been working on that. I`m happy to report at this time. I`ve been not -- I haven`t been told of any loss of life in the city. Now keep in mind, we have a metropolitan area and there may be some outside, but inside the city there`s been no reports to my knowledge. GUTHRIE: Fort Myers more or less took a direct hit, Mr. Mayor, what`s your sense of how this compares to other storms that Fort Myers has experienced? ANDERSON: I came here in the mid 70s. I was on the police department for almost 25 years, so a lot of storms here. This is by far the worst storm I have ever witnessed. They`re watching the water from my condo in the heart of downtown, watching that water rise and just flat out all the stories on the first floor. It was heartbreaking. KOTB: Boy, for -- Mayor for you who`s been there all those years and seen so many storms come and go to take a direct hit. So what is the plan now, like walk us through what will happen this morning and the days ahead? ANDERSON: So the first thing we need to do is make sure the roads are passable. And they`re safe. We do have a curfew in place for next 48 hours until we get a handle on everything. Once we get the roads cleared, you know, FPL will start working on the electricity. Our teams will be out there going through the neighborhoods trying to make sure people are safe, getting assistance, anyone who needs it. We`ll start working on getting the other utilities up and functioning getting cleaned up. We`ve gotten some great support pledge by the President and the governor. So I think I`m optimistic it`s going to be a long recovery but nonetheless we`re going to recover because Floridians are very resilient. [07:10:13] GUTHRIE: They are indeed. Mr. Mayor, thank you so much. Kevin Anderson of Fort Myers, you know, it`s going to be a busy day, so we thank you for your time. KOTB: All right, let`s -- ANDERSON: Thank you. KOTB: Thank you. Let`s turn now to Bill Karins. He`s been tracking the path of destruction where it`s heading and what it`s left behind, hey. BILL KARINS, NBC NEWS METEOROLOGIST: Yes, good morning. So we`ve been showing you where all the worst has been as far as the storm surge went, that was the Fort Myers area, Bonita Springs all the way down to Naples. Overnight, we`ve still had a lot of heavy rain. Our NBC affiliate in Orlando and meteorologists were saying in Kissimmee, there`s been houses with homes with one to two feet of water in them. The little McIver River in Seminole County located right about here is one foot over record flood stage. So again, there`s still problems and still water going into homes right now because of this situation. And look at Daytona Beach. A wind gust of 69 miles per hour, so this is down to a tropical storm, but it is not a pleasant morning in Volusia County, Flagler County heading up there to Jacksonville. That`s where the storm surge is going to be coming in during the day today. So even though it`s a weekend storm, there still could be some significant problems. And then it may actually intensify a little bit on its way up tomorrow in between Savannah and Charleston here to South Carolina, we may actually get landfall that either a strong tropical storm or as a hurricane tomorrow afternoon. And of course, we`re going to get heavy rain in this area, winds could gust possibly up to 70 miles per hour. And that way we could be dealing with some more power outages, guys, in this area too. And storm surge problems, which we`ll explain more about during the show today. GUTHRIE: All right, Bill, thank you. And as we`ve come on the air President Biden has officially declared the state of Florida, a major disaster. So that opens up funding and a lot of help hopefully today. NBC Nightly News anchor Lester Holt rode out the storm overnight in Bradenton just south of Tampa Bay. Homes there flooded, the area`s airport badly damage too. Lester, good morning, the view from where you sit. LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Well, Savannah, I went out to with my trusty flashlight a little while ago surveying the immediate area around us. There appears to be no major damage here. We spoke when heard from the mayor of Sarasota a while ago. He was venturing outside his home for the first time, saw plenty of damage. He`s not aware of anything catastrophic. But certainly during the night, we can hear this thing howling, ultimately dying down now. The rain has stopped and we`re feeling relative breezes after what we saw and went through yesterday. But we`re all OK. KOTB: Yes, difficult night for a lot of people. Lester, a lot of people spent the night in shelters. I`m sure they have tons of concerns about their homes. What are you hearing from them? HOLT: Yes, we went to a shelter a few hours before the eye wall came ashore and talked to people who made that choice. They`d heard the predictions. A lot of them thought it was a no brainer, immediately went into shelters. We talked to officials there who were very concerned that while they did have a number of people, they didn`t have nearly as many as they expected. And that`s why there`s a bit of trepidation this morning as the sun comes up here. You heard from one of the other mayors the sense of what they`re going to find now in the light of day in some of these neighborhoods. One couple of we talked to said they lived in a trailer home, very worried obviously about their neighborhood, the vulnerability. They decided to get out but so many of their neighbors did not. So that will be the big focus today, trying to get to those folks who rode it out and make sure they`re OK. GUTHRIE: All right, Lester, thank you. And of course, we`ll see you tonight on nightly news from Florida. I mean, bears (ph) repeating this is in the top five of strongest storms ever to hit the U.S. KOTB: Yes, that`s an incredible statistic. And as Bill mentioned, the worst of Ian now passing through Central Florida, seeing some heavy rain, strong winds, hitting Orlando, Blayne Alexander, is there, Blayne, good morning, what are you seeing? BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Well, Hoda, you can see just here in our live shot, just how powerful these winds are. In fact, we just spoke with an officer who said, not too far away from here, there was a tree that came down into a motel. But by far the real concern here is the rain and of course, the concerns over flooding. Just here in the Orlando area, we saw about a foot, more than a foot of rain overnight. Now to put that into perspective, that`s more than double the amount that this area typically sees in the entire month of September. And that`s what`s leading to incredible images like these. I think we can show you this. We`ve got a video from one of our affiliates, our local reporter, Tony Atkins with our affiliate WESH 2, actually rescued a woman who was stranded in her car in floodwaters. She told our affiliate that she was a nurse trying to drive to work. She was swept away by the flood. Unbelievable pictures of him actually carrying her on his back to safety. And officials believe that as this rain is expected to continue here, it`s only going to see, we`re only going to see more pictures like that. In fact, just north of where we are, we`re already getting more reports of rescues having to occur with people stranded in cars on an on ramp to a highway. We`re also getting reports of water coming into some businesses here in the Orlando area. Now the other wrinkle really that a lot of officials are watching is of course Orlando is known for its theme parks, it`s known for Disney , some for SeaWorld , Universal , all of those parks have been shut down at least through the end of today. But there were a number of people who already came into town, hoping to kind of take advantage of some of the clearer days toward the beginning of the week. [07:15:20] Well, now they`re being told to shelter in place in their hotels, as the storm has continued -- continuing to blow through. Guys, we`re expecting to see rain at this same speed and the same intensity of wind until at least noon if not later, guys. KOTB: All right, Blayne, thank you. I mean, hats off to that WESH reporter for helping that nurse. But hats off to that nurse who was getting in her car and driving to work to help people, so, wow. GUTHRIE: Incredible sight. KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: -- puts her on his back, I mean just incredible. KOTB: Wow. MELVIN: Thanks for helping the helper. KOTB: Yes. All right, let`s welcome in Craig. CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Hey, Hoda, Savannah, good morning. Good morning to you as well. Obviously the storm has brought air travel across much of Florida to a total standstill. headline: Meet the Press for October 2, 2022, NBC
story_text: [09:00:17] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CHUCK TODD, HOST, NBC`S "MEET THE PRESS WITH CHUCK TODD" (voice over): This Sunday, disaster zone. GOV. RON DESANTIS, (R) FLORIDA: Some of the damage was, you know, almost indescribable. TODD: Hurricane Ian`s punishing path across Florida leaves a staggering scale of destruction, entire neighborhoods wiped out. PRESIDENT JOSEPH R. BIDEN, JR.: It`s not just a crisis for Florida. This is an American crisis. TODD: Now the race to recover begins. But how should homeowners rebuild in the face of more extreme weather? And who should foot the bill? I`ll talk to Florida`s Republican senator, Rick Scott , and North Carolina`s Democratic governor, Roy Cooper . Plus, Putin`s land grab. Russian President Vladimir Putin announces the annexation of four regions of Ukraine, escalating the conflict and drawing widespread condemnation from around the world. BIDEN: America is fully prepared, with our NATO allies, to defend every single inch of NATO territory. TODD: Ukraine responds by asking to join NATO . So how real is the nuclear threat from Russia? I`ll talk to NATO`s secretary general Jens Stoltenberg . And, split issues. The two parties are divided when it comes to the major issues to focus on before Election Day. SEN. MITCH MCCONNELL , (R) KENTUCKY & MINORITY LEADER: Inflation, crime and open borders. TODD: While Democrats take a different path, centering on abortion. REP. ELISSA SLOTKIN, (D) MICHIGAN: A cold, heartless, violent approach to women`s health. TODD: Plus, new numbers from the NBC News/Telemundo poll. How decisive will Latinos be in deciding which party controls Congress? (on camera): Joining me for insight and analysis are Telemundo news anchor Julio Vaqueiro; USA Today Washington bureau chief Susan Page; Symone Sanders-Townsend, former chief spokeswoman for Vice President Kamala Harris ; and Stephen Hayes, editor of The Dispatch. Welcome to Sunday. It`s "Meet the Press." ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest-running show in television history, this is "Meet the Press" with Chuck Todd. (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: Good Sunday morning. For many it`s been a tough week. With 37 days until the midterm elections, it is a tale of two campaigns right now. For Republicans the midterm campaign that they`re trying to run is about inflation, immigration and crime. For Democrats, the campaign they`re trying to run is about access to abortion and the growing extremism of the Republican Party represented by a singular figure in Donald Trump . But with both parties so sure what they want the midterms to be about, it is worth keeping in mind Tom Brokaw`s favorite reminder to many of us during campaign seasons past, "Watch for UFOs." In this case -- it`s "The UnForeseen will Occur. It`s a guarantee," he says. Well, this week the unforeseen was represented by two major events. In Russia Vladimir Putin announced the illegal annexation of 15 percent of Ukraine, after a series of Russian setbacks on the battlefield. Putin`s war is already threatening to drive Europe into recession, soaring energy costs. And this week a massive explosion created four separate leaks in that critical natural gas pipeline between Russia and Germany. President Biden accused Russia of a deliberate act of sabotage. Then there`s Hurricane Ian. This is one of the five worst hurricanes in America`s recorded history. Ian is also one of the costliest storms ever to hit the United States. Early estimates suggest it could cost up to $47 billion just in insured losses alone. And as more extreme weather events hit the United States, there are some big questions about who should pay to rebuild, and more importantly where we should be rebuilding. Blayne Alexander is in hard-hit Fort Myers for us this morning. And, Blayne, I know the destruction is awful. The question is, are we going to find more people safe and alive? BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Unfortunately, that is the case. They`re still searching this morning, Chuck. And, you know, it`s scenes like these that really tell the story of Ian`s wrath. This entire area where I`m standing was once a marina. It was full of boats and shops. Now all of that is gone. And when you widen out and you take a bigger look at this entire area, unfortunately you just see more of the same. Now, where I`m standing right now is truly one of the hardest hit areas. But, Chuck, what`s even more devastating is the human toll. At least 77 people have lost their lives due to Ian. And, unfortunately, that number is only expected to rise. Right now crews are still sifting through the rubble. They`re trying to see if there are any lives that can still be saved. And they`re recovering those who unfortunately did not make it. This morning there are a number of people who are still unaccounted for. And, Chuck, making things only more complicated, there are at least two islands that are completely cut off from the mainland. The road was destroyed in the storm, so they`re using boats to bring people back and forth. You know, I`ve talked with countless people, and they tell me the reason they stayed is that they simply underestimated the power of this storm, Chuck. And, finally, we`ve learned that President Biden is going to come here to Florida to tour the devastation on Wednesday. Chuck? TODD: All right. Blayne Alexander in Fort Myers for us. [09:05:02] Blayne, thank you. And joining me now from Naples is Republican Senator Rick Scott of Florida. He`s also a former governor. Senator Scott, welcome back to "Meet the Press." SEN. RICK SCOTT (R-FL): Hi, Chuck. Boy, it`s a tough day for Florida and been a tough week for Florida. TODD: Sure has. Let me start with this. Look, in the first 72 hours, the people on the ground never feel like the recovery is coming fast enough. So I understand that. But tell me what you`re seeing. I know you`re in Naples. You`ve probably taken a look firsthand at Fort Myers. How`s the recovering going from your perspective, in the first 48 hours? SCOTT: Yeah, I`ve -- -- I`ve -- I`ve toured; I`ve been in Collier County, Naples. I`ve been up in Fort Myers, Lee County, and I did and aerial tour of all the areas and talked to first responders. I`ve been up to Sarasota, Charlotte -- Charlotte, where we got a lot of damage. People don`t realize that. Symone, how would you have handled that situation? SANDERS-TOWNSEND: Look, Karine Jean-Pierre has a very tough job. And I think she goes out there every single day. And a number of people could not do what she does every day. Look, I think it`s very clear that the president had a slip of the tongue, obviously. And I`m sure he is extremely apologetic to the family of the congresswoman if he caused them anymore trauma or agony. No one -- I mean, I think everyone understands that the president unfortunately uniquely understands how the family is feeling, and I`m sure he made that very clear to them when they came to the White House on Friday. I think just to acknowledge it, he had a slip of the tongue. Move on. It`s unfortunate. Again, life is here. He understands and empathized. I think that`s what`s most important here. And I think Karine did try to do that. TODD: People make mistakes, and you to try to go from there. SANDERS-TOWNSEND: Yeah. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. It is life. We`ve all done it before. TODD: Fair enough. All right. Before we go to break, this week on "Meet the Press Reports", the more armed Americans are, the more armed Americans are getting, and the farther the country moves away from agreeing on effective gun safety legislation. My colleague Cal Perry talks to a diverse group of gun owners about the safety measures they want, the ones they fear, and the impact of gun culture on American life. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MICHELLE DOUGLAS, MARYLAND 10TH CAVALRY GUN CLUB: You`re never going to get rid of the guns off the streets. That ship has sailed. It`s too late. There are too many guns out here on the street. And there are too many people that don`t follow the rules. So lift the restrictions on people like me. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: You can watch the full episode of Meet the Press Reports: America`s Gun Culture on YouTube , Roku, Apple TV, or wherever you get NBC News. And when we come back, new numbers from the NBC News Telemundo Poll. How critical will Latinos be in deciding which party controls Congress? (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:47:22] TODD: Welcome back. Data Download time. In 2020, Latino voters made up about 13 percent of the presidential vote. The bloc though is only growing, meaning these voters could be key to understanding where the nation`s electorate is headed. Our new NBC News Telemundo Poll offers some clues about how the Latino vote both differs from and aligns with the overall American electorate. Republicans do believe they can make some inroads. So let`s take a look. To start, this is where Democrats have an advantage. Latino voters are much younger than the overall electorate. Thirty-eight percent fall between the ages of 18 to 34. Only a quarter of American voters overall are in that age group. Latino voters are less likely to have a college degree than voters in the electorate overall. But it is a gap that has been closing over the last decade. And Latino voters, while they still lean pretty Democratic, this 21-point gap actually isn`t as big as it was in past elections. So there is that going on. And if you dig a little further, you`ll see a split in the Latino vote that is actually all too familiar in the broader electorate. It`s a political divide between urban and rural voters. So even though Latinos prefer a Democratic Congress by 21 points overall, the advantage varies significantly depending on where you live. As you can see here, urban Latinos give Democrats a 28-point advantage. That continues to decrease basically as you get closer to rural America. Suburban voters, the advantage is just 13 points, and it`s down to single digits. This is why Republicans think they can make inroads in South Texas. And then there are demographic divisions that also look similar. On the Supreme Court`s Dobbs decision to overturn Roe v. Wade, urban Latinos disapprove of that decision by 26 points. But again, as you move geographically, just over half of Latinos in suburbs disapprove, and in rural areas that gap was just four points. And then finally, Latino Republicans are actually more likely to identify with Donald Trump over the party than the overall GOP electorate. Check this out. Fifty-five percent of Latino Republicans still say they`re a Republican more than they`re a Trump supporter. But 40 percent call themselves a Trump supporter. It`s a 15-point gap. In our most recent poll of Republicans overall, it was a 25-point gap. Fascinating. Up next, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson makes history as she takes her seat on the Supreme Court. But she joins at a time of growing public distrust in the High Court. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:53:23] TODD: Welcome back. I want to dig more into our poll, and we did it with my friends here at Telemundo. Julio, a few other nuggets I want to throw out there. Among Latinos, the president`s job rating was at 51 percent. VAQUEIRO: Yes. TODD: That`s actually not good for a Democratic president. You know, we have a report in Nevada about how the biggest fear Democrats have is not Latinos voting Republican, it`s Latinos voting to not vote. VAQUEIRO: Yes. TODD: What is the mood of the Latino electorate? VAQUEIRO: So Latinos are the fastest-growing group of voters. And the numbers are there. Latino voters make up about one out of ten voters. But they are also very unhappy. I mean, the pandemic hit them very hard. The economy is hitting them very hard. Inflation is hitting. They are unhappy about the job quality. And if you see the main issues Latinos care about, they are right there. They`re economy, job quality. So yeah, this is a concern. And this can make things very difficult for Democrats. And also, the way Republicans are gaining space in that gap between Democrats and Republicans. TODD: You know, Symone, during the 2020 campaign, a lot of people were sounding this alarm. And whether it was because of the pandemic, did the campaign not respond well enough, or was that a pandemic issue? But it now looks more acute than ever. SANDERS-TOWNSEND: Look, I think it is very important that Democratic candidates -- Latino voters are persuadable. Voters, Black voters, are persuadable voters. TODD: But you have to treat them as persuadable voters, yeah. SANDERS-TOWNSEND: And you have to treat them as persuadable voters. And oftentimes, Democratic campaigns do not do that. [09:55:01] They show up late. They show up 37 days before Election Day, drop a couple ads, sprinkle a couple of leaflets, and think that that is enough. And that is not going to get the job done. TODD: Yeah. How much are Republicans counting on Latinos to get them? I mean, you look at South Texas. You look at Nevada, another state they`re trying to make inroads as the GOP? HAYES: Yeah. I mean, I wouldn`t say that Republicans are counting on them, but I think they see an opportunity there. If you look at the gains that Republicans made among Latino voters in 2020, a number of the post-mortem studies of that election show that Republicans did well, did better than expected. And I think if you look at the way that the economy is affecting Latino voters, it`s just like the economy`s affecting lots of voters. And there`s a polling question that we had that showed that 54 percent of Latinos say that they`re falling behind faster than the cost of living. That`s a problem for Joe Biden . TODD: You know, Susan, I want to put up the -- what Latinos` views on the Supreme Court decision, on Roe v. Wade, because what`s been interesting, and what you see here, is that it looks like the electorate overall, the approval for it is only 37 percent. That`s the electorate overall. Disapproval, a little lower, but not that much lower. But what`s interesting here, Democrats, for instance, are not talking about Dobbs in South Texas in those congressional races. It`s the one place. It is a slightly more conservative, religious conservative community. PAGE: And that`s always been an entree for Republicans toward Hispanic voters, because they are culturally more conservative. And one thing I think we`ve seen is where Hispanic voters used to be able to count on them for Democrats because of their ethnicity as an alliance with the party that has represented minorities. Now, I think they`re increasingly willing to vote their class, to vote the fact that they tend to be voters who do not have a college education, who are working in jobs that have been hard hit. And that`s I think account for some of the appeal, especially among Latino men who are drawn to Donald Trump . VAQUEIRO: Yeah, I think that`s something important that this polls shows off, is just how diverse the community is. And we talk a lot about that, but I don`t think it`s always understood. Latinos are just like any other ethnic group. It`s important where they live. It`s important their age, where they come from, how they got to this country. And that makes the Latino vote such a diverse vote. There`s no one Latino vote. TODD: Julio, I`m curious. The decision by Governor DeSantis to take Venezuelan migrants to Martha`s Vineyard, how did that play in South Florida with the Venezuelan community? VAQUEIRO: Well, I mean, we will have to wait and see November 8th. But I don`t think it was -- they didn`t receive it properly. Because this has been a party has been condemning governments in Nicaragua and Venezuela and Cuba, and yet you see these immigrants coming in, asking for asylum, and they are just turning their backs to them. So we will wait and see for the reaction on November 8th. TODD: But it certainly seemed like a riskier decision -- VAQUEIRO: Yes. TODD: -- the way South Florida politics works. Really appreciate you guys today. And before we go, "Meet the Press" was honored with an Emmy Award this week for Outstanding News Discussion and Analysis. More than a year after protests erupted across the country following the killing of George Floyd, our special broadcast was focused on schools, America, and race.
