headline: How To Identify Your Personal Breast Cancer Risks And The Steps You Can Take To Reduce It
story_text: [09:10:00] SHEINELLE JONES: We are back with our "Pink Power" series to mark the start of Breast Cancer Awareness Month. And this morning, we have a checklist of important information all women need to know from risk factors to screening and more. So, joining us now is Dr. Marisa Weiss , director of breast radiation oncology at Lankenau Medical Center in Pennsylvania. And Dr. Weiss is a breast cancer survivor herself. So, she certainly knows of what she speaks. Good morning to you. DR. MARISA WEISS, CHIEF MEDICAL OFFICER AND FOUNDER OF BREASTCANCER.ORG: Good morning. JONES: So, you and I we were just talking, it was 12 years ago. DR. WEISS: Yes. 12 years ago. JONES: That you were diagnosed? DR. WEISS: Yes. I am very grateful. I benefitted from early detection. And I am here today to share important information to help save other lives. JONES: I love that. So, with that, let`s dig in and get right to it. How do women assess their personal risk for breast cancer? I am hearing about women who have no family history getting breast cancer. DR. WEISS: Exactly. So, breast cancer is the most common cancer to affect women and 75 percent of the time, there is no family history. JONES: 76 percent? DR. WEISS: Yes. No inherited gene abnormality. But if you do have in your family breast cancer, ovarian cancer, prostate, melanoma in your family, you could be at higher risk of breast cancer because of an inherited gene. JONES: OK. DR. WEISS: So, that`s why it`s so important to share that information with your doctor, to assess your risk, you know, to take and make a plan to lower your risk. JONES: Absolutely. What do you mean by background? DR. WEISS: And consider genetic testing. JONES: OK. DR. WEISS: Background, well, you heard from Katie Couric about dense breast tissue? JONES: Yes. DR. WEISS: Putting you at higher risk, you might need extra test to find it. Also, black women are more likely to get breast cancer at younger ages at more advanced stages and have a more serious type of breast cancer. Jewish women are more likely to inherit an abnormal breast cancer gene. And age, our risk goes up as we grow older. But keep in mind, 20 percent of breast cancers happen before the age of 50. JONES: My goodness, which is why screening is so important. DR. WEISS: So important. Absolutely. MARTIN-BROOKS: Speaking of that, Dr. Weiss, earlier detection. DR. WEISS: Absolutely. MARTIN-BROOKS: And we talked a little bit about this in the green room. So, I have a history in my family. DR. WEISS: Yes. MARTIN-BROOKS: They told me 45 you start, this was five years ago. Now, is it 40? When should you start for these yearly mammograms? DR. WEISS: Yes. I say, please, everyone, get your yearly mammograms starting at age 40. And if you have -- MARTIN-BROOKS: Even if you don`t have family history? [09:15:00] DR. WEISS: If you don`t have family history, that`s right. And if you let things slip and slide because of the pandemic, call today to schedule your appointment. You also want to make sure that you get a comprehensive breast exam by your doctor or nurse practitioner once yearly and then, examine yourself on a regular basis just to make sure that you know what`s normal, what may have changed. And if you are at extra risk because of a strong family history, an inherited gene, or many you have dense breast, you might need extra tests like adding an ultrasound to your mammogram, then getting an MRI six months later and then, repeating that overtime. MARTIN-BROOKS: It`s really important information. DR. WEISS: It really is. Hey, Al. ROKER: So, Dr. Weiss, what should women be looking for, you know, when you talk about self-exams, things like that? DR. WEISS: Yes. Well, as it turns out, most breast cancers don`t produce signs or symptoms. They are found by mammography. But people regularly feel things or see things like a lump or an area of thickening in the breast or the armpit, area of swelling or a bulge or the skin might be dimpled or retracted, you might notice a nipple discharge or you might have, let`s say, pain or discomfort in the breast. If you have any of those symptoms that are new and persist, check them out. Call your doctor. Don`t wait. You want to find breast cancer as early as possible when it`s most treatable. ROKER: OK. DR. WEISS: Thank you. MELVIN: Dr. Weiss, what are some things that folks who are watching or listening can do to reduce the risk? DR. WEISS: Yes. Well, the good news is the same steps that reduce your risk of breast cancer improve your overall health. MELVIN: OK. DR. WEISS: Like getting to and sticking to a healthy weight, exercising regularly, even 10 minutes a day makes a big difference. You want to eat mostly a vegetarian-based diet with like meat, chicken, fish more as a sideshow. And then, reduce your alcohol use, since the more you drink, the higher the risk. And stop smoking because it increases the risk for all kinds of things. I say start with one step, then go to a next step. And before you know it, you will be in a healthier place. MELVIN: So, let`s just say you go to the doctor, you get the diagnosis. You get the dreaded C word. DR. WEISS: Yes. MELVIN: You hear it. DR. WEISS: Yes. MELVIN: Life is not over. How do you manage that part? DR. WEISS: It can really make -- I mean, I have been there. I am a doctor and a patient as it were. Well, it`s so important to get answers to your medical questions to reduce uncertainty and to know what to expect. Put your questions and concerns on a list and put the most important ones on the top and call, e-mail or text your doctor to get answers to your questions. Hey, don`t try to do it all. We women carry the weight of the world on our shoulders, right? So, delegate and reach out for help with like childcare, grocery shopping, you know, housework, all the things that don`t matter as much. Save your precious energy for your treatment. MELVIN: Lean on your friends and family. DR. WEISS: Absolutely. MELVIN: I want to ask you, you mentioned something a few moments ago, I want to follow up on. DR. WEISS: Yes. MELVIN: Genetic testing. Who should consider that? DR. WEISS: Anyone who`s got breast cancer who is -- can be -- can get genetic testing. But if you`re diagnosed at age 50 or younger, if you have a history of ovarian cancer in the family, there are men in the family with breast cancer, there`s a history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic cancer, melanoma, you should ask to get genetic testing. MELVIN: OK. DR. WEISS: If you`re of Jewish background, you should ask for genetic testing. MELVIN: OK. ROKER: And you mentioned men, doctor. DR. WEISS: Exactly. If you are a man who gets breast cancer, you are more likely to have an inherited genetic mutation, like BRCA1 and BRCA2. And you want to make sure, if there are any men in the family -- because men get breast cancer just as -- not as often as women, like about 1 percent of the time, but that goes along with higher risk of an inherited gene abnormality. ROKER: All right. MELVIN: Thank you. JONES: It`s important that we`re talking about it.; MELVIN: Thank you so much. DR. WEISS: Thank you. JONES: Dr. Weiss, thank you. DR. WEISS: You`re welcome. JONES: And for more information on breast cancer awareness, we put so much on our website. Just go to today.com/health. MELVIN: When we come back, former ambassador to the United Nations and governor of the greatest state in the country, South Carolina, Nikki Haley is here like. We`re going to talk about leadership, we`re going to talk about powerful women and of course, we`ll also talk about 2024. ROKER: Well, she lives in New York State, which is -- anyway. Then multi- talented actor and producer Kate Del Castillo is joining us in studio to talk about bringing back her international hit series. "3rd Hour of TODAY" will be right back live from New York State. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:20:00] JONES: We are back on this Monday morning. And we are reminded of a famous quote, this is from Margaret Thatcher . She said, if you want something said, ask a man. If you want something done, ask a woman. MELVIN: Former South Carolina governor, former ambassador to the United Nations under President Donald Trump , Nikki Haley took that advice to heart. In fact, it`s the basis of her new book. There`s the title, "If You Want Something Done...: Leader Lessons from BOLD WOMEN." In the book, she profiles that obstacles and accomplishments of 10 powerful women throughout history and weaves them in with her own story. And the former ambassador joins us this morning. Good to see you again. JONES: Good morning. NIKKI HALEY, FORMER SOUTH CAROLINA GOVERNOR, FORMER AMBASSADOR TO THE UNITED NATIONS UNDER DONALD TRUMP AND AUTHOR: Great to be with both of you. MELVIN: Welcome back. Welcome back. I just told you in the green room, I started reading the book this weekend. It`s a fantastic concept. We`re going to dig into the book in just a moment. But let`s start with -- because, I mean, the reality as you write this book about accomplished women and there has been some talk, perhaps you have heard, 2024, that maybe this accomplished woman would for president of the United States. I know you have said you haven`t made a decision. How are you going to decide? What factors will you consider and what`s your timetable? HALEY: Well, I mean, I think, first of all, our focus is November. You know, everybody`s looking at the November elections and I have been all over the country working on that. And then, after, you know, the first of the year, Michael and I will sit down. We`ll figure out if there is a place for me. If there is a place for me, I`ve never lost a race, I am not going to start now. We will put 1,000 percent in and we will finish it. If there`s not a place for me, I have fought for this country as long as I can remember and I will do it until my last breath. MELVIN: And you -- I think you said last spring that if your former boss, Former President Trump, if he does decide to run, that you will sit this one out, you won`t run. Is that still the case? And if so, why? HALEY: I mean, we`ll see if he runs. You know, we`ll see if he runs. He hasn`t said that he is going to run. And so, you know, we will make a decision after the first of next year and figure it out. MELVIN: Would you ever run against him? HALEY: It`s not something I think about. I was proud to serve with him in the administration. It`s something that, you know, I can tell you that I`m thrilled with the accomplishments we did together. We had a great working relationship. But right now, we will see what he does. JONES: You have been very involved in the midterm elections this year. As you know, some Republicans, you know, the candidates running have denied the results of the election. Do you think that`s a disqualifier? HALEY: Well, I mean, I think that the candidates I`m helping, they are really focused on the economy. They are very focused on crime. They are focused on education. Those are the things people are talking about. [09:25:00] I mean, do I think that the elections were real? Yes. Do I think that Joe Biden is the president? Yes. Unfortunately, I am not happy with that, but that is what it is. And the candidates that we`re talking about, real people, they are talking about the fact that it cost more money to go to the gas station, and that`s how they go to work. It cost more money at the grocery store, and that`s how they feed their family. JONES: So, they deny those election results though, you don`t think that`s a disqualifier? HALEY: I don`t know that I`ve talked to anyone that`s denied the election results. Everybody that I`m helping acknowledges the fact that the elections, you know, were real. MELVIN: Let`s talk about the book. What was the impetus? How did it come about? HALEY: You know, it`s -- this is a book about ordinary women that did extraordinary things. And if you are a parent, you know that if you raise strong women, they become strong -- if you raise strong girls, they become strong women and strong women become strong leaders. And so, I was a fan of Margaret Thatcher . And loved how she was very confident in herself. She believed in Britain but believed had herself. And then, when I went to the United Nations, I learned more about Jeane Kirkpatrick, who was my predecessor. And she was someone who was unapologetic about loving America. But then, I met people like Nadia Murad, who was in Iraq. She was part of the Yazidi community. They were overtaken by ISIS. She was gang raped. She was -- her family died and she came out, won the Nobel Peace Prize, fought for her community. Or people like Cindy Warmbier, where, you kno, her son, Otto Warmbier, we know was tortured in North Korea. But you find these stories that are just fantastic of women who had sheer will and knew that they were meant for great things, and they deserve to be in the room. And I hope that this is a reminder to every parent who has a child that we want those kids to know they deserve to be in the room. If you are someone who has had a female mentor or a leader, give them this as a thank you and say, thank you for believing in me. And these are inspirational stories. I hope it will inspire a lot of women. MELVIN: One of the things I found interesting in the book is this idea -- and I never knew this -- you, throughout the course of your career, you send notes to women who inspire you. Who have you sent notes to? HALEY: I mean, you know, any time I see a woman make a leap. You know, I think I sent one to the head of the New York Stock Exchange. I send it to the first female head of city. You know, I just sent it to the new female anchor at Fox News. You know, any time I see a woman do something, I think we have to give that and push them and say, go get them. You know, because women second guess themselves. And any time we can go and just push them a little further and say, you`ve got this, it`s important. MELVIN: Yes. JONES: And finally, listen, we just -- you just heard us talking about breast cancer awareness, we were talking so much about health and wellness for women. I was just reading that you`re running now. Did you just finish a half marathon? HALEY: I finished a half marathon in December. MELVIN: Wow. HALEY: Last I told you, I picked up running. MELVIN: Yes. HALEY: I finished a half marathon in December. JONES: What did (INAUDIBLE) finally? HALEY: You know, it`s a great way to tune out the noise. Like, a lot of people don`t realize I don`t live in the politics. MELVIN: Yes. HALEY: I have a regular life. But when you get out and run, it`s a great way to just kind of center your mind. You can take God with you and you just plan your day out and you can kind of figure out what really matters. It`s a great way to kind of forget the world for a while. So, it`s -- JONES: So, you`re just going to keep running? Marathon next? HALEY: I ran seven miles yesterday. I`m going to keep on going. MELVIN: Wow. JONES: OK. MELVIN: Tell Michael hello. Is he running with you? HALEY: Yes, he is. MELVIN: Love it. JONES: Good deal. MELVIN: All right. Thank you for your time this morning. JONES: Thank you. HALEY: Great to be with you. MELVIN: Congratulations again on the book. Again, it`s called, If You Want Something Done...: Leadership Lessons from BOLD WOMEN." It`s out tomorrow. JONES: Thank you. All right. Coming up, Kate Del Castillo joins us live. We`re going to find out about the highly anticipated return of her hit show. And then, later, we are stepping in our October "Start TODAY" walking challenge, speaking of fitness. And Stephanie Mansour is going to show us some moves to add to our walks. What are you guys doing? MELVIN: Way to go, Jill. JONES: We`ll be right back. MELVIN: Way to go, Jill. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:30:00] MARTIN-BROOKS: This morning, we are catching up with the incredibly talented Kate Del Castillo. You know her from blockbusters, of course, like "Bad Boys for Life" and the animated film "The Book of Life." JONES: And now, Kate is starring in the long awaited third season of Telamundo "La Reina del Sur" returning as anti-hero Teresa Mendoza. MELVIN: Kate`s character is taking on the male dominated cartels of South America, once again picking up four years after the events of season two. ROKER: So, Kate joining us now. Kate, good to see you. Thanks for being here. MELVIN: Hey, Kate. MARTIN-BROOKS: Good morning. KATE DEL CASTILLO, ACTRESS: Thank you so much for having me. Good morning, everyone. ROKER: So, you have been playing this character now. How is Teresa changed from when you first started playing her? DEL CASTILLO: Oh, my God. It`s been -- now, it`s been 12 years since we started the first season. It`s only three seasons. But, you know, they go for long. And now, is just more mature Teresa Mendoza. But she is always -- you know, she`s raw and she is bad spoken, and she is an anti-heroin. So, she drinks a lot, you know. Likes tequila a lot. But she steals the show. So, she`s still the same Teresa. It`s only that now she has a kid and her daughter is everything for her. And now, in this season she comes out of jail after being there for four years, totally isolated. So, she is in a different stage right now and she just wants justice. MARTIN-BROOKS: Well, she also loves action sequences as we saw a little bit in the B roll. DEL CASTILLO: Yes. MARTIN-BROOKS: And you shot in places like the Bolivia Salt Flat. What is that and what was that experience like? DEL CASTILLO: It`s a -- it`s -- I mean, there is no words to explain what it is. It`s like 129 kilometers of pure salt. So, it`s incredible. You don`t even have a reference, a point of reference ROKER: Wow. MARTIN-BROOKS: Right. DEL CASTILLO: So, we were going like so fast in the cars, because you don`t know how fast you are going. MARTIN-BROOKS: Going. DEL CASTILLO: And we had it almost for ourselves because, you know, we were there exactly in the pandemic. MELVIN: Oh, wow. JONES: Yes. DEL CASTILLO: So, we were -- yes, we shot in five different countries. We were in Cantina, Bolivia, Peru, Colombia and Mexico. JONES: Oh, my gosh. [09:35:00] DEL CASTILLO: And during the pandemic. So, this was really challenging. You know, Telemundo did an amazing job with all this. JONES: Do you love it when you do on those high-speed things? I was reading you and Jaime Camil, he`s your Latin Billboard co-host. You guys used to ride together. DEL CASTILLO: Yes, yes. He was my -- yes. He is one of my friends where I ride motorcycles with. And it`s just been long. And now, he is getting old, and me, too. MELVIN: No, you`re not. DEL CASTILLO: Now, we`re not riding anymore. JONES: You`re not riding motorcycles anymore? DEL CASTILLO: No, no, we don`t do that. Now, we host the Billboards. JONES: There you go. MELVIN: Let`s talk about the Latin Billboards here for a moment. DEL CASTILLO: Oh, yes. MELVIN: Christina Aguilera performing. DEL CASTILLO: Oh, my God. MELVIN: How was it? DEL CASTILLO: That was -- I mean, I get goosebumps. Really, she was stunning. headline: An Exclusive Interview With Katie Couric
story_text: HODA KOTB: All right, meantime, we are marking the start of breast cancer awareness month with a story that hits close to home. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE: Yes, our friend Katie Couric is with us. She has long been a cancer advocate using her platform, including her time here at Today to inform and educate the public. Well now she`s gone from cancer advocate to cancer survivor. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GUTHRIE (voice-over): Last week in a personal essay on the Katie Couric Media website she wrote, June 21st was the first day of summer, my eighth wedding anniversary, and the day I found out I had breast cancer. Like more than a third of women, Katie, was not up to date on her annual screening writing, had the pandemic given me a skewed sense of time? Had it messed with my memory? Six months overdue, Katie, went in for a mammogram and a breast ultrasound noting something suspicious in her left breast. Her doctor did a biopsy and it was cancer. After having a lumpectomy and 15 days of radiation, Katie, is sharing her story to educate others and once again save lives. In 2000, two years after her husband, Jay Monahan, died of colon cancer, Katie aired her own colonoscopy right here on Today. As a result, there was a 20 percent increase in screenings with the University of Michigan dubbed, the Couric effect. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Katie that smile right here please. GUTHRIE (voice-over): Now, she`s on a mission again. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTHRIE: And she`s right here with us. Hi, Katie, it`s so good to see you. COURIC: Hi, look at us all in pink. GUTHRIE: We are in pink. We got the memo. It is breast cancer awareness month. And the first question has to be, how you`re feeling? How are you doing? COURIC: I`m feeling great. I`m just getting over a cold. That`s why I wouldn`t give you all a hug this morning to protect you but I`m feeling just fine. You know, I finished radiation last week. They said it made you tired. I was actually not too tired from it. I had a lumpectomy in July. And my next stop I go on something called aromatase inhibitors which suppress estrogen because I have a hormone receptor positive, HER2 new negative tumor that they removed when I had my lumpectomy. But I just feel super lucky that it was diagnosed when it was that I went even though I was late that I went when I did. KOTB: Can you take us back because I think I mean, you are a cancer advocate, obviously but it`s a whole different ballgame when you go in, you think you missed your mammogram by six months, which is probably like most people at home right now. So you went in for your checkup? Tell us about that moment. COURIC: Well, I went in with my phone camera and I was going to share it with my followers and people who read my newsletter and go the website to say don`t forget, I forgot, I don`t want you all to. So when my rady -- breast radiologist Susan Rossmann said, can you turn off your phone? I was like, uh-oh, what does that mean. And she said I think there`s something we really need to biopsy and I want to do it today. [07:35:11] So I thought, oh, my God, you must be kidding me. And then which I found out the next days, she called me, I was pretty stunned. And I think those words, it`s cancerous or you have cancer, do stop you in your tracks. But she told me it was treatable. We needed to have a plan. So I went from feeling shocked to not that shocked, given my family`s history, and the, you know, and to relieved because my exposure to cancer with Jay and Emily and my mother in law, Carol Monahan, you know, they were all advanced, and the prognosis was really tough. So, I felt so grateful, honestly. And that`s why I`m so thrilled to be able to talk to you all about the importance of screening. And I know, Hoda you know about that, because Hoda and I had, you know, you have the same kind of tumor I had when you were in your 40s. When you talk about early detection, it was so funny, because when I was diagnosed here, I remember I sat with Corvo, David Corvo. And I told him what had happened. And he said, I`m going to tell you something. I said, OK. He said, I know a lot of friends who have breast cancer, and they all have one thing in common. And I said, what`s that? He said, they`re still here. And that was about just like, for you and for me to once you get the early detection, some of it, then it just becomes, now it`s medical. COURIC: Right, exactly. And there have been so many strides made. KOTB: Yes. COURIC: But likes -- I mean, as you said, a third of all women, I didn`t even know that number, didn`t get screened during COVID. And a lot of screening places shut down. I think our, the cadence of our lives changed. And I think we just got off track. And that happened to me as well. GUTHRIE: Before we get into some of the particulars, because I know you are a woman on a mission, and you have a really important message. I just, I immediately thought of Carrie and Ellie, your daughters, they`re in their 20s now. COURIC: Yes, Ellie is 31, if you can believe it, yes. GUTHRIE: You know, they experienced so much loss at a young age, you know, their father, their grandmother, their aunt? And I`m sure it was, that was a hard call to make even knowing that you, you know, had a really good prognosis. COURIC: Yes, it was -- I was nervous about it. I waited a few days, so I could process and really understand what we were dealing with and I FaceTime each of them. And Ellie is in LA. And Carrie never calls me back, so I basically had to FaceTime both of them. She`s here in New York. And, I told them, but I was very reassuring. But I saw in their faces, you know, it`s just hard to deliver that news, no matter how you do it. But, you know, I assured them that I was going to be fine. And Carrie came with me, when I got my lumpectomy, when I was being wheeled into the operating room. She was singing the "Arms of an Angel." She`s so funny. But anyway, but they`ve been incredibly supportive. And of course, I was worried about that. But again, just so grateful that they caught it early enough, so it could be treated. And by the way, you know, even when it`s at later stage than mine, I`m stage 1-A, there are so many treatments available. And a lot of women are living with breast cancer. But we need to do better. We need to come up with better treatments, and we need to get more women screened, I was surprised to see only 70 percent of women actually get breast cancer screening. And that number went down to 65 percent during the pandemic, but I think it`s probably went even lower. KOTB: Here`s a weird thing that we just saw on the American Cancer Society website. It says, and I think we have a graphic, women 55 and over should switch to mammograms every two years. They`re kind of giving you that window. You don`t need to go each year, you can go every two. COURIC: Yes, I mean, I think the recommendations have been all over the map. I mean, I`m not a doctor, and I`m trying to play one on T.V. but, you know, I think people should go every year. You should talk to your doctor. I think women have to advocate for their own health. And that`s why I`m so, you know, so excited to be able to talk about dense breasts, in particular. GUTHRIE: I wanted to ask you about that because you were someone that you`ve learned you have dense breasts. First of all, what does that mean, I thought I knew, I just asked you, you`re like, no, that`s not it. And what does that mean in terms of the kind of screening you need? headline: Herschel Walker , The GOP Candidate Who Has Called For A Ban On Abortion, Denying That He Paid For An Ex-Girlfriend`s Abortion More Than A Decade Ago
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Just 35 days before the Midterms, a new allegation is rocking that very tight Senate race in Georgia. Republican Herschel Walker strongly denying an accusation that he paid for a former girlfriend abortion. Here`s Kristen Welker. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, Republican candidate and former football star Herschel Walker forcefully denying an allegation that`s rocking the critical Georgia Senate race. A new accusation that Walker who supports an abortion ban after 15 weeks without any exceptions, paid for his then-girlfriend to have an abortion in 2009. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Do you know the woman that is making this allegation? HERSCHEL WALKER (R-GA), SENATE CANDIDATE: I have no -- I had no idea but it is a flat-out lie. WELKER: The explosive report appearing in The Daily Beast which did not name the woman citing privacy concerns. She says she and Walker agreed she would have the abortion. The Daily Beast publishing a photo of a get-well card she says this from Walker. The news outlet also says she gave them a receipt from an abortion clinic and an image of a $700 check she says his from Walker. NBC News has not seen nor independently verified any of the documents. WALKER: I never asked anyone to get an abortion. I never pay for an abortion and that`s a lie. WELKER: But tonight, Walker is facing fierce criticism from his 23-year-old son Christian saying Walker`s family urged him not to run because we all knew some of his past. CHRISTIAN WALKER, SON OF HERSCHEL WALKER : Don`t lie about your life at the expense of me, my mom, and all of the people that you`ve affected throughout your life. You don`t get to pretend you`re some moral family guy. WELKER: Herschel Walker tweeting I love my son no matter what. And blasting the allegations as a last-minute distraction by Democrats. WALKER: There`s inflation, the border wide open, crime. They don`t want to talk about that. So, they`re making up lies now because they need this Georgia seat. WELKER: Now, top national Republicans are rallying around him from former President Trump to Senator Rick Scott tonight saying Democrats know that Herschel Walker is winning so they have cranked up this smear machine. (END VIDEOTAPE) WELKER: Incumbent Democrat Senator Raphael Warnock not weighing in on the controversy, but saying he`s been a consistent abortion rights supporter. Lester? They still want to have the big holiday meal and all the gifts under the tree. But they`re going to try to cut some corners and do it differently. COSTELLO: The time to buy airline tickets say travel pros is now. Tom Costello, NBC News, Washington. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next for us tonight, fighting a crime wave. One city makes it easier for police to use private video surveillance. We`ll tell you about the controversy tonight. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: And now, our look at a controversial move by San Francisco on fighting crime. The city is now giving the police power to monitor private surveillance video as part of a new pilot program. Jake Ward explains. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JAKE WARD, NBC NEWS TECHNOLOGY CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Soon after Michael Su opened his San Francisco shoe store, it was robbed. MICHAEL SU, STORE OWNER: The perpetrator used the blowtorch to get in to bypass our alarm system. WARD: Thieves have hit the store three times. SU: When somebody breaks in, it`s like somebody`s breaking into your home. WARD: Now, a San Francisco ordinance gives police access to live private footage like Su`s. They need the owner`s permission, but they do not need a warrant. SU: I want to be the first one in line to give them access to my camera. WARD: San Francisco has seen a surge in retail thefts, including by this 2021 group that evaded police while robbing downtown stores. LONDON BREED, MAYOR, SAN FRANCISCO: Some of that potentially could have been avoided if they were able to watch the situation in real-time. WARD: San Francisco banned the use of facial recognition in 2019 and has championed alternative policing. But voters recalled its progressive DA this year as crime became more visible. Police data shows arrests are made in fewer than 10 percent of reported cases. But Mayor Breed says the city has to try something new. BREED: Sadly, people believe based on understanding the way the laws work in San Francisco that in most cases they can get away with something like this, even if they`re on film. WARD: You believe that state law is too lenient. BREED: I think it`s just a combination of things. And then when it does happen, we want to hold the perpetrators accountable. WARD: This ordinance requires special circumstances and internal clearance before officers can get footage. But those who voted against this ordinance say we are not seeing the bigger picture. CONNIE CHAN, SUPERVISOR, SAN FRANCISCO DISTRICT 1: Do they really help make us safer, you know? And that is the question. And when those video footages are already readily available to our law enforcement and yet we still cannot deliver safety results, where does this lead us? WARD: Michael Su says he`ll hand over access but within limits. SU: Obviously, they wouldn`t need to really see the inventory room. Cameras, I`m willing to share whatever it`s needed, you know, for the police to do their job. WARD: Jake Ward, NBC News, San Francisco. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, we`ll remember the queen of country music. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Finally, Loretta Lynn rose from humble beginnings to become one of the biggest country music superstars of all time. Here`s Kristen Dahlgren. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN DAHLGREN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): She was the Queen of Country Music who started as a coal miner`s daughter. Loretta Lynn was born in 1932 in Butcher Hollow, Kentucky, one of eight children with a hardscrabble upbringing that later fueled her music. LORETTA LYNN, SINGER: I write about my life. I mean, every song I`ve written. DAHLGREN: She was just a teen when she married 21-year-old war veteran Oliver Doolittle Lynn and started having babies. Eventually, the lullaby she crooned to her children led her to give professional singing ago. The song Coal Miner`s Daughter after catapulting her career became a best- selling book, then an Oscar-winning film starring Sissy Spacek and Tommy Lee Jones. Her marriage fraught with hardships. She sang about her husband`s cheating. LYNN: He says if it`s true, write it. So, that`s what it is. DAHLGREN: She tackled sensitive topics people just did not talk about like birth control. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Loretta Lynn. DAHLGREN: Lynn was the first woman to win the Country Music Association `s Entertainer of the Year. And her Grammys we`re joined by the Presidential Medal of Freedom. One of country music`s most enduring icons who never forgot her humble roots, or her father. LYNN: I`d give anything in the world if he would have been here when I recorded the Coal Miner`s Daughter. But I think he hears me. And one day, I will sing it to him. DAHLGREN: Kristen Dahlgren, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Loretta Lynn was 90. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. headline: Conversation With Clea Shearer, About Her Breast Cancer Journey
story_text: [08:10:00] CRAIG MELVIN: We are back. 8:12 with "Pink Power TODAY". Our special series for breast cancer awareness month. And this morning, this morning we`re checking in with our friend Clear Shearer. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE: Yes, "The Home Edit" co-founder was diagnosed with breast cancer earlier this year and she has decided to share every step in her journey, including her recent milestone of finishing chemo. HODA KOTB: Yes, throughout it all, though guys, there`s been a group of women she`s been leaning on. They talk every day but they had never met face to face until two days ago. They`re amazing women. They all came together from all across the country for a very special conversation. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CLEA SHEARER, "THE HOME EDIT" CO-FOUNDER: Look, all of your toys are so accessible. KOTB (voiceover): Clea Shearer finds joy in being a helper. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Will you guys help me? JOANNA TEPLIN, "THE HOME EDIT" CO-FOUNDER: I can`t get up there fast enough. SHEARER: Yes. TEPLIN: Like, show us the closets. SHEARER: Yes. KOTB (voiceover): She`s created a career out of it. Taking on clutter and organizing people`s lives as one half of "The Home Edit" team. SHEARER: Hey, guys. So, by now you probably read or heard that I have breast cancer. KOTB (voiceover): But after she shared her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year, Clea found herself asking for help from those who personally knew the fight she was facing. SHEARER: As you`re going through something so brutal, like chemo, everyone in your life wants to help, but there`s nothing quite like someone who`s actually been through it or going through it at the same time. KOTB (voiceover): A friend connected her to Maria Boschetti, a three-time breast cancer survivor who lives in California with her husband. The 42- year-old, who works in public relations, was first diagnosed when she was just 25. SHEARER: She`s taken so many copious notes. So, if I just say -- if I whip out any side effects she`s like, boop, boop, boop -- KOTB (on camera): Got it. SHEARER: -- page eight. She`s like, you`ll get over that real soon. KOTB (voiceover): Amy Jethway was 42 years old when she found a lump while on vacation with her boyfriend. The biotech sales account manager diagnosed with breast cancer just weeks after Clea. Their mutual friend passed along Clea`s number to Amy who lived hundreds of miles away in New Jersey. KOTB (on camera): These are strangers? People you`ve never met. SHEARER: I`ve never met them. KOTB (on camera): Just on text. Hey, girl? SHEARER: Well -- yes, literally. And I -- there are some of, you know, these women I talk to every day. If not every day, every week, and, you know, just to check in. They`re like my dear close friends. KOT (voiceover): A community connected through tough times. Dear friends who have never met. Meeting up in person for the first time. KOTB (on camera): Well, I think it`s a good time to meet them because it`s fun to text, but it`s more fun to see people in person. [08:15:00] SHEARER: Oh. Oh, my God. AMY JETHWAY, BREAST CANCER SURVIVOR: I can`t believe we get to see you. You`re real. You`re real. Oh, my God. SHEARER: It`s so good to see you. JETHWAY: I`m going to cry. Oh, my gosh. You`re so tall. KOTB (on camera): This is so cool in this moment to be sitting here. SHEARER: I can`t believe. KOTB (on camera): First of all, you haven`t met in person yet you -- SHEARER: No. Oh, my God. KOTB (on camera): -- but you know each other intimately. What did you think, Maria, when you first started connecting with Clea? MARIA BOSCHETTI, BREAST CANCER SURVIVOR: I was shocked she was so positive, right? Because it`s a terrifying time in your life. You were wanting to talk about it. You had questions but also you were -- wanting to help others. KOTB (voiceover): Others like Amy. JETHWAY: I reached out to you during your fourth AC -- SHEARER: Yes. JETHWAY: -- when you felt really horrible. SHEARER: Yes. JETHWAY: And she was so available to me. Like, that was really overwhelming to me because I was about to start my chemo journey. KOTB (voiceover): Did that make you scared or did that make you prepared? JETHWAY: I was so grateful for how open you were and how honest you were about things because if this is what`s going to happen to me, then this is going to happen. I wound up having a very different reaction with my fourth. SHEARER: I know. I was, like, so sorry. I scared you. KOTB (on camera): Oh, you were like, I`m cool. SHEARER: She was like, fine. JETHWAY: Yes. SHEARER: Meanwhile, this whole time I was, like, guys brace yourselves. It`s going to be awful. JETHWAY: Like, it aches everywhere. KOTB (voiceover): Clea`s openness about her hair loss empowering Amy as she started to lose her own. JETHWAY: I told my boyfriend, I`m going to shave this. Like, we`re -- we can do this. We can take this head on. And kind of, whatever parts of the journey you can own, you now, that`s something I got from you. KOTB (on camera): That`s important -- that`s something you got from Clea? JETHWAY: Yes. KOTB (on camera): What is that? JETHWAY: Like, owning what you can in the journey. KOTB (on camera): Were you reluctant, Clear, because there are parts that you want to share and then there are parts you want to keep. But it sounds like you were very -- SHEARER: Oh, I don`t keep much to myself. KOTB (on camera): You don`t? SHEARER: No. Hoda, you know me. I am a barrier soul kind of girl. KOTB (on camera): Yes. SHEARER: Not only did I tell everything pretty much to these ladies but, I mean, I would also tell our Instagram followers what was going on. And it made me feel understood, you know. And it`s also nice not to feel like an anomaly. KOTB (on camera): When you`re having a crummy day, you need someone who gets it. How important has that been, Maria, to have that? BOSCHETTI: It`s so important. I -- you know, I was so young the first time I was diagnosed. And I didn`t have anybody to talk to. You don`t process those emotions when you don`t have someone to talk to or ask question and that friendship. And now, you know, I was just texting Clea last night. I feel like you are this light of sunshine that`s even bringing the last eight years back in me. SHEARER: I`m sorry about that. KOTB (on camera): By the way -- BOSCHETTI: Don`t make me cry. I`m not a pretty crier. KOTB (on camera): But that`s so beautiful. That`s a really important point. BOSCHETTI: Yes, yes. KOTB (on camera): It like -- sometimes feelings lay dormant. SHEARER: Yes. JETHWAY: Yes. BOSCHETTI: Yes. KOTB (on camera): Until someone says, let`s unearth those. KOTB (voiceover): Clea, Maria, and Amy finding strength in each other and finding peace in the small things. KOTB (on camera): Everybody has their spot where they go to when they want to just, like, cleanse and clear and you all are walking in mine. This is Central Park. What`s your place, Clea? Where do you -- SHEARER: My back porch. KOTB (on camera): Your back porch? SHEARER: I have a chair. I read there. I listen to the rain there. I greet my kids after school there. KOTB (on camera): Uh-huh. SHEARER: I just -- it makes me so peaceful. KOTB (on camera): What about for you, Amy? JETHWAY: I have my one bench right on the Hudson -- SHEARER: Oh, that`s so nice. KOTB (on camera): Yes. JETHWAY: -- and that just go out. KOTB (on camera): Doing meditation, Maria, or anything that like -- BOSCHETTI: Yes. KOTB (on camera): You`re a meditator? BOSCHETTI: Yes, meditation and beach. KOTB (on camera): Meditation and beach? BOSCHETTI: Yes. KOTB (on camera): All right. So, this is a sisterhood. SHEARER: Yes. KOTB (on camera): This is something that you believe, Clea, is not for this moment. SHEARER: Uh-huh. It`s for life. KOTB (on camera): How do you know? SHEARER: You go through life and certain people enter it for a reason. I consider you one of those people, too, Hoda. Because I don`t lose friends. I only make them. So, we`ve been through something really incredible together. And also, and a little earth shattering. KOTB (on camera): Yes. SHEARER: A lot earth shattering. So, you`re stuck with me. KOTB (on camera): We`re stuck with clea. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: Wow. KOTB: So. sweet. And by the way, if you wonder if that friendship`s rear - - real, they`re planning a vacation October together. Also, Joanna, you know, Clea`s partner, was standing in the background the whole time. Weeping. Weeping. Like these friendships, the new old friendships or old friendships are all keeping her in. She also said about her hair, she talked about it. She said it`s very kind of peach fuzzy. She`s like, I`m not sure if I`m going to cover it. I think I might just -- finally, I`m free of all that stuff. SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS 3RD HOUR OF TODAY, CO-HOST: I think she looks beautiful. GUTHRIE: She has posted this week, actually, about her -- why she was wearing a wig to her kids` pickup. KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: She didn`t want to embarrass them. KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: And -- this is going to make me cry. Then her daughter said, mommy, you don`t embarrass me, I think you`re beautiful. So, she started -- yes. And you took them to your special place -- KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: -- in Central Park when you went through breast cancer? KOTB: Yes, that was my spot. It was very calming to me. It`s like -- you know, there`s no green space here but that was mine. So, I used to go there and feel very peaceful. And everyone had their little spot where they felt the warm hand. So, it was beautiful. I want to say thank you, of course, to Clea. She`s amazing and Maria and Amy. We also want to thank the Kent, that`s a beautiful space in New York. We had a great conversation there. So, we want to say thank you to them. MELVIN: That was wonderful. GUTHRIE: I`m so weepy today. MELVIN: That was wonderful. KOTB: All right. Mr. Roker, take us away. ROKER: Oh, special. OK. Guys, well, we are looking at a rainy, windy day here in the northeast and parts of New England. Sunshine through the southeast on into the Gulf where it will be nice and warm. Even up to the Great Lakes, we`re looking at a flood risk through the southwest. We`re going to continue to track that. And beautiful sunshine from Seattle to San Diego. [08:20:00] That`s what`s going on around the country. Here`s what`s happening in your neck of the woods. (LOCAL NEWS) ROKER: Don`t forget, if you`re heading out the door, head out to "TODAY" show Radio Sirius XM Channel 108. But right now -- KOTB: What time is it? ROKER: -- best time of the morning. GUTHRIE: All right. ROKER: In for Carson. KOTB: Come on, Sheinelle. JONES: We have good stuff for you this morning. KOTB: OK. We`re ready. JONES: OK. So, we`re going to start with "Black Panther: Wakanda Forever". Yesterday -- have you seen this? Marvel dropped a new trailer for the highly anticipated sequel. Of course, fans have been waiting to see how the franchise will handle the passing of its leading man, Chadwick Boseman. Well, this latest preview, giving audiences a closer look at the state of Wakanda and teasing the mysterious character stepping into the "Black Panther" suit. GUTHRIE: Who`s it going to be? JONES: We don`t know. I mean, we all have our guesses. KOTB: Yes. MELVIN: I`ll tell you what we do know. KOTB: What? MELVIN: That film`s going to make about a billion dollars. ROKER: Oh, right. KOTB: Yes. MELVIN: The first two weeks of it. JONES: Oh, it`s going to be huge. KOTB: Yes. JONES: "Black Panther: Wakanda Forever" it heads to theaters next month. Who do you think it is? GUTHRIE: What did you say, Al? ROKER: I think it`s going to be Michael B. Jordan. KOTB: Michael B. Jordan. GUTHRIE: Michael B. Jordan. OK. ROKER: Yes. GUTHRIE: All right. JONES: I thought it was going to be his sister. GUTHRIE: Yes, I wondered if anyone think it would be a woman. JONES: Right. GUTHRIE: I felt like it could be. MELVIN: This -- this is why it`s going to make a billion dollars. KOTB: yes. JONES: I know. Don`t tell me if you get there before I do. GUTHRIE: Well, they`ll have to reveal it at some point. MELVIN: That`s true. JONES: All right. Well, this is another good one. So, next up "The Crown". Calling up all Prince Harrys. A recently released casting announcement that Netflix is looking for an actor to play the adolescent royal redhead. According to the online note, they`re seeking someone with a strong physical appearance, if you guys know anybody, to play Harry from 16 to 20 years old. So, if you look like the Duke of Sussex or you know someone, you should throw your hat into the ring. Thank us later. The application closes next Friday and filming is scheduled to start in November. So, you`ll have to take off from or something, I don`t know. So, the clock is ticking. Do you know anybody? GUTHRIE: They have to have a posh English accent too. JONES: I mean, I bet you there`s somebody who we don`t know. Who -- this could be their next thing. GUTHRIE: A Harry doppelganger. JONES: Yes. GUTHRIE: For sure. JONES: All right. Next up, Paul and Linda McCartney. Yesterday, "Rolling Stone" co-founder, Jann Wenner stopped by "The Howard Stern Show" and revealed how he played matchmaker with one of his magazine`s photographers and a young superstar Beatle. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) HOWARD STERN, "THE HOWARD STERN SHOW" HOST: You didn`t realize Linda was a new hired to be a "Rolling Stone" photographer. She said, I want to go meet Paul McCartney . I want to photograph -- JANN WENNER , "ROLLING STONE" CO-FOUNDER: When she said, I want to (INAUDIBLE). I said, well, we don`t really need to spend the money, you know, sending you to London and cover. Why do you want to -- why do we need more Beatles. And so, just -- well, I want to meet Paul. I say, OK. You got the assignment. Go. STERN: Wow. Nice. WENNER : And then I started getting postcards from her every couple of weeks saying, you know, how she`s getting closer and then finally I got one said, we went out last night and had the most wonderful time. Thank you forever. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: Wow. JONES: How cool was that? And the rest they say is history. KOTB: Wow. JONES: That`s Jann Wenner , by the way. ROKER: Yes. KOTB: OK. Cool. GUTHRIE: It`s classical -- JONES: It was controversial but they thought, you know what -- ROKER: That`s amazing. GUTHRIE: You were there last night, right? JONES: It was phenomenal. Last night, Jimmy announced plans for an all-out `80s theme special -- MELVIN: They`re speaking your language -- JONES: -- featuring guests from retro movie hits like the "Karate Kid", "Last Chance", and "Back to the Future". headline: Republicans Rally To The Defense Of Georgia Senate Candidate Herschel Walker Facing Devastating Abuse Accusations From His Own Son And A Report He Paid For An Ex-Girlfriend`s Abortion
story_text: HODA KOTB: Meantime, the midterms just over a month away and a firestorm has erupted in a key Senate race in Georgia. Herschel Walker , the former football star now Republican nominee denying a report that he paid for his ex-girlfriend`s abortion. NBC`s Kristen Welker joins us with details on this sordid tale. Hey, Kristen, good morning. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: Hi, Hoda, good morning to you. Well, campaigns always brace for the possibility of an October surprise. Well, here it is in the critical Senate race in Georgia with a new controversy surrounding Republican Herschel Walker . Now GOP sources are telling NBC News that leading senators are preparing to stand shoulder to shoulder with him on the airwaves and on the campaign trail. But will it be enough with just five weeks until the midterms? (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) WELKER (voice-over): This morning Republicans are closing ranks around former football star Herschel Walker , their embattled Senate nominee in Georgia, a swing state that`s critical to Republicans fight to win control of the Senate. After "The Daily Beast" reported Walker in 2009, urged to then girlfriend to get an abortion after he got her pregnant, then reimbursed her for the procedure and sent her a get well card. Walker who says he wants to ban abortion after 15 weeks without exceptions, is denying the allegation. H. WALKER: It is a flat out lie. I can tell you right now, I never asked anyone to get an abortion. I never pay for an abortion. WELKER (voice-over): "The Daily Beast" says the woman asked not to be identified citing privacy concerns, adding she backed up her story by providing the get well card from Walker, an abortion clinic receipt, and a bank receipt with an image of a $700 check signed by Walker. NBC News has not independently verified the documents. CHRISTIAN WALKER, HERSCHEL WALKER`S SON: Everything has been a lie. WELKER (voice-over): Walker is also facing fierce criticism from his own son, Christian, a budding conservative influencer who says the family urged him not to run quote, because we all knew some of his past. C. WALKER: Family values people. He has four kids, four different women, wasn`t in the house raising one of them. He was out having sex with other women. Do care about family values? WELKER (voice-over): Herschel Walker later tweeting, I love my son no matter what. Walker is locked in a tight race with incumbent Democratic senator Raphael Warnock who won a special election by just two percentage points last year. Many Republicans are rushing to Walker`s defense led by former President Trump who`s endorsed him now saying Walker is being slandered and maligned by Democrats. It`s not the first controversy to rock his campaign. He`s falsely claimed he was a member of law enforcement and acknowledged fathering three children out of wedlock. Walker`s ex-wife has accused him of holding a gun to her head and threatening to kill her in incident Walker has blamed on his struggle with mental health. (END VIDEOTAPE) WELKER: Now his challenger again incumbent Democratic senator Raphael Warnock, not directly responding to the controversy. Instead, he`s stressing his long standing support for abortion rights. The big question here, will all of this make a difference? It`s just too soon to tell. But in close races like this one, even a few votes in either direction, could have an impact. Hoda? KOTB: Yes, those are some stunning allegations there. Kristen Welker for us there in Washington. The Marathon Man inspiring America. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening, everyone. With recreational marijuana use now legally in 19 states, it has been easy to forget pot is still very much illegal under federal law where the drug is classified right alongside LSD and heroin. But tonight, President Biden declaring it`s time to right the wrongs of what he called a failed approach to marijuana, announcing he is pardoning all prior federal offenses of simple possession of marijuana, and asking states where most pot convictions take place to do the same, potentially impacting thousands. It`s an effort to end what the President sees as unfairness in simple marijuana possession cases where he says Black and Brown people are more likely to be prosecuted. And he also wants a hard look taken and how the government classifies pot, which for now is regarded as more serious than fentanyl. Kelly O`Donnell has details. LATOYA CANTRELL, MAYOR OF NEW ORLEANS: So, the city of New Orleans is one that is grappling with violent crime like many other cities throughout the country, GUTIERREZ: Democratic mayor Latoya Cantrell blames the pandemic slowing down the court system as well as progressive prosecutors for the spike in crime. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We`re trying to stretch our money as far as we can possibly stretch it. IKEDA: To luring cautious customers, retailers including Kohl`s and Target jumpstarted their holiday deals today. And for the first time, Amazon will hold a second prime day-like event within one year. So, when sorting through the savings, shopping experts say, compare prices online. Look for retailers who offer price matching and use a cashback credit card to stretch your dollar the furthest as inflation curbs the power of your paycheck. Emily Ikeda, NBC News New York. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, the 100-year-old Marathon Man inspiring America. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Finally, we want to introduce you to a 100-year-old who has truly gone the distance and shows no sign of slowing down. Maggie Vespa with "INSPIRING AMERICA." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MAGGIE VESPA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Runners often strive to outpace time. MIKE FREMONT, 100-YEAR-OLD RUNNER: The nice thing about running at this age -- VESPA: Mike Fremont defies it. FREMONT: -- is that there`s very little competition. VESPA: At 100, the retired Cincinnati engineer and great grandfather of four logs five to 10 miles three times a week. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You are so sweet. VESPA: His 14-minute mile pace only slowed by starstruck fans. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You`re an inspiration to a lot of people. VESPA: Does that feel weird to hear that you`re a celebrity? FREMONT: Absolutely embarrassing. VESPA: With 60 marathons under his feet, Mike boasts four world records, fastest marathons for his age at 80 and 90. Fastest half marathons at 90 and 91. Running started his therapy in his 30s after the loss of his first wife. FREMONT: So, starting to run and it worked. VESPA: Decades later, after battling cancer, Mike went vegan and with the encouragement of his second wife, Marilyn, ran marathon after marathon. What do you think is fueling it? MARILYN WALL, WIFE OF MIKE FREMONT: I think he can`t quit. VESPA: Proving her point, his other hobby, canoeing. Of course, racing goes to. For people who think at 100, a person should be slowing down. What do you say to that? FREMONT: I think they ought to be speeding up. VESPA: Proof no matter your age, your best time may still lie ahead. Maggie Vespa, NBC News, Cincinnati. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And he just keeps going. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Thursday. Thank you for watching. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Goodnight, everyone. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. headline: Embattled Republican Senate Candidate Herschel Walker Defiant In The Face Of New Accusations From The Ex-Girlfriend Who Claims He Paid For Her To Have An Abortion
story_text: KRISTEN WELKER: All right, well, now to several new twists and what is arguably the most closely watched Senate race of next month`s midterm elections. Overnight, Georgia`s Republican Senate candidate Herschel Walker , speaking out to NBC News and standing by his claims that he didn`t know an ex-girlfriend had an abortion more than a decade ago. This is the same woman now says Walker wanted her to have a second abortion years later but she refused. NBC`s Allie Raffa is following all of these developments from Atlanta for us this morning, Allie, good morning to you. [07:10:00] ALLIE RAFFA, NBC NEWS CAPITOL HILL CORRESPONDENT: Kristen, good morning. Democrats controlled the Senate by just the thinnest of margins and keeping that hold could easily come down to this crucial Peach State Senate race where in just a few days has gone from too close to call to downright roiled in allegations. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) RAFFA (voiceover): This morning, all eyes on Georgia, the crucial Senate race between Trump-back to Republican Herschel Walker and incumbent Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock roiled in controversy after bombshell allegations this week by The Daily Beast that Walker paid for a former girlfriend`s abortion in 2009. And a New York Times report Friday that Walker pressured this same woman to have another abortion two years later, but she refused. Walker, who`s running on a staunch anti-abortion platform, repeatedly denying both claims. HERSCHEL WALKER , REPUBLICAN SENATE CANDIDATE, GEORGIA: I`m not going to back down. These things are way, way too high. RAFFA: But in a new twist overnight, the former football star confirming to NBC directly that his wife and the woman making the allegations revealed to be the mother of one of his children, were in contact Friday morning, the woman telling Walker`s wife that he paid for her abortion. Walker sharing copies of the text exchange with NBC News and saying "I`m not saying she did or didn`t have one. I`m saying I don`t know anything about that. I don`t know." Walker telling NBC this was the first time the woman ever mentioned the abortion to him or his wife. But the woman showed the New York Times and The Daily Beast a copy of a receipt from an Atlanta abortion clinic. A check that she claimed was reimbursement for the procedure. And the get well card she claims came from the former football star. We should note we have not seen this documentation. Walker telling NBC News "I don`t remember any card or check or anything. But I was dating her. I could have sent some money. I could have sent a card. But not for the reasons she is saying." Despite the spectacle, most congressional Republicans are still backing Walker. SEN. TED CRUZ, (R-TX): Herschel Walker is going to win that race. This is an effort from Democrats to hold on to power. RAFFA: While state Republicans` frustrations only grow. LT. GOV. GEOFF DUNCAN, (R-GA): Even the most staunch Republicans I think are rattled at the continued flow of information. RAFFA: Just 32 days before voters have their say. (END VIDEOTAPE) RAFFA: As of now, Walker doesn`t have any plans this weekend to meet with voters. But ultimately the choice is theirs. Republicans here tell me they don`t think this controversy will have any impact on this Senate race, while Democrats say this is just another reason they don`t think Walker is fit for Office, Kristen, Peter. WELKER: Allie Raffa, at the center of the political universe right now in Atlanta, thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.
