[09:30:00] And so exactly why it is that he seems to get- have this need and get this charge out of saying something that isn`t true, or other times convinces himself something is the case because it feels better. And then still other times, it sounds better. And I talk about that in the book, that sometimes he tells people, say XYZ. It sounds better. It`s all of the above. WELKER: And of course, we saw that play out in the oval office, as well, as he struggled with the truth over and over again. Now you have 219 candidates who fall into the category of election deniers. Do you think even Mr. Trump understood that he would have that impact on the party? HABERMAN: I don`t. I mean, I think that he looks at everything in terms of what works for him in short, ten-minute increments of time. I think that the effect that it could have on other people, I think he delights in it. I think he likes feeling like he`s powerful and like he`s shaping the party. But I don`t think that`s the reason, and I don`t think that`s the long-term strategy. WELKER: You also talk about his relationship with race over time. Goes back to his father. You also have this anecdote about how he pitches this idea to have an apprentice show that`s divided along racial lines, African American candidates versus Caucasian candidates. And he even confuses some Democratic staffers of color who are in the oval office with some of the serving staff. How do you think Mr. Trump has influenced race in America? HABERMAN: I think if you look at that clip that you played earlier in the show of Senator Tuberville saying what he said, I can`t imagine someone -- he`s a former high school football coach. I can`t imagine someone saying that a few years ago. I think he has created a permission structure for people to say what used to be known as the, quote/unquote, quiet part, in race-baiting politics, out loud. And now it`s just the doors are blown open. WELKER: I want to talk to you about yourself, Maggie Haberman the reporter. This has been covered, but I do want to delve into this, which is that the former president has said of you, I love being with her. She`s like my psychiatrist. You`ve kind of dismissed those comments. You`ve said that`s flattery. He says this to a number of different reporters. But at the same time, he does actually reach out to you more directly, arguably, than most other reporters. Why do you think that is? HABERMAN: I think he`s fixated with " The New York Times ". And I think that I am the person who covers him more often for the paper and who he identifies with the paper more. But it really is about this decades-old outer borough New York City guy trying to make his way in Manhattan and saw "The New York Times " as synonymous with the elites who looked down on him. He had this line that he said to the publisher of " The New York Times ", and we made this public back in 2019 when he was president, over the Resolute Desk, he`s talking about our- he`s complaining about coverage, which as you know, every president does. But in Trump`s case, he was complaining, I think I`m entitled to a good story from my paper, and if you want the clearest distillation of how he views "The New York Times ", that`s it. WELKER: And very quickly, you have said you think it`s more likely than not that he will run again in 2024. Is there anything other than health that you think prevents him from doing so at this point, Maggie? HABERMAN: I think a fear of losing and I think a disinterest in the process the way it is now. You know, there is a bitterness around him and a quickness to anger. That you know, he was always pretty quick to anger, but it has gotten more intense. Those are the reasons I could see. You know, something unforeseen, like something related to one of these cases, these legal cases, maybe. But I think he has backed himself into a corner and has to run. WELKER: Fascinating, fascinating stuff. It`s a fascinating read, "Confidence Man". Stick around, because you`re on our panel. We have a lot more to discuss with you, Maggie. Up next, with 30 days to go until the midterms, the battle for Senate control is heating up as the candidates finally debate the issues. Our panel is here. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:36:28] WELKER: We are back now with the panel. Maggie Haberman is still with us. And joining us are: Yamiche Alcindor, NBC News Washington correspondent and moderator of "PBS Washington Week"; Brendan Buck, former adviser to Speaker`s Paul Ryan and John Boehner ; and Jen Psaki , former White House press secretary and an NBC News contributor. Thanks to all of you for being here. Yamiche, let`s start with what`s happening on the ground in Georgia. You were there for many days. Is this Herschel Walker controversy resonating, or do you think he survives it? YAMICHE ALCINDOR, NBC NEWS WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT: Well, certainly a lot of people in Georgia are talking about it. But people, based on my reporting, are already in their camps. If you`re someone who didn`t like Herschel Walker like Lisa Gordon, this African American woman, who told me she had never even considered Herschel Walker because he was facing a host of domestic abuse claims. She didn`t think that he had the character to serve in the U.S. Senate . But I didn`t meet one Republican voter who was changing their mind. And that means, everyone that I talked to said, I don`t like this. Or maybe it`s made up. Maybe he`s telling the truth. Either way, it`s not changing my vote. And I`m thinking about this one voter; her name is Linda Oviot. She`s an elderly white woman. She told me, 100 percent I believe these allegations. I think Herschel Walker is lying right now. She told me, I`m still voting for him. People make mistakes. He`s now someone who is an opponent of abortion rights. And as a result, I`m going to continue to stick with him. And really, I think this is about people seeing politics as tribal, seeing Herschel Walker as a means to an end, and that end being more restrictions on abortion, maybe a better economy, maybe harsher policies on crime. Name it. That`s what Republican voters are telling me. WELKER: Well, and they also see it as a way to win the Senate. And Brendan, top Republicans are standing by him. I want to play a little bit of the sound that we heard from top Republicans this week and then get your reaction. (BEGIN VIDEO CIP) REPORTER: Do you stand by Herschel Walker ? SEN. TED CRUZ (R-TX): I believe Herschel Walker`s going to be the next senator. I`m proud to support Herschel Walker -- REPORTER: But do you want them to elect that Republican? CRUZ: Hell yes, I want every Republican running for Senate in this country to win. SEN. RICK SCOTT (R-FL): Herschel`s going to win. So they`re going to throw everything under the sun at him. Herschel is a great candidate. He`s focused on the right issues. (END VIDEO CLIP) WELKER: And NBC News has now confirmed that Scott and Tom Cotton are going to be campaigning with him this week. You`re from Georgia. You`ve been talking to your sources down there. What are folks telling you about how big of an impact this is having and whether this type of full-throated support may be risky for Republicans? BRENDAN BUCK, FORMER ADVISER TO SPEAKERS RYAN & BOEHNER: Well, they`re certainly circling the wagons, and that`s because of what`s at stake here. This seat could decide who controls the Senate. So it`s not surprising at all that Rick Scott , whose job is to get Republicans elected, is backing him. But it`s not hard to run into a Brian Kemp , Republican governor, Raphael Warnock voter in Georgia. And that`s the problem. I don`t think this is going to change a lot of things. I think it is relatively baked in. But you have to remember, Herschel Walker was losing before this happened. Herschel Walker needs to make up ground in the last month. People are going to be starting to vote very soon in Georgia. And the reason that the Republicans have been doing poorly in Georgia recently is the northern Atlanta suburbs. I know Yamiche spent some time in Marietta, Alpharetta, Roswell, these areas where Republicans have been losing educated women particularly. And this is a candidate who is raising the issue of abortion. That`s not going to help him get back to where he needs to be to get over 50 percent. ALCINDOR: And 1 or 2 percent percent, it makes all the difference in Georgia, right? Let`s also remember, all you need is that to make -- to win this seat. So that`s even if people are baked in. One or two percent of women changing their mind and Warnock wins -- WELKER: It makes a big difference. JEN PSAKI , NBC NEWS CONTRIBUTOR: But there`s also a potentially very long way to go here because this in all likelihood will go to a runoff in the beginning of December. And so while we`re looking at this last week and questioning, is it a game changer? Is it not a game changer? Frankly, I think Senator Warnock is probably doing the smart, strategic thing as of this moment, which is kind of letting Herschel Walker wallow in his muddy pit of scandal. [09:40:02] WELKER: So you don`t think he should take the gloves off at this point? PSAKI: I actually think, for the moment, and you always have to reevaluate in campaigns. You evaluate week by week. But again, this is -- could be a long call. What he is going to have to depend on, Senator Warnock, that is, is whether there`s going to be big spending to keep this in the minds of voters over the next month to two months. And then he may have to decide that he may have to take the gloves off, at some point. But I don`t think he needs to do that now. And I think he`s doing the right thing by letting Herschel Walker just wallow in his muddy scandal pit on his own here. WELKER: Maggie, one of the things that makes this moment so interesting is that it`s sort of like celebrity candidates on display, a lot of them handpicked by Trump. We talked about obviously Herschel Walker , but also Dr. Oz is another one. Is this a key test of celebrity candidates, and does it underscore kind of the challenge with it if you`re not Donald Trump ? HABERMAN: I think there`s a baseline challenge to that. Number one, he has been in public life as a celebrity for a very long time, dealing with the national media in a way that Herschel Walker was not, but in a way that Dr. Oz was more, right? I mean, so it just depends on which race you`re talking about and the specifics. The Oz-Fetterman race is very different than what`s happening in Georgia. I think that you`re going to have to isolate out these specific races. I don`t think that there is a blanket takeaway from this. I do think you will see more celebrity candidates, particularly among Republicans jumping in. And that is the Donald Trump effect. WELKER: That is a very good point. I want to talk about the battleground map broadly, now. It runs through nine key states. In order to win back control, Republicans have to flip one of the Senate seats currently held by Democrats in Georgia, Arizona, Nevada, or New Hampshire while holding on to seats in Pennsylvania, Ohio, North Carolina, Florida, and in Wisconsin. In Wisconsin, Republican Senator Ron Johnson, like many Republicans, is trying to put the focus on crime. Take a look at this recent exchange from a debate. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SEN. RON JOHNSON (R-WI): Whenever I see a police officer, I go up to them and I say, thank you for your service. And if I have time, I say, please, don`t be dispirited by the loud few who are trying to defund you. LT. GOV. MANDELA BARNES (D-WI): I`m sure he didn`t have the same interaction with the 140 officers that were injured during the January 6th insurrection. Let`s talk about the 140 officers that he left behind because of an insurrection that he supported. (END VIDEO CLIP) WELKER: Brendan, what do you make of that point/counterpoint? BUCK: Well, crime is a big issue. And we talk a lot about inflation; we talk about abortion. Most Republican candidates are running on crime. And particularly in Wisconsin, it is working to devastating effect on Mandela Barnes. Republicans -- Ron Johnson is someone who should be very vulnerable, but he has been hitting this crime issue. And in some places, it`s just going to work better than others. And in Wisconsin, it is working. I asked somebody, a plugged-in political operative in Wisconsin, why is it working so well there? He said, one word, Kenosha. WELKER: Jen? PSAKI: I would say I agree with Brendan that crime is an issue that Democrats have to speak to. I think there was a missed opportunity there for Mandela Barnes. When he talked about the insurrection, I think that was a little disconnected from what people in Wisconsin are feeling. I mean, Milwau -- crime is up in Milwaukee. If I were him or advising him - -which I`m not -- I would say, you should have made it about the use of gun violence and the fact that your opponent has done nothing to address gun violence. And that is what is showing rising crime in Wisconsin. Because that`s what people are thinking about. Their fears when they go out their door, less the insurrection, honestly. BUCK: There has not been a more potent political issue that I can remember in recent years than Defund the Police. And while Mandela Barnes may have not said he wants to defund the police, he does have a record of wanting to redirect funds away from police. And that is going to hurt, and that is showing up in the polls. ALCINDOR: But here`s the interesting thing. We had a country where a man was murdered, strangled, George Floyd. We had a country who then debated race relations and policing, and that backfired. So defund the police, while Democrats have continuously said --most Democrats have said -- we don`t support that, it stuck to them, because some people in this country were deeply uncomfortable with the fact that we were talking about the fact that Black people get killed at disproportionate rates than white people. We should also remind people that the FBI just this week said, murders are up. Violent crime is down. So a lot of this is about fear. But it`s fear on both sides because Republicans are saying, you should be fearing crime. You should be fearing the border. Democrats are saying, you should be fearing your personal privacy, and you should be fearing threats to democracy. WELKER: Yes. It`s certainly the closing arguments that we are seeing. All right. Stick around, guys. We do have a lot more. But when we come back, Elon Musk`s potential Twitter takeover and the surprising reality about how much it influences our politics. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:47:17] WELKER: Welcome back. It`s looking more and more like Elon Musk, the richest man on the planet, is going to purchase Twitter , kicking off conversations about what that could mean for the social media platform that plays a significant role in our country`s political discourse. That role is thanks in part to Donald Trump , who tweeted over 26,000 times as president before being removed from the platform after the January 6th Capitol insurrection. But although Twitter has played a dominant role in American politics, its reach is actually much smaller than you might think. Less than a quarter of Americans say they ever use Twitter . That`s a small fraction of some of the more dominant social media platforms like YouTube and Facebook . And of Americans who actually use Twitter , data shows a minority of very active users are producing the overwhelming majority of tweets. The top 25 percent of American Twitter users are producing 97 percent of tweets. The other three quarters of the platform`s users are just simply reading them. Data also shows that Twitter users lean pretty far left. About 32 percent of adults who say they are Democrats or that they lean Democratic say they use Twitter . That compares to 17 percent of Republicans, creating a 15- point partisan gap. Now, Facebook comes closest to having a balanced audience. Musk has indicated he plans to reinstate Donald Trump`s account, relax some of the platform`s content moderation rules -- which would likely allow a lot more disinformation -- and enhance its paid subscription option. So the question is, if Musk succeeds, how will his changes affect Twitter as a platform and its relevance to American politics today? When we come back, a look back at Donald Trump`s changing views on abortion, reversing the position he once made right here on this program. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) DONALD TRUMP , FORMER PRESIDENT: Well, look. I`m very pro-choice. I hate the concept of abortion. I hate it. (END VIDEO CLIP) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:52:52] WELKER: Welcome back. And the panel`s still here with me. I want to start this discussion by talking about President Biden and his wild week from the decision by OPEC to cut oil production, Jen, to these revelations at the end of the week in "The Washington Post " that investigators believe they do have enough evidence to charge Hunter Biden . It`s not clear he`s going to be charged, but how large is this looming over the president, over Democrats broadly? PSAKI: Well, it was a big week here in Washington. So much news. I don`t even know how you decided what to talk about this morning, Kristen. But the truth is, you know, I looked at a bunch of local front pages this morning. And if you look at the front page in Nevada, they`re talking about Trump`s rally there and what it means for candidates in turning out to vote. If you look at the front pages in Pennsylvania, they`re talking about, Mastriano, does he have a grassroots campaign or movement going? And obviously, Georgia is quite focused on every latest development in Herschel Walker . So the truth is: As much as there was so much news happening in Washington this week, it doesn`t always translate and often doesn`t translate to what voters are talking about in states. And I think that`s what we`re seeing currently. BUCK: What will probably translate what happened this week is with gas prices. One of the -- PSAKI: True, the OPEC decision. BUCK: One of the big pieces of news this week was that OPEC is cutting back production at the worst possible time for Democrats. And gas prices -- if you want to figure out the direction of politics, watch gas prices. And Democrats did better during the summer when they started to tick down. It`s very likely they`re about to start going back up, and that`s bad news for Democrats. ALCINDOR: And I was just talking to a voter who told me, at the end of the day, it`s the party in office that`s going to be blamed for this. And we know what White House officials have told me, that they look at this every day. And it`s a neon sign on the roads across America. What is the price of gas? My friend in- I have a friend who`s in Arizona. Just sent me a screenshot of $7 gas prices there, just talking about how worried she is. She`s not someone who`s deeply into politics, but she`s someone who really notices when the economy is going one way or the other. WELKER: Administration officials say, first thing they do is look at the gas prices in the morning. I do want to play this sound bite and pivot back to former President Trump. This is from 1999, right here on this program in October with Tim Russert and former President Donald Trump . [09:25:01] Take a look. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) TIM RUSSERT, FORMER NBC MODERATOR: Partial birth abortion, the eliminating of abortion in the third trimester. Big issue in Washington. Would President Trump ban partial birth abortion? TRUMP: Well, look. I`m very pro-choice. I hate the concept of abortion. I hate it. I hate everything it stands for. I cringe when I listen to people debating the subject. But you still -- I just believe in choice. And, again, it may be a little bit of a New York background because there is some different attitude in different parts of the country. And, you know, I was raised in New York and grew up, and work, and everything else in New York City. But I am strongly for choice, and yet I hate the concept of abortion. RUSSERT: But you would not ban it? TRUMP: No. RUSSERT: Or ban partial birth abortion? TRUMP: No, I would -- I would -- I am -- I am pro-choice in every respect and as far as it goes, but I just hate it. (END VIDEO CLIP) WELKER: Maggie, one of the things that hits me when you watch that clip, of course, it is former President Trump who appointed the three conservative Supreme Court justices who made it possible to overturn Roe v. Wade. And you were the first to report that Mr. Trump realizes the political place that that puts Republicans in in these midterm elections and possibly 2024. HABERMAN: There`s no question that Republicans are the dog that caught the car on this issue. And you see it with any number of candidates who are having trouble talking about it. Because, while I don`t think it is going to rise to the same level as the economy in midterms, it is animating a lot of Democrats to vote. What strikes me actually, listening to that clip, and I`ve listened to it several times, is he`s taking a very liberal position. He`s basically saying no limits on abortion. And this was, you know, 20-some-odd years ago. But he`s also just not answering the question. I mean, he`s basically trying to answer the question by saying, "Pro-choice, hate abortion," and Russert is trying to push him on specifics, and Trump is evading that. And that was part of how Trump was successful in 2015 and 2016, was he, you know, people would present him with this menu of options because he was so vague and jumping all over the place, and so much of his political career and frankly all of his career was about sort of bluffing and faking his way through things. And that was another example. WELKER: And, Brendan, obviously that was one of the things that made Republicans so nervous when he first announced his candidacy. And one of the points that Maggie makes in her book is actually, there was a lot of buzz about whether Donald Trump was going to run for the office of the presidency going back to 1999, right? But this issue has loomed very large over him. BUCK: Sure. And I think you can look at this issue narrowly at abortion, or you can look at it I think, which is probably the better way to describe where Republican politics is right no, and it`s a culture war. There`s a lot of people out there who believe that if you don`t support abortion, if you`re a Christian, that there are people out to get you, there are elites in Washington. And Donald Trump has very successfully taken the mantle of the person who`s there to defend. And it speaks to what Maggie spoke about earlier. He saw himself as an outsider in the outer boroughs trying to get into Manhattan. And so, this rich billionaire, how is he the working man`s person? He`s very successfully said, I am fighting for you. And people will go -- they really don`t care what he says at this point. They are going to stand with him because of that. PSAKI: But, what you`re seeing on the other side, which is also interesting, and it reminds me of the Affordable Care Act debate, is that when something is taken away it makes people very angry. And that`s what you`re seeing among Democrats. But also you`re seeing in places like New Hampshire -- which is a fascinating place in the abortion debate to me -- it`s more people saying, like, get out of my uterus. Live free or die. We live in New Hampshire. So this debate, I think, has become much more politically palatable for Democrats, and I think we even thought when I was sitting in the White House when these leaks were happening back in the spring. ALCINDOR: And quickly, you also have the fact that women in this country, they had all these labels. But now, those labels don`t make sense anymore because some people want restrictions and some want more limits. WELKER: What a great conversation. We are out of time. Thank you all. And thank you for watching. Chuck Todd will be back next week because if it`s Sunday, it`s "Meet the Press". END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: Top Republicans Traveling To Georgia To Campaign With Herschel Walker Amid His Abortion Controversy
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Just four weeks until the Midterms, today`s Senate Republican heavyweights rally behind Herschel Walker as he tries to weather the abortion controversy now overshadowing his campaign in all-important Georgia. Here`s Peter Alexander. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PETER ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, in Georgia, Republican reinforcements arriving to pollster embattled Senate nominee Herschel Walker . SEN. TOM COTTON (R-AR): It`s especially good to be here with the next United States Senator from Georgia Herschel Walker . ALEXANDER: Key senators Tom Cotton and Rick Scott standing by the former football great as he faces an allegation that he paid for an abortion for an ex-girlfriend more than a decade ago, while now campaigning on his opposition to abortion rights. Walker has strongly denied the accusation, but today for the first time publicly acknowledged he now knows who the woman is. The senators tonight insists the controversy will not cost Walker the race. SEN. RICK SCOTT (R-FL): Inflation, crime, parents not being involved in schools. That`s what people are going to vote on. ALEXANDER: Still, some state Republicans have criticized Walker. Lieutenant Governor Geoff Duncan writing, Walker has not yet earned my vote. He has four weeks left to change our minds. While, overnight, another critical clash over Ohio`s open Senate seat. In their first debate, Democratic Congressman Tim Ryan , accusing Republican J.D. Vance of lavishing praise on former President Trump. REP. TIM RYAN (D-OH): Ohio needs an ass-kicker, not an ass-kisser. ALEXANDER: While Vance attacked Ryan for voting 100 percent of the time with President Biden who remains unpopular with Ohio voters. J.D. VANCE (R-OH), SENATE CANDIDATE: We`re getting close to Halloween and Tim Ryan is put on a costume where he pretends to be a reasonable moderate. (END VIDEOTAPE) [19:10:07] ALEXANDER (on camera): Tim Ryan also tried to distance himself from President Biden saying he does not believe the President should run for reelection in 2024. Lester? HOLT: Peter, thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2022 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. headline: Dr. Mehmet Oz On Crime And His Campaign`s Attacks On Fetterman`s Health
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Just 25 days before the Midterms, tonight, we speak exclusively with Dr. Mehmet Oz, the Republican facing off against Democrat John Fetterman in that critical Pennsylvania Senate race. Our Dasha Burns pressing Dr. Oz on crime and his campaign`s attacks on Fetterman`s health. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Pennsylvania Republican Senate candidate and celebrity doctor, Mehmet Oz, has focused much of his campaign on crime and blasting Democrat John Fetterman on his votes as the head of the state`s Board of Pardons. He says he believes in second chances, the former president with his First Step Act, also was about giving second chances to prisoners who deserve it. Why don`t prisoners who prove good behavior, who are modeled prisoners, why don`t they deserve second chances? MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: The First Step Act had nothing to do with convicted murderers being released from prison, especially if they`ve been sentenced to life in prison. It`s a whole different game. When John Fetterman is asked, if you could wave a magic wand, what`s the one thing you would do, the one thing? And he says why get rid of life in prison? BURNS: Well, I asked him that. He actually said, it would be codifying Roe versus Wade and abolishing the Filibuster. OZ: Well, he`s answered it the way I just described in the past as well. And too often, John Fetterman seems to pay more attention to the feelings of the criminals than the innocent who were hurt. BURNS: We also asked about his campaign`s attacks on Fetterman`s health. He was off the campaign trail for months after suffering a stroke. One of your campaign staffers said that John Fetterman wouldn`t have had a stroke if he had "ever eaten a vegetable in his life." You`re a doctor. You`re a heart doctor. You of all people understand what John Fetterman is going through better than most. Why would you allow your campaign to mock him like that? OZ: I have tremendous compassion for what John Fetterman has gone through. I mean, not only do I, as a doctor, appreciate the challenges, but I know his specific ailment because it`s a specialty area of mine. BURNS: But would you ever talk to your patients like this? OZ: No. BURNS: He criticizes Fetterman for not releasing his medical records, while Fetterman accuses Dr. Oz of not being transparent on abortion rights. This is what he told us this week. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: Dr. Oz likes to make fun of me that I might miss a word. But you know, he`s missed, you know, two words. And that is a yes or no on the national abortion ban. BURNS: So, we asked him about Republican Senator Lindsey Graham`s bill that would ban abortions after 15 weeks. If you win, you`re going to be a colleague of his. You`re going to have to vote on bills like this. So, can you tell us right now, yes or no on that bill? OZ: I`m giving you a bigger answer than yes or no. I`m telling you. I don`t want any federal rules limiting what states do with abortion. It should be up to the states. (END VIDEOTAPE) BURNS: Lester, there was more we wanted to discuss. We had to ask for the same amount of time Fetterman gave us about 30 minutes, but the campaign said they had time constraints, so we only spoke for about half that time. Lester? HOLT: Dasha Burns, thank you. END Content and programing copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2022 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for October 14, 2022, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the search for answers after a deadly shooting rampage in North Carolina. (voiceover): A 15-year-old suspect in custody after the mass shooting that left five people dead in Raleigh. What we`re learning about the victims. Among them an off-duty police officer and a 16-year-old boy. What was the shooter`s motive? Also, tonight, the new move in the battle of her documents seized at Mar-a- Lago. What the DOJ is asking an appeals court to do regarding the special master. And Donald Trump sending a 14-page letter to the January 6 Committee after it voted to subpoena him. What it says? And the video from the day of the attack, Nancy Pelosi saying she wanted to punch Mr. Trump out. Our NBC News exclusive with Dr. Mehmet Oz, GOP Senate candidate in Pennsylvania. Does he stand by his campaign`s attacks on the health of his Democratic rival John Fetterman ? Does he support a federal ban on abortion and his anti-crime message? The holiday shopping season, why it`s off to an early start. Where to get big bargains right now? It`s America`s fastest-growing sport with fans like Tom Brady and LeBron James. How Pickleball is going pro. And remembering the actor who brought up a beloved Harry Potter character to life. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. We are going to begin with the tragic and frightening story that was breaking in North Carolina as we came on the air here last night. We now know five people died allegedly at the hands of a teenage shooter who held a Raleigh neighborhood in fear, forcing residents to barricade themselves inside their homes. North Carolina`s Governor calling it the nightmare of every community. Authority say the alleged shooter left a two-mile trail of victims and crime scenes behind him. Tonight, the 15-year-old suspect is being held and is in critical condition after a long standoff with police. The dead include an off-duty police officer and range in age from 16 to 52. Two other people were injured. And eyewitnesses are now describing to us their own harrowing encounters with the accused shooter. Blayne Alexander is in Raleigh and has late details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The crime scene stretched more than two miles from his quiet Raleigh neighborhood to a nearby walking path, a literal trail of terror all left by one gunman who police say is just 15 years old. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Officer down. We have an officer down. ALEXANDER: The first chance came just after 5:00 p.m. as neighborhood kids were getting off the school bus. Nayesha Royle (PH) was at home and heard screams outside. NAYESHA ROYLE, RALEIGH RESIDENT: A neighbor`s kids were knocking banging on the door. I`m telling her like open the door. Something`s going on. And you hear the kids say he has a gun. He has a gun. There`s a gun. ALEXANDER: And when you open the door, what did you see? ROYLE: Chaos. Chaos. ALEXANDER: She also saw the gunman and frantically started pulling neighbors and schoolchildren into her house. ROYLE: If you could have seen a fear in their eyes -- like, the little girl was like, he pointed the gun at me. And they`re kids. They`re kids. ALEXANDER: For more than four hours, police combed the area, bringing dogs and helicopters and telling residents to stay inside. Finally, they say they found the gunman hiding nearby. He was taken into custody and to the hospital in critical condition. MARY-ANN BALDWIN, MAYOR, RALEIGH: There are several families in our community waking up this morning without their loved ones. ALEXANDER: Among those killed according to officials, 29-year-old Gabriel Torres, an off duty police officer headed to work, 16-year-old James Roger Thompson a high school junior, the Sue Karnatz who was out for a run. Her husband says that was her biggest passion outside of their three boys. Nicole Connors, a caregiver at heart dedicated to her husband and their dog Sammy. And 35-year-old Mary Marshall set to get married in just two weeks. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Blayne, none of it makes sense. Did police said anything about a possible motive? ALEXANDER (on camera): Unfortunately, not yet, Lester. In fact, police are not saying what led up to that shooting, only that the entire thing is still under investigation. But we are learning more about charges. Tonight, the DA`s office confirms that even though the suspect is only 15 years old, he will be charged as an adult. Lester? HOLT: Blayne Alexander in Raleigh tonight, thank you. This evening, former President Trump`s response after the January 6 Committee voted to subpoena him as new video from inside the Capitol on that day shows the fear and frustration of congressional leaders. Kelly O`Donnell has late details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KELLY O`DONNELL, NBC NEWS SENIOR WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Former President Trump used 14 pages to vent his anger, disappointment, and complaint at the January 6 Committee for not investigating his claims of election fraud rejected by courts. With crowd photos, he embraced rioters as hard-working American patriots, but no answer on whether he will comply with a subpoena to testify. [19:05:22] SEN. CHUCK SCHUMER (D-NY): You know, the Capitol has been totally overrun. Answer my question. O`DONNELL: NBC News obtained 42 minutes of documentary footage shot by Speaker Pelosi`s daughter. CNN obtained additional clips that show congressional leaders of both parties. SEN. MITCH MCCONNELL (R-KY): Get them there in one hell of a hurry. Do you understand? O`DONNELL: Scrambling to get guard troops sent to the Capitol. SCHUMER: We need them there now, whoever you got. O`DONNELL: In another exchange -- REP. NANCY PELOSI (D-CA): Hi, Mr. Vice President. O`DONNELL: Speaker Pelosi reaches Mike Pence . PELOSI: I worry about you being in that Capitol building. Don`t let anybody know where you are. O`DONNELL: From concern, to fury at President Trump. PELOSI: I want to punch him out and I`m going to go to jail, and I`m going to be happy. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And Kelly O`Donnell joining us now. And there are also new legal developments, Kelly, in the search of the former president`s Mar-a-Lago estate. O`DONNELL (on camera): That`s right. The Department of Justice is asking an appeals court in the Mar-a-Lago documents case to end the use of an independent reviewer of those materials seized that Mr. Trump had requested. Lester? HOLT: Kelly, thank you. Just 25 days before the Midterms, tonight, we speak exclusively with Dr. Mehmet Oz, the Republican facing off against Democrat John Fetterman in that critical Pennsylvania Senate race. Our Dasha Burns pressing Dr. Oz on crime and his campaign`s attacks on Fetterman`s health. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Pennsylvania Republican Senate candidate and celebrity doctor, Mehmet Oz, has focused much of his campaign on crime and blasting Democrat John Fetterman on his votes as the head of the state`s Board of Pardons. He says he believes in second chances, the former president with his First Step Act, also was about giving second chances to prisoners who deserve it. Why don`t prisoners who prove good behavior, who are modeled prisoners, why don`t they deserve second chances? MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: The First Step Act had nothing to do with convicted murderers being released from prison, especially if they`ve been sentenced to life in prison. It`s a whole different game. When John Fetterman is asked, if you could wave a magic wand, what`s the one thing you would do, the one thing? And he says why get rid of life in prison? BURNS: Well, I asked him that. He actually said, it would be codifying Roe versus Wade and abolishing the Filibuster. OZ: Well, he`s answered it the way I just described in the past as well. And too often, John Fetterman seems to pay more attention to the feelings of the criminals than the innocent who were hurt. BURNS: We also asked about his campaign`s attacks on Fetterman`s health. He was off the campaign trail for months after suffering a stroke. One of your campaign staffers said that John Fetterman wouldn`t have had a stroke if he had "ever eaten a vegetable in his life." You`re a doctor. You`re a heart doctor. You of all people understand what John Fetterman is going through better than most. Why would you allow your campaign to mock him like that? OZ: I have tremendous compassion for what John Fetterman has gone through. I mean, not only do I, as a doctor, appreciate the challenges, but I know his specific ailment because it`s a specialty area of mine. BURNS: But would you ever talk to your patients like this? OZ: No. BURNS: He criticizes Fetterman for not releasing his medical records, while Fetterman accuses Dr. Oz of not being transparent on abortion rights. This is what he told us this week. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: Dr. Oz likes to make fun of me that I might miss a word. But you know, he`s missed, you know, two words. And that is a yes or no on the national abortion ban. BURNS: So, we asked him about Republican Senator Lindsey Graham`s bill that would ban abortions after 15 weeks. If you win, you`re going to be a colleague of his. You`re going to have to vote on bills like this. So, can you tell us right now, yes or no on that bill? OZ: I`m giving you a bigger answer than yes or no. I`m telling you. I don`t want any federal rules limiting what states do with abortion. It should be up to the states. (END VIDEOTAPE) BURNS: Lester, there was more we wanted to discuss. We had to ask for the same amount of time Fetterman gave us about 30 minutes, but the campaign said they had time constraints, so we only spoke for about half that time. Lester? HOLT: Dasha Burns, thank you. Now to the migrant crisis. The Biden administration announcing this week it will start expelling more Venezuelan migrants to Mexico. It comes as President Biden is under pressure to do more after a record number of illegal border crossings. Gabe Gutierrez reports now from Yuma, Arizona. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Each night, they rushed to turn themselves in, group after group of asylum seekers crossing the Arizona border. GISSELLE PALACIO, CUBAN MIGRANT: It`s beautiful coming to a free country. GUTIERREZ: Gisselle Palacio and her 3-year-old daughter came home from Cuba. Why did you come? PALACIO: I want to be free. I want to buy some food -- some food for my girl and work and deliver progress. American dream, you know? GUTIERREZ: This year alone is seeing hundreds of asylum seekers each night. And in just the last year, there have been more than 300,000 illegal border crossings in the area around Yuma. That`s three times the city`s entire population of nearly 100,000. It`s an all-time record. Is that sustainable? [19:10:13] DOUGLAS NICHOLLS, MAYOR OF YUMA, ARIZONA: It`s not sustainable. GUTIERREZ: Douglas Nicholls is Yuma`s mayor. NICHOLLS: I definitely do consider this a crisis. It`s a situation where numbers are multiple times higher than anywhere else in history. GUTIERREZ: The only hospital here estimates that over six months, it`s doled out $20 million in uncompensated medical care to migrants. DR. ROBERT TRENSCHEL, CEO, YUMA REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER: We have to stop that border flow. If you`re going to have the borders open like they are, then there has to be a payment source for these individuals. GUTIERREZ: Officials here say they`re not getting enough help from the federal government. Arizona`s governor has spent $6 million to bring in these shipping containers to close gaps in the border fence. The state is also spending $83,000 per bus to send migrants to Washington DC. FERNANDO QUEROL, AID VOLUNTEER: Politics play a big role. GUTIERREZ: But aid volunteers like Fernando Querol say there is no chaos. There`s immigrant rhetoric in an election year. QUEROL: None of these individuals are overwhelming, are overrunning the city. GUTIERREZ: Still, he views it as a humanitarian crisis. PALACIO: We spend like 25 days coming here. GUTIERREZ: One that brought a desperately Gisselle Palacio and her family to U.S. soil in search of a dream enduring a nightmare. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (on camera): Local officials say they expect border crossings here to rise again over the next few months as temperatures cool. Lester? HOLT: Gabe Gutierrez, thanks. Tonight, Russian President Vladimir Putin addressing the situation in Ukraine while a key Putin ally, the president of neighboring Belarus also speaking out. Keir Simmons spoke with him exclusively. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS SENIOR INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, after bombarding Ukraine, Russian President Vladimir Putin suggesting he could cause more destruction. There`s no need for massive strikes, he said, at least for now. As for the future, we`ll see. Mr. President. We met her key Kremlin ally, Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko , who insisted his crews also film our exclusive interview, but with no restrictions on questions. Do you think President Putin would use a nuclear weapon? ALEXANDER LUKASHENKO , PRESIDENT, BELARUS (through translator): If you put a person or a country in a corner, there is only one way out from there, to move forward? As far as the subtext of your question is concerned, never. Putin and the leadership of Russia never set the goal of using a nuclear weapon in Ukraine. SIMMONS : How would you describe President Putin state of mind right now? LUKASHENKO (through translator): Is that what you think in the western United States? He`s an absolutely adequate, healthy, athletic man. SIMMONS : President Lukashenko was supported by President Putin after a widely discredited election in 2020. And this week, Lukashenko supported Russia, at the U.N . Civilians being targeted, women and children. How can Belarus justify voting against the U.N . resolution to condemn the Russian offensive? LUKASHENKO (through translator): You know, there is an information war going on. The Ukrainians talk about mass graves, and the Russians similarly reveal mass crimes from the Ukrainian side. (END VIDEOTAPE) SIMMONS : And tonight, President Putin insisting his actions in Ukraine are correct and timely. They`re calling the situation unpleasant. Lester? HOLT: All right, Keir, thank you. In 60 seconds, holiday sales already kicking off as spending cools down. How stores are getting you by now. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Spending by Americans remain flat in September which is bad news for retailers but it may be good news for holiday shoppers already being lured with deep discounts. So, is Black Friday a thing of the past? Here`s Miguel Almaguer with tonight`s "PRICE YOU PAY." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: This is Black Friday now. MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): At some of the nation`s biggest retailers -- UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Black Friday deals for days. ALMAGUER: It`s beginning to look a lot like Christmas two weeks before Halloween. To jumpstart consumer spending that`s falling flat as inflation hits a 40-year, high big box stores like Best Buy , Target, and Walmart are tonight trying to unload excess inventory kicking off holiday sales earlier this year. [19:15:14] KIMBERLY PALMER, PERSONAL FINANCE EXPERT, NERDWALLET : Black Friday has already started because the sales have begun, the discounts have already been launched. ALMAGUER: Some of the deepest discounts could come on electronics, appliances, and computers, deal that 50, 60, and even 70 percent off by the real Black Friday may be the price retailers have to pay to get consumers to buy. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: If there`s a deal, of course, I`m just going to swipe that up. ALMAGUER: As families tighten budgets amid high-interest rates, steep gas prices and rising rents, more than 40 percent of Americans say they aren`t earning enough to cover the cost of holiday gifts this year. PALMER: Basically, retailers know that consumers are really stressed out financially by spreading out those sales over a multi-week, multi-month period. It makes it easier for consumers to keep spending. ALMAGUER: The best advice say experts, do your holiday shopping now and wait for the perfect sale. Last year, 50 percent of shoppers did their holiday shopping before Thanksgiving. Lester? HOLT: All right, Miguel, thanks. Up next, they`re a pivotal group of voters changing the political map. The race to connect with Latinos in our series "POWER OF THE VOTE." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Back now with our series the power of the vote. And tonight, the battle over the all-important Latino vote. As the political landscape rapidly changes, Tom Llamas takes us to South Florida where some long- standing expectations about Latino voters are being put to the test in the Midterms. [19:20:16] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM LLAMAS, NBC NEWS SENIOR NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In a state known for hurricanes, in 2020, a political earthquake hit Florida. CHUCK TODD, NBC NEWS POLITICAL DIRECTOR: This Latino thing is an issue here for the Democrats. LLAMAS: Joe Biden won the presidency but Donald Trump took nearly half of the Latino vote in Florida. CARLOS CURBELO , FORMER REPUBLICAN CONGRESSMAN FROM FLORIDA: Republicans figured out how to connect with Latino voters culturally. This is not about policy. This is about people`s view of the country. LLAMAS: A new NBC News Telemundo poll shows while Latinos lean Democrat and prefer Democratic control of Congress, support for the GOP is up 10 points over five midterm cycles. It`s why some are calling the Latino voter The Sleeping Giant. One of the tightest races in the country is happening in this Florida congressional district that includes parts of Little Havana. More than 70 percent of the voters here are Hispanic and this election as two Latinas going head to head. Congresswoman Maria Elvira Salazar , a daughter of Cuban exiles and former news anchor, flip this district read in 2020. The GOP has made so many gains when it comes to Latinos. Why do you think it`s happened? REP. MARIA ELVIRA SALAZAR (R-FL): Well, because we`re not stupid. And we want the same thing as other Americans, security, good jobs, good economy. LLAMAS: Her opponent, State Senator Annette Taddeo grew up in Colombia and fled after terrorists kidnapped her father. Do you think Democrats take Latino voters for granted? ANNETTE TADDEO (D-FL), CONGRESSIONAL CANDIDATE: Sometimes, yes, absolutely. As elections get closer, a bunch of money comes in at the last minute. I would like to see us all the time. LLAMAS: Part of the answer, recognizing there`s a diverse mix of Latino voters, many who fled socialist regimes. What are the things that are -- the issues that are on the minds of voters right now in this district? SALAZAR: Inflation, gas prices, good jobs. Number one is like, things are really bad. LLAMAS: Democrats are also hoping anger over abortion rights drives voters to the polls. TADDEO: We all come from places where the government tries to tell you what to do. And the last thing we want is the government or politicians making decisions that are so difficult and private. LLAMAS: And Taddeo is critical of her opponent for not speaking out about Florida Governor Ron DeSantis ` decision to transport Venezuelan refugees to Martha`s Vineyard. Do you think Governor DeSantis treated those refugees with dignity? SALAZAR: I think Governor DeSantis, just like any other governor, has no other -- has -- they are desperate and their -- the choices on the table are very small. LLAMAS: You think it was OK to ship. refugee families to Martha`s Vineyard where 50 people had one bathroom in a church and they were not prepared for them? SALAZAR: I am not OK with what`s happening on the border period. LLAMAS: A passionate fight for the Latino vote which could mean winning beyond this year`s Midterms. Tom Llamas, NBC News, Miami. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Up next, it`s being embraced by some of the biggest stars in sports. How Pickleball is going from a pickup game to pro. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) ROBBIE COLTRANE, ACTOR: You`re a wizard, Harry. (END VIDEO CLIP) HOLT: Sad news for Harry Potter fans. Robbie Coltrane, the Scottish actor who played Hagrid, the beloved half-giant gamekeeper at Hogwarts has died. Coltrane had a long career as an actor and comedian. He appeared in two James Bond movies and started the British crime series Cracker. He was 72. And finally, what do Tom Brady and LeBron James have in common besides being sports legends? Like a growing number of Americans, they`re obsessed with pickleball. Emilie Ikeda explains. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANNA BRIGHT, PICKLEBALL PLAYER: The ball has to bounce. EMILIE IKEDA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): 23-year-old Anna Bright is a product of Pickleball`s pandemic boom, picking up the game just a year ago. Now, she`s dominating the sport as a professional pickleballer. BRIGHT: I probably netted between 100 and $125,000 since late February. IKEDA: So, you`ve made six figures within less than a year of playing pickleball. BRIGHT: Yes. IKEDA: Once viewed as a pastime for the older athletes among us, pickleball, with its noisy pops of plastic, is somewhere between tennis and ping pong and proving it has no bounds. This is Major League Pickleball complete with color commentary. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Taddeo is flashing it all right now. IKEDA: Today, the first of a three-day tournament in Columbus, Ohio. 12 teams, 48 players. The top prize, $100,000. Pickleball is considered the fastest-growing sport in the U.S. with nearly five million players picking up a paddle last year. ANNE WORCESTER, STRATEGIC ADVISER AND BOARD MEMBER, MAJOR LEAGUE PICKLEBALL: There will be 40 million people playing pickleball by 2030. IKEDA: And some of the biggest names in sports are paying attention. TOM BRADY, NFL STAR: All right, Pickleball. IKEDA: Tom Brady, LeBron James, and Kim Clijsters are among the growing list of superstar pro athletes buying up professional pickleball teams. What makes pickleball appealing as an investor? KIM CLIJSTERS, FORMER PROFESSIONAL TENNIS PLAYER: The growth margin. I think it`s really cool to see that there is still so much potential. The reason why I did MLP is because it`s equal pay. Men and women are starting on an equal playing field. IKEDA: Major League money is following the fans as professional pickleball takes its swing. Emilie Ikeda NBC News, Columbus, Ohio. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: It sounds like it`s time to get in the game. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. headline: Behind The Scenes Of Carrie Underwood`s Epic New Tour
story_text: SHEINELLE JONES: I am excited for this. So, this morning, we have a "TODAY" exclusive. A first look at what to expect when country superstar Carrie Underwood hits the road for her Denim and Rhinestones tour. It`s her first in three years since she took me back stage in South Carolina where it all kicks off. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CARRIE UNDERWOOD, SINGER: It`s a good time. A lot of hard work has gone into the show and very, very proud of it. People are going to have fun. JONES (voiceover): It`s been a few years since a Carrie Underwood tour has made its way across the country. And no one seems more excited than the superstar herself.\\ JONES (on camera): What is the one thing you miss about touring? UNDERWOOD: The crowds. I love to sing. When I`m on stage, I feel like I am at home. And just to feel the energy from people and you look out at all these seats and every single person that is there. JONES (voiceover): The eight-time Grammy winner embarking on a 43-stop arena tour, kicking it all off with a huge show in Greenville, South Carolina. And yours truly is given an all-access pass. JONES (on camera): This gives me like the feels. UNDERWOOD: It`s pretty awesome. It looks bigger. I feel like from up here. JONES: From here? UNDERWOOD: Yes. JONES (voiceover): The stage for her "Denim and Rhinestones" tour lit in dramatic purple will include pyrotechnics and even Carrie performing some high-flying aerial stunts. UNDERWOOD: I am always looking to do things I`ve never have done before. JONES (on camera): Like fly? UNDERWOOD: Like fly. JONES (voiceover): Carrie, taking a page out of her CMT Awards performance. UNDERWOOD: And it`s important to me to make sure like everybody gets a good view. So, we want to figure out some cool ways to get from point A to point B. JONES (on camera): How exciting is that? JONES (voiceover): It`s all part of her goal to bring something new to the arena tours. UNDERWOOD: I want everything to feel different. I don`t want somebody to be like, no, I saw a Carrie Underwood show, you know, four years ago and I`m good. JONES (voiceover): Something definitely worth the price of admission, Carrie`s stunning wardrobe. JONES (on camera): Like this is -- UNDERWOOD: It`s a lot. There`s a lot going. JONES: It`s amazing. Look how beautiful it is. UNDERWOOD: The last part is adding more rhinestones. JONES: I don`t know if you could add any more rhinestones. UNDERWOOD: You always can. I mean -- JONES (voiceover): But something no amount of rhinestones can replace, Carrie`s time with her kids on the tour and at home. [09:35:00] UNDERWOOD: They will be out to visit. This tour, I`m going home a lot more than I ever have before. There is a way to get me home even if it`s just for the day. JONES (on camera): So, are your kids aware of what mommy does? I mean, they`ve been on tour with you before but they are young. UNDERWOOD: I feel like Israel who is seven and a half, he is becoming more aware that it`s not normal, probably because of people around him. So, he`ll go to school and somebody will be, like, I saw your mom on TV last night. JONES (voiceover): One of the Carrie`s few must-haves, a mobile gym. JONES (on camera): This is good. Do you ever work out to your own music? UNDERWOOD: No. JONES: No. UNDERWOOD: It`s weird. JONES (voiceover): A U.S. arena tour, a long way from Carrie`s "American Idol" days. JONES (on camera): Let me take you back. UNDERWOOD: Yes. JONES: It was in 2005. I was a reporter in Tulsa, Oklahoma, and I had the assignment to meet you at the door. The whole town was going nuts because a local girl made it on "American idol." And you walked in and your hands were like -- and I grabbed your hand. I was like, are you ready? If you look at this picture, like this girl right here, do you remember what you were feeling in those early days? UNDERWOOD: At that point, it was all very new, very fresh. And I am, like, OK, you know, let`s enjoy this and have fun and, you know, keep trying to, you know, move forward, but it could all go away at any second. And I think it`s kind of important to treat everything like that, you know, because it just makes you grateful. So, I still -- I`m waiting for the moment where I`m like feeling like I belong. JONES: Are you kidding me? JONES (voiceover): And while I had her, I just had to ask. (MUSIC PLAYING) JONES (on camera): One of your fellow "American Idol" winners, you know, Kelly Clarkson, does her Kellyoke. Have you heard her sing "Before He Cheats?" UNDERWOOD: I have. I have. I feel like she`s one person that you`re like, please, don`t sing my song because you`re going to make me look bad. JONES: Are you joking? You all are both like powerhouses. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: That`s funny. I was asking her, you know, if she stays in touch with some of the -- you know, the folks who she, you know, was on "Idol" with years ago. And she has -- great. She says she still talks to Simon, you know, that whole thing. DREYER: Oh, that`s great. JONES: One thing I will say about Carrie is she is so humble and it`s not lost on her. Because I`m like, oh, my god, look at all these clothes and look at all of this. And she is like, yes. You know, she just -- it keeps it -- DREYER: It seems like it hasn`t gone to her head. JONES: Not at all. DREYER: She`s walking around like, can you -- JONES: She is still saying, can you believe it? DREYER: Yes. JONES: I know. DREYER: That`s great. JONES: The tour kicks off tomorrow and tickets are on sale now. There will be pyrotechnics. She flies, as we talked about. She even -- she`s like, I am humble and even -- SOBOROFF: I want to see you get up on the flying thing. JONES: I loved it. Yes. ROKER: Oh, yes. DREYER: With that old hairstyle. JONES: Exactly. DREYER: Yes. JONES: Exactly. DREYER: All right. Coming up, another icon is here with us in studio. She`s -- SOBOROFF: There she is. DREYER: Stella McCartney . You`re going to fashion, family and so much more, right? STELLA MCCARTNEY , FASHION DESIGNER: Absolutely. DREYER: OK. When we come back. SOBOROFF: Don`t go anywhere. JONES: Gorgeous. Gorgeous. SOBOROFF: Nice done. Nice walk off. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:40:00] JONES: We have our life therapist here. She`s also -- SOBOROFF: Really have a good time JONES: -- a fashion royalty with us this morning here in studio. SOBOROFF: Stella McCartney has made a name for herself designing clothes for celebrities like Meghan Markle , Amal Clooney, Beyonce Johnson, so, so many more. DREYER: She launched her brand in 2001, pioneering animal free and ecofriendly fashion. ROKER: And Stella joining us now fresh off her Paris fashion show. JONES: Yes. ROKER: Good morning, Stella. JONES: Good morning. STELLA MCCARTNEY , FASHION DESIGNER: Hi. SOBOROFF: Good to see you. MCCARTNEY: Good morning. ROKER: So, you made this a part of your mission, you know, sustainable ecofriendly. I mean, Bella Hadid`s Met`s dress in the Paris fashion show you making a big splash. How important is that to you and why did you decide so early on? I mean, you were really ahead of the curve on this. MCCARTNEY: You know, I grew up on an organic farm in England as a vegetarian and I basically wanted to be a fashion designer and I was lucky enough to be one and I thought, I can`t compromise my ethics for my career. I don`t want to kill animals. You know, billions of animals get killed for handbags and shoes and leather jackets. So, I was like, I can`t do that. I need to find an alternative. headline: TODAY WITH HODA & JENNA for October 14, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) [10:00:16] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (voice over): Today, a Hollywood star who is doing it all, actress, entrepreneur, musician and mom, Zooey Deschanel.
