JENNA BUSH HAGER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (voice over): It`s TODAY with Hoda and Jenna, it all starts right now. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB (on camera): Hi guys, it`s Friday, October 14th, middle of the month. HAGER: Smack in the middle of October. KOTB: Halfway to Halloween. HAGER: Yes, halfway to Christmas. No? But we`re closer. KOTB: Don`t you love a Friday? HAGER: It`s feeling like fall in the northeast. KOTB: I know. Have you looked at the leaves yet? HAGER: Yes. KOTB: You did? HAGER: Did you look at the leaves? KOTB: I saw them the other day. HAGER: They`re changing. KOTB: Sometimes you get busy and you miss the most obvious thing in the world. HAGER: Don`t miss -- by the way, they`re right behind you. KOTB: They`re changing. HAGER: They`re right behind us and they`re changing but yes, a Friday feeling. KOTB: Yes, we hope you guys -- we hope you guys have a great weekend, savor and linger. Let your weekend last. HAGER: And look at the leaves. KOTB: Roll it out. Yes, enjoy. All right, so, there is a gentleman in his 40s who is turning heads because he looks fine like wine. HAGER: OK, we`re talking about Chris Pine. He has a new hairdo. KOTB: OK, look at his before picture. HAGER: Which was kind of blonde. KOTB: Shoulder length. HAGER: Blondish. KOTB: But if you look deeply into the picture on the left, it`s very gray with blonde ends. HAGER: Yes. KOTB: And he decided he was going to just kind of -- HAGER: Go for it. KOTB: Go for it. HAGER: Shave it all off. KOTB: OK. Wow. What do you think of -- do you think that is? HAGER: First of all, he`s not my favorite Chris. I know there`s a lot of Chris`s. Who`s your favorite again? KOTB: I can`t remember. HAGER: There`s so many. KOTB: There`s too many Chris`s. There`s so many. HAGER: There`s too many Chris to even count. But anyway, now with that hairdo, he`s in the top two, or three. KOTB: He`s moved. He was that (INAUDIBLE). HAGER: I don`t know who else there is. There`s Chris Hemsworth. There`s Chris Stapleton. KOTB: Chris Pratt. HAGER: Chris Pratt. Anybody else from -- Chris Evans. KOTB: Chris Evans, of course. Chris Hemsworth. HAGER: There`s a lot of Chris`s. KOTB: There`s so many. Wouldn`t you hate to be a Chris? There`s just too many cute ones. HAGER: Kris Kringle. KOTB: OK, you`re really getting weird as usual. HAGER: Yes, I feel like Chris was that name that I always named my Ken Doll. It was either Chris or Chad. You know in the 90s -- 80s, 90s. KOTB: Chad was very bougie (PH). HAGER: Right? Yes, bougie. Chad with the thing around his neck. KOTB: Right. Tying the sweater. Who wore sweaters like that? HAGER: In the 80s. KOTB: Drape it. Did you do that? HAGER: No. KOTB: Did you wear chinos? Do you know what chinos are? HAGER: Khakis? KOTB: Yes, they`re like khakis. HAGER: I mean, my mom might have dressed me but I don`t think anybody would have called me bougie if they saw my baby picture. I was (INAUDIBLE) were about to size is too small and like a huge t-shirt. KOTB: Do you remember -- do you remember one of your first day of school outfits? Do you remember liking that or whatever? Do you remember what those outfits were you were like, it`s the first day? HAGER: I remember always towards the end of August wanting to like plan out my outfits, being excited about it. But I didn`t ever have any way to do it. So, I`d look through the Archie comic books and see what Veronica was wearing. I like Veronica, did you? KOTB: Yes, I love the Archie comics. I don`t know that I ever looked at Veronica and say I want to wear her outfits. HAGER: I look at her outfits and I`d like circle them. But the saddest part is they would never come to fruition. You know, it was like my -- would I wear this on the first day? KOTB: Isn`t that cute? HAGER: But our mom didn`t really. KOTB: My mom loved to pick out our outfits. I remember an orange vest with an orange long color and an orange skirt. Thinking I was wow. And I remember walking like, does everybody see me? HAGER: Wow. KOTB: Because I thought that was really something. I remember the feeling. HAGER: I wish I had this picture and maybe you`ll do. I remember a mustard yellow shirt with a kilt and a tie that I believe my sister made a matching tie for my cat. But it was like mustard yellow and a mustard yellow tie. And I had glasses. KOTB: Glasses. We all had glasses. HAGER: And it just was a terrible look. KOTB: I just feel like the more I think about those of us who went through all those different phases, compared to now, I just think -- [10:05:03] HAGER: It gets better later. KOTB: It gets greater later. No, but people who had a more difficult childhood have a more -- have an easier adulthood I think. I think you go through a lot. And you`re like, oh, that`s nothing. I`ve been through that. I`ve had that. HAGER: Well, I mean, I look at pictures of myself in fourth grade with a full mustache. And I`m like, where did that hair go? I mean, I know I waxed it for a period of time. KOTB: You did? HAGER: Not on fourth grade, but later, you know, and I`m just like, wow, you know? KOTB: I know. Anyway, if you`re going through an awkward stage, or if your kids are, just hang on. HAGER: Yes, totally. KOTB: Hang on. HAGER: It gets greater later. KOTB: Debbie Smith said that, greater later. HAGER: We agree with it. KOTB: All right. HAGER: OK. So, if you`re looking for love. Anybody around here that could be. OK, this is what you want to do. You might want to just go to the grocery store. KOTB: Apparently, there`s some strange code of grocery shopping that will let a prospective partner know that you`re in the market. You might see someone go, he`s cute. I`m going to give him a signal. There`s a signal you can give with the produce that you`re shopping for. HAGER: And you know what not, somebody made this up. We don`t know who, but I think he was a bachelor star. So, they know what happens. KOTB: It was Brittney Hockey (PH). HAGER: OK. She said, here`s the deal. KOTB: This is her. She said this, the girl from the Bachelor show. HAGER: She knows. OK, she said bananas are faced up in your cart. KOTB: Face up. What does that mean? Then, you`re single. HAGER: But if you`re not looking, put your banana down. KOTB: Upside down, curve down. HAGER: Honey, I hope you`re putting your banana down. Leave your banana down. KOTB: Can you imagine if you`re just grocery shopping and then suddenly and you -- HAGER: I don`t think people really do this. KOTB: Nobody does. OK, next. HAGER: People are too busy. KOTB: This is a good one. You`re aware of this one. HAGER: I am not aware of this one. KOTB: No, you were aware of the concept. HAGER: You`re talking to me? KOTB: Of the concept. HAGER: OK. Evidently if there`s an upside down pineapple. Upside down -- upside down. What does upside down means? KOTB: It means that the pointy stuff is down. HAGER: OK, upside down pineapple, that means you`re in a couple. But you`re still actively looking. KOTB: What`s the pineapple? HAGER: Evidently, a pineapple signifies that you`re -- KOTB: Why would you know that? HAGER: I only know it because I have a pineapple light. KOTB: Like a nightlight? Like a real light? HAGER: A chandelier. I know. OK, don`t make fun of me. KOTB: No, I`m not, I`m just curious. HAGER: I have a pineapple thing and somebody -- lamp. And somebody came into my home and they were like, do you know what that means? And I was like, no, I just thought it was a lamp that was a gift. Well, a pineapple lamp means that you could be looking for extracurricular. KOTB: OK. All right, and if you want -- if you want a relationship, you`re supposed to grab a peach from the peach section and put it in his cart. HAGER: Well, could he put a peach in your cart? KOTB: Yes, he could. HAGER: So, what is a peach symbol of? KOTB: I don`t -- I don`t -- ask them. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Juicy. HAGER: Juicy. Will you ever put a peach at anybody`s cart? KOTB: No, they`d be like, did you drop this in my cart? I think it would be you`re thinking it`s like some hot gesture and they`re like, this is my cart lady. You`re like, oh, sorry. Can you imagine? Coming up next, a social media challenge from none other than Ricky Gervais. HAGER: Oh, I`m scared. We`re going to scroll through this week`s best viral videos and post, after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [10:12:40] KOTB: We are in for a good time whenever our good friend stops by. She`s the host of the Midnight Snack podcast. Michelle Collins. MICHELLE COLLINS, MICHELLE COLLINS PODCAST HOST: Oh my God. HAGER: We`ve been waiting because Michelle lives on the other side of the pond, so we`re so happy. Did that -- did that have that accent I wanted? The pond. Michelle is back to run through those buzzy social media posts you might have missed in a segment we like to call Let`s Scroll. COLLINS: Oh my God, I`m so happy to here. How are you? HAGER: We`re good. KOTB: We start with Ricky Gervais. What is he up to? COLLINS: Ricky is always causing problems and you know, people love him and hate him but he had this tweet that went viral where he asked the question you can only keep three -- ladies, I want you to look at this list. KOTB: You can only keep three. HAGER: Bottled water, hair dryers, stretching, taxis, social media, lying, potatoes KOTB: Parties. HAGER: Sitting down, gossiping, umbrellas, radio? COLLINS: And condiments. Which ones -- now, I`ll say, I know what three I would pick. Do you know which three? HAGER: The radio we can listen to on Spotify. KOTB: But you can have other things that are like that? HAGER: Or just three. COLLINS: I would say those three as far as I know from Ricky`s rules. KOTB: Nothing else. HAGER: Nothing else. KOTB: Nothing else on the planet Earth. I`d have to have radio because I need music. If that`s the only way to get music. I`m taking music HAGER: Only these three things? COLLINS: It`s really, really tough. HAGER: What are yours? COLLINS: Well, OK, publicly, it would be on NBC. It would be sitting down, parties and umbrellas because I`ve always fancied myself a bit of an impressionist painting. Like I like that for me. But I think privately it would be gossiping, lying and parties. What about you girls? HAGER: Definitely parties. COLLINS: It has to be. KOTB: Parties, music, radio. I think I need water. HAGER: Condiments. Oh, water. COLLINS: Are we diva? We need water. OK, let`s scroll, next thing. KOTB: All right, what`s the next one? COLLINS: I know how much you girls love Serena Williams. KOTB: Yes, love. COLLINS: So, you know, she`s retired. I mean, she wasn`t calling it that. But she stepped away from tennis. And now we`re seeing what she`s doing. HAGER: Is she on a girl`s weekend? COLLINS: She`s not, she`s in Mexico. She`s dancing to my new hit single itty bitty bomb bomb (PH). You`ll see it. KOTB: Wait, I want to see. COLLINS: Let`s watch this. KOTB: Yes, let`s watch. HAGER: Is she making s`mores? COLLINS: Making s`mores, no kids. HAGER: Oh my gosh. KOTB: How happy does she look? HAGER: That looks so fun. COLLINS: You know, and I feel like -- you know, if anybody deserves a break, don`t you think it`s time Serena gets a break? HAGER: Yes. [10:15:04] KOTB: It`s time. HAGER: I think we should go to Mexico too. KOTB: I would love that. HAGER: Right? Let`s go to Mexico with or without s`mores. COLLINS: I thought she was talking about me, I was like I`d like to come. HAGER: No, with you. I`m not saying with or without you. COLLINS: Of course, OK, let`s scroll. HAGER: We love it when Michelle is here. COLLINS: We love dating posts. I know how much -- KOTB: Yes, yes. Yes. COLLINS: Amber Rose is funny. So, she posted this thing. Why is it so hard to find an intelligent, sexy, rich, successful tatted gentleman that also has kids but is not an abusive narcissists and he`s definitely an atheist but also a feminist. She can`t find this man. Do you think people at home that Amber Rose is asking for too much? Yes or no? HAGER: Maybe. KOTB: Maybe. COLLINS: Well, I feel like every single man I meet is a narcissist. Is that possible? HAGER: Maybe. Is that possible? COLLINS: And none of them are tattooed though, which is fine by me. KOTB: But what? So, they`re just talking about themselves the whole time you`re on the date? COLLINS: Yes. HAGER: Do they ask you a question? COLLINS: No, they do. But it`s just I feel like all these men out there, she`s right. That she`s looking for this perfect man. The truth is if they have eight teeth and a working nostril hole. I`m like, oh my God, he`s the one. KOTB: Working nostril hole. COLLINS: If he has a working nostril. HAGER: Just one hole? COLLINS: Well, sometimes it`s all you need Jenna. And should we scroll on? KOTB: Yes, scroll on. COLLINS: This is really cute. OK, you know, people wonder, what are your fans at home look like? Please watch this lovely lady Emily Wilson. She`s biggest fan watching. Let`s take a look at this. This is the audience you want, Jenna. HAGER: Oh my gosh. I was wondering where we heard this yell. COLLINS: So, she has a reaction shot to all of our shenanigans. HAGER: Everyone? COLLINS: Yes. KOTB: Oh my God. HAGER: Love you, Michelle. COLLINS: Thank you. HAGER: You guys, check out Michelle on her podcast Midnight Snack. KOTB: All right, coming up next, Actress Zooey Deschanel on her signature style and her real life Hollywood love coming up after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [10:21:07] KOTB: "Elf", "New Girl", "500 Days of Summer" movies and T.V. shows that all have a single thing in common. This lovely lady right here Zooey Deschanel. She`s been acting since she was a teen, also an entrepreneur, a musician, is trial -- a style trendsetter, a mom, hi. ZOOEY DESCHANEL, ACTRESS: Nice to see you. KOTB: It`s so great to see you. A couple of years ago, we have the Scott brothers here all the time, they`re always fixing. DESCHANEL: They`re the best, right? KOTB: Yes, and I was so excited when I saw -- whatever the posts were early on that you and Jonathan were dating. DESCHANEL: Yes. KOTB: First of all, he`s in love with you. You can tell. How did you -- when did you know like this relationship feels right for me? DESCHANEL: Well, you know, he`s just so kind, always so nice and thoughtful and considerate. And I always try to be that way. But you know, when somebody else is being that way, you know, and it kind of encourages you to like, keep it up and like, oh, well, he`s so nice. So, you know, I want to be even nicer. So, he`s just such a thoughtful kind person. and he`s just so fun. KOTB: Was it so immediate? Sometimes when you know, you know? DESCHANEL: Yes, it was. Yes, you know, we`re both like, I was like 39 when we met, he was like, maybe 41. Like, we were, you know, not young. So we kind of knew, you know? It`s great. KOTB: That`s so sweet. Now, I picture him making all the like design decisions only because he`s that guy. Do you got -- how does that work for you, too? DESCHANEL: You know what he`s really collaborative. Because I`m very, like, I have a distinct point of view. KOTB: You got a style. DESCHANEL: And he was, you know, he has certain things that are really important to him. And I have certain things that are really important to me. And luckily, they`re not the exact same thing. So, he`s really into all the architectural stuff and -- KOTB: And you`re into more of this style? Yes. Your style is so cool. DESCHANEL: Thank you. KOTB: So, when I picture you as a little girl. When you were a little girl, were you the one like I`m going to wear this with this mom and dad. I`m going to do it my way. DESCHANEL: Yes, I was always I had my own style. KOTB: Which one is you in this two? DESCHANEL: The little. Yes, I`m sure I had these smock dresses that my grandma and my aunt would make. And I would always be wearing dresses. I liked dresses, and I liked the smocking with the little, you know, all those little like Christmas dress. KOTB: Yes. Can I see that picture one more time? Because I am noticing something else that`s similar, bangs. You`ve had bangs your whole life. Is that -- has that been your signature since you were little? DESCHANEL: I mean, you know, when you`re a little kid they just cut your hair, right? And that`s how it was cut and then it just kind of looks better on me. I grew them out once and it didn`t look as I want to. KOTB: It wasn`t for you? DESCHANEL: No. I look better with the bangs. KOTB: That was like no. DESCHANEL: I looked into the mirror. I`m like nobody recognizes me with -- KOTB: Proof that I have a forehead. You`ve got really cool parents. DESCHANEL: I do. KOTB: You hit the parent jackpot. How many years have they been married? DESCHANEL: 50. Yes, they just had their 50th wedding anniversary this summer. KOTB: Oh my God. So, what -- watching them, I mean, they`re obviously teaching you things about a relationship and how to keep a relationship work. What do you think you`re learning or you`ve learned from them? DESCHANEL: We have like family dinners all the time. Yes, it`s, you know, they`re just a fantastic couple. And they both have their own independent things that they do. They`re both very independent people. But they always come together. And you know, they just like being together. So, I think that`s the most important thing. KOTB: There is an app that you are associated with that you -- that you`re crazy about, tell me about it. DESCHANEL: Yes. So, I`m a co-founder of this app called Merryfield. And it`s kind of like couponing. But it`s easy. I feel like couponing is kind of hard. And you have to be good at math. [10:25:00] So, this is just specifically for better for you brands. When I had my first kit, I got really into, you know, health and wellness. And it really kind of upset me that it seemed like, you know, it was kind of difficult to eat healthy on a budget, and it felt oh my gosh, it was so expensive. I`m like, wait, why is it expensive to buy fresh food that`s healthy for you? KOTB: Right. DESCHANEL: So, I started at a company called Lettuce Grow, and we do like hydroponic growing devices. So, I was like, I want to do 20 percent of my growing home, like grow food. KOTB: OK. DESCHANEL: But then what about the other 80 percent? So, Merryfield is like the solution for the other 80 percent. We give rewards and cashback for buying better for you, or ecofriendly brands. KOTB: So, if you buy healthy, something healthy you get? HAGER: Yes, better our brands, and our brands are all vetted through like a very strict set of standards. KOTB: OK. HAGER: And yes, it`s been amazing. The response has been incredible. A lot of people who are saying, you know, these brands were kind of out of their reach, you know, they couldn`t afford them before now. Now it allows them to afford these Better For You brands and we`re helping people eat healthier. KOTB: They feel better in the end. DESCHANEL: I know. KOTB: Zooey, it`s so good to see you. Congratulations on what`s happening in your life right now. I`m really happy for you. Coming up next, Jenna and I are going to sit down with a breast cancer survivor who`s inspirational stories touching so many lives, coming up after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [10:29:57] KOTB: First, a look at how she created a whole new life for herself with a very meaningful mission. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) RICKI FAIRLEY, FOUNDER, TOUCH, THE BLACK BREAST CANCER ALLIANCE: I tried to like let everything go, and just paddle, and just feel the water. And see to feel the sun or the wind. Feel God around me. KOTB (voice-over): Ricki Fairley starts most of our days like this, alone, and at peace on the Chesapeake Bay. But this mother of two didn`t always know how to slow down. Like most caregivers, Ricki was constantly on the go. FAIRLEY: I was a crazy busy typical mom, working mom. I actually had been married for 30 years, and I was the breadwinner for our family, traveling every week on the road. KOTB: After a routine mammogram, the words triple negative breast cancer stopped her in her tracks. FAIRLEY: My doctor said, we found five spots on your chest wall. You are now metastatic, you have two years to live. Get your affairs in order. We don`t have anything for you. And I said, well, I can`t really die right now. I have a daughter at Dartmouth. I have to pay for her tuition. So, me, you, and gotten some drugs or something, we got to work this out. KOTB: It was a long road of surgeries, chemotherapy, radiation, and experimental drugs. But it worked. And Ricki was cancer free. She decided to quit her old life and start fresh. FAIRLEY: I knew I had to get rid of all the cancers in my life. I divorced my husband of 30 years, I quit my business partner of 10 years. I sold my house in Alpharetta, Georgia with a pool and two acres. And I moved to my little one bedroom condo on the beach. KOTB: She also did a lot of research and learned about the disparity in breast cancer for black women. FAIRLEY: This disease for black women is a different disease. And now, we have a growing body of data that validates that a black breast cancer cell looks different from a white one. We have a 41 percent higher mortality rate than white women. We have a 39 percent higher recurrence rate of breast cancer than white woman, which is crazy. KOTB: So, with her new home, her new fiance and her new way of life, came a new purpose, a nonprofit called, Touch, The Black Breast Cancer Alliance. FAIRLEY: I wanted to change the game on how the world thinks about black women and breast cancer. I want to advance the science. I want to stop the dying. I wanted to bring pharmaceutical companies to the table to say deal with this. Help us. KOTB: 11 years after she was told she was going to die. Ricki is still cancer free and has been able to watch her oldest daughter get married and have a family of her own. FAIRLEY: I work for my granddaughters. I don`t want them to ever think about this disease. I don`t want them to have to talk about it. I don`t want them to -- I don`t want it to be in their existence. KOTB: As for her younger daughter, Hayley, Ricki got her wish and watched her graduate college. They now work side by side to help other women going through the unthinkable, HAYLEY BROWN, DAUGHTER OF RICKI FAIRLEY: Seeing my mom, firsthand, being sick, and dealing with all of the things that come with it. And now, just the things that even come with survivorship. Just being a support to some for these women has been a large part of my mission. And so, what I`m trying to do now for the breast cancer community is also create that safe space. KOTB: Looking back, Ricki has advice for her younger, busier self. FAIRLEY: Your peace nonnegotiable. Take care of yourself. Check your breath, give yourself a minutes, give yourself a pause. It`s OK to say no. KOTB: And as she sits with her family, four generations of strong women, Ricki`s mission is clear. FAIRLEY: I`m a miracle. I know a miracle. I shouldn`t be here. So many women that with that had what I had didn`t make it. And I know that God left me here to do this work. To be an advocate for other women. It`s my purpose. (END VIDEOTAPE) KOTB (on camera): Ricki, I mean, we are in awe of you. Your purpose came with that horrible diagnosis. FAIRLEY: Yes. So, in 1978, the old one was knocked down and a new wood rose in its place. Now, it`s getting a fresh coat of paint ahead of its big birthday. headline: Meet the Press for October 16, 2022, NBC
story_text: [09:00:17] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CHUCK TODD, NBC HOST (voice over): This Sunday, the battlegrounds. With the midterms now just 23 days away, the candidates in the Senate races that will determine party control are making their final pitch to voters and facing off on the debate stage, in Georgia... HERSCHEL WALKER , GEORGIA REPUBLICAN SENATE NOMINEE: That was a lie, and I`m not backing down. SEN. RAPHAEL WARNOCK , (D) GEORGIA: My opponent has a problem with the truth. TODD: ... Pennsylvania... MEHMET OZ, PENNSYLVANIA REPUBLICAN SENATE NOMINEE: We should have had a debate already. LT. GOV. JOHN FETTERMAN , (D) PENNSYLVANIA: I actually have a record in fighting crime. TODD: ... and Wisconsin. SEN. RON JOHNSON, (R) WISCONSIN: We have to keep violent criminals in jail. LT. GOV. MANDELA BARNES, (D) WISCONSIN: It is absurd when people say that I`m soft on crime. TODD: I`ll speak with two independents, Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Utah`s independent Senate candidate, Evan McMullin. Plus, Trump`s testimony. REP. BENNIE THOMPSON , (D) MISSISSIPPI & CHAIR, SELECT COMMITTEE ON THE JANUARY 6 ATTACK: He must be accountable. TODD: The January 6th committee issues a subpoena for former President Trump to testify about his role in the attack on the Capitol... REP. LIZ CHENEY, (R) WYOMING & VICE CHAIR, SELECT COMMITTEE ON THE JANUARY 6 ATTACK: We are obligated to seek answers directly from the man who set this all in motion. TODD: ... while new video reveals congressional leaders pleading for help... SEN. CHUCK SCHUMER , (D) NEW YORK & MAJORITY LEADER: Why don`t you get the president to tell them to leave the Capitol? TODD: ... and new questions emerge on how the Secret Service handled advance warnings of the threat. I`ll talk to Democratic congresswoman Stephanie Murphy of Florida, who sits on the committee. And political polarization, why the state of Wisconsin best represents the deep divide playing out in our national politics. My reporting on the ground behind what`s driving the red and blue divisions. (on camera): Joining me for insight and analysis are Amy Walter, editor in chief of the Cook Political Report; Politico "Playbook" co-author Eugene Daniels; former North Carolina Pat McCrory ; and Maria Teresa Kumar, president of Voto Latino. Welcome to Sunday. It`s "Meet the Press." ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest-running show in television history, this is "Meet the Press With Chuck Todd." TODD: Good Sunday morning. There are just over three weeks to go until Election Day. Nearly 2 million Americans have already voted, just another 120 million to go. So with Republicans still favored to win control of the House, both parties are actually keeping their attention and money right now focused on the battle for control of the Senate, in particular these nine battleground states. These are the nine closest Senate races in the country because they`re trying to keep their top targets in play. In order to win back control, Republicans have to flip one of the Senate seats currently held by the Democrats, Georgia, Arizona, Nevada or New Hampshire, while also holding onto all of their seats that are in play here. Pennsylvania, Ohio, North Carolina are open seats. Florida and Wisconsin feature incumbents. On the Democratic side, Nevada Senator Catherine Cortez Masto is arguably the most vulnerable Democratic incumbent. Republicans are also trying to pick off Georgia Senator Raphael Warnock . But they`ve struggled a bit as allegations about domestic abuse and now abortion seem to saddle Republican Herschel Walker . Georgia now, by the way, has the highest price tag in the country of any mid-term race. More than $140 million has been spent on ads since the primary. By the way, that total is more than what both Bush and Gore spent in the year 2000, if you want to see how much funding has grown exponentially. So the number here will get even bigger, especially if this Georgia race goes into another overtime, as it happened two years ago. This time the runoff would be on December 6th. On Friday night the candidates met in what may be -- may be their only debate, where Walker again denied that he paid for the mother of one of his children to have an abortion. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) WALKER: As I said, that`s a lie. And I said that was a lie, and I`m not backing down. And you have Senator Warnock, people that would do anything and say anything for this seat. But I`m not going to back down because this seat is too important to the Georgia people for me to back down right now. MODERATOR: You`ve been vocally pro-life, supporting a ban on abortions without exceptions. Would you support a complete ban on a national level? Thirty seconds. WALKER: First of all, see, that`s not true, either. I said I support a -- a heartbeat bill, and I said that has exceptions in it. MODERATOR: Do you believe there should be any limitations on abortion set by the government? And you have 60 seconds. WARNOCK: I think that the women of this country and the women of this state woke up one summer morning and a core protection that they`ve known for 50 years was taken from them by an extremist Supreme Court. And I stand where I`ve said I stand in the past, that a patient`s room is too narrow and small and cramped a space for a woman, her doctor and the United States government . (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: By the way, early voting in Georgia starts tomorrow. Let`s turn now to a few of the Democratic opportunities here. Just two Republican incumbents, as I noted, are in battleground races. [09:05:02] That`s Wisconsin and Florida. But nominees that essentially were hand- picked by Donald Trump in those three open races have made those states more competitive as well. The cycle`s second highest ad price tag is in the state of Pennsylvania. More than $95 million has been spent on ads just since the primary in May. My colleague Dasha Burns had exclusive interviews this week with both Senate nominees. NBC News agreed to Democrat John Fetterman`s request to use a transcription program during the interview because he`s still experiencing some auditory processing issues from a stroke he had in May. Outside, though, of releasing a letter from his cardiologist on June 3rd, the campaign has denied additional requests for his medical records. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Don`t voters deserve to know your status now? FETTERMAN: Being on -- in front of thousands and thousands of people and having interviews and getting around all across Pennsylvania, that gives everybody, and the voters decide, you know, if they think that it`s -- it`s really the issue. Dr. Oz likes to make fun of me that I might miss a word, but, you know, he`s missed, you know, two words, and that is "yes" or "no" on the national abortion ban. BURNS: One of your campaign staffers said that John Fetterman wouldn`t have had a stroke if he had, quote, "ever eaten a vegetable in his life." You`re a doctor. You`re a heart doctor. You of all people understand what John Fetterman is going through, better than most. Why would you allow your campaign to mock him like that? OZ: I have tremendous compassion for what John Fetterman is going through. I mean, not only do I as a doctor appreciate the challenges, but I know his specific ailment because it`s a specialty area of mine. BURNS: Doesn`t the buck stop with you? Isn`t that what a leader accepts? OZ: Oh, I accepted responsibility. And -- and I -- you know, I deal with issues as they come up. But he has his own set of issues. We should have had a debate already. BURNS: But would you ever talk to your patients like this? OZ: No. (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: In Wisconsin the race between Republican Senator Ron Johnson and Democratic Lieutenant Governor Mandela Barnes comes in at $76 million spent on ads, in just two months since the primary. This puts Wisconsin third on the overall spending list. Many of the ads have focused on the issue of crime, at least the ads coming from Republicans. And in a debate this week, those attacks by Johnson continued. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JOHNSON: We need law enforcement. And the problem with the whole Defund movement, which he has been a big supporter of, it dispirits law enforcement. They`re having a hard time recruiting members. BARNES: No police officers in this country were more dispirited than the ones who were present at the United States Capitol on January 6th. (APPLAUSE) JOHNSON: I immediately and forcefully and repeatedly condemned the violence on January 6th, unlike my opponent... (AUDIENCE BOOING) MODERATOR: Audience, please. JOHNSON: ... who basically just ignores the 570 riots, the 2,000 law enforcement officers injured during the summer riots. And he incited the Kenosha riots. BARNES: He called those folks "patriots." He called them "tourists," the people who were beating up police officers in the United States Capitol, the people that were there to protect him. (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: Mandela Barnes was endorsed early in the primary by Senator Bernie Sanders . It helped vault Barnes to lead in that primary. Meanwhile Senator Sanders has been cautioning Democrats to stay as focused on economic issues in the final weeks of the race as the party has been on the issue of abortion rights. And Senator Sanders joins me now. Senator, welcome back to "Meet the Press." SANDERS: Good to be with you. TODD: Look, I want to focus on your -- this was an op-ed you wrote about a week or so ago. And you`ve said this in other -- other programs. So walk me through what you`d be doing right now, you`re -- if you`re in one of these battleground races. You`ve said abortion rights should be front and center. How would you be talking about the economic issues? SANDERS: Well, number one, what the Supreme Court did was totally outrageous. It is women who should control their own bodies, not the government. Number two, too many people have fought and died to defend American democracy. We cannot let right-wing extremists undermine what is so important to this country, and that is the right of all people to participate in the political process. Thirdly, and terribly important, we live in a moment, Chuck, in which we see an economy where the people on top are doing phenomenally well, while working people are struggling. You`ve got more income and wealth inequality today than any time in the history of the United States, three people owning more wealth than the bottom half of the people in our society. That is insane. So what I think is Democrats should talk about the economy. I think they should contrast their views with the Republican positions. I believe, and most democrats believe, that at a time when half our people are living paycheck to paycheck, we should raise the minimum wage to a living wage. No Republicans support that. I think we should make it easier for workers to join unions. Republicans don`t support that. I believe that, when you have billionaires start paying a nickel, in some cases, in federal income taxes, yeah, we should demand that the rich and large corporations start paying their fair share. Now, what Republicans are saying, Chuck, which is quite amazing to me, is that, in the midst of these difficult economic times for seniors and for other people, you know what they say? "We`ve got to cut Social Security; we`ve got to cut Medicare; we`ve got to cut Medicaid." [09:10:12] I think that that is grotesque. And I think Democrats have got to hold them accountable for those reactionary positions. TODD: Senator, do you accept the criticism that the American Rescue Plan passed in early 2021 contributed to the current inflation issue we`re dealing with now? SANDERS: No, I don`t. Inflation right now, as I`m sure you know, Chuck, is an international problem. In Germany it is 10 percent; U.K., it is 10 percent; Canada, it is 7 percent. Inflation globally is caused by the pandemic and the break in supply chains. It is caused by, in my view, the war in Ukraine, obviously. TODD: Yeah. SANDERS: And it is also caused by incredible corporate greed. And I hope everybody understands that, when you go to the gas tank, you fill up your car today, the oil companies are making huge profits. TODD: Yeah. SANDERS: The food companies are making huge profits. They -- prescription drugs are high. Pharmaceutical industry is making huge profits. We`ve got to deal with that issue. TODD: Why do you think... SANDERS: And Republicans won`t, by the way. TODD: We have a majority of economists now that believe a recession in the next 12 months is likely. First of all, do you think the Federal Reserve is currently helping or hurting the situation? SANDERS: I think they`re hurting the situation. I think that it is wrong to be saying that the way we`re going to deal with inflation is by lowering wages and increasing unemployment. That is not what we should be doing. This inflation thing is a real issue. It is a global issue. But at a time when working families are struggling and the people on top are doing phenomenally well, I don`t think you go after working people. TODD: So you wouldn`t be raising interest rates anymore, at this point? The damage has already been done, in your view? SANDERS: Yes. TODD: Let me move to a couple of races, and I want to get your take on a few things. John Fetterman in Pennsylvania, look, you had -- you had some health issues on the trail during your presidential race. You did -- you were asked to release more of your medical records. You didn`t release all of your records, but you did release quite a few letters from your doctors. And frankly, you were on the trail being who you are and going all over the country. I think folks saw that your health was in good shape. Do you think Mr. Fetterman should be releasing more of his medical records, since he`s asking for a six-year term here? SANDERS: Well, Chuck, you know, I don`t know enough about John`s medical situation. But I think the contrast is very clear. I do know John Fetterman . I`ve known him for years. And John is somebody who is going to be a real fighter for the working class of this country. He is prepared to take on the greed of corporate America. And I hope very much he joins us in the United States Senate . TODD: In Wisconsin Mandela Barnes getting hit hard on the issue of crime. This -- you`ve heard the phrase "Defund the police." He`s not alone. A lot of Democrats are being hit with these ads. How would you be handling these attacks? SANDERS: Well, what -- you know, obviously it`s -- it`s not true, the attacks on him. I know that Mandela believes very strongly that we need good law enforcement, non-racist law enforcement. And I agree with him on that. I think, at the end of the day, if we`re going to solve the crime problem; if we`re going to solve the terrible drug problem that we`re seeing all over this country, we`ve got to get at the root causes of those problems. And that means we have a better educational system, that we make sure that our young people have the decent jobs that they need. I think January 6th, especially what happened this week, didn`t generate the kind of headlines and the kind of wall-to-wall coverage -- [09:55:06] TODD: Subpoenas wasn`t a headline enough for you-- WALTER: Subpoena, no. I think voters expect, of course, he`s going to get subpoenaed. If they said, we`re indict -- we believe that he should be indicted. We know that the real issue here is, until there is some legal action taken, this is still all background noise. TODD: We got defamation testimony this week in that defamation lawsuit that apparently the former president, Jean Carroll, that, that he`s worried about. That happens Wednesday, Eugene. DANIELS: Yeah. I mean, it`s just over and over and over and over again. WALTER: Yeah. DANIELS: Right? It`s January 6th. It`s Mar-a-Lago. It`s this defamation case. We talk to Republicans, and you probably would feel the same way, it`s that they`re like, it`s just too much chaos, and, we don`t want -- we want you gone. Please go away, and he wants to be at the center of attention all the time. TODD: All right. Well, I`ve got to play for you what Paul Ryan said earlier this week, because he said something that both seems obvious and yet I want to say naive at the same time. Take a listen. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) PAUL RYAN , FORMER SPEAKER OF THE HOUSE: I think Trump`s unelectability will be palpable by then. We all know that he`s so much more likely to lose the White House than anybody else running for president on our side of the aisle. So why would we want to go with that? (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: I`m old enough to remember, Pat, when that was Scott Walker`s argument in 2015 about why people need to rally around somebody other than Donald Trump . MCCRORY: Well, there are about 20 Republican - TODD: Yeah. MCCRORY: - candidates for the presidency that are running right now. TODD: Who really believe this too, right? MCCRORY: Who really believe this, too, and they can`t say it because they don`t want to upset the core 30 percent who are with Trump regardless. And, by the way, the Democrats are running away from Biden in this election, too. They do not want -- the Democrats don`t want Biden on the stage. TODD: Well, no, no, no. Oregon Democrats do. MCCRORY: Yeah, and the Oregon governor`s race is now close-- TODD: I know. Right. MCCRORY: Democrats don`t want Biden or Harris either, and Republicans frankly don`t want Trump. And they`re the ones trying to consume the TV time. TODD: Well, I don`t think Biden`s actually -- (CROSSTALK) KUMAR: I think -- TODD: -- White House seems to be fine -- KUMAR: Yeah. Yeah. TODD: -- with this. I`ve talked to folks at the White House like, hey, we`re all on the same message. We`ll go to Oregon and Florida? Okay. (CROSSTALK) DANIELS: It doesn`t matter. KUMAR: Yeah. KUMAR: You tell us where to go. But, I also think that with Biden, his challenge is that he hasn`t been able to communicate to the American people what he`s done. I mean, we can say that the difference between Donald Trump and the difference within Biden is Biden is a policy president. So he has - - he`s going to make fundamental changes for a generation. KUMAR: It`s his legacy of undermining elections. MCCRORY: Biden -- KUMAR: And it`s not just him, it`s not him, but he actually has a cadre of individuals right now seeking office that are election deniers. MCCRORY: But -- but -- but -- KUMAR: And that legacy is far more dangerous for a modern-day president than any other thing -- MCCRORY: But Biden can`t go on-- TODD: Last word. KUMAR: -- because it believes in undermining our democracy. MCCRORY: Biden can`t go on TV because 401(k)s are down 20-25 percent, because the price of eggs is more than we`ve ever paid in our lifetime, because of gas is going up. The Democrats don`t want Biden around. Republicans right now, the last four weeks, they just want the super PAC ads-- TODD: Well, Democrats do want one Democratic president campaigning for them. It`s the former Democratic president, who we`re going to see a lot of I think in the last three weeks anyway. Terrific panel, terrific show. Just 23 days. You ready, Amy? Are you ready? headline: Conversation With Elizabeth Heiskell About Her Breast Cancer Journey
story_text: HODA KOTB: We are back. 8:13. The "Pink Power TODAY". And this morning story hits close to home for us. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE: Yes, our beloved "TODAY" food contributor Elizabeth Heiskell was diagnosed with stage two breast cancer this past summer. KOTB: Like a lot of women this can happen, too. She was in the best shape of her life. She has no family history. She says breast cancer wasn`t just -- well, not on her radar. Elizabeth, we love you. You are here with us. ELIZABETH HEISKELL, " TODAY" FOOD CONTRIBUTOR: Yes. KOTB: We are going to talk to you in a second. OK. But first, let`s check out her story. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) HEISKELL: I was diagnosed with stage two breast cancer. KOTB (voiceover): Elizabeth found a lump by chance. HEISKELL: I went to just scratch my chest and I found a lump. I thought that I had had a mammogram eight months ago. I wasn`t that concerned, honestly. KOTB (voiceover): But she had the lump checked by her doctor. HEISKELL: She felt around and she started to look very panicked. We got to get a mammogram. We got to get an ultrasound. We need to get a biopsy. KOTB (voiceover): Elizabeth thought she was up to date with her mammogram screenings but the doctor informed her otherwise. HEISKELL: She said, Elizabeth it`s been two years, almost two and a half years since you had it. KOTB (voiceover): The news she had breast cancer came as a complete shock. HEISKELL: When my doctor did call me and told me that I had invasive ductal carcinoma, I didn`t know invasive or ductal meant but I knew carcinoma. I knew that was cancer. It was like the wind had been knocked out of me, like somebody punched me. I was not prepared for this. I was in the best shape of my life. I had just lost a good amount of weight. Breast cancer was not on my radar at all. It took me to my knees. [08:15:00] I have no family history of breast cancer. That was another reason I was so blindsided by this. As hard as it is for somebody to tell you that you have cancer, as hard as that is to hear, it is impossible to say the words to your family. Honestly, I didn`t think I was going to be able to process it to say that sentence to my family. It took weeks and weeks for it to even sink in. I just finished my third chemo treatment. I am just now grasping the fact that I have cancer. KOTB (voiceover): Cooking brought some comfort. HEISKELL: I must have made meat loaf, mashed potatoes, and sort of green peas with cream sauce. This was what -- what my mother made for me. I don`t even know how many times I made that meal because it did, it brought me such comfort. I was diagnosed three weeks before mama passed away. So, it`s been a lot. We are going to do these great easy salads that we can -- KOTB (voiceover): As a well-known chef and "TODAY" contributor, Elizabeth says she is passionate about cooking and taking care of others, but cancer has forced her to focus on herself. HEISKELL: It`s not my nature. I bring the casseroles. I bring the food. I am the doer. I am the one that makes sure that everyone else is OK. And it`s easy to let that take over and you forget to take care of yourself. You just have to take it step by step, day by day. But you will, you will get there. You will get to the top of the mountain. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB (on camera): Yes, you will. Yes, you will, Elizabeth. GUTHRIE: yes. KOTB: We are so happy that you are sitting here on this couch. We want to know all about it. But just in this moment, like, how are you -- tell me the prognosis. How are you feeling today? HEISKELL: You know, I am so unbelievably grateful. So, we went back to MD Anderson and that little tumor has shrunk 78 percent. GUTHRIE: Wow. Wow. Wow. KOTB: Come on. HEISKELL: That was only -- that was after three chemo treatments. KOTB: Wow. HEISKELL: I mean, it`s unbelievable. And I`m just -- I am -- I`m so grateful that I`m almost -- I feel guilty at times, you know, because I have the most amazing support system. I have you all. I have family and friends. And, you know, an incredible health care. And, you know, it`s good. It`s good. GUTHRIE: So, you`re halfway through your chemo. You`ll have your surgery. But -- I mean, to have that kind of, it`s working? HEISKELL: Yes. GUTHRIE: The feeling must be such, such a -- you know, just an inspiration? HEISKELL: It was unbelievable. And the lady that did my ultrasound, she -- her -- my mother`s name was Sheila (ph). Her name was Sheila (ph). She spelled it just like my mother did. And then her daughter`s name was Elizabeth and we have the same birthday. GUTHRIE: Oh, my gosh. HEISKELL: So, if you don`t tell me that my mama wasn`t all up in that room. GUTHRIE: Oh, wow. HEISKELL: But you know, the thing is, is that this is -- it is a journey. You know, it is a climb. And I`m leaning in and I`m learning. You know, I`m learning so much. And, you know, it`s -- I had worked myself up. When I was getting ready for that first chemo treatment, honey, fear had taken over. It was driving the bus. You would have thought that I was going to go in there and they were taking off all my fingers, all my toes. Like, I was petrified. KOTB: Yes. HEISKELL: And so, I got through that day and Luke was with me and I literally -- everything they did, I said, oh, that wasn`t so bad. KOTB: Yes. HEISKELL: Well, I mean, that wasn`t so bad. So, by the time I got home, I called my girls and I said, look -- I said, fear is not going to drive this bus. It -- to dream, it`s -- you use the same exact brain, the same exact creativity to make those horrible nightmares as you do to dream. And I am not doing it any more. KOTB: That`s it. HEISKELL: I am not holding back. You all think that I`ve always been 100 percent. There is something that I have been holding back and I`m not going to do it anymore. I am not fearing. KOTB: You said there are things that cancer could -- is teaching you that nothing else could have taught you. Because everyone knows that adage of God only gives you as much as you can handle. HEISKELL: Yes. KOTB: You actually don`t believe that? HEISKELL: No, I don`t think that`s the case. I think it`s time for you to lean in and learn something new. And, you know, the lessons that I have learned -- I mean, it`s look for silver linings even in this mess. There was this sweetest lady when I was at the clinic. And, you know, they give us these warm robes. So, it -- kind of, for five minutes you feel like you are at a spa, until they take your boob and they stick it into a vice grip. For that minute, you know -- and so, as she looked at me and she is sitting there with her bald head and sunken eyes, and she said, oh -- she said, aren`t these robes just the silver lining? And I had just been diagnosed, and I thought silver lining my butt. We are sitting here, you know. And then it came to me. And then she said, you know, where you live? And I said, I live in Oxford. She said, bus -- but my sister-in-law lives here in Houston so I have a place to stay. She goes, another silver lining. And it was almost like she was catching butterflies. I am not kidding you. And so, if you stay there in that silver lining, that silver lining is going to be the thing that you`re going to wrap yourself in. That`s all you`re going to see is the silver. And I`m telling you, these are the lessons that I would have -- I mean, and I know we talk about it and we say, you know. But to really believe -- KOTB: Believe it. GUTHRIE: Yes. HEISKELL: -- and every day you are looking for the silver lining butterflies. [08:20:00] KOTB: One of your silver linings is standing over there. You talked about your tribe. HEISKELL: Yes. KOTB: Your people. Who do we have? HEISKELL: So, I have my daddy, who I love more than life itself. And it`s his birthday tomorrow. And then I have Mindy and my sweet husband, Luke who -- let me tell you something, Luke looked at me in my first cancer treatment. And he looked over and I was sitting there and he had tears in his eyes when they went to put the first chemo drug in my body. And he looked at me and I know he was thinking, if only I could just take this and put this in me right now. He has been everything. You cannot even imagine. And my girls. Oh, my gosh, and my friends. KOTB: Is that one of your brothers? HEISKELL: And my friends -- no. And that`s Molly. And we have Margie (ph) and Peter. And -- you know, I do. I have a whole tribe. I have a little boy that every day when he goes to school, he tells his dad to honk the horn and -- so that I know that they are praying for me that morning. I mean, there is -- you cannot imagine. I have somebody who sent me a night light because I`d said that when the fear was taking -- driving the bus, I was up late nights. I mean, it was tough. And so, she sent me a night light that I could turn on when I was up scared at night. I mean, these are the people that I have. And, you know, I hope that people that, if you know somebody that has breast cancer or cancer or that`s struggling, please go out of your way. It doesn`t have to be much. KOTB: Right. HEISKELL: A honk of the horn or a night light, anything. KOTB: And sometimes people think, well, you know what, they may want their family time. They may want their privacy. But reach out, right? HEISKELL: Lean into them. KOTB: Lean in, yes. HEISKELL: Get under them. KOTB: Yes. HEISKELL: Hold them up. KOTB: Hold them. HEISKELL: And carry them up that mountain. I mean -- KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: Call, don`t text. KOTB: Yes. HEISKELL: Yes. And they did call me. You all they called me. KOTB: Of course. HEISKELL: And of course, when I was driving back from Memphis, we had been to the oncologist when you called, and I was like, oh God. Lord. Look, Hoda`s on the phone. Stop the car. Because we were about to go through a dead area. I was like, Hoda never calls me. Just stop the car. And then Savannah called. And it was just amazing. KOTB: Well, we -- GUTHRIE: We love you. KOTB: You`re our family. GUTHRIE: You are our family. KOTB: We`re part of your tribe, too. HEISKELL: Well, that -- I have been looking forward to being back here with you all so much. And you are -- I mean, I am. I`m back with family. I`m with Debbie and my producer, who I -- who really, I mean, she is my family. KOTB: Well, we adore you. You need to -- all of this is, like, the most inspirational. GUTHRIE: I know. It really is. KOTB: I`m sure you helped a ton of people today. We love you. HEISKELL: Go get your mammograms. KOTB: Yes. HEISKELL: I literally thought it was eight months. It had been two years people. KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: Yes. HEISKELL: It had been two years people. KOTB: You got it. HEISKELL: You put it on your calendar right now. You stop what you`re doing. I`m serious. KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: Yes, absolutely. KOTB: We love you. We love you. GUTHRIE: We love you. By the way, Elizabeth wrote a beautiful and personal essay, shares more of her story, and you should read it. Check it out today.com. And we just love you. KOTB: Yes. HEISKELL: I love you. GUTHRIE: Al, over to you. ROKER: Silver lining butterflies. Oh, I`ll remember that. KOTB: We love that. ROKER: That and hotter than the hinges of hell. GUTHRIE: Yes. ROKER: All right. Let`s show you what we got going on. Heavy snow in the U.P. of Michigan today. Some showers in the northeast. Look for some wet weather also down through the Florida Peninsula. Heavy rain down through Southern Texas. Warm and dry out west. That`s what`s going on around the country. Here`s what`s happening in your neck of the woods. KOTB: "POP Start" too. GUTHRIE: OK. JONES: "POP Start" is good too. ROKER: Yes, it is. JONES: All right. We`re going to try to give you some good stuff today. First up, Robbie Coltrane. Tributes are pouring in after the beloved actor died at the age of 72 over the weekend. He was best known for his role as Hagrid in the "Harry Potter" movie franchise. His agent shared in a statement that he would, "Be best remembered for decades to come as Hagrid in the Harry Potter films. A role which brought joy to children and adults alike all over the world. Prompting a stream of fan letters every week for 20 years." Coltrane`s "Harry Potter" co-star Daniel Radcliffe also paid tribute in a statement writing, Robbie was one of the funniest people I`ve met and used to keep us laughing constantly as kids on set. I feel incredibly lucky that I got to meet and work with him and very sad that he has passed. All right. Next up, Carrie Underwood. As we mentioned on Friday, the country superstar is hitting the road for her "Denim and" -- I was going to say diamonds -- "Rhinestones" tour. Highlighting her greatest hits and new music from her latest album. Underwood kicked off her tour with a sold-out show in Greenville, South Carolina, over the weekend. Here`s a look at one of her epic opening night performances. [08:25:00] (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CARRIE UNDERWOOD, SINGER: Yes, I`m one of those crazy angels. Tilted halo with a neon shine. Call me one of those crazy angels. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: Pretty cool. KOTB: Wow. JONES: She said she wanted to do something new and she certainly did. Underwood plans to make stops in 43 U.S. cities. That`s a lot of shows. Next up is Indianapolis, Indiana. You can catch the "Denim and Rhinestones" tour through March 20th through the 23rd. headline: The New Pledge From President Biden, If Democrats Keep Control Of Congress, He`ll Immediately Move To Pass National Abortion Rights
story_text: LESTER HOLT: 21 days before the Midterms, President Biden trying to keep abortion rights front and center, but polls show voters worrying most about the economy and soaring inflation. Peter Alexander reports on the new clashes between candidates in key battlegrounds. [19:05:09] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PETER ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): With just three weeks until the Midterms and Republicans slamming Democrats over the economy and record inflation, President Biden tonight trying to amplify the politically divisive issue of abortion rights, urging voters to keep Democrats in control of Congress. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Here`s the promise I make to you and the American people. The first bill that I will send to the Congress will be to codify Roe v. Wade. ALEXANDER: But some Democrats fear the potency of that message may be waning. Tonight, a new poll shows 44 percent of likely voters cite the economy or inflation as the number one problem facing the country while just five percent list abortion as their top issue. And now, Republicans have a four-point lead when voters are asked which party`s candidate they`d support. In Ohio, one of several crucial races that`ll determine control of the Senate. Republican candidate J.D. Vance hammered Democrat Tim Ryan over skyrocketing prices in a heated final debate. J.D. VANCE (R-OH) SENATE CANDIDATE: That rising energy price that people see at the pump, that they see in the utility bills, that was the direct result of policies enacted by Joe Biden and Nancy Pelosi and supported 100 percent by Tim Ryan . ALEXANDER: While Ryan slammed Vance for embracing former President Trump. REP. TIM RYAN (D-OH): You were calling Trump America`s Hitler. Then he kissed his ass -- VANCE: It`s not true. RYAN: It is true. And then you kissed his ass, and then he endorsed you. And you said he`s the greatest president of all time. ALEXANDER: There are critical governor`s races too in the battlegrounds of Arizona and Michigan and a rematch in Georgia between Republican Governor Brian Kemp and Democrat Stacey Abrams . Their one and only showdown last night. STACEY ABRAMS (D-GA), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: We live in a state of fear. And this is a governor who for the last four years has beat his chest but delivered very little for most Georgians. ALEXANDER: Kemp touting his early moves to reopen the state during the pandemic and going after Abrams. GOV. BRIAN KEMP (R-GA): Miss Abrams is going to lie out my record because she doesn`t want to talk about her own. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Peter, President Biden is going to pivot to the economy tomorrow focusing on high gas prices. ALEXANDER (on camera): Yes, Lester, that`s right. Looking to lower those prices, the President is going to announce that the administration will move forward with the release of as many as 15 million additional barrels of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It`s a controversial move that comes amid Russia`s war in Ukraine and after Saudi Arabia snub the President`s request to boost oil production. Lester? HOLT: Peter Alexander at the White House, thank you. There`s breaking news and a trial involving a murder they went unsolved for 25 years. A California man convicted late today for killing Kristin Smart, a college student who disappeared in 1996. Paul Flores, a former classmate of Smart`s wasn`t arrested for the crime until last year. Flores` father who was accused of helping move Smart`s body was found not guilty. Smart`s remains were never found. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for October 18, 2022, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the arctic blast of cold putting tens of millions on alert across the eastern half of the country. (voiceover): Frost and freeze warnings across 25 states, 86 million impacted. For many, the coldest air of the season yet. More than a foot of snow falling in parts of the Midwest less than a month into fall. Al Roker is tracking it. Also, tonight, just three weeks until the Midterms. The new pledge from President Biden, if Democrats keep control of Congress, he`ll immediately move to pass national abortion rights. Will it be enough with polls showing voter concerns focused on the economy right now? More than 25 years after the disappearance of Kristin Smart, the verdict in the murder trial or for former college classmate. Blackouts in Ukraine after officials say Russia destroyed nearly a third of its power stations in little over a week. Growing fears for an Iranian climber after she competed without a hijab. The worries about her safety tonight. The deadly crash. A plane slamming into a car dealership. The FDA pushing to take a controversial pregnancy drug off the market. Why some doctors and moms say it`s a mistake And the Wikipedia warrior fighting to get some remarkable women the recognition they deserve. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC Nightly News with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. In a year defined by some of the most extreme heat we`ve ever seen, along with one of the strongest hurricanes to hit the U.S. mainland, tonight, making headlines for unseasonable cold and early snow. In the East, autumn interrupted by a sudden and dramatic detour into winter, a climate change whiplash leaving 86 million people currently under freezing alerts from the northern tip of Texas across the south and up into the Northeast. More than 40 record lows possible this evening across 18 states. Several cities in the south could see their earliest freezes on record. Al Roker will lay it out for us in a moment but first let`s go to Maggie Vespa feeling the big chill in Michigan. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MAGGIE VESPA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Less than a month into fall, a frigid blast blanketing swaths of the Midwest in white. Did you have to dig out the winter coats? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We did. We just need to go for a walk tonight. We got to go home. VESPA: And tonight, leaving at 6 million Americans across 25 states under freeze alerts. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`ve never seen anything like this. This is super early. VESPA: In particular, parts of northern Michigan and Wisconsin slammed with more than a foot of snow. Whitecaps crashing on the Great Lakes. The storm knocking out power for thousands and closing schools. It`s paralyzing impact stretching into Illinois and Indiana where roads today were impassable. Snow falling as far south as Kentucky and Tennessee. The system`s powerful punch landing more than two months before the official start of winter. East of the Rockies, temperatures are 10 to 25 degrees below average. Even seasoned locals shutter. And is it a birthday gift or is it a problem. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It`s a problem. VESPA: Countless families forced to crank the heat just as heating bills are expected to hit a 10-year high, leaving some left to wonder whether this unseasonably severe cold snap is a sign of brutal winter weather to come. Is any part of this painful given that we`re like mid-October? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It`s going to be a long winter. A really long winter starting this early. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And Maggie joining me now. I know the timing of this story made the impact much worse. VESPA (on camera): Yes, Lester, that`s right. Here in the Upper Peninsula where you can see snow is still falling, utility crews are reportedly finding a lot of downed trees that hadn`t shed their leaves yet, meaning they were likely toppled by snow because this early in fall, they`re that much heavier. Lester? HOLT: Maggie Vesper, thank you. Let`s get right to Al Roker who is tracking this cold wave. Al, what can we expect for the rest of the week? AL ROKER, NBC NEWS WEATHER ANCHOR: Lester, we`ve got this storm system over the Great Lakes. It`ll be moving out but probably dump another one to three inches of snow, so that`s out of here. But still here, 86 million of us are going to be under some sort of frost advisories, freeze watch, freeze warning from the plains all the way to northeast, down to the Gulf. We got that Jetstream dipping way down. Records possible in 18 states from Texas, Kansas, on into Kentucky, in the east southeast and down to the Gulf. And then tomorrow, temperatures still below average anywhere from 10 to 15 from Philadelphia, Baton Rouge, St. Louis. Those will start to moderate late this week. And then next week, warmer in the east, colder out west. HOLT: Al, thanks. 21 days before the Midterms, President Biden trying to keep abortion rights front and center, but polls show voters worrying most about the economy and soaring inflation. Peter Alexander reports on the new clashes between candidates in key battlegrounds. [19:05:09] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PETER ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): With just three weeks until the Midterms and Republicans slamming Democrats over the economy and record inflation, President Biden tonight trying to amplify the politically divisive issue of abortion rights, urging voters to keep Democrats in control of Congress. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Here`s the promise I make to you and the American people. The first bill that I will send to the Congress will be to codify Roe v. Wade. ALEXANDER: But some Democrats fear the potency of that message may be waning. Tonight, a new poll shows 44 percent of likely voters cite the economy or inflation as the number one problem facing the country while just five percent list abortion as their top issue. And now, Republicans have a four-point lead when voters are asked which party`s candidate they`d support. In Ohio, one of several crucial races that`ll determine control of the Senate. Republican candidate J.D. Vance hammered Democrat Tim Ryan over skyrocketing prices in a heated final debate. J.D. VANCE (R-OH) SENATE CANDIDATE: That rising energy price that people see at the pump, that they see in the utility bills, that was the direct result of policies enacted by Joe Biden and Nancy Pelosi and supported 100 percent by Tim Ryan . ALEXANDER: While Ryan slammed Vance for embracing former President Trump. REP. TIM RYAN (D-OH): You were calling Trump America`s Hitler. Then he kissed his ass -- VANCE: It`s not true. ALEXANDER: There are critical governor`s races too in the battlegrounds of Arizona and Michigan and a rematch in Georgia between Republican Governor Brian Kemp and Democrat Stacey Abrams . And this is a governor who for the last four years has beat his chest but delivered very little for most Georgians. ALEXANDER: Kemp touting his early moves to reopen the state during the pandemic and going after Abrams. GOV. BRIAN KEMP (R-GA): Miss Abrams is going to lie out my record because she doesn`t want to talk about her own. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Peter, President Biden is going to pivot to the economy tomorrow focusing on high gas prices. ALEXANDER (on camera): Yes, Lester, that`s right. Looking to lower those prices, the President is going to announce that the administration will move forward with the release of as many as 15 million additional barrels of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It`s a controversial move that comes amid Russia`s war in Ukraine and after Saudi Arabia snub the President`s request to boost oil production. Lester? HOLT: Peter Alexander at the White House, thank you. There`s breaking news and a trial involving a murder they went unsolved for 25 years. A California man convicted late today for killing Kristin Smart, a college student who disappeared in 1996. Paul Flores, a former classmate of Smart`s wasn`t arrested for the crime until last year. Flores` father who was accused of helping move Smart`s body was found not guilty. Smart`s remains were never found. Worldwide concern tonight about what will happen to a celebrated female athlete from Iran who competed without a headscarf as the country deals with unprecedented anti-government protests driven by women. Andrea Mitchell has the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF FOREIGN AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, another Iranian woman in the spotlight. Elnaz Rekabi, a 33-year- old elite rock climber, the first female athlete on an Iranian team known to have competed without her country`s mandatory headscarf or hijab. During international competition in South Korea, Rekabi`s long hair flowing uncovered, prompted concerns for her safety. Hours later, a post on her Instagram account read, I encountered a problem with my cover during the final. Adding, she was returning to Iran with her team as planned. The circumstances under which it was posted remain unclear. Human rights activists are worried about her fate and around where women and girls have been beaten and jailed for not following the dress code. What are your concerns about the fate of the woman climber who took off the hijab in competition in South Korea? NAZANIN BONIADI, IRANIAN-BORN ACTRESS AND ACTIVIST: We`re very concerned that she`s going to end up in solitary confinement and be tortured into making a false confession. And we need to internationally stand up for her. MITCHELL: U.S. leaders are voicing support. What can America do to stand by the women of Iran? REP. NANCY PELOSI (D-CA): Well, we can make sure everyone is paying attention to it. This is organic. It`s initiated by the women, and we should all take great pride in that. And these women in Iran are just so remarkable. MITCHELL: Tonight, the resistance in the face of the regime`s furious crackdown undiminished. Andrea Mitchell, NBC News Washington. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: A building materials company that operates across the U.S. agreed to plead guilty today to supporting terrorists who killed Americans. Officials say it`s the first U.S. prosecute mission of a company for supporting terrorism. Here`s Justice Correspondent Ken Dilanian. [19:10:06] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEN DILANIAN, NBC NEWS JUSTICE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): One of the world`s largest corporations admitting tonight it funneled millions of dollars to ISIS. LISA MONACO, U.S. DEPUTY ATTORNEY GENERAL; Corporate crime that has reached a new low and a very dark place. DILANIAN: French cement company Lafarge , which operates plants in dozens of countries and 43 U.S. states pleading guilty to paying terrorists in Syria between 2013 and 2014 so it could keep a cement plant running as ISIS and other groups fought for control. Payments made at the same time the terror group was capturing and beheading U.S. hostages, including James Foley and Steven Sotloff. Prosecutors say the company sent ISIS and the al-Qaeda-linked Nusra Front more than $10 million, then tried to cover it up. BREON PEACE, U.S. ATTORNEY, NEW YORK EASTERN DISTRICT: Lafarge made a deal with the devil, foreign terrorists who pledged to in fact did harm the United States, its people, and its national security. DILANIAN: The company agreed to pay a settlement of nearly $800 million to the U.S. government . French authorities in 2018 charged eight former Lafarge executives with financing terrorism. The company now owned by a Swiss firm said today it deeply regretted what happened, adding that the executives involved no longer work there and that none of the conduct involve us employees. (END VIDEOTAPE) DILANIAN (on camera): In a disturbing twist, court documents show Lafarge was doing business with ISIS and al-Qaeda at the same time, its concrete was being used to build One World Trade Center on the site where terrorists destroyed the Twin Towers in 2001. President Zelenskyy warning today that 30 percent of Ukraine`s power stations had been destroyed, causing massive blackouts. New airstrikes today left hundreds of thousands of people without power or water. Concern is growing as cold weather sets in. Now to our reporting from inside Russia and the impact of President Putin`s partial draft. We`ve seen the traffic jams of young men fleeing the country to avoid it. Keir Simmons with some who have left. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS SENIOR INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, as Russia`s President Putin attempts to force Ukrainians into capitulation with deadly drone strikes, he`s under pressure at home with many Russian men deciding to leave. We traveled to Kazakhstan to meet some of the thousands who came here to escape the partial draft. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I don`t want to kill people. I don`t want to die. SIMMONS : With their possessions on their back, these men not wanting their faces on camera. This is the bag that you left Russia with? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes. SIMMONS : Just this? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes. SIMMONS: Dimitri, not his real name, is homeless and heartbroken. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I feel very sad about it because I feel a connection with my motherland. SIMMONS : You love your country. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Of course. Of course, I love -- I love Russia. SIMMONS : We met a group of Russian artists putting on street performances as a thank-you to the people of Kazakhstan for welcoming them. Alexander`s friend got his draft papers, and they decided to leave that same day, just grab anything they could. And what happened on the border? We flew, then found a car, he says. But there was 10 miles of traffic at the border. So, we walked. No longer facing life on the front line, but their lives changed forever. What do you see in the future? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I can tell you nothing about my future because I see like only in two weeks. SIMMONS: Back in Russia, the only independent pollster here tells us support for President Putin remains strong but the partial mobilization is having an impact. DENIS, VOLKOV, DIRECTOR, LEVADA POLLING CENTER: More than half our population feel anxious about it. SIMMONS : What are they anxious about that? VOLKOV: That the husbands, sons, might be recruited. (END VIDEOTAPE) SIMMONS : The Kremlin says the partial draft will soon be over with 300,000 enlisted. But ultimately, it`s President Putin`s decision. Lester?
