(BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): For Americans earning reward points for every gallon of gas, rental car, airline ticket, and cup of coffee, loyalty may not be worth what it once was, as companies rewrite their reward rules, often requiring more purchases, not fewer. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m very disappointed in Dunkin. COSTELLO: Dunkin Donuts has faced a social media backlash after raising the cost of earning a free cup of coffee from $40 to $50 and doing away with free birthday drinks. There is drama in the Dunkin world right now tweeted one customer. I no longer run on Dunkin. But Dunkin says its revamped program gives customers more options and a wider variety of food and beverages. Chipotle is also requiring more purchases to earn a free burrito. P.F. Chang`s now offers extra reward points for a monthly fee. As inflation drives up restaurant costs, forcing many to trim expenses. R.J. HOTTOVY, HEAD OF FINANCIAL RESEARCH, PLACER.AI: We`ve seen from Chipotle. We`ve seen it from Dunkin. We`ve -- probably we`ll see it for many others before we`re all set and done. COSTELLO: For many customers, the points make the difference. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes, big difference. They save -- they save a lot of people a lot of money. COSTELLO: Meanwhile, you can now earn a mile on Delta Airlines for each dollar you spend at Starbucks , just as Delta will require passengers to spend more on tickets to earn top tier status and free upgrades. The advice if you`ve been gathering points -- TED ROSSMAN, SENIOR INDUSTRY ANALYST, BANKRATE: You don`t want to hoard these just for hoarding sake. You want to earn and burn strategically. COSTELLO: Use them or lose them. Tom Costello, NBC News, Washington. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Up next, a terrifying scene. The deadly plane crash slamming into a car dealership. And the controversy over a drug meant to prevent premature births. Why the FDA wants to pull it. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: Fiery images out of Ohio today when a small plane crash into a car dealership parking lot in Marietta. Investigators say the pilot and a passenger were both killed when the plane went down about 30 minutes after takeoff from Columbus. No injuries were reported on the ground. Also, tonight, the battle over a controversial pregnancy drug. The FDA wants to take it off the market but some doctors and moms say it`s a lifesaver for babies born prematurely. We get more now from Ann Thompson. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANNE THOMPSON, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): They are the littlest Americans. Nearly 400,000 children born prematurely each year, 10 percent of all births, 14 percent in the African American community. Tony Blake delivered her first two children at 28 and 32 weeks. TONY BLAKE, MOTHER OF PREMATURE BABIES: I didn`t want another kid in the NICU. Like you just don`t want that because you want to have that bonding time. THOMPSON: So, her doctor prescribed McKenna for her third pregnancy, a synthetic version of the hormone progesterone. She carried her daughter Rain to 33 weeks. BLAKE: It helped me to not actually go into labor. THOMPSON: Now the FDA wants to pull McKenna from the market saying trials show Tony story is the exception, not the rule. DR. PATRIZIA CAVAZZONI, DIRECTOR, FDA CENTER FOR DRUG EVALUATION AND RESEARCH: Based on the evidence available today, McKenna is not shown to be effective. Its benefit-risk profile is unfavorable, and it shouldn`t be withdrawn from the market. THOMPSON: Once fast track for approval, regulators say, along with no benefits, there are risks to mothers, including blood clots and depression. But Dr. Kristin Lyerly wants to keep prescribing McKenna to her patients. DR. KRISTIN LYERLY, OB/GYN: Why not leave it on the market while we are investigating further? Because the potential to reduce preterm birth has an incredible impact on patients and their families for their entire lives. THOMPSON: Especially, she says, for African American moms with higher rates of premature birth. Others disagree. Is there any evidence that African American women benefit from this drug? DR. MICHAEL CAROME , DIRECTOR, PUBLIC CITIZEN HEALTH RESEARCH GROUP: The available evidence based upon data reviewed by the FDA doesn`t support that the drug is effective for those patients. THOMPSON: McKenna`s manufacturer says the drug should be kept on the market while additional study is undertaken. The advisory committee will vote tomorrow, but the final decision is still months away. Anne Thompson, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Up next, raising the profiles of women and minority scientists. Her mission to tell their stories. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Millions turn to Wikipedia for answers but as Stephanie Gosk reports, when one physicist noted there were few entries on women and minorities in science, she got writing. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) STEPHANIE GOSK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): From the Boxer Rebellion to the history of the banana. Wikipedia has instant information on everything. At least that`s what British physicists Jess Wade believed until she noticed a gaping hole in the online encyclopedia`s content. JESS WADE, BRITISH PHYSICISTS: Women is so underrepresented, and people of color are so underrepresented. GOSK: And then, the 33-year-old got to work. How many entries do you have in Wikipedia? WADE: 1757 or 1756, but who`s counting? GOSK: She`s dedicated on top of a day job spent in the lab. WADE: I get home, I have my dinner, and I have my designated Wikipedia time where I just kind of research and then write and then read and then edit and then write some more. GOSK: Writing bios on women like Gladys West. WADE: She was born in Virginia in 1930. She went to a historically black College and university. She studied Math. She became a math teacher at high school and then she worked for the U.S. government on GPS. GOSK: Jess Wade plucked her story out of forgotten history, leading to West`s 2018 induction into the U.S. Air Force Hall of Fame. It`s nice to think that you were able to give her just a little bit of nudge. WADE: Like, I don`t -- I didn`t do anything, right? She`s the magic. I just -- I`m just that person who just kind of taps it closer to the goal line, and then she shoots, and she scores. GOSK: Wade says society is doing better getting young women interested in math and science but it`s not enough. WADE: We`re not doing enough to retain them in the system. And part of that is because we`re not celebrating them. GOSK: Now, with her help, everyone can type in a search and give a round of applause. Stephanie Goss, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Tuesday. Thank you for watching. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. headline: TODAY for October 18, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. It`s Tuesday. Hope you have those winter coats handy. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes, and in several cities, they`re already breaking out the snow shovels. It is October 18th. And this is Today. Deep freeze, nearly 100 million people waking up to brutally cold temperatures from Colorado to New England all the way down to Florida, some places in between coping with the earliest snowfall in years. It`s going to be a long winter. We are alive where the flakes are falling and Al will have your full forecast. Breaking overnight, cities across Ukraine facing a new barrage of Russian airstrikes, this time, cutting power and water supplies to tens of thousands of civilians, the very latest in a live report from the front lines. Growing concern, an Iranian athlete in the international spotlight after competing in a high profile event without her hijab, so was it a show of support for women protesting on the streets back home, her new message overnight and what she`s facing as she returns to Tehran. Three weeks to go, with the midterms fast approaching candidates from coast to coast clashing in closely watched debates overnight, just ahead, we will break down the key races where they stand and the biggest issues on the minds of voters. All that, plus, burgers, tacos, fries, oh my, those sky high prices now hitting a staple for millions of Americans, fast food, what you need to know and how to save on your next meal. And just for kicks, the Los Angeles Chargers use a big Monday night rally to collect your field goal. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The kick is good. And the Chargers win it in overtime. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: And knock off the Denver Broncos in a nail biter, today Tuesday, October 18th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Well, good morning. Good to see you. It`s a Tuesday morning. We`re so happy that you`re with us. GUTHRIE: Oh, yes, and burr, that cold snap affecting much of the country, we started talking about it yesterday. Well today, it`s here. KOTB: More specifically it is here. The snow really whipping up this morning in northern Michigan near the shores of Lake Superior and while it may not be snowing where you live, the chances are it is getting cold. GUTHRIE: Yes nearly 100 million Americans under frost and freeze warnings this morning with that winter like weather extending from Colorado all the way up and down the East Coast. KOTB: And that early Cold is a cause for concern for many Americans who are already bracing for higher heating costs. Al is standing by. He`s got his forecast. But first, NBC`s Maggie Vespa joins us now from a snowy Michigan. Maggie, we can`t believe what we`re seeing in there. MAGGIE VESPA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: I know guys, good morning. This is crazy, right? You wouldn`t know it based on this snow globe of a live shot. But we are less than a month into fall right now. And obviously this looks like a winter wake up. And to be clear, we`re in the Negaunee, Michigan like Upper Peninsula Michigan, so a dusting of snow this time of year is not unusual. But look at our handy dandy tape measure. Here in Negaunee, we`re at roughly eight inches and counting. And again, this chill is not just affecting the Midwest, this cold snap is stretching all the way to Florida. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) VESPA (voice-over): Overnight, fall quickly turning to winter in the Midwest. (on camera): Is a part of this painful given that we`re like mid-October? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It`s going to be a long winter. VESPA (voice-over): And early season storm dumping more than a foot of snow in northern Wisconsin and Michigan. And making for a treacherous drive in Indiana. The weight of the heavy snow knocking out power to tens of thousands, Monday, and causing trouble for plows. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We have hard times for our plows to get through because the trees are hanging over the roads. VESPA (voice-over): Autumn leaves blanketed in white as Chicago saw its first flurries of the season. The October chill bringing the first freeze of the season to 89 million people this week. Today Kansas City Omaha and dozens of other cities waking up to record breaking cold as low as the teens. Americans forced to crank the heat just as heating bills are expected to hit a 10-year high. The frigid blast arriving nearly a month ahead of schedule and also surging south, sending temperatures tumbling from Tennessee to the Florida Panhandle this week. Alabama and Mississippi set to feel even colder than Boston Wednesday. While in South Carolina farmers are scrambling to harvest before the frost. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It isn`t fun to lose crops. We will harvest what we can and we`ll continue to harvest tomorrow. VESPA (voice-over): A change of season and a taste of winter come early. (on camera): What is it looks like this when your trip trick or treating? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m going to freeze my butt off. (END VIDEOTAPE) [07:05:03] VESPA Yes, guys, the stakes are high. All right so back out here live, again, we have this handy dandy thermometer now. And you can see it`s right around freezing, so just hold it up for the snow to keep piling up. And for reference, by the way, the first day of winter isn`t until December 21st. And for those of you down south, it sounds like you`ll be waking up to your coldest morning tomorrow morning, your coldest temperature is tomorrow morning. The good news is it sounds like you won`t need those jackets for long. Hoda, I`ll send it back to you. KOTB: All right, Maggie Vespa for us, Maggie, thank you. GUTHRIE: She`s got all the gadgets in her tricks. And Al has got even more. AL ROKER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: I know she doesn`t have a big wall like this. GUTHRIE: Yes, come on. ROKER: But we can show you all that snow that`s going to be coming in and it`s going to be hanging around a bit. We`re going to talk about that later. But let`s get to that cold. As you can see stretching from the Rockies all the way to the northeast down to Mobile, Alabama, almost 90 million people impacted by frost advisories, freeze watches and warnings. Right now it`s 22 in Des Moines, 39 in Cincinnati, Fort Smith, Arkansas at 40 degrees, Pittsburgh 38. The Jetstream dips down to the south the eastern half of the country. Out west, they`ve got some record warmth in the Pacific Northwest. But for this afternoon, only 46 in Detroit, that`s 14 degrees below average, Memphis 53, 20 degrees cooler than average, Knoxville 50, that`s 10 degrees cooler. And then tomorrow morning, we look for possible records in Raleigh Savannah, Knoxville, Tupelo, Little Rock Tulsa, on into Austin and Baton Rouge. However, we will see temperatures start to temper just a bit as we move toward the end of the week by Friday at 60 in New York City, 68 in Cincinnati on Friday, Memphis will be 77. And by next week, we`re going to flip the script, out west colder than average. And here in the east, it`s going to be warmer than average. So just hang in there. Good news is coming guys. GUTHRIE: Yes. KOTB: Cool. All right, Al, thank you. Breaking overnight, a new wave of attacks across Ukraine, explosions have been felt across the capital of Kyiv and other cities, even as the death toll rises from yesterday`s barrage of Russian strikes. NBC`s chief foreign correspondent Richard Engel has the very latest. Hey, Richard, good morning. RICHARD ENGEL, NBC NEWS CHIEF FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT: Good morning, Hoda. Russia is now attacking Ukrainian cities daily and with impunity. This was the main flower market here in the city of Mykolaiv was hit by a Russian missile overnight. And just down the street, Russia attacked an apartment building killing at least one person according to Ukrainian officials. And Ukrainian say by attacking sites like these that have no military value, Russia is trying to break the Ukrainian spirit. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ENGEL (voice-over): Russia is flattening Ukraine, one market at a time. Death by a thousand cuts. For Irina Shipchenko (ph), whose flower shop was destroyed overnight in Mykolaiv, what Russia is doing is nothing less than state terror. We clean up and continue living. What else can we do and we will win, she says. Over the last two weeks, Russia has intensified attacks on Ukrainian cities, claiming to be destroying the country`s infrastructure and its ability to wage war. But Russia is firing directly on civilians attacking an apartment building overnight in Mykolaiv, too. Officials say Russia launched a guided missile, killing one person. The strikes came hours after an airplane mysteriously crashed in Russia. State media reporting that a pilot on a training mission took off from an occupied part of Ukraine and ejected, the aircraft smashing into a building and killing four Russians. Ukrainians wonder if it was an accident or sabotage from within. President Putin personally dispatched investigators to the scene. Discontent is growing in Russia after the Kremlin imposed the draft, rounding up conscripts across the country. And with precision weapons in short supply, Moscow is increasingly relying on Iranian made dive bomber drones, launching them in swarms at Ukrainian cities including Kyiv with deadly effect. Overnight in his daily address, President Zelenskyy called for more air defenses. Secretary of State Blinken condemned Iran for supplying Russia with weapons. The United States gives Ukraine billions of dollars in military support, but not long range weapons, trying to find a perhaps impossible balance of supporting Ukraine without antagonizing Moscow excessively. In a sign, both sides seemed to recognize this will be a long war. Russia and Ukraine exchanged prisoners 108 Ukrainian women for captured Russian soldiers in a one to one swap. (END VIDEOTAPE) ENGEL: Over the last several days, we`ve been talking a lot about how Russia is using those Iranian made drones. The drones are highly effective. They have a long range but they don`t carry very much explosive power. Certainly not enough to cause damage like this or to dig a crater in the ground anything like this. You see it can even expose the city`s earlier foundation. And President Zelenskyy today commenting on this attack says it is more evidence why his country needs better air defenses. And he wants Russia to be held accountable. Hold? [07:10:14] KOTB: All right, Richard Engel for us there in Ukraine. Richard, thank you. GUTHRIE: There is international concern this morning for the safety of an Iranian athlete after she represented her country in a recent climbing competition without wearing the customary hijab. NBC`s Meagan Fitzgerald has that story for us this morning. Meagan, good morning. MEAGAN FITZGERALD, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Savannah, good morning. Elnaz Rekabi competed on Sunday with what appeared to be a headband her hair uncovered which is a violation of Iran strict dress code. Now this morning, an apology on her Instagram page, but there`s still growing concern for her safety. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) FITZGERALD (voice-over): This morning, concerns for a young female Iranian athlete after she competed without wearing a hijab. Elnaz Rekabi, a prominent rock climber, took part in a competition in South Korea this weekend, notably climbing with her head uncovered. In the past, Rekabi has worn the traditional headscarf while climbing. The hijab has been a focus of recent extraordinary protests in Iran, sparked by the death of 22-year- old Mahsa Amini who was detained by the morality police for breaching the dress code. She died three days later. Women across Iran have protested by cutting their hair and appearing in public with their heads uncovered. After the appearance in South Korea, Rekabi is headed home. The Iranian embassy in Seoul tweeting she departed yesterday. Human rights groups have been concerned about pressure she may face from authorities. MAHMOOD AMIRY-MOGHADDAM, DIRECTOR OF NGO IRAN HUMAN RIGHTS: I think they will put her under tremendous pressure. There is fear of torture, ill treatment, psychological pressure. FITZGERALD (voice-over): Rekabi this morning posting on Instagram that her job had issues before she was called to climb. Now back in Iran, the regime has been under pressure as protests led by young women continue, many watching Rekabi`s returned to the country with concern. And let`s start right there with the issues that voters say matter to them. And what that`s telling us about what might happen here and these elections. So you see the momentum in these final weeks. Let`s talk about the issue of crime, not high on the list of voters concerns and yet it seems to be making an impact in certain races. KORNACKI: It`s fascinating because we showed you the top issue voters have, crime doesn`t rate high there, doesn`t mean it`s not on their mind. So let`s show you a place where I think it is having an impact. This is Wisconsin, one of the key Senate races, Ron Johnson to term Republican incumbent. He leads in the polling average over his Democratic challenger. Now Johnson has been leaning heavily on crime. [07:15:00] Interesting poll that came out of Wisconsin this week they asked things a little bit differently. They basically asked, are these issues important to you? That`s what`s being asked here. Inflation tops the list. But look at crime. It`s close to 90 percent. And I think also striking, abortion is under 80 percent. Republicans running heavily on crime, Democrats running heavily on abortion, and it looks like in this Wisconsin race, crime may have more resonance than abortion does. GUTHRIE: Making a big difference in Pennsylvania Senate race as well, it appears. But let`s talk about Georgia, because it may just be Georgia, Georgia, Georgia to quote our friend Tim Russert. If nobody gets 50 percent and here`s that Senate race, Raphael Warnock , Herschel Walker , Warnock leading but nobody had 50. If nobody cracks 50, it`s a December 6th runoff, could have control of the Senate on the line. They did have a debate last Friday. We`re waiting to get a readout from some polls haven`t really seen it yet if that change anything there. GUTHRIE: Real quickly, the governor`s race is interesting because it doesn`t look like people are at least telling pollsters they`re going to vote straight down party lines. KORNACKI: We thought this type of voter was extinct, the split ticket voter. What pollsters say they`re seeing here is there`s a suburban voter outside Atlanta who doesn`t like Biden, doesn`t like the Democrats but also doesn`t like Donald Trump . And, you know, Brian Kemp went to political war with Donald Trump and he survived in that voters eyes. Kemp`s OK. Walker`s got some convincing to do. story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good Thursday morning from Washington and New York. Our top story, all eyes once again on Ukraine. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Tension there building after new attacks and new threats. It is October 20th. This is Today. Leave immediately, this morning, thousands of residents in southern Ukraine being forced to flee their own homes. Mass evacuations underway after a warning of imminent attacks and martial law declared by Vladimir Putin . And this morning, mounting concern over power outages ahead of a harsh winter, we`ll have the very latest and a live report straight ahead. On the road, President Biden hits the campaign trail today in the closely watched battleground of Pennsylvania. Can he move the needle for the undecided voters with less than three weeks to go? Feeling the freeze, another day of bitter cold across much of the country, parts of the south waking up two record lows, but Al says, hang in there, a big warm ups on the way. They`ll have your full forecast. Consumer alert, the new warning from police after a string of robberies in cities across the country tied to popular online marketplaces. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CMDR. RODNEY G. HILL, CHICAGO POLICE DEPARTMENT ENGLEWOOD DISTRICT: Nine times out of 10, if you see a deal that is too good to be true, it is. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: This morning what you need to know before you click. Those stories, plus, "The Crown" and the controversy. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It is with regret, the Prince and Princess of Wales are separating. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: The growing backlash against the hit show`s upcoming storyline. Why an Oscar winner wants it to come with a disclaimer and how "The Crown`s" creator is responding. And smash hit. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: At the wall looking up, see you later. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: The Astros defeat the Yankees in game one of the ALCS while the Padres rally to tie up their series with the Phillies in a game for the record books. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Aaron Nola against Austin Nola, little brother against big brother. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: The battle of the brothers going down in history, today, Thursday, October 20th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie live from Washington, D.C. and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Well good morning. Good to see you. So happy you`re joining us on a Thursday morning. Savannah is joining us in D.C. And SG, can you imagine being the mom and dad you`re like, I`m cheering for both my sons. You go, no you go. It`s got to be a tough one. GUTHRIE: I know. Yes, moms are always like, no, I don`t have a favorite. No really, I don`t. Well, a lot more of those highlights in just a bit. Plus nearly two thirds of the country waking up to another morning of bitter cold, I know you`re feeling it there in New York, here Washington too. Record low temps expected in the south today. Al is tracking it and he has some good news on when it`ll feel a little more like fall. KOTB: But we are going to start this morning in Ukraine where new evacuations are being ordered. It comes as residents are being told to charge their devices after drone strikes knocked out key power stations, rolling blackouts now common. And this is just as the brutal Ukraine winter is approaching. NBC`s Cal Perry is in Ukraine for us. Cal, good morning. Give us the latest. CAL PERRY, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Hey, good morning to you, Hoda. Fresh strikes overnight, the target once again that vital energy infrastructure of Ukraine. It is what has prompted the mayor here to tell people turn off your electricity, save power. All the while as you mentioned, the bitter cold from the winter has arrived, the temperatures plunging overnight, all the while the strikes continue across Ukrainian cities. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PERRY (voice-over): This morning, the people of Kherson are caught in the middle. Thousands in the port city that has been under Russian occupation for months, now being ordered to evacuate by Russian installed leaders. Some getting text messages that read, dear residents, evacuate immediately. There will be shelling of residential areas by the armed forces of Ukraine. We`ll see that change later in the week. For the day, today, sunny and warm out west, easing chilly conditions here in the East, sunshine from the plains down to Texas.
