headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for October 25, 2022, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the chilling new details of the deadly shooting at a St. Louis High School. (voiceover): Investigators revealing today the 19-year-old gunman had an AR-15-style rifle and 600 rounds of ammunition. That disturbing handwritten note he left behind. What we`re learning about the victims, the stories of survival, and what police a prevented even more bloodshed. Also, tonight the spike in children hospitalized with RSV as flu season ramps up and President Biden getting his Omicron booster. His warning to Americans ahead of another potential winter COVID surge. WNBA star Brittney Griner losing her appeal in a Russian court. Where does that leave negotiations for a prisoner swap? What the White House is saying? Just two weeks until the Midterms and the high stakes showdown tonight in Pennsylvania. Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz facing off in their first and only debate with control of the Senate on the line. Adidas dropping its deal with Kanye West after his antisemitic comments caused a firestorm. NBC News investigates the breast cancer diagnoses missed in more than two dozen women. How did it happen? And the mission to rescue tourists stranded in the Grand Canyon Caverns 200 feet underground. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. We will never know exactly how much higher the death toll would have been in yesterday`s school shooting in St. Louis had police not killed the attacker. But today, there is chilling new evidence the 19-year-old killer intended it to be a bloodbath. Today, police revealing the gunman used an AR-15-style rifle to shoot his victims. A teacher and a student were both killed, four others were wounded. In addition, three people were injured during the chaos at Central Visual and Performing Arts High School. Authorities also saying the shooter, a former student, was carrying 600 rounds of ammunition. But the most revealing evidence may be what police say they found in his car, entries in a notebook that may offer a disturbing roadmap into his state of mind. Emilie Ikeda is in St. Louis tonight with new details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) EMILIE IKEDA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, a trove of evidence shedding light on what may have driven a 19-year-old to storm his alma mater, gunning down a sophomore and teacher and injuring at least seven. Investigators discovering a letter in the suspect`s car parked outside Central Visual and Performing Arts High School. MICHAEL SACK, INTERIM CHIEF, ST. LOUIS METROPOLITAN POLICE DEPARTMENT: He spoke about his desire to engage in this incident to conduct the school shooting. IKEDA: The handwritten note reads in part, "I don`t have any friends. I don`t have any family. I`ve never had a girlfriend. I`ve never had a social life. I`ve been an isolated loner my entire life. This was the perfect storm for a mass shooter." A mass shooter that claimed the lives of beloved health and physical education teacher Jean Kuczka and sophomore Alexandria Bell. The student`s father calling her death a nightmare. ANDRE BELL, FATHER OF ALEXANDRIA BELL: No matter how I felt, I can talk to her and it was -- it was alright. That was my baby. IKEDA: Armed with an AR 15 style weapon and 600 rounds of ammunition, police say the suspect Orlando Harris` shooting rampage could have been even worse. SACK: Oh, this could have been a horrific scene. It was not by the grace of God and that the officers were as close as they were. IKEDA: Officers who already happened to be in the area for another event, said they arrived on scene within five minutes of the first 911 call, and made it to the government on the third floor within another eight minutes. The suspect shot dead. Police would not say how the team broke into the school or obtained a long gun plus a stockpile of ammunition. When you got there, what did you see? MICHAEL BISHOP, STUDENT PARENT: It was chaos. IKEDA: Student parent Michael Bishop applauds the police`s rapid response, but knows the trauma will follow his daughter and her classmates. BISHOP: She`s going to second guess going into any school, any building with people for who knows how long and it`s heartbreaking. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Emilie, there`s going to be a lot of looking back at this point. Were there any red flags in the gunman`s history? IKEDA (on camera): Lester, police say the suspect did not have a criminal history but may have been suffering from a mental illness. Law enforcement underscoring the importance of see something, say something, encouraging people to speak up if someone makes concerning comments or is struggling. Tonight, a community still in shock as school officials say that it may be weeks before students can return for in person instruction here. Lester? HOLT: OK, Emilie, thank you. Tonight, pediatric emergency rooms around the country say they are beyond capacity because of that surge in children with respiratory viruses including RSV. It comes as they deal with COVID and flu as well. Here`s Tom Costello. [19:05:16] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In Northern Virginia, the respiratory virus known as RSV has made its way into 4-year-old Nova Louis`s lungs. How are you feeling? NOVA LOUIS, HAS RSV: Sick. COSTELLO: Struggling to breathe with an existing heart condition, her mom rushed her to the ER this morning. SUMMER LOUIS, MOTHER OF NOVA: It`s very troubling and worrisome because everyone`s getting sick, and she just had COVID this summer for the first time. COSTELLO: The medical director at the Inova Children`s ER says they`re in crisis mode. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Three days of fever and cough congestion. COSTELLO: Overwhelmed like many hospitals with a dangerous viral tripledemic. The start of the flu season, the ongoing COVID threat, and RSV infecting large numbers of children who spent much of the pandemic isolated and virus free bubbles. Already, this children`s er has broken its yearly record for treating patients./ DR. RICK PLACE, PEDIATRIC MEDICAL DIRECTOR, INOVA L.J. MURPHY CHILDREN`S HOSPITAL: We`ll have 70 patients in the department at any one time in the evenings. COSTELLO: With just 21 beds. PLACE: With 21 beds. COSTELLO: It`s not unique to this hospital. Nationwide, 73 percent of pediatric inpatient beds are full right now. Here in Virginia, 76 percent. Many hospitals are now out of pediatric ER beds. PLACE: Not only are there a lot of sick kids right now, there`s no place for them to go. COSTELLO: Meanwhile, the country is still averaging 367 COVID deaths per day, but only 8.5 percent of Americans have received updated COVID boosters to cover the latest variants. Today, President Biden received his new COVID Booster while urging Americans to get both flu and COVID boosters by Halloween. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Your old vaccine or your previous COVID infection will not give you maximum protection. (END VIDEOTAPE) COSTELLO (on camera): Here at Inova, they`ve now moved to an emergency operation status and they`ve added this tent outside because if the patient count continues to grow at this pace, they`ll be forced to move triage outside. Lester? HOLT: All right, Tom Costello, thank you. A court in Moscow today rejected WNBA star Brittney Griner`s appeal, meaning she will face a possible eight more years in prison for drug possession. Andrea Mitchell has the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF FOREIGN AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Brittney Griner today appearing via video link from behind bars, pleading for leniency against long odds. BRITNEY GRINER, WNBA PLAYER: This has been very traumatic experience waiting for this day. I just beg that the court takes in all the states that were overlooked during the first court and reassess my sentence here. MITCHELL: But the judge has quickly ruled she must serve another eight years for smuggling less than a gram of cannabis, worse than she`d feared. MARIA BLAGOVOLINA, ATTORNEY FOR BRITTNEY GRINER: I think Brittany herself is quite -- is quite pessimist about the outcome. MITCHELL: Griner`s former Olympic coach after seeing her today. DAWN STALEY, BRITTNEY GRINER`S FORMER OLYMPIC COACH: You hear the hopelessness in her voice. You know you hear her trying to be strong, probably trying to be strong for her wife, Cherelle, and her family. MITCHELL: On Griner`s 32nd birthday last week, she wrote from her cell, "Thank you everyone for fighting so hard to get me home." Secretary of State Blinken now tweeting, "Today`s result is another failure of justice compounding the injustice of her detention." Her agent calling Griner, "A hostage, a political pawn." Her last hope, a prisoner swap. President Biden tonight saying they`re in constant contact with the Russians. BIDEN: So far, we have not been meeting with much positive response, but we`re not stopping. (END VIDEOTAPE) MITCHELL (on camera): The President could make the case to Vladimir Putin at next month`s G-20 hopefully before Grindr is sent to one of Russia`s notorious penal colonies. Lester? HOLT: Andrea Mitchell tonight, thank you. Just two weeks until the Midterms, and tonight, the only debate in that crucial Senate race in Pennsylvania, as our new poll shows Republicans gaining momentum nationwide. Kristen Welker has late details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, just hours before the critical one and only debate, Pennsylvania Democratic Senate Candidate John Fetterman`s campaign, with a striking attempt to lower expectations, declaring Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz has a huge built-in advantage saying, Fetterman is dealing with a lingering audio processing challenge after his stroke in May. And writing Fetterman is going to win this race, even if he doesn`t win the debate. Tonight`s debate is unprecedented with Fetterman requesting closed captioning monitors like the ones he used in an interview with NBC News. Fetterman with this explanation over the weekend. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: It`s the elephant in the room having a stroke. There`s a monitor right now using captioning so I can fully, you know, understand everything in terms of from hearing. WELKER: The debate comes as Dr. Oz has been gaining in the polls. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: The debate we`re having tomorrow night is going to reinforce John Fetterman`s radical positions. [19:10:03] WELKER: Our latest NBC News poll showing Republicans with momentum to him in their fight to take back control of Congress. 71 percent of Americans now saying the country is on the wrong track, and Republicans leading in congressional preference among likely voters, 48 percent to 47 percent. Republicans with a nine-point enthusiasm edge. While in Florida, a fiery debate between Republican Governor Ron DeSantis and Democrat Charlie Crist . Chris pressing DeSantis who is seen as a likely presidential contender. CHARLIE CRIST (D-FL), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: Will you serve a full four- year term if you`re re-elected governor of Florida? It`s not a tough question. GOV. RON DESANTIS (R-FL): Well, listen, I know that Charlie is interested in talking about 2024 and Joe Biden , but I just want to make things very, very clear. The only worn-out old donkey I`m looking to put out to pasture is Charlie Chris. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Kristen, you mentioned veterans challenges. Dr. Oz also faces challenges tonight. WELKER: That`s right, Lester. After Dr. Oz`s campaign was criticized for attacking Fetterman`s health, there will be a lot of scrutiny on his tone. Plus, he`ll have to answer those charges that he`s a celebrity candidate who`s not from Pennsylvania. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker in our Washington studio, thank you. Tonight, we look at the essential role of poll workers who help voters get their ballots they find themselves under increasing pressure and in some cases are deciding to quit. Blayne Alexander reports in our series "POWER OF THE VOTE." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Angie Jones never thought she would become a poll worker. ANGIE JONES, POLL WORKER: I voted, you know, as most Americans do, but I`ve never really been involved in the political process. ALEXANDER: But the 2016 election changed all of that. JONES: After that election happened, that I needed to be part of the solution. ALEXANDER: Her solution, training to become a poll manager in Fulton County, Georgia. People who come to your polls and say, I don`t trust this process. What do you want them to know about the work that you do? JONES: Well, first of all, come join us. Take the training. If people would understand the process more, I feel like they would be less fearful that their votes are not secure. ALEXANDER: Angie has worked every election since 2018, but none like Georgia`s 2021 runoff that gave Democrats control of the Senate. After the 2020 election, did you notice a change? JONES: Immediately I noticed a change. I had a lot of voters that came in angry, distrustful. ALEXANDER: And election workers were increasingly targeted by conspiracy theories like Shaye Moss and her mother Ruby Freeman, who also worked in Fulton County. SHAYE MOSS, FULTON COUNTY POLL WORKER: It turned my life upside down. ALEXANDER: According to the Brennan Center for Justice, one in five election workers say they are unlikely to serve through 2024. One in six have personally experienced threats. Angie says she will never forget asking a friend to sign up. JONES: She said, no. She was afraid. And I remember she said to me, people will say things to me that they would never say to you. ALEXANDER: Because she`s a woman of color. JONES: Because she`s a woman of color. ALEXANDER: Georgia was at the center of efforts to overturn the 2020 election, something election official Gabriel Sterling called Dangerous. GABRIEL STERLING , CHIEF OPERATING OFFICER, GEORGIA SECRETARY OF STATE: It has all gone too far. All of it. ALEXANDER: Are you concerned that there could be similar threats this time around? STERLING: I`m sure there will be. You got to be aware of it, but you can`t over-prepare for it. ALEXANDER: Do you ever think about just walking away? JONES: No, never. Never. My responsibility is to do everything that I can do within my power at that precinct to protect the vote. ALEXANDER: Blayne Alexander, NBC News, Atlanta. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Shining some light on important work and important people. In 60 seconds, missed cases of breast cancer. The detection delayed in dozens of patients and the hospital at the center of the controversy. Our investigation is next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:15:00] HOLT: There`s no question that mammograms save lives were the early detection of breast cancer, but a review of cases at one hospital showed many cancers were initially missed even though they appeared on the scans. Kristen Dahlgren has our investigation. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN DAHLGREN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Jim and Pat Ratliff had a 54-year love story. JIM RATLIFF, WIFE HAD BREAST CANCER: We were attached at the hip. DAHLGREN: Through ups and downs, including Pat`s breast cancer more than a decade ago, which is why she was so diligent about screening and concern when she noticed changes in her other breast. She had imaging at a nearby hospital, part of NIH Northern Arizona Health Care. And they told her what? RATLIFF: They couldn`t find anything. DAHLGREN: Eventually, Pat saw breast surgeon Beth DuPree. DR. BETH DUPREE, BREAST SURGEON: I literally couldn`t believe what I was seeing. It was screaming cancer. DAHLGREN: Advanced breast cancer. Two years later, Pat was gone. Dr. DuPree had just moved to Sedona to develop a state-of-the-art Breast Center at NIH . Pat was just the first patient she says who came to her with a cancer missed on previous scan. DUPREE: These were misses that are not subtle. DAHLGREN: The hospital has an exclusive contract with Northern Arizona Radiology. DuPree who says she continued to flag misread mammograms push them to hire dedicated breast imagers, including Mike Ulissey who couldn`t believe some of what he says was missed. MIKE ULISSEY, BREAST IMAGER: I said my god, Beth. That`s the size of a tangerine. I don`t understand how they can call it normal. DAHLGREN: The hospital requested the radiology group have those new breast imagers review more than 6000 patients whose scans had initially been read by a particular general radiologist. Ulissey says they found cancer in an additional 25 women. CHRISTIE GALLO, HAD BREAST CANCER: The recommendation was returned to me here. DAHLGREN: Among them Christie Gallo (PH). GALLO: My question was, how can I go from normal to having three tumors in one year? That didn`t make sense to me. DAHLGREN: Dr. DuPree believes the number of patients with missed cancers was much greater than the 25 detected in the review. She made a poster with all of her patients whose diagnoses she says were delayed, hoping to show it to the hospital board. We`re only showing those who gave us permission. It must be hard to look at their faces. DUPREE: It is. DAHLGREN: NBC News obtained an email from one of the breast imagers to the radiology group sent before the review was complete, warning of the gravity of the situation. After the review, there was still concern. ULISSEY: We thought that there were a significant chance that additional patients were in harm`s way. We need to expand our investigation. DAHLGREN: But Dr. Ulissey says the radiology group did not. In his statement to NBC, NIH points out the radiology group is a separate entity and says in part, "The hospital quickly acted to address these concerns. We ensured these mammograms were reread specifically by a team of breast fellowship-trained radiologists, saying very few required any follow-up. And since this review, all mammograms are read by specialized breast radiologists." The hospital`s Chief Counsel spoke on a Zoom with community advisors. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: So, the quality process works. There was an error. We`re humans. Doctors are human. GALLO: They messed up and they don`t want to fess up to it. DAHLGREN: Northern Arizona radiology called the review results well within national standards. In a statement, it says, "All radiologists are board certified and meet all requirements, including those under the Mammography Quality Standards Act. DuPree and three out of four new breast imagers including Dr. Ulissey have now left. NBC News has learned the general radiologist who was the subject of the review is now working in another state. As for Gallo, her cancer is in remission, but she`s not sure the questions will ever go away. GALLO: Maybe if they had caught it sooner, it could have been a just a lumpectomy instead of a whole mastectomy choice, but I didn`t get that choice. DAHLGREN: Kristen Dahlgren, NBC News, Sedona, Arizona. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next for us, late news about today`s earthquake in California. Plus, top brands cut ties after antisemitic comments by music and fashion mogul Kanye West. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: Back with the new troubles for Kanye West. Adidas ended its deal today with the music mogul and designer who now goes by Ye over his recent antisemitic comments. Hours later, Gap said it is immediately removing West`s clothing line from its stores. Forbes reports that without his lucrative Adidas deal, West is no longer a billionaire. Some scary moments in Northern California today when an earthquake struck near San Jose. The quake had a preliminary magnitude of 5.1 according to the U.S. Geological Survey . Seismologists say it`s the biggest quake to hit the Bay Area in more than eight years, but there are no reports of injuries or significant damage. Up next, the dramatic rescue. Tourists trapped hundreds of feet underground at a cavern in Arizona. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally, the tourists stranded 200 feet underground and the mission to rescue them from the depths of the Grand Canyon Caverns. Here`s Miguel Almaguer. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The four-hour rescue unfolded more than 200 feet underground. This narrow and dark elevator shaft the only way up for four tourists trap 21 stories down after the elevator malfunctioned at the base of the Grand Canyon Caverns. FELICIA JIMENEZ, TRAPPED AT THE GRAND CANYON CAVERNS WITH HER FAMILY: That`s when we start realizing like this is real. ALMAGUER: Suddenly stuck, Felicia Jimenez and her family needed help from the local sheriff`s department in Peach Springs Arizona who used manpower and a series of ropes and levers to winch up the stranded from the cavern floor. The steep stairway to the popular tourist attraction not an option for the four older members of Jimenez`s family with mobility issues. JOHN PAXTON, COCONINO COUNTY SHERIFF`S OFFICE: If you can picture a fire escape on the side of a tall building, you know, like I think -- we think of New York, and you`d have to do that for 21 floors. JIMENEZ: We`ve all agreed on this. Grateful for our family members because things could have gone way worse. When they got hoisted out, somebody could have fell. ALMAGUER: The stranded stuck for 26 hours did have access to this single hotel suite run by the company who operates inside the cave, but not by choice. JIMENEZ: I just feel a lot of love for my family. It makes you not want to take anything for granted. ALMAGUER: After a 30-minute tour became nearly a 30-hour ordeal, tonight, everyone is back above ground after a rocky start to a deep excursion. Miguel Almaguer, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Quite a drama and quite a rescue. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Tuesday. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2022 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. headline: Herschel Walker Facing A New Allegation Of Paying For An Abortion Of A GOP Senate Candidate Is Responding Tonight
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Let me turn now to Kristen. Kristen, there`s a new headline in that tight Georgia Senate race, an anonymous allegation against Herschel Walker . What do we know? KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, that`s right. This latest allegation comes from an anonymous woman who spoke on Zoom without showing her face in a press conference arranged by Attorney Gloria Allred, an allegation Herschel Walker is strongly denying tonight. Now, the woman claims she had an affair with Walker, the football star turned Republican Senate candidate, and got pregnant nearly 30 years ago. She says Walker pressured and paid for her to have an abortion, but she did not provide any evidence to support those claims. Now, Walker fired back today calling the claims foolishness and a lie, saying his Democratic opponent Senator Raphael Warnock "lost the debate and Democrats will now say anything to win." The woman`s claim comes after another woman accused Walker of paying for her abortion which Walker also strongly denied. The Georgia race is a toss-up that could determine Senate control. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker, thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2022 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. headline: The Fallout From A High Stakes Showdown In Pennsylvania With Control Of Congress Hanging In The Ballots
story_text: [19:00:00] LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the fallout from a high stakes showdown in Pennsylvania with control of Congress hanging in the ballots. (voiceover): Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz facing off in their first and only debate. Fetterman`s health struggles in the spotlight months after he suffered a stroke. Oz under scrutiny for an answer he gave on abortion. The reaction from voters just 13 days before the Midterms. Also, tonight, Herschel Walker facing a new allegation of paying for an abortion of a GOP Senate candidate is responding tonight. The verdict in the trial of a Wisconsin man who killed six people when he plowed his SUV into a Christmas parade. The deadly school shooting in St. Louis. The warning the shooters family gave to police and they`re pleas to take a gun away from him months before the rampage. Vladimir Putin overseeing nuclear drills as Russia pushes unproven dirty bomb allegations against Ukraine. And the American fighter killed in Ukraine two months ago finally on his way back home. Hospitals filling up with children infected with RSV. What parents need to know. The critical shortage in a medication millions used to treat ADHD. And he went from homeless to shooting college hoops. The basketball star inspiring America. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. Just 13 days before the Midterm Elections, and a flood of political ads are saturating the airwaves on the heels of another marquee debate reminding just what is at stake in hard-fought congressional races, power and control of Congress. In the House, Democrats trying to defend their majority with all 435 seats of the body up for election. Dems facing the same challenge in the U.S. Senate with 35 seats are up for election. The balance of power in the Senate could be determined by a handful of tight races, including Pennsylvania where last night`s debate pitted Republican Mehmet Oz against Democrat John Fetterman sparring over abortion, fracking, and immigration. But not before Fetterman call out what he described as the elephant in the room, his health. Dasha Burns starts us off tonight with the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, Pennsylvania Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz back on the campaign trail following last night`s critical one and only face-off. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: Pennsylvania deserves better than Fetterman. BURNS: His opponent, Democrat John Fetterman , not yet making any public appearances after the fierce clash. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: It`s something called the Oz rule that if he`s on TV, he`s lying. OZ: And this is the only debate I could get you to come to talk to me on and I had to beg. BURNS: A debate the Fetterman`s health front and center. Fetterman whose campaign says suffers from auditory processing challenges after a stroke six months ago, requesting these closed captioning monitors in the studio. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke. He`s never let me forget that. And I might miss some words during this debate. Mush two words together, but it knocked me down, but I`m going to keep coming back up. BURNS: Fetterman did miss some words during the hour-long showdown, at times of struggling to answer questions, including this moment. Fetterman was asked about his changing position on fracking, which he now says he supports. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: There is that 2018 interview that you said, "I don`t support fracking at all." So, how do you square the two? FETTERMAN: I do support fracking. And I don`t --I don`t -- I support fracking and I stand -- and I do support fracking. BURNS: Fetterman would not commit to releasing his full medical records. FETTERMAN: My doctor believes that I`m fit to be serving, and that`s what I believe is where I`m standing. BURNS: And in one of the biggest clashes of the night going after Dr. Oz on abortion rights. FETTERMAN: He celebrated when Roe v. Wade went down and my campaign would fight for Roe v. Wade, and if given the opportunity, to codify it into law. BURNS: And tonight, the Fetterman campaign zeroing in on this response from Oz. OZ: I want women, doctors, local political leaders letting the democracy that`s always allowed our nation to thrive to put the best ideas forward so states can decide for themselves. Local political leaders. Local political leaders. BURNS: Turning it into a campaign ad against his opponent. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Oz is too extreme for Pennsylvania. BURNS: But Oz calling Fetterman the extreme candidates throughout the night, especially on the issue of crime. OZ: We have taken away the ability of police to do their job and that son John Fetterman . BURNS: The momentous matchup coming just two weeks before Election Day. Voters with strong reactions about Dr. Oz. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: His comment about political leaders, you know, determining what a woman -- a woman can and cannot do with her body is -- was very telling. [19:05:09] BURNS: And Fetterman. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I just don`t think he`s capable at this time to be in that position. I mean, if you have somebody that can`t even handle a debate that has to, you know, read from this prompter. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And Dasha, some big names could soon be campaigning there on both sides. BURNS (on camera): Yes, Lester. Plans are coming together for both President Biden and former President Obama to campaign with Fetterman, and the Democratic candidate for governor. And former President Trump will campaign with Dr. Oz and the Republican gubernatorial candidate. Lester? HOLT: Dasha Burns, thank you. Let`s bring in Andrea Mitchell and Kristen Welker. Andrea, first to you. What are you hearing there in Pennsylvania about the impact of that debate? ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, Democrats here are telling me that they think Fetterman will be OK, given his labor support and Oz`s missteps on abortion and the minimum wage. But they acknowledge that this format did not work for Fetterman. Republicans say they`re pleased with how it went. The fact that this race is even close, though, tells you Republicans have momentum right now and it`s happening nationwide. In the Senate, enough incumbent Democrats could lose, giving Republicans several chances to take control. And in the House Democrats are in trouble in states like Oregon and New York, which are normally safe. Last night there was a debate for New York Governor where Republican Trump ally Congressman Lee Zeldin is within striking distance of Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul , which is remarkable in a solid blue state. Lester? HOLT: Andrea, thanks. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2022 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. And he went from homeless to shooting college hoops. The basketball star inspiring America. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. Just 13 days before the Midterm Elections, and a flood of political ads are saturating the airwaves on the heels of another marquee debate reminding just what is at stake in hard-fought congressional races, power and control of Congress. In the House, Democrats trying to defend their majority with all 435 seats of the body up for election. Dems facing the same challenge in the U.S. Senate with 35 seats are up for election. The balance of power in the Senate could be determined by a handful of tight races, including Pennsylvania where last night`s debate pitted Republican Mehmet Oz against Democrat John Fetterman sparring over abortion, fracking, and immigration. But not before Fetterman call out what he described as the elephant in the room, his health. Dasha Burns starts us off tonight with the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, Pennsylvania Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz back on the campaign trail following last night`s critical one and only face-off. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: Pennsylvania deserves better than Fetterman. BURNS: His opponent, Democrat John Fetterman , not yet making any public appearances after the fierce clash. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: It`s something called the Oz rule that if he`s on TV, he`s lying. OZ: And this is the only debate I could get you to come to talk to me on and I had to beg. BURNS: A debate the Fetterman`s health front and center. Fetterman whose campaign says suffers from auditory processing challenges after a stroke six months ago, requesting these closed captioning monitors in the studio. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke. He`s never let me forget that. And I might miss some words during this debate. Mush two words together, but it knocked me down, but I`m going to keep coming back up. BURNS: Fetterman did miss some words during the hour-long showdown, at times of struggling to answer questions, including this moment. Fetterman was asked about his changing position on fracking, which he now says he supports. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: There is that 2018 interview that you said, "I don`t support fracking at all." So, how do you square the two? FETTERMAN: I do support fracking. And I don`t --I don`t -- I support fracking and I stand -- and I do support fracking. BURNS: Fetterman would not commit to releasing his full medical records. FETTERMAN: My doctor believes that I`m fit to be serving, and that`s what I believe is where I`m standing. BURNS: And in one of the biggest clashes of the night going after Dr. Oz on abortion rights. FETTERMAN: He celebrated when Roe v. Wade went down and my campaign would fight for Roe v. Wade, and if given the opportunity, to codify it into law. BURNS: And tonight, the Fetterman campaign zeroing in on this response from Oz. OZ: I want women, doctors, local political leaders letting the democracy that`s always allowed our nation to thrive to put the best ideas forward so states can decide for themselves. Local political leaders. Local political leaders. BURNS: Turning it into a campaign ad against his opponent. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Oz is too extreme for Pennsylvania. BURNS: But Oz calling Fetterman the extreme candidates throughout the night, especially on the issue of crime. OZ: We have taken away the ability of police to do their job and that son John Fetterman . BURNS: The momentous matchup coming just two weeks before Election Day. Voters with strong reactions about Dr. Oz. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: His comment about political leaders, you know, determining what a woman -- a woman can and cannot do with her body is -- was very telling. [19:05:09] BURNS: And Fetterman. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I just don`t think he`s capable at this time to be in that position. I mean, if you have somebody that can`t even handle a debate that has to, you know, read from this prompter. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And Dasha, some big names could soon be campaigning there on both sides. BURNS (on camera): Yes, Lester. Plans are coming together for both President Biden and former President Obama to campaign with Fetterman, and the Democratic candidate for governor. And former President Trump will campaign with Dr. Oz and the Republican gubernatorial candidate. Lester? HOLT: Dasha Burns, thank you. Let`s bring in Andrea Mitchell and Kristen Welker. Andrea, first to you. What are you hearing there in Pennsylvania about the impact of that debate? ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, Democrats here are telling me that they think Fetterman will be OK, given his labor support and Oz`s missteps on abortion and the minimum wage. But they acknowledge that this format did not work for Fetterman. Republicans say they`re pleased with how it went. The fact that this race is even close, though, tells you Republicans have momentum right now and it`s happening nationwide. In the Senate, enough incumbent Democrats could lose, giving Republicans several chances to take control. And in the House Democrats are in trouble in states like Oregon and New York, which are normally safe. Last night there was a debate for New York Governor where Republican Trump ally Congressman Lee Zeldin is within striking distance of Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul , which is remarkable in a solid blue state. Lester? HOLT: Andrea, thanks. Let me turn now to Kristen. Kristen, there`s a new headline in that tight Georgia Senate race, an anonymous allegation against Herschel Walker . What do we know? KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, that`s right. This latest allegation comes from an anonymous woman who spoke on Zoom without showing her face in a press conference arranged by Attorney Gloria Allred, an allegation Herschel Walker is strongly denying tonight. Now, the woman claims she had an affair with Walker, the football star turned Republican Senate candidate, and got pregnant nearly 30 years ago. She says Walker pressured and paid for her to have an abortion, but she did not provide any evidence to support those claims. Now, Walker fired back today calling the claims foolishness and a lie, saying his Democratic opponent Senator Raphael Warnock "lost the debate and Democrats will now say anything to win." The woman`s claim comes after another woman accused Walker of paying for her abortion which Walker also strongly denied. The Georgia race is a toss-up that could determine Senate control. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker, thank you. In Wisconsin this evening, the man who plowed his car through a Christmas parade guilty on all counts, bringing his chaotic trial to an end. The charges included multiple counts of intentional homicide after he killed six people. Miguel Almaguer has more. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We the jury find the defendant Darrell E. Brooks guilty of first-degree intentional homicide. MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The verdict was a clean sweep for prosecutors. Darrell Brooks guilty of all 76 criminal charges including intentional homicide, reckless endangering safety, and hit and run causing death. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Are those your true verdicts? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes. ALMAGUER: After just three hours of deliberation, the chaotic three-week trial came to an end as Brooks sat slumped over. SUSAN OPPER, DISTRICT ATTORNEY, WAUKESHA COUNTY: We are satisfied that this defendant has been held accountable for his actions. ALMAGUER: It was last year at this Christmas Parade in Waukesha, Wisconsin when Brooks plowed his car through the crowd, killing six and injuring dozens. Among the victims, the elderly and children. TYLER PUDLEINER, SURVIVOR: Were stronger than him and it`s been proven today. Just another step forward in the process. ALMAGUER: Maintaining his innocence -- DARRELL BROOKS, DEFENDANT: I am a lot of things. A murderer is not one of them. ALMAGUER: Brooks, who represented himself, showed a range of emotions in what became a circus-like trial, deciding to plead not guilty by reason of mental defect. JENNIFER DOROW, JUDGE, WAUKESHA COUNTY CIRCUIT COURT: Mr. Brooks, you`re interrupting me yet again. BROOKS: No, you weren`t just speaking, so -- DOROW: All right, Mr. Brooks, you are now going to be removed to the courtroom. BROOKS: I don`t concent to that. ALMAGUER: Brooks repeatedly interrupted the trial, at one point removing his shirt and staring down the judge who removed him from court. DOROW: I need to take a break. This man right now is having a staredown with me. Frankly, it makes me scared. (END VIDEOTAPE) ALMAGUER (on camera): In Wisconsin, conviction of first-degree intentional homicide carries a mandatory life sentence. Darrell Brooks will be formally sentenced in the coming weeks. Lester? HOLT: All right, Miguel Almaguer, thank you. Tonight, new details emerging about the 19-year-old gunman who killed two people and injured seven others at a St. Louis high school on Monday. Emilie Ikeda has the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) EMILIE IKEDA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Months before storming a St. Louis high school with a long gun and 600 rounds of ammunition, police said the accused killer`s family worked with law enforcement to have his gun removed from their home. MICHAEL SACK, INTERIM COMMISSIONER, ST. LOUIS METROPOLITAN POLICE DEPARTMENT: It`s -- and it`s hard to tell when somebody is going to be violent or act out or if they`re just struggling. [19:10:06] IKEDA: His family played an active role in getting a medical help involving therapy, medication, and committing him on several occasions according to police. Was the family aware of the arsenal of ammunition he had? SACK: They were aware that he had acquired a firearm. IKEDA: The ATF is still tracing where he originally bought the gun and how it landed back in his possession after law enforcement had transferred it to another adult. SACK: How he acquired it after that, you know, we don`t know. IKEDA: It`s believed to be the same AR-15-style weapon used to gun down sophomore Alexandria Bell and teacher Jean Kuczka, both of whom Ashley Wrench knew well. ASHLEY WRENCH, TEACHER: And you can hear just pop, pop, pop, pop. IKEDA: The longtime math teacher walking by her classroom for the first time since the shooting spree. What do you remember from Monday? WRENCH: Everything. The terror, the intruder trying to get in my room two, three, four times. IKEDA: That day, the school doors were locked, and seven unarmed security guards were on site. But authorities say the government managed to avoid the school`s checkpoints. Can you tell us if he had to break glass to get into the building though? SACK: You did have to force entry. And that`s good for us because that buys us time. (END VIDEOTAPE) IKEDA: And Lester, we`re learning tonight authorities believe the gunman was targeting the school and certain individuals. But the rapid police response and a potentially not functioning gun helps prevent even more bloodshed. Lester? HOLT: And the details that keep coming out are stunning. Thank you. A show of force in Russia. President Vladimir Putin observing annual drills led by Russia`s strategic nuclear forces as Russia continues with unfounded claims that Ukraine intends to use a dirty bomb in the war there. Also, today, Russian authorities returned the body of an American man killed in August while fighting for Ukraine. The remains of 24-year-old Joshua Jones were handed over to Ukrainian officials in a Russian- controlled part of Ukraine. Let`s turn to that big increase now in cases of RSV infections in children, with many hospitals saying they`re in crisis mode now. Tom Costello has the warning signs for parents. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): 3-year-old Izzy Bankey is today almost back to her old self, but she`s been through rough few weeks. Homesick, a two-hour wait in an urgent care clinic, a second urgent care visit, an ambulance ride to Children`s National Med Center as she struggled to breathe. Then, admitted with RSV-caused pneumonia. KATE FOSTER-BANKEY, MOTHER OF IZZY BANKEY: Nobody wants to like, hold their kid down and hold a mask on their face. And so, she`s screaming and trying -- and trying to rip the breathing tubes out. And that breaks your heart as a parent. COSTELLO: RSV is an ever-present respiratory virus but especially serious in kids with low immunity after isolating during the pandemic. Now, hospitals nationwide say they`re overwhelmed with sick kids. 74 percent of pediatric hospital beds nationwide are occupied. 89 percent in Missouri, 91 percent in Texas, 99 percent in Rhode Island. Seattle Children`s tells NBC News it`s a 200 percent capacity in the ER. At UW Health Kids in Madison, Wisconsin, the chief medical officer is urging parents to stay on top of the symptoms before kids have to go to the ER. DR. JOSHUA ROSS, PEDIATRIC EMERGENCY MEDICINE PHYSICIAN, UW HEALTH -KIDS: Suctioning the nose, nasal passages, staying well hydrated, using anti- fever medications usually do the trick. We really want to pay attention to as kids under about 18 months of age that can develop more significant respiratory symptoms. COSTELLO: Seek immediate help if a child is in respiratory distress, breathing fast, nose flaring, using their shoulders or pulling under their ribs to breathe, and turning blue. DR. RICK PLACE, PEDIATRIC MEDICAL DIRECTOR, INOVA L.J. MURPHY CHILDREN`S HOSPITAL: If you think your child is in danger, you need to go to the E.R. I mean that`s a flat-out message. COSTELLO: Trust your gut, say doctors. Tom Costello, NBC News, Washington. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: In 60 seconds, the nationwide shortage of Adderall, a key medicine that helps kids and adults with ADHD. What`s behind it and what families are doing to bridge the gap. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:15:00] HOLT: Back now with a disorder that impacts so many Americans, including more than six million children, ADHD. For those who treat it with Adderall, a nationwide shortage has them scrambling to fill prescriptions. Anne Thompson explains. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANNE THOMPSON, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Giovanni is the center of Lyon and Kandy Flood`s world. KANDY FLOOD, SON HAS ADHD: Oh, nice. THOMPSON: It turned upside down by the Adderall shortage. When they told you the prescription wasn`t available, I mean, did your heart sink? K. FLOOD: Absolutely. My anxiety went up and my heart sank, and I was at a loss. THOMPSON: For a week, the third-grader had no Adderall manage his ADHD. Giovanni, what was it like for you to go without your medicine? GIOVANNI FLOOD, HAS ADHD: Uncomfortable. LYON FLOOD, SON HAD ADHD: His teacher came to us, threw her hands up and said, can you do something because he was way out of control, doing cartwheels in the class, and rolling on the floor. K. FLOOD: Rolling on the floor, yes. DR. LENARD ADLER, PSYCHIATRIST, NYU LANGONE: We`re fielding several phone calls a day. THOMPSON: Dr. Lenard Adler leads the adult ADHD program at NYU Langone Health. ADLER: I`ve had a patient having to call about 15 pharmacies before they finally got to -- THOMPSON: 15? ADLER: 15 pharmacies before they got their prescription filled. THOMPSON: This month, the FDA revealed the shortage blaming increased demand for the control substance and manufacturing issues at Teva , the largest drug maker. In a statement, Teva says the shortages are temporary and it expects inventory recovery in the coming months. ADLER: If you`re at the end of your prescription, I wouldn`t suggest doing anything on your own. I would have a discussion with your physician. Sometimes that means trying a new pharmacy. It can be. If necessary, trying a new medication. THOMAS: Kandy`s daily phone calls to her pharmacy paid off. They got a month`s refill, but there`s no guarantee they won`t face this again and soon. Anne Thompson, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, the verdict in the case against three-man accused of supporting the plot to kidnap Michigan`s governor. Plus, voter intimidation and efforts to combat it in our series "POWER OF THE VOTE." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: In Michigan today, three men were found guilty in state court for supporting a plot to kidnap Governor Gretchen Whitmer out of anger over her COVID restrictions. Two other men were convicted on federal conspiracy charges in August. Whitmer said, today`s verdicts are quote further proof that violence and threats have no place in our politics. Also, tonight, less than two weeks to the midterms, Arizona election officials are stepping up security after what they call vigilantes were spotted near ballot drop boxes. Gabe Gutierrez is there. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Amid complaints of armed masked groups wearing tactical gear and recording voters, the sheriff in Maricopa County, Arizona has now stepped up security near ballot drop boxes. PAUL PENZONE, SHERIFF, MARICOPA COUNTY: It troubles me that suddenly others feel compelled to act out in a way that is potentially criminal intimidation or criminal threats, trying to undermine democracy under this cloak of patriotism. And in doing so, what they`re doing is they`re destroying the most important institution in our nation, you know, the freedom and the right to vote. GUTIERREZ: He also says his office is investigating this incident captured on cell phone video where a woman tried to take a picture of one of their license plates and was pushed. We spoke to the woman. She asked us not to use her name or show her face for fear of backlash. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You know, a lot of people are intimidated. And when people are standing around, you know, with handguns on them and sometimes tactical gear, you know, it really does scare the average person. GUTIERREZ: At least six complaints of alleged voter intimidation here have now been referred to the State Attorney General`s Office and the Department of Justice. Across the country, election threats are ramping up ahead of the Midterms. LEIGH CHAPMAN, ACTING SECRETARY, PENNSYLVANIA COMMONWEALTH: A lot of these threats are fueled by missing disinformation. GUTIERREZ: Law enforcement Nationwide is on alert. MERRICK GARLAND , U.S. ATTORNEY GENERAL: The Justice Department has an obligation to prevent to guarantee a free and fair vote. GUTIERREZ: Back in Arizona where early votes are already been counted, Republican election officials have called these armed drop box watchers uninformed vigilantes. As a Republican, how frustrating is it to you that some of these groups have latched on to conspiracy theories? STEPHEN RICHER, MARICOPA COUNTY RECORDER: Well, it`s been an interesting last two years. And you know, for the party of facts and logic, at times, we have fallen short from, in my estimation, on facts and logic. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (on camera): Voter rights organizations have now sued to temporarily block at least some of these groups from monitoring these ballot drop-off boxes. Lester? HOLT: All right, Gabe, thank you. Coming up, at $700 million, it`s one of the biggest Powerball jackpots in history. Could there be a winner tonight? Plus, he was homeless before he found his place on the court. "INSPIRING AMERICA" is next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Tonight`s Powerball jackpot has grown to a massive $700 million, the fifth largest in the game`s history. No one has won since August. The odds are one in 293 million. If you bought your tickets, good luck to you. And finally, the student-athlete beating formidable odds with a former NBA point guard coaching them on. Kathy Park with tonight`s "INSPIRING AMERICA." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KATHY PARK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Jeremiah Armstead picked up a basketball at 14, the same age he realized life wasn`t a game. JEREMIAH ARMSTEAD, BASKETBALL PLAYER: I felt like I wasn`t in at 14. That`s what I feel like. Because that`s when they really picked up homeless and stuff like that. PARK: For years, Jeremiah says he moved from shelter to shelter with his mom and two siblings. ARMSTEAD: I was living off food stamps. PARK: What would you say were some of the darkest times in your life? ARMSTEAD: Sleeping at bleachers. People walking by, looking in the car. Stuff like that builds character, so I can`t be mad to stuff like that. PARK: Homelessness pushed Jeremiah to fight harder for his goals. ARMSTEAD: Can`t is not in my vocabulary. PARK: He excelled as a student in California and as an athlete, a winning combination that got him into Fisk University in Nashville, and a spot on the basketball team. KENNY ANDERSON, FORMER NBA PLAYER: The grit definitely sets him apart. PARK: Former NBA point guard Kenny Anderson now coaches a rising star and sees a lot of himself in Jeremiah. ANDERSON: My best year of my high school career, I was -- I have the way to live. We got evicted. PARK: The NBA legend beat the odds and believes Jeremiah can too. Meanwhile, his cheering squad couldn`t be prouder. MINDY BROOKS, MOTHER OF JEREMIAH: This is a child who deserves to just show what he can do. PARK: What`s the end game for you? ARMSTEAD: My first goal which is get my mom and my sister out to shelter that they`re in. PARK: Family first while making moves on and off the court. Kathy Park, NBC News, Nashville. headline: Democrat John Fetterman And Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz Face Off
story_text: [07:00:17] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. It`s Wednesday, all eyes were on Pennsylvania overnight. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes. The first and only Senate debate there with control of Congress hanging in the balance. It is October 26th, this is Today. Center Stage, Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz face off on the issues. JOHN FETTERMAN (D), PENNSYLVANIA SENATE CANDIDATE: My campaign would fight for Roe v. Wade. MEHMET OZ (R), PENNSYLVANIA SENATE CANDIDATE: John Fetterman picks everything to an extreme and those extreme positions hurt us all. GUTHRIE: And ongoing concerns over Fetterman`s fitness to serve. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke, he`s never let me forget that. GUTHRIE: This morning the candidates in their own words and the takeaways in one of the nation`s most important midterm contests. Inside the Rampage, new details on the gunman behind that deadly school shooting in St. Louis, with a letter found in his car is revealing about a possible motive, and the stories of bravery now emerging. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I really credit my students a lot because even with the gunshots that close, they did not scream. GUTHRIE: That harrowing firsthand account just ahead. Cooling Off, housing prices falling fast after soaring to record highs. So is now the best time to buy, and what does it mean if you`re in the market to sell. We`ll break it down. All of that plus, Chaos and Controversy. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Miss USA is Texas. GUTHRIE: The Miss USA pageant embroiled in scandal. Some contestants claiming it`s rigged. The organization`s president now suspended and an investigation underway. The very latest straight ahead. And breaking news, what scientists are now saying about whether you really need to rake those leaves and it could make your weekend a lot more enjoyable. Today, Wednesday, October 26, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is TODAY with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. GUTHRIE: Good morning, everybody. Welcome back to TODAY. It is Wednesday morning, nice to have you along with us. This raking story, you want to get back those hours of your childhood raking leaves, don`t you? KOTB: Can you imagine -- you go remember all the time your parents said you got to go out and rake the leaves and stuff them into hefty bags. Who knew that we didn`t have to do that? GUTHRIE: Science is saying something different this morning. We`ll get to that. KOTB: Yes. We got a busy morning a lot to get to including we`ve got some rare good news. It`s tied to the economy at least if you`re planning to buy a house. GUTHRIE: Yes. Prices are now going down at a record rate. Tom Costello is going to have everything we need to know. KOTB: Of course, we will begin with last night`s big debate in Pennsylvania. GUTHRIE: This was highly anticipated not only because of questions concerning Democrat John Fetterman`s health after his stroke six months ago, but also because this race could decide which party controls the Senate. And that will affect every single American come next year. We`ll show you how it all played out. Let`s start this morning with NBC`s Dasha Burns in Harrisburg. Dasha, good morning. DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Savannah, good morning. This debate was highly anticipated not just by voters here in Pennsylvania but people across the country. It`s an extremely tight race, just a couple of points separating these candidates in the polls. And in a battle against one of the most familiar faces on American television, many tuned in to see how Fetterman would fare after suffering a stroke earlier this year, and the stakes could not have been higher. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BURNS (voice-over): In a race that could help decide the balance of power in Congress, Pennsylvania Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Mehmet Oz neck and neck in the polls finally face to face on the debate stage. FETTERMAN: I`m running to serve Pennsylvania. He`s running to use Pennsylvania. OZ: John Fetterman picks everything to an extreme and those extreme positions hurt us all. BURNS (voice-over): Fetterman acknowledging what he called the elephant in the room, the stroke that nearly killed him five months ago. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke, he`s never let me forget that. And I might miss some words during this debate, mush two words together. I`m also fighting for any forgotten community all across Pennsylvania. They ever got knocked down that had to be -- to get back up. And I`ve made my entire career dedicating to those kinds of pursuits. BURNS (voice-over): Fetterman using closed captioning to assist with auditory processing battling Dr. Oz. FETTERMAN: It`s about supporting and helping young earners -- excuse me, young students to give them a break. BURNS (voice-over): But experiencing some stumbles throughout the debate particularly during an exchange over fracking challenged by the moderators for past contradictory comments. FETTERMAN: I do support fracking and I don`t -- I don`t -- I support fracking and I stand and I do support fracking. [07:05:03] BURNS (voice-over): Fetterman says he`s fit to serve citing a letter from his doctor, but he would not commit to releasing his full medical records. FETTERMAN: I believe if my doctor believes that I`m fit to serve, and that`s what I believe is appropriate. BURNS (voice-over): The celebrity TV doctor never directly addressing Fetterman`s health but saying this during an exchange on education. OZ: Visited vocational schools. I`ve been answered but John, because obviously, I wasn`t clear enough for you to understand this. BURNS (voice-over): One point where Oz has not been clear how he`d vote on a 15 week abortion ban introduced by Republican Senator Lindsey Graham . OZ: I want women doctors, local political leaders, letting the democracy that`s always allowed our nation to thrive, to put the best ideas forward so states can decide for themselves. BURNS (voice-over): A clear difference from his opponent. FETTERMAN: My campaign would fight for Roe v. Wade, and if given the opportunity to codified into law. BURNS (voice-over): Oz also trying to court moderate undecided voters. But it was former President Trump`s endorsement that helped get him onto the Republican ticket here. MODERATOR: Donald Trump has supported you. He has endorsed you. Why won`t you fully commit to supporting him in 2024? OZ: Oh, I do. I would support Donald Trump if he decided to run for president. (END VIDEOTAPE) BURNS: And, Savannah, speaking to media after the debate, the Fetterman spokesperson said the campaign was thrilled with his performance saying he won "countless exchanges against Oz." And we asked the Oz spokesperson what the Republican meant when he said that decisions about abortion should be made between "a woman or her doctor and local political leaders." The campaign responded that he is "prolife" with exceptions for rape, incest and the life of the mother. And, Savannah, voters that we talked to overnight said that they wish they`d seen more substance and fewer attacks, Savannah. GUTHRIE: All right. Dasha Burns leading us off, thank you. Let`s turn to NBC`s Hallie Jackson. You watch the debate as well, Hallie. I mean, John Fetterman said the elephant in the room was his health, his recent stroke, his fitness to serve, how did it play in the room? HALLIE JACKSON NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: So I talked to some folks are in the room. I was on the phone with a campaign advisor right after the debate last night, Savannah. And here`s where I think it`s coming down at this point for Democrats, who are largely acknowledging that, yes, John Fetterman , it`s very evident, is clearly still recovering from a stroke. There were accommodations made, as Dasha talked about, the closed captioning, to be able to have him conduct this debate. But I will say that there is a sense among people close to the lieutenant governor that voters will understand that he had a health issue, that he is recovering, that he is putting himself out there. They`re going after Oz for the line about abortion access being between a woman, a doctor and local political leaders. I would expect to see some potential attack ads on that in the coming days. But he also talked with Democratic allies, Savannah, who questioned whether it will actually help that Fetterman was on the debate stage and questions overall on both sides of the aisle on how this is going to move the needle for Pennsylvania voters. This is such a close race. Every vote will matter in his race. It has bigger stakes nationally. And there is still a question mark of how voters will respond and react. GUTHRIE: And on the issues, we saw some themes play out that have obviously been -- it`s kind of a microcosm of what`s happening in other races where Republicans are hitting hard on the economy and crime, Democrats turning to abortion and we saw that last night. JACKSON: It was on full display, Savannah. You`re totally right. When you look at, for example, the abortion access, the answer from Oz. When you look at how Oz went after Fetterman on crime and the economy, we are seeing that not just in Pennsylvania. But you look at other debates that were happening overnight in places like New York, for example, where crime in the economy were also issues that Republicans were really trying to hit hard on Democrats. story_text: [07:00:17] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. It`s Wednesday, all eyes were on Pennsylvania overnight. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes. The first and only Senate debate there with control of Congress hanging in the balance. It is October 26th, this is Today. Center Stage, Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz face off on the issues. JOHN FETTERMAN (D), PENNSYLVANIA SENATE CANDIDATE: My campaign would fight for Roe v. Wade. MEHMET OZ (R), PENNSYLVANIA SENATE CANDIDATE: John Fetterman picks everything to an extreme and those extreme positions hurt us all. GUTHRIE: And ongoing concerns over Fetterman`s fitness to serve. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke, he`s never let me forget that. GUTHRIE: This morning the candidates in their own words and the takeaways in one of the nation`s most important midterm contests. Inside the Rampage, new details on the gunman behind that deadly school shooting in St. Louis, with a letter found in his car is revealing about a possible motive, and the stories of bravery now emerging. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I really credit my students a lot because even with the gunshots that close, they did not scream. GUTHRIE: That harrowing firsthand account just ahead. The organization`s president now suspended and an investigation underway. The very latest straight ahead. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is TODAY with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. GUTHRIE: Good morning, everybody. Welcome back to TODAY. It is Wednesday morning, nice to have you along with us. This raking story, you want to get back those hours of your childhood raking leaves, don`t you? KOTB: Can you imagine -- you go remember all the time your parents said you got to go out and rake the leaves and stuff them into hefty bags. Who knew that we didn`t have to do that? GUTHRIE: Science is saying something different this morning. We`ll get to that. KOTB: Yes. We got a busy morning a lot to get to including we`ve got some rare good news. It`s tied to the economy at least if you`re planning to buy a house. GUTHRIE: Yes. Prices are now going down at a record rate. Tom Costello is going to have everything we need to know. KOTB: Of course, we will begin with last night`s big debate in Pennsylvania. GUTHRIE: This was highly anticipated not only because of questions concerning Democrat John Fetterman`s health after his stroke six months ago, but also because this race could decide which party controls the Senate. DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Savannah, good morning. This debate was highly anticipated not just by voters here in Pennsylvania but people across the country. It`s an extremely tight race, just a couple of points separating these candidates in the polls. And in a battle against one of the most familiar faces on American television, many tuned in to see how Fetterman would fare after suffering a stroke earlier this year, and the stakes could not have been higher. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BURNS (voice-over): In a race that could help decide the balance of power in Congress, Pennsylvania Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Mehmet Oz neck and neck in the polls finally face to face on the debate stage. FETTERMAN: I`m running to serve Pennsylvania. He`s running to use Pennsylvania. OZ: John Fetterman picks everything to an extreme and those extreme positions hurt us all. BURNS (voice-over): Fetterman acknowledging what he called the elephant in the room, the stroke that nearly killed him five months ago. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke, he`s never let me forget that. And I might miss some words during this debate, mush two words together. I`m also fighting for any forgotten community all across Pennsylvania. They ever got knocked down that had to be -- to get back up. And I`ve made my entire career dedicating to those kinds of pursuits. BURNS (voice-over): Fetterman using closed captioning to assist with auditory processing battling Dr. Oz. FETTERMAN: It`s about supporting and helping young earners -- excuse me, young students to give them a break. BURNS (voice-over): But experiencing some stumbles throughout the debate particularly during an exchange over fracking challenged by the moderators for past contradictory comments. FETTERMAN: I do support fracking and I don`t -- I don`t -- I support fracking and I stand and I do support fracking. [07:05:03] BURNS (voice-over): Fetterman says he`s fit to serve citing a letter from his doctor, but he would not commit to releasing his full medical records. FETTERMAN: I believe if my doctor believes that I`m fit to serve, and that`s what I believe is appropriate. BURNS (voice-over): The celebrity TV doctor never directly addressing Fetterman`s health but saying this during an exchange on education. OZ: Visited vocational schools. I`ve been answered but John, because obviously, I wasn`t clear enough for you to understand this. BURNS (voice-over): One point where Oz has not been clear how he`d vote on a 15 week abortion ban introduced by Republican Senator Lindsey Graham . OZ: I want women doctors, local political leaders, letting the democracy that`s always allowed our nation to thrive, to put the best ideas forward so states can decide for themselves. BURNS (voice-over): A clear difference from his opponent. FETTERMAN: My campaign would fight for Roe v. Wade, and if given the opportunity to codified into law. BURNS (voice-over): Oz also trying to court moderate undecided voters. But it was former President Trump`s endorsement that helped get him onto the Republican ticket here. MODERATOR: Donald Trump has supported you. He has endorsed you. Why won`t you fully commit to supporting him in 2024? OZ: Oh, I do. I would support Donald Trump if he decided to run for president. (END VIDEOTAPE) BURNS: And, Savannah, speaking to media after the debate, the Fetterman spokesperson said the campaign was thrilled with his performance saying he won "countless exchanges against Oz." And we asked the Oz spokesperson what the Republican meant when he said that decisions about abortion should be made between "a woman or her doctor and local political leaders." The campaign responded that he is "prolife" with exceptions for rape, incest and the life of the mother. And, Savannah, voters that we talked to overnight said that they wish they`d seen more substance and fewer attacks, Savannah. GUTHRIE: All right. Dasha Burns leading us off, thank you. Let`s turn to NBC`s Hallie Jackson. You watch the debate as well, Hallie. I mean, John Fetterman said the elephant in the room was his health, his recent stroke, his fitness to serve, how did it play in the room? HALLIE JACKSON NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: So I talked to some folks are in the room. I was on the phone with a campaign advisor right after the debate last night, Savannah. And here`s where I think it`s coming down at this point for Democrats, who are largely acknowledging that, yes, John Fetterman , it`s very evident, is clearly still recovering from a stroke. There were accommodations made, as Dasha talked about, the closed captioning, to be able to have him conduct this debate. But I will say that there is a sense among people close to the lieutenant governor that voters will understand that he had a health issue, that he is recovering, that he is putting himself out there. They`re going after Oz for the line about abortion access being between a woman, a doctor and local political leaders. I would expect to see some potential attack ads on that in the coming days. But he also talked with Democratic allies, Savannah, who questioned whether it will actually help that Fetterman was on the debate stage and questions overall on both sides of the aisle on how this is going to move the needle for Pennsylvania voters. This is such a close race. Every vote will matter in his race. It has bigger stakes nationally. And there is still a question mark of how voters will respond and react. GUTHRIE: And on the issues, we saw some themes play out that have obviously been -- it`s kind of a microcosm of what`s happening in other races where Republicans are hitting hard on the economy and crime, Democrats turning to abortion and we saw that last night. JACKSON: It was on full display, Savannah. You`re totally right. When you look at, for example, the abortion access, the answer from Oz. When you look at how Oz went after Fetterman on crime and the economy, we are seeing that not just in Pennsylvania. But you look at other debates that were happening overnight in places like New York, for example, where crime in the economy were also issues that Republicans were really trying to hit hard on Democrats. These are issues that are going to matter to voters in the next 13 days before Election Day. You saw them on stage and they`re going to continue to play out over the next two weeks. GUTHRIE: All right. Hallie Jackson, thank you very much. KOTB: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito says that leak of the draft opinion to overturn Roe vs. Wade endanger the life of justices. Those comments came last night during an event at the Heritage Foundation . Alito says the leak was "a great betrayal of trust," and it put targets on their backs. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: In May, the Supreme Court martial launched in an investigation to identify the leaker. No findings from that probe have been made public. GUTHRIE: Also this morning, new details are emerging from the investigation into that deadly high school shooting in St. Louis. Police say a letter left behind is shedding light on what may have led a former student to carry out that attack. NBC`s Emilie Ikeda has more on the story joins us from St. Louis. Emilie, good morning. EMILIE IKEDA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Savannah, good morning. Investigators say one of the most revealing pieces of evidence was found in the suspect`s car, a hand written note where the teenage gunman called himself an isolated loner. [07:10:04] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) IKEDA (voice-over): Armed with this AR-15 style weapon and an arsenal of ammunition, police say the St. Louis school shooter`s rampage could have caused far more bloodshed had officers not arrived within minutes, MICHAEL SACK, ST, LOUIS INTERIM POLICE COMMISSIONER: But appears that he came into the building with more than 600 rounds of ammunition. IKEDA (voice-over): The chilling details emerging as police examined the suspect`s trail of evidence, including a handwritten notebook from the accused killer Orlando Harris`s car. Police say the 19-year-old wrote, "I`ve been an isolated loner my entire life. This was the perfect storm for a mass shooter." ASHLEY RENCH, MATH TEACHER: You heard boom, boom, boom, boom. IKEDA (voice-over): Math teacher Ashley Rench recalled the sounds of gunfire right outside her classroom. RENCH: I really credit my students a lot because even with the gunshots that close, him pulling on the door trying to get in, they did not scream. They just huddled together. IKEDA (voice-over): Rench knew both of the victims. St. Louis Public Schools identifying teacher Jean Kuczka who`s being hailed a hero for reportedly standing in front of students to protect them and sophomore Alexandria Bell, dying just weeks before her 16th birthday. KACY SHAHID, PRINCIPAL, CENTRAL VISUAL AND PERFORMING ARTS HIGH SCHOOL: They very bright student, very charismatic, beautiful spirit, a wonderful dancer. IKEDA (voice-over): This morning, a growing memorial outside the school still riddled with grim reminders of a terror the community will never forget. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: You do a short term sacrifice of paying a higher rate now for maybe the next 12 to 18 months. MELVIN: So this time of the year. GUTHRIE: All right. Let`s check the weather outside the answer. ROKER: You know, a lot of folks take Mississippi River cruises. This was late September last year. You can see how lush it is. This year, October of 2020, look at how dry it is. And that is continuing. And in fact we are looking at record low river levels. Memphis reaching its lowest river level since 1954. And the big problem is the drought. When this is an economic lifeline, the Mississippi River, $13 billion in shipping, a 35,000 related jobs. It accounts -- get this, 92% of our nation`s agricultural exports. So it is a lifeline literally, and the big problem has been the extensive drought in the western half of the Mississippi River basin. Problem is going into the winter, doesn`t look like we`re going to get much relief, so going to continue to have problems along the Mighty Mississippi. For Today, we`re looking at sunshine returning through the southeast into the gulf, plenty of sun from Texas on up into the plains, some mountain snows where they`re going to use that for those great ski resorts and we`re looking at sunshine from San Diego, some showers in Seattle. That`s what`s going on around the country. Here`s what`s happening in your neck of the woods. (LOCAL WEATHER) ROKER: And that is your latest weather. Guys? GUTHRIE: Thank you, Al. By the way, you`re about to hit the road for a very special lend-a-hand. ROKER: Yes. We`re really, really thrilled to be doing this. We`re going to see you tomorrow morning from Fort Myers Beach, Florida. [07:45:00] This is one month after Hurricane Ian roared ashore. We`re going to give you a firsthand look at a community`s resilience and determination to rebuild. Plus, we`re going to meet some heroes who are putting their own recovery on hold just to help others. We`re looking forward to sharing their inspiring stories live from Fort Myers Beach, Florida tomorrow on Today, in our great station down there, WBBH NBC2. We`re going to be working with them as well. KOTB: Cool. MELVIN: I love that you`re doing that. I love that you`re doing that. Up next, to rake or not to rake, apparently that is the question this morning. This morning scientists have been answered that a lot of you are really going to love. We`ll have that for you right after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (CLIP FROM "IT`S THE GREAT PUMPKIN CHARLIE BROWN") MELVIN: Classic, classic. KOTB: Yes. MELVIN: Back with our beloved holiday special, "It`s the Great Pumpkin Charlie Brown." And, Carson, there`s reason we picked that scene. CARSON DALY, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: There`s got to be a reason for that. That means fall is here. Pesky task of raking leaves but that chore might be a thing of the past. According to experts, leaving at least some of those leaves on the ground can actually help your lawn improving the health of grass and encouraging plant growth. Let`s discuss it and let`s predicate this by saying I don`t rake my leaves anymore. I have when you landscaping engineers to do that. MELVIN: There you go. GUTHRIE: I like that. KOTB: Carson, did you rake when you were a kid? DALY: Yes. KOTB: Did your parents make you? DALY: Yes. MELVIN: Of course. KOTB: Did your parents make you? ROKER: Absolutely. And in fact, I did -- when I was in high school, I did a whole thing. A whole research project to convince my father that we did not have to rake leaves. And that we just take the leaf catcher, that lawnmower, and mulch it (inaudible). And I`ve talked to the Queens` cooperative extension guy. He said it`s fine. I was -- oh -- GUTHRIE: You were ahead of your time. Did you rake leaves? KOTB: We raked, that was a definite chore. GUTHRIE: I grew up in the desert, we didn`t have leaves. (CROSSTALK) DALY: Yes. But would you leave -- they`re saying you should leave all the leaves on the lawn, it`s good for it. They break down, it`s natural -- GUTHRIE: Is this a great show for people because, first, kids find out that the video games are good for them. Now they don`t have to rake leaves anymore. MELVIN: Keep watching kids. GUTHRIE: It`s like no school, candy for breakfast, what`s next? MELVIN: Did you`re dad but it? ROKER: Yes, yes, he did. Because he wasn`t doing it, you know -- GUTHRIE: OK. ROKER: -- for a while DALY: But I love it after the leaves have been raked, and then just a few kind of scattered on the green lawn, how beautiful that looks. KOTB: Yes, it`s cool. DALY: I`m more likely to compost. MELVIN: You`re welcome kids. You`re welcome. DALY: How long can you hold your breath for?
