headline: The Today Show for October 26, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:00:00] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS TODAY, CO-ANCHOR: It`s 8:00 on "TODAY." Coming up, center stage. Inside the Pennsylvania Senate race, Democrat John Fetterman facing off against Republican Mehmet Oz sparring over the issues. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LT. GOV. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA): I`m running to serve Pennsylvania. He is running to use Pennsylvania. DR. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATE NOMINEE: John Fetterman takes everything to an extreme. And those extreme positions hurt us all. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: And John Fetterman`s health. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) FETTERMAN: I had a stroke but it knocked me down. And I`m going to keep coming back up. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: Why this race could help decide the balance of power in Congress. Then tripling down. New warnings about that oncoming tripledemic, COVID, flu and RSV. What experts are saying this morning about keeping you and your loved ones safe. Plus, all in the family. Jenna sits down with the Queen Consort Camilla`s nephew Luke Parker Bowles. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LUKE PARKER BOWLES, QUEEN CONSORT CAMILLA`S NEPHEW: I have this name. And if I use it for something that helps people, then all the better. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: What brought him to the United States and what he hopes to accomplish here. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JENNA BUSH HAGER, HODA & JENNA HOST: If somebody had told you when you were 18, you are going to be in New Jersey when you get older, what would you say? PARKER BOWLES: I`d say what`s New Jersey? (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: Today, Wednesday, October 26, 2022. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From Vernon, Texas. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Celebrating our golden anniversary. CROWD: Friends for 35 years. CROWD: Visiting from Irvine, California. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Girls trip. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: From Philadelphia. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: To the "TODAY" show. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Shout out to my daughter. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: In Merrimac, Virginia. CROWD: From Lake Charles, Louisiana. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Because today. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m turning 70. (END VIDEO CLIP) CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Aw. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS TODAY, CO-ANCHOR: Aw. GUTHRIE: Aw. Hello. Good morning. Welcome back to "TODAY." What a great crowd out there. A beautiful fall morning. Relax. You don`t have to rake your leaves today. KOTB: Yes. Exactly. GUTHRIE: That`s what we`ve learned this morning. MELVIN: So, far. Yes. KOTB: Happy birthday, Lake Charles. Cool. GUTHRIE: Let`s get to the news, 8:00 on a Wednesday morning. With control of the U.S. Senate at stake, all eyes on that Pennsylvania rates last night. And the only debate, hitting Democrat John Fetterman against Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz. And it comes amid questions concerning Fetterman`s health after his stroke six months ago. NBC`s Dasha Burns joins us with some of the key moments last night. Hi, Dasha. Good morning. DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS REPORTER: Hey, Savannah. Good morning. This debate was highly anticipated, not just by voters here in Pennsylvania, but across the country. This is an extremely tight race. Just a couple of points separating these candidates. And in the battle against one of the most familiar faces on American television, many tuned in to see how Fetterman would fair after suffering a stroke earlier this year and the stakes could not have been higher. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BURNS (voiceover): In a race that could help decide the balance of power in Congress, Pennsylvania Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Mehmet Oz neck-and-neck in the polls finally face to face on the debate stage. LT. GOV. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA): I`m running to serve Pennsylvania. He is running to use Pennsylvania. DR. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATE NOMINEE: John Fetterman takes everything to an extreme. And those extreme positions hurt us all. BURNS (voiceover): Fetterman acknowledging what he called the elephant in the room. The stroke that nearly killed him five months ago. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke. He`s never let me forget that. And I might miss some words during this debate, mush two words together. I am also fighting for any forgotten community all across Pennsylvania that ever got knocked down that had to be made -- to get back up and I have made my entire career dedicating to those kinds of pursuits. BURNS (voiceover): Fetterman using closed captioning to assist with auditory processing, battling Dr. Oz. FETTERMAN: It`s about supporting and helping, you know, young earners, excuse me, young -- young, uh -- young, you know, students to give them a break. BURNS (voiceover): But experiencing some stumbles throughout the debate, particularly during an exchange over fracking, challenged by the moderators for past contradictory comments. FETTERMAN: I do support fracking and I don`t -- I don`t -- I support fracking and I stand -- and I do support fracking. BURNS (voiceover): Fetterman says he is fit to serve, citing a letter from his doctor. But he would not commit to releasing his full medical records. FETTERMAN: I believe if my doctor believes that I`m fit to serve and that`s what I believe is appropriate. BURNS (voiceover): The celebrity TV doctor never directly addressing Fetterman`s health, but saying this during an exchange on education. OZ: I visited vocational schools. I have an answer. But, John, because you -- obviously, I wasn`t clear enough for you to understand this. BURNS (voiceover): One point where Oz has not been clear, how he would vote on an abortion ban introduced by Republican Senator Lindsey Graham . OZ: I want women, doctors, local political leaders leading the democracy that`s always allowed our nation to thrive to put the best ideas forward so states can decide for themselves. BURNS (voiceover): A clear difference from his opponent. [08:05:00] FETTERMAN: My campaign would fight for Roe V. Wade. And if given the opportunity to codify it into law. (END VIDEO CLIP) BURNS (on camera): And, Savannah, and speaking to media after the debate, the Fetterman spokesperson said the campaign was thrilled with the Democrat`s performance saying he won, "Multiple exchanges against Oz." We also asked the Oz spokesperson about that line you just heard there where Oz said that decisions about abortion should be made between, "A woman, her doctor, and local political leaders." The campaign said that Oz is, "Pro- life with exceptions for rape, incest and the life of the mother." Savannah. GUTHRIE: All right. Dasha Burns, thank you very much. KOTB: With fears of a winter tripledemic growing, President Biden is urging Americans to get their flu and their COVID boosters as soon as they can. The president, who tested positive for COVID twice this summer, got his updated COVID shot yesterday. He noted that the virus is constantly changing but said that nearly all COVID deaths can now be prevented if enough people get vaccinated. Meantime, three quarters of all pediatric hospital beds around the country are now full because of an outbreak of RSV among children. MELVIN: Clorox is recalling eight of its Pine-Sol disinfecting cleaning products because they could contain harmful bacteria. The recall covers 37 million containers of Pine-Sol cleaners. They were made at a plant in Georgia. The CDC says the bacteria can cause blood and lung infections in people with compromised immune systems. For more information on the recall, go to our website, today.com. GUTHRIE: The International Space Station had to do defensive driving this week to avoid a potential collision with a piece of Russian satellite debris. NASA says the ISS had to fire its thrusters for more than five minutes on Monday. That raised its altitude a bit and allowed it to dodge the space junk. MELVIN: Wow. GUTHRIE: That maneuver did not affect normal operations. The debris was created by Russia`s test-firing of a missile last year that destroyed one of its old out of commission satellites. MELVIN: Space is really getting crowded. GUTHRIE: Yes. MELVIN: Really getting crowded. KOTB: All right. Guys, we got the news covered. Now, how about a boost? MELVIN: Yes. KOTB: All right. So, a UPS driver in South Dakota is the hero of the neighborhood because he made one incredible shot after he made a delivery. So, he dropped off a package, heads back to his truck, he`s walking past a driveway basketball game. The ball rolls towards the street, picks it up, and he fires off a one-handed shot. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: No way. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: No way. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: No way. MELVIN: Oh. KOTB: Oh, my gosh. After a brief celebration, the delivery man just climbs back in the truck, off he goes. MELVIN: Wow. KOTB: What a nice moment. MELVIN: That`s impressive. KOTB: That`s cool. GUTHRIE: So happy about the ring cameras sometimes. KOTB: I know. MELVIN: Yes. GUTHRIE: I mean, otherwise, they`d be like, no. But, seriously, I was away. KOTB: He did it. GUTHRIE: I did it. MELVIN: We got lots more ahead on a Wednesday morning, including our first look at a holiday special from the Marvel Universe. I can hear Al Roker screaming now. We`re going to show you the beloved star who is going to make a great cameo. GUTHRIE: But first, Jenna`s one-on-one with an extended member of the royal family, the queen consort`s nephew who lives right here in the northeast, New Jersey. Sharing his story for the first time. And Jenna, we`re looking forward to that conversation. Right after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:10:00] MELVIN: And welcome back. Welcome back. In the wake of Queen Elizabeth`s death, the eyes on the world are on the new monarch, King Charles and Queen Consort Camilla. GUTHRIE: Well, I learned something new today. One of their biggest supporters lives right here in the U.S., very close to us. Camilla`s nephew Luke Parker Bowles. KOTB: And Jenna met up with him to hear his intriguing story. Who knew he lived in Jersey. JENNA BUSH HAGER, HODA & JENNA HOST: I mean, he -- you would have thought you had to go across the pond. KOTB: Yes. BUSH HAGER: I just had to go in the hole and tunnel. After growing up of Parker Bowles, he`s began a new life right here in New Jersey. He is smart, charming, lovely. And now he is sharing his story for the first time. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BUSH HAGER (voiceover): It`s an unlikely story, an unofficial British ambassador for the royal family living among the rolling hills of picturesque Montclair, New Jersey. LUKE PARKER BOWLES, QUEEN CONSORT CAMILLA`S NEPHEW: This town is so much about film and culture. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): I met with up with Luke Parker Bowles, nephew of queen consort Camilla, while he was busy promoting the Montclair Film Festival. BUSH HAGER (on camera): I never really thought I`d find a little slice of England in New Jersey. But tell me how you came here. PARKER BOWLES: I came to America, I met a beautiful woman who is now my wife. And I was in England making movies there. One of Hugh Grant`s films, "Love Actually" and everything, and I moved over here and started doing independent film. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): The father of three has lived in the United States for more than a decade. Lured away from the U.K. by the bright shiny lights of Hollywood and big dreams of an acting career. PARKER BOWLES: And after a while I -- it would -- it became very clear that I did not have the skill set, but I loved film more than anything. And so, I realized I wanted to be behind the camera. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): Far different from his life in London. He grew up the nephew of Camilla Parker Bowles, by her first marriage to Andrew Parker Bowles. His last name often casting a large and dramatic shadow as his aunt was in the spotlight. BUSH HAGER (on camera): I read that when you were younger, you were actually sometimes bullied. PARKER BOWLES: It was a rough time. It was not a great time to be a Parker Bowles. But it hasn`t scarred me. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): His family focused on using its name for good. PARKER BOWLES: All of us, I think. My cousins, my brother, and myself, we`ve always have been involved in charity. It`s much more important to be doing charitable things, not to be holier than thou, just because it gives you a focus. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): One of the charities close to his heart is the Queen Elizabeth II Garden in Lower Manhattan which pays tribute to his countrymen lost on 9/11. PARKER BOWLES: His majesty, very kindly become our trustee and helped us get this garden going, and then her late majesty allowed us to name it after her. And it`s a place for people to go down and reflect and remember. BUSH HAGER (on camera): Your heart is here. Your kids are here. Your wife is here. Your job is here. Part of you is still there. And by giving back here, you are keeping that part of you alive. PARKER BOWLES: I think my shrink would say there is some guilt involved, maybe, that I`m not over there. It goes back to the fact that I have this name. And if I can use it for something that helps people, then all the better. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): He says, it`s an example set from the very top. He admired Queen Elizabeth and her dedication to service, working for the British people up until the very end. BUSH HAGER (on camera): Watching the outpouring of love -- PARKER BOWLES: Yes. BUSH HAGER (on camera): -- for her majesty, Queen Elizabeth, we were in Scotland. So, to get to see little girls lining the street with hand- colored papers for her. PARKER BOWLES: I think, for the most part, she left this world feeling that everything was in its right place. BUSH HAGER (on camera): And she was such an example -- PARKER BOWLES: Oh, yes. BUSH HAGER (on camera): -- of service. PARKER BOWLES: Oh, yes. BUSH HAGER (on camera): -- and dedication. PARKER BOWLES: Yes. BUSH HAGER: I mean -- PARKER BOWLES: And flinchingly and never seeking thanks or approval. It was her job and she took it very seriously. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): Now, with the next generation leading the monarchy into a new area, Parker Bowles says he is optimistic and excited for the future. PARKER BOWLES: It`s been a big change for the U.K. of late. You know, we are in a lot of trouble with our financial situation, with our political situation. [08:15:00] And I think that it`s no surprise that the one ray of light, at the moment, is -- I have to get used to the queen. BUSH HAGER (on camera): Yes. PARKER BOWLES: Is his majesty and my aunt, and also Kate and William. BUSH HAGER (on camera): Yes. PARKER BOWLES: You know. I think that the queen, before she died was very smart about making sure that the four of them were front and center to the public and were showing that they actually are working. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): Parker Bowles now focuses on his business called Cinema Lab, restoring old movie theaters in the U.S. PARKER BOWLES: And it was really spurned on by seeing my daughter and her friends and my friends` daughters and sons, all hanging out at CVS car parks, or whatever it may be. BUSH HAGER (on camera): There was no movie theater for them to go? PARKER BOWLES: There`s no center. We want to bring back the community. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): That need of community and a place to come together is universal, whether it`s in London or across the pond in a small town in New Jersey. BUSH HAGER (on camera): If somebody had told you when you were 18, you are going to live in New Jersey when you get older, what would you have said? PARKER BOWLES: I`d say, what`s New Jersey, probably? Truly. But I -- it`s the best decision I ever made. (END VIDEO CLIP) BUSH HAGER: Don`t you love that, what`s New Jersey? KOTB: Wow. BUSH HAGER: It just shows you never know where life is going to take you. MELVIN: Yes. BUSH HAGER: But he talked about how important giving back was to his family. That his dad had three rules. One of them was to be kind. One was to not get caught, what he said, that one that we couldn`t break. And the other one was to do service. And I think that those were good rules to take back to our kids. But do not get caught. MELVIN: CARSON DALY, NBC NEWS HOST: Two out of three ain`t bad. GUTHRIE: Yes. BUSH HAGER: Yes, two out of three is pretty good. But he is a very charming, funny guy. And he said that Camilla is the same way, the queen consort. KOTB: Yes. BUSH HAGER: Is that same way -- has that funny -- KOTB: Wit. BUSH HAGER: -- not humor which -- you know -- KOTB: You -- GUTHRIE: Yes. KOTB: Yes, I was going to say I know someone who loves that kind of humor. GUTHRIE: People say she is fun to -- she`s the one you want to sit next to at a dinner party. KOTB: Yes. BUSH HAGER: Yes. GUTHRIE: That was the word up there in London. KOTB: Cool. GUTHRIE: Cool. KOTB: That was cool. KOTB: Thanks, Jen. MELVIN: Thanks, Jenna. KOTB: That was great. BUSH HAGER: Thank you. KOTB: All right. Mr. Roker, how about a check of the weather? AL ROKER, NBC TODAY WEATHER ANCHOR: All right. Let`s show you what we`ve got. In New Jersey and the other 49 states, we`re looking at some wet weather around the Great Lakes stretching all the way down into Northern Florida. We have also got some snow in the Rockies and up into the Western Plains. For today, temperatures, awfully chili. Alaska 20s and 30s. 80s down in Hawaii. 50s as you make your way into the Pacific Northwest. 80s in Southern Texas on into the southeast. We are looking for plenty of sunshine as you get down mid-Atlantic states down to the Gulf Coast on into the Plains up into the Great Lakes. Some mountain snows out west. Heavy rain for our friends in parts of eastern New England. That`s what`s going on around the country. Here`s what`s happening in your neck of the woods. (LOCAL NEWS) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) ROKER: And that`s your latest weather. Best time of the morning. DALY: I don`t know about that. Let`s go over some of it. ROKER: I think so. MELVIN: No. It`s -- it is. DALY: "POP Start", looking pretty solid today. We`re going to start with "Guardians of the Galaxy". Marvel`s gang of misfits is back together for a holiday special. In the trailer, Mantis and Drax are trying to cheer up their buddy Star-Lord with an extra special Christmas gift. And it leads to one heck of a celebrity cameo. Take a look. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) POM KLEMENTIEFF, ACTRESS: Maybe if we go to Earth for a really wonderful Christmas gift, it would make him happy. Something special he will never forget. DAVE BAUTISTA, ACTOR: What about someone special. KLEMENTIEFF: We are looking for the legendary Kevin Bacon. BAUTISTA: We`re looking for the legendary Kevin Bacon. KLEMENTIEFF: I just said that, Drax. BAUTISTA: But your voice is small and mousy. I think, maybe he didn`t hear you. You`re coming with us, as a Christmas present. (END VIDEO CLIP) DALY: That`s a good present. Have a new year with Kevin Bacon. KOTB: Oh, that`s cool. DALY: It makes perfect sense. ROKER: Fantastic. DALY: "The Guardians of the Galaxy" holiday special is going to start streaming November 25th on Disney Plus. MELVIN: That`s fantastic. DALY: Next up, Sir Elton John. It`s been almost 50 years since the "Rocket Man" launched into his superstardom with that legendary performance at Dodger Stadium. Next month, it`ll be a full circle moment when Elton makes that same venue his final stop in the north American farewell tour. KOTB: Wow. DALY: The Grammy is going to return for the show that`s set to live stream on Disney Plus. MELVIN: Wow. [08:20:00] DALY: The three-hour broadcast is going to pay tribute to the singer and his iconic 1975 Dodger Stadium concert. In a statement, Elton sharing his excitement for the upcoming show, calling it truly extra special. And you can catch that on November 20th. KOTB: Wow. DALY: That`ll be great. MELVIN: All right. DALY: Next up -- you owe me $5. Taylor Swift, made it in "POP Start", three for three this week. MELVIN: Every day. DALY: Seems like "Midnights" is everywhere. Swift`s new album has been showing up also in some pretty unexpected places, including one city`s local traffic report. You might remember Sheila Watko from our Philadelphia station. Over the summer, Sheila worked in more than a dozen Beyonce songs, like, titles of the songs in her live report to celebrate the release of "Renaissance". Well, she`s back. MELVIN: Uh-oh. DALY: She went full Swifty with another amazing music themed segment. Take a look. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SHEILA WATKO, NBC10 PHILADELPHIA ENTERTAINMENT REPORTER AND TRAFFIC ANCHOR: The avenue -- this is not a glitch, Lucy. Looking great out there. Sweet nothing in both directions. This is our karma for dealing with that earlier construction on 95 in Delco. We`re dealing with an earlier vehicle fire. And if we take a wide look at the area, you`re going to see most of the map is actually bejeweled with these green roads. (END VIDEO CLIP) DALY: But Sheila -- KOTB: Go girl. ROKER: Impressive. DALY: -- Sheila got in all 20 tracks. MELVIN: Wow. GUTHRIE: That`s impressive. ROKER: Impressive. DALY: That`s impressive. MELVIN: Wow. GUTHRIE: She`s very clever. ROKER: Yes. DALY: All 20 tracks from "Midnights". MELVIN: Way to go Sheila. KOTB: Cool. DALY: There you go. Next up, People`s Choice Awards. We have a "POP Start" exclusive announcement this morning. The scoop on who is going to be hosting this year`s big show. Uncle al, drum roll please. It is our buddy Kenan Thompson. MELVIN: Yes. DALY: Emmys -- ROKER: He is on fire. DALY: -- just last month. Yes. I think he did the SPs this month -- ROKER: Yes. DALY: -- this year, too? Kenan back to host the PCAs for the second year in a row. Also, he`s nominated comedy TV star category for his work on "SNL". In a statement, Kenan said, I`m so grateful to be nominated. Shoutout to the fans and congrats to all the nominees. Get ready for round two. You can catch Kenan and the 2022 People`s Choice Awards, of course, here on NBC and E!, that`s Tuesday, December 6th. And finally, "Avatar: The Way of the Water". Fans have been excited for this sequel. It`s more than a decade in the making. James Cameron`s epic sci-fi flick is coming. And ahead of its December release in theaters, the cast now opening up about a surprising skill set that they had to learn onset. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JIMMY FALLON, "THE TONIGHT SHOW STARRING JIMMY FALLON" HOST: So, you had to learn how to, like, hold your breath for a long time. SIGOURNEY WEAVER, ACTRESS: We did. FALLON: Because a lot of it is under water. WEAVER: Yes, we had to learn free dive. And the first thing -- and we had this amazing teacher named Kirk Krack who teaches the Navy SEALs. You know, I actually got up to six and a half minutes. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: Minutes? DALY: Six and a half minutes underwater. ROKER: Wow. DALY: In an interview with " The New York Times ," James Cameron said that he didn`t want to use CGI for the underwater sequences -- MELVIN: Wow. DALY: -- because he wanted it to look real. GUTHRIE: Wow. DALY: Which I guess is the Tom Cruise , "Top Gun: Maverick" approach to filmmaking now. ROKER: Yes. NBC senior consumer investigative correspondent Vicky Nguyen is here. She`s got everything we need to know. Hey, Vicky. Hey, good morning, Hoda, Savannah and Craig. [07:40:00] NGUYEN: Travel experts are calling fall the shoulder season. It`s that period after Labor Day but before Christmas, and vacation prices in a lot of places typically go way down. In this tough economy, many families who put off their summer vacations are now taking advantage. This morning we have the trips you can book right now to get the most bang and family fun for your buck. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) NGUYEN (voice-over): Move over summer vacation fall is now the hot season for family getaways. More than a quarter of American travelers say they plan to take a trip in October. Travel agency sales for vacation airline tickets up 9% this fall, and average ticket prices way down for many family friendly destinations. Flights to Honolulu now 30% less, Denver down 20%, and Fort Lauderdale 15% less, with working remotely making vacations easier than ever for working parents. Many are itching to get away after being homebound during the pandemic. DANNY GENUNG, CEO, HARR TRAVEL: Compared to last fall, we`re seeing an almost 500% increase in families booking close and travel. NGUYEN (voice-over): Mom Stacy Mackenzie from Maine is actually pulling her three kids out of school this week for a long postponed vacation to Disney World and Universal Studios in Orlando. STACY MACKENZIE, MOTHER: We decided to go in the fall just because I thought it would be cooler weather and less people. NGUYEN: This vacation was too good to pass up after all that time cooped up. MACKENZIE: Yes, yes. And I`m one of those that cries at Disney commercials because I want to go so bad. So we are so excited to be going I`m so excited. NGUYEN (voice-over): Though average hotel rates are higher, up 22% compared to last year, demand is still soaring with the number of rooms booked in September surpassing the same month in 2019 for the first time. If you want the best vacation deals for your family, experts say consider getting onboard a cruise. Book a future trip this week on Royal Caribbean and Norwegian, and your kids can sail for free. Blackout dates excluded. With COVID vaccine requirements now eliminated, families are signing up in droves. Nebraska mom, Miriam Hamilton, her husband and twin boys just went on an eight day Caribbean cruise for 50% off the regular price. MIRIAM HAMILTON, MOTHER: Prices are always better for traveling in the fall. It`s usually quieter for the kids. The activities are not as full for kids so they get better chances at doing things and doing them more often. (END VIDEOTAPE) KOTB: All right, Vicky. And there are some people who do not want to pull their kids out of school. Is there an option for them for a cheaper fall vacation? NGUYEN: Well, definitely if you don`t want to pull your kids out of school, Thanksgiving week going overseas for that dream European vacation. That`s the time to go because they don`t celebrate over there, great prices. If you want to go this month, Hoda, October, San Diego is your destination. KOTB: Oh is it? NGUYEN: All kinds of deals on restaurants, attractions, hotels for kids. You (inaudible) the kids out. GUTHRIE: I love San Diego. It`s a good city. OK, cool. KOTB: Thank you, Vic. MELVIN: So this time of the year. GUTHRIE: All right. Let`s check the weather outside the answer. ROKER: You know, a lot of folks take Mississippi River cruises. Well guess what, hey, those have been delayed or some canceled. Take a look at the Mississippi River. The not so mighty Mississippi, it`s dry and it`s causing big problems for shipping. This was late September last year. You can see how lush it is. This year, October of 2020, look at how dry it is. And that is continuing. And in fact we are looking at record low river levels. Memphis reaching its lowest river level since 1954. And the big problem is the drought. When this is an economic lifeline, the Mississippi River, $13 billion in shipping, a 35,000 related jobs. It accounts -- get this, 92% of our nation`s agricultural exports. So it is a lifeline literally, and the big problem has been the extensive drought in the western half of the Mississippi River basin. Problem is going into the winter, doesn`t look like we`re going to get much relief, so going to continue to have problems along the Mighty Mississippi. For Today, we`re looking at sunshine returning through the southeast into the gulf, plenty of sun from Texas on up into the plains, some mountain snows where they`re going to use that for those great ski resorts and we`re looking at sunshine from San Diego, some showers in Seattle. That`s what`s going on around the country. Here`s what`s happening in your neck of the woods. (LOCAL WEATHER) ROKER: And that is your latest weather. Guys? GUTHRIE: Thank you, Al. By the way, you`re about to hit the road for a very special lend-a-hand. ROKER: Yes. We`re really, really thrilled to be doing this. We`re going to see you tomorrow morning from Fort Myers Beach, Florida. [07:45:00] This is one month after Hurricane Ian roared ashore. We`re going to give you a firsthand look at a community`s resilience and determination to rebuild. Plus, we`re going to meet some heroes who are putting their own recovery on hold just to help others. We`re looking forward to sharing their inspiring stories live from Fort Myers Beach, Florida tomorrow on Today, in our great station down there, WBBH NBC2. We`re going to be working with them as well. KOTB: Cool. MELVIN: I love that you`re doing that. I love that you`re doing that. Up next, to rake or not to rake, apparently that is the question this morning. This morning scientists have been answered that a lot of you are really going to love. We`ll have that for you right after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (CLIP FROM "IT`S THE GREAT PUMPKIN CHARLIE BROWN") MELVIN: Classic, classic. KOTB: Yes. MELVIN: Back with our beloved holiday special, "It`s the Great Pumpkin Charlie Brown." And, Carson, there`s reason we picked that scene. CARSON DALY, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: There`s got to be a reason for that. That means fall is here. Pesky task of raking leaves but that chore might be a thing of the past. According to experts, leaving at least some of those leaves on the ground can actually help your lawn improving the health of grass and encouraging plant growth. Let`s discuss it and let`s predicate this by saying I don`t rake my leaves anymore. I have when you landscaping engineers to do that. MELVIN: There you go. GUTHRIE: I like that. KOTB: Carson, did you rake when you were a kid? DALY: Yes. KOTB: Did your parents make you? DALY: Yes. MELVIN: Of course. KOTB: Did your parents make you? ROKER: Absolutely. And in fact, I did -- when I was in high school, I did a whole thing. A whole research project to convince my father that we did not have to rake leaves. And that we just take the leaf catcher, that lawnmower, and mulch it (inaudible). And I`ve talked to the Queens` cooperative extension guy. He said it`s fine. ROKER: -- for a while DALY: But I love it after the leaves have been raked, and then just a few kind of scattered on the green lawn, how beautiful that looks. KOTB: Yes, it`s cool. headline: Today for October 27, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. It`s Thursday. Big developments overnight in two key races that kind of decides who`s in charge in Washington. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: With just 12 days to go until the midterms, we`re going to break it all down for you. It is October 27th. This is Today. New accusations, another woman comes forward claiming Herschel Walker urged her to have an abortion. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I do not believe that Herschel is morally fit to be a U.S. senator. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: While in Pennsylvania, John Fetterman addresses his debate performance. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LT. GOV. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATOR CANDIDATE: During that debate wasn`t exactly easy. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: We got it all covered. Crisis mode, hospitals nationwide being forced to take drastic measures to handle the tripledemic surge of flu, COVID, and RSV. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Not only are there a lot of sick kids right now, there`s no place for them to go. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Just ahead, the new message from health officials all families need to hear. Breaking overnight, a new wave of protests in Iran, despite authorities intensifying a brutal crackdown, this morning the powerful scenes playing out across the country. Under pressure, Tesla reportedly facing a criminal investigation over its autopilot claims after a string of high profile crashes. So has the popular automaker misled consumers about how safe their cars really are? Those stories, plus, members only. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Contrary to popular belief, you can be any age to join AARP. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: From AARP to AAA, the surprising clubs you can sign up for to save big. And feeling lucky. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Here are tonight`s winning numbers. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: With no winner overnight, the Powerball jackpot jumps to a whopping $800 million, one of the largest prizes ever now up for grabs. Today, Thursday, October 27th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Well, good morning. It is so good to see you, happy that you`re here joining us. It is a Thursday morning. GUTHRIE: Well, you got it lined up if you want to get those Powerball tickets. The drawing is this weekend so you have time to get your tickets but jackpots up to 800 million. KOTB: It is. We`re going to have a lot more on jackpot fever coming up. But we`re going to start with another big countdown. We`re talking about the one to the midterm. GUTHRIE: Yes, 12 days to go now, and the spotlight is intensifying on two major races in Georgia and Pennsylvania. What happens there could impact the lives of every American. KOTB: Here`s what`s at stake, the balance of power in the Senate and the direction of key issues from the economy to abortion rights to rising crime rates, NBC`s senior Washington correspondent Hallie Jackson has the very latest for us. Hey, Hallie, good morning. HALLIE JACKSON, NBC NEWS SENIOR WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT: Hey Hoda, hey Savannah. You have laid out the stakes and it is crunch time now, right, for candidates in these really important really close races with big guns like former presidents in both parties set to hit the campaign trail in the coming days. And the focus today turning to Georgia, where there`s a new abortion allegations surfacing, and one of the country`s most closely watched matchups. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JACKSON (voice-over): With less than two weeks to go this morning, the future of the Senate could hang on to key states with neck and neck races in Pennsylvania and Georgia, where there`s now another twist, Republican Herschel Walker who`s campaigned on an anti-abortion platform now denying a new allegation from a second woman who says Walker pressured her to have an abortion in the early 90s. HERSCHEL WALKER (R-GA), SENATOR CANDIDATE: What I`m saying, this is a lie and I`ve said it once and I`ve moved on my campaign. JACKSON (voice-over): The anonymous woman sharing her voice only came forward in a Zoom press conference arranged by Attorney Gloria Allred. The accuser saying after she became pregnant in 1993, Walker encouraged her to have an abortion, adding she first couldn`t go through with the procedure, but that Walker encouraged her to go back driving her to a Dallas clinic where she had the abortion. The woman explaining why she`s speaking up now. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I am a registered Independent and I voted for Donald Trump in both elections. I do not believe that Herschel is morally fit to be a U.S. senator. JACKSON (voice-over): NBC News has not verified her allegations and the woman did not provide evidence Walker was involved in her abortion. WALKER: I`m done with this foolishness. JACKSON (voice-over): The Republican candidate and former football star also denied allegations earlier this month from another former girlfriend who says Walker paid for her abortion in 2009. In a statement the campaign for Walker`s opponent, Senator Raphael Warnock says Walker has a problem with the truth, a problem answering questions, and a problem taking responsibility for his actions. That match up, very close with recent polling showing Warnock leading by just five points. And in another closely watched race in Pennsylvania a tossup with polls ranking Democratic Lieutenant Governor John Fetterman and Republican candidate Dr. Mehmet Oz within the margin of error. [07:05:11] FETTERMAN: During that debate wasn`t exactly easy, you know, I knew it wasn`t going to be easy after, you know, having a stroke after five months. JACKSON (voice-over): Fetterman appearing at a campaign rally in Pittsburgh after raising $2 million, his team says, in the hours after his one and only debate against Republican Mehmet Oz. Fetterman facing questions about his at times halting debate performance with lingering auditory processing issues after a stroke five months ago. Oz also on the campaign trail hammering the issue of crime and on defense against a new Democratic ad highlighting his debate comments on abortion. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is who Dr. Oz wants in charge of women`s health care decisions. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATOR CANDIDATE: I want women, doctors, local political leaders, local political leaders. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTHRIE: Meanwhile, Hallie, the President hitting the campaign trail today, what do you expect? JACKSON: He is all about the economy, Savannah, in this kind of closing argument here trying to highlight his administration`s record on something we know that voters care about the economy plus cost of living. The top issue that voters say matters to them come Election Day. The President is going to be at Upstate New York to argue that Democrats economic policies are better than Republicans, even as many GOP candidates have pointed to high inflation in their midterm campaigns. You`ve also got the president`s cabinet fanning out across the country too. All of it is part of this full core press ahead of Election Day. Savannah? GUTHRIE: Twelve days to go. Hallie Jackson, thank you. And we turn now to growing concerns over the dangerous tripledemic of viruses nationwide flu, COVID, and the respiratory illness, RSV. With cases surging, some hospitals even in areas of warmer weather, are running out of beds. NBC national correspondent Gabe Gutierrez is inside Phoenix Children`s Hospital this morning with more. Gabe, good morning. GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Savannah, good morning. It`s only October but doctors here and across the country are dealing with patient numbers that they usually don`t see until much later in winter. And overnight we met one mother who barely heard of RSV until she ended up here with her newborn son. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (voice-over): This morning, the latest wave of child respiratory illnesses is spreading prompting more concerns of a tripledemic this winter. In Arizona, RSV cases are up 344 percent over a typical season. CHEYENNE SHIELDER`S (ph), SON DIAGNOSED WITH RSV: Terrifying, this is serious illness. You know, with him being this young. He doesn`t have an immune system to fight it off. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): Cheyenne Shielder`s (ph) two-month-old son Ryder (ph) was in the hospital overnight. (on camera): What would you tell other parents? SHIELDER: Look up the symptoms of RSV and trust her gut to because I was on the border about coming or not to the hospital. And I feel like I probably should have come a little bit sooner. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): Last year and now this year, Phoenix Children`s Hospital has been dealing with an unusually high number of RSV cases, though the facility is not at capacity, it`s bracing for a rough winter DR. WASSIM BALLAN, PHOENIX CHILDREN`S HOSPITAL CHIEF OF INFECTIOUS DISEASES: COVID-19 combined with a potentially bad influenza season and now we`re seeing RSV going up at the same time, that obviously makes us concerned that we might get into this triple pandemic situation. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): This year, even western and southern states with warmer temperatures are seeing a significant rise in RSV and flu cases. In Arizona, 87 percent of pediatric hospital beds are occupied, in Texas 91 percent, Seattle Children`s tells NBC News it`s at 200 percent capacity in the ER. DR. ASHISH JHA, WHITE HOUSE COVID-19 RESPONSE COORDINATOR: Under normal circumstances, about 90 percent of kids end up getting RSV at least once, by the time there are two. Because of the pandemic, some of the kind of standard patterns have been disrupted so we`re seeing a lot of RSV at once. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): Parents now worried sick across the country from San Diego where Fernanda Costanarez (ph) is caring for baby Alejandra (ph). FERNANDA COSTANAREZ (ph), DAUGHTER DIAGNOSED WITH RSV: She was struggling to breathe. She was struggling breathing. And we got scared because she had no color at all on her skin. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): To Washington, D.C. where three-year-old Izzy Banki (ph) is recovering. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Nobody wants to like hold their kid down and hold a mask on their face. And so she`s screaming and trying and trying to rip the breathing tubes out. And that breaks your heart as a parent. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ: And while COVID cases are trending downward nationwide, right now, there are concerns about new strains this winter. And of course, Savannah, concerns about that flu season that is already hitting many states hard around the country. Savannah? GUTHRIE: All right, Gabe Gutierrez, thank you. KOTB: Meantime, new unrest is rocking Iran with massive protests across the country more than a month after a young woman`s death while being held by the nation`s morality police. Some of those demonstrations turned deadly, emitted ongoing crackdown and that`s led to new sanctions from the United States, NBC`s chief international correspondent Keir Simmons has been following this story for us. Hey Keir, good morning. [07:10:00] KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS CHIEF INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Hoda, good morning to you. And we`re just getting more incredibly impactful video from the city of Mahabad in north western Iran. Take a look at this. This is a just this morning. You can see protesters targeting a building there. Later they seem to be throwing stones there. Looks like there is tear gas. The Kurdish rights group that posted this video says a number of government buildings have been taken over and that it`s also rounds the funeral of a man who was shot dead during protests yesterday. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) SIMMONS (voice-over): This morning, a powerful image seen around the world. A young woman not wearing a headscarf stands on the roof of a car hands in the air as crowds attempt to reach the grave of Mahsa Amini. And near the cemetery, this video from an independent Kurdish human rights organization, captioned the resistance is glorious. Huge numbers across Iran determined to mourn and to protest the death of the 22-year-old, marking 40 days after she died in the hospital, the morality police targeting her for allegedly violating the country`s strict clothing code. In the capital of Tehran, clashes with the security forces and the sound of gunfire. In Mahsa`s hometown, they shouted women, life, freedom. And these demonstrators daring to chant freedom, freedom, enough of the despotism. Then images like this one, smoke rising told them another violent crackdown there. Reports say live rounds were used and tear gas. The Iranian authorities switching off the internet in the city. But a semi official news agency reporting at least 10,000 demonstrated. Thousands of miles away the White House announcing sanctions targeting more than a dozen Iranian officials. KARINE JEAN-PIERRE , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: Our message to Iran is very, very clear, stop killing your people and stop sending weapons to Russia to kill Ukrainians. SIMMONS (voice-over): A dramatic change from earlier this year when the Biden administration was trying to negotiate a nuclear deal with Iran. But this morning, there is no sign of compromise in Tehran and no backing down by these young female protesters and the many men out on the streets in support. (END VIDEOTAPE) SIMMONS : And just underscoring how incredibly tense it is in Iran, Hoda, a news of a shooting that was not related to the protests, 15 worshippers were killed, ISIS claiming responsibility for that. The government blaming foreign terrorists. It just emphasizes how incredible it is that these protesters are coming out on the streets day after day to support Mahsa Amini. KOTB: Yes, and worth repeating, too, that as you said, it`s not just women on those streets, it looked like equal numbers of men that we were seeing in those videos all with the same cause. All right, Keir Simmons for us in London. Kier, thank you. GUTHRIE: Back home, we`ve got new concerns about energy bills this winter. We haven`t even handed out the candy to trick or treaters. But in recent weeks, a lot of us have gotten that early taste of the cold and it doesn`t bode well for what`s to come. NBC`s Tom Costello over in the Bronx with that story this morning. Tom, good morning. TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Hi, Savannah, we are at an oil terminal facility here in the Bronx. So oil comes out of this facility and into homes across the Northeast. And millions of people use heating oil to heat their homes in the Northeast leading oil stocks right now, the lowest in decades. But there is no talk of rationing. It doesn`t matter if you heat your home with heating oil, gas, or electricity, you`re going to pay more to stay warm this winter. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) COSTELLO (voice-over): From the Northeast and Midwest to parts of the south, Mother Nature has already given millions of us a sneak peek at what`s ahead. And this morning, the forecast for America`s collective wallet this winter may also be a bit frigid. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It`s a very, very high bill. COSTELLO (voice-over): Across the board, energy costs are expected to be higher than last year. The federal government expects the biggest jumps for customers who use heating oil or natural gas to stay warm up, 27 and 28 percent. Two factors are driving the spike the global market affected by Russia`s war in Ukraine and OpEx plan to slash production of crude oil. The supply of heating oil in New England is also about a third of where it typically is. BRIAN DEESE, NATIONAL ECONOMIC COUNCIL DIRECTOR: We are operating right now at unacceptably low inventory levels. COSTELLO (voice-over): Still, and this is important, experts say that is not cause for concern. CHRIS HERB, CONNECTICUT ENERGY MARKETERS ASSOCIATION PRESIDENT: Supply is tight. That is undeniable. We have enough fuel to supply people`s needs at this time. And for over a century, our industry has never failed. COSTELLO (voice-over): Right now, the cost for a gallon of heating oil is about 5.70 per gallon. That`s up more than $2 from last year with eight states paying even more. DONNA HUBER (ph), RHODE ISLAND RESIDENT: There are people that are going to have to choose between feeding their families or heating their home. And that`s scary. You know, it`s really scary. COSTELLO (voice-over): Experts say the best ways to say, check windows for leaks and seal or replace if needed. Adjust your thermostat when you`re sleeping or out of the house. And schedule routine services to maintain your heating systems. [07:15:05] UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This will heat about 2,000 square feet. COSTELLO (voice-over): Donna Huber (ph) in Rhode Island is among many Americans looking for alternatives to stay warm. Recently installing a wood stove in her home. HUBER (ph): I bought three quarts of wood for under $800. If I wanted to heat my house solely on the wood, that would take me through the season. That`s less than half of a tank of oil. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTHRIE: Tom, there are also local programs that people can turn to for help. COSTELLO: You know, this is important, every state has Home Energy Assistance Programs, so if you have trouble paying your bill, and the bills are going to get expensive this winter, turn to those programs. And you might even check with your own utility company to see if they offer assistance. And by the way, if you can pay your bill, if it`s no problem, and you can round off, you know, most states offer that option, roundup your bill to help those in need, this may be the win or two offer an extra dollar to help those in need. Savannah? GUTHRIE: Tom, it`s a great idea, round up. Tom, thank you very much. KOTB: All right, 7:15 time to cut to the chase. You did not win the big prize in last night`s Powerball. But we got good news, nobody else won on the jackpot, once again on the rise. So let`s look at the latest number, $800 million. That`s the latest number. It`ll probably even go up from there. So if someone wins it, it would be the second largest Powerball jackpot of all time. The next drawing Saturday night, you got plenty of time to get your tickets. Start planning what you`re going to do with your dough. Yes, plenty of time. GUTHRIE: All right, let`s get a first check of the weather, Al is on the road this morning in Fort Myers Beach, Florida. Sun is coming up, a pretty shot there. Al, good morning. AL ROKER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Hey, good morning, guys. And we`re here to lend a hand to this hard hit community, ground zero for Hurricane Ian, which hit a month ago tomorrow. We`ll talk about that in just a little bit. But let`s talk about the risk of for some more severe weather as we head down south, we`re talking Texas and parts of Oklahoma. Storm hazards today, wind gusts of up to 60 miles per hour, isolated tornadoes, damaging hail. Tomorrow that moves to the east to eastern and southern Texas, Victoria, Houston on into San Antonio for more gusts and the possibility of tornadoes. Heavy rain as well, some places localized flooding possible. So as you see this wide swath of one to three inches of rain and the tropics not done yet. We`ve got two areas of development that we`re watching currently anywhere from a 40 to 50 percent chance. The one area we`re watching that somewhere down south of Bermuda subtropical depression, possible by the weekend. It`s going to be meandering throughout the southeast. We`re going to be watching that spinning offshore throughout the weekend and we`ll continue to track it. We`re going to get to your local forecast coming up in the next 30 seconds. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (LOCAL NEWS) ROKER: And that`s your latest weather, more from Fort Myers Beach, Florida in just a little bit. Guys? GUTHRIE: I`m excited, Al. You`re going to do a lot of good out there this morning. Just ahead, word that Tesla is facing a criminal investigation this morning over claims about some of its cars. Stephanie Gosk is with us. STEPHANIE GOSK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Yes, Savannah. This has to do with that autopilot we`ve talked a lot about. According to Reuters, Tesla has been under investigation since last year. There have been a number of high profile crashes that they are looking into. And it is a criminal probe. Back to you. [07:19:15] KOTB: All right, also then Vicky Nguyen, she`s going to be here to save you some money. She scouted out some unexpected places that you can find some deals including there`s a surprising trend that has young people joining AARP. But first, this is Today on NBC. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) GUTHRIE: Still ahead, an image touching hearts across the country. KOTB: Yes, have you seen this? A Kentucky coal miner who raced right from work to take his three-year-old son to a basketball game, we`re going to hear from him and tell you something really special that came from that photo. But first, your local news and weather. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:26:21] (LOCAL NEWS) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (LOCAL NEWS) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:30:19] GUTHRIE: We are back 7:30. What a pretty sunrise in Fort Myers Beach, Florida. It`s been hard times there in the last month, one month since Ian hit. Well, Al Roker has arrived along with our lend a hand truck. And we are really hoping to do some good there this morning. We`ll see that community really coming together battling to rebuild and it`s happening. We`ve got some special things planned. SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: It`s good. KOTB: I love when Roker arrives. Meantime, inside Studio 1A Sheinelle is here, Craig is on assignment. Shall we get to our 7:30 headlines? JONES: Let`s do it. KOTB: All right, let`s do it. A Wisconsin man has been convicted of killing six people injuring dozens of others when he drove his SUV through a Christmas parade. It took the jury a little more than three hours to find Darrell Brooks guilty of all 76 charges. Police say he drove his vehicle into the parade in downtown Waukesha last November, despite police warnings to stop. headline: MEET THE PRESS for November 6, 2022, NBC
story_text: [09:00:18] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CHUCK TODD, HOST, NBC`S "MEET THE PRESS WITH CHUCK TODD": This Sunday... PRESIDENT JOSEPH R. BIDEN, JR.: Vote. Get out and vote. TODD: ... battle for control. GOV. RON DESANTIS, (R) FLORIDA: I think Republicans are going to win the House and the Senate. I think they`re going to do both. TODD: Republicans need to flip just one seat to gain control of the Senate and only five seats to win control of the House. KEITH PEKAUI, CANDIDATE FOR U.S. REPRESENTATIVE, (R) ILLINOIS: I want you to watch Nancy Pelosi hand me that gavel. (APPLAUSE) TODD: This morning, the results of our final NBC News poll before the midterms and what it says about the GOP`s chances of taking complete power back on Capitol Hill. Plus, democracy at risk. BIDEN: You can`t love your country only when you win. TODD: President Biden issues a dire warning about election deniers and the risk for our electoral system. But will those warnings from Democrats resonate with economically challenged swing voters in the final push before Election Day? And, very soon... FORMER PRESIDENT DONALD J. TRUMP: I will very, very, very probably do it again, OK? TODD: Will former President Trump announce his 2024 bid before we finish counting the 2022 vote? My guest this morning, Florida`s Republican Senator Rick Scott , the chair of the GOP`s campaign arm; and New York Congressman Sean Patrick Maloney , the chair of the House Democratic campaign arm. Plus... (UNKNOWN): Are you ready to meet the press? TODD: Seventy-five years, from presidents to prime ministers, dictators to Civil Rights leaders, we mark 75 years as the destination where newsmakers come to make news. Joining me for insight and analysis are NBC News chief White House correspondent Kristen Welker; former Democratic senator from Missouri Claire McCaskill; former Republican governor of North Carolina Pat McCrory ; and Amy Walter, editor in chief of the "Cook Political Report." Welcome to Sunday. It`s "Meet the Press." ANNOUNCER: From NBC News headquarters in New York, the longest-running show in television history. This is a special edition of "Meet the Press With Chuck Todd." TODD: Well, good Sunday morning. On our 75th birthday, from our election headquarters here at Rockefeller Center in New York City, with just two days until Election Day, more than 40 million people have already cast ballots in the first national election since the January 6th attack on the U.S. Capitol. By the way, we expect a record midterm turnout, 120 million to 125 million, when all the votes are counted. At stake, all 435 House seats. Republicans need a net gain of just five to take control of that chamber. It is the smallest number of seats that the out-of-power party has needed since 1932. Thirty-five Senate seats are at stake this cycle. Republicans, of course, need just one Democratic seat to flip control of that chamber. There are also 36 governor`s races, including in some key 2024 presidential battlegrounds like Arizona, Florida, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. And in our final pre-election poll, conducted over the last three days, Republicans do appear to have the momentum. Just how big is that momentum? The question is whether Democrats can prevent what former President Obama once called a "shellacking." The president`s travel in the final stretch says it all about how the Democrats believe the election is going. Outside of the Philadelphia stop with Obama yesterday, President Biden has spent the final days of his campaign not in purple states but in blue states, California, New Mexico, Illinois and New York, where he`ll be campaigning later today in suburban New York City, Westchester County. And here`s why. Biden`s job approval rating sits at 44 percent in this final NBC News poll. By the way, all-time low with independents. His approval rating is just 28 percent. And let me put this in context for you. What does a job rating mean? Some people believe it`s the single most important indicator to understand where a midterm election is going. Bill Clinton`s 44 percent job approval rating translated into a 54-seat loss for his party. A 45 percent job approval rating for President Obama in 2010 translated to 63 lost House seats. Forty-six percent for President Trump, 40 House seat loss for his party. So what will 44 percent give us? And here`s, to me, the number you probably ought to care about the most in this poll, the state of the U.S. economy. Eighty-one percent tell us they are dissatisfied. This is the second highest number we`ve ever recorded. The last time it was this high was just before the 2010 election. And you know how that one went. All right. The generic congressional ballot here. We have it dead even, 47- 47. It`s a slight uptick for the Republicans from two weeks ago, when it was 47-46. Here`s something to keep in mind. Essentially a tie race probably gives the Republicans the five or six seats they need. [09:05:06] For every percentage point that they lead the Democrats, that`s probably anywhere from another five to 10 seats that would be added to their total. Just something to watch for on election night. All right. This is key, and this is something that should make Democrats relieved this weekend. Interest in this election, enthusiasm. Democrats have now matched the Republicans, dead even. In 2018 they had a slight lead. And of course the Democrats had the better night. But let me go inside the numbers, and why there`s still some warning signs here for the Democrats. There are two enthusiasm numbers in particular that I want to point -- I want to highlight here, African-American voters and young voters. And as you can see, remember Democrats had a good night in 2018. And right now African-American voters are not quite at their 2018 levels, and young voters are not quite at their -- at their 2018 levels, but look at seniors. Seniors are a little bit more. So this is why Republicans feel good about the end of this. We also asked folks to send us what message -- if you could send a message with your vote to Congress, what would you say with it? And here`s our word cloud response. And as you can see, "Fix Economy," the number one message that was sent from voters. And essentially tied for second here, "End Partisanship" and "Women`s Rights." So essentially the three big issues of the economy, abortion rights and the democracy, all represented here. And you can see the voters are engaged on this. By the way, given what happened to Paul Pelosi, we asked voters about the current climate of political violence. Voters are now more likely to view our political rhetoric as an important contributing factor, rather than seeing what happened as some isolated incident. And when we asked who is responsible for this elevated rhetoric, social media companies come out on top, almost universally blamed for our current political climate. Cable news media nearly matches them, then Trump, then Republican officials, Democratic officials, and President Biden there at the bottom. Let`s turn back now to the battle for the House. Because I want to point out some key numbers here for you to keep track of. In the seven times since the Truman era, when the president`s job rating has been below 50 percent in his first midterm election, which is what we`re staring at with this one, that president`s party has lost an average of 43 House seats. And guess what? This cycle, there are 44 Democratic held seats that are rated as lean or toss-up by the Cook Political Report, and there`s just 20 Republican held seats that are in those same categories in the House battleground. In 2018, you can see it was a much more lopsided battleground here, with the Republicans basically defending almost everything and Democrats barely defending anything. In this cycle, the defense for the Democrats includes the district where Congressman Sean Patrick Maloney is running after redistricting. He also chairs the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee charged with getting House Democrats elected and keeping their majority. And Congressman Maloney joins me now. Welcome back to "Meet the Press," two days before the election, sir. REP. SEAN PATRICK MALONEY , CHAIR OF DEMOCRATIC CONGRESSIONAL CAMPAIGN COMMITTEE & (D) NEW YORK: Good to be with you. TODD: Well, let me start with this. What constitutes -- what constitutes a good night for Democrats on Tuesday? MALONEY: We`re going to hold this majority. That constitutes a good night. We`re going to defend our -- our mainstream democratic values against the threats to our democracy. We`re going to protect women`s reproductive freedom and voting rights. We`re going to give you cheaper prices for gas and groceries, healthcare and housing. And we`re going to give you safer streets by funding good local policing with accountability, but also doing something about gun violence. And that is a plan for the future. And because our candidates have real plans, they`re going to do better than people think on Tuesday night. TODD: Do you acknowledge, though, that all the data seems to point in the other direction? MALONEY: Oh, look, I think the polls you just showed shows it`s basically tied with the numbers in 2018, which, if I recall, was a pretty good year for Democrats. I think this race is razor-close. And I think everybody who cares about the extremism in this MAGA movement, the racism, the anti- Semitism, the violence, needs to get out and vote. And that`s not just Democrats. That`s independents and fair-minded Republicans who watched the January 6th hearings, who know what we`re up against, who listen to Republicans oppose things like Social Security and Medicare, want to put it on the chopping block every five years. That`s your next guest, by the way. That`s his plan. And we`ve got a plan to cap seniors` out-of-pocket costs in Medicare. There are big differences. I want everybody to go out and vote. TODD: If you lose your race, does that mean this was a wave? MALONEY: Oh, come on. I`ve always had a tough race, Chuck. I beat a Republican to have this seat. I`m the first gay person ever elected to Congress from New York. I`m raising an inter-racial family in a county Donald Trump won in 2016 by 20 points. It has always been improbable that I would serve in the Congress. I have to go out and earn it every two years. And I`ve... TODD: So you don`t believe... MALONEY: I`ve won five times because... TODD: ... if you happen to lose, you don`t think that somehow is part of the national wave that something -- that you got, sort of, rolled out that way? [09:10:10] MALONEY: Well, I guess what I`m not going to do is play hypotheticals with you when we`re two days out from an election, and... TODD: Fair enough. MALONEY: ... I`ve won times in a district where everybody said I couldn`t. I mean, if I -- if we were having this conversation in 2012, you would have made fun of me for even running, because I was running against a Republican incumbent with a bunch of money, and nobody -- nobody thought I could win. So people like me weren`t supposed to serve in Congress from New York until I did it. So with all due respect, what Democrats are going to do right now is going to go out and fight with everything we have got, for seniors who need costs capped in Medicare; for people worried about gun violence in our schools; for people who want to have a real plan to go forward together, without the anger and the fear and the hatred, fighting for women`s reproductive freedom and voting rights. That`s what we`re going to do. And I`m going to let the pundits, kind of, make predictions. We`re going to let the voters speak on Tuesday. TODD: I want to talk about a couple of messaging things that we`ve seen pop up. There`s a lot of blue state Democrats on the House level that are in these competitive seats, Oregon, New York, California. And I`m curious, do you think the abortion message doesn`t work as well in blue states because voters don`t believe it will ever be illegal in their state, but it does work pretty well for some of your red state Democrats? Have you noticed this yourself? MALONEY: Well, of course. When -- when abortion is literally being taken away by an initiative like in Kansas, of course people are going to pay more attention. But of course Pat Ryan won a race none of you thought he could win in upstate New York, leaning in to protecting women`s reproductive freedom, right here in New York. My own opponent pretends there`s no threat to it in New York, but of course he voted to ban abortion when he was in the assembly. And if he had his way, every state in the country could ban it for any reason without exceptions. So the threats are real. If these guys control Congress, the first thing they`re going to do is they are going to try to pass a national abortion ban. And bear in mind, 75 percent of the Republicans now in the Congress support a national abortion ban. That means California and New York and other big blue states are on the chopping block, too. And so of course they want to disguise it and try to confuse or lull voters into a false sense of security. But when the wolf comes to the door, it`s wearing sheep`s clothing. And that`s what voters in blue states need to understand. TODD: Do you -- do you believe the Democrats should have worked sooner on getting a better crime message? It`s an argument Stan Greenberg, Bill Clinton`s longtime pollster, has made, and said that Democrats didn`t learn, even though many in the party said the right things about avoiding the phrase "defund the police," that there wasn`t enough done fixing the problems that clearly showed up in 2020 House races. What say you? MALONEY: Well, let`s look at the record. I mean, for one thing, we passed the most important gun safety legislation in 28 years, stood up to the NRA , stood up to the big gun lobbies, and no Republicans except a handful were willing to help. That`s really important. In addition to that, we have passed the most important local police funding, $300 million over the next five years, out of the House. That`s called the Invest to Protect Act. And if you look at our frontline candidates, my goodness, whether it`s Steven Horsford in Nevada, who`s put billions of dollars through his legislation into violence prevention initiatives that are evidence-based, or you`re talking about Matt Cartwright in Pennsylvania, who`s been a leader in getting cop grants out there to hire and train more police officers. In my own district, I`ve brought back $7 million for local police departments, including new technologies like ShotSpotter technology, like license plate readers, like body cameras. We`ve got a record of delivering for public safety. And we`re proud of that record. TODD: Yes, and there`s a bill, though, that was going to be a pretty big bill that every single national law enforcement group supported. It was called the Community Oriented Policing Services bill. "COPS" was short of it. The -- let me show you the bill`s co-sponsors here because it`s a who`s who of who Republicans are targeting in these House races, Tom O`Halleran , Arizona 1; Elissa Slotkin , Michigan 7; Angie Craig , Minnesota 2; Elaine Luria , Virginia 2; and Abigail Spanberger , Virginia 7. Was it a mistake not getting this bill passed? You could have gotten it passed. These -- these members of Congress needed it, and they`re all on the front line. MALONEY: I just told you, those members were in the lead on passing $300 million of funding for police departments under 125 officers. That`s every precinct -- every town, and cop, you know, in my district is in a department under 125 officers. Those members took the lead. And so the fact is that, together with the gun safety legislation, which the cops demand, because they don`t want to roll up to a scene and have a kid with an AR-15. We have done real things. Now, let`s contrast that to what our opponents have done, which is nothing on gun violence, which is nothing on supporting our police. My own opponent cut police budgets in Westchester County when he had the chance. [09:15:02] I mean, my goodness, at some point the record should matter here. And we`ve got a strong record of supporting police. TODD: Final question here. Midterm results are very much always connected to presidential job rating. How much responsibility do you think President Biden has for this political environment? MALONEY: I think the president gets a bum rap. By the way, he`s been a leader on public safety his whole career. He`s also fixing our roads and our bridges. He`s bringing jobs back from China. He`s -- he`s capping seniors` out-of-pocket costs in Medicare. He took on the big drug companies. But we`re going to get some clues about the House very early on. [09:50:00] Virginia and Indiana, their polls close by 7:00 p.m., and they`re both fast-counting states. So here`s what we`re going to learn. Elaine Luria , this should be the first district Republicans should be able to pick up. If they`re not picking this up, it`s suddenly a much better night for Democrats than people thought. Virginia 07 and Indiana 01 should be the next two that Republicans flip if they`re going to have as good of a night as they think they`re going to have. Let me add another district here. If for some reason this turns into a red tsunami, keep an eye on the 10th congressional district in Virginia. That was the one Barbara Comstock held. If that flips, then you know a huge Republican night. Now, did African Americans turn out? Two places to watch: Milwaukee County and Philadelphia County. Democrats need huge margins here. And if the African American vote shows up and it looks like 2018, then they should feel pretty good. But if those numbers are lower, then you know that there was a problem. How about young voters? Dane County`s a good place to check in Wisconsin, home of the University of Wisconsin . Centre County`s home of Penn State University . Will the Democrats get these margins and the raw vote that they need? That`s two places to look for. Now as for Republicans, they want a huge rural turnout. Well, Putnam County in Ohio, look at that. He had a 62-point margin in 2018. Will it get bigger? That`s something to watch there. Chattooga County in Georgia, this is Marjorie Taylor Greene`s district. How big will the Republican turnout be? That should matter. And then also, if Republicans are going to have a really good night, they`ve got to improve their numbers in suburban counties. Delaware County`s a place to look here. Well, this is a place Democrats have been inching and eroding the Republican gains here. Will that continue or not? Cherokee County, sort of an exurb if you will of Atlanta. Democrats have been making some progress there. Let`s see what happens in 2022. So bottom line is this -- those are the places to watch. But it`s going to be election week, not election night. JOHN KERRY (D-MA): This war can be ended, and it should be ended now. TIM RUSSERT, NBC NEWS MODERATOR: Full wrath. That`s a very strong statement to the Afghans this morning. headline: The Governor`s Race In Georgia Too Early To Call Between Brian Kemp And Stacey Abrams
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Dozens of governors seats are also in play being driven by issues ranging from inflation to abortion. Blayne Alexander is following the key races. Blayne, what should we know? BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, Lester, when I`ve spoken to voters, both of those issues came up and more. So much of it just depends on the state. And tonight, Lester, many of those key governor`s races are very tight. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) B. ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, it`s not just control of Congress that`s at stake, also what for grabs, 36 critical Governor seats, including here in Georgia, Republican Governor Brian Kemp`s rematch against Stacey Abrams . A win would make her the first Black woman governor in U.S. history. A big focus for Kemp, his early decision to reopen Georgia during COVID. GOV. BRIAN KEMP (R-GA): She was criticizing me for just simply giving you the opportunity to go back to work or to open your business. B. ALEXANDER: Abrams, like many Democrats around the country emphasizing abortion access. STACEY ABRAMS (D-GA), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: We know for women in Georgia, this is the lethal decision. B. ALEXANDER: In Arizona, it`s a marquee matchup between Democrat Katie Hobbs and Kari Lake, a Trump-backed Republican who has repeatedly denied the 2020 election results and is already casting doubt on this election. KARI LAKE (R-AZ), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: We`re so ready for fair elections, aren`t we? I`m worried about tomorrow. KATIE HOBBS (D-AZ), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: When people like Kari Lake denied the results of the election, we stood firm. B. ALEXANDER: TWO other contests to watch feature Democratic incumbents in tight races. Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer in a tough fight against Republican Tudor Dixon and perhaps most surprising in deep blue New York where Governor Kathy Hochul is facing a serious challenge from Republican Lee Zeldin , who is focusing on rising crime. LEE ZELDIN (R-NY) GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: Voters of all walks of life, Republicans, Democrats, and Independents, they`ve had enough. (END VIDEOTAPE) B. ALEXANDER (on camera): And Georgia officials say there have been very few lines at polling places today, they point to a record 2.5 million people who cast early votes. Lester? HOLT: Blayne Alexander, thank you. I want to bring in now our political director and moderator of "MEET THE PRESS," Chuck Todd. Chuck, you`ve been digging into the exit polls. What do voters seem to be most concerned about? CHUCK TODD, NBC NEWS POLITICAL DIRECTOR (on camera): Well, it will not surprise you. The number one issue overall, inflation. What`s interesting is that there`s only a five-point difference. Abortion came in second 27 percent. And then you see the other three issues you saw a lot in TV ads, crime, gun policy, and immigration. Inflation-breaking Republican, abortion-breaking Democrat. Crime-breaking Republican. Gun, if you pick guns, you broke Democrat and immigration by Republican. Let me show you by party. As you can see here, among Democrats, the most important issue was abortion. Among Republicans, the number one issue is inflation. And here`s the tiebreaker perhaps, the difference between getting 49 percent and 51 percent in some of the Senate races. Independents picked inflation. Now, let me give you a little teaser about some of the state polls, Lester. In two of our Senate battlegrounds, abortion topped inflation, Pennsylvania and New Hampshire. Just something to keep in mind tonight as we figure out who`s going to control the Senate. HOLT: Interesting trends starting to emerge. All right, Chuck, thanks very much. And our Chief Washington Correspondent Andrea Mitchell joins us now with some concerns that figured tough numbers about our exit polls. ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Exactly. Well, as Chuck was just pointing out, the top issue was inflation. But abortion was a top concern among a lot more voters than we had expected and crime less than expected. But there`s something else that really stuck out to me. This early exit poll shows that 46 percent of voters say President Biden`s policies are hurting the country. Only 36 percent say they`re helping the country. 16 percent say his policies are not making a difference. Even some of Mr. Biden`s base voters, including Black voters and young voters, are not convinced that his policies are working. The President in the final weeks of the campaign has been saying that this election is a choice between his party and the Republicans and not a referendum on his presidency. But if voters ended up making their decision based on how they feel about his record -- his record, that`s not a good sign for Democrats. Lester? HOLT: All right, Andrea, thanks for that. Washington could look dramatically different in the days to come. How Congress have the Biden administration are strategizing for a big shift. Plus, we`ll take you inside a vote-counting center. Why it could take a while before the full picture of the elections is known. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: The Issue That Turned Out To Be A Game-Changer In States Red And Blue
story_text: [19:20:00] LESTER HOLT: In the wake of the Supreme Court overturning Roe v Wade, the Midterm Elections saw a record number of abortion-related measures on the ballot. And in every state where voters had a direct say, they opted against restricting access. Here`s Yamiche Alcindor. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) YAMICHE ALCINDOR, NBC NEWS WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, Democrats across the country are celebrating sweeping wins for supporters of abortion rights. JOSH SHAPIRO (D-PA), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: A woman`s right to choose one. SEN. MAGGIE HASSAN (D-NH): I will always, always keep fighting to protect a woman`s fundamental freedom. GOV. GRETCHEN WHITMER (D-MI): We will make Michigan a leader, a place where women make their own decisions. ALCINDOR: In Michigan, residents voted to enshrine abortion rights into the state constitution, an issue Governor Gretchen Whitmer and her running mate been a central part of their successful reelection campaign. WHITMER: This is a right that we are not going to go backwards on. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m proud of my state. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I don`t want the government in my bedroom. ALCINDOR: And abortion rights did drive people to the polls. It was the second most important issue to voters behind inflation. In addition to Michigan, voters in California and Vermont codified abortion rights into their state constitutions. And it wasn`t just blue states, voters in Kentucky and Montana shot down measures that could have restricted access. What do you make of that nationally? WHITMER: I think it`s a sign that the American public has had rights for 49 years. We`re not going to go backward. And so, whether it`s state by state we see this happen or hopefully at some point, you know, a national effort again, I think that this is where the fight is at the moment. ALCINDOR: Those against abortion rights not processing the results. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I believe abortion is first-degree murder. ALCINDOR: Eric Scheidler from the Pro-Life Action League says he`s gearing up to continue their push. ERIC SCHEIDLER, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, PRO-LIFE ACTION LEAGUE: If we`ve learned anything over the past 50 years as a movement is that we`ve got to be able to take a punch. ALCINDOR: Still, Americans in five states send a clear message about reproductive rights. Yamiche Alcindor, NBC News, Detroit. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Coming up, their new mission: training troops to become teachers in "THOSE WHO SERVE." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal.
