KIMBERLY ATKINS STOHR, SENIOR OPINION WRITER, THE BOSTON GLOBE : And I know that the DOJ and Merrick Garland want to keep things unpolitical. But I think that`s one of the things that he should`ve thought about in making the decision, either to do it from the beginning. I think that he didn`t need one at all. The regulations don`t mandate this. He could have continued this investigation, and it should`ve gone a little faster. TODD: Doesn`t it feel like he is a character from the pre-Trump era? ATKNS STOHR: Yes. TODD: And that`s sort of like what Garland`s -- you know, whatever you think, he`s just sort of, isn`t this the way we`re supposed to do it? BAKER: It`s the old fashioned. TODD: And you`re, like, it`s not the way in the Trump world, yeah. BAKER: It`s a new era. Right. A new era. But there is one thing that might be indicated here. Merrick Garland has made a threshold decision perhaps, that it is okay to charge a former president, or a presidential candidate, if the elements of the law are met, because otherwise, he wouldn`t have bothered to appoint a special counsel. That`s a pretty big step, if in fact that`s what`s going through his mind right now. TODD: All right, the other big event this weekend was this Republican Jewish Coalition event. You know, Anna, it was interesting. Donald Trump , he, he ended up satelliting it in because I think he realized Ron DeSantis was stealing the show no matter what. But he gave this rambling answer about the midterms, correctly noting the impact of abortion, but he never said the word. Meanwhile, Mike Pence is here telling me it`s the greatest achievement of the administration. PALMER: I mean, one of the biggest divides, right? You have Donald Trump , who was pro-choice. I mean, Mike Pence , ever since I`ve covered politics, this is very core to who he is. TODD: Yeah. PALMER: Clearly, not afraid that the American public might not be in the same place that Mike Pence is. But that`s one of the few distinguishing factors, right, when you look at the two of them. Mike Pence kind of twisting himself into a pretzel in this whole interview, where he didn`t really want to say that, that the former president was wrong, that what happened on January 6th was wrong. TODD: Brendan, he wants -- he wants to run on the Trump administration more than Trump does. BUCK: Pence is running what seems to be leading up to a campaign that would make a lot of sense if Donald Trump wasn`t still around. He`s the natural next -- next in line. All the great things that we did. I`m separating myself from him a little bit. But he refuses to actually take on Donald Trump . In reality, you know, he`s running for president. Donald Trump is going to be a candidate -- TODD: He`s going to take him on. BUCK: Exactly. TODD: Trump will take Pence on. BUCK: Exactly. And so we have a situation where, once again, you have Republicans sort of just hoping that he goes away, and unwilling to attack him. Donald Trump is going to attack Mike Pence . He`s going to attack Ron DeSantis . And to think that you can just sit there and wait for him to implode I think is a little naive. TODD: But is there a little bit of Trump fatigue? I feel like I`m sensing it in the rank and file. ATKINS STOHR: I think there`s more than a little bit. The midterms were evidence of that. But it`s not fatigue among the people, like including Mike Pence , who stood right next to -- TODD: Well because -- because they`re afraid of Trump`s base. ATKINS STOHR: Well, but it`s an opportunity to say, this is waning and we`re going to break free, and we`re going to take a different path. But instead, Mike Pence tried to excuse Trump for everything, other than trying to stop the certification of the election. It was -- it was Fauci`s fault that something, it was Mark Meadow`s fault that he talked about disinfectant. It was someone else`s fault. It was lawyers` fault that he -- PALMER: But where Mike Pence is, is very different, I think where you`re seeing a lot of the Republican Party saying, that was, you know, a three- time loser. You have members -- TODD: Pence doesn`t want to go there. PALMER: Not at all. TODD: No. PALMER: I mean, it`s pretty -- it`s stunning compared to where the rest of the Republicans are. TODD: Well, he`s self-aware in that who else was going to make him vice president? Ultimately, that`s the issue he has. All right, guys. I have to go. Enjoy your Thanksgiving weekend. You guys are terrific. There`s an unedited version of my Mike Pence interview, including approximately 30 minutes that we weren`t able to air here at MeetThePress.com. Please take a look at it. That`s all we have for today. Thanks for watching. Enjoy the Thanksgiving holiday. We`ll be back next week. We don`t bring leftovers. We`ll be bringing real "Meet the Press" because if it`s Sunday, it`s "Meet the Press". END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for November 23, 2022, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, another deadly mass shooting in America, this time at a Virginia Walmart just before Thanksgiving. (voiceover): The gunman, a store manager laughing before opening fire in the Walmart break room according to witnesses and police. At least six killed before the shooter took his own life. The horror unfolding as the store was filled with holiday shoppers. We`re on the scene. It comes just days after the massacre at an LGBTQ club in Colorado. The suspect making a first court appearance today slumped over in a wheelchair with visible facial injuries. What happened at that hearing? Also, tonight, the busiest day on the roads as nearly 55 million Americans travel for Thanksgiving. And the holiday storm threat. We`re tracking it. Russia`s new missile strikes on Ukraine. A maternity ward hit. A newborn infant killed. The first bombings in Jerusalem in years. The deadly blasts being called a terrorist attack. New details in the murders of four University of Idaho students. And now, the other unsolved stabbing case. Police are looking at it. Is there a link? The countdown to Black Friday. Where to find the best deals despite soaring inflation? And the spirit of a holiday. What kids say they`re most thankful for this year. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. We keep ending in the same place, don`t we? Morning victims who could have been any of us, scratching our heads over possible motives, and reciting the growing list. All those places where mass violence has snuffed out or threatened to take innocent lives. Tonight, just days after the Colorado Springs attack, we`re absorbing details of the latest horrific mass shooting in this country. Six people at a Chesapeake, Virginia Walmart shot to death by a long-time store employee who opened fire with a handgun. Several others were wounded. A survivor is saying the attack in an employee break room was preceded by the gunman`s laughter. The 31-year-old took his own life before police arrived. The killer described by a senior law enforcement official as a disgruntled employee. But what that means as to a specific motive is unclear. In a statement, President Biden speaking with many are thinking tonight, there are now even more tables across the country that will have empty seats this Thanksgiving. NBC`s Cal Perry is in Chesapeake with the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CAL PERRY, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tragedy in Chesapeake, Virginia. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: How many medics do we have left in the city right now? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Currently six medics available. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Go ahead and dispatch all of them. PERRY: 911 receiving its first call to the Walmart Supercenter at 10:12 p.m. Officers arriving within two minutes. We got a whole scene out here but it`s crazy out here right now. They everywhere. The 31-year-old shooter who police say worked at the store since 2010 came armed with a handgun and multiple magazines. One senior law enforcement official tells NBC News he was a disgruntled employee. BRIANA TYLER, WITNESS: I literally was frozen. I just stood there. I`d like I literally could be dead right now. It didn`t kick in until I looked at my coworker and she was bleeding out of her neck. PERRY: Six people were killed ranging in age from 16 to 70. At least four others were wounded before the shooter turned the gun on himself. MARK SOLESKY, CHIEF, CHESAPEAKE, VIRGINIA POLICE DEPARTMENT: The investigation is still ongoing, and we`ll be processing that scene for days. GOV. GLENN YOUNGKIN (R-VA): The most important thing we need to do is come around families and support them. It`s unimaginable what they`re dealing with today. PERRY: 24-year-old Jalon Jones had been working at the Walmart for about a year. He`s recovering at a nearby hospital. KIMBERLY SHUPE, MOTHER OF JALON JONES: He knew he was being shot. He made it to the front of the store. And then when he made it to the front door, he was shot again. PERRY: 28-year-old Jessie says it was just her fifth day on the job. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I saw a lot of bad thing that happened to really good people. And I didn`t understand it. And it didn`t feel real. PERRY: She says she was in the break room when the shooter came in laughing and started firing. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: He got the gun pointed at me and he looks at me and he puts it up in the air. And all he said was just to go home. I ran. I didn`t look back. I want to look back. PERRY: Do you know why he let you go, Jessie? Do you have any idea? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: No, I know. PERRY: So far, there`s no word on motive, and it`s unclear if the victims were targeted. Authorities today cordoned off this vehicle in the parking lot saying it`s a vehicle of interest. DR. JESSICA BURGESS, SENTARA NORFOLK GENERAL HOSPITAL: It`s heartbreaking. PERRY: Chesapeake, Virginia, just the latest community left grappling with yet another senseless shooting. [19:05:01] BURGESS: It was just two days ago that I was contacting one of my colleagues in Colorado Springs wishing her well and checking in to see how she was doing after she had just taken care of shooting victims. So it`s very disheartening that now I`m in the same position with my colleagues from across the country checking in on me. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Cal, what are investigators focusing on right now? PERRY (on camera): Lester, investigators are focused on any connection they can find between the victims and the shooter. For example, if any of the victims worked with the shooter, that could go a long way in finding a motive. Lester? HOLT: All right, Cal Perry tonight, thank you. In Colorado Springs today, the first court appearance by video from jail for the suspect in the killing of five people at that LGBTQ nightclub four days ago. The suspect who was subdued and beaten by club patrons was released from the hospital yesterday. The suspect, on public defenders, identify as non-binary person, was ordered held without bail and faces possible murder and hate crime charges. We have been through this so many times this year. By one count, there have been 608 mass shootings defined as four or more people shot. That`s not far from last year`s record. Here`s Tom Costello. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): On this Thanksgiving Eve, America is reckoning with the violence that is tearing up the national fabric. This afternoon, four high school students shot in Philly. Every week, nearly 13 mass shootings, so many we too often forget those that happened last week or last month. 21 children and teachers killed in Uvalde, Texas. 10 people gunned down in a Buffalo grocery store. Five and Raleigh, four in Memphis, four in Tulsa, six in Sacramento. The list is excruciatingly long. ROB BONTA, ATTORNEY GENERAL, CALIFORNIA: We know that this is America`s disease, unique in the world. COSTELLO: David Hogg, one of the high school students from Parkland, Florida where 17 people died, tweeted at 2:24 this morning, I am tired of waking up to texts about another mass shooting in America. DAVID HOGG, PARKLAND SHOOTING SURVIVOR: It`s going to continue happening. And we have to work together to actually stop this from happening. COSTELLO: Nationwide, 49 people die in gun violence every day. STEVEN DETTELBACH, DIRECTOR, ATF: My biggest fear is that somehow as a country, we become callous or to kind of accept or think that this is OK, that this is somehow part of our national story. COSTELLO: Pediatrician Emily Lieberman was with her children in Highland Park, Illinois when a gunman killed seven people on July 4. Now, she`s leading a group of doctors demanding the Senate pass more than the gun safety measures enacted after Uvalde. EMILY LIEBERMAN, PEDIATRICIAN: Now, the number one cause of death of children in this country is gun violence. It`s time to start tackling gun violence as a public health problem and listening to people like physicians who know how to solve this problem. (END VIDEOTAPE) COSTELLO (on camera): The country holding a mirror to itself with politicians expected back in D.C. next week. And the decades-old gun control debate likely to be a dinner table topic tomorrow. Lester? HOLT: Tom Costello, thank you. We`ll take a turn out of the busy Thanksgiving travel rush. Almost 55 million Americans expected to travel this year nearly hitting pre pandemic levels. And we`re also tracking storms that could bring heavy rain to the south and Gulf Coast tomorrow. Erin McLaughlin joins us now from Los Angeles. Erin, what`s the traffic like there? ERIN MCLAUGHLIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, things are looking pretty good here, Lestrer, especially for Los Angeles. Nearly 49 million Americans are expected to hit the road this Thanksgiving. That`s slightly compared to last year with the national average price of a gas, a gallon of gas, just below that $5.00 mark we saw back in June. Meanwhile, across the nation`s airports tonight, some good news for the most part. Flights have been on time thanks largely to clear skies and good weather across the country. Here in Los Angeles at LAX airport, they`re expecting some 200,000 passengers today alone. It`s the busiest they`ve been since the beginning of the pandemic. Lester? HOLT: Erin McLaughlin in Los Angeles, thank you. Two bombings in Jerusalem today killed a teenager and injured at least 18 others including two Americans. The explosions were near bus stops during the morning rush hour. Israeli police say the bombs were left at those locations and blamed Palestinians for the attacks. It`s the latest in a surge of violence between Israelis and Palestinians. And in Ukraine, Russia launching a new barrage of missile strikes. Ukrainian officials say a newborn infant was killed when a missile hit a hospital maternity ward in the southern part of the country. Much of Ukraine without power after Russians attack the energy infrastructure in Kyiv and several other cities. Tonight, new details from the police in the killings of those four college students in Idaho. Lots of leads and progress reported in the case but still no suspect identified. Gadi Schwartz has the latest. [19:10:06] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GADI SCHWARTZ, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): For the 11th day in a row, investigators saying still no suspect, no motive and the killings of four Idaho university students, but trying to assure the public they are making headway. COL. KEDRICK WILLS, IDAHO STATE POLICE: At this crime scene, we collected 103 pieces of individual evidence. SCHWARTZ: But frustration is growing among family members who fear investigators fell behind during the first crucial 48 hours of the case. WILLS: No tip is too small and we would urge anybody that has any information whatsoever to please provide that to help us solve this case. SCHWARTZ: Those who live in Moscow also asking about a recent dog mutilation that happened three miles away from the murders. Jim and Pam Colbert say about a month ago, someone grabbed their dog at 2:00 a.m. and skinned him in a field in front of their home. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Right over there. Right over -- SCHWARTZ: Took his fur but left his unbuckled collar behind. So, somebody actually had to unclasp it. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Unclasp it right here. See, that stays. And somebody had to undo it. Because if you had a knife, wouldn`t you have cut it? SCHWARTZ: But Moscow police say they don`t think that case has anything to do with the murders. Police also asked about an unsolved murder 300 miles away in Oregon, in which a masked intruder attacked a couple with a knife in their sleep. JAMES FRY, CHIEF, MOSCOW, IDAHO POLICE: Actually, I had a tip come in on that case and I`ve ordered it to our tip line. SCHWARTZ: Meanwhile, the University of Idaho giving students the option of finishing their semester remotely while families of the victims are struggling with the thought of Thanksgiving without their loved ones and praying that the killer won`t strike again. Gadi Schwartz, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Also tonight, the so-called tripledemic, RSV, the flu, and COVID, is already pushing hospitals to the brink. The U.S. facing shortages of pediatric beds, medical staff, and now even some medications. Here`s Gabe Gutierrez. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In Buffalo, some store shelves normally filled with children`s Tylenol are empty. Pharmacists say a spot shortage of the drug in Canada triggered by mounting cases of RSV is spilling over the border. DON ARTHUR, PHARMACIST: Apparently, up in Canada, the liquid forms of Tylenol are unavailable. GUTIERREZ: Johnson and Johnson , the maker of Tylenol, says there`s no overall shortage in the U.S., telling NBC News we are experiencing high consumer demand and they`re doing everything we can to make sure people have access to the products they need. Still, the FDA currently lists amoxicillin as being in short supply. And it all comes as the healthcare industry braces for a potential tripledemic this winter. RSV, flu, and COVID colliding. In New York, Ella Rose Giam (PH) is home after a week in the hospital. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It was surreal. Like, seeing your daughter on a breathing mask and she`s only three and a half. GUTIERREZ: Adding to the strain on the system, an increasingly dire staffing shortage. More than half a million people in the healthcare and social services industries quit their positions in September. Were you burnt out? Extremely. Yes, sir. Reece Brown in Louisiana is no longer a traveling nurse. REECE BROWN, NURSE: That joy which is literally being sucked out of us. We were doing everything that we could and we just -- it was never enough. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (on camera): As for COVID, the CDC says new data shows the Omicron boosters offer better protection against variants than earlier doses. Still, they are not as effective as the original COVID vaccine was against the initial virus. Lester? HOLT: All right, Gabe Gutierrez, thanks. In 60 seconds, new abortion restrictions and the agonizing decisions they are forcing some families to make. Our in-depth look at the issue coming up next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: The Georgia Supreme Court today reinstated a ban on abortions after six weeks of pregnancy while it considers an appeal. And while a few states including Georgia make exceptions when a fetus has life-threatening problems, most states with new abortion restrictions do not. Blayne Alexandre has more. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Jill Hurtle could not wait to become a mom. She still remembers the second she found out. JILL HURTLE, HAD ABORTION: I was like sobbing. I was so excited. [19:15:02] ALEXANDER: You felt like a mom. HURTLE: I felt like a mom in that -- in an instant. ALEXANDER: Her husband, Matt, dreamed of being a girl dad. They even picked out a name Ivy Grace. Every doctor`s appointment brought good news until the 18-week scan. HURTLE: And our world`s like came crashing down. She came in and she said her heart isn`t what it is supposed to look like. I think in that exact moment, my stomach dropped and I think I truly knew that it was going to be a really severe situation. ALEXANDER: It was. A condition known as hypoplastic left heart syndrome, HLHS. Doctor said her baby`s case was especially severe, and her daughter would likely not survive long after birth. HURTLE: I didn`t want her to have to go through so much pain and suffering. ALEXANDER: After more tests and more devastating news, Jill and her husband made the painful decision. HURTLE: If she were to live an hour or 10 days, I didn`t want her to just - - I didn`t want her to know nothing but pain. So, my protective instinct was to do what I knew what was best for her, which was to send her to heaven. ALEXANDER: Every year, congenital or fetal anomalies impact one in every 33 babies born in the U.S. and range from minor to life-limiting or life- threatening. Since the Supreme Court decision overturning Roe v. Wade, at least 16 states have successfully enacted laws further restricting abortion access. Only three have exceptions for lethal fetal anomalies. DR. DAVID LEVINE, NEONATOLOGIST: We`re not dealing with one size fits all. We can`t make laws for one size fits all. ALEXANDER: Dr. David Levine is a neonatologist who opposes abortion access and believes the baby should be carried to term even with a grim prognosis. LEVINE: Most families who have decided to spend time with their babies however short it might be, by and large, have benefited from it. They`ve been able to bond with their baby. ALEXANDER: Is it therefore a law to make that decision for a parent? LEVINE: There are many decisions that are taken out of our hands. Is it fair for the mother to make that decision to take a baby`s life away from him. ALEXANDER: Jill had to leave South Carolina and wait two weeks for an appointment in Washington, DC. HURTLE: Those two weeks were probably the hardest two weeks I`ve ever experienced in my life. Every time you feel her kick or move, it`s just a dagger to the heart. ALEXANDER: She believes abortion bans should have exceptions for cases like hers, giving women the chance to make a choice, however painful. HURTLE: I am a mom. I`m a mom to an angel in heaven. And I know that she`s at peace. ALEXANDER: Blayne Alexander, NBC News, Charleston, South Carolina. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, as the holiday shopping rush begins, top tips on where and how you can save in our series "RACE TO DELIVER." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: As you may have noticed, many retailers have already rolled out their Black Friday deals. So, where can you save the most? NBC`s Brian Cheung has been shopping around for our series "RACE TO DELIVER." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BRIAN CHEUNG, NBC NEWS BUSINESS AND DATA REPORTER (voiceover): Tonight, amid a growing unease in the nation`s economy, the dash for holiday deals is on. With consumer prices up 7.7 percent compared to last season and one in three households saying their finances are worse off from a year ago, shoppers are left with tighter budgets. TRAE BODGE, SMART SHOPPING EXPERT, TRUETRAE.COM: Retailers are aware of the fact that consumers only have so much to spend. CHEUNG: That`s why even before Black Friday, many retailers are already offering deep discounts vying for your holiday dollars. The most discounted items this season, everything from TVs, laptops, to home appliances, and beauty products. For electronics, consider older models for an even better deal. Many clothing retailers are also offering extra deep discounts this season in part because of excess inventory falling supply chain lock-ups last year. BODGE: We are seeing a lot of overstock still and retailers have been spending the last couple of months trying to sell through that merchandise. CHEUNG: Which could lead to even deeper discounts. BODGE: I do expect to see discounts deeper than usual in categories like casual apparel, TVs, furniture, home decor. And so, in addition to the exciting cyber weekend sales that we`ll see, we`ll also see kind of extra discounts as retailers look to clear out all those overstocks. CHEUNG: Experts say shopping with strategy will save you big bucks. Start by creating a shopping list with a spending cap. Then compare prices online and in store. And check your credit card for additional discounts and offers. (END VIDEOTAPE) CHEUNG (on camera): And don`t forget about gift cards which are always a hot item every year. Many can actually be bought at a discount. Lester? HOLT: All right, Brian, thanks. Up next, what are you thankful for? Some children will tell us right after the break. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally, a lot of news has been especially grim this week, but we thought you might be uplifted or find a smile in listening to the gratitude expressed by some New York school kids we spoke to about Thanksgiving. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) HOLT (voiceover): At Manhattan Country School, today`s lesson is all about giving thanks. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Thank you God for a mother. HOLT: And after two years of holidays overshadowed by COVID, many students told us they`re grateful for a Thanksgiving that feels a little more normal. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m thankful for like, family and friends because like, during COVID, I wasn`t able to see -- I wasn`t able to see like, a lot of my friends. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m very grateful that me and my family -- or my family and I have been healthy and happy and able to see each other. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m really thankful for the school and for my teachers and my friends. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m thankful for my dog. She`s good at comforting people especially me. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m thankful for my family because they give me comfort and I just love them. HOLT: Of course, on Thanksgiving -- UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I love cooking. HOLT: Comfort also comes in the form of turkey, stuffing, and potatoes. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We bake and we coconut we have this huge feast at the end. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We make an angel fruitcake which I really love to do with my grandma. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m definitely looking forward to eating because we do cook pretty good Thanksgiving meal. HOLT: When you`re in grade school, there`s something else to look forward to. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We get a lot of days off from school. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The first thing I think about it is wrapped up in a blanket drinking hot chocolate and watching a movie, and I just get really excited about that. HOLT: A moment of peace with the people you love, to give thanks, isn`t that what the day is all about? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: When I think about the holidays, I think about community and spending time with the people that I love and giving back to them and hopefully receiving the same. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And thank all of you for being here tonight. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS. Be sure to tune in for the Macy`s Thanksgiving Day Parade at 9:00 Eastern here on NBC and Peacock. Thank you for watching and Happy Thanksgiving, everyone. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. headline: The Today Show for December 8, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:00:00] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS TODAY, CO-ANCHOR: It`s 8:00 on "TODAY." Coming up, flu fears. New concerns over medication shortages as cases spike from coast to coast. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: There`s hardly anything to choose from. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Coming up, what you can do to ensure your family is prepared this flu season. Plus, breast cancer breakthrough. The just-released study sparking hope for women with breast cancer who want to start a new family. What the promising new data shows about a safe path forward. And Garten`s variety. The Barefoot Contessa herself, Ina Garten, joins us for a full hour to help spruce up our holiday tables, from a new spin on some tasty treats to becoming the host with the most. Plus, a glimpse into some of our most treasured traditions. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CROWD: Three, two -- yahey. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Blast off. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: We`ve got a fun-filled hour ahead with a few surprises along the way. Today, Thursday, December 8, 2022. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Best friends. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And "TODAY" super fans. CROWD: From Parkersburg, West Virginia. CROWD: From Pullman, Washington. CROWD: And Lynwood, Illinois. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: From Hagerstown, Maryland. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Celebrating our 25th anniversary. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Friends for 20 years. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: From El Paso, Texas. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Here with my grandson. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From Mechanicsville, Virginia. CROWD: Hello from Woodbine, Iowa. CROWD: And Cincinnati, Ohio. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Celebrating Vicky`s birthday. CROWD: From Baton Rouge. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Here to experience a magic. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Of Christmas in New York. CROWD: From Mizpah, Minnesota. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Welcome back. How do we say thank you for coming out -- SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS TODAY, CO-ANCHOR: I know. KOTB: -- every morning? This crowd, it`s like six people thick. It`s a big crowd. We cannot wait to get outside and visit with everybody in just a bit. But what do you say we get to our news at 8:00? CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes. KOTB: An early surge in flu cases is sending more Americans to the hospital and it`s actually causing pharmacies to run out of both prescription and over-the-counter treatments. NBC Sam brock has the latest on how long this might last and what you should do in case your drugstore shelves are empty. Sam, good morning. SAM BROCK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Yes. Hoda, good morning. The mere fact that the flu season has arrived weeks in advance, as you said, has put parents in quite a crunch, pretty much across the board from antibiotics to antivirals. I know at the very end there she was sent to a notorious penal colony in Russia. MITCHELL: Exactly. At the beginning of November after her appeal was lost, she was taken from the detention jail where she had been at least more accessible to occasional visits from US embassy officials and taken to this penal colony. And the conditions, we understand, were terrible. That the rule that they were fed, not nutritious, no hot water, one bathroom for as many as 80 women prisoners, very little exercise. And this woman is six foot nine (inaudible) had already been kept in a cell that was way too small for her. She`s missed, you know, an entire season 10 months of physical fitness and of conditioning, and of her career at the peak of an athlete`s life and career. So she has suffered immeasurable loss. We`re just hoping when she gets to that medical facility in San Antonio that the wonderful doctors who have taken care of all of our service members for so many years of conflicts, that they will know exactly what to do about PTSD, about whatever else she may be suffering from, and about getting back in shape. KOTB: And it`s worth kind of underscoring why she was arrested in the first place. They originally said that she was charged with smuggling drugs. And was she was contending that she just had some cannabis oil that she had medical permission to use for some of her ailments. So that was the genesis of why -- GUTHRIE: In the context at the very moment that Russia was launching its war in Ukraine. So many people, Andrea, feel she was swept up in geopolitics. MITCHELL: Absolutely, it was February 17th when they were about to launch the war in February 24th. And the fact is it was less than a gram. There was no testimony. So there`s no question that she was not doing anything that would warrant this. In any case, even if there weren`t -- if she weren`t being held hostage geopolitically, there`s no excuse at all. KOTB: And it`s also, Andrea, worth noting this is exactly what she said when she was in trial. I never meant to hurt anybody. I never meant to put in jeopardy the Russian population. GUTHRIE: Peter at the White House and I want to talk about the Whelan family because the statement, which I said is quite lengthy and very nuanced, very generous of course to Brittney Griner. He is a US businessman, but notably, he is a former US Marine. And it`s on that basis that Russia has been making its case. The US says wrongfully that he was there serving as a US spy. The US has repeatedly denied that. We are now hearing from some of the officials here as this news is breaking. They are saying this is a big day. It is a great day they say but it would sure be a lot better in the words of one of these officials if Paul was coming home as well. So that`s what makes this particularly bittersweet right now. And we should note, I mean, this is the President ultimately who signed off on this. But Victor Bout, he is a significant prisoner that the US had in custody. As we have said a convicted arms dealer, the merchant of death, Savannah, as you noted earlier. There were conversations in the back and forth that took place over the course of the last several months where the Russians appear to have expressed interest into one of their citizens who was an assassin, who was being held in Germany by the German government . But that was a nonstarter in the course of the back and forth. [08:55:20] But as Andrea indicated, at the end of the day, when the Russians said they would give up Brittney Griner and Brittney Griner, the president of United States made the decision to go with it. GUTHRIE: All right. Peter, thank you very much. This has been NBC News Special Report covering the release of Brittney Griner. And we`ve learned this morning she has been traded, as Peter mentioned, for a notorious Russian arms dealer who had been convicted and served about three quarters of his sentence, Victor Bout. That trade has secured her release. She is on route to San Antonio where we understand she`ll be receiving medical treatment. KOTB: And it was nice to see her wife, Cherelle, up there at the podium saying that at this moment, although there`s still a lot going on, she`s going to take this moment to pause and smile. headline: TODAY WITH HODA & JENNA for Dec 26, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [10:00:17] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (voiceover): Today, get ready to be inspired. Donna shows up at the door of a beloved neighbor and gives him the ultimate sweet surprise. Plus, writer and poet Yung Pueblo. How his millions of followers are learning and healing from his every word. And the breast cancer survivor whose personal journey is touching and saving the lives of countless women. JENNA BUSH HAGER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (voiceover): It`s TODAY WITH HODA -- KOTB: -- & JENNA. It all starts right now. HAGER: It all starts right now. KOTB (on camera): Hey, guys, happy day after Christmas. It`s Monday, December 26th. We hope that you all had a very merry one and a happy one. All the wrapping paper the bows and all that stuff tucked away. HAGER (on camera): Waking up with family still in the house. It`s -- what were they called this day in the U.K.? Boxing Day? KOTB: Boxing Day? They do? HAGER: Yes. I`m not sure why. KOTB: Oh, just like to decorative -- HAGER: But let`s celebrate Boxing Day. Why not? KOTB: OK. I like that. HAGER: And we`ve got an amazing show today that`s going to leave you feeling inspired and feeling good. Just as this day should. KOTB: Oh my God, this is -- this is our kind of show. HAGER: It sure is. KOTB: Because we love -- loves -- love things that feel like that. HAGER: Wait, in fact, can you just talk about the way you start your day? And the way you end your day? Because Henry is reading a book called Think Like A Monk by Jay Shetty. KOTB: Jay Shetty, yes. HAGER: And he says a lot of people think about the morning routine, but people forget about the end. KOTB: You know what`s funny? The morning routine I packed with inspirational readings and quotes and prayers and writing in my journal and all these kinds of things at night. I usually read and we have Yung Pueblo on today, a couple of lines from his book. And just before I close my eyes. Like last thing in, last thing in. I also try to say -- usually you think of like three things you`re grateful for. Yes, but a twist on that and this sounds vain, but it isn`t. Three things I appreciate about myself. Now, think about for right now, just freeze for a second. In this moment, what are three things you appreciate? Not that you`re grateful for? So, what is it that you`ve done that you appreciated? And it`s only for you, you`re not bragging. But what did you -- what have you done so far that you appreciate? And sometimes they`re small things like I gave my kids space, so that they could say what they wanted to say and then I received? OK, that`s the thing. And so, that`s the way -- HAGER: Yes. Or the way you handle situations. KOTB: Yes. Yes. HAGER: Yes, it`s so -- it`s so interesting, because I think we don`t even realize the negative stuff we say to ourselves, which is constant. Why did you do that? Why did you do that for? Why did you -- KOTB: I`m telling why (INAUDIBLE) should -- HAGER: You shouldn`t have said that. KOTB: Yes. HAGER: But -- so imagine just filling that time with? Oh, look, what you did there. You know, saying nice things. And I think it really does make a difference. KOTB: You know, Michelle Obama`s book that`s been out for a little bit is so beautifully written. But she talks about in one part, how we have a rectangular-sized shield that we put between us and the world. And she`s talking about the phone. HAGER: Oh, interesting. KOTB: And she says, what we`re doing every day is we are missing micro connections. You`re in the line at the bank, but I`m playing Candy Crush, so I don`t even look up to say hello, or I`m here and I`m doing something small. What your day -- she talked about how every day a micro connection and actually matters. It shows that we`re -- we may be different, but we`re human. But if you`re -- if there`s something in your ears and something in front of you, because people keep saying why are we drifting further apart? Tiny interactions that we would normally have. HAGER: Thank you. Yes. KOTB: Please, hi on the street. HAGER: The kind of smile that kind of makes you feel good. KOTB: Yes. Yes. HAGER: Wait, do you know -- so, when I first went back to work after having Mila, she`s 9, so about nine years ago, I got assigned the story. And I swear, it was like some sort of gift. Because the story was all about how basically kids are feeling like they`re not interesting. There was this doctor at Harvard who was studying what this -- what this does to a child. So, pretend you`re saying, Mommy, mommy -- KOTB: Hey, mom, mom, I want to tell you something. No, mom, mom, mom? HAGER: Hear. Hear. Hear. So, the words -- KOTB: Right. This is more important. HAGER: This is more important than this. KOTB: Than you. Than you. HAGER: And it was the best gift because what I realized is I was putting emphasis on work everything -- KOTB: I got to get this deal. Very important. HAGER: -- and you`ll (INAUDIBLE) instead of looking into my baby`s eye. KOTB: Yes. HAGER: And well, it`s not true. I mean, no mom thinks this is more interesting than their child. KOTB: Or, we don`t even realize -- we think how of just doing one quick thing, just one quick thing. HAGER: Anyway, that`s -- that could be a New Year`s resolution for a lot of people out there, and it`d be for mine. KOTB: Yes, yes. Me, too. [10:05:05] HAGER: OK. So, there`s research that recently was published in the Economic Times. It says humor at work actually accelerate creativity, motivation, and promoting productivity. KOTB: You know what, here`s the funny thing. I`m sitting next to this one. So, here`s the funny thing about you. Sometimes, I worry as we`re sitting here, because the things you say are so crazy and funny that I`ll just lose it instantly. But here`s the funny thing. I feel like there are ways -- there are ways of connection. HAGER: Yes. KOTB: For us, we have it. I think we have a deep kind of spiritual connection. But when you make me laugh, I feel so weirdly and crazily connected. Like I am -- sometimes I think about what you say much later in the day, and I`ll literally just be like, and goes what, I got nothing. It was something -- I can`t even explain. HAGER: You called me the other day. And you go, all I have to say is pirate and hung up. KOTB: You know why? Because I thought I was wearing a pair of cute black pants, black boots, but they didn`t meet in the middle. So, Jenna goes, hey, pirate. And literally, I was -- I just laughed, but that`s the whole thing. They say, it`s the whole thing. If you have them laughing, you have them listening. HAGER: That is such a good one. KOTB: And teachers who are -- yes, teachers who are -- who make kids laugh, kids lean in, they listen. HAGER: Totally. But laughing also is so much fun. I feel like that`s -- I mean, I`m coming up with all my New Year`s resolutions. Somebody, write this down. KOTB: What is it? HAGER: My other New Year`s resolution is to laugh more. KOTB: Yes. How? HAGER: Like why are we too busy? I mean, we laugh a lot because that`s our -- KOTB: Because we have -- and we also have space too. If we didn`t, if we were rushing through, you know, the whole -- HAGER: Rushing and doing this, and -- here`s your paper. Like, laugh instead, right? KOTB: Get in the next segment. I know. HAGER: Why don`t we just laugh more? KOTB: Yes, we do. HAGER: I mean, we do. In life, why don`t we -- KOTB: We all, collectively. OK, shall we see this video that`ll make us feel good. HAGER: Yes, yes. All right, this is the father of a bride in Jersey. So, the wedding videographer mic`d up the dad for his big walk down the aisle. So, let`s take a listen. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Nice and slow, honey. Look at his face. You see nothing but smiles. I love you, you know? Take care of her. Give me a hug, too. You`ll be fine, kiddo. I`ll be always by your side. You`ll never be alone, OK? (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Oh my gosh. HAGER: There were so few words yet they were so beautiful. KOTB: We were talking about laughing. HAGER: It`s good, now we`re crying. But you know what I think about crying? If you`re crying, you`re listening, too. KOTB: Yes, yes, yes. It works for both. All right, coming up, if you love a surprise we got a good one for you. HAGER: And Donna shows up unannounced to surprise a beloved neighbor right after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [10:10:00] HAGER: Now to our series, "KNOCK KNOCK SURPRISE!" And this is a surprise that`s going to fill your heart, for sure. KOTB: Yes. So, a few months ago, a viewer wrote in to tell us about her incredible neighbor of 20 years. His name is Ernie Mann. He lives in Rensselaer, New York. So, we sent Donna there to surprise him with something we knew he`d love. Check it out. DONNA FARIZAN, NBC NEWS HOST: This is so exciting, ladies. I`m here with Amy Mooney who nominated Ernie for National Good Neighbor Day. We`re walking up to his door right now. I`m going to leave you right there, Amy, OK? And I`m going up. I am -- we were hiding in the bushes for quite some time, a little bit nervous of what was going to happen, and how he`s going to react. Amy said that he`s going to be in shock. So, I`m going to knock on the door right now. And hopefully, Ernie will come out and be surprised. We can`t wait. There`s a crowd of over 30 here with us. This neighborhood loves him so much. And I don`t know how he`s going to react, but I`m hoping he`s going to be happy. So, let`s see what Ernie has to say. We`ve knock knocked the doors. Hi, Ernie, surprise! Ernie, come on out here. I`m Donna -- I`m Donna from the TODAY SHOW. And you are live. Come on over here with me, Ernie. It`s nice to meet you. You are so beloved as you can feel and see. And I don`t know if you know this, Ernie, but we can go right here. It is National Good Neighbor Day today. And we wanted to honor you because you are a pillar of this community. FARIZAN: Well, let me fill you in a little bit more. Amy right here -- Amy right here nominated you. You are on live television on the TODAY SHOW right now. But anyway -- FARIZAN: So, Ernie, we know that Hoda and Jenna want to say something, too. So, we just are going to give you these earbuds, so you can listen to what`s going on. He was a teacher for over 30 years, and he was also an active volunteer firefighter. He was our fire chief. [10:15:09] My kids would play wiffle ball in his backyard. Ernie`s like a dad to a lot of us, and he would do anything for any of us. Ernie and his wife, Jan moved into the neighborhood. That was almost 20 years ago. Ernie is a Yankee fan. So, there`s a healthy rivalry going on. Ernie`s sense of humor can be summed up in a card that our daughter received at Johns Hopkins Hospital, he sent her a beautiful get well card and signed it Derek Jeter . Ernie is a person who has gone above and beyond, and now it`s time for us to honor him. He`s going to be so pissed at me. You have no idea. (END VIDEO CLIP) FARIZAN: Is that true? How do you feel right now? MANN: I`m overwhelmed, honestly. FARIZAN: I`ll take -- I`ll take these out. I know -- MANN: Totally, I don`t know what to say. FARIZAN: Have you always loved Rensselaer this much? MANN: Yes, I have. Yes. My father was born in Rensselaer. And before it was Rensselaer, actually. And now, I`ve lived through all my life. FARIZAN: Well, thank you for all that you do. You`re such a great representation of not only calm but a good neighbor. MANN: Thank you so much. FARIZAN: And you know, I wanted you to put the earbuds in one more time because I heard Ernie that you are a big Yankees fan. Is that right? MANN: Yes, that`s true. FARIZAN: So, well, in honor of that, I think there`s a member of the team that wanted to say hello to you if that`s OK, let`s take a listen. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) NESTOR CORTES: Nestor Cortes here with the New York Yankees . I just want to congratulate you on being a good neighbor. We`ve heard all about you and what you`ve do -- and what you`ve done with the community. By the way, we have a special gift coming for you. So, stay tuned. And go Yankees . (END VIDEO CLIP) FARIZAN: Well, I know that you just saw Nestor Cortes, Jr. through the screen. But you know what, can we just grab some Yankees swag? OK, this is for you. I think you`re going to need it because, Ernie, we are getting you four tickets to Yankee Stadium, so you can go see Nestor (INAUDIBLE) and you have a lot of people to choose from to take with you. How do you feel? MANN: I`m, honest to God, I`m overwhelmed. And I totally didn`t see any of this coming. I don`t know -- FARIZAN: Well, you know, thank you so much for being a great neighbor. MANN: Well, I`ve had great neighbors around me. It`s been pretty easy. All the people around me, they`re wonderful people. FARIZAN: As we send it back to Hoda and Jenna, is there one piece of advice you would give people to become a better neighbor? MANN: If you just look out for each other, if you look and see if somebody`s up against it, try to help them a little bit. You can do it quietly. You don`t have to make a big fuss. And if just people are nicer to each other all over. It`s easy to do. FARIZAN: Thank you, Ernie. It`s easy to do with you. KOTB: Oh my gosh, how much do we love Earnie. HAGER: We love Earnie. He`s such a sweet, sweet man, and what a great group of neighbors, a beautiful community. KOTB: Incredible. Incredible. Coming up next, a mother of two who wouldn`t let breast cancer beat her, and now she`s helping other women get a fighting chance coming up after this. [10:20:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HAGER: All morning long, we`re celebrating people whose stories inspire us to live our very best life. KOTB: Breast cancer survivor Ricki Fairley is one of those people. After defying the odds, she created a brand new life for herself with a very important mission. Take a look. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) RICKI FAIRLEY, BREAST CANCER SURVIVOR: I try to like let everything go and just paddle and just feel the water and see that -- feel the sun or the wind. Feel God around me. KOTB (voiceover): Ricki Fairley starts most of our days like this, alone and at peace on the Chesapeake Bay. But this mother of two didn`t always know how to slow down. I actually had been married for 30 years, and I was the breadwinner for our family, traveling every week on the road. KOTB: She also did a lot of research and learned about the disparity in breast cancer for black women. FAIRLEY: This disease for black women is a different disease. KOTB: So, with her new home, her new fiance and her new way of life came a new purpose, a nonprofit called Touch: The Black Breast Cancer Alliance. FAIRLEY: Your piece is non-negotiable. Take care of yourself, check your breasts, give yourself a minute, give yourself a pause. It`s OK to say no. (END VIDEOTAPE) KOTB (on camera): Ricki, I mean, we are in awe of you. Your purpose came with that horrible diagnosis. A huge change. I said, no, I have to go now. HAGER: You know, the best thing about this is that you had the second life and you`re using it to help other women. You -- those statistics that we heard in the piece are unacceptable. You could have just read those and thought, OK, but instead, you`re fighting them. And that just seems like an incredible mission. FAIRLEY: I work for my granddaughters. I don`t want them to ever think about breast cancer, and we have a lot of work to do to save black women. FAIRLEY: That will be awesome. You know, we have this movement called When We Trial. PUEBLO: You know, it`s a bit of a risk and but it worked out for us. headline: 50 Years After Roe v. Wade, America Is An Abortion Battleground After The Supreme Court Decision Overturning It
story_text: LESTER HOLT: We have new details on the Supreme Court`s probe into the stunning leak last year, that draft opinion overturning Roe v. Wade. The Supreme Court Marshal revealed today she spoke with each justice in addition to court employees, but investigators were not able to identify the leaker. And this weekend marks 50 years since the Roe v. Wade decision. In the months since it was overturned, the U.S. has become a patchwork of laws varying from state to state. Anne Thompson with more now on the deep impact on clinics. [19:15:07] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANNE THOMPSON, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The days are nonstop at Florida`s Jacksonville Health Center. 50 years after roe versus wade and seven months after the Dobbs ruling that overturned it, demand for abortion at this Planned Parenthood Clinic hasn`t slowed says Manager Jessica Wannemacher. JESSICA WANNEMACHER, MANAGER, PLANNED PARENTHOOD CLINIC, JACKSONVILLE: It`s getting worse. THOMPSON: What do you mean? WANNEMACHER: The amount of patient load that we need to be able to see more patients. THOMPSON: Four years ago, the clinic offered abortion services once a week. Now, it`s up to five days. Dr. Shelly Tien specializes in high-risk pregnancies. Of the 63 patients you`re seeing today, how many of those are seeking abortion services? DR. SHELLY TIEN, PLANNED PARENTHOOD CLINIC: The vast majority. THOMPSON: Has it been like that since the Supreme Court decision? TIEN: It has. THOMPSON: Florida bans abortions after 15 weeks with narrow exceptions. It also requires two in-person doctor`s visits at least 24 hours apart, but the outright bans and heartbeat bills in neighboring states have more than doubled the out-of-state patients here. For opponents of abortion rights like Andrew Shervill, it is a frustrating consequence of the Supreme Court decision. ANDREW SHIRVELL, FOUNDER AND EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, FLORIDA VOICE FOR THE UNBORN: It`s extremely -- actually, it`s extremely infuriating because here Florida`s leading on so many other issues, but we should not be in this position at all. THOMPSON: So, what`s next? SHIRVELL: What`s next? Here in Florida, we`re pushing for a complete abortion ban. THOMPSON: But at the clinic Dr. Tien believes any restrictions come with dire consequences. TIEN: Women are going to die because of what has happened to reproductive rights in this country. THOMPSON: A recent Commonwealth Fund study analyzed data from 2020 and found maternal death rates were 62% higher in states that had abortion restrictions. The battle is now in states like Florida. SHIRVELL: I think the Dobbs decision properly returned the public policy fight to the states, and that for the foreseeable future is where activists on both sides are going to be engaged. THOMPSON: Should medical doctors have a role in crafting abortion law? SHIRVELL: No, I don`t believe so. THOMPSON: Dr. Tien disagrees. TIEN: It must be shared decision-making between the patient, her family and her healthcare team. THOMPSON: Do politicians have a role in this? TIEN: Absolutely not. Absolutely not. THOMPSON: Rulings may change, but the debate has no end in sight. Anne Thompson, NBC News, Jacksonville. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: All right, coming up, it may say organic, but is it food fraud? headline: On This 50th Anniversary Weekend Of The Roe Versus Wade Decision That Was Overturned Last Year
story_text: [07:00:18] JOE FRYER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning and thanks for starting your weekend with us and it might be a good one to stay inside with another big storm impacting much of the country. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: And another one is close behind. It`s January 21st. This is TODAY. Severe weather watch. Millions in the south preparing for a heavy dose of rain today with the potential of flash floods before the same storm heads up the East Coast. Threatening to bring up to a half a foot of snow in the Northeast. We`ll have the full forecast. Battle Cry. On this 50th anniversary weekend of the Roe versus Wade decision that was overturned last year, tens of thousands take to the streets of the nation`s capital as part of the March for Life rally. Where does the abortion fight go from here? Record surge. The government reporting the number of illegal border crossings at its highest level ever since President Biden took office. What can officials do to slow down the influx? Caught on camera. Police take down. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Drop it! Drop it! WELKER: Harrowing moments inside an Indiana Wal-Mart captured on police bodycam after a former employee opened fire. This morning, the woman police are credited with helping to stop the bloodshed from getting worse. All that, plus football frenzy. Fans from coast to coast getting ready for this weekend`s NFL playoffs divisional round. Eight teams facing off including that highly anticipated rematch between the Buffalo Bills and Cincinnati Bengals . It all kicks off today, Saturday January 21st, 2023. ANNOUNCER: From NBC News, this is TODAY with Peter Alexander and Kristen Welker. WELKER: Welcome to TODAY and thank you so much for joining us on this Saturday morning. Peter is enjoying the morning off. We`ve got Joe Fryer here. And Joe, you are here for a big weekend in softball, a big weekend for my beloved Eagles taking on the Giants. FRYER: We know what you`re going to be e doing tonight. We definitely know who you`re going to be cheering for. WELKER: Fly Eagle fly. I got the whole family in town. We are ready. FRYER: I know you are and I might be jumping on your bandwagon because the Giants beat my Vikings last week and I`m still bitter. WELKER: Yes, you know where your allegiances are. FRYER: Exactly. WELKER: I like that. All right. Good. FRYER: Exactly. We`re going to talk football and a little bit. We`re going to be begin though by covering several developing stories this morning. That includes the marches planned this weekend for activists on both sides of the abortion rights debate. We`re going to hear what anti-abortion rights protesters are hoping for next today after that big March for Life rally here in D.C. WELKER: And we`ll also tell you about tough times for the tech industry. Google `s parent company announcing on Friday at slashing 12,000 jobs. They`re joining other companies like Microsoft , Amazon and Meta making mass layoffs. FRYER: But let`s begin this morning with our top story. The weather as the south prepares for intense rain today and the Northeast gets ready for a round of snow that could bring up to six inches. WELKER: Some area saw a preview of that on Friday for the very latest on all of it. Let`s bring in Somara Theodore. Somara, you`ve been tracking this. What should folks be bracing for? (LOCAL NEWS) [07:05:16] WELKER: Somara, thanks. Maybe a good weekend to stay indoors for a lot of people. We`ll get the rest of your forecast in just a few minutes. FRYER: This weekend marks the 50th anniversary of the Supreme Court`s decision on Roe v. Wade. And a half century later the debate over abortion rights still looms large, especially after the Dobbs decision last year overturning Roe. On Friday the March for life took place just one of several marches this weekend on both sides of the issue. NBC`s Marissa Parra was at the march and joins us with more. Marissa, good morning to you. WELKER: Good morning. MARISSA PARRA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Joe and Kristen, good morning to you. Another busy day in D.C. as usual, right? WELKER: Yes. PARRA: Well crowds for the march we`re in the tens of thousands. And we know that the march was originally started to protest Roe versus Wade. So, there was a big celebratory mood in this new post Roe era, right? This is what they`ve been fighting for. But activists on both sides of the abortion debate are really galvanized in different ways, especially as we get closer to 2024. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PARRA (voice over): This morning, the battle over abortion access far from over. Roughly seven months after Roe v. Wade was overturned, the nation`s capital seeing the nation`s first march for life in a post Roe world. REP. STEVE SCALISE (R-LA): And today, we celebrate Roe is gone. It`s important to keep your focus on what the mission is. But every step of the way. It`s also critical that we celebrate victories along the way. PARRA: Changing the route to reflect a change country, stopping in front of both the Supreme Court and the Capitol. A symbolic nod to the role they both have and continue to play abortion law. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It`s up to the states now so we need to raise awareness and each of the states. PARRA: Counter protesters reading their own fight to win back lost ground. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: That is why I`m here. It is to show that we will not let America be bullied out of the right to abortion. PARRA: The path to a full nationwide victory for either side an uphill battle. It`s been 50 years since Roe v. Wade was first signed into law. But in the months since its reversal last summer, almost two dozen states have either banned abortion or they`re close to it, with several legislative sessions actively debating what their laws will be on a state level. This says federal action fails to move forward. Senator Lindsey Graham`s federal abortion ban proposal failed last fall and the Biden administration`s hopes of a federal right to choose. KARINE JEAN-PIERRE , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: We need to codify Roe. PARRA: Unlikely and a Republican-controlled House. And with new FDA guidance making abortion bills more accessible over the counter, a new abortion battleground is headed to the pharmacy. (END VIDEOTAPE) PARRA: Now that new FDA guidance was a small victory for abortion rights activists and we know tomorrow is the 50th anniversary of that original decision. So, there are bigger than Roe pro-choice marches scheduled across the country. Joe and Kristen? FRYER: All right. Kristen -- Marissa Parra, thank you so much. Appreciate it. WELKER: Great to see you, Marissa. Really appreciate it. Well, just one day after the Supreme Court announced it couldn`t find who was behind the leak of that draft opinion of the decision to overturn Roe v. Wade. Former President Trump is calling on the journalists who revealed the leak to be jailed. And this morning the Biden administration is fighting back. NBC`s Monica Alba is tracking all of it from the White House. Monica, good morning to you. MONICA ALBA, NBC NEWS WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: Kristen, good morning. After an eight-month investigation that leaks still could not be pinpointed with former President Trump pushing stricter measures to root out the leaker. The probe led by the courts chief security officer determined hackers were likely not responsible. after interviewing 97 employees. The search found that 82 had access to digital or hard copies of the draft. But now we`re learning more about who else was questioned in the matter. The court investigator revealing Friday she spoke with each of the nine justices several on multiple occasions and all cooperated in the process. Every credible lead was explored and none of them implicated the justices or their spouses according to the court. And soon after the 20-page report came out that couldn`t identify the leak, the former president called for the reporters who broke the news to be arrested, along with possibly their editor and publisher saying they should be put in jail "until the answer is given." Within hours, the White House released a statement defending freedom of the press saying it`s the responsibility of all leaders to protect First Amendment rights. Kristen? WELKER: Yes. Just remarkable that that investigation could not determine who was behind the leak. Monica, another big headline you are tracking we`re also in the midst of this debt ceiling standoff between the White House and Republicans but we`re hearing that the President will meet with House Speaker Kevin McCarthy to discuss a path forward. What are you hearing? ALBA: That`s right, Kristen. While speaker McCarthy did accept President Biden`s offer to meet soon, no date has been set yet by the White House. But a contentious back and forth Friday about the debt ceiling show just how difficult resolving this issue may be. [07:10:07] House Republicans don`t want to increase America`s ability to borrow without promises of future spending cuts. While the President says there`s no room for negotiation when the stakes are so high. Warning of unprecedented financial calamity if the U.S. doesn`t meet its credit obligations for the first time in history. Experts say it could even lead to a recession or stock market crash if it happens, as the treasury secretary is already using extraordinary measures to keep paying the nation`s bills effectively buying time by shifting money around but that will only last until June. Kristen? WELKER: A major test and showdown for all of Washington. Monica Alba at the White House. Thank you, Monica. FRYER: Illegal crossings at the U.S.-Mexico border last month surged to a record number since President Biden took office. The government says it stopped migrants more than 250,000 times along the border. Up 40 percent from the prior December. The extraordinary influx came shortly before Mr. Biden introduced measures to deter migrants from Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua and Venezuela. Republicans say his lacks border policies have led to the flood. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.
