headline: Meet the Press for January 22, 2023, NBC
story_text: (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) [09:00:19] CHUCK TODD, NBC HOST (voice over): This Sunday, another document discovery. The FBI searched President Biden`s Delaware home on Friday and found more classified materials. Six documents, including some from his time as a senator, were found. Biden insists he did nothing wrong. PRESIDENT JOSEPH R. BIDEN, JR.: I think you`re going to find there`s nothing there. I have no regrets. TODD: Plus, warning signs. American politics teetering on the edge, from the court to Congress, to special counsel probes and rising extremist threats. After losing an election and claiming it was rigged, a Republican candidate is arrested and charged in connection with shootings at the homes of four Democratic lawmakers. (UNKNOWN): An attack on an elected official is an attack on democracy. TODD: New Mexico, just the latest example of election denialism sparking political violence. And, post-Roe. Fifty years after the landmark Supreme Court decision granting a constitutional right to abortion, the debate over reproductive rights has shifted, with the ruling now overturned. (UNKNOWN): We didn`t learn anything after overturning of Roe v. Wade. We buried our head in the sand. TODD: But if you think either side is open to finding a middle ground, think again. My guests this morning, Democratic Senator Joe Manchin of West Virginia and Republican Congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina. Plus, lasting impact. FORMER PRESIDENT WILLIAM JEFFERSON CLINTON : I did not have sexual relations with that woman. TODD: The Lewinsky scandal and its consequences still influencing American political life 25 years later. Joining me for insight and analysis are NBC News chief White House correspondent Kristen Welker; Republican strategist Brendan Buck; New York Times chief White House correspondent Peter Baker; and Kimberly Atkins Stohr, senior opinion writer for the Boston Globe . Welcome to Sunday. It`s "Meet the Press." ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest-running show in television history, this is "Meet the Press With Chuck Todd." TODD: Good Sunday morning. Boy, our democracy and our politics, they feel like we`re at a breaking point. We have rising political violence fueled by election denialism, economic brinksmanship in Congress, a Supreme Court relationships between the justices so strained after an unprecedented leak, they have yet to issue an opinion this term. And trust in the court from the public never been lower. And this morning we`re waking up to reports of another mass shooting with at least 10 dead at a lunar new year event in Monterey Park, California. Details are still coming in. No need to jump to conclusions, but, let`s be honest, these events do not exactly bring comfort to our current political system. We don`t handled these well or solve these problems. And if all of this wasn`t enough, adding to this instability, we have both the current and former presidents under investigation. And on Saturday night the White House revealed more classified information was found at Biden`s Wilmington home, after what was a remarkable 13-hour FBI -led search on Friday of the home of a sitting president. It wasn`t a subpoena; it was a cooperative search. It was done with the president`s legal team acknowledging it. They said they offered to provide prompt access to his home, and that six more items with classified markings were indeed found, including documents from Biden`s time as a senator as well as vice president. And this FBI search comes just days after Biden said he had no regrets about how he`s handled the issue of classified documents and how he`s talked to the public about it. But it`s likely to prompt more comparisons between the current and former presidents, though of course Mr. Trump and his advisers are also being investigated for obstructing their probe. Then we have the issue of election denialism. That`s been fueled by Donald Trump . And, sadly, it appears it`s given some of his supporters a permission slip to commit political violence. The case in New Mexico this week is just the latest in a string of violent incidents rooted in election denialism, from the assault on Brazil`s capitol by supporters of the former president there, where Trump allies actually helped sow doubts about those election results. We had the attack on Paul Pelosi just days before the midterm elections as well. And then, finally, we have this manufactured crisis here in Washington, this escalating rhetoric over the debt limit. It`s a reminder of just how fractured right now the Republican Party is, because it`s Republicans wanting to have this fight in an attempt to re-brand themselves as the party of fiscal discipline, if you will, after they oversaw an explosive rise in the national debt under President Donald Trump . So Republicans are trying to use this debate to try to unify them around an issue, cutting spending. Democrats, of course, now see an opportunity to paint House Republicans as extremist. The reality is, of course, at the end of the day, this debt limit is going to get raised. We just don`t know how it gets done. Even Republican Senate Leader Mitch McConnell concedes this point. SENATE MINORITY LEADER MITCH MCCONNELL, (R) KENTUCKY: America must never default on its debt. It never has and it never will. QUESTION: Should we be concerned about a financial crisis? [09:05:01] MCCONNELL: No, I would not be concerned about a financial crisis. (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: And joining me now is Senator Joe Manchin of West Virginia. Senator Manchin, welcome back... MANCHIN: Chuck, it`s always good to be with you. TODD: Look, I want to get into the debt ceiling. I want to get into all this stuff. But I -- we got some developments overnight with this classified documents, an FBI search. The White House said it was coordinated with the FBI , but we now have an FBI searching of former President Trumps`s... MANCHIN: Sure. TODD: Now we have an FBI search into President Biden`s residence. What`s your assessment of how the president has handled this situation? MANCHIN: Well, I mean, it`s just hard to believe that -- that in the United States of America we have a former president and the current president basically in the same situation. How does this happen? You know, only thing I can tell you, Chuck, is when I go into the SCIF with the secured documents, they always ask, "Are you clean," when you walk out. They want to make sure you`re not carrying anything out. You know, and there might be a mistake. You might just put it in your other papers. But you double-check right there. So that -- to be held accountable and responsible is what we all are. And to put those in unsecured spaces is irresponsible. TODD: Do you see similarities or do you see more differences in how President Trump versus how President Biden`s handled this? MANCHIN: I`m not going to make that decision, but I think that Merrick Garland did the right thing by putting a special counsel. TODD: You do? MANCHIN: And I think that we should wait until the special counsel rather than making this a political circus. Let them find out the facts. What, was one more damaging? Are they both about the same, did not cause any problem? Or is one more reckless and irresponsible than the other? I can`t answer that question, but I think the special counsel will do a better job than the politicians and the political circus that`s going to follow. TODD: President Biden said he had no regrets on how he handled this. Do you have any advice for him on how he should handle this... MANCHIN: Oh, I think he should have a lot of regrets, yeah. I would... TODD: What are they? MANCHIN: I would think that. And I`d say, whoever`s responsible -- I mean, if I hold people accountable and I use, whether it be my staff or my -- you know, my -- my staff, that we`re doing this, and I`m looking at it, then I`m going to hold someone accountable. But, basically, the buck stops with me. TODD: So you think he should be out there, and "Look, I -- I messed up." MANCHIN: That`s all. Just say... TODD: "Maybe I didn`t do it" -- just say it? MANCHIN: "I made a mistake." TODD: Just fall on your sword here? MANCHIN: We`re all human. TODD: Yeah... MANCHIN: We make mistakes. I can tell you, I don`t think anyone intended - - he sure didn`t intend for it to fall into wrong hands and use it against our country. I know they didn`t intend that to happen. Could it have happened? I don`t know. And, yeah, you just might as well say, "Listen, it`s irresponsible. It was something we should have had a better check and balance on. TODD: Now, former President Trump defied a subpoena. So, in that sense, the way each has handled is different. Do you acknowledge that? MANCHIN: Absolutely... TODD: Yeah. TODD: ... much different than the other. One`s -- one`s saying, "OK, I hope I didn`t make any mistakes. I hope no one was compromised. I hope we didn`t hurt our country." And the other says, "Oh, I`m -- believe me." Well, you know what? (LAUGHTER) What they said, verify. You have to verify? TODD: Trust, but verify. MANCHIN: Trust, but verify. Let`s find out. And that`s what the special counsel is... TODD: And that`s what you want here? Both special counsels to, sort of, resolve... MANCHIN: First of all, every one of us in our life have to be held accountable and responsible for our actions. TODD: Yeah. MANCHIN: People want accountability. And they want, basically, when you`re held accountable, are you responsible or not? If you are, would you -- can you fix that? Did you make a mistake? Fine. You know... TODD: And that`s what you think, the president needs to get out and there just get in front of it. MANCHIN: Cicero said, "To err is human." You`re a human being. You`re going to make mistakes. Did you intend to make it? Did you intend to harm somebody? Did you intend to basically do an irresponsible thing? I don`t think, hopefully, either one of them did. TODD: Right. MANCHIN: But it sure -- sure turned out to be irresponsible. TODD: Let`s talk about the debt ceiling. You`re -- as always, you`re trying to find a compromise and middle ground. MANCHIN: Yeah. TODD: I -- I know your instinct here. (LAUGHTER) But why should Republicans get the benefit of the doubt on the debt ceiling here, considering that it`s -- that they`re, sort of, manufacturing a crisis that`s a bit unnecessary right now? MANCHIN: Well, first of all, if one side thinks that the other one`s more responsible for the debt, at $31.4 trillion, that`s -- that is totally not accurate, and it`s deceptive. We`re all responsible. We`ve got a $31.4 trillion debt. It`s a runaway debt, and no one`s holding themselves accountable. And basically, I think you said it, use the budget process. I`ve been here 12 years. We haven`t had a budget yet. TODD: Yeah, I -- that`s what I don`t get here. MANCHIN: We haven`t had a budget yet. TODD: And that`s what I question... MANCHIN: Yeah, you should. TODD: You want to do this special committee here. MANCHIN: I`m... TODD: And I`m sitting here going, why add more bureaucracy? We have a budget committee. We have two budget committees. We have a joint committee on taxation. We have all these different committees that have already been created to deal with this process. Why can`t we use the congressional bureaucracy that exists? MANCHIN: We have 12 appropriations committees that`s supposed to do their job. Why don`t you basically put a time certain on what you can... TODD: Right. MANCHIN: ... and what can`t do and when you do it. I can`t speak for that. I was a former governor of the State of the West Virginia. TODD: Right. MANCHIN: I was responsible for a balanced-budget amendment and basically staying within the realms of my constitution. So, you know, I met every week; every week like clockwork they walked into my office, on a Tuesday or Wednesday, and sat down and go over it. You`re either going to be -- have to make some cuts now, make some adjustments now so we end the year with a balanced budget... TODD: Sure. MANCHIN: ... or a surplus. There`s nothing that holds us accountable -- nothing at all. We can say, "Oh, we`re going to do it." As I`ve said before, 12 years, haven`t had a budget. That`s ridiculous. TODD: So let me -- you want to do this, sort of, you and Senator Romney, to have a committee that deals with the trust fund issues. [09:10:01] But right now neither party wants to touch that. I mean, in that sense, you have Donald Trump came out, and certainly Democrats, nobody wants to touch Social Security and Medicare. MANCHIN: Well, first of all... TODD: So how do you separate those two out and deal with our fiscal... MANCHIN: Why would you scare the bejeezus out of people that basically -- I`m going to say, in West Virginia, I`ve got 60 -percent of my population that that`s all they have is Medicare and Social Security. You think I`m going to go down that path and put them in jeopardy? No, but there are so much other things that -- basically wasteful spending that can be corralled in without scaring the bejeezus, depending on what political side you`re on. TODD: Let me ask you about wasteful spending. Because one of the -- the three most hypocritical words I hear are "waste, fraud and abuse." (LAUGHTER) Right? Everybody says, "Oh, waste, fraud and abuse." MANCHIN: And it`s all there. It`s all there. (LAUGHTER) TODD: OK, but -- but waste, fraud and abuse isn`t going to balance a budget, OK? At the end of the day, there`s going to have to be choices that have to be made. What is something that ought to be on -- in the discussion of, you know, maybe we`re spending too much? MANCHIN: Well, we know we`re spending too much because we`re not balancing our budget... (CROSSTALK) MANCHIN: ... have more debt. The bottom line is, it`s in the eyes of the beholder. That`s the problem that we have, 535 people say, "Wait a minute, yeah, what you`re doing is wasteful, Chuck; I think you ought to cut that." TODD: Right. MANCHIN: And you`re going to say, "OK, Joe, how about yours?" TODD: But -- but your -- your spending that you think is mandatory, another person thinks is wasteful, right, or abuse? MANCHIN: Yeah, and just think, for every dollar -- just get it down -- break it down to the dollar. Is there any savings within that dollar you think that there`s wasteful or abuse that we could at least have a target to set. Is it a penny? Is it five pennies? Is it a nickel? TODD: Yeah. MANCHIN: Where is it? TODD: But here`s what gets lost here, is nobody will put anything on the table. Everybody says, "We`ve got to cut spending." Well, what? And nobody wants to... (CROSSTALK) MANCHIN: Chuck, you hit it dead on the head. The process isn`t working. How come we`re not held accountable to have a -- to have the appropriation bills done at a certain time before the end of the fiscal year? TODD: You tell me. MANCHIN: Well, that`s what I... TODD: I mean, what does Chuck Schumer say? What does Mitch McConnell say? MANCHIN: You know what happens? It rolls -- it rolls over into an omnibus bill at the end, and everything`s thrown into it, and OK, "Here, we`ve got it, guys, that`s it." It makes no sense. TODD: So what should -- so it sounds like you actually think the debt ceiling is a moment we should use to focus on... MANCHIN: Well, if you`re going to use the debt ceiling for anything except for theatrics, OK, which is what probably might happen for a while -- we`re going to pass the debt ceiling. You are exactly correct. It has to pass. You know, we have the currency of the -- you know, good faith of the United States dollar and the currency of the world. You just can`t let it default and basically hold us in jeopardy from where we stand in -- in the world -- world order. With that being said, is how do you get to it? Do you use this moment? Do you come to a responsibility? What -- what are we paying for interest now? For 10 years, it was zero; it was funny money. We`re not -- you know, it doesn`t put any burden. We`re just raising debt, but we`re not basically harming how we have to meet that debt through our interest payments. Now we`re talking real money on interest rates. We`re almost up to what our defense budget is, paying in interest. TODD: I guess I come back to, and I don`t think you have the answer, either, which is, what is the moment to force this confrontation? MANCHIN: This is a moment -- if Kevin McCarthy coming in -- coming in new, says, "OK, this is -- we`re -- it`s serious, and he takes it from the standpoint -- and he knows... TODD: What does he need to do that you would take him seriously on this? MANCHIN: Well, you know, Chuck... TODD: You know what I mean by that, like, how do you know when he`s being serious and how do you know when he`s playing politics? MANCHIN: Well -- well, the bottom line is he has a hell -- a heck of a political hand that`s not -- not very good right now. He`s not -- he`s not holding a lock, if you will. And he has 10 or 12 -- it`s pretty much out there. He has to make a decision on how he wants to govern and how he wants this next two years and this 118th Congress. You know, I just -- it was amazing. I just saw the Ohio legislature -- I don`t know if you paid any attention to it. TODD: I did, yeah. MANCHIN: The Ohio legislature, which is Republican controlled, basically chose their new speaker, a Republican, with as many if not more votes from the Democrats. Because they wanted someone they can work with. That`s a coalition. Why can`t we put coalitions together here? TODD: Well, that`s... MANCHIN: Some moderate, centrist Democrats, coming over and working, whoever`s the majority, and saying, "You don`t have to -- you don`t have to bow and kowtow to the extremes." TODD: You don`t have to work about primaries. A lot of your colleagues have to worry about primaries. Isn`t that why this doesn`t happen? MANCHIN: Let me tell you one thing. Meanwhile, this week marks 25 years since news broke that President Bill Clinton had an extramarital affair with a young White House intern. It`s a scandal that forever transformed Washington`s politics, the media, and the American public. Monica Lewinsky`s lawyer joined this program to discuss the president`s future just after the story broke. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP, JANUARY 25, 1998) TIM RUSSERT, MODERATOR, MEET THE PRESS: Do you believe the president can survive this crisis? WILLIAM GINSBURG, ATTORNEY: I don`t know. I don`t want to call myself a country lawyer, but I certainly am not a Beltway lawyer and I`m not a political pundit. RUSSERT: Does it influence you, affect you in any way to know that the fate of the country, the fate of Bill Clinton , is in effect in your hands and in Monica Lewinsky`s hands? GINSBURG: In addition to the fact that I don`t believe that the government of the United States is in Monica Lewinsky`s hands or in my hands, short of that, you bet you it scares me. It scares me that my country could be in this kind of a crisis. I`m not political, but I am a citizen of this country and I do respect the presidency. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: When we come back, just how much did the Lewinsky scandal change the course of our political history? Trust me, we are still living with the consequences today. Our panel is next to discuss. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:53:36] TODD: Welcome back. This week marks the 25th anniversary of an event that arguably launched our current moment in our politics, when Matt Drudge on the Internet broke the news that "Newsweek" was sitting on a story about former President Bill Clinton having an affair with a young White House intern named Monica Lewinsky . So, here`s what happened next -- a presidential lie, an investigation, disappointing Republican midterm, impeachment, Senate acquittal, round-the- clock media coverage and speculation, and the takeoff of a more partisan cable TV news environment. It remains one of the more significant forks in the road in modern political history, and it turns out we`re perhaps still living in that moment. Peter Baker, you and I were both, sort of, younger, very much reporters in this moment. And I think at the time we were all blown away. I guess looking back last week, it just sort of hit me, my God, we`re still stuck in this loop. BAKER: Yeah. We are stuck in this loop. That`s exactly right, I was just remembering. I remember walking home at night, at 2:00 in the morning after we published the first story on this in "The Washington Post " at the time, thinking, oh my God. What have we done? What have we unleashed here? This is an extraordinary story. The president of the United States, sex in the White House, investigation of lying under oath. But to your point, I think it changed our politics. It wasn`t just a one- off sex scandal, which we`ve had a number in our history. It was a moment when we made our politics more tribal, in which we decided we were going to make any investigation, any scandal about us versus them. And that`s what we`ve seen time and time again ever since. [21:25:01] We saw it with Trump. We`ve seen it with other presidents. And I think that we redefined our ideologies to suit which side are we on. TODD: You know, before 1998 we had had one impeachment in this country. Since that time, Brendan Buck, we`ve had three. I mean you just can`t -- we live in this moment constantly and the way Democrats rallied around Bill Clinton , we saw Republicans rally around Donald Trump . And you can`t help but ask yourself -- without Clinton, does Trump ever happen? BUCK: Yeah. I think the tribalism is the right point. It`s, while I don`t like what you did, you`re my guy and I would never give the other side a win. And I think that`s how everything is viewed. It`s much less, what my team is for, as being against what the other team is. It turned politics into a soap opera. And that`s what we still have today. Most -- I won`t say "most" -- a lot of politicians now are much more entertainers in their own minds than they are public servants. And it corrodes our politics, and there are so many outlets for it. Of course, the media, there are so many more platforms for them to play the role and to entertain, and it leads us to where we are now. TODD: No, you definitely saw the partisanship of cable exploded. The idea that cable news is a prime time destination didn`t exist until Monica. But, Kimberly, we also know the fact that this was an incredibly misogynist thing that happened. This was a -- you know, when we talk about Me Too -- and I`ve had younger staff. They say when they learn the history of it, they don`t understand why there was no discussion of the power dynamic. And it`s like, that`s how immature our debate was back then. ATKINS STOHR: Yeah. Two decades before Me Too. You know, over the years, I`ve had discussions with people who have said their viewpoint about Monica Lewinsky then has changed so profoundly than it is now. That someone -- this 22-year-old intern, you think about the kids that you see walking around -- TODD: Twenty-two-year-old intern. We all have 22-year-olds walking around our offices. ATKINS STOHR: Right, and the attacks that were done. I mean, just, I couldn`t imagine being a part of that. She seems to have come out of that with a lot of grace and respect now in retrospect, but it really shows the difference in how up until then --aside from Clarence Thomas -- there wasn`t a sex scandal that was this public. Now, we treat things very differently. TODD: Do we though? WELKER: Well, and -- ATKINS STOHR: No. Not differently enough. But at least there is that change. WELKER: I do think that that is one of the biggest impacts, this cultural shift. And Monica Lewinsky herself describes herself as patient zero for Internet shaming. And she has talked about being bullied and what that experience was like. And the way that she was treated by this country, by the world has not aged well. And in many ways, it is the seeds of the Me Too movement. And I think it`s been fascinating to watch her reclaim her story. And as you say, Kimberly, so many people have changed their perspectives about how they view that moment, how they viewed her and how they treated her. TODD: Peter, the question I wonder: It`s going to take some outside event to shift us to another fork in the road and get out of this doom loop we`re in, but I don`t know what that looks like. BAKER: I don`t know what that looks like. I mean, we had 9/11, and we kind of changed -- TODD: Temporary respite. BAKER: -- our politics for about a year or so, right? TODD: Yeah. BAKER: And that didn`t make a permanent difference. And I don`t know what will happen now that will be the equivalent of that. I mean, we have these big crises. We have these big issues. We have the debt ceiling issue. We have a crisis of our democracy. We have the crisis of the war in Ukraine. So many crises, and we can`t come together on things. TODD: Everything is worse since 1998 in this moment. That`s the bottom line, sadly. Before we go, sign up for our free daily newsletter, First Read. You`ll get the best analysis, polling, and political news every morning: wisdom before it becomes conventional. Scan the QR code on screen or go to NBCNews.com/FirstRead. That`s all we have for today. Thanks for watching. We`ll be back next week; because if it`s Sunday, it`s "Meet the Press". END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. headline: Nationwide Marches On Anniversary Of Roe v. Wade
story_text: KATE SNOW: Today, the landmark abortion ruling, Roe v. Wade turns 50 years old. But the controversy surrounding last year`s reversal or Roe is heating up once again, with marches across the country. And now, more than six months after that decision, where does the battle over abortion rights stand? Marissa Para reports from Madison, Wisconsin. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We will win. I believe that we will win. MARISSA PARRA, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, on the 50th anniversary of Roe v. Wade, abortion rights activists drumming up defiance, moving their main women`s march bigger than Roe, from the capitol to the Midwest. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: This time, we move the National March to Madison in order to kick off our newfound campaign to the states, which is where battle is taking place. PARRA (on camera): So, I have the main march here in Madison, Wisconsin, that is because we are just weeks away from a primary judicial election and a state Supreme Court seat is up for grabs. And if it is filled with a pro- abortion rights candidate, then the Wisconsin abortion ban could be overturned. PARRA (voiceover): Sister marches in hundreds of cities across the country, just days after the National March for life against abortion and just seven months after Roe v. Wade was overturned in a five-four decision, sending both sides of the debate into action. The state of play, a murky patchwork. Roughly two dozen states have either a total abortion ban or are close to it. Some state laws changed immediately, like Wisconsin`s abortion ban. Some, like neighboring Illinois, later passing abortion protection. And last fall, historically red states, Kansas and Kentucky, voted down antiabortion ballot measures. Today, Vice President Kamala Harris once again calling to codify Roe. KAMALA HARRIS , U.S. VICE PRESIDENT: Congress must pass a bill that protects freedom and liberty. PARRA (voiceover): But with Republicans in control of the House, the federal abortion debate remains in a deadlock, making mobilizing on a local level more important than ever. From Madison, Wisconsin, Marissa Parra, NBC News. (END VIDEO CLIP) SNOW: Still ahead, a goodbye at Graceland, the moving tributes from celebrities and fans today for Lisa Marie Presley. How her mother remembered her. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:50:00] SNOW: A violent protest in Downtown Atlanta is under investigation tonight. It happened late Saturday. A group demonstrating against a new police training center got out of hand. Police say some people smashed windows and set a patrol car on fire. Others were carrying explosive devices. Six people were arrested and charged with domestic terrorism, arson, and criminal damage. A small plane made an emergency landing northwest of Houston Today. Take a look at this. The single engine aircraft reported that it lost power and it went down, crashing on top of an 18-wheeler. The plane then caught fire. The most astonishing thing about all this, the pilot and the truck driver were not injured. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. BRACH: Flattens, comes in a bunch of sizes. Flattering on all shapes and sizes, really great color assortment. And you can never go wrong with a pair of white sneakers. KOTB: Yes. (LOCAL NEWS AND WEATHER) [09:00:00] [09:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) AL ROKER, NBC TODAY WEATHER ANCHOR: This morning on the "3rd Hour of TODAY," deep sea discovery. New haunting video of the "Titanic" captured nearly 40 years ago. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It was really literally entering a preserved museum, and the deeper you got into the ship, the more preserved it was. (END VIDEO CLIP) ROKER: Why it`s just now being released and what researchers found inside the doomed ship. Then, later, a "TODAY`s Checklist" for men and women. How to take care of your hair and what to do if you`re losing it. Plus, an icon in the house. NBA legend Kareem Abdul-Jabbar is here. How does he really feel about his all-time scoring record being broken and his important heart health message? And Taye Diggs joining us live in studio with big news for fans of his hit show, today, Thursday, February 16, 2023. ANNOUNCER: Live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza, this is the "3rd Hour of TODAY." SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS 3RD HOUR OF TODAY, CO-HOST: Good morning and welcome to the "3rd Hour of TODAY." I`m Sheinelle here with our whole team. The gang`s all here this morning. Al and Craig. First of all, can we just say, I was downstairs with everybody in the concourse, is what we call it here, and we look up at the monitor -- CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes. JONES: -- and you guys were having like a lovefest or something. What was happening? ROKER: Well, it was the "Titanic." You know, Joe Fryer, who`s about to do a story about the Titanic. JONES: OK. ROKER: And we had the video of Jack and Rose. And I just -- I was inspired. MELVIN: I was moved by the spirit. JONES: So, did you just -- you got moved by the spirit and you just decided to just -- ROKER: Yes. MELVIN: Yes. ROKER: Yes, just kind of like -- MELVIN: It was fun. ROKER: King of the world. JONES: I love it. Well, so -- DYLAN DREYER, NBC NEWS 3RD HOUR OF TODAY CO-HOST AND METEOROLOGIST: I mean, you guys have also recreated the pottery scene from "Ghost." MELVIN: The "Ghost" scene. ROKER: Yes. JONES: Oh, "Ghost" scene. DREYER: So -- ROKER: That`s right. JONES: We need to do a mash-up. ROKER: No, we are not going to recreate the "Dirty Dancing" scene. MELVIN: No. No, we`re not. JONES: Come on. MELVIN: No. JONES: That`s -- that would be the trilogy. DREYER: Yes. MELVIN: I mean, so you`re so light, I could probably do it. JONES: You could probably do it now. All right. Well, to be continued. We`ll try to make that happen and do like a mash-up. But there is a reason we`ve been talking about the "Titanic" this morning. Here`s the latest, some never-before-seen footage. It was shot back in 1986. It`s just been released. Now, at the time, this was the first expedition to actually find the Titanic. Look at this. DREYER: Look at this. JONES: The ship is so cool. It`s gone unseen at the bottom of the Atlantic for more than 70 years. So, we have NBC`s Joe Fryer here. He`s following the story for us this morning. DREYER: Oh, the chandelier. JONES: It`s like so beautiful. Why are we just now seeing it, you know, now? JOE FRYER, NBC NEWS NOW ANCHOR: Yes. So, there was this tiny little independent film made 25 years ago called "Titanic." Perhaps you heard of it. And it`s just now starting to get some buzz. This is the 25th anniversary of the Titanic. So, it kind of to commemorate that. JONES: OK. FRYER: This video is finally being released. I mean, let me give you the background here. JONES: OK. FRYER: First of all, remember, the Titanic went down in 1912. It took decades to find. It wasn`t until 1985 that a crew was able to find it, more than 12,000 feet below the surface. Robert Ballard, who you heard from at the beginning of the show, he was on that crew. So, months later, back then in 1986, they went down, they took this footage. It`s really the first-time humans laid eyes on the wreckage of the Titanic. But the footage, basically, most it has remained private until now. It was not released publicly. It`s 81 minutes. It`s uncut. DREYER: Wow. FRYER: It`s unnarrated. And you can really just stare at it. DREYER: Which is really exciting because now so much of it is disintegrating. We can`t see anything new. So, we think all of our new Titanic stuff, we can`t get anymore. And, wow. JONES: Boom. DREYER: It`s like you see chandeliers, you see things from 1986 that were still in such good condition. FRYER: Yes, you see that. And the chandelier is really one of the most haunting images. ROKER: Yes. FRYER: But you see the front of the bow of the ship. You know, you see the first officer`s cabin. There are so many details you see. And things that look different, you know, back in the `80s than they even do now because it is disintegrating. There`s this metal-eating bacteria that`s actually sort of turning the remnants of Titanic -- MELVIN: That sounds really sci-fi. FRYER: I know. -- to dust. And so, you get to see all these -- JONES: Oh, it turns it to dust. FRYER: -- incredible images, the promenade window. And it really gives you a look into early 20th century life. And this footage probably does a better job of it than some of the high-definition cameras that have gotten down there more recently. Robert Ballard says it was like a tombstone when he remembers seeing it for the first time. ROKER: Sure. DREYER: Oh, my goodness. FRYER: And one of the most haunting images for him, he remembers seeing, you know, a mother`s shoes next to a baby`s shoes. I mean, really just some images that stick with you. ROKER: Wow. DREYER: Heartbreaking. JONES: Wow. ROKER: Joe, that was haunting. JONES: It`s interesting. Joe Fryer, thank you. MELVIN: Thanks, Joe. ROKER: Appreciate it. DREYER: Yes. ROKER: All right. So, another big story we`re watching this morning, 2024 presidential race starting to take shape. We`ve got former South Carolina governor and U.N . ambassador, Nikki Haley, officially in. Craig. MELVIN: In fact, Mr. Roker had the chance to catch up with the former ambassador right after her first campaign event yesterday in Charleston, South Carolina. We talked about her decision, some of the biggest campaign issues, and the support she`s receiving from her family. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) [09:05:00] MELVIN (voiceover): Your former boss said that you had a hard time making the decision, said that you would never run against the president, he did a great job, he was the best president in my lifetime, his words, told Nikki to follow her heart. She`s polling at 1 percent. Not a bad start. Your response to that? NIKKI HALEY, FORMER U.N. AMBASSADOR: What I`ll tell you is I think he was a good president. There was so much that he did that was good. What I`m talking about -- MELVIN: Well, then why not support him this time? NIKKI HALEY: Because I think we need to have a new generation, for Republicans. We have lost the last seven out of eight popular votes for president. It means Republicans need to do something different. MELVIN: Is it the message or is it the messengers? NIKKI HALEY: I think it`s always both. It`s always got to be someone who really does listen to the people, that has their pulse on the ground of what real families are going through. But I also think it`s how you communicate. I don`t want just Republicans with me, I want everybody with me because I believe that everybody wants to be proud about America. MELVIN: Let`s talk about abortion for a moment. A senior senator from South Carolina, Lindsey Graham, has proposed a federal ban on abortion. Would you sign that? NIKKI HALEY: We need consensus on this. Our goal -- MELVIN: Consensus on abortion? Would you support a federal ban? NIKKI HALEY: I think we -- not a full out federal ban, because I don`t think that`s been put on the table. I think what Lindsey Graham has put on the table is 15 weeks. And I think, if we`re looking at 15 weeks, what we need to understand is that we are not OK with abortion up until the time of birth. And so, we should at least decide when it is OK. MELVIN: A decade ago, you supported significantly scaling back Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid. Should those social safety nets be scaled back? NIKKI HALEY: Should we reform those entitlements? Yes. But should we take anything from people who have already been promised? No. MELVIN: When you say reform, what do you mean? NIKKI HALEY: You go and everybody that`s been promised money, they get it. We don`t take it from anybody. But these new ones coming in, they know what`s going to be broke by the time they get there. Those are the ones we fix. The younger generation, we go and do a new system on how they`re going to get it. MELVIN: So, you would phase out Social Security -- NIKKI HALEY: Not phasing -- MELVIN: and Medicare and Medicaid, as we know it. As we know it now, you would phase it out? NIKKI HALEY: You would change it. You`re not phasing it out. MELVIN: Well, it seems like semantics, if you`re saying -- NIKKI HALEY: You are saying change it out. MELVIN: So, you want to reform it? NIKKI HALEY: I want to reform it, yes. MELVIN (voiceover): A plan for the future as Nikki Haley looks at a long campaign trail ahead. But she isn`t doing it alone, her husband Michael and kids Rena and Nalin are by her side. NIKKI HALEY: You can`t do this without your family. You just can`t. And so, to have them there for support, it`s everything. MELVIN (on camera): We`ve got a wedding that`s about to happen in the Haley family. So, are you helping plan a wedding and a presidential campaign simultaneously? NIKKI HALEY: We are. But this has been really sweet. We`ve had a lot of fun with this. RENA HALEY, NIKKE HALEY`S DAUGHTER: We have. NIKKI HALEY: I mean, between like picking songs and picking flowers and all of those things, it`s kind of a sweet spot to be able to do this. MELVIN: Did you go to your family before you decided to run for president and say, you know what, this is what I think I want to do? NIKKI HALEY: I did. MELVIN: How`d that conversation go? NIKKI HALEY: I did. Nalin has always been very involved in everything I do politically. He, of course, was like, yes, you should do this. And Rena`s response was, why do you want to live in someone else`s house again? Literally, it wasn`t what it was. MELVIN (voiceover): Haley`s son not only encouraged his mom to run, he`s even working on her campaign this summer. MELVIN (on camera): Do you ever provide unsolicited political advice to mom? NIKKI HALEY: Every day, all day. MELVIN: Really? NIKKI HALEY: By text message, by phone call, and everything in between. Nonstop. NALIN HALEY, NIKKI HALEY`S SON: I`m her biggest supporter, but also her biggest critic. MELVIN: Wow. NIKKI HALEY: It`s very true. It`s very true. MELVIN: What kind of mom was Nikki Haley? NALIN HALEY: A tough one, but also a very loving one and caring one. MELVIN: Rena? RENA HALEY: She was tough but loving. She always made sure to show up to any events we had, came in and supported us, but we always had our house rules we had to follow. MELVIN: Were you surprised at all when she said, you know what, I think I want to do this? MICHAEL HALEY, HALEY`S HUSBAND: No, I wasn`t surprised. MELVIN: I would imagine from time to time you would see or hear something that`s said or written about your wife and you -- M. HALEY: You know, when you wade in this water, you know, it`s going to happen. NIKKI HALEY: I think it`s tougher on them than it is on me. And they do take it personally. And politics is a blood sport. And it`s a shame that it is, but it is. They know that the key is, you know, you have your faith, you trust in the love we have as a family, and this, too, shall pass. That`s the beautiful thing about campaigns, is there`s a start and an end. And the goal is just pray every day and let`s get through it. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: So, you know, I`ve covered ambassador for a number of years now, and when I saw the kids yesterday, it was pretty interesting because I`ve seen, you know, the kids off and on for years. In fact, I think we`ve got a picture from her first inauguration as governor. DREYER: Oh, my goodness. JONES: Wow. MELVIN: So, those are the two kids there. DREYER: All grown up. MELVIN: All grown. JONES: This is a hot topic. DR. WOLFELD: It`s a very hot topic. JONES: All right. So, let`s first start with -- I mean, even just breakage. DR. WOLFELD: Right. WOLFELD: Anything too rough or strenuous can maybe damage and break your hair. [09:15:00] JONES: And you know there`s a thing going around where they`re telling girls, if you want your hair to be thicker and longer, to brush it. So, kids are just brush, brush, brush. WOLFELD: You want to avoid tension on your hair. So, any tight hairstyles are no good. JONES: Yes. DR. WOLFELD: Avoid any very hot treatments, hot hair blowers are not very good. I -- well, the basics. You see God only made so many perfect heads. The rest he covered with hair. So, you`ve got to take care of your scalp, right? DR. WOLFELD: That`s right. That`s right. So, just in your daily life, from the products you may use, from sweating, from just grime from the environment may build up in your scalp so you want to really cleans your scalp. ROKER: Right. DR. headline: Clearing Up Some Common Nutrition Myths With The Registered Dietitian
story_text: SAVANNAH JONES: Welcome back this morning on Your Health. Common myths and maybe misguiding your diet decisions. Nora Minno is a registered dietician and she`s here to clear these things up once and for all. Nora, good morning to you. NORA MINNO, REGISTERED DIETICIAN: Good morning, Sheinelle. JONES: So we have five nutrition myths that we`re going to debunk. I should say there are three of us here because congratulations. MINNO: Yes, thank you. JONES: She was so worried as nutritionist people are going to be like, oh, she`s got little (inaudible). No, no, there`s a little baby in there. MINNO: Exactly. JONES: We are girl, we don`t know, OK. First things first, I should avoid all carbs. This is a big one. MINNO: Yes. JONES: I know so many people who just -- they feel like if they touch a carb, they explode. MINNO: I agree. And I have good news for all you carb lovers. I`m pretty sure as everybody body, right? Carbs are your friend. In fact, there are a really important part of a healthy balanced diet. They do a lot for us. They are our body`s preferred source of fuel, same with our brain. They help our digestion and they actually just make us feel good. JONES: So then, what are we doing wrong then? Because a lot of people, you know, I guess obviously probably shouldn`t have carbs before bed, but where are we going wrong? MINNO: Exactly. So really, when it comes to carbs, it is just about the quality of carbs that you`re picking and the quantity that you`re consuming. That`s really where a lot of people go wrong over consuming things like refined carbs, sweets, white breads, things like that. But if you focus on portions, choose more complex carbs. JONES: What`s a good carb? Give me a couple of example. MINNO: Fruits, vegetables, whole grains, oatmeal, things like that, you should be in the clear. JONES: All right. So myth number two, fresh produce is healthier than frozen or canned. What would you say? MINNO: No. This is not true at all. In fact, sometimes your frozen or canned options can be actually more nutritious. There was a study done that found that vegetables can lose 15% to 55% of their vitamin C by the time they`re picked, by the time they make it to your grocery shelf. So frozen, they typically flash freeze right on the spot. So you`re packing a lot more nutrients. And they`re actually a little bit better for your wallet too. JONES: I was just about to say there`s a cost benefit as well. MINNO: Exactly. Less food waste, oftentimes they are more budget friendly. And then you just have some good things on hand if you want to make a smoothie, a salad, things like that. JONES: Absolutely. OK, our next myth, this is a good one. Plant milk is healthier than dairy milk. What say ye? MINNO: All right. Well, this is not always the case. This one really comes down just to preference because you know, now it just seems like there`s a million different plant milks out there. There are options galore, which is great, but cow`s milk is still a really great option. One cup of skim milk packs in 10 grams of protein and a quarter of your daily calcium needs. Whereas plant milk like an almond milk has one gram of protein per serving. JONES: You know what it is, I guess also just depends on, you know, whether you`re lactose intolerant, you know, if you have a dietary issue. MINNO: Exactly. So this one -- one is not better than the other, it`s just going to come down to choice. And if you are picking a plant milk, you want to pick varieties that have low or no added sugar, and ones that are more fortified with things like calcium, vitamin D that you might not be getting if you`re picking that -- JONES: I will admit that the plant milks, I didn`t realize some of them do have a lot of sugar. MINNO: Some do. JONES: I just didn`t realize that. MINNO: Some do. So be a savvy reader. JONES: All right. Let`s talk about fat there. Remember for a while everything was low fat this, low fat that. MINNO: Yes. MINNO: So the nutrition or the myth number four all fat is bad. Obviously it`s not. [08:45:05] MINNO: It`s not. And thank goodness that low fat craze in the `90s and thereafter is over because we know now that fats, most importantly, mono and polyunsaturated fats are really good for us. It is still American Heart Month, and we want to get those fats in from things like avocados, nuts, seeds, olive oils, and even our fatty fish to help protect our heart boost that HDL, which is our good cholesterol, and lower LDL, which is our bad cholesterol. JONES: Sounds good. And I think sometimes when you`re eating, you just don`t know which one is right. MINNO: Exactly. So we do want to avoid certain fats, there are facts called saturated fats, that the American Heart Association says we should stay at or below 13 grams a day -- JONES: Oh wait, that`s good advice. MINNO: -- for a hearth healthy diet. JONES: All right. Si when you get a package is something flipped over the back. MINNO: Yes. JONES: And if you see saturated fats, how many grams did you say it should be layered? MINNO: 13, approximately around 13 per day. JONES: Per day. MINNO: So if you have four ounces of kind of lean ground beef, you`re already at that 13 mark. So you want to be a real savvy label reader. JONES: OK, all right. Myth number five soy, I`m actually interested in what you`re going to say. Soy increases risk for breast cancer. MINNO: Yes. You know, I hear this one all the time. JONES: Me too. MINNO: And it`s still very common and abundant. So this myth really stems from the fact that soy contains something called phytoestrogens. And we know that estrogen can sometimes be linked to an increase in breast cancer. JONES: Right. MINNO: But the estrogens in soy are very different than mammalian estrogens, ones that we have in our body, and they act differently. And in fact, they can be protective against things like breast cancer, because what we`ve seen in Asian countries where they consume more soy, is that breast cancer risk is actually much lower. JONES: Does it depend on the product or what kind of soy you`re consuming? No? MINNO: Not really. And again, the American Heart Association said 25 grams of soy protein per day can actually be heart protective. So you can get your tofu, your (inaudible), your soy milk, your edamame at a sushi restaurant, right? Lots of really great options to pack some good soy protein. JONES: There you go. So you don`t have to avoid it. Nora, thank you. MINNO: That`s OK. Thank you, Sheinelle. JONES: All right. headline: The Today Show for February 20, 2023, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:00:00] SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS 3RD HOUR OF TODAY, CO-HOST: It is 8:00 on "TODAY." Coming up, surprise visit. Overnight, President Biden making history arriving in Ukraine. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , U.S. PRESIDENT: I`m here to show our unwavering support for the nation`s independence, and sovereignty, and territorial integrity. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: A major sign of support from the U.S. as the war in Ukraine approaches its one-year anniversary. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BIDEN: That`s how long we`re going to be with you, Mr. President, for as long as it takes. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: We`re live with the latest. Then, holiday sales. Hoping to save some money this long weekend. We have a look at all the best Presidents` Day deals, everything from furniture to appliances, electronics, and cars. Plus, the three questions you should ask yourself before making a purchase. And royal treatment. The Prince and Princess of Wales joining stars from around the world for the so-called British Oscars. We`re highlighting all the best moments including an emotional tribute to Queen Elizabeth. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) HELEN MIRREN, ACTRESS: Cinema at its best does what her majesty did effortlessly, bring us together and unite us in a story. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: So, what films took home the night`s biggest awards? All that and more. Today, Monday, February 20, 2023. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Spending Presidents` Day. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: On the plaza. CROWD: From Fort Worth, Texas. CROWD: Murrysville (ph), Pennsylvania. CROWD: Huntsville, Alabama. CROWD: St. John, Indiana. CROWD: And New Lenox, Illinois. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Celebrating milestone birthdays. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: My 30th. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And my 60th. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: From Jacksonville, Florida. CROWD: Lea`s (ph) turning 18. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Shout out to our NBC family. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: At KOMU 8 News. CROWD: In Columbia, Missouri. CROWD: Happy Presidents` Day. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: Welcome back to "TODAY." We certainly appreciate you being with us on this Monday morning. And take a look at all of these folks. We are happy to see this happy holiday crowd. This is on -- in our corner of the woods here at Rockefeller Plaza. TOM LLAMAS, NBC NEWS SENIOR NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Yes, they came from all over the country. We always love that. JONES: Uh-huh. LLAMAS: A lot of states represented. Savannah and Hoda, you know them, will be back tomorrow, of course, and it will be a big morning here in Studio 1A. JONES: That is right. Grammy winning superstar Pink will be here. She`s coming out with a new album and heading on tour. So, a lot to talk about. Plus, she`ll treat us to a live performance when she joins us for our 8:00, 9:00, and 10:00 hours. So, join us tomorrow. JACOB SOBOROFF, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: I am not going anywhere. LLAMAS: Yes. JONES: Right SOBOROFF: I`m going to stick around for that. JONES: It`s going to be a party. LLAMAS: She always brings it. Like, live -- JONES: She does. LLAMAS: -- Pink live is always amazing. JONES: She does. And we`ll get back outside and say hi to all those folks coming up in just a bit. Meantime, it is a busy morning. So, let`s get to your news at 8:00. In an unprecedented show of support for Ukraine, President Biden took a high stakes trip to the war zone overnight. His surprise journey to Kyiv coming just days before the first anniversary of the Russian invasion. NBC`s Erin McLaughlin is in the Ukrainian capital with more on this historic visit. Erin, good morning. ERIN MCLAUGHLIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Good morning, Sheinelle. President Zelenskyy calling the visit historic, timely, and brave. The visit began here in the capital at the presidential palace. President Biden was greeted by President Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena. He signed a guest book and announced a $500 million military aid package and delivered this message. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , U.S. PRESIDENT: One year later, Kyiv stands and Ukraine stands, democracy stands. America stands with you and the world stands with you. (END VIDEO CLIP) MCLAUGHLIN: From the palace, they made their way to St. Michael`s Cathedral. I watched as air raid sirens echoing in the distance. The two presidents walked out this way and paid tribute to the thousands of fallen Ukrainian soldiers in the memorial behind me. From there, President Biden made his way to the U.S. embassy where he met with staff before departing the capital. In Russia, this visit is being seen as a provocation. But here in Ukraine, it is being seen as a remarkable show of support and solidarity by America. Back to you. JONES: All right. Erin, thank you. LLAMAS: And as we just saw there, the president`s secret trip showing his unwavering support for Ukraine, even as some in NATO and in Congress are questioning the ongoing commitment. NBC`s Chief White House Correspondent and Weekend TODAY co-anchor Kristen Welker joins us now live from Poland where the president will be marking this week`s first anniversary of the war. Kristen, good morning. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT AND "SATURDAY TODAY" ANCHOR: Hi, Tom. Good morning to you. That`s right. [08:05:00] This trip was so secret because of the dangers that it posed, that only a handful of the president`s inner staff was aware that he was actually traveling to Kyiv. And that keen message just adding to what Erin said, the president saying, we`re not leaving. But executing on that is going to be more challenging to keep the global community on board and Congress, with some Republicans, already saying they are not going to write a blank check to Ukraine. So, what happens now? Well, he travels here to Poland. He`s going to be meeting with the president of Poland. He will be meeting with leaders of the critical eastern flank and then he`s going to deliver his capstone address in the same location where he spoke in Warsaw when he visited when the war was just a month old. And I am told in talking to top officials, that part of his message is going to be a condemnation of Vladimir Putin building on what we heard from the vice president over the weekend, that Putin has committed crimes against humanity and should be held accountable. Now, this all comes amid new concerns about China, it`s believed that China is providing nonlethal aid to Russia. The secretary of state, over the weekend, saying that they believe China is considering providing lethal aid as well. The secretary of state warning that would be met with serious consequences, all as this war enters a pivotal new phase. Tom. LLAMAS: All right. Kristen Welker with a lot of new developments there. Kristen, thank you. SOBOROFF: Breaking overnight, North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles towards Japan today, it`s second weapons test in the last three days. The missiles landing in the waters off the west coast of Japan. The test prompting Tokyo to call for an emergency meeting of the United Nations Security Council . Over the weekend North Korea also launched an intercontinental ballistic missile, and in response, the U.S. military yesterday held bilateral air drills with South Korea and Japan. JONES: All right. We`ve covered the news. Now, are you ready for a "Morning Boost"? LLAMAS: Yes. SOBOROFF: Yes, please. JONES: All right. This is a good one. A young Australian basketball fan was in tears after watching his team, the Tasmanian Jackjumpers get knocked out of the playoffs during a game in New Zealand. While on his way back to the locker room the Australian captain noticed the heartbroken fan and knew that he had traveled a long way to come see the game. So, he walked over to comfort him and even gave him a pair of sneakers. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: How is that, mate? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Amazing. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Wow. CLINT STEINDL, TASMANIA JACKJUMPERS BASKETBALL TEAM CAPTAIN: As much as I try to put a smile on his face, he still had the tears. But maybe puts them up in his bedroom or something, gives him something to aspire to. And that`s what we`re trying to do in Tasian (ph), you know, I just try to help the little fella out. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: Oh, that`s sweet. A little classy move. Keeping in mind that the player has got to be hurting too from that season ending loss. Listen, there are fans young and old, and it hurts when you lose, you know. LLAMAS: Yes, that`s -- SOBOROFF: Shout out to the Jackjumpers. JONES: There you go. LLAMAS: Tasmanian Jackjumpers. I like those jerseys too. SOBOROFF: Nice. JONES: Learn something everything. LLAMAS: Those are pretty cool. All right. Coming up, the Prince and Princess of Wales rubbing elbows with the stars of Hollywood. We`re going to take you live to London for an inside look at the big night at the British version of the Oscars. JONES: But first, expert tips you need to hear to make the most of today`s holiday sales. We`ll get to that in a moment right after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:10:00] JONES: Welcome back this morning on "TODAY`s Consumer". We are focusing on those Presidents` Day sales. LLAMAS: Yes, inflation is putting a strain on your budget, it could be a great day to find a few deals, but, of course, there are things you need to consider. JONES: Joining us now is CNBC`s Senior Personal Finance Correspondent Sharon Epperson. Sharon, good morning to you. SHARON EPPERSON, CNBC`S SENIOR PERSONAL FINANCE CORRESPONDENT: Good morning. JONES: All right. Before we get into it, you say, before we get to the deals, you have three questions you want people to ask themselves. EPPERSON: Very important questions to ask. JONES: OK. EPPERSON: First of all, do you need it? JONES: Fair. EPPERSON: Do you love it? And can you pay it off immediately? JONES: Fair enough. EPPERSON: And so, it`s not just can you afford it. Because you`re probably going to put it on a credit card. JONES: Yes. EPPERSON: You don`t want to carry that interest on the credit card. You want to pay that off immediately or that savings is really something you`re going to be paying for, for months and months in interest. JONES: So, can you pay it within the month before you get that bill? EPPERSON: Exactly. JONES: All right. Fair enough. LLAMAS: I feel that`s a good life lesson -- JONES: It is. MINNO: And it`s still very common and abundant. So this myth really stems from the fact that soy contains something called phytoestrogens. And we know that estrogen can sometimes be linked to an increase in breast cancer. JONES: Right. MINNO: But the estrogens in soy are very different than mammalian estrogens, ones that we have in our body, and they act differently. And in fact, they can be protective against things like breast cancer, because what we`ve seen in Asian countries where they consume more soy, is that breast cancer risk is actually much lower. JONES: Does it depend on the product or what kind of soy you`re consuming? No? MINNO: Not really. And again, the American Heart Association said 25 grams of soy protein per day can actually be heart protective. So you can get your tofu, your (inaudible), your soy milk, your edamame at a sushi restaurant, right? Lots of really great options to pack some good soy protein. JONES: There you go. So you don`t have to avoid it. Nora, thank you. MINNO: That`s OK. Thank you, Sheinelle. JONES: All right. Next, a remarkable couple who made their dreams come true, opening a unique restaurant here in New York during the pandemic. How it`s become one of the hottest tickets in town, we`ll take you there. But first, this is TODAY on NBC. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) DREYER: We are back with this morning`s Plaza Pics. Kathy and her family, they`re visiting us from tower Minnesota to celebrate Kathy`s 63rd birthday. SOBOROFF: I love Minnesotans. I had fun getting to know David and his mom Bibi. They`re from Raleigh, North Carolina and joining a mother-son trip to New York. The cutest. JONES: I love that. And here I am with Ginny and her son Tyler from Middleton, Maryland. Every morning before school, they watch the TODAY Show together. LLAMAS: Oh that`s so sweet. JONES: Yes, cute. LLAMAS: OK. We want to turn out to our discover Black Heritage Series. And this morning a young married couple making waves in the restaurant industry here in New York. JONES: Kevol and Ria Graham have a remarkable story when it comes to their Caribbean-inspired restaurant. They opened Kokomo in July of 2020, four months into the COVID locked down, and right before their second child. Can you imagine? [08:50:06] Now, it is one of the hottest restaurants in Brooklyn and I paid a visit to find out their recipe for success. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JONES (voice-over): Kevol and Ria Graham are living a life they never could have imagined. KEVOL GRAHAM, KOKOMO OWNER: I love hospitality. I never thought that I would have my own restaurant. But as we look back, we kind of see that every step that we took was actually leading us to this moment. JONES (voice-over): Today, they are the parents of three young children and will celebrate five years of marriage. But it`s their journey to this point running Kokomo, a popular pan-Caribbean restaurant with Indian and Asian flavors that combines their passion for food and hospitality. (on camera): Clearly, you both had some kind of restaurant background -- K. GRAHAM: (Inaudible) on nightlife and then became our roving chefs. The guys that I grew up with. RIA GRAHAM, KOKOMO OWNER: At the time, I was a marketing manager for a Caribbean restaurant as well. JONES (voice-over): They were soon married and hesitantly decided their next move together would be a restaurant. So they took the social media documenting everything about acquiring and opening a restaurant. As they were just about to open, the pandemic hit. Against all odds, they officially opened in the summer of 2020. (on camera): How challenging was it? R. GRAHAM: I would say it was like mental warfare, because you really did not know what to expect. But I think because we were so open about our feelings to our social media, people wanted to genuinely support. K. GRAHAM: Something that`s very inspirational, because Ria was a part of every step during pregnancy that motivated me to even work harder. JONES (voice-over): The couple describes the menu as elevated Caribbean fare, served up in an atmosphere that feels like the Caribbean. R. GRAHAM: I would say if you`re looking for a vibe, come here. K. GRAHAM: To represent all different parts of the Caribbean. We definitely appeal to all ethnicities, you know, whether it`s Afro Caribbean, Latin Caribbean, you know, Asian Caribbean. JONES: Did you get inspiration for different recipes? I mean, how did you do it? K. GRAHAM: We were very passionate about like bringing out things that we grew up on, you know, tapping into our Caribbean heritage. JONES: Do you feel like you are blazing a trail? R. GRAHAM: Real trailblazers for us are the grandmas, man, because there`s nothing like a Caribbean grandma in that kitchen showing her stuff. And now we`re just trying to modernize it and just make it into something fresh and new. JONES (voice-over): Some of their hottest Caribbean dishes are on flatbread. K. GRAHAM: (Inaudible) flatbread or any given day, because it`s a -- it`s something that we reinvented because I think everybody comes in and like they can get that anywhere. It serve with shrimp, foxtail, chicken. R. GRAHAM: Once we saw that brick oven, we knew we had to do O to Brooklyn by having a brick oven pizza crust, and then we`d have on top of it a tomato (inaudible) sauteed shrimp with ackee, which is the national food of Jamaica. JONES (voice-over): I had to give the food a try. K. GRAHAM: So this is our Rasta balls. JONES: OK. K. GRAHAM: Crockett fry Italian Alfredo sauce that we infuse with some jerk seasoning. Aioli only on top. JONES: Can I try it? K. GRAHAM: Of course. The flavors bursting in your mouth. JONES: Oh my gosh. This alone would have me coming back. (voice-over): As they embrace this family run business, they reflect on this moment in time. R. GRAHAM: Everything that you need to succeed is within you. K. GRAHAM: We come from very humble beginnings. Our parents struggled, I know how hard, excuse me. I know how hard they worked to leave a path for myself. In heart, we as parents worked for us to be where we are. I take nothing for granted. And you can achieve anything you want if only you believe in yourself. (END VIDEOTAPE) JONES: They are two of my new favorite people. So I`ll be texting you guys and you`ll be sick of me. (INAUDIBLE) K. GRAHAM: Can I come? JONES: Sunday (inaudible) things. So Kev and Ria say their parents also helped them run the restaurant. In the spring, they`re opening up another restaurant nearby. They`re calling it Ox Kale (ph) specializing in innovative Caribbean cuisine that`s healthy. Isn`t that -- I`m telling you, I told them, I`m like if you can make it healthy and yummy -- DREYER: Is that (inaudible) speaks for the rest of the menu? JONES (voice-over): Yes. DREYER: This is -- JONES: So, they also make their own in house coconut rum. LLAMAS: Wow, OK. JONES (voice-over): Merry Christmas. LLAMAS: Cheers. (Inaudible) JONES: So there you go. Cheers. What did you just say? SOBOROFF: Chill. I will talk about during the break. JONES (voice-over): OK. Coming up on Hoda and Jenna, actress Rosario Dawson plus a manicures to the stars which will be sharing three hot new nail trends. DREYER: But first in our 3rd Hour, a couple doing the impossible making bagels even better. JONES: Yum. LLAMAS: See, I told you. DREYER: The most delicious food you`ve ever had. You`ll have that after your local news. JONES: Cheers. (LOCAL NEWS AND WEATHER) [09:00:00] END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.
