headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for February 23, 2023, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the bombshell testimony. Alex Murdaugh taking the stand at his murder trial. (voiceover): The South Carolina attorney denying he killed his wife and son, but then stunning the courtroom, admitting he lied to police about his alibi that night. The paranoid thoughts he said he thought he was having and the moment Murdaugh broke down as he described finding the bodies. Then the prosecution`s turn. The tough questions he faced under cross- examination. Also tonight, a deadly winter storm on the move. More than a million customers without power. In the Midwest, a downed power line killing a firefighter. A parking garage collapsing under snow. The new threat in the west. Rare blizzard warnings in southern California. Al Roker is here. New clues in the toxic train derailment in Ohio. The NTSB saying it was 100 percent preventable. The preliminary report finding an alarm went off just before the wreck. What investigators say about the crew`s actions and the potential cause. The shooting spree in Florida. A TV reporter and a 9-year-old girl killed. New body cam of police arresting the suspect. The new details. And the Emmy-winning star of Abbott Elementary, Sheryl Lee Ralph on the obstacles she has overcome and inspiring a new generation. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT: Good evening. For the defense, accused murderer Alex Murdaugh taking the witness stand today in South Carolina. Dramatic and at times tearful testimony from the man at the center of the country`s most closely followed criminal trial. Murdaugh under questioning from his lawyers saying I didn`t shoot my wife or son. And addressing what has appeared to be some of the prosecution`s strongest evidence. Murdaugh from the witness box admitting he lied about his whereabouts the night his wife and 22-year-old son were shot to death. Shocking at the lies to an opioid addiction and paranoia. Under cross-examination, Murdaugh, a former lawyer also admitted to stealing from clients. The prosecution has maintained the murders were part of Murdaugh`s attempt to escape accountability for financial misdeeds. We begin tonight with Catie Beck reporting from Walterboro, South Carolina. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CATIE BECK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): After nearly five weeks of testimony, a stunning surprise. ALEX MURDAUGH, ACCUSED OF KILLING HIS WIFE AND SON: I am going to testify. I want to testify. BECK: The trial`s most anticipated witness takes the stand. Alex Murdaugh testifies in his own defense. The first questions aimed at the heart of the case. JIM GRIFFIN, DEFENSE LAWYER: Did you take this gun or any gun like it and blow your son`s brains out on June 7th, or any day, or any time? MURDAUGH: No, I did not. GRIFFIN: Did you take another blackout such as this and fire it into your wife Maggie`s leg, torso, or any part of her body? MURDAUGH: No, I did not. BECK: Quick to confront what is perhaps the prosecution`s strongest evidence, the video taken by Paul Murdaugh at the dog kennels, placing Alex at the crime scene minutes before the murders. He`s told investigators he wasn`t there, but admits now he was lying. GRIFFIN: Alex, why did you lie? MURDAUGH: As my addiction evolved over time, I would get in these situations or circumstances where I would get paranoid. BECK: Murdaugh says he didn`t trust state law enforcers, and regrets the lie that led to many others. GRIFFIN: Did you continue lying after that night, did you not? MURDAUGH: Once I lied, I continued the lie, yes, sir. BECK: Emotional and crying throughout, Murdaugh`s testimony largely rewrites his timeline on the night of the murders, showering and changing clothes before dinner, and describing the moment he discovered the bodies, again saying he checked for signs of life. MURDAUGH: I know I tried to turn him over. GRIFFIN: When you say you tried to turn him over, why were you trying to turn him over? MURDAUGH: I don`t know. I don`t know. I don`t know why I tried to turn him over. My boy`s laying face-down. BECK: Later in testimony, Alex admits a long-time addiction to opioids, that he stole clients` funds, but denies being overly concerned about getting caught prior to the murders. CREIGHTON WATERS, CHIEF PROSECUTOR: What kind of cases did you normally do? BECK: On cross-examination, prosecutors began by pressing Murdaugh on the fraud cases, where he admits he stole money from his clients and lied to them. And prosecutors suggesting all the stolen money wasn`t going to fund his pill addiction. WATERS: You were generating millions of dollars in fees. That was not enough for you? Would you concede that? [19:05:08] MURDAUGH: If by concede that, you mean was I also stealing money that I shouldn`t have, yes, sir, I agree with that. I`ve said that, repeatedly. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Catie, what do we know about how the jury was taking all this in how they may have reacted? BECK (on camera): Well, Lester, the jury was captivated, so attentive to Alex Murdaugh`s testimony on the stand today. At times, Murdaugh was repositioning his body to face the jurors directly and answer the questions directly to them. At one point, when Murdaugh got extremely emotional, one juror that was sitting close to him actually slid a Kleenex box in his direction. Lester? HOLT: All right, Catie Beck, thank you. Let me bring in our Senior Legal Correspondent Laura Jarrett now. Laura, what was the defense strategy here, and how does it appear to be playing out? LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, this is the defense team going on offense. Clearly, the goal was to try to take the sting out of the damning evidence that the prosecution would raise on cross-examination, and that`s likely why he was forced to admit that he lied to police and to his family, all while trying to plant seeds of reasonable doubt. But testifying at all, it`s a risky gamble. Already the prosecution has tried to highlight his inconsistencies and also pierce through his folksy demeanor on cross-examination to try to show this jury that he is an accomplished lawyer who knows how to cover his tracks. Lester? HOLT: All right, Laura, thank you. Now to that deadly crippling winter storm that is stretching right now across the country and a separate threat here in the West. Gabe Gutierrez is watching it all from Minneapolis. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, devastating snow, ice, and wind pummeling even more of the country. This time knocking out power to nearly a million people across the Midwest. Most of those outages in Michigan where a volunteer firefighter was killed when a tree brought down a high-voltage line. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: A volunteer just died in here for free. He gave his life for free. GUTIERREZ: In Wisconsin, authorities say snow likely caused a partial collapse of a parking garage at a shopping mall. Today, Minneapolis under a snow emergency. Over the last few hours, we`ve seen a very rapid snowfall here. The road conditions are getting worse. Snow totals not as high as predicted earlier in the week, still around a foot blanketed the twin cities over three days. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is a big one. For all coming down at once, like, yes, this is a pretty big one. GUTIERREZ: Coast-to-coast, treacherous road conditions. Portland, Oregon recording its second snowiest day on record with more than 10 inches. This 20-car pileup in Southern California injuring at least eight people. A separate system now prompting the first blizzard warnings since 1989 for the mountains near L.A. The nationwide weather whiplash is remarkable even for February. Across the Mid-Atlantic and southeastern U.S., record heat, unusually high temperatures as far north as Philadelphia. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Having a 70-degree day is just such a welcome break. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (on camera): But air travel is still dicey. More than 2,000 U.S. flights canceled just today, Lester. HOLT: All right, Gabe, thank you. And that takes us to Al Roker . Al, as one storm moves out, another moves in impacting the West Coast. AL ROKER, NBC NEWS WEATHER ANCHOR: Lester, we have six million folks out west looking at winter weather advisories, winter storm warnings, blizzard warnings, including the San Bernardino Mountains. First blizzard warning ever issued there. Record lows likely. We`re looking at morning lows in Reno in the 20s. Vegas into the 30s. Even Los Angeles into the upper 30s. Salt Lake City in the 20s. We`re looking at five to eight feet of snow back through the Sierra, but also the San Bernardino Mountains and the Santa Barbara Mountains as well. We`re also looking upwards of 10 inches of rain through Southern California. Significant roadway flooding and airport delays likely. Lester? HOLT: All right, Al Roker , thank you. And new tonight, a preliminary finding about the cause of that toxic train disaster in Ohio as the Transportation Secretary visited for the first time. Ron Allen is there. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) RON ALLEN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, with the scene being cleaned up, new details about what caused the fiery derailment. Federal investigators saying a preliminary investigation shows an overheated wheel bearing likely to blame. JENNIFER HOMENDY, CHAIR, NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION SAFETY BOARD : This was 100 percent preventible. ALLEN: The NTSB says the train passed over two detectors, which showed the bearing was heating up. By the time it hit a third detector, it was 253 degrees above air temperature, triggering an audible alarm to warn the crew, who then slowed and stopped the train. HOMENDY: This is a community that is suffering. This is not about politics. What I care about is figuring out how this happened. ALLEN: The NTSB chair says there is no evidence the crew did anything wrong. In a statement, Norfolk Southern says our highest priority is the safety of our people and the communities we serve. Adding, it will continue to support the NTSB `s investigation. While today, Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg visited for the first time after criticism from some residents that he should have come sooner, demanding the nation`s rail operators stop resisting safety measures to cut costs. [19:10:19] PETE BUTTIGIEG, U.S. SECRETARY OF TRANSPORTATION: Let`s get people from both sides of the aisle to the table and come to agreement on some steps that are needed, even if the rail industry is pushing back. ALLEN: Meanwhile, near the crash, this Figleys only comes back to the farm to check on things like their chickens. They`re part of a class action lawsuit that attorneys say includes over 500 residents. MARILYN FIGLEY, RESIDENT, EAST PALESTINE: I live out of my car and at my daughter`s house. It`s awful. I feel homeless. ALLEN: Why won`t you come back home? FIGLEY: Because I don`t know what I`m coming home to, and I`m 70 years old. ALLEN: Ron Allen, NBC News, East Palestine, Ohio. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Now to Florida, where a series of shootings left three people dead, including a young girl and a reporter. Two more are hospitalized. A suspect is under arrest. Guad Venegas is there for us. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Get on your (BLEEP) face! GUAD VENEGAS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the Orange County Sheriff releasing bodycam footage of the arrest of Keith Moses, the 19-year-old suspect accused of a deadly shooting spree in Orlando. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Roll him on his side real quick. VENEGAS: Three victims killed, including a news reporter and a 9-year-old girl, two others critically wounded. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We`re getting multiple gunshots wound calls in the Hialeah Street area. VENEGAS: The first shooting happened Wednesday morning where authorities found 38-year-old Natacha Augustin dead from a gunshot wound. Officials say the victim was an acquaintance of the suspect. Hours later, a news crew covering that incident was ambushed in their car, deputies say. The gunfire killing 24-year-old Spectrum News 13 reporter Dylan Lyons and critically wounding cameraman Jesse Walden. I just happened to catch a bullet. But he kept shooting at me as I ducked behind the wheel of my car, and he walked forward and shot into my car and ended up striking our reporter. VENEGAS: Authorities say the suspect then fled the scene and entered a nearby home. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`ve got two more victims, 9-year-old female. VENEGAS: Deputies say he then opened fire again, killing a 9-year-old girl and critically injuring her mother. The suspect was arrested a short time later. JOHN MINA, SHERIFF, ORANGE COUNTY, FLORIDA: We recovered a Glock 40, a semiautomatic handgun from inside of his pants. That gun was still hot to the touch, meaning it had just been fired. VENEGAS: Moses is now charged with first-degree murder. (END VIDEOTAPE) VENEGAS (on camera): And tonight, officials are still investigating a motive, but they say the 19-year-old suspect had a lengthy criminal history, including eight felony and 11 misdemeanor arrests. Lester? HOLT: Guad Venegas, thank you. In 60 seconds, the battle over abortion. How an imminent court ruling about a widely used abortion drug could have an impact nationwide. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: It could be the most consequential abortion decision since Roe v. Wade was overturned. A Texas judge will soon decide whether to block access to a commonly used abortion pill nationwide. Dasha Burns reports. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CROWD: We can`t go back! DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Amarillo, Texas now at the center of America`s abortion debate. CROWD: I believe that we will win! BURNS: Here, a group of anti-abortion doctors and medical organizations are suing the FDA , challenging the approval of Mifeprex, generically known as Mifepristone, part of a two-drug regimen commonly used for abortions that has been approved by the FDA since 2000. Alliance Defending Freedom arguing the FDA didn`t adequately evaluate the drug`s safety. ERIK BAPTIST, SENIOR COUNSEL, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM: We`re asking the court to do what is right, to follow -- and ask the FDA to follow the law by taking these dangerous drugs off the marketplace. BURNS: Presiding over the case, a conservative judge appointed by former President Trump. An injunction would set off access to Mifepristone nationwide. If the plaintiffs win this lawsuit, what will be the effects? [19:15:01] DR. SERINA FLOYD, MEDICAL DIRECTOR, PLANNED PARENTHOOD OF METROPOLITAN WASHINGTON, DC: It will be devastating. Even in places where they`ve worked very hard to secure access to abortion, states like California, New York, here in D.C. BURNS: Abortion providers like Dr. Serina Floyd say the lawsuit is based on misinformation. How dangerous is this medication? FLOYD: It`s not dangerous at all. The evidence is solid, the science is solid. The complication rate is less than one percent. BURNS: The FDA told NBC News it does not comment on ongoing litigation. But in the court filings said the claims in the lawsuit are unsupported by any evidence. Since 2000, more than five million women have taken mifepristone with 28 deaths associated with the drug reported. Millions of women have taken these drugs safely. Doesn`t that paint a contrary picture to your complaint? DR. CHRISTINA FRANCIS, AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF PRO-LIFE OBSTETRICIANS AND GYNECOLOGISTS: I`m seeing these women in my own practice. My emergency room physicians, they`re telling me how frequently they`re seeing these complications, that women come in with retained tissue, with heavy bleeding, with serious life-threatening infections. BURNS: In a court brief, the country`s leading group of OBGYN say the mifepristone is "exceedingly safe and effective, calling the lawsuit ideological and not scientific. The result if you win is that abortion access will be significantly limited. Is that the goal of this lawsuit? BAPTIST: No, the goal of this lawsuit is to protect American women and girls from dangerous chemical abortion drugs. BURNS: There is another drug, Misoprostol, that can be used for abortions, but doctors say it can be less effective on its own. Back in Amarillo, Amanda Barnes travelled from Atlanta to protest this case. AMANDA BARNES, ACTIVIST: It`s ridiculous that just because, you know, we were born with a uterus and certain body parts that we should have to be subjected to this treatment. BURNS: The next frontier in America`s abortion battle. Dasha Burns, NBC News, Amarillo, Texas. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Coming up, our exclusive report in the flow of goods into Russia, despite sanctions. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: As the war in Ukraine approaches the one-year mark, the U.S. is pushing for more sanctions against Russia. But are the ones already in place having an impact? Keir Simmons went inside neighboring Georgia to find out how Russia is getting around them. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS SENIOR INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): If you want to know how the Russian economy is surviving amid punishing western sanctions, you might come here. We`re just across the border in Georgia, and it`s lined with trucks. President Putin`s supply line. You`re going from Turkey to Russia? To Moscow? He`s carrying xerox printer ink, he says. Since Putin`s invasion and unprecedented Western sanctions, satellite images along with international trade data shows this mountain pass becoming much busier. That`s not surprising. At the outset of the war, Russia dropped most import restrictions on things like cars. The Russian border is about 25 miles that way, but police tell us they`ve closed the road because of an avalanche risk. Business has stopped, but only temporarily. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Hello! SIMMONS : Then hidden in the snow, a stunning discovery. Two brand-new American ram pickups. American cars, American trucks? It was never driven, he says. Take a look at this. Look, it`s still got the protection on the dashboard. Look, they`re brand-new. Where are they going? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: To the Moscow. SIMMONS: To Moscow, he tells me. The men tell us they`ve sold both vehicles for around $170,000 each. They say they are moving cars every week. Does it matter that there is a war on? Where is that war, he asks. It doesn`t matter for us. We have obtained one of the vehicle ID numbers and asked the manufacturer who told us it was legally sold to a private customer by an authorized distributor in Abu Dhabi, that they cannot prevent that customer from reselling it, and the company complies with all U.S. and international sanctions. And it`s not only Georgia. Satellite images also show lines of trucks on the roads to Russia from China. President Putin and China`s top diplomat meeting yesterday, pledging to strengthen ties. China already provides crucial economic help to Russia. Back in Georgia, the road reopens, and we pass a construction site where China is helping build a new tunnel through the mountain. The half-billion project was started before the Ukraine invasion. But the plan will be more trade with Russia. Clearly, not every country wants this to be the end of the road for moscow. (END VIDEOTAPE) SIMMONS (on camera): Despite all the sanctions, the IMF says Russia`s economy is actually set to grow this year, though only by 0.3 percent. Lester? HOLT: Keir Simmons tonight, thank you. Up next, our inspiring one-on-one with actress and singer Sheryl Lee Ralph. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: She is the star of a hit sitcom, an Emmy winner, and recently sang at the Super Bowl. Sheryl Lee Ralph now on the hurdles she overcame and why she is only just getting started. She spoke with Dana Griffin. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DANA GRIFFIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): With a career spanning nearly five decades in showbiz, Sheryl Lee Ralph is back in the spotlight. Do you still have pinch me moments, especially now when you see we`re sitting in the middle of Hollywood? SHERYL LEE RALPH, SINGER: Yes. I have real pinch me moments in life, because, you know, I`ve lived most of my life as a very regular normal human being. I will go to the 99 Cent Store, the Dollar Tree or whatever. I will do that. And now when I go, I`m like, what in the world are they staring at? And then, I`m like, oh my God, it`s me. GRIFFIN: The entertainment icon has had a whirlwind of recent success, inspiring a new generation. RALPH: Now, who took that picture of me? GRIFFIN: Last year, she won an Emmy for supporting comedy actress for her role in Abbott Elementary where she plays teacher Barbara Howard. What was that moment like for you? RALPH: First of all, I was -- I was listening to the whole thing, and I was like getting ready to be happy for somebody. And I realized, no, this is very real. She just called my name. GRIFFIN: And more recently, the critics choice awards where her message resonated with many. RALPH: When you look in the mirror, you better love what you see. GRIFFIN: Her Broadway, TV and film career dates back to the `70s. In 1981, she starred in the original Broadway cast of Dream Girls. Her latest performance, Super Bowl LVII, singing Lift Every Voice And Sing. But stealing the show hasn`t always been easy. RALPH: They used to say you`re too dark. Your lips are too big. Your hair is too nappy. Suppose I listened to them? GRIFFIN: But Ralph persevered. What else do you want to accomplish? RALPH: More. I want to tell stories that deserve to be told, characters whose voices were dimmed or dulled or muted just because they were Black. Now is the time to tell those stories. GRIFFIN: Dana Griffin, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And that`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Thursday. Thanks for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. story_text: SAVANNAH GUTHRIE: We are back with our series Shop This List TODAY. This week`s picks, affordable products that can help you rest and recharge we got Shop All Day contributor Chassie Post here to share them with us. You can shop along. You just scan the QR code. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for February 25, 2023, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:30:18] JOSE DIAZ-BALART, NBC NEWS HOST: Tonight, a historic storms slams the state of California. Millions still under life threatening flash flood alerts after a rare system dumped heavy snow, torrential rain, and caused damaging wind gusts. The daring rescues and dangerous conditions as the storm moves east. Overseas, Ukraine heads into its second year of war. The images of solidarity emerging from across the globe. What the conflict could look like six months from now? Plus today, the CDC is out in East Palestine three weeks after that toxic train derailment as residents come forward with new health concerns (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MELISSA BLAKE (ph): They poisoned me. They shouldn`t get away with that. (END VIDEO CLIP) DIAZ-BALART: And any day now, a Texas judge could make one of the biggest rulings on abortion access since Roe v. Wade was overturned. Could a popular and FDA approved abortion pill be pulled off the shelves nationwide? Plus, what we now know about a top college basketball star being linked to a fatal shooting. And the dancing grannies hit the streets during Mardi Gras. Why it was so much more than just a celebration. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Jose Diaz-Balart. DIAZ-BALART: Good evening. We begin tonight with a rare storm that hasn`t been seen in California in decades. As we come on the air, millions are under life threatening flash flood alerts after an historic system pummeled the state. Just listen to this, a blizzard warning was issued for the first time ever in San Bernardino County, where they saw more than five feet of snow. Other parts of the state saw hurricane force winds and torrential rains. Rescue workers were raced against the clock to save stranded drivers. And now that storm system is pushing east. Our Dana Griffin is in Los Angeles with the very latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DANA GRIFFIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Life threatening flooding in the Golden State. In Southern California`s Ventura County, multiple RVs swept into the river. Watch this dramatic rescue, one of several in the region. A driver stuck in raging floodwater flings to a rescuer. They`re both hoisted swinging in the wind before safely landing on solid ground. This morning, near Los Angeles, a dangerous light show. A live wire fell into the water, setting a car on fire. The historic winter weather walloped California with heavy snow. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Now we`re having of trouble because the snow is making it slippery. GRIFFIN: Torrential rain in some areas, nearly an entire month`s worth in 48 hours. And strong wind gusts creating blizzardlike conditions in the San Bernardino County mountains. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: First time seeing snow in a long time. GRIFFIN: With San Francisco seeing its lowest temperatures in over a century. And Los Angeles experiencing its first blizzard warning in more than 30 years. In San Diego, several water rescues today. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We just had a vehicle that was in the deep water, unable to drive out, and two occupants of the vehicle that needed to be rescued and brought back to dry land. So, we anticipate doing this a few more times. GRIFFIN: The stunning system now headed east toward Oklahoma City, Wichita and Kansas City, where 9 million are at risk for large hail and even tornadoes. In Michigan, more than 400,000 remain without power from an ice storm earlier this week. Back in Southern California, tonight, the mess the storm left behind and the dangers this system could still bring to the area. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: Dana Griffin joins us from hard hit Los Angeles. Dana, what threat remains even as the storm now moves out? GRIFFIN: While, Jose, those lingering impacts could include mudslides and additional flooding. Just take a look at the Los Angeles River, it is moving so swiftly at such a dangerous pace, and the water level is usually not this high. Jose? DIAZ-BALART: Dana Griffin in Los Angeles. Thank you. And now to the war in Ukraine. The conflict entering its second year with no end in sight. And around the world today, signs of solidarity in support of the war-torn country. Erin McLaughlin reports tonight from Kyiv. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ERIN MCLAUGHLIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): From New York to Taipei, Toronto to Tbilisi, a sea of yellow and blue. Outside the Russian embassy in Warsaw, protesters blasting the sound of air raid sirens. Ukraine is waking up under the sounds of real Russian bombs and rockets, she says. [18:35:10] A global show of support for Ukraine as the Russian assault enters its second year. The United States now pledging $2 billion more to help the Ukrainians fight. But President Biden Friday ruling out sending Ukrainian President Zelenskyy F-16 fighter jets for now. JOE BIDEN , (D) U.S. PRESIDENT: We`re sending him what our seasoned military thinks he needs now. He needs tanks, he needs artillery. MCLAUGHLIN: All things Ukrainian officials agree they need to win this war and quickly. (On camera): Where do you see this war in six months? MYKHAILO PODOLYAK, ADVISER TO PRESIDENT VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY (through translator): If we get the necessary types and quantities of weapons, primarily shells and missiles, I think in six months we will be approaching the finalization of this war. MCLAUGHLIN: An optimistic outlook as U.S. officials allege China is considering sending lethal aid to Moscow. China denies the claims and on Friday put forward a peace proposal between Russia and Ukraine, a proposal U.S. officials have dismissed. President Zelenskyy, however, says he`d like to meet with the Chinese leader. Meanwhile, the war grinds on in the east and more lives are lost. Among the dead, a U.S. Army veteran, according to his family, 28-year-old Andrew Peters was killed in action last week fighting for the International Legion. Andrew had a strong sense of right and wrong. The family said in a statement, we are all extremely proud of his bravery and selfless sacrifice. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And Erin joins me from Kyiv. Erin, more than a year into the war, it often seems like a stalemate, what could make a difference going forward? MCLAUGHLIN: Jose, an advisor to the Ukrainian military tells me that at this point, both sides are running out of ammunition and that the key to victory for Ukraine could be if it receives enough supplies from its western allies. Jose? DIAZ-BALART: Erin McLaughlin in Kyiv, thank you. Back home, we are just learning about another possible Norfolk Southern train derailment, this time in North Carolina. It comes as fears grow among residents in East Palestine, Ohio, about their health. Here`s Jesse Kirsch. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JESSE KIRSCH, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): More than three weeks after that toxic train derailment, the CDC in East Palestine today encouraging residents to participate in a survey. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I think it`s important for residents to understand that in order for us to get a better idea of what their potential exposures may have been, what might be causing any potential health effects. KIRSCH: The latest outreach comes as President Biden defended his administration`s response late Friday, saying for now, he has no plans to visit. BIDEN: I`m keeping very close tabs on it. We`re doing all we can. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The government has got to be responsible and make sure that everything is done. KIRSCH: Already, more than a dozen lawsuits have been filed against rail company Norfolk Southern . ERIN BROCKOVICH, FAMED ENVIRONMENTAL ACTIVIST: And everything happens so quickly. KIRSCH: Famed environmental Activist Erin Brockovich is among those organizing legal challenges. BROCKOVICH: You will ask questions, you will demand answers. KIRSCH: She spoke to hundreds of residents Friday. BROCKOVICH: They are confused. They don`t know who to believe or who to trust. And I have learned in every community I`ve been in they need to trust themselves. KIRSCH: Melissa Blake (ph) lives less than a mile from the derailment. Two days later, she says she evacuated and went to the emergency room. (On camera): They quarantined you at the ER. MELISSA BLAKE (ph): Yes. They didn`t know what was on me about the fumes and all that, the chemicals. They told me that it was acute bronchitis due to chemical fumes. KIRSCH: She says she`s now using an inhaler to help breathe and says she talked to a lawyer. BLAKE (ph): They poisoned me. They shouldn`t get away with that. KIRSCH: Norfolk Southern says it can`t comment on litigation and promises to do right by the community. (On camera): Cleanup continues, and the NTSB says it`s still investigating. Meanwhile, here in East Palestine, the trains keep moving through town. Jose. DIAZ-BALART: Jesse Kirsch in East Palestine, Ohio. Thank you. Tonight, abortion rights activists are waiting on what could be the most consequential ruling on abortion access since Roe v. Wade was overturned. A judge in Texas could decide to pull a popular abortion pill off the market nationwide. Ali Vitali has more. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ALI VITALI, NBC NEWS CAPITOL HILL CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): A new fault line in the battle over abortion access. This one centered on the so-called abortion pill. Both sides bracing for a Texas judge`s decision that could restrict access to one of two drugs used to induce medicated abortion. Mifepristone is one part of a two-step regimen, long approved by the food and drug administration and currently the most prevalently used form of abortion care in the United States with overwhelming evidence that it`s safe and effective. KAMALA HARRIS , U.S. VICE PRESIDENT: Most Americans could look in their medicine cabinet, where they will find medication prescribed by a doctor that they use on daily basis. Mifepristone is no exception to that process. [18:40:05] VITALI: The federal judge in Texas appointed by former President Donald Trump could render his ruling any day now, setting off a national chain reaction long anticipated by abortion rights advocates and the White House. In some states, particularly rural ones with limited clinics that present a travel barrier to care, limitations on the pill could be keenly felt. In states like South Dakota, where we met Nurse Misty (ph) last year, limits on the pill were already the next battle. MISTY (ph), NURSE: Because it`s not access at all. Claiming that those medications aren`t safe just is so false. VITALI: Here on the steps of the Austin federal courthouse, the national divide encapsulated. (On camera): This as much as it`s a small scene, is a very telling one. Like, this is what (inaudible) this is the national debate playing now? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It is the national debate, but at the same time, the majority of Americans, the vast majority of them are pro-choice and pro- abortion. MELANIE SALAZAR: I believe that chemical abortion pills are the next battle that anti-abortion people have to be fighting. (END VIDEOTAPE) VITALI: Jose, if the judge rules against the pill, expect the Biden administration to challenge it, a move that could ultimately put this decision before the Supreme Court. DIAZ-BALART: Ali Vitali in Austin, Texas, thank you. And now to a brutal attack in a Florida high school where a student allegedly beat a staffer after she took away his video game console. Our Emilie Ikeda has the details. I want to warn you that some of the video may be disturbing. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) EMILIE IKEDA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Tonight, this Palm Coast, Florida high school under the microscope after a brutal attack on a teacher`s aide. It happened Tuesday, all caught on camera. You first see her walk into view. Then she`s attacked from behind by a 6-foot-6, 270-pound student. The paraprofessional falls to the ground unconscious. The student stomping on her back and repeatedly throwing punches in a beating that lasts roughly 25 seconds. Even as students and staff try to help her. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This could have been homicide. When you push people down like that, they hit their head. You never know the outcome. IKEDA: The 17-year-old, who is not being named since he`s a minor, has been charged with felony aggravated battery with bodily harm. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Am I going to jail? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes, you are. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: For how long? IKEDA: According to the arrest report, the suspect told investigators that he was upset that the employee took his Nintendo switch game away from him and made comments that when he comes back, he is going to kill her. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: If I`m the prosecutor, I`m going to listen to that evidence and I`m going to ask myself, what does that say about the state of mind of the student when this was happening? IKEDA: The president of the Florida Education Association calls Tuesday`s attack a consequence, in part, of understaffing. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Florida has been dealing with a massive teacher and staff shortage issues. When you don`t have enough staff, you -- it`s harder to manage students in our schools. IKEDA: The district superintendent says, creating a safe learning and working environment on our campuses is critical. Violence is never an appropriate reaction. The violence landing that school staffer in the hospital who is now facing a long road to recovery. Emilie Ikeda, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: Still ahead tonight, why a college basketball star is being linked to a fatal shooting. Also, hospitals are supposed to be posting prices, so why are patients still shocked at their high medical bills? (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:45:58] DIAZ-BALART: Tonight, a college basketball star is under growing scrutiny after being linked to a fatal shooting last month. Morgan Chesky has the details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MORGAN CHESKY, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): On the court he`s a top NBA prospect, but it`s his role off the hardwood, putting a growing spotlight on Alabama freshman Brandon Miller. KURT HELIN, NBC SPORTS PROBASKETBALLTALK MANAGER EDITOR: They`ve been one of the top teams in the nation all year, and Miller is a large part of that. He is going to be a top five NBC draft pick if these red flags don`t change that dynamic. CHESKY: The controversy stems from a murder investigation tying the 20- year-old to the scene of a deadly January shooting. NATE OATS, UNIVERSITY OF ALABAMA MEN`S BASKETBALL COACH: The whole team understands how tragic and serious the situation that we`re dealing with is. CHESKY: On January 15, police say 23-year-old Jamea Harris was fatally shot near campus. Investigators arrested Michael Davis and Alabama player Darius Miles, who was subsequently released from the team. Both men are now charged with capital murder, and investigators say Miles admits he provided the gun used in the shooting to Davis. But in a court hearing this week, police testified it was Miller who brought the handgun to his former teammate after getting text messages to pick him up and bring Miles gun. In a statement, Miller`s attorney said Brandon never touch the gun, was not involved in its exchange to Mr. Davis in any way, and never knew that illegal activity involving the gun would occur. Miller hasn`t missed a game since the investigation began. The university is stressing he`s fully cooperating with authorities and is not considered a suspect. OATS: Make decisions based on available facts, and that`s what we did here. CHESKY: Tonight, the mother of Jamea Harris upset Miller was allowed to play today, saying had there been no gun, her daughter would still be alive. DECARLA HEARD, JAMEA HARRIS` MOTHER: I haven`t stopped being angry. I haven`t stopped long enough to grieve because I`m so angry. She has a five- year-old son that`s still at home waiting on his mom to come home. And she never come home. CHESKY: Morgan Chesky, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: All right, we are back in a moment with the failure to comply, why some hospitals still are not posting prices for patients despite a law saying they have to. Plus, the deadly crash that killed two bicyclists into Arizona. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:50:49] DIAZ-BALART: We are back at the scene of a deadly crash in Arizona, where a pickup truck struck a large group of bicyclists riding across a bridge. At this time, there are two confirmed fatalities and eleven others injured. Officials say the driver stayed on the scene and police are investigating the incident. Two years ago, laws were put into place that required hospitals nationwide to post the prices of medical procedures so that patients knew how much they would have to pay for treatment in advance. But patient advocates say many hospitals still are not posting prices, and customers are being shocked by the large medical bills. Marissa Parra has more. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MARISSA PARRA, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): The pressure of paying for medical procedures has haunted Jeff King in Kansas for years. JEFF KING, SURPRISE MEDICAL BILLS VICTIM: I went back to my follow up appointment. They said, how are you doing? I said, well, your medical bill about put me into AFib again. PARRA: But it is his right to know how much a procedure costs in advance, and it has been since January of 2021, when federal price transparency became federal law. CHIQUITA BROOKS-LASURE, CENTERS FOR MEDICARE AND MEDICAID SERVICES ADMINISTRATOR: It`s so incredibly important. PARRA: Chiquita Brooks-LaSure, the Administrator for Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services , also oversees hospital transparency. In a report released last week, CMS says that of the 600 hospitals they sampled, 70% were in full compliance, up from the 27% the year before. But patient advocacy groups are dissatisfied. CYNTHIA FISHER, PATIENTRIGHTSADVOCATE.ORG FOUNDER: It is not happening fast enough. PARRA: And they`re challenging CMS`s survey results. PatientRightsAdvocate.org released their own report weeks ago, analyzing the websites of 2000 hospitals within the nation`s largest hospital systems, their findings only 25% were in full compliance. Patient Advocate Cynthia Fisher shows us what patients should see on a compliant hospital`s website. FISHER: It`s showing all of the codes. PARRA: And she showed us what she found on many instead. FISHER: Instead of prices, they put N/As in the field. PARRA: So we took it to CMS. (On camera): Would this hospital be considered compliant? BROOKS-LASURE: Yes, because N/A according to our rules means we don`t do the procedure. PARRA: Which would mean if they provide these procedures? BROOKS-LASURE: They should be telling us how much it costs. PARRA: In the two years since the law took effect, CMS has only issued two fines given as NBC was pressing the HHS secretary last summer. (On camera): The buck stops with you. You`re the secretary. (Voice-over): Brooks-LaSure says they`ve given 500 warning letters to hospitals, and now the maximum fines have been increased from $100,000 to $2 million. So we asked, what`s the biggest hold up? CMS blames the pandemic. BROOKS-LASURE: So they haven`t always had all of the staff to really focus on some of the IT system changes that need to happen. PARRA: The American Hospital Association , which represents healthcare networks and hospitals, says health systems remain, "deeply committed, despite considerable strains on the hospital workforce over the past three years." PARRA: Who hurts the most? FISHER: It`s the American people. It`s the hard-working. PARRA: In Washington, Marissa Parra, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: When we come back, the heartwarming reason these grannies are dancing through the streets of the Big Easy. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:56:45] DIAZ-BALART: There is good news tonight about the power of friendship and how love and dancing help heal the pain. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: For the famous Milwaukee Dancing Grannies, this week`s visit to New Orleans was the trip of a life. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Ladies and gentleman, the Milwaukee Dancing Grannies. DIAZ-BALART: A chance to perform in one of the city`s Mardi Gras parades. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Oh, they were amazing. DIAZ-BALART: But for Jan Kwiatkowski and the rest of the group, it was about so much more. (On camera): Jan, what was it like to be in New Orleans for Mardi Gras? JAN KWIATKOWSKI: It was the probably absolute most amazing, profound, exciting lifegiving thing that not only myself, but all of us have done. DIAZ-BALART: She says the celebration was also a time of healing. That`s because in November 2021, three of their members and a dancer`s husband were killed along with two other people during the Waukesha Christmas parade when a man driving an SUV intentionally plowed through the crowds. (On camera): In that senseless, horrible tragedy, how do you all as a group go forward? KWIATKOWSKI: The reality is you don`t heal unless you`re healing in community. DIAZ-BALART: Community they found in the New Orleans dance group called The 610 Stompers. They call themselves extraordinary men with extraordinary moves. And they invited the grannies to Mardi Gras as a sign of solidarity. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I cannot begin to tell you how much that means to all of us. (CHEERING & APPLAUSE) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Why can`t we just come together and try to heal and -- DIAZ-BALART: Stompers Chris Second (ph) and Brett Patron just knew their city would welcome them with open arms. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m going to tell you that right now. They are hard to handle. But they were so much fun. DIAZ-BALART: The two dance groups now forever friends with joyful memories they`ll never forget. KWIATKOWSKI: It`s just such a tangible way of saying you`re not alone. That meant a lot. I can`t even put into words. I`m going to cry now how much that meant. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: The Grannies hope to have The 610 Stompers join them in a parade sometime this year back in Wisconsin. That`s NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for this Saturday. Kate Snow will be here tomorrow night. I`m Jose Diaz-Balart. Thank you for the privilege of your time, and good night. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: Meet the Press for February 26, 2023, NBC
story_text: (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) [09:00:19] CHUCK TODD, HOST, NBC`S "MEET THE PRESS WITH CHUCK TODD" (voice over): This Sunday, defending democracy. One year after Russia invaded Ukraine, President Biden promises to stand strong against the threat from Vladimir Putin . PRESIDENT JOSEPH R. BIDEN, JR.: Ukraine will never be a victory for Russia -- never. But what does victory look like? And are we giving them enough to win the war, or just survive it? (UNKNOWN): If you want victory, we have to do more. TODD: Plus, rising tensions. (UNKNOWN): You are approaching Chinese airspace. Keep a safe distance or you will be intercepted. TODD: As the U.S. continues to warn China about sending weapons to Ukraine, tensions are rising in the South China Sea. Is the Pentagon preparing to move more troops to Taiwan? My guests this morning, the national security adviser to President Biden, Jake Sullivan, and Republican Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska. And, off the rails. FORMER PRESIDENT DONALD J. TRUMP: I sincerely hope that, when all of the politicians get here, including Biden, they get back from touring Ukraine, that he`s got some money left over. TODD: Donald Trump travels to the site of the toxic train derailment in Ohio to bash the Biden administration for focusing more overseas, creating the first real split-screen moment of the 2024 campaign. (on camera): Joining me for insight and analysis are NBC News chief White House correspondent Kristen Welker; NPR White House correspondent Tamara Keith; Republican strategist Al Cardenas; and journalist and author Jonathan Alter. Welcome to Sunday. It`s "Meet the Press". ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest-running show in television history, this is "Meet the Press With Chuck Todd." (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: Good Sunday morning. As the war in Ukraine enters its second year, the question is, what will victory look like? It`s pretty clear no one involved, not the United States or our European allies, Ukraine or Russia, can afford for this war to be in the same place it is today going into year three, a year from now. And yet both sides, President Biden in a surprise visit to Kyiv, and Vladimir Putin , this week in Moscow, prepared the world for a drawn-out conflict. JONATHAN ALTER, NBC NEWS CONTRIBUTOR: I just don`t think the split screen hurts Biden at all. He`s on a very successful trip and his messages were the arsenal of democracy, the FDR message. [09:40:03] He`s backing the modern Winston Churchill, Zelenskyy. What is Trump doing? He`s saying to the people of Palestine, have a good time. He`s handing out MAGA caps. That`s not a very good impression for him. WELKER: And I was in Poland with President Biden, and just to add to that point, he was making this broader case. This war is not just about the war in Ukraine. It`s about democracy. It`s about upholding American ideals. And his surprise trip to Ukraine, if you talk to Republicans and Democrats, they say it may be one of the strongest counterpoints yet to this narrative that he`s too old for a second term. TODD: No, I think that was a big moment for him on his -- on his vibrancy. KEITH: Absolutely. It was not an easy trip. No president has done what he did, which was spend 25 hours in a country at war, a country where the U.S. doesn`t have a base of operations. I mean, that is -- a ten-hour train ride each direction is a remarkable feat for this White House to have pulled off and they are quite happy that they pulled that off. TODD: But I want to talk about the fact that I was thinking about we`ve had three one-term presidents in our lifetimes, essentially. And two of them lost arguably due to foreign policy issues. Jonathan, you profiled one of them in Carter. And that was the Iran hostage crisis. George H.W. Bush, Bill Clinton successfully sort of used a message that Trump was using, which is, hey, he`s so concerned overseas. It`s the economy stupid here. This war can`t drag on into `24, can it? ALTER: Well, I think it very well might. TODD: Yeah. ALTER: The question is whether it will swamp Joe Biden the way events overseas ended up swamping Jimmy Carter . In his first half of his term, Carter was very successful. But these events kind of really burdened him. The difference is inflation. So basically -- TODD: Speaking of the thing that could hurt both of them, right? ALTER: So events overseas with the Iranian revolution in 1979, that kicked off a whole new round of inflation. So Carter was running for reelection with double-digit inflation and double-digit interest rates. And these overwhelmed many of his quite big achievements, which few people remember now. So if Biden can manage to keep inflation in check in the next couple of years, even if there`s a stalemate in Ukraine, I think he`ll be okay. TODD: Al, go ahead, but I want you to address the growing divide in your party. I mean, you`re a hawk against authoritarianism, as somebody that`s - - good South Florida Republican. What`s going on with DeSantis here? CARDENAS: Yeah, that`s a great question. I mean, here`s someone who`s served in the military after going to Harvard and Yale. I mean, he had the world in front of him with those records, and yet he went into the military. You would think, like Dan Sullivan, that he`d be on Dan Sullivan`s track, not the track of the dissenter. So I -- that`s one I can`t figure it out. Maybe he`s concerned about the base that follows Donald Trump . And maybe that`s a reason. But that one I can`t figure out. I did want to say that of all of the comments we`ve made about presidents losing elections, the one that didn`t participate in a election but whose circumstances are more similar to Biden was Lyndon Johnson. He`s in the middle of a war with you know Russian-backed people. And his numbers kept falling. And then he said, you know what, I`m stepping down. ALTER: But he had 500,000 troops there. CARDENAS: My point is I think-- TODD: That`s a big difference. CARDENAS: -- Biden may be facing the Lyndon Johnson predicament -- TODD: Oh, wow. CARDENAS: -- before you consider his running for reelection. TODD: All right. I`m going to have to leave that there. But that`s a fascinating conversation, and the point is if this gets into `24, we don`t know how this is going to play with the American people. Up next, the Ohio train disaster was 100 percent preventable, according to federal investigators. Trains are still, though, some of the safest options for transporting hazardous chemicals. I`m going to show you why after the break. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:46:54] TODD: Welcome back, Data Download time. That East Palestine train derailment and the chemical spill it caused raised some renewed questions about the safety of rail travel and using it to transport toxic chemicals. Just how safe is shipping toxic cargo by train? The answer is somewhat complicated. Let me show you. Train derailments overall have actually been going down over the last 10 years. We had over 1,300 derailments in 2013, just over 1,000 in 2022, about three a day. Good news is not all these train derailments are trains carrying hazardous materials. Now, though, let`s compare hazmat spills on railway incidents. So we had 667 hazmat spills in 2013 on the tracks -- railroad tracks. It`s down to 355 in 2022, so you can see it`s actually been getting safer by rail. Now, contrast that by hazmat spills on the highways. Look at this: In 2013 we had nearly 14,000. It`s actually been going up. We had over 23,000 hazmat spills by highway, just 355 by train. So clearly it`s safer to do this and better to do this by train, right? Well, you start to look at it financially, it`s a different story. Let`s take 2022 as an example. There were over 23,000 incidents that happened on highways. The cost of those cleanups: $21 million. The 355 incidents by rail? The cost of that was more than double that: $45 million. Now, why is that? It`s mainly due to one large rail spill in May. It was a train carrying petroleum products that derailed in Harmar Township, Pennsylvania. Spilled over 3,000 gallons into a creek, cost over $30 million in damages. By the way, the rail operator of that train? None other than Norfolk Southern , the same one behind this month`s incident in East Palestine. When you have these derailments, they can be gigantic accidents. When we come back, more Americans believe abortion should be legal in all or most cases. It`s becoming a major political problem for the GOP. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:52:38] TODD: Welcome back. The Republican Party has an abortion problem. That is the unmistakable conclusion of this new national survey from the Public Religion Research Institute. Of 20,000 Americans, it is easily the most comprehensive survey on abortion attitudes we have seen since the Dobbs decision. This was able to do both national polling and 50 separate state polls. Two- thirds of Americans, 64 percent, say abortion should be legal in all or most cases. This is an increase from 2010, from 55 percent. And Republicans right now look like they`re more out of step, just 36 percent favor legal abortion compared with 86 percent of Democrats. And look at this number: 68 percent of Independents. The Republican number has not moved since 2010. But support among Democrats and Independents has actually grown by double digits. State by state, you can see here solid majorities favor legal abortion. In the six historically closest presidential states, the battleground states, all of them but one over 60 percent. And in the three most vulnerable Democratic-held Senate seats, look at those states: Montana, Ohio, and West Virginia, also with very high percentages on legal abortion. Al Cardenas, what does the GOP do here? They seem to be in a box on abortion. CARDENAS: Well, look, everybody was thankful for Roe v. Wade. The Republicans and Democrats didn`t want to touch it for 60 years for obvious reasons. Now, Donald Trump decided he wanted to do evangelicals a favor and name three Supreme Court justices who were committed to looking at this issue. And now, we`ve got the political explosion of having made that Dobbs decision. And in my opinion, that`s not the only one they`re going to make. The Supreme Court of the United States has become the Democrats` best ally -- TODD: Wow. CARDENAS: -- when you come to what`s going on, in spite of the fact that Republicans were rejoicing that they -- TODD: Right. CARDENAS: -- had a 6-3 majority. TODD: Tamara, they don`t -- that`s the thing. They don`t know what their position is now as a party. KEITH: That`s correct. Well, because they don`t actually agree. There are some people like former Vice President Mike Pence , very likely presidential candidate, who says, we need to stand strong, stand firm on abortion. We need to take a strong position here. Then you have someone like Trump saying, "You know, Republicans could be in real trouble here with this issue. So it`s one of the many things that probably won`t be settled by 2024. [09:55:01] But in terms of the identity of the Republican Party, it is a challenge, because when you start talking about specifics -- when something has been taken away and then you start talking about specifics, people actually care about this issue. And that`s what showed up in this poll, is just a spike in support. TODD: And the White House has been, look, I saw Vice President Harris did an event earlier this week. WELKER: Oh yeah. TODD: I mean, look, I`m going to look back on 2022 and start to think that we`re overrating the impact of the Trump candidates and underrating the impact of the abortion decision. WELKER: That`s right. I mean, we saw the power of Dobbs in the midterm elections. And I`m told the vice president is going to be out front on this issue. You can expect that over the next two years. In terms of the strategy within the Republican Party moving forward, when you talk to Republicans, one person said something so interesting to me, which is that Roe was overturned and then the focus became on banning abortion in the states. Instead of talking about maternal health, talking about adoption, talking about what happens to these families. Another person said, we`re going to focus on the economy. Well, that`s a risky strategy. What is the economy going to look like in the next year and a half? And it`ll be a test. Is the economy as motivating as the abortion issue? ALTER: And the abortion pill is going to be a huge issue. There`s a decision coming out in Texas. TODD: Oh my goodness, if that goes away, yeah. ALTER: So right now, 55 percent of all abortions are medical abortions with the abortion pill, up from 45 percent just a couple of years ago. And if this decision comes down the way people are expecting, and then it`s upheld at the U.S. Supreme Court , as people expect, a lot of women who want to use the abortion pill are not going to be able to. And they`re going to be awfully upset about that. TODD: I`m going to bring it back. You`re my Floridian pal here, Al. I sense Governor DeSantis is uncomfortable on what to say about abortion right now, because he has the 15 week, but I notice he doesn`t want this session of the legislature to touch abortion, does he? CARDENAS: No, he doesn`t. He`s shied away from this issue. He`s acknowledged from the outset it`s not a winning issue. He hasn`t mentioned the issue. And he`s acting like, hey, I`m Governor from Florida. I don`t need to get involved with this. Let this be a national issue. So far, it`s working for him. Nobody`s really taking him on, primarily because the Democrat Party has imploded in Florida. But if I was them, I would certainly try to put him in a corner, but they haven`t. TODD: But with the Jon Tester news this week, and you see those abortion numbers, I finally -- look, I was pretty pessimistic about this Senate map for Democrats. But suddenly you see those abortion numbers and you`re like: I see the path for Tester. I see the path for Brown. KEITH: They can talk about this issue and make it about people`s rights. And not just about -- TODD: Make the libertarian argument. KEITH: -- a healthcare procedure. Yes. WELKER: But, Chuck, I think it`s interesting. Tam, to your first point about the divisions within the Republican Party, one of the biggest ones is about this 15-week national abortion ban. A lot of Republicans are saying Senator Lindsey Graham should`ve never introduced this, because the whole point of Dobbs was to send this back to the states. TODD: Except he was actually looking for a compromise number here. I don`t know if Democrats will ever get to even 20, let alone 50. WELKER: Well, and now every Republican candidate is going to have to weigh in on that. TODD: All right. Before we go, this week on the Chuck Toddcast, I spoke with former ambassador to Russia, Mike McFaul, Washington Post`s Dan Balz. And after the broadcast today we`re going to have a post-game discussion with Jonathan Alter, talk a little bit about Jimmy Carter . headline: MEET THE PRESS for March 5, 2023, NBC
story_text: (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) [09:00:18] CHUCK TODD, HOST, NBC`S "MEET THE PRESS WITH CHUCK TODD" (voice over): This Sunday, crime and punishment. President Biden backs down from fighting a Republican effort to block D.C.`s more lenient`s approach to crime. PAUL VALLAS , (D) CHICAGO MAYORAL CANDIDATE: We will make Chicago the safest city in America. (APPLAUSE) TODD: Just after the perception of rising crime took down Chicago`s mayor. MAYOR LORI LIGHTFOOT, (D) CHICAGO: We fought the right fights. TODD: Can Biden`s moves help Democrats from being seen as soft on crime going into 2024? Plus, divide and conquer. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis isn`t officially in the race yet, but he`s eagerly courting Trump`s base. GOV. RON DESANTIS, (R) FLORIDA: I think there`s a strong anti-woke majority out there across the country. TODD: The primary fight has kicked into high gear as more candidates consider challenging Trump. FORMER PRESIDENT DONALD J. TRUMP: For those who have been wronged and betrayed, I am your retribution. TODD: I`ll talk to New Hampshire Republican Governor Chris Sununu , who`s considering his own White House run. And, confronting China, a bipartisan push to face the growing threats from Beijing. REP. MIKE GALLAGHER , (R) WISCONSIN: This is an existential struggle over what life will look like in the 21st Century. TODD: Tensions continue to escalate as the U.S. warns about supplying arms to Russia and new concern over COVID`s origins. CHRISTOPHER WRAY , DIRECTOR, FEDERAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION: The origins of the pandemic are mostly likely a potential lab incident in Wuhan. TODD: In a joint interview, I`ll talk to the chair and ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee, Republican Mike Turner of Ohio and Democrat Jim Himes of Connecticut. (on camera): Joining me for insight and analysis are NBC News senior Washington correspondent Hallie Jackson; former Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson; USA Today Washington bureau chief Susan Page; and former Republican governor of North Carolina Pat McCrory . Welcome to Sunday. It`s "Meet the Press." ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest-running show in television history, this is "Meet the Press with Chuck Todd." (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: Good Sunday morning. This may be the week where we saw the 2024 presidential campaign kick into full gear, and not just on the Republican side. President Biden`s decision to block a D.C. crime law caught many Democrats off guard. Because it`s going to be the first time in 30 years that Congress has nullified a law in D.C. And it`s a Democratic president and a Democratic Senate. But if you view it through the lens of political calculation, it may make perfect sense. President Biden decided that neither he nor his party, with a big Senator map to defend with a lot of red areas to defend, could afford to look soft on crime heading into 2024. Republicans tried to make crime a central issue in the 2022 midterms, and they certainly had some success in New York State and a few other areas. But the results this week in the Chicago mayor`s race, where voters fired the incumbent, are a reminder that crime and policing are still important to urban voters as well, a huge part of the Democratic coalition. Democrats have been twisted in knots on the crime issue because it`s a problem with swing voters. And Biden is trying to provide them with a way forward. The mirror image of, sort of, being twisted in knots for Republicans is the abortion issue. But no one in the GOP, at least to date, is taking the lead to try and come up with a modified solution to that political problem for them. If anything, the Republicans are more fractured, and not just on the abortion issue but about the general direction of the party. It`s a divide that has been on full display this weekend. But there`s one issue where there is little divide these days, and it is on China, with its rising national security threats. The secretary of state, Antony Blinken , issued yet another direct warning to China about sending lethal aid to Russia for the war in Ukraine. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SECRETARY OF STATE ANTONY BLINKEN: China can`t have it both ways. It can`t putting itself out as a force for peace in public while it, one way or another, continues to fuel the flames of this fire that Vladimir Putin started. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: If we want to dig deeper into this, joining me now are the chair and ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee, appearing here together, Republican Congressman Mike Turner of Ohio and Democratic Congressman Jim Himes of Connecticut. Gentlemen, welcome back to "Meet the Press," and thank you for coming on together. REP. MIKE TURNER , (R) OHIO & CHAIR OF HOUSE INTELLIGENCE COMMITTEE: Thanks for having me. REP. JIM HIMES, (D), CONNECTICUT & RANKING MEMBER, HOUSE INTELLIGENCE COMMITTEE: Thanks for having us. TODD: Before we start on this stuff, your -- this train derailment overnight happened in your congressional district. I know the shelter in place order is no longer. What -- what more can you tell us? What more have you learned, and is the federal government responding? TURNER: Sure. This truly is outrageous. You know, Ohio is really the crossroads of America, both on the road and in the rail. An unbelievable amount of goods travel through Ohio, some hazardous. What we`ve seen recently with the risk to communities is -- is unacceptable. Luckily, it seems we may have missed a bullet in this one, that this train may have been empty, and it looks like hazardous materials is not going to be a threat to the community. We`ll have to see. TODD: Is it clear -- do you think it`s clear that the freight industry isn`t well-regulated and needs to be? TURNER: Oh, absolutely. And the fact that we`re having derailment after derailment shows really the lack of investment -- the disinvestment in our infrastructure, and that needs to change. [09:05:04] TODD: Let me move to this -- Congressman Himes, I`ll -- I`ll start with this. I know both of you have been getting these briefings. Another warning to China. We heard it from the secretary of state about arming Russia. Our reporting indicates that this actually came from our intelligence inside of Russia, confirmed (inaudible). How serious is this threat, and do we know if China has made a final decision? HIMES: Well, no question it`s a serious threat. We`ve seen the Russian military obviously come apart. The Chinese could reverse in the same way that the Iranians are helping the Russians right now. I think the administration is doing the right things by saying "Don`t do this." Now, it doesn`t surprise me at all that there`s a debate inside China about whether they should do this. Hopefully, wisdom prevails. I -- I couldn`t help but note, in the Chinese proposed peace plan, the 12th point said we need to focus on rebuilding China -- rebuilding Russia. I can imagine the Chinese see a lot of business there. Obviously, if they`re part of the Russian assault on Ukraine, they will not get that business. So, no, I don`t think a final decision has been made, but I do think it`s wise for us to say "Don`t go there." TODD: Congressman Turner, you -- you`ve noted that we have a different posture now on our intelligence. We`re releasing more of it. Do you think more of it should be released to make sure the world believes us? TURNER: Right, well, and obviously you`re seen with the CIA director, even calling out to China on this issue that they`re considering it has a huge shift in policy. And what we`re seeing is the administration using intelligence to try to impact the outcome of -- of policy, right? So they`re not just saying "We happen to know this" in looking to hold someone accountable. They`re trying to thwart them, to stop them from doing this. You know, the problem with China entering this is because, you know, you`ve got the West giving weapons to Ukraine. You`ve got Russia depleting their stores. We obviously, the West together, have an ability to impact Ukraine greater than Russia alone does. It would be an inexhaustible source of weapons if China and its production capacity supported Russia. And that would change the dynamics. TODD: What kind of intel do we have on the state of the Russian army, Congressman Himes, meaning, like, we`ve seen some reports that they may be running out of munitions; they have some issues. What does our folks say? HIMES: Well, so neither Mike nor I can get too deep into any particular intel, but, you know, you don`t need to get too deep into intel. Consider the fact that you see every single day on television, which is the entire Russian army cannot take a town that nobody had ever heard of a year ago, the town of Bakhmut. Now, you know, Mike and I have been doing this long enough that we remember when we literally devoted hundreds of billions of dollars and much of our national security apparatus to this beast of a Russian military. Today we see that they can`t, even with the push of the president, Vladimir Putin , they can`t take a town. That doesn`t mean they`re not still dangerous. They have nuclear weapons. But they are not what we thought they were. TODD: I want to play something. Sergey Lavrov was at the G-20, Congressman turner. And wait -- I mean, wait until you hear the reaction to something he said here. Let me play it. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SERGEY LAVROV , RUSSIAN FOREIGN MINISTER: The war which we are trying to stop and which was launched against us using the Ukraine... (LAUGHTER) ... Ukrainian people... (CROSSTALK) LAVROV: of course influenced -- influenced -- influenced the policy of Russia. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: You know, there`s nothing like being able to say the phrase, "The world was laughing" at them. HIMES: Completely. TODD: The world was laughing at them. TURNER: Spontaneously. TODD: What should -- what should the West use a moment like that for? TURNER: Well, the thing about both Putin, Lavrov and even Medvedev, although he`s supposed to be the new, new face of a new Russia, come from an era where, you know, they controlled Eastern Europe. They could say things that were not true and people believed them because they controlled information. Today information can`t be controlled. So the -- the laughability of what they`re saying, and the ridiculousness of what they`re saying is easily exposed. TODD: All right. Let me move to the issue of these classified documents. Nobody seems to be satisfied with -- with what you`ve got. Congressman Himes, does that include you? Were you satisfied with the briefing? HIMES: So we have a lot more work to do. Look, I think, as the leaders of the Intelligence Committee, our number one job is to make sure that the DNI, the FBI , whoever needs to do it, does everything they need to do to protect the sources and methods that might have been exposed were any of those documents to have been out in the wild. So there`s a lengthy process to figure out that. And -- and I can`t speak for Mike, but I will tell you that, though we have been briefed, we`ve got a lot more to do to make sure that the government is doing what it should be doing. TODD: Well, let me ask specifically, do you know what the Trump docs are, Congressman Turner? TURNER: We -- we... TODD: Do you know what the Biden docs are? And do you know what the Pence docs are? TURNER: No, but we -- there are some things that we do know. And, first off, I want to... TODD: Let me stop there. No? They didn`t share with you those things in a classified setting? TURNER: Right. TODD: Why? TURNER: Well, first off, we -- in the things that we do know, one of the things we know is that the FBI is not being forthcoming. They`re -- they`re not giving us the information. They`re claiming that it`s going to affect the outcome of their investigation, which of course it can`t because the people who are the targets of their investigation know what`s -- what are in those documents. And we have the clearance and the ability to look at these documents. We also know, from Averil Haines, that she said that -- that she was not consulted prior to the raid on -- on Trump`s Mar-a-Lago home, that in fact there -- it was not a national security basis. [09:10:08] So as we go through this process, as they give us the category of the documents and their assessment as to who had access to them, who did not have access to them, we`re beginning to build an understanding. But the thing that we know is that it`s unbelievable that administration after administration is apparently sloppy and messy in their use of classified documents. And that`s one thing, on a bipartisan basis, we have to address well beyond just this. This has to change, where classified documents are under a certain amount of control. TODD: But, Congressman Himes, do you -- do you know -- do you at least know the classification levels of these docs? Do you know -- is there a -- is there a distinction between the Trump docs, the Biden docs and the Pence docs, or not? HIMES: So we have not been shown anything that would allow us to draw that conclusion. And we`ve got to be a little careful here, because what we were shown wasn`t shown in the... TODD: So you weren`t briefed much? HIMES: Well, we were -- we were briefed, but I -- but let`s just say that neither one of us are satisfied that we got enough information to execute our primary responsibility of making sure that sources and methods have been protected. We`ve got more to learn before we can be satisfied on that. TODD: So right now you have no idea whether these were the highest level... HIMES: Well, we didn`t say no... TODD: ... or the mid-level. HIMES: We didn`t say no idea. TODD: OK. HIMES: Again, we can`t get too into the details. We got a flavor for what was there. And I won`t speak for Mike, but I will tell you, having been given a flavor, this is a very serious issue. This wasn`t stuff that we can say clearly does not matter. It matters. TODD: In all three cases? HIMES: Well, again... TODD: Or you don`t know? HIMES: We don`t know yet. TURNER: One thing I would say, Chuck, which is important, which is also the symbolism of the fact that Jim and I are here together. TODD: I was just going to say, Devin Nunes and Adam Schiff... (LAUGHTER) ... I don`t know would have done this together. TURNER: Right. We -- we have shifted. And it takes two to shift to a bipartisan basis. And you see it on the Senate side, too, with Marco Rubio ... TODD: Right. TURNER: ... Senator Warner. And the approach to this issue of the Biden docs and the Trump docs and the Pence docs, we`re looking at holistically, what do we have to do to fix this? How do we address this? What were the risks involved? And you have to understand, also, that without Congress having asked, there wasn`t even a risk assessment being done. We were the ones who initiated this. That`s -- that`s part of the concern. TODD: I get the sense that the -- that the intel community doesn`t trust Congress, and you guys -- is that fair? Do you think you guys have to rebuild your -- you have to prove to them that you`re trustworthy with secrets? TURNER: I would say it`s more of a tension between the FBI and Congress than it is the intelligence community. Because we`re having... TODD: Just more FBI and Congress? TURNER: Absolutely. And I think that`s going to come to a head over the next couple years. You`re seeing it in a number of areas where they`re just not -- you know, they are not special; they don`t have greater privileges than the president does. And they`re continuing to act as if they have some privilege to be able to operate without congressional oversight. TODD: Congressman Himes, I`m curious what you -- that piece about, sort of, the tension between main Justice and the FBI having to do with retrieving the classified documents from Mar-a-Lago. It looks like there was fear going in of retribution. The FBI , are they more concerned about perception than whether they`re doing their job? Are you worried about this? HIMES: Well, two things about the FBI . First of all, and Mike`s right, they are subject to congressional oversight. Secondly, they do have to preserve the integrity of their investigation. And there are investigations on board right now. So we need to work with them because both of us, everybody, wants them to be able to do investigations in an unsloppy manner. We`ve got too much of a history of investigations in a somewhat sloppy manner. But of course there was consternation. Look, it`s one thing to conduct a raid on an average Joe citizen. To conduct a raid on a former president who, and I hope I don`t insult my good chairman here, who was, sort of, known for his, you know, aggressive retribution against people he didn`t like, I`m sure that got a lot of discussion. But, you know, look, the lesson to be drawn here is, if you don`t want a raid on your -- on your home, don`t take a year to cough up documents that we know are out there. TODD: The COVID origin. TURNER: Or -- or six years. (LAUGHTER) Because Biden... (CROSSTALK) TURNER: ... Biden took six HIMES: Fair enough. fair enough. (LAUGHTER) TURNER: The one aspect that`s -- that`s important here is that Merrick Garland did an unbelievable, terrible political miscalculation. He appointed a special prosecutor against Trump, not realizing he was going to end up having to appoint one against his own boss. TODD: Right. TURNER: And that`s going to -- how that`s going to play out is going to be amazing. TODD: Let`s talk about the -- the COVID origin situation. I think a lot of people were surprised to learn that the Energy Department had an intelligence agency and, in fairness, and I -- you know, some of us know that`s true. They deal with our nukes. There`s a reason for it. But a lot of people didn`t know. But I want to -- they labeled it "low confidence." So how should the public take that? TURNER: Well, it`s not actually been released yet. These are all leaks that are reporting this. TODD: Great. All the more helpful to... (LAUGHTER) TURNER: Right, right. TODD: ... messing up the story, but fair.
