headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for April 6, 2023, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the dramatic showdown over guns in Tennessee. (voiceover): The state`s Republican-led house voting on removing three Democrats from office after they led a protest on the floor demanding stricter gun laws after the Nashville school shooting that killed six people. The rare punishment used only three times before since the Civil War. Outside the building, the massive protest and what happens now with the ousted Democrat seats? Also, tonight, in the new report of the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan, the White House largely blaming the chaos and decisions by Former President Trump and the actions it says the U.S. should have taken even sooner. The rising tensions of the Middle East. Israel striking back tonight after the biggest barrage of missiles from Lebanon in more than 16 years. Tracking severe storms on the move tonight in the Mid-Atlantic on the heels of that deadly tornado outbreak. NBC News investigates after our report on toxic air concerns near a Louisiana school. What the EPA is now doing about it. And it was 20 years ago we lost a member of our NBC News family covering the war in Iraq. Tonight, my conversation with David Bloom`s widow about the lives his story may have saved. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC Nightly News with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening and welcome. The tears of grief that consume Nashville, Tennessee just 10 days ago over the murders of young children and school staffers are replaced tonight by cries of anger and accusations after an extraordinary move by Tennessee House Republicans to seek the expulsion of three Democratic members for their roles in a gun safety protest on the House floor last week. All day, angry supporters and gun safety advocates crowding the state house where the GOP majority was putting the resolutions up to a vote one by one, declaring the three participated in disorderly behavior when they led supporters in chants demanding stricter gun safety measures. Expulsion, a rarely exercise right of the Tennessee House that critics on the left tonight are calling anti-democratic. NBC`s Priscilla Thompson is in Nashville following it all for us. Where do things stand right now, Priscilla? PRISCILLA THOMPSON, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, Lester, just moments ago, a vote to expel one lawmaker narrowly failed. And this after earlier today, another lawmaker was expelled. That third lawmaker is in the chamber pleading his case right now. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) THOMPSON (voiceover): Outrage tonight in Nashville in reaction to Republican-led efforts to expel three Democratic lawmakers from the state legislature. CAMERON SEXTON, SPEAKER, TENNESSEE STATE HOUSE: I hereby declare of Representative Justin Jones of the 57 representative district expelled from the House of Representatives of the 113th assembly of the State of Tennessee. The three Democrats in question, state representatives Justin Jones, Gloria Johnson, and Justin Pearson were accused of disorderly behavior following their participation in a demonstration on the house floor last week. JUSTIN JONES (D-TN), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: We need action! We need action! We need action! THOMPSON: They joined advocates calling for stricter gun safety measures following the mass shooting at the Nashville private school that left six people dead on March 27th. Their chants with a bull horn from the podium in the house well led to today`s showdown. JONES: We called for you all to ban assault weapons and you respond with an assault on democracy. THOMPSON: While Tennessee`s Constitution allows for any member of the state legislature to be expelled with the two-thirds vote, it has only happened three times before. Demonstrators today filled the halls of the state capitol. But arguments from Democrats did little to sway the Republican super majority. JONES: This does not seem like America. To expel voices of opposition and dissent is a signal of authoritarianism and it is very dangerous. THOMPSON: The Republican Speaker of the House says today`s actions were about the rules. SEXTON: It did break rules by going to the well and showing that they were at the well, they were speaking, they pulled out a bull horn, and rolled out of order before there was a recess. THOMPSON: But protesters here told us they felt today`s vote was a distraction from the urgent issue of gun violence. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: What`s happening in Tennessee right now is abhorrent and our legislators are not listening to what we are saying. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Priscilla, what happens next? THOMPSON (on camera): Lester, counties will appoint interim representatives to fill the seats of those expelled lawmakers until a special election is set. And that would be set by the governor. And as for those expelled lawmakers, here in Tennessee, they are still eligible to run and could potentially be re-elected for those seats in that special election. Lester? [19:05:07] HOLT: Priscilla Thompson tonight, thank you. Tonight`s other top story, a Biden administration review partially blaming the Trump Administration for the chaotic and deadly U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan, prompting a backlash from Republicans. Kristen Welker is at the White House with more. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, nearly two years after the deadly and disastrous American withdrawal from Afghanistan, those stunning images of Afghans desperately chasing U.S. planes and the airport terror attack which killed 13 U.S. service members. The Biden Administration releasing its after-action review trying to pin much of the blame on Former President Trump who had left office eight months earlier including citing sharp drawdowns of U.S. troops. JOHN KIRBY, STRATEGIC COMMUNICATIONS COORDINATOR, NATIONAL SECURITY COUNCIL: It is also undeniable that decisions made and the lack of planning done by the previous administration significantly limited options available to him. WELKER: Though acknowledging the Biden Administration should have started the evacuation earlier. Despite facing withering criticism, President Biden at the time called the withdrawal a "extraordinary success." JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: No nation -- no nation has ever done anything like it in all of history. WELKER: And today, this pushback from a White House spokesperson. KIRBY: For all this talk of chaos, I just didn`t it. Not from my perch. I just won`t buy the whole argument of chaos. It was tough in the first few hours -- WELKER: But a former top Trump official tonight firing back. MIKE POMPEO , FORMER U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE: They came in, took the plan that we had, and just botched it. It is outrageous for them to somehow try and blame anyone but Joe Biden . WELKER: We pressed the White House. Does the president take responsibility for the withdrawal and everything that happened thereafter? KIRBY: He`s the commander-in-chief. And he absolutely has responsibility for the operations that our men and women conduct and the orders that he gives. Meanwhile, in Taliban -controlled Afghanistan tonight, women face new oppression and Afghan interpreters who helped the U.S. are in hiding. We asked Jeff Phaneuf, a veteran trying to get translators out about the report. JEFF PHANEUF, VETERAN: It doesn`t do enough to take full ownership of the continued problem looking forward to save the 160 to 200,000 of our Afghan partners who were left behind. (END VIDEOTAPE) WELKER (on camera): Just last month, the CENTCOM commander warned ISIS in Afghanistan could conduct terror attacks against U.S. interests abroad in under six months. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker at the White House, thank you. Tonight, Israel launching new strikes in Gaza after getting hit by a wave of rocket attacks fired by militants in Lebanon. Raf Sanchez is in Tel Aviv tonight. Raf, what more do we know about this? RAF SANCHEZ, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, in the last hour, Israeli jets have begun striking targets in Gaza belonging to the Hamas militant group. And we are hearing sirens going off in southern Israel which suggests Palestinian militants are shooting back. We don`t yet know if there are casualties, but we do know Israel blames Hamas for those rockets from Lebanon earlier in the day. And all of this comes after violent scenes yesterday between Israeli police and Palestinians at the Al-Aqsa mosque in Jerusalem, the third holiest site in Islam. Lester? HOLT: Raf Sanchez, thank you. Despite growing China tensions, a U.S. delegation is in Taiwan after talks in California between Taiwan`s President and House Speaker Kevin McCarthy. Courtney Kube reports now from Taiwan. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) COURTNEY KUBE, NBC NEWS PENTAGON CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, despite threats from China, including this warship seen off the coast, a top delegation of American officials arriving in Taiwan for critical high- level talks. The bipartisan group meeting with Taiwan`s Vice President Lai, and later this weekend, President Tsai after her historic visit with house Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California. TSAI ING-WEN, PRESIDENT, TAIWAN: Taiwan is grateful to have the States of America by our side. KUBE: China blasting the show of support from the U.S. for Taiwan vowing to firmly defend national sovereignty and territorial integrity. China says the island democracy of Taiwan is part of its territory. REP. MICHAEL MCCAUL (R-TX): The United States stands by you and will protect you. KUBE: Tonight, a top House Republican Michael McCall saying the U.S. needs to arm and train Taiwan`s military. While Taiwan`s Vice President says they are already on the front lines of combating China`s authoritarianism, U.S. intelligence says China`s President Xi has instructed his military to be ready to invade Taiwan by 2027. We met Enoch Wu a former Special Forces Soldier now using his training to prepare Taiwan`s civilians to be ready. ENOCH WU, FORMER TAIWANESE SPECIAL FORCES: It was important for us to stand up a volunteer corps trained in crisis response. KUBE: He believes the threat of an invasion is higher now than ever. WU: If you can`t defend it, it`s not yours. Protecting Taiwan, protecting our home is our own responsibility. [19:10:01] (END VIDEOTAPE) KUBE (on camera): Despite the sharp comments, some U.S. officials tell me Chinese President Xi Jinping is unlikely to put on a large military show of force while French President Emmanuel Macron is in China on a state visit. But once President Macron leaves, President Xi could respond more forcefully. Lester? HOLT: Courtney Kube in Taipei, thank you. We`re tracking more severe weather here at home as the storm that ripped through parts of the Midwest now pushes into the Mid-Atlantic. 10 million people are at risk. Damaging winds the main concern. Fortunately, the tornado threat has diminished. We`ll turn to abortion now and what has been a consequential week for both sides of that battle as it plays out across the country. Blayne Alexander has the story for us. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): It`s been nearly 10 months since the end of Roe v Wade and the beginning of abortion access falling solely under state control, with major developments in four states this week. In Idaho, the governor signed a controversial new law making it a felony for non-parent adults to help a minor cross state lines for an abortion, the first law of its kind nationwide. Planned Parenthood is slamming the measure as extreme saying it will put young people in dangerous and isolating situations. What would you say to critics who call this unnecessarily cruel? TODD LAKEY (R-ID), STATE SENATOR: I think again it`s important that we protect the life of the unborn child. When it comes to minors, what the legislation requires is that parents essentially be informed. ALEXANDER: In Florida, protests and arrests after the state senate passed the so-called Heartbeat Protection Act reducing abortion access from 15 weeks to six. LAUREN BOOK, (D-FL), STATE SENATOR: If you vote for this ban, things will get worse. Women will die. ERIN GRALL (R-FL), STATE SENATOR: For 50 years, the killing of innocent children has been legal. Legal does not equate to right. ALEXANDER: It all comes amid a pair of victories for abortion rights advocates. In Michigan, Governor Gretchen Whitmer signed a repeal of the state`s abortion ban on the books since 1931. GOV. GRETCHEN WHITMER (D-MI): Abortion rights are now enshrined into our state constitution. ALEXANDER: And in Wisconsin, abortion was at the heart of Tuesday`s high- stakes election for a seat on the state supreme court now set to be filled by the liberal candidate all but ensuring abortion access in the state. JANET PROTASIEWICZ, JUSTICE-ELECT, WISCONSIN SUPREME COURT: Wisconsin voters have made their voices heard. ALEXANDER: Tonight, several more states are considering legislation that would either expand or restrict access to abortions. Blayne Alexander, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: In 60 seconds, what residents say is a long-time toxic threat to a school near a production plant in Louisiana, and what the EPA is now doing about it following our investigation, next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Three weeks ago, we first reported on the Fifth Ward Elementary School in Reserve Louisiana located next to a plant emitting what the EPA has long said was a likely carcinogen. Cynthia McFadden returned with the head of the EPA who was now taking action. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MICHAEL REGAN , ADMINISTRATOR, EPA : Our work isn`t done. CYNTHIA MCFADDEN, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL AND INVESTIGATIVE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): 18 months ago, the newly appointed head of the EPA , Michael Regan took what he called a journey to justice tour that brought him here. REGAN: I vowed that EPA would take action. MCFADDEN: Today, he returned to make good on that promise proposing a staggering slate of emission standards for 80 toxic chemicals. REGAN: We`re sending a safety standard that we believe is the lowest you can set that is detectable with technology. MCFADDEN: Including chemicals being emitted from the Danka plant here in Reserve. On our last visit here, we met George and his great-grandmother Mary Hampton who`s been battling for years to get the Denka Plant next door to George`s elementary school to stop emitting where the EPA has long said are unsafe levels of two of those toxic chemicals. One of your neighbors says it`s like sending the kids to a gas chamber. MARY HAMPTON, RESIDENT, RESERVE, LOUISIANA: Exactly, exactly. [19:15:00] MCFADDEN: We also met Robert Taylor who had been fighting with her for years. He didn`t have much confidence the EPA would do anything. So, when the agency called the night our story aired and suggested we meet up with Michael Regan in Louisiana, we agreed. One of the things that Mr. Taylor said to me the first time I came to visit was that this was a sacrifice zone. REGAN: What I can tell you is there are none of these facilities in Beverly Hills. There`s no coincidence if you look at who`s on the front lines, most of these individuals are Black, Brown, or tribal and or low-income. So, there`s a consistent pattern here. If the new standards announced today are put into effect, they become much more enforceable. MCFADDEN: I think what angers a lot of people is though the Denka plant has been emitting at these historically high levels for years now. Why not shut the plant down while everything else is being sorted out. REGAN: We are using every tool in our toolbox. And if I have more powers, trust me, I would use them. MCFADDEN: Denka told us it`s reduced emissions and says it`s breaking no laws denying it`s putting the folks who live here at any increased risk for cancer. REGAN: I wish that we could move more expeditiously to take action to protect George, to protect Mr. Taylor, to do all the things that we want to do yesterday. MCFADDEN: As for Bob and Mary, they said today has filled them with hope. What`s the best part of today? ROBERT TAYLOR, RESIDENT, RESERVE, LOUISIANA: We got the attention of our politicians. HAMPTON: It`s not over. TAYLOR: It`s not over but we`ll be here when it ends. I tell them all the time. I was here from day one. I`ll be there till day zero. MCFADDEN: Cynthia McFadden, NBC News Reserve, Louisiana. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: We`ll take a short break. Up next, sticker shock, the soaring cost of buying a new car. What`s driving it up in "THE PRICE YOU PAY." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: If you`ve been shopping for a new car, then you know that prices and monthly payments have been soaring. Miguel Almaguer reports on why and what you can do in "THE PRICE YOU PAY." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): For Americans already facing sticker shock on the sales lot, tonight, car payments are also accelerating towards record levels. Admins revealed the average annual percentage rate or APR on a newly financed vehicle has now ballooned to seven percent. The typical payment for a new car in overdrive hitting $730 a month. It could be enough for Sharon Divestern to pump the brakes on buying new. SHARON DIVESTER, LOOKING TO BUY A CAR: If you find something that you like, you just save money. ALMAGUER: As car payments become more expensive than ever, tonight, one in six buyers who finance new are paying more than $1,000 a month. The staggering price to sit behind the wheel rivaling the cost of putting a roof over your head. IVAN DRURY, DIRECTOR, EDMUNDS INSIGHTS: Unless you have a lot of cash on hand to kind of mitigate those APRs, you will be looking at a number you probably have never seen before if you bought a car in the last 10 years. ALMAGUER: With more drivers going into delinquency, the average cost of a new car has nearly hit $50,000. Many buyers are no longer in the driver`s seat when it comes to monthly payments. Supply remains tight. Inflation is driving up costs and the Fed continues to raise interest rates. There is some good news though. Experts believe rates will soon stabilize. But for now, it`s a bumpy road ahead for drivers buying new. Miguel Almaguer, NBC News Los Angeles. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And next tonight, I`ll remember a beloved NBC News colleague, David Bloom, and his important Legacy 20 years later. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: This is a somber anniversary for all of us at NBC News and for journalism at large. It was 20 years ago we learned our colleague David Bloom had died while embedded with the front-line elements of the U.S. invasion of Iraq. How David died was a shock in itself and a wakeup call still impacting lives today. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DAVID BLOOM, FORMER NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: This is the U.S. Army `s third infantry division. We`re with the second brigade, the 315 Infantry. HOLT: It`s where we like to be on the big story out front. David Bloom rolling into combat on live T.V. with the Army`s 3rd Infantry Division trailed by a customized satellite truck known as the Bloom Mobile. BLOOM: Basically, what we`ve done is we`ve established the ability transmit live from this vehicle using a pretty sophisticated camera which can be outside the vehicle and take the bumps and the jars. HOLT: Paul Nassar was David`s producer on the journey. BLOOM: We`re just rolling along. It`s nighttime now. PAUL NASSAR, PRODUCER: The difference with the Bloom Mobile is it was the first time that you had live television on the move in the middle of an invasion. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Rocket, rocket, rocket. BOOM: Tom, we`re under attack right now. HOLT: David traveled aboard a cram tank recovery vehicle. What was your level of concern about him going off and working in a battlefield. MELANIE BEAL, WIFE OF DAVID BLOOM: I was very concerned. And what I knew about David though is that`s the only place he would be. He really had a calling to be a journalist. HOLT: His wife Melanie worried about the war, unaware he faced another threat. BEAL: Two nights before his death, he had called me and he said, you know, I just can`t sleep another night in that tank with my knees pulled up to my chest. I`ve been having these leg cramps. HOLT: What no one including David knew he had developed a blood clot. NASSAR: The that he died, he kind of woke up and he said that he wasn`t limping anymore. It had gotten much better. And we were all relieved but what was evident now is that the blood clot had moved from behind his knee to other parts of his body. HOLT: Specifically, his lungs were a pulmonary embolism proved fatal. David was just 39 and left a wife and three young daughters behind. After David`s passing, Melanie committed herself to increasing awareness about deep vein thrombosis, DVT, the condition that took David`s life and affects hundreds of thousands of lives each year. BEAL: 50 percent of the time there are signs of a clot in your leg, and those signs can be swelling, redness, pain, cramps in David`s case. But 50 percent of the time it`s silent and you don`t really know that the clot is there. HOLT: The message she believes is getting through. BEAL: I think changes have been made. People now are aware when they get on planes to get up and walk around, stretch their legs. HOLT: Do you think his story has ultimately saved lives? BEAL: I know that it has saved lives. I really do believe that. And David dedicated his life to informing the American people in his role as a journalist. And I couldn`t think of a better legacy for him than to inform the American people about what took his life. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: David and his family in our hearts tonight. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS. Thank you for watching. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: The Issue Of Abortion, In Idaho, Doctors Are Facing Difficult Decisions
story_text: LESTER HOLT: On the issue of abortion, in Idaho, doctors are facing difficult decisions. Some choosing to leave the state due to its restrictive abortion laws. Kristen Dahlgren explains. [19:10:08] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN DAHLGREN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Not far from Idaho`s Capitol building, Dr. Kylie Cooper and her family are packing up and moving out of the state. The high-risk pregnancy specialist says she can no longer safely practice under one of the nation`s most restrictive abortion bans. DR. KYLIE COOPER, OBSTETRICIAN-GYNECOLOGIST: My husband and I are finding ourselves having conversations about what we would do if I were charged with a felony. DAHLGREN: Idaho only has exceptions for rape, incest, or averting the mother`s death. COOPER: Do I make the medically appropriate decision and commit a felony or do I follow the law and then watch as this person in front of me gets sicker and sicker? DAHLGREN: A recent survey shows about half of OBGYN`s in Idaho are considering leaving the state in the next year. All but two of those polled say the state`s abortion ban is the reason. So, you don`t think doctors are leaving the state. RAUL LABRADOR , ATTORNEY GENERAL, IDAHO: I don`t think there`s a huge outflow of doctors. DAHLGREN: GOP State Attorney General Raul Labrador . LABRADOR: I think maybe they just need more education on what the law allows. DAHLGREN: So, you`re saying the doctors are misinformed? LABRADOR: I think I`ve heard a lot of things that that borders on misinformation. But I think doctors are safe as long as they`re following the law. DAHLGREN: Many doctors say the law can be confusing. In fact, just hours after talking to us, Labrador withdrew a widely circulated letter to a state senator, in which he stated the law prohibits doctors from providing abortion pills or referring women out of state for abortions. Now saying it was not intended as a guidance document, and an updated law made it moot. For Dr. Cooper, it`s a hard day leaving patients like the one who recently asked -- DAHLGREN: Is it safe for me to be pregnant in Idaho? And my unequivocal answer was no, it`s not. DAHLGREN: But she doesn`t think it`s safe for doctors either. Kristen Dahlgren, NBC News, Boise, Idaho. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: We`ll be back in 60 seconds with a chilling new video showing a tech executive moments after he was stabbed. Plus, the shocking moment that shut down the Masters. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: At the Masters Golf Tournament in Georgia today, this is a terrifying moment high winds knocked down three trees near the 17th tee. Take a look. You can see people scrambling to get out of the way. There are no reports of injuries, but tournament play when suspended and the grounds evacuated because of dangerously high winds, lightning, and approaching thunderstorms. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for April 7, 2023, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the growing political firestorm over lawmaker expulsions in Tennessee. (voiceover): Outraged after two Black legislators who were expelled for interrupting debate over gun violence, while a White member kept her seat. Maybe she says because of the color of her skin. Republicans pushing back. Vice President Harris making a quickly arranged visit to Nashville. Plus, the new questions about if the expelled lawmakers could be reinstated. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas speaking out saying he did nothing wrong by accepting and not disclosing luxury trips over two decades paid for by a Republican megadonor. Violence escalating in the Middle East. Two Israeli sisters shot to death in their car in the West Bank. A new attack in Tel Aviv after new Israeli airstrikes on southern Lebanon and Gaza. The shocking moment at the Masters. High winds toppling three trees falling next to spectators. The newly released surveillance video showing the tech executive pleading for help moments after he was stabbed. An urgent new warning to parents about the dangers of sleeping with their infants. And the stunning act of forgiveness. My story about the man who called for the release of his father`s killer. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening and welcome, everyone. The expulsion from office of two Tennessee Democratic state reps over their boisterous call for gun safety reform has sparked national outrage on the left and left Tennessee House Republicans defending against accusations of unequal treatment and racial motivations. The GOP supermajority voting out to Black state representatives while sparing a White female lawmaker who faced the same accusations, accused of leading a disorderly protest for stronger gun laws in the House chamber last week. The deaths of six people in a Nashville school shooting less than two weeks ago have sparked a wave of activism in Nashville and elsewhere and demands for stricter gun measures. But the extraordinary step of selectively removing outspoken lawmakers has cast a chill being felt all the way to the White House tonight. Priscilla Thompson now has late details from Nashville. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PRISCILLA THOMPSON, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, growing fallout in Tennessee after last night`s historic vote. Two Black lawmakers were expelled by the state legislature while Representative Gloria Johnson was not. GLORIA JOHNSON (D-TN), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: Maybe I`m a White lady. I don`t know what else it was. THOMPSON: The trio was accused of breaking house rules and disorderly behavior. JUSTIN JONES (D-TN), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: No action? CROWD: No peace. THOMPSON: After protesting for stricter gun laws in the well of the chamber days after a Nashville school shooting left six people dead. JUSTIN PEARSON (D-TN), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: Surely justice will come. THOMPSON: Republican Lowell Russell who voted to expel Representatives Justin Jones and Justin Pearson but not Johnson says Johnson`s actions were not as severe and did not warrant an expulsion. LOWELL RUSSELL She didn`t shout and she didn`t bring the megaphone in. She didn`t use the megaphone. She didn`t engage on the people in the gallery. THOMPSON: But Jones says this type of action has never been taken against White colleagues who he says have committed far more severe infractions. JONES: One was admitted child molester, one was convicted of domestic violence, one peed in another member`s chair, and none of them were ever expelled. THOMPSON: A concern echoed by Pearson. PEARSON: The rules will be the in all and be all of this house, then that needs to apply equitably to everyone. THOMPSON: Jones calling the expulsions a political lynching. JONES: A state in which the Klu Klux Klan was founded is now attempting another power grab by silencing the two youngest Black Representatives. THOMPSON: Republicans say unequivocally, this was not about race. WILLIAM LAMBERTH, (R-TN), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: Our members literally didn`t look at the ethnicity of the members that were up for expulsion. CROWD: The people united will never be divided. THOMPSON: Still, their actions are drawing widespread condemnation from Democrats across the country, including President Biden, calling the expulsion shocking, undemocratic, and without precedent. Those expelled lawmakers` futures could soon be back in the hands of voters determined by a special election should they decide to run again. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Priscilla joining me now. As we await that special election, Priscilla, what happens now? THOMPSON (on camera): Lester, counties will appoint interim representatives in the meantime. Already, Nashville`s Metro Council has scheduled a meeting for Monday where Justin Jones is expected to be reinstated immediately. And we`re getting late word tonight that President Biden has spoken with all three of those Democrats, inviting them to the White House. Lester? [19:05:09] HOLT: Priscilla Thompson, thank you. Escalating violence tonight in the Middle East with deadly attacks in Tel Aviv and the occupied West Bank. And Israel striking back at Palestinian militants in southern Lebanon and Gaza. Raf Sanchez is in Israel with late details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) RAF SANCHEZ, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, a new wave of attacks shaking Israel. In Tel Aviv, Israeli police say they shot dead an attacker who rammed his car into tourists on a city promenade, killing at least one person. Hours earlier, two Israeli sisters killed in a suspected Palestinian ambush in the occupied West Bank. Their mother flown to the hospital in critical condition and fighting for her life. Israel`s Prime Minister at the scene of the attack warning our enemies are once again testing us. The wave of violence sweeping the Holy Lands darkening which should be a sacred week for believers celebrating Ramadan, Passover, and Easter. It began on Wednesday with Israeli forces storming into the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem, Islam`s third holiest site. And this morning Israeli jets pounding targets in Gaza and unusually southern Lebanon. Airstrikes across two regions aimed at the Hamas militant group, which Israel says was responsible for a barrage of rockets from Lebanon, the largest in nearly 20 years. U.N . peacekeepers in Lebanon assessing the damage and trying to prevent a rush to all-out war. (END VIDEOTAPE) SANCHEZ (on camera): And Israeli police say all the victims in Tel Aviv tonight we`re tourists visiting during this holy period. Meanwhile, a major manhunt is underway for the gunman who killed those two sisters. Lester? HOLT: Raf Sanchez tonight, thank you. Also, this evening, Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas says he violated no disclosure laws by not reporting luxury vacations he reportedly took four years paid for by a top Republican donor who he says is a longtime family friend. Laura Jarrett has late details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight Justice Clarence Thomas breaking his silence after a report detailed his secret lavish vacations paid for by a top Republican donor. Thomas writes, real estate mogul Harlan Crow is among his dearest friends and that colleagues advised him this sort of personal hospitality from close personal friends who did not have business before the court did not need to be reported. According to ProPublica , Thomas joined Crow on swanky trips for over two decades, including to this Lakeside resort, taking private jet rides, and island hopping in Indonesia on this super yacht, virtually none of which was disclosed. The luxury travel, a stark contrast to the more modest image the conservative justice has projected. CLARENCE THOMAS , ASSOCIATE JUSTICE, U.S. SUPREME COURT: I prefer going across the rural areas. I prefer the R.V. parks. I prefer the Walmart parking lots to the beaches and things like that. There`s something normal to me about it. JARRETT: NBC News has not independently verified the ProPublica report, which claims Thomas`s fellow travelers include GOP donors and corporate executives. JUSTIN ELLIOTT, REPORTER, PROPUBLICA : There`s also just an enormous amount we don`t know about what happens on these trips and who gets invited along. JARRETT: Crow says Thomas never asked for any of this hospitality. And he has never sought to influence Justice Thomas on any legal or political issue. The Supreme Court does not have an ethics code. And under federal law, Justices don`t have to disclose meals, stays at private homes, or other entertainment that is personal hospitality. Tonight, Thomas says he always sought to comply with disclosure guidelines and intends to follow new rules that trips on private jets must be reported. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And Laura, there are calls for more rule changes now. JARRETT (on camera): That`s right, Lester. Democratic lawmakers want to pass a bill that would require the court to establish a formal code of conduct. But the Chief Justice says they don`t need one, effectively leaving his colleagues to police themselves. HOLT: And Laura, we`re also watching some breaking news about a high-stakes lawsuit in Texas over the abortion pill. What do you know? JARRETT: Yes, that`s right, Lester. This just coming down minutes ago. This decision a partial victory for a group of anti-abortion advocates and doctors that had asked a federal judge to block access to the drug most widely used to induce abortions. Now, the plaintiffs had asked that judge to remove it from the market entirely nationwide immediately, but the judge didn`t go that far. Instead, he has suspended the original approval of the drug, acknowledging the plaintiffs do have a right to sue in this case, acknowledging their arguments about safety concerns, but there`s no immediate effect of this ruling. The judge has instead giving the Justice Department seven days to appeal, something Biden administration has almost certainly going to do very quickly. They have signaled that previously. HOLT: All right, Laura Jarrett, thank you for all that. On the issue of abortion, in Idaho, doctors are facing difficult decisions. Some choosing to leave the state due to its restrictive abortion laws. Kristen Dahlgren explains. [19:10:08] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN DAHLGREN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Not far from Idaho`s Capitol building, Dr. Kylie Cooper and her family are packing up and moving out of the state. The high-risk pregnancy specialist says she can no longer safely practice under one of the nation`s most restrictive abortion bans. DR. KYLIE COOPER, OBSTETRICIAN-GYNECOLOGIST: My husband and I are finding ourselves having conversations about what we would do if I were charged with a felony. DAHLGREN: Idaho only has exceptions for rape, incest, or averting the mother`s death. COOPER: Do I make the medically appropriate decision and commit a felony or do I follow the law and then watch as this person in front of me gets sicker and sicker? DAHLGREN: A recent survey shows about half of OBGYN`s in Idaho are considering leaving the state in the next year. All but two of those polled say the state`s abortion ban is the reason. So, you don`t think doctors are leaving the state. RAUL LABRADOR , ATTORNEY GENERAL, IDAHO: I don`t think there`s a huge outflow of doctors. DAHLGREN: GOP State Attorney General Raul Labrador . LABRADOR: I think maybe they just need more education on what the law allows. DAHLGREN: So, you`re saying the doctors are misinformed? LABRADOR: I think I`ve heard a lot of things that that borders on misinformation. But I think doctors are safe as long as they`re following the law. DAHLGREN: Many doctors say the law can be confusing. In fact, just hours after talking to us, Labrador withdrew a widely circulated letter to a state senator, in which he stated the law prohibits doctors from providing abortion pills or referring women out of state for abortions. Now saying it was not intended as a guidance document, and an updated law made it moot. For Dr. Cooper, it`s a hard day leaving patients like the one who recently asked -- DAHLGREN: Is it safe for me to be pregnant in Idaho? And my unequivocal answer was no, it`s not. DAHLGREN: But she doesn`t think it`s safe for doctors either. Kristen Dahlgren, NBC News, Boise, Idaho. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: We`ll be back in 60 seconds with a chilling new video showing a tech executive moments after he was stabbed. Plus, the shocking moment that shut down the Masters. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: At the Masters Golf Tournament in Georgia today, this is a terrifying moment high winds knocked down three trees near the 17th tee. Take a look. You can see people scrambling to get out of the way. There are no reports of injuries, but tournament play when suspended and the grounds evacuated because of dangerously high winds, lightning, and approaching thunderstorms. Police in San Francisco are combing through disturbing newly released surveillance video hoping to find new clues in the stabbing death this week of a Silicon Valley tech titan. Miguel Almaguer reports. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): This Chilling surveillance video could be a key piece of evidence. The dailymail.com which obtained CCTV says after tech executive Bob Lee was stabbed multiple times, he appears to try and wave down a passing car for help before the motorists drives away, wounded and stumbling into clear view around 2:35 a.m. Tuesday. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The location is 365 Main, across from Folsom and Harrison. There`s been stabbing. ALMAGUER: The San Francisco Standard says Lee called 911 and screamed help, someone stabbed me. BROOKE JENKINS, DISTRICT ATTORNEY, SAN FRANCISCO: That 911 call of course gives us a sense of time, but unfortunately unless someone says who did it or what happened specifically, its usefulness can be limited. ALMAGUER: San Francisco`s D.A. says she cannot confirm reports a knife was found near the crime scene, but says cellphone data is key. JENKINS: We want to know who he has been communicating with just before he was stabbed, who he was with, what cell phone towers that cell phone was hitting. Those are all critical pieces of evidence for us tracing backward to the moment that this stabbing occurred. [19:15:05] ALMAGUER: Perhaps best known for creating the mobile payment service, Cash App -- BOB LEE, TECH EXECUTIVE: We still need solutions for the unbanked. ALMAGUER: -- Lee was a tech icon who used to live near the area where he was killed. The police chief facing pressure as the city safety remains under blaring scrutiny amid a rash of negative headlines. BILL SCOTT, CHIEF, SAN FRANCISCO POLICE: We do have some good things to follow up on his case. And they are working tirelessly. ALMAGUER: Tonight, the high-profile murder mystery of a tech titan. Miguel Almaguer, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: We are back in a moment with a warning for parents about the big risks over where your baby sleeps. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [20:20:00] HOLT: We have an important warning for parents. Doctors are reporting a jump in infant deaths linked to unsafe sleeping conditions and co-sleeping with parents. Tom Costello now with what you need to know. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Cook Children`s in Fort Worth calls it alarming. 30 babies in just 15 months who likely died during unsafe sleeping conditions suffocating next to the adult in the bedding or pillows. DR. GEETHA DEVDAS, EMERGENCY MEDICINE PHYSICIAN, COOK CHILDREN`S MEDICAL CENTER: Co-sleeping is not something that we recommend. We recommend that babies really have their own bed, crib, or bassinet to sleep in. COSTELLO: Last month, the CDC reported a 15 percent increase of sudden infant death cases among African Americans in 2020 during the pandemic. Providers say multi-generational homes where parents sleep with children and have poor access to health care could be contributing factors. Nationwide, each year, 3400 sleep-related infant deaths. The risk is five to 10 times higher while bed-sharing with an adult even higher on a couch or chair. Tragically, it happened to pediatric cardiologist Sam Hankey in 2010. His 3-week-old son Charlie fell asleep on his chest as Sam also slept. [19:20:30] SAM HANKE, PEDIATRIC CARDIOLOGIST: When I woke up, Charlie never did. And this tragedy is something that happens way too often in our country. COSTELLO: Pediatricians say children should sleep and PJs or sleeping sack flat on their backs on fitted sheets, no blankets, pillows or stuffed animals. Sam hanky and his wife have started Charlie`s Kids. HANKE: What we`ve learned is that we`re not alone in this tragedy. COSTELLO: Teaching safe sleep to prevent another baby from dying. Tom Costello, NBC News, Washington. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And I`ll be back with a remarkable story of forgiveness in this season of renewal. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Finally, tonight, in this season of grace and renewal, we have a remarkable story of forgiveness. It`s a story of a man who was willing to open himself up to the humanity and potential of a stranger who took the life of someone dear to him. [19:25:02] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: I`ve done a lot of interviews with newly released incarcerated people and generally they have been exonerated. That`s not your story. RANDALL BAGLEY, INCARCERATED FOR MURDER: That`s not my story. HOLT: You did it. BAGLEY: I did it. HOLT: You killed a man. BAGLEY: I did. HOLT (voiceover): In 1998, Randall Bagley shot and killed Donald Mitchell during a Maryland robbery. BAGLEY: I turn to say something to him, and the gun went off. HOLT: In an instant, a man robbed of his life and the victim`s young son robbed of a father. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: You`re the Boogeyman. HOLT: Last September, 24 years later, Idris Mitchell spoke in a Maryland court where that man who killed his dad was asking for a second chance, a reduction of his sentence. Audio recordings captured the hearing. IDRIS MITCHELL, SON OF DONALD MITCHELL: You are the nightmare. I`ve never seen you. I never knew what you look like. HOLT: But then, he stunned the courtroom. MITCHELL: I fundamentally, wholly and wholeheartedly forgive you. HOLT: Mitchell asked the judge to release Begley from his life-plus 35 years sentence. When Idris spoke, what was going through your mind? BAGLEY: I thought it was unreal. I thought it was unreal. HOLT: Mitchell even surprised himself. MITCHELL: I didn`t want to say that I forgave him. HOLT: But more than for forgive him, you also called for his release. You said -- MITCHELL: No, that was unexpected. HOLT: It was unexplained. MITCHELL: That was unexpected. I was going to stop there. And I think what changed, and even advocating for his release was again hearing what he had done. HOLT: In Bagley, Mitchell says he found things in common, both high achievers. Mitchell, a Yale grad. Bagley accepted into the first class of Georgetown University `s bachelor degree program for the incarcerated. MITCHELL: Not to be funny, but he had a better GPA than I did at Yale. So, I was like, OK, slightly better. I had a good one. But I think that he simply -- he simply dedicated himself to improvement. HOLT: Mark Howard heads Georgetown`s Prisons and Justice Initiative. MARK HOWARD, DIRECTOR, GEORGETOWN`S PRISON AND JUSTICE INITIATIVE: When he started explaining what happened in that courtroom and also the role that this program had played in his journey of getting him to that point, it was very emotional. HOLT: A judge recently slashed Bagley sentence, and he was released in January. In some ways setting two men free. MITCHELL: You wait 23 years to say something. And then when you do, you find yourself actually advocating for the man who killed your father. That`s not -- I don`t think that`s conventional, but it`s what felt right. HOLT: Did you deserve that level of forgiveness? BAGLEY: I don`t deserve anything. I took a man`s life. I don`t deserve anything. I`m grateful. Happy, but I don`t deserve anything. MITCHELL: Randall, Mr. Bagley, which do you prefer? BAGLEY: Whatever. MITCHELL: Whatever? BAGLEY: Randall, yes. MITCHELL: Randall, OK. Are you OK? BAGLEY: Yes. MITCHELL: OK. BAGLEY: Are you OK? MITCHELL: We`re working on it. We`re working on it. BAGLEY: Idris. MITCHELL: So, what`s going on? BAGLEY: I`m still trying to process it. HOLT: And as they recently met for the first time, one question lingered in the air -- why? BAGLEY: What made you do it when you could have said so many other things other than I forgive you? MITCHELL: Because I -- because I think people can change, all right. People can change. You`re 22. It`s been 24 years. BAGLEY: It takes a lot to do what you`re doing. It takes a lot. It takes a lot. MITCHELL: I appreciate that. BAGLEY: Takes a lot, bro. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: A powerful moment of healing. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Friday. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: Abortion Rights Activists Vowing To Fight, Others Celebrate The Rule, As The Biden Administration Says It Will Appeal
story_text: JOSE DIAZ-BALART: President Biden is vowing to fight the Texas ruling. It`s the beginning of what`s expected to be yet another contentious round of court battles over abortion. Monica Alba reports from the White House. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MONICA ALBA, NBC NEWS WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: The battle over abortion rights could again be headed for the Supreme Court, with the Department of Justice planning to appeal the Texas ruling that would jeopardize access to the most commonly used abortion pill, setting up a legal showdown, less than a year after the court overturned Roe v. Wade. [18:35:07] President Biden vowed to fight the decision, writing Friday, if it were to stand, there will be virtually no prescription approved by the FDA that would be safe from these kinds of political ideological attacks. The Texas case now goes to the conservative Fifth Circuit, but in the short term, the drug is still available. It`s unclear whether the Washington State ruling which asks for the medication to be kept on the market will also be appealed. If both are heard at the circuit level, it`s unlikely this will be resolved in the courts anytime soon. CAROL LAM , FORMER SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA U.S. ATTORNEY: I would not expect there to be much change in the actual law for at least several months, perhaps upwards of a year. ALBA: With the Supreme Court, which currently has a conservative majority watching to see how that plays out. LAM: What is most likely to happen is that there will be a split in the circuits. So the Fifth Circuit will rule one way, the Ninth Circuit will rule a different way. And the Supreme Court will say now there is a conflict between two circuits. And that means we should probably hear this case and decide the issue on the merits. ALBA: As Vice President Harris, who has been the administration`s leading voice on abortion access, slammed the Texas decision as a dangerous precedent. KAMALA HARRIS , U.S. VICE PRESIDENT: There is no question that the President and I are going to stand with the women of America. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And Monica joins us now from the White House. What else Monica, could the Biden administration do here? ALBA: Well, the Justice Department could file an emergency appeal with the High Court, while it also tries to get the Texas order blocked by the Fifth Circuit, a strategic call that likely will become apparent in the next week or so. Jose? DIAZ-BALART: Monica Alba at the White House, thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. headline: Major Fallout After A Federal Judge Suspends Approval Of The Commonly Used Abortion Pill Set To Begin Within Day
story_text: [18:30:17] JOSE DIAZ-BALART, NBC NEWS HOST: Tonight, major fallout after a federal judge suspends approval of the commonly used abortion pill set to begin within day. Abortion rights activists vowing to fight, others celebrate the rule, as the Biden administration says it will appeal. New confusion today after another judge rules in favor of the pill. Will the Supreme Court decide the issue? Is their mole in the Pentagon? The race to find out who may be leaking top secret intelligence, the Department of Justice and Pentagon now investigate. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: They put ourselves at risk, they put our allies at risk. DIAZ-BALART: China`s major escalation launching massive military drills off Taiwan`s coast just as U.S. lawmakers visit the island. Our correspondent is there. Gunfire at the beach, six people shot most of them teenagers enjoying a senior skip day. Video so the chaotic moments shots were fired. Terrifying new footage of trees falling at the Masters are these the luckiest people on earth. Watch his three trees just barely missed them. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Trees are falling off of the ground. DIAZ-BALART: Why play was halted again today. And the need for speed. The new push across the country to raise the speed limit. How fast is too fast. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Jose Diaz-Balart. DIAZ-BALART: Good evening, a new front has opened to the nation`s ongoing battle over abortion rights. Not even a year after Roe v. Wade was overturned leaving it up to the states to determine whether abortions are legal. A federal judge issued a ruling that would halt the use of the commonly used abortion pill nationwide. The decision came down late on a Friday of a holiday weekend. But the reaction today was swift with some small protests across the country. The suspension doesn`t go into effect for seven days. And the Biden administration is vowing to stop it. The case seems destined to rocket up the legal system possibly all the way to the Supreme Court. We have two reports tonight beginning with Dasha Burns, who has been with activists on both sides. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Tonight activist outraged over a Texas judge`s ruling late Friday, suspending the FDA approval of the abortion pill Mifeprex generically known as mifepristone. Judge Matthew Kacsmaryk writing in his opinion, the court does not second guess the FDA`s decision making lightly. But here the FDA acquiesced on its legitimate safety concerns. But he stopped short of an immediate nationwide ban, instead allowing the federal government seven days to appeal the decision. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is an assault on the humanity of women. This is an assault on basic reproductive rights. It`s also an assault on democracy. BURNS: The outcomes celebrated by the plaintiffs. ERIK BAPTIST, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM LEAD ATTORNEY: This is a significant victory for the doctors and medical associations we represent. And more importantly, the health and safety of women and girls. BURNS: We sat down with Alliance Defending Freedom before the ruling the conservative group behind the lawsuit that was also instrumental in overturning Roe v. Wade. BAPTIST: The goal of this lawsuit is to protect American women and girls from dangerous chemical abortion drugs. It`s not we are not seeking a nationwide abortion ban. BURNS: The drug has been approved by the FDA since 2000. Since then, more than 5 million women have taken mifepristone with 28 deaths associated with the drug reported. It`s the most common method for terminating pregnancies in the U.S. But just minutes after the Texas ruling came down a federal judge in Washington State dropped a contradictory decision protecting access to the abortion pill in 17 states and Washington D.C., the dueling rulings now so in chaos and confusion across the country. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And Dasha joins us now from New York City`s Washington Square Park where, Dasha, a small group of protesters have gathered? BURNS: That`s right, Jose. Activists here and nationwide criticizing the judges timing, the ruling coming ahead of a holiday weekend. Still protesters here telling me the stakes are too high to stay home as this decision could impact abortion access here in New York and nationwide. Jose? DIAZ-BALART: Dasha Burns in New York. Thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. headline: Meet the Press for April 9, 2023, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:00:00] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CHUCK TODD, NBC HOST (voice over): This Sunday, the abortion legal wars. A Texas federal judge suspends FDA approval for the abortion pill Mifepristone. Another in Washington State directly contradicts him, setting up a likely Supreme Court standoff on the abortion bill. MIKE PENCE, (R) FORMER VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: The FDA went beyond their legislative authority. REP. ALEXANDRIA OCASIO-CORTEZ (D-NY): The contents of this judge`s ruling is frankly shocking. TODD (voice over): As the abortion issue gives liberals their first majority in the Wisconsin Supreme Court in 15 years. REP. GLORIA JOHNSON (D-TN): Everything we care about is on the line. TODD (voice over): Wisconsin, just the latest in a string of statewide defeats on the abortion issue for the GOP. Is anyone in the party going to listen to voters? Plus, lawmakers expelled. Two Black lawmakers are ousted by the Tennessee Legislature after protesting on the House floor for stricter gun laws. JUSTIN JONES (D), FORMER TENNESSEE STATE REPRESENTATIVE: We called for you all to ban assault weapons, and you respond with an assault on democracy. CAMERON SEXTON, (R) SPEAKER OF THE TENNESSEE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES: They had a protest against House policy. TODD (voice over): The effort to expel a third Democrat failed. JOHNSON: I was a (inaudible) white lady. I don`t know what else it was. TODD (voice over): I`ll talk to the two ousted lawmakers, Justin Jones and Justin Pearson. And Trump charge -- ALVIN BRAGG , MANHATTAN DISTRICT ATTORNEY: These are felony crimes in New York State, no matter who you are. TODD (voice over): As the New York case progresses, it`s the probe into his mishandling of classified documents that may put Trump in greater legal jeopardy. I`ll talk to one of Trump`s attorneys in that case, James Trusty. And finally, defying China. My exclusive interview with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Mike McCaul as he wraps up his own trip to the Island of Taiwan. Joining me for insight and analysis are NBC News Senior Legal Correspondent Laura Jarrett; Amna Nawaz, co-anchor of PBS NewsHour; Republican Strategist Brendan Buck; and Symone Sanders Townsend, Former Chief Spokesperson for Vice President Kamala Harris . Welcome to Sunday. It`s `Meet The Press`. (END VIDEOTAPE) ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest-running show in television history, this is `Meet The Press` with Chuck Todd. TODD: And a good Sunday morning, Happy Easter, Passover and Ramadan. The spring holidays are here. Pope Francis presided over a crowded mass this morning in Vatican City, St. Peter`s Square. He is, of course, in a wheelchair right now after his release from the hospital a week ago. But he did ride through the crowd on this Easter Sunday morning to the cheers of many. But despite the celebrations this morning, let`s be honest, this was no ordinary holiday week. In fact, come November of 2024, let me look back at this week as the most consequential to the future of the Republican Party and to our overall electoral politics, from the dueling abortion rulings Friday night to overt partisan warfare in Tennessee. Ironically, the least consequential event may very well be the former president`s legal troubles, at least the Manhattan case, though it`s still important obviously. But what`s happened this week in Texas, in that courtroom in Wisconsin at that ballot box and in Tennessee in that State House may reverberate the most in our political culture as a widening divide corrodes our institutions from our State Houses to the courts. The national divide was crystallized on Friday night in those dueling abortion rules. Less than an hour apart on specifically the abortion pill over (ph) federal judges, these are legal efforts that were pushed by the political activists, seeking a decision by the Supreme Court. There was no actual medical event, no misuse of this pill to trigger this look at the drug. It was simply political activism. BUCK: Yeah. We`ve made a deal with this part of the party for a very long time and made a lot of promises. And I think a lot of people -- look at it in a political sense, there are a lot of people who firmly believe that this is the right moral position to have and so you can`t just walk away from that. But if you take a bigger picture look at it, the politics of it are devastating for us. We can`t win without them. But obviously, winning with them is coming at a significant cost. TODD: Symone, feels like a long way away, remember when Joe Biden`s abortion position was getting questioned -- SYMONE SANDERS-TOWNSEND, MSNBC HOST, "SYMONE": Oh my, goodness. TODD: --by Democratic activists in the primary? SANDERS-TOWNSEND: I remember vividly. I think I was there -- TODD: I guess we`re a long way away from that. SANDERS-TOWNSEND: Very long way away, Chuck. Look, I think what Brendan said should be underscored here because for a very long time, this is what the Republican Party apparatus organized around. They did not organize around jailing women for getting an abortion, fining and jailing, potentially jailing doctors. They did not organize around forcing girls to have babies by their rapists. But that is exactly what is happening because of the positions they have advocated for. So when "The Wall Street Journal" says, they`ve got to get their position straight with the voters, I`m confused and don`t understand because I think they`ve been quite clear on what their position is. TODD: Well, I think that`s the problem though, isn`t it? BUCK: Yeah. We said that we were going to send this back to the states because we were going to have some reasonable limitations on abortion. And now state by state doesn`t look very reasonable and we are at the mercy of a bunch of state legislatures. And there`s not a very good way to run a party. TODD: Speaking of being at the mercy of the local state legislatures, this situation in Tennessee, Symone, look, there are loud echoes from our recent past in the south and in the `60s. [09:30:02] But this also feels like the inevitable moment that you have when you have these gerrymandered super-majorities that have become calcified. SANDERS-TOWNSEND: Absolutely. TODD: Because this is what it felt like: a whole bunch of people who just don`t deal with dissent. SANDERS-TOWNSEND: Absolutely. I mean, look, I was down in Nashville. I spoke with the Tennessee Three and state legislators there. What is happening in Tennessee, and frankly across the South, is in fact Jim Crow. What Jim Crow was blocking Black people from the ability to have participation in their government, disenfranchising lawmakers. And it`s again -- it`s not just Tennessee. Look at what`s happening in Mississippi coming into Jackson and the state legislature stepping in. Look at what`s -- Governor Abbott in Texas. Look at what`s happening in Florida. This is an all out assault. TODD: Government Abbott -- I know we wanted to be quick, and I appreciate you doing that with time -- but he looks like he`s okay if there`s a pardon of a Travis County, a blue county, prosecution, a murder conviction of a Black Lives Matter protester. SANDERS-TOWNSEND: He put out a statement and said, I welcome the pardon on my desk so I can sign it. And so it is an assault. And I think these young people, young state legislators, who stood up, they have galvanized the movement. TODD: Brendan, not a single national Republican leader has supported what Tennessee has done. It is no doubt in my mind the silence is at least sending a message of, oh my God, that looks terrible, but I don`t think it`s helping the party`s image. BUCK: No. I mean, what do they do? I mean, this happened in Congress in 2016. We had a sit-in where Democrats took over the House floor and we had members who wanted us to arrest them, wanted us to arrest John Lewis on the House floor. But you realize that`s a bad look. And here`s another situation where you have a statue legislature who is defining the party. No one is in charge. And there`s no consequences for any of these legislatures. As you said, their districts are such that they`re not going to be voted out because they did this -- TODD: Half of them didn`t face any opponent, Brendan. Half of them didn`t face any opponent at all. It`s stunning. BUCK: Yeah. Well, this is again a situation where there`s no infrastructure. There`s nobody calling the shots. We are being defined as extreme and it`s why Republicans are on the run in just about everywhere across the country. TODD: All right. When we come back, despite the widening partisan divide, there is one area this week where U.S. lawmakers were unified, and intentionally so -- defying China`s display of military force in Taiwan. Despite the domestic political divisions on full display this week, the effort that the United States made this week to show a united front on Taiwan was extraordinary, when you think about it, as lawmakers at home and abroad met with Taiwan`s president and promised a U.S. commitment to the island`s security. It was bipartisan. MCCAUL: We have every right to be here, to meet with President Tsai. And it actually strengthens our resolve. TODD: The Taiwanese themselves seem to be downplaying this. And, and secondly is the combat training that is occurring on the island. We need to ramp that up to a larger scale so they can provide that projection of strength and deterrence. They`re not where they need to be right now. TODD: Do you have a sense of what the Taiwanese people want? And I say that in that we know pre-sort of what China did before it took over Hong Kong, it was always this sense that you know, a lot of people in Taiwan wanted some sort of relationship with mainland China that was negotiated, that was sort of respectful. Is that what they still want? Or do they think some sort of military confrontation is now going to be inevitable? MCCAUL: Well, they don`t want a military confrontation. We certainly don`t want that. I think after Hong Kong, it was a wake-up call for the people of Taiwan. President Tsai, we spoke with her today. That obviously helped her in her re-election. headline: The Beginning Of What Is Set To Be The Biggest Battle Over Abortion Rights Since The Overturning Of Roe V. Wade
story_text: [18:30:00] KATE SNOW, NBC NIGHTLY NEWS ANCHOR: Tonight, the beginning of what is set to be the biggest battle over abortion rights since the overturning of Roe v. Wade. Protests over a judge`s ruling that would halt the use of the abortion pill. Some healthcare providers are now stockpiling the drug. The Biden administration vowing today to fight the decision as some Democrats call on the president to simply not enforce any ban. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Everything is on the table. (END VIDEO CLIP) SNOW: Political firestorm in Tennessee. Why at least one of the Democratic lawmakers expelled by Republicans there may be back in his seat tomorrow. Stand-off at sea. Navy ships from Taiwan and China face off as China launches massive war games, including this simulation showing how they could strike the island. Growing violence in the Middle East. Israel attacked by rockets from inside Syria. The retaliation tonight. Should this convicted killer walk free? The governor of Texas vows to pardon a U.S. army sergeant who shot a Black Lives Matter protester. Tiger Woods drops out of the Masters with another injury. New questions tonight about his future in the sport. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: That is not easy to see. (END VIDEO CLIP) SNOW: On this Easter Sunday, the pope`s message to the world just a week after leaving the hospital. ANNOUNCER: This is "NBC Nightly News with Kate Snow." SNOW: Good evening and Happy Easter to you. The decision from a federal judge in Texas Friday is still reverberating as we head into a new week. That judge suspended the FDA`s approval of the abortion pill. The president has vowed his administration will fight that decision. Any appeal must be filed by Friday. The pills are already banned in 13 states that have made abortion illegal. If this ruling were to hold up, the pills would then be banned nationwide. The anti-abortion groups that brought the lawsuit argue the drug is not safe. The White House says if a judge can overrule the FDA on this medication, any judge could ban any drug. We begin tonight with Allie Raffa. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) ALLIE RAFFA, NBC NEWS WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, battle lines drawn. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I am very worried about women who need this medication. AMY O`DONNELL, TEXAS ALLIANCE FOR LIFE COMMUNICATIONS DIRECTOR: We applaud the judge`s action to issue the stay on the chemical abortion drug, mifepristone. RAFFA (voiceover): After the most consequential abortion ruling since the reversal of Roe v. Wade, a Texas federal judge suspending FDA approval of the most commonly used abortion pill, giving the federal government seven days to appeal before the ruling goes into effect. XAVIER BECERRA , U.S. SECRETARY OF HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES: We intend to do everything to make sure it`s available to them, not just in a week but moving forward, period. RAFFA (voiceover): Reporter: the health and human services secretary, Xavier Becerra , vowing the Biden administration is considering all legal options. BECERRA: Well, we`ve already filed an appeal of this court`s ruling. RAFFA (voiceover): The issue will likely be decided by the Supreme Court after a federal judge in Washington State ruled to protect the drug in more than a dozen states. One Republican lawmaker threatening cuts to FDA funding if the White House fights the Texas ruling. REP. TONY GONZALES (R-TX): It may become a point where House Republicans on the appropriations side have to defund FDA programs that don`t make sense. RAFFA (voiceover): Some healthcare providers are now stockpiling the pill, fearing an all-out ban. While some Democrats urge the Biden administration to go even further. REP. ALEXANDRIA OCASIO-CORTEZ (D-NY): I believe that the Biden administration should ignore this ruling. It is up to the Biden administration to enforce, to choose whether to enforce such a ruling. RAFFA (voiceover): HSS secretary, Becerra, not committing to that specific option. BECERRA: Every option is on the table. (END VIDEO CLIP) SNOW: And Allie joins us now from the White House. Allie, will the drug still be available as this case makes its way through the courts? RAFFA (on camera): Well, legal experts say the drug will likely remain available as these cases make their way through the courts, a process that could take months, possibly even years, Kate. SNOW: All right. Allie Raffa at the White House for us, thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: The Future Of The Pill Used For More Than Two Decades Uncertain After Competing Rulings By Two Federal Judges
story_text: LESTER HOLT: This evening, the divide over abortion is centered on a pill used for more than 20 years. But now the focus of competing rulings by two federal courts. Dasha Burns reports and the growing fallout. [19:05:07] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the fallout from dueling court rulings. The future of the abortion pill is hanging in the balance after a Texas judge invalidated the FDA`s approval of mifepristone. The Department of Justice is now appealing that decision. JENNIFER KLEIN, WHITE HOUSE GENDER POLICY COUNCIL: What this ruling effectively is a backdoor ban on abortion. BURNS: What options are available to the administration here? KLEIN: We`ve been waiting for the judge to rule. And what we did is what we believe is the best strategy which is to appeal this decision immediately. BURNS: Minutes after the Texas judge`s decision on Friday night, a federal judge in Washington State with equal authority dropping a contradictory ruling ordering the FDA to maintain access to the drug. It all sowed confusion nationwide and created a legal standoff. Use with another drug, mifepristone is the most common method for terminating pregnancies in the U.S. It`s been approved since 2000 and used safely more than five million times. But the plaintiffs in the Texas case, a group of anti-abortion doctors and medical organizations, allege the drug is dangerous and the FDA didn`t follow proper protocol when approving it. I spoke with the group behind the lawsuit before the ruling. The result if you win is that abortion access will be significantly limited. Is that the goal of this loss? ERIK BAPTIST, SENIOR COUNSEL, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM: No, the goal of this lawsuit is to protect American women and girls from dangerous chemical abortion drugs. It`s not -- we are not seeking a nationwide abortion ban. BURNS: Meanwhile, today, lawmakers in blue states vowed to do whatever necessary to protect reproductive rights. GOV. MAURA HEALEY (D-MA): It harms patients, undermines medical expertise, and takes away freedom. BURNS: Tonight, Mifepristone remains legal as the battles rage on in the courts. Dasha Burns, NBC News . (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Let me bring in now Senior Legal Correspondent Laura Jarrett. Laura, there was movement on both of these cases in court today. LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): A flurry of court filings today, Lester. The Justice Department and the pill manufacturer both hoping to convince a conservative-leaning court of appeals to hit pause on that Texas decision, to give everyone time to make their arguments without this deadline looming of the ruling set to go into effect on Saturday. The court just minutes ago asking to hear what the plaintiffs have to say about all that, but the FDA also wants Clarity from a federal judge in Washington State who ordered the drug to stay on the market about how to reconcile that order with the Texas ruling. HOLT: This feels like this could be heading to the Supreme Court. JARRETT: Yes, it really could, and fast. If the Fifth Circuit doesn`t block the Texas decision, the DOJ will take it to the Supreme Court as soon as this week. And if DOJ wins, the plaintiffs could appeal there as well. HOLT: All right, Laura, thanks very much. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc.
