It all sowed confusion nationwide and created a legal standoff. Use with another drug, mifepristone is the most common method for terminating pregnancies in the U.S. It`s been approved since 2000 and used safely more than five million times. But the plaintiffs in the Texas case, a group of anti-abortion doctors and medical organizations, allege the drug is dangerous and the FDA didn`t follow proper protocol when approving it. I spoke with the group behind the lawsuit before the ruling. The result if you win is that abortion access will be significantly limited. Is that the goal of this loss? ERIK BAPTIST, SENIOR COUNSEL, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM: No, the goal of this lawsuit is to protect American women and girls from dangerous chemical abortion drugs. It`s not -- we are not seeking a nationwide abortion ban. BURNS: Meanwhile, today, lawmakers in blue states vowed to do whatever necessary to protect reproductive rights. GOV. MAURA HEALEY (D-MA): It harms patients, undermines medical expertise, and takes away freedom. BURNS: Tonight, mifepristone remains legal as the battles rage on in the courts. Dasha Burns, NBC News . (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Let me bring in now Senior Legal Correspondent Laura Jarrett. Laura, there was movement on both of these cases in court today. LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): A flurry of court filings today, Lester. The Justice Department and the pill manufacturer both hoping to convince a conservative-leaning court of appeals to hit pause on that Texas decision, to give everyone time to make their arguments without this deadline looming of the ruling set to go into effect on Saturday. The court just minutes ago asking to hear what the plaintiffs have to say about all that, but the FDA also wants Clarity from a federal judge in Washington State who ordered the drug to stay on the market about how to reconcile that order with the Texas ruling. HOLT: This feels like this could be heading to the Supreme Court. JARRETT: Yes, it really could, and fast. If the Fifth Circuit doesn`t block the Texas decision, the DOJ will take it to the Supreme Court as soon as this week. And if DOJ wins, the plaintiffs could appeal there as well. HOLT: All right, Laura, thanks very much. I want to turn now to that political drama in Tennessee. Late today, the Nashville Council voting to reinstate one of the Black state lawmakers expelled last week over a gun protest. Kathy Park reports he has just been sworn in again. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Thank you, vice mayor. I would like to nominate Representative Justin Jones. KATHY PARK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, a political showdown in Nashville. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Ayes 36. PARK: With former Tennessee lawmaker Justin Jones back to the state house just days after his expulsion. The Metro Nashville Council voted unanimously in favor of his reappointment. FREDDIE O`CONNELL, MEMBER, METROPOLITAN NASHVILLE COUNCIL DISTRICT 19: This is a message that partisanship has gone so far as to be a force in violating basic principles of democracy. PARK: This special meeting comes after a rare move by House Republicans to remove three Democratic lawmakers after they joined a gun control rally on the House floor which Republicans say violated the rules. CAMERON SEXTON (R-TN), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: You can call it peaceful, you can call it whatever, but they had a protest against house policy on the floor. JUSTIN JONES (D-TN), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: No action -- CROWD: No peace! PARK: Among the Tennessee three, only one survived the vote, Gloria Johnson. GLORIA JOHNSON (D-TN), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: It might have to do with the color of our skin. GOP leaders say their decision was not based on race but that Johnson didn`t go as far as her two freshman colleagues. CROWD: No justice, no peace! PARK: Representative Justin Pearson will learn his fate Wednesday in his own district with a special meeting in Memphis. Meanwhile, the political battle doesn`t end for Jones as he awaits a special election and he`s vowing to return. (END VIDEOTAPE) PARK (on camera): And moments after the critical vote to reappoint Justin Jones, hundreds of his supporters began rushing out of the metro council chambers and began marching straight toward the state capitol. Lester? HOLT: All right, Kathy Park, thank you. There is growing concern tonight about whether U.S. intelligence sources were compromised by the leak of dozens of classified documents. Andrea Mitchell has the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF FOREIGN AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The leaked documents include sensitive and top secret intelligence about U.S. adversaries and allies potentially jeopardizing U.S. spies in hostile countries and electronic surveillance. JOHN KIRBY, STRATEGIC COMMUNICATIONS COORDINATOR, NATIONAL SECURITY COUNCIL: We don`t know uh who`s responsible for this and we don`t know if they have more that they intend to post. [19:10:07] MITCHELL: The documents show Ukraine running low on ammunition and using U.S. intelligence to strike a Russian target. Russia`s military is struggling in Ukraine. South Korea reluctant to help the U.S. supply artillery to Ukraine. Is the worst damage the Russian sources and methods behind the inside information from Russia on the defense ministry? JOHN BRENNAN, FORMER DIRECTOR, CIA: I think the greatest concern is that some of our sources both human as well as technical collection systems could be compromised as a result of this. Another document has the leaders of Israel`s intelligence service, the Mossad , backing anti-government protests though Israel denies it. RON DERMER, MINISTER FOR STRATEGIC AFFAIRS, ISRAEL: The senior director of the Mossad and our senior officials in the Mossad were not involved in any way. MITCHELL: The stolen intelligence first showing up on a chat server for the Minecraft video game according to open-source intelligence agency Bellingcat before appearing on other sites. The slides showing conflicting Russian casualties in Ukraine indicate some of the documents could have been doctored but officials believe most are real. (END VIDEOTAPE) MITCHELL (on camera): The Justice Department is investigating to find the source as officials fear the leak has exposed critical vulnerabilities in U.S. intelligence. Lester? HOLT: And Andrea, separately, there`s news tonight about that Wall Street Journal reporter detained in Russia. What can you tell us? MITCHELL: That`s right, Lester. Secretary of State Blinken has determined the reporter Evan Gershkovich is wrongfully detained falsely charged with spying. Now, the U.S. hostage envoy can begin working with his family to try to get him out. But in violation of Russia`s legal obligations, U.S. diplomats had still not been able to visit him almost two weeks since he was jailed. Lester? HOLT: All right, Andrea Mitchell, thank you. Former President Donald Trump is trying to block Former Vice President Mike Pence from testifying before a federal grand jury investigating Mr. Trump`s rule in efforts to overturn the 2020 election. Lawyers for Trump are asking a federal appeals court to reverse a lower court`s decision ordering Pence to appear. With nearly 600 days until the next election, President Joe Biden turned heads today with an admission on live T.V. that he plans to run again. Kristen Welker joins us from the White House. Kristen, the timing came as a bit of a surprise. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (on camera): That`s absolutely right, Lester. President Biden making his most definitive comments yet that he`s running for reelection in 2024, talking to our Al Roker during the annual White House Easter Egg Roll. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) AL ROKER, NBC NEWS WEATHER ANCHOR: Help a -- help a brother out. Make some news for me. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: .No, no, no. I plan on running now but we`re not prepared to announce it yet. (END VIDEO CLIP) WELKER: Top White House advisors are preparing to make final decisions on launching his re-election campaign according to several sources familiar with the discussions. Several considerations include no major Democratic Challenger has emerged despite Mr. Biden`s sagging poll numbers. Former President Trump who`s running for the GOP nomination has been indicted and is consuming the political spotlight. Still, source familiar with President Biden`s thinking tell NBC News, don`t expect to hear a final announcement until possibly next month, if not later. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker at the White House tonight, thanks. In 60 seconds, a grand jury indicts the mother of a six-year-old boy who shot his teacher in a Virginia classroom. The charges she faces tonight plus what her legal team is saying. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: A Virginia grand jury has indicted the mother of that 6-year-old boy who brought a gun to his school and shot his teacher. Miguel Almaguer reports on the charges she now faces. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I have a report of a teacher shot. MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, three months after the shocking school shooting, the mother of the 6-year- old Virginia boy who shot and seriously wounded his first-grade teacher is facing criminal charges. Today, a grand jury in Newport News indicting 25- year-old Deja Taylor on charges of felony child neglect and a misdemeanor count of recklessly leaving a loaded firearm so as to endanger a child. GEORGE PARKER, FORMER SUPERINTENDENT, NEWPORT NEWS PUBLIC SCHOOLS: Who would be prepared for a 6-year-old to bring a loaded weapon onto school or a weapon on the school. [19:15:06] ALMAGUER: After authorities announced the 6-year-old would not be charged with a crime, the Commonwealth`s Attorney saying today every criminal case is unique in its facts and these facts support these charges, but our investigation into the shooting continues. ABIGAIL ZWERNER, TEACHER: I just will never forget the look on his face that he gave me while he pointed the gun directly at me. That`s something that I will never forget. It`s changed me. It`s changed my life. ALMAGUER: Abigail Zwerner who told Savannah Guthrie the bullet still remains lodged in her body is suing School administrators for $40 million alleging gross negligence. Zwerner said staff failed to act on several warnings that the 6-year-old had a gun or made threats. There were failures in accountability at multiple levels that led to Abby being shot and almost killed, writes her attorney. We will not allow school leaders to escape accountability for their role in this tragedy. (END VIDEOTAPE) ALMAGUER (on camera): A lawyer for Deja Taylor, the mother of the 6-year- old, tells NBC News she plans to turn herself in later this week. Lester? HOLT: All right, Miguel, thank you. Up next, she was the target of an Internet conspiracy theory claiming she had died after getting vaccinated. Now, for the first time, Tiffany Dover speaks out. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Few Americans know what it`s like to be the target of a conspiracy theory. But since the day nurse Tiffany Dover fainted while getting her COVID vaccine, life has never been the same. And tonight, she`s speaking out for the first time in an exclusive interview with NBC`s Brandy Zadrozny. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BRANDY ZADROZNY, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tiffany Dover wants the world to know one thing. TIFFANY DOVER, NURSE: My message is simple it is that I am alive. I`m well. ZADROZNY: That`s it? DOVER: I hope they believe it. ZADROZNY: They are the massive online community of conspiracy theorists who`ve been convinced she`s dead for more than two years. I made a whole podcast about it. Tiffany wasn`t ready to share her story then, but now -- DOVER: I`m ready to just put my story out there, all my story. ZADROZNY: That story begins in 2020. Tiffany was working as a nurse manager at CHI Memorial Hospital in Chattanooga, putting in grueling hours on a COVID unit. When vaccines arrived that December, Tiffany became one of the first people at her hospital to get the shot. DOVER: I felt OK during that. ZADROZNY: Then she stood up to answer questions. DOVER: I`m sorry. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: You want to sit down? DOVER: I ended up passing out. So, that created the opposite effect of what I would have wanted. ZADROZNY: But you got right back up. DOVER: I did. And this is something that`s happened to me my whole life. I do have episodes where I pass out. ZADROZNY: But in that moment, a conspiracy theory was born. DOVER: People thought that I was dead. People thought that I was an actress paid to do this, that I was paid off by a big firm. It was completely overwhelming to be honest. ZADROZNY: It snowballed fast. DOVER: I had people showing up at my house. I had people reaching out to my friends, to my family. I`ve been -- received death threats. ZADROZNY: Were you afraid for your family? DOVER: Absolutely, yes. ZADROZNY: Through it all, Tiffany kept silent. And that only made the online frenzy worse. Why not come out and dispel these rumors? DOVER: Initially that was exactly what I wanted to do. And unfortunately, I was told that that absolutely would not happen. ZADROZNY: The hospital told you not to speak out. DOVER: Correct. Yes, it would be irrecoverable damage is what I was told if I was to speak out and have another episode. ZADROZNY: Instead, the hospital put out this video intending to show she was alive. But the so-called Tiffany Truthers picked it apart and used it as fuel. Online, anti-vaxxers and the movement are sort of using you as their poster girl. DOVER: It`s hard to think that you are being used to detour somebody from getting the vaccine. And that was really hard for me to cope with. ZADROZNY: Are you saying you blamed yourself? DOVER: Yes, absolutely. I wish that we would have used it as a platform to speak out on the fact that people do pass out after getting shots, vaccines, but that is not a reason to not proceed with getting them. ZADROZNY: CHI Memorial has repeatedly denied knowledge of any directive asking Tiffany not to speak or post, including in an interview for our podcast. KAREN LONG, MEDICA COMMUNICATIONS SPECIALIST, CHI MEMORIAL: I`m not aware of anything that asked Tiffany not to respond. ZADROZNY: The hospital recently telling NBC News we have no new information. A year ago, Tiffany left CHI Memorial. and while she hopes to work as a nurse again one day, for now, she`s focused on reclaiming her life. Even after all of this, there will be people who say, we don`t believe you. What then? DOVER: At this point, you know, I`ve done what I needed to do. I`ve put it out there that I`m alive. They have to choose whether they believe that or not. And that`s all I can do is put out the truth. ZADROZNY: Brandy Zadrozny, NBC News Higdon, Alabama. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And for the bonus podcast, scan the Q.R. code on your screen or search for Tiffany Dover wherever you get your podcasts. When we come back, a masterful performance by one of golf`s rising stars. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: It`s not often you see a 23-year-old compete at the Masters, let alone outplay some of the best golfers on the planet. Stephanie Gosk with why Sam Bennett is inspiring America. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) STEPHANIE GOSK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Sometimes, the significance of the moment can be lost on the young, but not this moment. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Nothing can top this at 18. GOSK: The magic of a standing ovation at the masters on a Sunday is not lost on amateur, Sam Bennett. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: He`s overwhelmed with emotion. GOSK: The Texas A&M senior was greeted by his mother to celebrate a remarkable 16th-place finish for someone his age at Augusta National, one of the most difficult golf courses in the world. SAM BENNETT, GOLFER: I haven`t had a kid yet, so that walk up to 18 was definitely the coolest experience of my life. GOSK: Bennett stunned golf fans with his first two rounds of the tournament, shooting back-to-back 68s. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: What a start for the amateur. GOSK: Not just making the cut, the second-best start for a masters in amateur history. At the end of the day on Friday, he was alone in third place paired up with pro golfer Jon Rahm who went on to win the whole thing. BENNETT: If you would have told me I was going to be here when I was a kid, I would have -- I would have thought you were crazy. GOSK: For inspiration, Bennett has a tattoo, words from his father who died from early-onset Alzheimer`s in 2021. Don`t wait to do something, it says, right there on his left arm every time he swings. Stephanie Gosk, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Monday. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. headline: The Battle Over An Abortion Pill: Big Pharma Pushing Back Against The Ruling As Some States Start Stockpiling Drugs
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Major backlash tonight from the drug industry to that abortion pill ruling by a federal judge. And now, some states are stockpiling abortion drugs as the legal battle plays out. Laura Jarrett has the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): A show of force from big pharma now waiting into the battle over a widely used abortion pill. More than 600 drug makers and biotech leaders signing on to a scathing condemnation of that ruling by a federal judge in Texas invalidating the FDA`s longtime approval of mifepristone, accusing the judge of activism. DR. AMANDA BANKS, FORMER CEO, BLACKFYNN THERAPEUTICS: Now -- it`s now been shown that courts can step in and overturn a scientific decision. Dr. Amanda Banks, a former CEO of Blackfynn Therapeutics, who co-authored the letter says the judge`s ruling sets a dangerous precedent that extends beyond the abortion issue. BANKS: If one medicine is subject to this kind of outcome, really any medicine is. JARRETT: President Biden also slamming the decision today. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: My thoughts are completely out of bounds what the judge did. JARRETT: While the anti-abortion group that filed the Texas lawsuit is doubling down. Writing in a statement, "The FDA failed to abide by its legal obligations to protect the health, safety, and welfare of girls and women." With the Texas order is set to go into effect early Saturday unless blocked in the courts, Democratic governors are not wasting any time taking matters into their own hands. GOV. GRETCHEN WHITMER (D-MI): We`re taking a close look at all of our options. JARRETT: Massachusetts, Washington State, New York, and California all now stockpiling years` worth of mifepristone or an alternative abortion pill. GOV. KATHY HOCHUL (D-NY): So, I`m proud to announce that New York State will create a stockpile of misoprostol, another form of medication abortion. JARRETT: It`s all in preparation for a decision that would apply nationwide. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: So, Laura, where does all these stand right now as far as the courts are concerned? JARRETT (on camera): So, late tonight and tomorrow, we should see more court filings from both the plaintiffs that filed the Texas lawsuit and the Justice Department, which is asking the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals to freeze that judge`s order. Once all those are in midday tomorrow, we could see a decision from that appeals court anytime. HOLT: All right, Laura Jarrett, thanks very much. In 60 seconds, the tough new auto emission standard is about to be announced. Will they push more Americans toward electric vehicles. Plus, spring is here and already setting some record temperatures in a lot of cities, next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Spring is here but much of the country is seeing record highs temperatures in places like Phoenix, and Las Vegas, even South Dakota hit the 90s. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for April 11, 2023, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the terrifying images just released of a Louisville mass shooting. (voiceover): Police body camera video showing how officers confronted the gunman who police say ambush them after shooting and killing five of his fellow bank workers using an AR-15 he bought legally. One officer shot at and getting back off to reengage. Officers being hailed as heroes for stopping him from killing more people. Were there warning signs and what his neighbors are saying? Damage control. New revelations from those leaked classified intelligence documents putting U.S. alliances in question. The Manhattan district attorney sues a top House Republican claiming interference in the investigation of Donald Trump . The battle over an abortion pill. Big pharma pushing back against the ruling as some states start stockpiling drugs. Tough new auto emission standards about to be announced, but will they push more Americans to go electric. A big upside of artificial intelligence detecting cancer much earlier and predicting when it might strike. And the young bold athletes sharing their culture and moves with skateboarding superstar Tony Hawk . ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening and welcome. Once again in the tragic aftermath of a mass shooting, we`re getting a heart-stopping first person look at police risking their own lives to stop and active shooter. Late this afternoon, Louisville police releasing body cam video of officers rushing to a downtown bank yesterday. Immediately coming under fire from a bank employee. He was armed with an AR-15 assault-style rifle carrying out a murderous rampage, fatally shooting five people. The gunman killed by police. Tonight, one of those officers who rushed to stop the gunman, a rookie just days on the streets remains in critical condition. And tonight, there is a deeper understanding of just how close to home these shootings are for many Americans. A new survey out tonight finding one in five U.S. adults say they have been threatened with a gun. Maggie Vespa leads us off tonight with new details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MAGGIE VESPA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Echoes of gunfire as officers speed up to the scene. Tonight, a firsthand look at police say seven minutes of horror playing out inside a Kentucky bank. Police body camera and cell phone video showing Louisville Metro officers view Monday morning as they race to confront a lone gunman. One taking gunfire as windows shatter, falling, then jumping right back up. Minutes later, killing the shooter. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I think he`s down. VESPA: What was it like to watch that body camera video? JACQUELYN GWINN-VILLAROEL, INTERIM CHIEF, LOUISVILLE METRO POLICE: It is really -- it shakes the core. It shakes the core to know that life was being lost. VESPA: Investigators say Connor Sturgeon seen here on surveillance cameras was armed with an AR-15 rifle which he bought legally from a local dealership six days before the massacre, adding the 25-year-old was a current employee at Old National Bank and knew the colleagues he targeted. Overnight, officials confirming a fifth victim died, 57-year-old Deanna Eckert. Meanwhile, dispatch audio indicating the shooter may have tried to warn a friend before the attack. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: The shooter, 25-year-old white male Connor Sturgeon, 6`4. He texted a friend -- called a friend, left voicemail saying he`s going to kill everyone at the bank, feeling suicidal. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We know he left a note. We know he texted or called at least one person to let them know he was suicidal and contemplating harm. VESPA: Neighbors of surgeons home which investigators searched yesterday shocked by the news. KERA ALLGEIER, NEIGHBOR OF THE GUNMAN: I can`t say nothing really bad about the guy. He`s very quiet, soft spoken. I just don`t understand. VESPA: Doctors also struggling. DR. JASON SMITH, CHIEF MEDICAL OFFICER, UNIVERSITY OF LOUISVILLE HEALTH: There`s only so many times you can walk into a room and tell someone they`re not coming home tomorrow. And it just breaks your heart. When you hear someone screaming mommy or daddy, it just becomes too hard. VESPA: Tonight, three remain hospitalized, including officer Nickolas Wilk still in critical condition. The chief adding Wilk was on his fourth shift less than two weeks out of the academy. His twin brother just started. Also wounded with minor injuries, officer Corey Galloway, who investigators say killed the shooter. MONESSA BARD, MOTHER OF JULIANA FARMER: I can`t hear her voice anymore. I can`t touch her. I can`t tell her how much I love her. VESPA: The details do nothing to numb Monessa Bard`s pain. Her 45-year-old daughter Juliana Farmer among the dead. Amid a successful career in banking, she was just recruited back to Louisville and Old National Bank three weeks ago. [19:05:11] How do you make sense of that? She just got back there. BARD: There is no sense to be had. I just feel like that man stole her from us. I don`t understand his reasoning. I don`t understand why she`s gone. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And Maggie, officials I know are applauding the heroism displayed by police even after the shooter was down. VESPA (on camera): Yes, Lester, that`s right. They tell us here yesterday, EMS agencies were actually short-staffed, so a Louisville police lieutenant improvised, jumping in the front seat of an ambulance and driving it to the hospital allowing EMS workers in the back to keep caring for a wounded patient. Lester? HOLT: Maggie Vespa in Louisville, thank you. And there was yet another deadly mass shooting today, this one in Washington D.C., as a new survey shows just how much Americans are affected by gun violence. Here`s Gabe Gutierrez. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): As a funeral for a shooting victim wrapped up in D.C. today, gunfire erupted again. One man killed, three others hurt. From workplace violence to school shootings, according to a new survey from the Kaiser Family Foundation , a majority of U.S. adults have either personally or had a family member who has been impacted by a gun-related incident, including suicide. Nearly one in five Americans have lost a family member to gun violence with people of color disproportionately impacted. So, is this about mental health or is it about easy access to guns? JACKIE ROWE-ADAMS, FOUNDER, HARLEM MOTHER S.A.V.E.: It`s about both of them. GUTIERREZ: Jackie Rowe-Adams lost two sons, Anthony and Tyrone, to gun violence. She now runs a support group in Harlem. ROWE-ADAMS: When I hear about this constant shooting, it pains me. It hurt so bad because I know another family, I know the mother, father, family is hurting for the loss of their loved one. GUTIERREZ: As the nationwide debate over access to guns heats up a day after the mass shooting in Louisville, the city`s mayor fumed over a state law that requires confiscated firearms like the rifle the killer used on Monday to be resold at auction. CRAIG GREENBERG, MAYOR OF LOUISVILLE, KENTUCKY: It`s time to change this law and let us destroy illegal guns and destroy the guns that have been used to kill our friends and kill our neighbors. GUTIERREZ: While in Tennessee, Republican Governor Bill Lee today called for stronger background checks for gun purchases. GOV. BILL LEE (R-TN): The executive order will for one thing set a 72-hour clock for reporting new criminal activity. GUTIERREZ: Other states like Maryland, Washington, and Colorado are moving forward with new restrictions as gun rights advocates push back on what they consider unconstitutional overreach. DUDLEY BROWN, PRESIDENT, NATIONAL ASSOCIATION FOR GUN RIGHTS: No amount of gun control is going to stop a criminal hell bent on murder from gaining some tools to do it. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ: The Kaiser survey also showed that about a third of adults have avoided large crowds due to the possibility of gun violence. Lester? HOLT: All right, Gabe, thank you. Tonight, U.S. officials are scrambling to control the damage from the disclosure of intelligence secrets after dozens of classified documents were leaked online. Andrea Mitchell now with the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF FOREIGN AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, those leaked documents causing tough conversations between Washington and U.S. allies. On Ukraine, a U.S. intelligence assessment that Ukraine`s military will fall well short of retaking most of the territory it`s lost to Russia according to a document obtained by the Washington Post . And a document seen by NBC News revealing Ukrainian agents launched drone attacks against targets in Russia and its ally Belarus, including just outside Moscow despite promising the U.S. it would not strike Russia. Secretary of State Blinken spoke with Ukraine`s Foreign Minister today. Are you concerned about cross-border attacks? ANTONY BLINKEN , U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE: Ukraine has to make decisions about how it can most effectively defend itself against Russian aggression. MITCHELL: Another leaked documents says Egypt`s President El-Sisi recently ordered 40,000 rockets to be produced for Russia according to The Washington Post . Egypt denies it. Since Camp David in 1978, Egypt has received more than $50 billion in military aid and $30 billion in economic aid from the U.S. more than any other country in the Middle East except Israel. How could intelligence officials not know sooner about the leaks? Sir, why didn`t you know about it before April 6? That means that they were up for at least many weeks if not months before U.S. intelligence knew that they were in the public domain. GEN. LLOYD AUSTIN, U.S. SECRETARY OF DEFENSE: They were somewhere in the web. And in where exactly and who had access at that point, we don`t know. (END VIDEOTAPE) MITCHELL: The Pentagon is now in damage control, limiting the number of people who can see such highly classified documents. Lester? HOLT: Andrea Mitchell, thank you. In New York, the Manhattan D.A. prosecuting former President Trump is suing the House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan. Garrett Haake joins me now from Capitol Hill. Garrett, explain what this means. [19:10:10] GARRETT HAAKE, NBC NEWS SENIOR CAPITOL HILL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, Lester, Manhattan D.A. Alvin Bragg has asked a federal judge to block a House Judiciary Committee subpoena for a former top prosecutor in his office who`s being ordered to testify next week. Now, Bragg also asked the judge to void any subpoenas that might be filed against him or his current staff. The Democratic D.A. argues that Congress has no power to supervise the state criminal prosecutions and the efforts by Republican Committee Chairman Jim Jordan to force testimony or acquired documents related to his prosecution of Donald Trump are purely political with no legislative purpose. Jordan responding tonight in part in a tweet that reads, first, they indict a president for no crime, then they sued to block congressional oversight. Lester? HOLT: Garrett Haake, thank you. Major backlash tonight from the drug industry to that abortion pill ruling by a federal judge. And now, some states are stockpiling abortion drugs as the legal battle plays out. Laura Jarrett has the latest. DR. AMANDA BANKS, FORMER CEO, BLACKFYNN THERAPEUTICS: Now -- it`s now been shown that courts can step in and overturn a scientific decision. headline: The Battle Over Access To Abortion Pills Headed To The Supreme Court
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Now to the escalating fight over access to an abortion pill. The Justice Department says it will now ask the Supreme Court for emergency action to stop new restrictions from taking effect. Laura Jarrett has late details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): A fierce battle over abortion now headed to the U.S. Supreme Court . The Attorney General vowing to challenge a ruling from a federal appeals court that could jeopardize access to mifepristone, a commonly used abortion pill. KARINE JEAN-PIERRE , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: We believe that the law is on our side. JARRETT: Overnight, that appeals court blocked a portion of a Texas ruling that invalidated the approval of mifepristone, allowing the drug to remain on the market for now. But the judges also rolled back several FDA moves in recent years that made the drug easier to obtain. If the Supreme Court doesn`t step in, women may soon be required to visit a doctor`s office in person to receive the pill instead of taking it at home. It will no longer be available through the mail. The generic version also off the table. And the pill will only be approved through seven weeks of pregnancy instead of 10. DR. LAURA MACISAAC, OBSTETRICIAN-GYNECOLOGIST, MOUNT SINAI: Having more in- person visits means women will have to take time off of work, get childcare often during the work week. If the medication can`t get into the hands of the people that need it quickly, then it isn`t available. JARRETT: Doctors like Laura McIsaac who practice for over three decades alarmed by the ruling. MACISAAC: That will absolutely increase pregnancy complications and increase maternal mortality. JARRETT: Restricting access to mifepristone at the heart of the original Texas lawsuit. ERIN MORROW HAWLEY , SENIOR COUNSEL, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM: The FDA has basically sanctioned mail-order abortions. JARRETT: Erin Hawley represents the advocacy groups and doctors that sued the FDA . HAWLEY: The Fifth Circuit`s decision is a huge victory for women and for the rule of law. The FDA did not have a valid basis for approving that drug. JARRETT: While the fight continues in the courts, tonight, a clash at the State House. In Florida, anger erupting on the House floor. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Show the bill passes. JARRETT: As the Republican-controlled legislature passed a six-week abortion ban headed to the governor`s desk for signature soon. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: So, Laura, when do all these restrictions take effect? JARRETT (on camera): So, those restrictions should begin early Saturday. I say should because tonight a federal judge in a different case in Washington State reiterated that the Biden administration must not make any changes to the availability of this drug. The government will likely tell the U.S. Supreme Court it simply cannot comply with all these conflicting rulings. HOLT: All right, Laura, thanks very much. headline: The Supreme Court Putting A Temporary Hold On A Lower Court Ruling That Would Limit Access To An Abortion Pill Keeping It Widely Available For Now
story_text: LESTER HOLT: A late and dramatic development in the battle over that abortion pill. Late today, the Supreme Court stepping in and putting a temporary hold on a lower court ruling that would limit access. Laura Jarrett has details for us. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the U.S. Supreme Court moving quick to block a federal judge from rolling back access to the abortion pill mifepristone at least for now. Justice Samuel Alito handing down an order within hours of the Justice Department`s emergency appeal that had warned of chaos and profound disruption if the high court didn`t step in. At issue in the case, a legal morass of complex FDA regulations over the drug that had recently been made easier to obtain. KAMALA HARRIS , VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: They attacked medication that for 20 years the FDA ruled as being safe. JARRETT: But the advocacy groups and doctors that sued to ban the drug claim the FDA ignored safety risks. Those plaintiffs now have until Tuesday to submit their legal arguments to the justices. At the same time, access to abortion now largely cut off throughout much of the south. After the Supreme Court overturned Roe v Wade, many women traveled to Florida for abortions. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Show the bill passes. JARRETT: Now, the state has banned anyone from seeking an abortion after six weeks of pregnancy though the law won`t go into effect right away. FENTRICE DRISKELL (D-FL), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: You just don`t want women to have choice. CHASE TRAMONT (R-FL), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: Here we value life from conception to the casket. JARRETT: Governor Ron DeSantis signing the bill with a private gathering overnight, a far cry from the jubilant celebration he put on for a 15-week ban passed last spring highlighting a rising tension within the GOP on the issue. As some are mindful of the public polling largely favoring abortion, other presidential hopefuls are leaning into their conservative base with eyes on 2024, including Senator Tim Scott who spoke exclusively to NBC`s Ali Vitali today. TIM SCOTT (R-SC): If I were President of the United States, I would literally sign the most conservative pro-life legislation that they can get through Congress. JARRETT: But for now, the issue of abortion access rest with the Supreme Court, with the justices poised to rule next week. Laura Jarrett, NBC News (END VIDEOTAPE) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. headline: The Battle Over Abortion Rights Is Now Headed Back To The Supreme Court
story_text: [18:30:21] JOSE DIAZ-BALART, NBC NEWS HOST: Today tonight, the battle over abortion rights is now headed back to the Supreme Court. Protesters out in force today from Los Angeles to Washington, D.C., as the fate of access to abortion pills could be decided within days. New revelations from those leaked intel documents, reports of up to four more Chinese spy balloons and new questions about why it took authorities so long to notice the leaked documents. Terrifying moments as a bomb is thrown at Japan`s Prime minister. He is rushed to safety before it explodes. What we know about the suspect. A violent coup d`etat playing out right now in Africa. The American ambassador and his staff forced to take shelter. The deadly police mistake caught on video. Officers at the wrong address. When the homeowner opens the door with a gun, they opened fire. How could this have happened? NBC News with rare access as law enforcement busts a giant retail crime ring. Nearly $200,000 in merchandise recovered. And there`s good news tonight. The daughter who reveals to her father after his life saving kidney transplant, she was his donor. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m really proud of her. I can`t believe she did it. (END VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Jose Diaz-Balart. DIAZ-BALART: Good evening. The nation`s highest court is once again wading into the country`s most divisive issue, abortion rights. Today, there were protesters outside the Supreme Court as well as rallies across the country. The past week has been a dizzying string of competing and contradictory court decisions, some restricting access to the abortion pill, others protecting it. The Supreme Court now says it will take up the issue, setting a deadline just five days away. At stake, access to mifepristone, the abortion pill the most common way women and pregnancies in the U.S. The Supreme Court could rule to suspend its use nationwide. We begin tonight with Monica Alba. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And we didn`t backed down. CROWD: No. MONICA ALBA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Protests from coast to coast tonight. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Standup don`t back. ALBA (voice-over): As the fate of the nation`s most commonly used abortion pill hangs in the balance. After a week of uncertainty, the Supreme Court weighing in Friday, keeping mifepristone available for at least the next four days. The temporary action allows the full court to review emergency appeals from the Biden administration and one of the drug makers and gives the plaintiffs a group of doctors and advocacy groups until Tuesday to submit their arguments. ERIN HAWLEY, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM SENIOR COUNSEL: It`s really time that the FDA was held to account for putting politics above women`s health and safety, as well as unborn lives. ALBA (voice-over): The high court expected to rule on Wednesday as abortion rights activists expressed concern about what the conservative majority that overturned Roe v. Wade could do now. WENDY FROSH, WASHINGTON, D.C. ABORTION RIGHTS PROTESTER: The same could happen with any other medication if we allow judges to exercise this outrageous authority or misuse of authority. ALBA (voice-over): If the Fifth Circuit ruling is upheld, women would have to get the drug in person at the doctor`s office. It would no longer be available by mail and the window for prescription would be narrowed from 10 weeks to seven. The White House standing by the FDA`s, quote, evidence- based approval. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I think it`s outrageous what the court has done relative to concluding that they`re going to overrule the FDA . ALBA (voice-over): With Vice President Harris making a surprise stop at the Los Angeles women`s march Saturday, vowing to stand up and fight for abortion access. KAMALA HARRIS , VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: This is a moment that history will show required each of us. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: And Monica joins us now from the White House. Monica, what could the Supreme Court do Wednesday? ALBA: Well, it`s unclear how the justices will rule, but it`s possible the court could extend the temporary pause, keeping things as they were before the Texas ruling, until this can play out in the lower courts. Jose? DIAZ-BALART: Monica Alba, thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: Here at home, an evacuation order has been issued for parts of Georgia after a massive fire reignited at a plastic resin plant in Glenn County . The fire first broke out early this morning and was contained before reigniting later in the day. There are no reports of injuries. [18:40:11] Growing questions in New Mexico tonight after a call for help went horribly wrong. Body cam captured police showing up at the wrong house and then fatally shooting the homeowner. Shaquille Brewster has details. A caution in some of the video is disturbing. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) SHAQUILLE BREWSTER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Tonight, new body camera video capturing the fatal police shooting of a homeowner in New Mexico. The videos from April 5th show three Farmington officers responding to a domestic violence report around 11:30 p.m. identifying themselves as police three times. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Farmington police. BREWSTER (voice-over): But the department says officers went to the wrong address. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It might have been 4308. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Was it 43 or 53? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes, it might have been 5308. BREWSTER (voice-over): Fifty-two-year-old Robert Dotson opens his front door wearing a robe, investigators say pointing a gun at police. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Hands up. BREWSTER (voice-over): All three officers fired their weapons. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m good. I`m good. I`m good. BREWSTER (voice-over): Dotson died at the scene. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: One down at the doorway. BREWSTER (voice-over): His wife is heard screaming inside. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Please don`t. BREWSTER (voice-over): Appearing to open the door when police say she begins firing. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Get her in cuffs. BREWSTER (voice-over): Minutes later, she surrendered. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Where`s the gun at? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: He dropped it and she picked it up and pointed it at us. BREWSTER (voice-over): Upstairs are two children heard on a 911 call released by the Farmington Police Department. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: There were gunshots in the house and my dad is shot. BREWSTER (voice-over): The police chief offered his condolences the next day. STEVE HEBBE, FARMINGTON, NEW MEXICO POLICE CHIEF: Mr. Dotson was not the subject of the call that our officers were responding to. And this ending is just unbelievably tragic. I`m extremely sorry that we are in this position. BREWSTER (voice-over): The department is not naming the three officers who are now on paid administrative leave. CARMEN BEST, NBC NEWS LAW ENFORCEMENT ANALYST: BREWSTER (voice-over): It is a tragedy, no doubt. BREWSTER (voice-over): Former Police Chief Carmen Best, who watched the video, says the shooting appears to be consistent with police training. BEST: I would not expect my officer to have a gun pointed in their direction and not react. BREWSTER (voice-over): A reaction stemming from a mistaken address now being investigated by state police. Shaquille Brewster, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: Still ahead, ten years after the shattering events of the Boston Marathon bombing, the survivors who never backed down. Also, a rare inside look as law enforcement takes down giant retail theft rings. Look at all the things they recovered. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:45:15] DIAZ-BALART: A day of hope and healing in Boston, with the city marking 10 years since a horrific marathon bomb attack that claimed the lives of three people and injured hundreds more are. Kathy Park takes us inside the survivor`s decade long road to recovery. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KATHY PARK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): A powerful tribute today as thousands gathered at the Boston Marathon finish line, a place so many have raced through. But today, everyone was still. Here 10 years ago, an unthinkable attack. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And we heard the two explosions. And my family and I knew something was wrong right away. PARK (voice-over): Back to back explosions that killed three people and injured hundreds more. This was Michelle Blackburn 10 years ago, cheering on a friend. The blast nearly took her leg. MICHELLE BLACKBURN, BOSTON MARATHON BOMBING SURVIVOR: I think that anytime you go through a trauma, it`s very fluid. They spent many years just avoiding it altogether. PARK (voice-over): And this is Michelle today, training to run this year`s marathon until a recent injury took her out for now. BLACKBURN: But I always say forward is the only way forward. So that`s what we`re doing. It`s nothing that`s going to preclude me from running again. JEFFERSON DRISCOLL, BOSTON MARATHON BOMBING WITNESS: I actually knew them. PARK (voice-over): Jefferson Driscoll was 10 when the bombing happened. He grew up with the family of Martin Richard, the youngest victim killed at age eight. Now 20, Jefferson is running his first marathon. (on camera): What inspired you? DRISCOLL: The Richard family, their resilience, their kindness, their peace. It`s been amazing. You learn endurance and it teaches you Boston is one family, one big, strong family. PARK (voice-over): Boston strong still on full display a decade later. Kathy Park, NBC News, Boston. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: We are back in a moment with rare access as police track and catch the suspects behind a massive retail theft ring. And life-saving surprise, a father battling for his life learns of the incredible sacrifice made by his daughter. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:50:03] DIAZ-BALART: A retail theft is on the rise across America. You`ve surely seen the videos of brazen thieves smashing windows and stealing merchandise. Well, police now and the stores themselves are working together to catch them. George Solis, now with a rare inside look at one operation. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: What do you want me to do with it? GEORGE SOLIS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): As the radio calls come in. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: OK. All right. Copy. SOLIS (voice-over): California Highway Patrol squads close in. The drama unfolding just before dusk in this Southern California neighborhood. Months of surveillance into an organized retail crime ring. LT. ADAM SMITH, CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY PATROL : One was going into the stores on multiple occasions over the past three months, gathering as much items as they could. SOLIS (voice-over): All leading up to this. Three suspects arrested on suspicion of organized retail theft, according to law enforcement. This is California Highway Patrol `s specialized organized retail crime task force in action recovered a handyman`s paradise worth of high end tools. (on camera): What was the dollar figure that was recovered in tools yesterday? CAPT. JEFF LOFTIN, CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY PATROL : It was about $150,000. SOLIS (voice-over): According to the CHP , this case involved two brothers who repeatedly stole power tools from Home Depots across Southern California and their fences, or the third party they were selling to. LOFTIN: They were concentrating on Milwaukee, DeWitt. You see over here, Makita. SOLIS (voice-over): This high stakes operation, first flagged to the task force by Home Depot , a partnership between law enforcement and major stores to combat the rampant rise of organized retail crime. LOFTIN: As long as we let these people get away with what they`re doing, you and I are going to pay for it. SOLIS (voice-over): Home Depot`s own investigators were on site to ID the stolen items. RORY STALLARD, HOME DEPOT WESTERN DIVISION AP INVESTIGATION SENIOR MANAGER: That makes a huge difference when we prosecute the case, because now everything`s under one umbrella. We`re dealing with one prosecutor. SOLIS (voice-over): Organized retail crime is different than shoplifting. The goal is to resell stolen items for a profit, resulting in tens of billions of dollars lost by retailers each year, many instances caught on camera nationwide, from smash and grabs at luxury stores to dragging entire displays out the door. (on camera): This is not just one battery charger. This is a whole kit of them. LOFTIN: Right, entire boxes. SOLIS (voice-over): Since its creation in 2019, the Highway Patrols` unit has recovered more than $28 million worth of stolen goods. Because of that, California Attorney General Rob Bonta has made fighting organized retail crime a priority even across state lines. ROB BONTA, CALIFORNIA ATTORNEY GENERAL: We will hold you accountable. We will bring felony charges against you. SOLIS (voice-over): The crime surge forcing retailers to drastically increase security. (on camera): Home Depot deploys a number of security measures to ensure their products stay safe from security cameras that watch your every move to products that are secured and locked in place. STALLARD: We call it hardening the target. SOLIS (voice-over): If the thieves manage to thwart these growing security measures, the task force says they won`t get far. SMITH: We`re going to be following you, and we`re going to catch you. George Solis, NBC News, Los Angeles. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: When we come back, the amazing moment, this young girl sees the world like never before. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:55:53] DIAZ-BALART: There`s good news tonight about the sacrifices we make for the ones we love. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): This is a magical moment the Scarborough family in Tucson, Arizona, will never forget. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Casey. DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): That`s Henry and Maraena`s baby girl Ireland putting on glasses for the very first time. Now clearly seen, she`s surrounded by so much love. There were other unforgettable moments too. Here`s army major Eric Cusick, a few weeks back, surprising his kids at their schools in New York after a 10-month mission overseas, a homecoming that means so much to this military family. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Oh, my God. DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): And in St. Louis -- UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Are you kidding me? DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): That`s John Ivanowski, shocked to find out his daughter Delaney was his kidney donor. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It`s fine. DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): It`s a secret she kept for months preparing for the procedure when his kidney disease got worse. The gift of life, helping him heal. JOHN IVANOWSKI: I think about it every day. She`s my hero. I`ll take care of her the rest of my days here. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I need you to read something for me. OK. DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): Across the country, students were celebrating good news like Stephen Russell. STEPHEN RUSSELL, STUDENT: That you are to be admitted. DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): The multi sports star with Special Olympics, Georgia. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Here it goes. DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): Overwhelmed when he found out he got into Kennesaw State University . UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Way to go Stephen. DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): But this was the moment that moved everyone to tears. That`s South K High School Senior Joshua Alvarado in Los Angeles, surprised with a $50,000 scholarship. He plans to study engineering at Stanford. Joshua embraced by his mom, Erine (ph), and his two sisters. The moment bittersweet. That`s because his dad, Mario, died five years ago. Joshua prayed to him after the celebration. (on camera): What did you tell him? JOSHUA ALVARADO, SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL STUDENT: I told him that I hope he`s watching. DIAZ-BALART: He`s proud. No doubt. You should know that. ALVARADO: Thank you. DIAZ-BALART (voice-over): The family has overcome struggles, even homelessness. As a first generation son of Mexican immigrants, Joshua hopes his story inspires others.\\ (on camera): How would you define the American dream? ALVARADO: The American dream to me, has always been reaching for something more. That belief that there`s better out there and that it`s within your reach if you just work hard enough. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: That`s NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for this Saturday. I`m Jose Diaz- Balart. Thank you for the privilege of your time. Good night. headline: Meet the Press for April 16, 2023, NBC
story_text: (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) [09:00:19] CHUCK TODD, HOST, NBC`S "MEET THE PRESS" (voice over): This Sunday, supreme uncertainty. The Supreme Court keeps the abortion pill available for now, with a final decision potentially coming in days. VICE PRESIDENT KAMALA HARRIS: They attack medication that for 20 years the FDA ruled as being safe. SEN. LINDSEY GRAHAM , (R) SOUTH CAROLINA: I do believe in common-sense restrictions on abortion. That`s where America`s at. TODD: As Republican presidential hopefuls continue to struggle with the abortion issue, post-Roe. SEN. TIM SCOTT, (R) SOUTH CAROLINA: I would literally sign the most conservative pro-life legislation that they can get through Congress. QUESTION: Even if it was six weeks? SCOTT: I`m not going to talk about six or five or seven or 10. TODD: And the gun debate, after more mass shootings in Tennessee and Kentucky. (UNKNOWN): Oh, my God, there`s an active shooter there! TODD: The NRA holds its annual meeting and Republicans pledge support. FORMER PRESIDENT DONALD J. TRUMP: With me at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue, no one will lay a finger on your firearms. TODD: Can the two parties find common ground on issues that have divided the nation for decades? My guests this morning, Democratic Senator Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin and Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana. Also, rising tensions. Israel is facing crises at home and criticism abroad. PRESIDENT JOSEPH R. BIDEN, JR.: They cannot continue down this road. TODD: My exclusive interview with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu . ISRAELI PRIME MINISTER BENJAMIN NETANYAHU: People will see at the end that Israel was a democracy, is a democracy and will be even a stronger democracy after this democratic reform. TODD: Finally, how did a 21-year-old gamer, an Air National Guardsman, gain access to the nation`s top secrets? (on camera): Joining me for insight and analysis are NBC News senior Washington correspondent Hallie Jackson; former Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson; Leigh Ann Caldwell of The Washington Post ; and Stephen Hayes, editor of The Dispatch. Welcome to Sunday. It`s "Meet the Press". ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest-running show in television history, this is "Meet the Press With Chuck Todd." (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: Good Sunday morning. Debates over guns and abortion have roiled this nation for decades. This week those debates feel a bit more intense than they have in a while, and there are some deepening tensions between activists who wield power inside Republican primary circles and the overall electorate. Today mark the 16th anniversary of the Virginia Tech shooting. At the time it was the deadliest mass shooting in U.S. history. Thirty-two people were killed. Now, sadly, it`s been surpassed by mass shootings in Las Vegas and Orlando. After five people were killed this week in a mass shooting in Louisville, Kentucky, six more killed two weeks ago at a school in Nashville, 2024 Republican hopefuls gathered at the NRA Convention and rejected the idea that gun restrictions could somehow limit violence -- gun violence. And the NRA continued to demand unlimited political allegiance from the GOP. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) WAYNE LAPIERRE , CEO, NATIONAL RIFLE ASSOCIATION: Gun-hating politicians should never go to bed unafraid of what this association and all of our millions of members can do to their political careers. TRUMP : The issue is not too many guns; the issue is too many thugs, hoodlums and savage criminals on our street. GOV. KRISTI NOEM, (R) SOUTH DAKOTA: Little Miss Addie, who is almost two, I want to reassure you, she already has a shotgun and she already has a rifle. (LAUGHTER) (APPLAUSE) And she`s got a little pony named Sparkles, too, so the girl is set up. (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: A Gallup poll conducted before the Louisville and Nashville shootings showed 63 percent of Americans are dissatisfied with the nation`s gun laws. But a majority of Republicans, 54 percent, are satisfied. And so far that overall dissatisfaction number hasn`t translated to the ballot box. Not a single pro-gun elected politician has been thrown out over the issue. But that`s not true on abortion. Nowhere is the gap between the Republican base and the overall general electorate greater than on this issue, particularly after the overturning of Roe V. Wade. On Friday the Supreme Court put a temporary hold on a lower court ruling on the abortion pill, while the court considers the Biden administration`s request to preserve FDA approval of the drug. The state keeps the abortion pill widely available for now, with perhaps another decision expected by Wednesday to try to clear some of this up. Of course, in theory, with the Dobbs decision, the court thought it was sending abortion back to the states. Clearly, that is not the case. The Dobbs decision is not popular with the public. While 61 percent of voters disapproved of the court`s decision to overturn Roe in a fall NBC News poll, 69 percent of Republicans approved of it. Republican elected leaders are well aware of the political challenges abortion presents right now. In 2024 presidential hopefuls have struggled to answer simple questions about where they stand on abortion rights and access. This week Florida Governor Ron DeSantis quickly signed a six-week abortion ban before a speech at evangelical Liberty University . [09:05:02] But he did it behind closed doors, and then he never mentioned what he did in his speech. Donald Trump has repeatedly refused to say whether he would even support a federal law that would restrict abortion. And you`ll hear Tim Scott, Nikki Haley, even Mike Pence , all of them are struggling to define their views on this issue. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) QUESTION: Is it encouraging a culture of life, though to propose the death penalty for women who get abortions? FORMER VICE PRESIDENT MIKE PENCE: I -- I must tell you that I don`t -- I`m not familiar with those proposals, and I don`t -- I don`t -- I don`t have a way of responding to that or confirming it. SCOTT: I would literally sign the most conservative pro-life legislation that they can get through Congress. QUESTION: Even if it was six weeks? SCOTT: I`m not going to talk about six or five or seven or 10. FORMER GOV. NIKKI HALEY, (R) SOUTH CAROLINA: I don`t want unelected justices deciding something this personal. We`re not going to let this be a political football. Let`s let the states work this out, if Congress decides to do it, but don`t get into that game of them saying "How many weeks? How many weeks?" No, let`s first figure out what we agree on. (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: And joining me now is Democratic Senator Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin, who announced this week that she plans to run for a third term. Senator Baldwin, welcome back to "Meet the Press." SEN. TAMMY BALDWIN , (D) WISCONSIN: It`s a delight to join you. TODD: Let me start with the Supreme Court`s decision to put a temporary hold on the ruling having to do with Mifepristone and the future of medicated abortion in this country. Do you think five days is enough time to -- for the Supreme Court to get all the information they need in order to make this decision? BALDWIN: Well, who knows how long that will take, but I`m certainly glad for the five days. But, look, what we have in Texas is a -- a judge who was not guided by science but is part of an extreme Republican concerted effort to ban abortion nationwide. And we do not need judges, politicians or government telling women about what sort of healthcare they can have. It is an issue that is not only playing out in the court in Texas but in -- in the State of Florida, with the governor signing a near six-week ban, Idaho forbidding travel out of state for minors, Wisconsin, where we`ve gone back to literally 1849. That is the date our criminal abortion ban was passed. And that`s 174 years ago. We are fighting back. TODD: If the Supreme Court decides to allow the circuit`s ruling to hold, which would roll back FDA approval of Mifepristone essentially to pre-2016 regulations -- if that happens, what do you want the Biden administration to do? For instance, do you want them -- do you think they should resubmit Mifepristone to the FDA and get a new approval? BALDWIN: Yeah, so we don`t know what the ruling is going to be. We know that this is a drug that was proven safe and effective back in 2000. We know there have been further FDA regulations and -- and the drug has been made available now in a recent ruling over the counter. And I don`t think that there should be second-guessing of the scientific-based process that FDA goes. It has such repercussions beyond the drug Mifepristone to -- you know, we want to be able to rely on a science-driven process that the FDA has. TODD: Let me ask you about, sort of, federal versus state here. In Wisconsin, assuming that the newly configured Supreme Court decides that the 1800 law is essentially null and void, that it`s obsolete, it`s likely that Wisconsin`s abortion law would -- would revert to a law that was passed in the `80s that would essentially make 20 weeks, I believe, the limit on when you can get an abortion. Your bill in the Senate would be Roe v. Wade, which is essentially 24 weeks. Do you think there`s a meaningful difference between 20 and 24 weeks, as this debate moves forward? BALDWIN: Yeah, so the Women`s Health Protection Act codifies Roe v. Wade, but it takes the additional step to tell states that they can`t pass laws that unduly limit access to that right. In Wisconsin you -- you talk about the 1980s law, but there have been laws passed in the `90s and, frankly, quite recently that further restrict a woman`s access to full reproductive healthcare, whether those are waiting periods, mandatory counseling... [09:10:03] TODD: Right. BALDWIN: ... invasive ultrasounds. These are the types of state interference that the Women`s Health Protection Act would eliminate. TODD: I`m just curious, though, how rigid are you on this? In order to get two-thirds of what you`re hoping to get, and you could get 60 votes with 20 weeks, would you do it? BALDWIN: I -- I certainly would look at that, but here is what the bill does. The bill talks about pre-viability and viability and relies on medical expertise. Because that -- that time may change as medicine advances. So we recognize that from the get-go, and I think that`s the appropriate way to do it. But I do want to get this measure passed. TODD: But you are willing to have some compromise if that was the price of getting more Republicans on board? If you could get them on board at 20 weeks rather than 24? We even heard Senator Tim Scott saying that, if 20 weeks is all he could get, looking at it through the other way, that perhaps he would support that. Is that at all... BALDWIN: I`m not... TODD: ... something worth... BALDWIN: I`m not going to negotiate... TODD: I understand that. Is that all something worth at least looking at? BALDWIN: Certainly it`s worth looking at, but I think the way to go is to have medical science establish what`s pre-viable and what`s post-viability, and that`s what the bill does. TODD: I want to ask you a couple of political questions. Over the last two presidential elections... BALDWIN Yes. TODD: ... just one U.S. senator was able to win re-election despite the presidential candidate of the same party winning their -- not winning their state. It was Susan Collins in Maine in 2020. BALDWIN: That`s right. TODD: Do you think you can win re-election if Joe Biden can`t carry Wisconsin? BALDWIN: Well, I think Joe Biden will carry Wisconsin. Obviously, we don`t know who the Republican nominee will be, but despite Republican national efforts to put the spotlight on Wisconsin by hosting their convention there and having the first Republican primary debate in Wisconsin, I think we will prevail. And I think you can look at last week`s momentum in our state supreme court race. What people said resoundingly is we want our rights and freedoms back, and we`re willing to work hard, go to the polls and win elections in order to do that. That will not diminish in 2024. And if any Republican thinks that voters have simmered down on the abortion issue, they are wrong. It`s going to -- that is going to continue well into the next presidential race. TODD: Senator Dianne Feinstein is recovering from a tough bout with shingles. There has been some calls for her to resign now. Where do you stand on this? BALDWIN: Well, I certainly wish Senator Feinstein well and am pleased that she has made the decision to have a fill-in on her seat on the Judiciary Committee. I think that is really an important, a responsible thing to do during her absence, because we have President Biden`s nominees waiting for hearings and votes, and we want to keep that moving. But I wish her well and hope she returns to the Senate very soon. TODD: Do you think these calls for her to resign are appropriate? BALDWIN: Look, it`s up to Dianne Feinstein and her family to decide whether she wants to keep on serving, and she`s had a remarkable record, and I respect that. TODD: Senator Tammy Baldwin , Democrat from Wisconsin, running for a third term. I appreciate you coming on and sharing your perspective with us. BALDWIN: Thank you so much. TODD: And joining me now is Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, the top Republican on the Senate Health and Education Committee, also, by the way, a medical doctor. Senator Cassidy, welcome back to "Meet the Press," sir. SEN. BILL CASSIDY, (R) LOUISIANA: Thank you, Chuck. TODD: I want to start with the dispute over Mifepristone. You`re somebody who -- you`ve not wanted for a while this drug to be available by mail. So I`m curious, why were you not one of the 11 Republican senators to sign on to a brief supporting the Texas ruling? CASSIDY: I`m not quite sure what you`re asking there. I mean, I sign on briefs all day. I`m not sure that has any great importance. I think what is important is that we have a political process by which we resolve these issues. That particular ruling seems to be going through -- it was on a process-oriented thing. Among the reasons that they ruled that way, I`m told, is that the FDA did not follow correctly the Administrative Procedures Act. Now, that`s a question of fact. It can be resolved by the courts. It`s actively being resolved. I think the broader question is how do you resolve the issues in general? TODD: Yeah. CASSIDY: I think that returning it to the states to allow a state`s values to guide is very important. [09:15:02] In -- in Massachusetts, in New York, California, nothing changes. In my state, a law written by a Democratic female state senator and signed into law by a Democratic governor established a more pro-life statute. That`s the way I think it`s going to resolve politically, I think it`s going to resolve socially and culturally. TODD: And on the decision on Mifepristone, do you believe that the scientific community should, sort of, take precedent here? The American College of Obstetrics -- Obstetrics and Gynecology says that Mifepristone is safe and effective. You have said their word matters when it comes to over-the-counter birth control. Should their word matter when it comes to the use of Mifepristone? CASSIDY: So I think you`re going back to the kind of assertion that the principal basis of the court case in Texas was about the safety. And I think specifically it said that it was supposed to -- the accelerated pathway was supposed to approve a drug to treat an illness. It is a stretch to call a pregnancy an illness. And so -- and of course, obviously, we know what happens to the unborn baby. And so I`m not quite really sure that you`re framing this question accurately. Now, beyond that is also a cultural and social issue. In my state we are a pro-life state. We have a legislation -- we have legislation which is far more pro-life than it is in, say, California. But the Californians keep their law and we keep our law, and that`s the way it`s going to work out nationally. TODD: Right. I guess, though, on this Texas decision, it does seem like it`s going to call into question other FDA approvals on other drugs. I mean, do you worry about the up-ending a status quo and, sort of, up-ending the FDA`s authority in a way that will be -- create, sort of, chaos in the pharmaceutical industry? CASSIDY: I think that`s totally alarmist. It`s totally alarmist. And, by the way, when did the FDA think it can go above the law? It can ignore -- it can ignore the Administrative Procedure Act, which every other agency has to follow, theoretically, but they don`t have to? So I mean, I think that`s alarmist, and I also think that the FDA should not be above the law. TODD: I want to get you to respond to something Governor Chris Sununu said about the larger debate about Roe v. Wade and this. Take a listen. I`m curious what -- your reaction. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) GOV. CHRIS SUNUNU , (R) NEW HAMPSHIRE: Roe v. Wade, whether you agreed with it or not, there was a 50-year precedent there. There`s a 20-year precedent with this thing. So now, to the American public, it looks like Republicans are coming in and trying to massively change and blow up the system and all of this sort of thing. TODD: Do you think he has a point? CASSIDY: If he`s speaking about the public`s perception, I would say that be the case -- that would be the case. There was a doctor from New Jersey who was testifying before Congress and just, you know, grieving about how all of her patients were fearful. And I`m thinking, nothing`s going to change in New Jersey. She doesn`t understand the law, or if she understands it, she`s deliberately mischaracterizing it. So there is a perception issue out there. But what Dobbs does, it returns to the states the decisions to allow the decision to be reflective of the state. In New Jersey, it doesn`t change. In Louisiana, it reflects our values -- again, a law written by a Democratic female state senator signed into law by a Democratic governor. So I`m not quite -- so I agree with, kind of, the premise, but -- of what Governor Sununu said, but I`m, kind of, disagreeing with how you`re presenting it. TODD: Are you still -- are you still glad that Roe v. Wade was overturned, or do you think, in hindsight, this was -- you know, you`ve always said this is an uncomfortable -- you know, it`s hard to find a middle ground. Did it turn out Roe v. Wade was the uncomfortable middle ground for America? CASSIDY: I think Dobbs is the uncomfortable middle ground, where people will confront that there is a diversity of opinion, and no one group has the ability to impose their will upon the other. headline: The Supreme Court Preserving Access To The Abortion Pill For Now In The Most Significant Case Since Roe v. Wade
story_text: [19:00:00] LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the breaking news from the Supreme Court of the future of that abortion pill. (voiceover): The Supreme Court preserving access to the abortion pill for now in the most significant case since Roe v. Wade. So, what are the next steps? We`ll break it down. The severe storm threat moving east after tornadoes ripped through Texas and Oklahoma. At least three dead, flash flooding and water rescues in Austin, golf ball-sized hail in Illinois, even a water spout in Florida. Millions at risk heading into the weekend. Charges against Alec Baldwin officially dropped. And new details about the gun that killed the Rust cinematographer as production resumes. The new images from inside the film`s Montana set. An American killed in Sudan as fighting rages on. Plus, the latest from U.S. officials on the other Americans trapped. Alarming new findings about climate change. A new report says the melting of glaciers is off the charts. Can anything be done? Is the future of food grown in a lab? It`s better for the climate but what does it taste like? And back in the groove with record sales rising. Why so many are turning to turntables this weekend. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening, everyone. Facing an 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time deadline of its own choosing and a day of high drama, the U.S. Supreme Court has just weighed in on another pivotal and consequential question in the nation`s divide over abortion. The justices tonight deciding what`s next for a Texas Court ruling that said the FDA`s 23-year-old approval of a commonly used abortion drug is no longer valid, a ruling temporarily paused from taking effect up until now. That has had the potential to impact medical abortions even in states where abortion remains legal. Senior Legal Correspondent Laura Jarrett is standing by with late details. Laura, what is the court saying here? LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Hey, Lester, good evening. Just minutes ago, the U.S. Supreme Court issued an order to keep a widely used abortion pill on the market. The justices have flatly blocked that lower court decision from Texas that had invalidated the FDA`s longtime approval of Mifepristone and would have made the drugs substantially harder to obtain. Now, Justice Thomas, Justice Alito dissenting to that decision from the rest of their colleagues. The FDA and the drug maker had strongly urged those justices to step in, warning essentially if they hadn`t stepped in, all manufacturing and distribution of this drug would have come to a screeching halt. But for now, women can continue to receive the pill by mail and use it until 10 weeks into their pregnancies while this case continues to play out in the court below. Lester, the Biden Administration just issuing obviously a statement praising it. You know, the groups that had filed this suit originally had claimed that the FDA ignored safety risk, something that the FDA and the Biden Administration put -- pushed back on very strongly, Lester. HOLT: All right, so Laura, legally, what happens next? The next steps here. JARRETT: OK, so, now the case will head back to a federal appeals court for further evaluation of the merits of the lawsuit. This Supreme Court decision was just a temporary issue just because it came up so quickly. Now the case will head back to a three-judge panel on the fifth circuit. It`s made up of mostly conservatives but we don`t know who exactly on that court will hear this case now that it`s back there, Lester. HOLT: All right, Laura Jarrett on that breaking news. I`m joined now by Peter Alexander at the White House. Peter, the president as we heard just reacted to this move. What are you learning? PETER ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Yes, Lester, that`s right. The White House has been bracing for this decision for days. Abortion medications have become an increasingly critical flash point of the states` limit or ban abortions after the Supreme Court`s ruling last year overturning Roe v Wade largely because abortion medication can be sent by mail and taken at home. As for the president, he just moments ago weighed in, releasing a statement that reads in part, Mifepristone remains available and approved for safe and effective use. While we continue this fight in the courts, the president adding, that his administration will continue to defend the FDA`s independence to review, approve, and regulate a wide range of prescription drugs. The President says the stakes for women could not be high higher and denounces what he called politically driven attacks on women`s health, Lester. The White House had warned if the court upheld the lower court`s decision, it would have put women`s health at risk and have undermined the FDA`s ability to keep safe and effective medications available for those people who need them. Lester? HOLT: All right, Peter Alexander -- Peter, thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc.
