headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for May 5, 2023, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the stunning video just released a former president Trump`s deposition in a civil trial. (voiceover): His testimony played for the jury, considering writer E. Jean Carroll`s allegations in her civil lawsuit that he raped her and defamed her. His strong denial and what he says about Carroll, a photo with her and his wife, and an infamous comment he once made about women. The Supreme Court puts the execution of an Oklahoma death row inmate on hold. My interview with Richard Glossip was said to be his last. Instead, relief for supporters who say his trial was unfair. Their reaction, the moment the news came in. The war in Ukraine, why a Russian mercenary group is threatening to quit fighting in a key city. It`s ultimatum to Russia. Is the U.S. ready for more migrants expected to come to the Southern Border? We put the question to the Homeland Security Secretary. More good news about jobs, but the new warning from President Biden about a potential government default. Will birth control pill soon be available over the counter? The FDA set to consider it. And the coronation of King Charles now just hours away. Thousands filling the streets for a royal ritual not seen in 70 years. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening and welcome everyone. Former President Trump has not testified in the civil lawsuit in which a writer accuses him of raping her more than 20 years ago and then defaming her by saying she made up the allegation. But today, a video deposition given by Mr. Trump was made public for the first time. In it, the former president strongly denies the accusation, intense questioning from E. Jean Carroll`s lawyer. Mr. Trump was also asked about comments he made about women in that infamous Access Hollywood Tape that came to light before the 2016 election. It`s where we begin tonight with Senior Legal Correspondent Laura Jarrett. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, former President Donald Trump seen under oath, blasting the rape accusation against him from writer E. Jean Carroll. DONALD TRUMP , FORMER PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: She`s accusing me of rape, a woman that I have no idea who she is. It came out of the blue. JARRETT: Released publicly for the first time today, Mr. Trump`s deposition in a civil case. Carroll is suing him for allegedly defaming her. She says he raped her in a department store dressing room more than 20 years ago. TRUMP: It`s the most ridiculous, disgusting story. It was just made up. If it did happen, it would have been reported within minutes. JARRETT: This week, a jury in Manhattan watch clips of the deposition. Carroll`s attorney turning the focus to that now infamous Access Hollywood Tape. TRUMP : You can do anything. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Whatever you want. TRUMP: Grab them by the (BLEEP). UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And when you`re a star, they let you do it. You can do anything. Grab them by the (BLEEP). You can do anything. That`s what you said, correct? TRUMP: Well, historically, that`s true with stars. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It`s true with stars that they can grab women by their (BLEEP). TRUMP: Well, that`s what, if you look over the last million years, I guess that`s been largely true. Not always, but largely true, unfortunately or fortunately. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: You consider yourself to be a star. TRUMP : I think you can say that, yes. JARRETT: Mr. Trump had repeatedly said Miss Carroll was not his type. TRUMP: It`s not politically correct to say it, and I know that, but I`ll say it anyway. JARRETT: But then he mistook Carroll for his ex-wife, Marla Maples, when shown this old photo of him shaking Carroll`s hand. TRUMP : I don`t even know who the woman. Let`s say I don`t know who -- it`s Marla. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You say Marla is in this photo? TRUMP: That`s Marla. Yes, that`s my wife. JARRETT: Throughout the deposition, Mr. Trump steadfastly denying Carroll`s accusation and going after Carroll`s attorney. TRUMP : You know, it`s not true too. You`re a political operative also. You`re a -- you`re a disgrace. JARRETT: Later, turning to her physical appearance. TRUMP : You wouldn`t be a choice of mine either, to be honest with you. I hope you`re not insulted. I would not, under any circumstances, have any interest in you. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Laura, this is the only time the jury is going to actually hear from Mr. Trump. JARRETT (on camera): Right, Lester. Mr. Trump`s attorney has opted not to put on a defense case. The judge is giving the former president until 5:00 p.m. Sunday to change his mind. If not, closing arguments are expected on Monday. Lester? HOLT: Laura Jarrett, thank you. The Supreme Court has stepped into temporarily halt the planned execution this month of an Oklahoma man whose case has drawn support from both sides of the death penalty debate. Tonight, my exclusive interview with Richard Glossip on the day a dramatic new twist in his case unfolded. [19:05:00] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) HOLT (voiceover): Less than two weeks before his scheduled execution, Richard Glossip once again waits at death`s door, like he has so many times before. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And incarcerated individual at Oklahoma State Penitentiary. HOLT: Richard, how many execution dates have you had? RICHARD GLOSSIP, PRISONER CURRENTLY AT DEATH ROW: Nine. HOLT: And three of those, you were within minutes of being executed. GLOSSIP: Yes, three of them. I was fed my last meals. HOLT: Each time he was given a last-minute stay. This morning, Glossip called me from Oklahoma`s death row, his last interview before his new date to die, believing he had 13 days to live. Glossip, a former motel manager, convicted of organizing the 1997 murder of his boss, Barry Van Treese, but he maintains his innocence. I think you know the question I have to start off with and that is did you have anything to do with the murder of Barry Van Treese? GLOSSIP: I did not. HOLT: And you might be surprised who believes him and is fighting for him. KEVIN MCDUGLE (R-OK), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: These people should be ashamed. They should be arrested. These two men are not Glossip`s defense attorneys. They are pro-death penalty conservative lawmakers, Oklahoma representatives J.J. Humphrey and Kevin McDugle. MCDUGLE: I don`t think they`ve got enough to convict him of Jay Walking. J.J. HUMPHREY (R-OK), STATE REPRESENTATIVE: There`s no doubt, no doubt that he`s innocent of murder. HOLT: McDugle and Humphrey are desperate to save Glossip`s life. They point to two independent reviews. Both determine the original investigation was corrupt. HUMPHREY: This is unjust. I mean, this is a case where literally the prosecution team has tried to hide everything that they`ve done. One of the prosecutors, literally, we have it in writing, that she tried to change the testimony of the actual murderer. HOLT: Even the state`s Republican attorney general doesn`t think Glossip should be put to death. And in a rare move just this week, the A.G. asked the Supreme Court to grant a stay of execution. The answer came today in the middle of our interview. None of us saw it coming. I just handed a note. The U.S. Supreme Court halts execution of Oklahoma death row inmate Richard Glossip, whose case has drawn support from state`s Republican attorney general. MCDUGLE: Yes, that`s awesome, awesome. HUMPHREY: I tell you, we thought they would do it. Oklahoma is finally going to have the opportunity to look under the hood. The decision granting a temporary stay of execution, giving the court more time to review Glossip`s case. Minutes after the decision, we spoke to Glossip`s attorney Don Knight. DON KNIGHT, ATTORNEY FOR RICHARD GLOSSIP: We are thrilled that this -- that the court granted this stay of execution. This is something that we`ve been asking for a long time. We know that Rich Glossip is innocent. HOLT: Yet another reprieve for Glossip for now, but maybe not forever. GLOSSIP: I either let this consume me or I make peace with it and try to live the best I can with what life I have left. And that`s what I try to do. I`m scared to death. Don`t get me wrong. I don`t want anybody to think that I`m taking it lightly or anything, but you have to make peace with the situation. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT (on camera): We have reached out to both the district attorney and the victim`s family after today`s news but have not heard back from either. However, after a recent hearing, the family members said they believe Glossip is guilty. As the war in Ukraine grinds on, tonight, a major rift has escalated between the head of a Russian mercenary group fighting in eastern Ukraine and Russia`s military leaders. And he`s given them an ultimatum. Richard Engel has the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) RICHARD ENGEL, NBC NEWS CHIEF FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): It`s been called the biggest land battle since World War II, Bakhmut in eastern Ukraine. For months, a group of mercenaries known as the Wagner group has been leading the charge here where Russia has gained ground. Much to the embarrassment of the Russian army, which to undercut its rival has, according to the mercenaries, been blocking the delivery of supplies. Today, the head of Wagner standing over the bodies of his fighters said he`ll quit Bakhmut next week unless his men get more ammunition. Russia is feeling the pressure. It accuses the United States of conspiring with Ukraine to carry out a drone attack against the Kremlin itself, calling it an attempted assassination on President Putin. Allegations the U.S. and Ukraine strongly deny. JOHN KIRBY, STRATEGIC COMMUNICATIONS COORDINATOR, NATIONAL SECURITY COUNCIL: One thing I can tell you for certain is that the United States was not involved in this incident in any way. ENGEL: Today, Russia`s Foreign Minister promised a response with what he called concrete actions. And negotiations aren`t going well. In Turkey, talks over access to the Black Sea got heated when a Ukrainian delegate photobombed a Russian negotiator, the frustrated Russian turn back and snatched the Ukrainian flag. Turkey condemned the behavior as undiplomatic. (END VIDEOTAPE) [19:10:06] ENGEL: When asked about the Wagner group`s potential pull out from Bakhmut, the Kremlin`s response was no comment. Lester? ENGEL: Richard Engel tonight, thank you. We have breaking news about the death of a man in a New York City subway. Jordan Neely died this week after he was put on a choke hold by another passenger. Some riders said Neely had been threatening people on board. NBC has learned that the case is expected to go to a grand jury to decide if charges will be filed against the man who put Neely in that choke hold. He was questioned by police and released. Now, to the border crisis with officials bracing for a rush of migrants when that pandemic border restriction known as Title 42 expires next week. The Biden administration facing bipartisan criticism. And tonight, the Homeland Security Secretary is responding in an interview with Julia Ainsley. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JULIA AINSLEY, NBC NEWS HOMELAND SECURITY CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, just a week from the lifting of that border restriction known as Title 42, growing numbers of migrants crossing into the U.S. All as the Border Patrol expects illegal border crossings will spike to 10,000 per day when Title 42 lifts. Are you worried about Title 42 lifting next week? ALEJANDRO MAYORKAS, U.S. SECRETARY OF HOMELAND SECURITY: I`m not worried about Title 42 lifting. We recognize the challenge at the border. Our responsibility is to plan and to execute on those plans. And that is indeed what we have done and continue to do. AINSLEY: Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas here to talk to border agents. The Biden administration has faced criticism over its border policies amid a record number of illegal border crossings. Mayorkas insisting the policies are working. Is our border secure? MAYORKAS: Our border is secure. The border is secure because we are maximizing our resources to deliver the most effective results to our border with the most extraordinary workforce in the world. AINSLEY: But Hidalgo County Sheriff Eddie Guerra disagrees. Is our border secure? EDDIE GUERRA, SHERIFF, HIDALGO COUNTY: Well, I can tell you no. There`s a lot of places on the southwestern border that the -- our federal partners do not have control. (END VIDEOTAPE) AINSLEY: As for the bipartisan proposal in Congress to extend Title 42, Secretary Mayorkas told us that the Biden administration has already tried to end Title 42 several times, and now is the time to do so. Lester? HOLT: All right, Julia, thank you. Just ours are now, something that Britain and the world have not seen in seven decades, the core nation of a new British monarch. Keir Simmons is watching it all for us from London. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS CHIEF INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The night before the biggest day of his life, King Charles smiling and laughing. Palace officials say he`s shown no sign of nerves. Today, the Princess of Wales pictured with two first ladies, Jill Biden and Ukraine`s Olena Zelenska . The King, William and Catherine greeting the public earlier. WILLIAM, PRINCE OF WALES: How are you doing? SIMMONS : The Princess asked how the children are feeling. Prince George will be a page of honor tomorrow. CATHERINE, PRINCESS OF WALES He`s excited, a bit nervous. Obviously with a big day ahead. But, No, can`t wait actually. SIMMONS : Even taking a cell phone to console someone`s American relative too ill to make it. CATHERINE: I hope you get back as soon. SIMMONS : The crowds have already camped along the world-famous Mall for a glimpse of history tomorrow morning. At 5:20 Eastern, a small procession will leave Buckingham Palace with the King to Westminster Abbey. Then the solemn service, not seen this century, will commence. The moment of crowning is expected around 7:00 a.m. Next, a breathtaking spectacle. From the Abbey, a 4,000-strong military parade would escort the King along this route. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: And he won`t answer questions about why. SIMMONS : But polls show enthusiasm for the monarchy waning and protesters will be out too. GRAHAM SMITH, CEO, REPUBLIC: I would think the monarchy is in a lot of trouble because they`ve lost their star player. SIMMONS : The King is looking to answer those critics by combining tradition with change tomorrow. Manju Malhi, a chef, has been invited for her charity work. MANJU MALHI, CHEF: I feel included and very inclusive and part of British history being a daughter of an immigrant. (END VIDEOTAPE) SIMMONS : Meanwhile, Prince Harry is here in London tonight. He will not play a formal role tomorrow. But Buckingham Palace is not saying who will appear on the famous balcony behind me. They say we`ll find out when it happens. Lester? HOLT: All right, Keir Simmons in London, thank you. In 60 seconds, the landmark moment in the fight against COVID. Plus, why trade schools are becoming the bold new trend in education. And the battle over birth control. The FDA is set to consider whether a pill can be sold over the counter. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:15:00] HOLT: We are back with a remarkable announcement from the World Health Organization that the COVID global health emergency is officially over. It`s a milestone three years after the start of the pandemic that killed millions in upended economies across the globe. Officials say vaccines and high levels of immunity significantly cut the risk, but they caution the virus is still a threat. Turning out of the economy less than four weeks away from the country potentially defaulting if there`s no deal to raise the debt ceiling. Economists say that will be catastrophic. Still, markets close sharply higher today as the economy added 253,000 jobs last month and unemployment fell to 3.4 percent. Catie Beck now on the uncertainty that lies ahead. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CATIE BECK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): President Biden today highlighting the good. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Unemployment rate is at 3.4 percent, which is the lowest in 50 years. BECK: But accusing Republicans who want spending cuts of putting the economy at risk over the debt ceiling. BIDEN: They`re trying to hold the debt hostage to us to agree to some draconian cuts, magnificently difficult and damaging cuts. BECK: A possible default on the debt along with rising interest rates and ongoing turmoil among banks fueling fears of a recession. But an uncertain economic future is something Abbie Carlson is preparing for. Her decision to go to trade school wasn`t easy one. ABBIE CARLSON, STUDIES AT A TRADE SCHOOL: People are finding out that with a four-year degree, they`re not making a whole lot of money off the bat and they`re ending up with all of debt. BECK: She`ll graduate with none thanks to state funding for the program. Carlson will finish her training in welding in October. Is the common knowledge among students, we`re going to be hired right away when we leave here? CARLSON: Yes, 100 percent. If you don`t leave with a job, it`s on you. BECK: Tennessee College of Applied Technology President Nathan Garrett says there`s a waitlist to get in. NATHAN GARRETT, PRESIDENT, COLLEGE OF APPLIED TECHNOLOGY: I think at the end of the day, people are really looking at where`s the value at? BECK: Trade program enrollment is surging with big spikes in construction up almost seven percent, and mechanic and repair programs up five percent last fall, while undergraduate college enrollment has declined in recent years. CARLSON: I have hope for the future like I never did before. BECK: Hopeful for opportunity even in an uncertain economy. Catie Beck, NBC News, Nashville. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Still ahead tonight, the battle over birth control as the FDA gets sent away in and whether to sell pills without a prescription. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: A revolutionary change could be coming to birth control, pills sold without a prescription. A group of FDA advisors is set to meet next week to consider the measure. Maggie Vespa has details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MAGGIE VESPA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In an era of historic shifts in reproductive health, a push for an American first over the counter, birth control pills. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I think that`s great. I feel like it`s necessary. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Without a doubt, this is a right that everybody should have access to. VESPA: Advisors to the Food and Drug Administration meeting next week to review drug maker Perrigo`s application to sell its oral contraceptive, Opil, over the counter. It`s been available for 50 years with a prescription like all birth control pills in the U.S. Perrigo aiming to offer it to all women and teens, no doctor needed. DR. KRISTYN BRANDI, FELLOW, AMERICAN COLLEGE OF OBSTETRICIANS AND GYNECOLOGISTS : I`m surprised that this hasn`t happened already. People can self-screen. People can read instructions. And so, we shouldn`t be limiting people`s access to care. VESPA: It`s unclear how much Opil would cost, whether it would be available on store shelves or behind a pharmacist counter and whether a minor would need parental consent. An initial FDA review, flagging concerns about whether adolescents can understand the label`s instructions and whether current and former breast cancer patients, who the FDA says should not be on hormonal birth control, would know to avoid it. Perrigo writing its application demonstrates that Opil is safe and effective. Experts noting any decision on Opil will have no impact on other prescription birth controls or on lawsuits over the abortion pill, Mifepristone. (END VIDEOTAPE) VESPA (on camera): The FDA`s final decision on the push to sell Opil over the counter is expected this summer. Lester? HOLT: All right, Maggie, thank you. When we come back, London`s monarchy mania. Just how far some travel to be in the middle of all the royal excitement. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally tonight, the Royal fans who traveled across the pond for a front-row seat to King Charles` coronation. Here`s Kelly Cobiella. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KELLY COBIELLA, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the flags are flying, the horses prancing, the crowds dressed in their best red, white, and blue for the first coronation in 70 years. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It`s just an awesome time to witness history. I mean, we haven`t done this in our lifetimes. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes. COBIELLA: The monarch`s smiling face is everywhere, from windows to fridge magnets. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: He`s our king. He`s going to be our super king. COBIELLA: A super king with super fans. And we found plenty of Americans. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I just love it. I just absolutely eat it up. COBIELLA: Braving the rain for a front-row seat to history. Cassandra Estrella Rocha from California changed her vacation plans to be here. Have you been camping here? CASSANDRA ESTRELLA ROCHA FROM CALIFORNIA, AMERICAN TOURIST: Yes. COBIELLA: Oh, my gosh. ROCHA: And I`m not a camper. COBIELLA: Why? ROCHA: I want to be a part of history. Like, I just think -- you know, in America, we don`t have things like this, right? COBIELLA: As the skies cleared, surprise handshakes from the King, telling greatest hits radio London News -- CHARLES III, KING OF THE UNITED KINGDOM: Rain`s a blessing, except for your camera. COBIELLA: A smiling king, a cheering crowd, and tomorrow, the crowning moment. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I think he`s an amazing, amazing guy, and I`m proud to be a Brit. Long live the queen -- the king. COBIELLA: Kelly Cobiella, NBC News, London. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And NBC`s coverage of Charles` coronation starts at 5:00 a.m. Eastern tomorrow morning. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Friday. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. headline: New Guidelines For Breast Cancer Screening
story_text: LESTER HOLT: There is major news tonight about women in breast cancer. Government experts now say mammograms should begin much earlier, at age 40. Erin McLaughlin has details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ERIN MCLAUGHLIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, a leading health panel now recommending mammogram screenings for breast cancer begin for women at age 40, a full decade sooner than the panel`s previous guidelines. Experts say it`s about time. DR. MAXINE JOCHELSON, CHIEF OF BREAST IMAGING, MEMORIAL SLOAN KETTERING : The science has always been there. That`s why many of us have been recommending 40 for years. MCLAUGHLIN (on camera): So, finally this panel is listening to that science? JOCHELSON: Yes. MCLAUGHLIN (voiceover): The draft recommendations come from the U.S. preventative Services Task Force. They say the new guidelines could save 20 percent more lives across the board for all women, emphasizing the new guidelines are especially important for black women. DR. CAROL MANGIONE, US. PREVENTIVE SERVICES TASK FORCE: Black women are 40 percent more likely to die from breast cancer than white women if they get it. They also are more likely to get more aggressive forms of breast cancer. MCLAUGHLIN: The panel stopping short of recommending annual mammogram screenings, maintaining that women still screen every two years. MCLAUGHLIN (on camera): Does this recommendation go far enough? JOCHELSON: No. MCLAUGHLIN (voiceover): She argues women 40 and over should get screenings every year and says women should start talking with their doctors about risk factors at age 25. Still, experts are hopeful these new recommendations will help send a more consistent message. [19:15:13] MANGIONE: The most important thing for women to know is to begin screening at the age of 40 because it just might save your life. MCLAUGHLIN: Erin McLaughlin, NBC News. HOLT: In a moment, NBC News investigates work contracts with the nation`s largest hospital chain nurses say they`ve been a threat to their health and yours. headline: Frustrated Over Getting Quality Care: What Mothers To Be Want In The Delivery Room
story_text: [19:20:00] LESTER HOLT: As Mother`s Day approaches, we`re reminded pregnancy and childbirth can come with health risks. And for Black women, those risks are significantly higher. Zinhle Essamuah now on why more mothers are working with doulas. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ZINHLE ESSAMUAH, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Kanaiah King`s (ph) first pregnancy in 2021 was traumatic. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Good job. Everything that could go wrong went wrong. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): She went into labor early at just 24 weeks and had a serious infection. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You know, doctors kind of use the big words, thinking you would know, but I didn`t. It was my first time. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): But the St. Louis native had support from a doula, Robin Lloyd. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Ms. Robin would literally stop them like, hey, stop. Let me talk to her. And she would tell me exactly what it meant. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): Birthing doulas are trained nonclinical professionals who support clients through pregnancy, labor, delivery, and postpartum. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We all are going through the same thing. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): The doulas offer one-on-one education. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: No question is a dumb question. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): And group courses for expectant and new moms. Kanaiah credits Robin for helping her get through it all? ESSAMUAH: What are you feeling? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m very grateful for her. I`m very grateful for her. Because if she wasn`t there, I don`t know what would have happened. ESSAMUAH: Do you think you would be here and your kids would be here if you hadn`t had a doula? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Not at all, no. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists finding doulas-improved outcomes for women and labor. They`re especially critical for Black women, who are three times more likely to die from a pregnancy-related cause than White women. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You`re so cute. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): Kanaiah`s doula, Robin, works with the nonprofit Parents as Teachers, motivated by her own life-threatening delivery. The nonprofit received state funding, making it possible to provide doula services to families cost-free. Of the nearly 320 families they serve, many unhoused, 95 percent are people of color, and all of their doulas are Black women. ESSAMUAH: Why is it particularly important for women of color and Black women to have access to them? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Well, I think -- I think access is the key. We wanted to make sure that we had Black doulas serving those families that resemble them. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): Now, Kanaiah is expecting a baby boy in just a few weeks with Robin by her side. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m going to be there. You know, you`re going to have that support and not to worry. ESSAMUAH (voiceover): Zinhle Essamuah, NBC News, St. Louis, Missouri. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, the moving reunion for one man who nearly died in a supermarket and the hero nurses who saved his life. headline: A Federal Appeals Court Hearing Arguments On Limiting Access Nationwide To A Widely Used Abortion Pill, A Fight Ultimately Heading To The Supreme Court
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Now to the battle over abortion. A federal appeals court hearing arguments on limiting access nationwide to a widely used abortion pill, a fight ultimately heading to the Supreme Court, while some states restrict abortion further. Here`s Laura Jarrett. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the most commonly used abortion pill still on the market, but its legal future uncertain. A federal appeals court appearing deeply skeptical today of arguments from the Biden administration and pill manufacturer as they try to keep Mifepristone available. JAMES HO, JUDGE: I don`t understand this theme. The FDA can do no wrong. We are allowed to look at the FDA, just like we`re allowed to look at any agency. JARRETT (voiceover): The three-judge panel must decide what to do with that controversial decision out of Texas last month, which invalidated the FDA`s longtime approval of the drug. One judge hearing the case appointed by George W. Bush , the other two by Donald Trump. All have a history of supporting abortion restrictions. Judge James Ho calling abortion a moral tragedy in a 2018 case. The stakes of what happens to a pill women can currently get in the mail even higher now with new abortion restrictions emerging at the state level. TIM MOORE, HOUSE SPEAKER, NORTH CAROLINA: We needed to take action to protect the unborn. JARRETT (voiceover): Overnight in North Carolina, a GOP supermajority banned most abortions after 12 weeks with few exceptions, overriding the governor`s veto. DR. BEVERLY GRAY, OBSTETRICS AND GYNECOLOGY ASSOCIATE PROFESSOR, DUKE UNIVERSITY : The law is incredibly arbitrary. And it was crafted by people who are not physicians. It`s really important to note that when there`s a list of exceptions, someone is always left out. JARRETT (voiceover): North Carolina had been an outlier among the sea of states that restricted access after the Supreme Court decided women don`t have a constitutional right to an abortion. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Every pregnancy threatens the life of mothers. JARRETT (voiceover): In neighboring South Carolina, a six-week ban like Florida`s is on the horizon. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for May 17, 2023, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Tonight, Prince Harry and wife Meghan pursued by paparazzi. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) HOLT (voiceover): Conflicting accounts of what happened late last night in the busy streets of New York. Was it a near catastrophic car chase for more than two hours as a spokesperson for Harry claims or what the police called a challenging trip home as photographers pursued them with no reported collisions or injuries? We talked to the cab driver who drove them. An Idaho grand jury indicts Bryan Kohberger accused of killing four college students. The new details just revealed. As a federal court set to restrict access to a widely used abortion pill, the battle bound for the Supreme Court as North Carolina enacts a restrictive abortion law. President Biden heads overseas while striking an optimistic tone that the country will never default as negotiators race to reach a debt limit deal. A former Green Beret killed in Ukraine. What he told NBC News about why he decided to join the fight. The teenager missing for six years finally found after a TV show and a tip. How thieves are getting into your iPhone and stealing everything. The threat and how to protect your data. The first state of the country to ban TikTok. But will it hold? And the Titanic as we`ve never seen it. Spectacular new images that may shed light on why it sank. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. (END VIDEO CLIP) HOLT (on camera): Good evening and welcome. What happened on the streets of New York City last night involving one of the world`s most famous couples was either a near catastrophic car chase as their spokesman says or arrived that law enforcement sources say was simply a bit chaotic. That spokesman for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, Harry and Meghan, describing a dangerous two-hour long chase pursued by highly aggressive paparazzi, resulting in multiple near collisions. The episode rekindling grim memories of the wild pursuit that led to the death of Harry`s mother, Princess Diana in a Paris highway tunnel nearly 26 years ago. But tonight in New York, officials are describing what happened to Harry and Meghan as something less harrowing than reported. And that`s where we start tonight with Gabe Gutierrez. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Meghan! Meghan! Meghan! GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan Markle , seen here leading a charity event in New York. And tonight, there appeared to be differing accounts about what happened next. A spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex admonishing photographers for a relentless pursuit that lasted two hours and resulted in multiple near collisions involving other drivers on the road, pedestrians, and two NYPD officers. Adding, the near-catastrophic car chase came at the hands of a ring of highly aggressive paparazzi. ERIC ADAMS, MAYOR, NEW YORK CITY: The briefing I received, you know, two of our officers could have been injured. I thought that was a bit reckless and irresponsible. GUTIERREZ (voiceover): Though tonight, at least three law enforcement sources tell NBC News, the couple was followed, not chased, and that the incident was a bit chaotic, not near catastrophic. ADAMS: I would find it hard to believe that there was a two-hour high-speed chase. GUTIERREZ (voiceover): In a written statement, the NYPD says numerous photographers made the couple`s transport challenging, but there were no reported collisions, injuries, or arrests. GUTIERREZ: Harry and Meghan had private security as they left this venue. And two law enforcement sources tell NBC News that they wanted to return to Manhattan`s upper east side, where they were staying with a friend, and did not want the paparazzi to follow. GUTIERREZ (voiceover): So, the law enforcement sources say the couple was driven up and down Manhattan for more than an hour with a police escort. Then the pair was taken to this police precinct where a taxi picked them up. GUTIERREZ: Would you describe it as chaotic? SONNY SINGH, TAXICAB DRIVER: Yes, chaotic. You could say chaotic. With me - - GUTIERREZ: Catastrophic? SINGH: I don`t know what happened previous in the day, right? With me, it was chaotic, but not crazy, crazy, right? GUTIERREZ: Do you think the paparazzi went too far? SINGH: You know, I don`t know. When we were -- they kept their distance when they were following us in my cab. GUTIERREZ (voiceover): Sonny Singh told us he`s the taxi driver who picked up the couple. But he says they drove around for only 10 minutes before the street was blocked by a garbage truck. SINGH: People just came out of nowhere with cameras and started snapping pictures. GUTIERREZ: Did they seem worried? SINGH: They seem worried. They seem worried and nervous as well. GUTIERREZ (voiceover): He then says he dropped them back off at the police precinct where a different car eventually took them home. Prince Harry , of course, has railed against the paparazzi for much of his life, accusing them of invading his privacy. HARRY, DUKE OF SUSSEX: I had to do everything I could to protect my family. GUTIERREZ (voiceover): Though critics say Harry and Meghan also court the cameras and publicity pointing to their Netflix docu-series. HARRY: No one sees what`s happening behind closed doors. [19:05:02] GUTIERREZ (voiceover): It was 26 years ago this summer that his mother, Princess Diana, died during a car chase in Paris. HARRY: You get followed, photograph, chase, harassed. The clicking of cameras and the flashes of cameras makes my blood boil. It makes me angry. It takes me back to what happened to my mom I experienced when I was a kid. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: All right, Gabe joined us from outside that police precinct. Gabe, was there any video of the pursuit? GUTIERREZ (on camera): Well, Lester, source close to Harry and Meghan says that there is a security video that captured the encounter, but it has not yet been publicly released, Lester. HOLT: All right, Gabe, thanks. Let me turn now to Keir Simmons in London. And Keir, a lot of people immediately thought about Princess Diana when they heard about this. KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS CHIEF INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: And you know, Lester, inevitably, that is one of the first things that Prince Harry will have thought of when this happened, that terrible night when he lost his mom. Listen, there are parallels. Princess Diana was trying to escape the paparazzi just like Harry and Meghan this week. Princess Diana had lost her royal protection. Prince Harry no longer has royal protection. But there`s also Lester, important context here, too. Prince Harry is fighting a legal battle with the British press. This isn`t just about the past for him. This is about the future. He seems determined to keep fighting, even to change the media. But Lester, there are those who question whether he can win that fight. HOLT: All right, Keir Simmons in London, thank you. New developments this evening in the brutal killings of those four University of Idaho students. The suspect has been indicted. And as Erin McLaughlin reports, we will see him in court soon. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ERIN MCLAUGHLIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight in Moscow, Idaho, Bryan Kohberger, the man charged with stabbing four college students to death, now indicted by a grand jury. The indictment includes four counts of murder in the first degree and one count of burglary. If found guilty, he could be sentenced to death. Kohberger has yet to enter a plea, but his previous attorney said he believes he`ll be exonerated. The indictment follows his December arrest at his family home in Pennsylvania. More than 45 days after Maddy Mogen, Kaylee Goncalves, Xana Kernodle, and were found brutally murdered in this college house. According to court documents, Kohberger`s DNA was found on a knife sheet at the crime scene. And his white Hyundai Elantra scene driving here during a routine traffic stop. It was also allegedly caught on camera in the area the night of the killings. One of two surviving roommates telling police, she saw a male figure with bushy eyebrows, a mask, and black clothing in the home that night. MCLAUGHLIN: So, this grand jury indictment simplifies the process for the surviving witnesses. JEAN FISHER, FORMER DEPUTY PROSECUTING ATTORNEY, ADA COUNTY, IDAHO: Absolutely, because they don`t have to testify in front of Kohberger during this preliminary proceeding. MCLAUGHLIN (voiceover): News of the indictment is the latest twist in a grisly case that`s left a small university community heartbroken. Last weekend, Kaylee and Maddy both received posthumous degrees. (END VIDEOTAPE) MCLAUGHLIN (on camera): Kohberger will be arraigned on Monday. Legal experts say once he enters a plea, the trial must begin within six months unless he waves his right to a speedy trial. Lester? HOLT: Erin, thank you. Now to the battle over abortion. A federal appeals court hearing arguments on limiting access nationwide to a widely used abortion pill, a fight ultimately heading to the Supreme Court, while some states restrict abortion further. Here`s Laura Jarrett. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the most commonly used abortion pill still on the market, but its legal future uncertain. A federal appeals court appearing deeply skeptical today of arguments from the Biden administration and pill manufacturer as they try to keep Mifepristone available. JAMES HO, JUDGE: I don`t understand this theme. The FDA can do no wrong. We are allowed to look at the FDA , just like we`re allowed to look at any agency. JARRETT (voiceover): The three-judge panel must decide what to do with that controversial decision out of Texas last month, which invalidated the FDA`s longtime approval of the drug. One judge hearing the case appointed by George W. Bush , the other two by Donald Trump . All have a history of supporting abortion restrictions. Judge James Ho calling abortion a moral tragedy in a 2018 case. The stakes of what happens to a pill women can currently get in the mail even higher now with new abortion restrictions emerging at the state level. TIM MOORE, HOUSE SPEAKER, NORTH CAROLINA: We needed to take action to protect the unborn. JARRETT (voiceover): Overnight in North Carolina, a GOP supermajority banned most abortions after 12 weeks with few exceptions, overriding the governor`s veto. DR. BEVERLY GRAY, OBSTETRICS AND GYNECOLOGY ASSOCIATE PROFESSOR, DUKE UNIVERSITY : The law is incredibly arbitrary. And it was crafted by people who are not physicians. It`s really important to note that when there`s a list of exceptions, someone is always left out. JARRETT (voiceover): North Carolina had been an outlier among the sea of states that restricted access after the Supreme Court decided women don`t have a constitutional right to an abortion. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Every pregnancy threatens the life of mothers. JARRETT (voiceover): In neighboring South Carolina, a six-week ban like Florida`s is on the horizon. (END VIDEOTAPE) [19:10:07] HOLT: So, Laura, help me understand where we are. The -- it`s for the abortion pill. The justices agreed last month to keep it on the market during the appeal process. JARRETT (on camera): That`s exactly right, Lester. And there`s no deadline for the appeals court to rule on Mifepristone. But once it makes a decision, the case is inevitably headed back to the Supreme Court for a final say. HOLT: All right, Laura Jarrett, thanks. JARRETT: Sure. HOLT: President Biden is heading to Asia tonight for the G7 summit as the U.S. inches closer to a critical default deadline. Kristen Welker is in Hiroshima. Kristen, the President with a clear message before leaving today. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: Lester, that`s right. President Biden projecting optimism with just 15 days to reach a deal to raise the debt limit or risk economic calamity. While still in Washington, the President said he`s confident the country won`t default, calling a meeting with top congressional leaders this week productive. The president has cut short part of this critical diplomatic trip to deal with the crisis. But despite that, Republican House Speaker Kevin McCarthy blasting Mr. Biden this afternoon for going overseas at all before a deal is done. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker, thank you. Breaking news from Ukraine tonight. Another American volunteer, former Green Beret, has been killed in battle there. Molly Hunter has more on his decision to fight as new images show the immense toll of war in the east. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MOLLY HUNTER, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, as this grinding war continues to rob young Ukrainian lives on the battlefield, the family of American volunteer soldier Nicholas Maimer telling NBC News he was killed on Ukraine`s front lines. The 45-year-old Idaho native, now one of at least 10 Americans killed since the war started. He arrived on his own to join the fight in May 2022. And months before his death, he spoke to NBC`s Raf Sanchez, protecting his identity, going by the name Sema. The 20-year U.S. Army veteran training volunteer soldiers outside of Kyiv. NICHOLAS MAIMER, AMERICAN KILLED IN UKRAINE: I had that strong internal debate on whether I should, what I could contribute, you know, should I accept the risk? And ultimately, I decided that it was worth it to help Ukraine. HUNTER (voiceover): And worth the risk. RAF SANCHEZ, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT: Have you been to the east? MAIMER: I signed up knowing that but with the statement that I was willing to fight. HUNTER: Ukraine says they now have the momentum in Bakhmut, fighting hard for what little remains. Today, new satellite imagery appears to show the devastating toll from May 2022 to the charred earth of this month. (END VIDEOTAPE) HUNTER (on camera): Tonight, Russia is claiming they destroyed launchers, part of U.S.-made Patriot Air Defense Systems in that massive attack yesterday. Well, tonight, two U.S. officials telling NBC News a Patriot system incurred damage, but is fully operational. Lester? HOLT: Molly Hunter, thank you. In 60 seconds, a mystery solved. A girl missing for six years found. The new details about the tit that led to her discovery all after a TV show about the case. Stay with us. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: We have new details in the shocking case of a missing girl finally found alive after six years thanks to a tip from a teen who saw the girl`s story on a true crime show. Maggie Vespa reports. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KAYLA UNBEHAUN, SIX YEARS MISSING: Hi, this is Taylor here. I have a cat. MAGGIE VESPA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, new details in the crucial tip that brought Kayla Unbehaun home. Six years after police say her mother, who did not have legal custody, kidnapped her. Investigators in North Carolina now say a teen girl working at an Asheville clothing store Saturday spotted Kayla and recognized the now 15-year-old. JONATHAN BROWN, ASHVILLE, NORTH CAROLINA POLICE DEPARTMENT: The employee of the store had a personal connection through their childhood. VESPA (voiceover): The tipster also crediting the hit show Unsolved Mysteries which featured Kayla`s case last fall. BROWN: The media attention that this case has received over the years up to and including the Netflix documentary most likely heightened her awareness. [19:15:08] VESPA (voiceover): Kayla and her mom, police say, initially giving officers fake names and birthdays. Kayla seeming calm. BROWN: She looked relatively healthy, didn`t appear to be in any type of physical trauma. VESPA: Police soon uncovered the pair`s true identities. Tonight, they say Kayla is back home in Illinois. Her mother, Heather Unbehaun charged with kidnapping. The remarkable homecoming following years of pleas from Kayla`s dad, Ryan Iskerka, on multiple true crime shows. RYAN ISKERKA, FATHER OF KAYLA UNBEHAUN: My daughter was gone. VESPA: Tonight, Iskerka writing in a statement, I`m overjoyed that Kayla is home safe, adding we ask for privacy as we get to know each other again and navigate this new beginning. (END VIDEOTAPE) VESPA: Heather Unbehaun is out on $25,000 bond. Her attorney declined to comment. Lester? HOLT: Maggie Vespa, thank you. Still ahead, the first state to ban TikTok, but will it hold? Plus, a new warning, thieves stealing iPhones, passcodes, and even locking you out of all your data. How to protect yourself? Next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Montana today became the first state to ban TikTok. The governor is signing a bill that will bar the Chinese-owned video app from operating in the state because of privacy and security concerns. It will also prohibit mobile app stores like Apple and Google from offering TikTok in the state. A challenge on First Amendment grounds is expected as Congress debates limiting TikTok. Turning now to the important warning. Thieves are stealing iPhones and passwords to hijack all your personal information. Stephanie Gosk explains how they`re doing it and how to protect yourself. [19:20:15] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) STEPHANIE GOSK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Just behind the locked screen of an iPhone, a goldmine of money, memories, and connections, and thieves have found a way in. JOANNA STERN, SENIOR PERSONAL TECH COLUMNIST, WALL STREET JOURNAL: They`re stealing your passcode. GOSK: It`s so sinister. STERN: It`s so sinister but also so simple. GOSK: So, they go to places where people are vulnerable. STERN: Drunk. People are vulnerable. They`re drunk. They`re having good time. GOSK (voiceover): Joanna Stern covers tech for the Wall Street Journal. She`s done a series of reports exposing a new crime wave. Phones being ripped off at bars leading to tens of thousands of dollars stolen and Apple accounts locked. STERN: I was blown away by how many people I heard from that had been to different cities across the U. S. GOSK (voiceover): NBC`s digital team also helped uncover a ring of thieves allegedly targeting gay bars in Manhattan. Victims are drugged. Their phones stolen. Two men John Umberger and Julio Ramirez overdosed and died. Three suspects are charged with murder. Taylor Ashie says he too was drugged and a victim of theft, waking up after a night out and realizing his phone was gone. TAYLOR ASHIE, VICTIM OF THEFT: I immediately got up, went to check my computer to see what was going on. I had about 20 to 25 fraud alert emails. GOSK (voiceover): He says the thieves changed his Apple ID password, locked him out, and then went on a shopping spree. ASHIE: They added my credit cards to Apple Pay which I had not previously used, and then they went around New York City using my phone as a credit card. GOSK (voiceover): Ashie would get roughly $15,000 back but what he couldn`t get restored was his Apple account. ASHIE: Hours of conversations with Apple , support staff. I never received my information back. GOSK: We`re talking about personal photos, contacts? ASHIE: Both. GOSK (voiceover): The key is getting the passcode. GOSK: How quickly can you change my Apple ID? STERN: All right, so I`m going to tap here at the top. This is your iCloud or Apple ID area. I`m going to password and security. I`m going to change password. I`m going to put in your passcode. It`s in. Is that right? GOSK: And you`re there. STERN: And I`m there. GOSK (voiceover): It took her 18 seconds. But there`s more. STERN: These thieves on the streets know how to enable something that`s a pretty hidden setting. It`s called this recovery key. GOSK (voiceover): The recovery key is supposed to add another layer of protection. STERN: The problem is that the thieves have the recovery key. Once you`ve changed someone`s Apple ID password and turned on this recovery key, it`s basically game over for the person whose account that is. GOSK (voiceover): In a statement, Apple says we take all attacks on our users very seriously no matter how rare. We work tirelessly every day to protect our user`s accounts and data and are always investigating additional protections. There are some steps to take. Make the passcode on the iPhone stronger like using six digits instead of four. STERN: You can also go here to passcode options and do a custom alphanumeric code. GOSK (voiceover): Another option is going to screen time, then content and privacy restrictions where there are several places you can add a four- digit code that will block access. The changes will make the phone less convenient. ASHIE: I feel like it`s Fort Knox on my phone now. GOSK (voiceover): But with life`s most important information in the palm of your hand, the hassle may be worth it. Stephanie Gosk, NBC News New York. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: When we come back, the astonishing new images of the Titanic like you`ve never seen it before. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally, astonishing new 3D images of a Titanic providing the most captivating view yet of the shipwreck. Here`s Tom Costello. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The images are breathtaking in their clarity and detail. The Titanic broken in two, 1200 feet below the North Atlantic. Too big for a single photo, the new 3D scan combining 700,000 images reveals the full scale of the disaster. The bow covered in rust. It`s anchor still attached. The boiler room where workers shoveled coal to keep the lights on. The propeller, its serial number, still legible. Scattered on the ocean floor unopened champagne bottles, shoes, hats and jewelry. 1500 people died that day in 1912. Edith Haisman was just 16 on board with her parents. We talked to her in 1996. EDITH HAISMAN, TITANIC SURVIVOR: I`ll never forget it, see all the dead bodies floating in the sea. It was terrible. COSTELLO (voiceover): A deep sea mapping company used submersibles to create this 360-degree view. Coming soon, a documentary looking at how an iceberg cut open a ship once branded unsinkable. COSTELLO: This makes the Titanic tragedy much more real. ANTHONY GEFFEN, CEO AND CREATIVE DIRECTOR, ATLANTIC PRODUCTIONS: There`s no doubt about that. People around the world will be able to walk around the Titanic for themselves and they`ll be able to see the wreck, they`ll be able to see the debris field. This is a history where we can live in the past. COSTELLO (voiceover): A virtual view preserved forever. Tom Costello, NBC News, Washington. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: The fascination continues. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Wednesday. Thank you for watching. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. story_text: (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) [09:00:18] CHUCK TODD, HOST, NBC`S "MEET THE PRESS WITH CHUCK TODD" (voice over): This Sunday, taking on Trump. The Republican primary field will be expanding this week as Florida Governor Ron DeSantis and South Carolina Senator Tim Scott both jump into the 2024 race. GOV. RONALD DESANTIS, (R) FLORIDA: I think the party has developed a culture of losing. SEN. TIM SCOTT, (R) SOUTH CAROLINA: It`s time for us to be proud to be Americans and proud of our president. TODD: Can either candidate make the case he`s the better alternative to Donald Trump and unite the party in the process, in the primary battle ahead? I`ll talk to Republican Congressman Byron Donalds of Florida, who`s currently backing Donald Trump . Plus, flirting with disaster. Debt ceiling negotiations break down, restart and then stop again. PRESIDENT JOSEPH R. BIDEN, JR.: Default is not an option. HOUSE SPEAKER KEVIN MCCARTHY, (R) CALIFORNIA: This White House will not acknowledge that they`re spending too much. TODD: What`s really going on inside the talks? Is either side negotiating in good faith? And how serious is the June 1st deadline for a catastrophic default? I`ll talk to Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen . And, abortion politics. Republican lawmakers in Nebraska and North Carolina pass new abortion restrictions, as Democrats prepare to fight back. GOV. ROY COOPER , (D) NORTH CAROLINA: Politicians shouldn`t push their way into the exam room with women and their doctors. (APPLAUSE) TODD: President Biden`s 2024 campaign is already planning to focus on the new ban in the swing state of North Carolina. How will the battle over abortion rights impact the 2024 race? I`ll talk to North Carolina`s Democratic Governor, Roy Cooper . (on camera): Joining me for insight and analysis are NBC News managing Washington editor, Carol Lee; Dan Balz, chief correspondent for The Washington Post ; former Republican Congressman Carlos Curbelo ; and Simone Sanders-Townsend, former chief spokesperson for Vice President Kamala Harris . Welcome to Sunday. It`s "Meet the Press." ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest-running show in television history, this is "Meet the Press With Chuck Todd." TODD: Good Sunday morning. This is going to be one of the busiest weeks yet in the presidential campaign, as the 2024 Republican field grows. So do concerns among some Republicans that none of Donald Trump`s current rivals are going to be able to beat him in a primary. South Carolina Senator Tim Scott is announcing his campaign tomorrow in his hometown of North Charleston before heading to the early states of Iowa and New Hampshire. And Florida Governor Ron DeSantis expected to formally file paperwork for president this week, a bit of a soft launch of his campaign, with a video and a donor retreat at the Four Seasons in Miami before formally having the big campaign rally announcement later in the month. But when the year began, DeSantis had the look and feel of not just a front-runner but of a potential juggernaut. But the last months have not been kind. Trump has relentlessly attacked him, and under those attacks, DeSantis has floundered a bit. He has struggled with big donors who have complained quite publicly that he, quote, "doesn`t even return phone calls." Others don`t like his position on abortion, the six-week ban, and believe it would be a problem in a general election. And still others worry about his charisma. He launched a book tour. It was immediately overshadowed when he called the Ukraine war "a territorial dispute." He walked it back after some donors complained. Then there`s the fight with Disney , where he took a political advantage and a victory, and it has now turned into a political problem. The DeSantis slump has made more Republicans who believe Donald Trump cannot win a general election flirt with jumping into this race themselves, from New Hampshire Governor Chris Sununu to North Dakota Governor Doug Burgum to former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie . And if no alternative materializes there, donors are likely to keep shopping for Republicans with general election appeal, like Governor Ryan Kemp or Governor Glenn Youngkin, who himself rolled out a curious video this week that cast himself as the successor to Ronald Reagan . In the meantime, it appears that the first big fight between the two current front-runners for the Republican nomination will actually be over the issue of abortion and whose position makes them more electable. Ironically, that electability fight may not be about January 6th and Trump`s growing legal baggage. This week Trump said that, quote, "Many people within the pro-life movement feel (DeSantis`s six-week abortion ban) was too harsh," while DeSantis responded to Trump earlier this week. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) DESANTIS: As a Florida resident, you know, he didn`t give an answer about would you have signed the heartbeat bill that Florida did, that had all the exceptions that people talk about. The legislature put it in. I signed the bill. I was proud to do it. He won`t answer whether he would sign it or not. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: And joining me now is Republican Congressman Byron Donalds of Florida. Donalds, by the way, introduced DeSantis at his election night party in November. But last month, he became one of 11 Florida congressional Republicans to endorse Donald Trump . [09:05:04] Congressman Donalds, welcome to "Meet the Press." REP. BYRON DONALDS, (R) FLORIDA: It`s good to be with you, Chuck. TODD: Before we start with the politics, sort of, the political junkie conversation, I want to talk about the debt ceiling. You`re a member of the Freedom Caucus on here. Where -- are you going to be comfortable with a deal that you probably personally won`t like, but it`s a deal that, sort of, maybe progressives don`t like and the Freedom Caucus doesn`t like, but it`s -- it can pass? Are you going to be able to accept a deal like that? DONALDS: Chuck, to be blunt with you, we`re not really sure what deal is even on the table. The White House is not serious. They came up with a proposal to spend another $30 billion more than they already wanted to spend. They`re not taking a look at the reality of where our country is fiscally. Look, Joe Biden is saying that he`s cut $1.7 trillion from the deficit, but everybody`s saying that`s not true. CARLOS CURBELO , NBC NEWS POLITICAL ANALYST: So, look, two different kinds of candidates getting into the race this week. Tim Scott, who`s going to try to get around Donald Trump , and Ron DeSantis , who doesn`t have a choice but to try to go through Donald Trump in order to get that nomination. I think, you know, if the brawl between DeSantis and Trump gets nasty enough, candidates like Scott could become interesting, could become attractive. And I also think it`s a little early to write off Ron DeSantis . I mean, if any of us were starting a presidential campaign today and we had all that money, all the resources he has -- TODD: And already in double digits -- CURBELO: And -- TODD: -- by the way. CURBELO: -- in second place, we would probably be happy. On top of that, DeSantis has a strong record to run on for a Republican primary. In a general, you know, the social issues might be a challenge, but he has a strong economic record to run on. So look, been a tough last few months. But it`s a bit early to say this guy can`t make it. TODD: Symone, what have you learned here? You were involved in a massive, what some people thought was going to become, a demolition derby on the Democratic side in 2019. All of a sudden, I think we thought we were going to have a smaller field, the field is growing. By the way, is Tim Scott the Pete Buttigieg of this crowd, meaning that he may pop here if people don`t, if people aren`t careful? SYMONE SANDERS-TOWNSEND, HOST, "SYMONE": Is he the Pete Buttigieg , or is he the Cory Booker , the person that everyone liked, but just could not catch fire with the voters? And I say that, and I like Cory Booker personally, but we saw what happened in the 2020 election. If there were less candidates then, if maybe if there were other people not in the race, could someone like Cory Booker , could have caught fire? I think it`s a question that Tim Scott himself has asked him a couple of times, his team. Obviously, this is something they`ve had to weigh. And they`ve weighed that it`s better to get in than stay out. Look, I think -- I`m with you. I think it`s early, but it`s also late. And, you know, we had this conversation -- TODD: Yogi Berra. Exactly. SANDERS-TOWNSEND: -- earlier this week, you know? It`s late early because it`s early, first debates, Republican primary debate is not until the end of August. But it`s late because Republican primary voters start voting on January 8th. That`s the Iowa caucuses. TODD: Yeah. SANDERS-TOWNSEND: So how do you build the infrastructure? How do you -- how do you become a national candidate that can connect with voters from state to state? TODD: Well, the other issue, of course, is the abortion issue. I want to put up this graphic, Carol, that we put together. Since Dobbs, it is a consistent issue here for Republicans across the board. So in 2022, you had the Kansas abortion referendum. You had a special congressional election in New York. And you, of course, you had the midterms themselves, where it was clear abortion was a huge issue. And then look what we just learned over the last couple of months. You had the Supreme Court race in Wisconsin, that abortion rights clearly helped the left there. And you have new mayors on the Democratic side in Jacksonville and an Independent; Republicans knocked out in Colorado Springs, all of them over being perceived as too out of the mainstream on social issues. Will this Republican primary even matter in the presidential because of those numbers? LEE: Well, I can tell you that the Biden team is certainly looking at this and thinking that this is an opportunity for them to expand the map in North Carolina, as well as Florida. A Biden official has told me that they think the six-week ban that Governor DeSantis signed is very significant. That they -- TODD: That`s why they want to go to Florida, you think? LEE: And they are already, they`re, quote/unquote, testing the waters there. They`re on the air. They see an opportunity here. And it all comes down to abortion. TODD: And, Dan, you pointed out in your terrific piece today two key groups in 2022 showed up for Democrats that they didn`t expect -- women without a college degree, and voters under the age of 35. BALZ: Yeah. And I think that the women without college degrees are a prime target. But I think it was the abortion issue that drew them. And I don`t know whether that`ll be the case in 2024. They could easily slip back to the Republicans. TODD: All right. We have more time, I promise. Up next, the COVID public health emergency has been declared over. So after living with three years of this virus, what was the real impact? Data Download`s next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:47:41] TODD: Welcome back. Data Download time. Earlier this month, the national emergency that surrounded the COVID-19 pandemic was officially declared over. So we wanted to take a look at just how much this three-year pandemic impacted the country as a whole. And let`s start with the greatest statistic of all, the loss of life. Overall, more than a million Americans died of COVID-19 since it first appeared here in early 2020. That is more people than the populations of Austin, Texas or Jacksonville, Florida, and it`s more people than live in the entire state of Montana. But the good news is, the current death number are among the lowest they`ve ever been. Look at this, just 281 reported last week nationwide. At its peak in early January of 2021, nearly 26,000 Americans lost their life in just a week, just a week. Now, speaking of that -- of those vaccines, according to the CDC, over 81 percent of Americans received at least one dose of a COVID vaccine. That number dropped off a little bit on second doses, as you could see here, nearly 70 percent. Well, let me tell you this. The boosters? They`re not getting -- they`re not getting bought -- used by many folks very often. Mostly, this is folks over the age of 65. It`s an indication of just how comfortable we are now living beyond this virus. But, of course, the economic impact was huge with this pandemic. Did you know we threw over $4 trillion in money from the government to try to offset what was just a huge disruption in the American economy? And even though we threw all that money at the economy, it still impacted our overall national economic trends here -- $14 trillion in lost economic activity from 2020 through the end of last year, according to researchers from the University of Southern California . Before we go to break, this week, special counsel John Durham released his long-awaited report on the Russia investigation. Well, back in 2001, Bill Clinton investigator Robert Ray joined "Meet the Press" days after striking a deal with the president to avoid an indictment, and he talked about the lessons he learned as an independent counsel. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) ROBERT RAY, INDEPENDENT COUUNSEL: The most important thing I learned is that achieving a just result for a prosecutor`s not so easy. I -- one can think exclusively within the box of being a federal prosecutor, but the position of independent counsel brings I think a larger responsibility not only to the, to the interests of justice, but also to the country`s best interests. And achieving a result that`s satisfactory to all of those concerns is not, is not an easy one. [09:50:08] It is important for the country`s confidence to know that law enforcement with regard to the integrity of public officials can work. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: We look forward to hearing from John Durham . We`ve invited him to be on this show. When we come back, we`re going to look at the impact of the Durham report on the FBI , and what role it may play for an institution that`s increasingly under partisan attack. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) TODD: Welcome back. If you only consume media on the right, you might be excused for thinking this week`s 306-page Durham report on the Russian inquiry was a "bombshell" and "damning" and that the investigation was an "abomination" and a "soft coup". But special counsel John Durham`s actual sharpest conclusions after a four- year investigation were that the FBI suffered from confirmation bias and, quote, discounted or willfully ignored material information that countered the narrative of collusion between Donald Trump and Russia. The report recommended no wholesale changes to FBI rules for regulations or wiretaps, and Durham did not send a single person to jail, even though former President Trump once predicted that Durham would uncover the crime of the century. That said, Dan Balz, this is not an FBI that should feel good about what Durham discovered because at a minimum, this issue of confirmation bias, it goes to the heart of how James Comey seemed to worry so much about what the perception of the FBI was that he -- whether it was overdid or underdid Hillary stuff and then overdid or underdid Trump stuff. [09:55:00] BALZ: Well, since, since Comey, the FBI has been under attack. And the Durham report in many ways confirms what the DOJ IG -- TODD: It`s almost identical, really. BALZ: It`s almost identical. TODD: Yeah. BALZ: And in some ways backed off some of the rhetoric that they had going into it. But the FBI `s been in a compromised position. And part of that has to do with the nature of our politics today. The FBI has become a politicized institution and a political target, and this is going to make it much more difficult for Merrick Garland as he goes forward with these investigations, and I don`t see any way out of that in the -- anywhere in the near future. TODD: No. And let me throw in this headline from your newspaper, Dan. FBI misused surveillance tool on January 6th suspects, BLM, Black Lives Matter arrestees and others. Symone, I -- look, trust in the FBI is eroding left and right. Feels like we`re in a moment that we need a real Church Committee, that this is a moment like J -- when the J. Edgar Hoover FBI clearly was no longer helping the American people, there was a moment. This feels like we might be in one of those moments. SANDERS-TOWNSEND: I would say yes and no, okay? Yes, because obviously, we -- I mean, as Dan was talking, I thought about the activists -- the civil rights activists, Black Lives Matter activists, Black Panthers -- TODD: Who have also been -- SANDERS-TOWNSEND: -- who have been targets of the FBI for eons and years, okay, going back to well before this current political climate that we sit in. But FBI agents, law enforcement across the country, people who work for the government, they are in a precarious position because of this belief in the, quote/unquote, deep state that does not -- I would argue it doesn`t exist. But depending on what you read about this report, you could be persuaded to believe that it does. FBI agents` offices have been targeted, right? Their lives have been put in danger. And so, would a Church Committee do anything but play to -- right into the hands of those in the far wing spaces and places of America? TODD: I hear you, but we got to -- it seems like we have to do something to restore trust. We have to -- and it has to be moderate trust. CURBELO: And the reason, Chuck, is that the FBI -- you know, the opponents of the FBI , the conspiracy theorists, the people who want to diminish our institutions, they just need, you know, 10 percent of the truth, 15 percent of the truth -- TODD: Yeah, if that. CURBELO: -- to make a living and to bring down the institution. So the FBI has to raise its standards because they can`t even give these people an inch. With an inch, they can bring down these institutions. TODD: And I`ll be honest. Christopher Wray hides. LEE: Well -- TODD: He hides. He does -- he only goes before Congress, and he doesn`t defend the institution publicly. LEE: There is a lot of consternation within the FBI about that, about the way he postures publicly. There`s a couple places where this is really going to come to a head this year, and that is the two special counsel investigations, the Hunter Biden investigation and the reauthorization of Section 702 of -- TODD: With those FISA warrants, yeah. LEE: The FISA warrant. And that is something that`s going to be a huge fight. The White House has been worried about it already for months. TODD: Yeah. LEE: It`s going to get worse. And all of this is going to be on display at that time, at the -- by the end of the year. TODD: All right. I have to end it there. Before we go, it has been 54 years since we first landed astronauts on the moon, and now the U.S. is in another space race: back to the Moon and then to Mars. Watch our latest episode of "Meet the Press Reports": "The Race to Mars". It`s on Peacock, YouTube , or after this broadcast, on NBC News NOW. That`s all we have for today. Thanks for watching.
