headline: Meet the Press for June 18, 2023, NBC
story_text: (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) [09:00:19] CHUCK TODD, NBC NEWS HOST (voice over): This Sunday, former Vice President Mike Pence responds to the federal indictment of Donald Trump . MIKE PENCE, FORMER VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I don`t know why some of my competitors in the Republican primary presume the president will be found guilty. Look, all we know is what -- what the president has been accused of in the indictment. TODD: If you were President Biden, would you pardon him right now? PENCE: I just think this whole matter is incredibly divisive for the country. TODD: As he launches his own run for the White House, he explains where he differs with his former running mate. PENCE: In 2016 Donald Trump promised to govern as a conservative. But he makes no such promise today. TODD: His criticism on how Trump would lead on the world stage. PENCE: My former running mate, seeing war raging in Eastern Europe, is signaling an ambiguous message, not even able to say who he would prefer to see win the war in Ukraine. TODD: And now he thinks he can build support for his own campaign. Who is a Pence supporter, and how does it differentiate right now from a Trump supporter? PENCE: I know the people in our movement. TODD: My exclusive interview with Mike Pence , making history as the first former vice president to ever directly challenge his running mate in a primary. Joining me for insight and analysis are NBC News senior Washington correspondent Hallie Jackson; New York Times chief White House correspondent Peter Baker; Kimberly Atkins Stohr, senior opinion writer for the Boston Globe ; and Stephen Hayes, editor of The Dispatch. Welcome to Sunday. It`s "Meet the Press." ANNOUNCER: From NBC News in Washington, the longest-running show in television history, this is "Meet the Press With Chuck Todd." (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD (on camera): Good Sunday morning, and a happy Father`s day to all the dads out there. As one former prosecutor put it pretty bluntly this week, two years from now, Donald Trump could be in prison or he could be president. With Trump holding a commanding lead over the Republican field this week, his opponents face the question that will dominate this race over the next six months. Will they, can they and should they go after the former president over his federal indictment and Trump`s legal issues that are likely to come. First, let`s tackle the "Will they?" Clearly, it would be the best way for any Republican candidate not named Trump to get some attention. But so far the most direct criticism has come from single-digit candidates Chris Christie and Asa Hutchinson. Hutchinson called on Trump to drop out of the race after the indictment, saying "It`s simply wrong to be discussing a pardon." And Christie said "The conduct (in the indictment) is awful." But as Trump appeared in a Florida courtroom, even opponents who have criticized the charges as "serious" and as -- Donald Trump`s behavior as "reckless", have diminished that very criticism of Trump with attacks against the Justice Department for bringing the charges against him in the first place. And before the case was even tried, they`ve been leaping to a promise of a pardon. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) VIVEK RAMASWAMY , (R) PRESIDENTIAL CANDIDATE: This is my commitment, on January 20, 2025, if I`m elected the next U.S. president, to pardon Donald J. Trump . NIKKI HALEY, (R) PRESIDENTIAL CANDIDATE & FORMER FLORIDA GOVERNOR: I think it would be terrible for the country to have a former president in prison for years because of a documents case. So I would be inclined in favor of a pardon. But I think it`s really premature at this point, when he`s not even been convicted. GOV. RON DESANTIS, (R) FLORIDA & PRESIDENTIAL CANDIDATE: We`re going to clean house at FBI and Justice. We`re going to do a lot. But part of it is using your Article II powers to redress wrongs, including, potentially, pardons. If there was a distant standard, we`re going to be very inclined to grant clemency in those situations. (END VIDEOTAPE) TODD: Let`s tackle part two of this question. Can they go after him on this? In a Quinnipiac poll this week, Trump leads the Republican field by 30 percentage points, garnering 53 percent of the vote, so over a majority. And in an NPR/PBS/Marist poll, while just 43 percent of Americans overall believe Trump should continue running for president given this indictment, a whopping 83 percent of Republicans believe he should keep running. Only 13 percent of Republicans believe Trump has even done anything illegal. Changing those voters` minds in a conservative media ecosystem that, at least for now, plans to defend Trump under any circumstance, will be an uphill battle. The final part of this question, should they go after him? One candidate who has a pretty explicit take on the seriousness of protecting classified information, regardless of someone`s money or position, was candidate Donald Trump in 2016. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) FORMER PRESIDENT DONALD J. TRUMP: In my administration, I`m going to enforce all laws concerning the protection of classified information. No one will be above the law. We can`t have someone in the Oval Office who doesn`t understand the meaning of the word "confidential" or "classified." [09:05:07] One of the first things we must do is to enforce all classification rules and to enforce all laws relating to the handling of classified information. (END VIDEO CLIP) TODD: Now, perhaps that applies to thee and not to me in that case. That was 2016, and his opponent was Hillary Clinton . Now, as one Republican strategist put it, if you aren`t willing to criticize Trump, ask yourself why you`re running to defeat him? The bottom line, the question for all of Trump`s opponents is what kind of party are they running to lead? On Friday I sat down in Huntsville, Alabama, with Trump`s one-time running mate, former Vice President Mike Pence . He`s now challenging him for the nomination. And of course I began by asking him about Trump`s indictment this week. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TODD: Do you think, if these allegations are true, he deserves to be convicted? FORMER VICE PRESIDENT MIKE PENCE: Well, first, you know, in moments like this, I think it`s important for leaders in this country and those of us who aspire to leadership to return to first principles. The first principle is no one`s above the law. The second principle is that every American is entitled to a presumption of innocence. Now, I -- I`ve read the indictment in detail. And the allegations in the indictment are serious. And I can`t defend what is alleged. But the former president deserves his day in court. He deserves the opportunity to make his defense in a court of law. And so I want to -- I want to reserve judgment about this until he`s had an opportunity to -- to take his case into the courtroom and take his case to the American people. I will never diminish the -- the importance of protecting our nation`s secrets, particularly those that bear upon our national security. I have a son in the Marine Corps. I have a son-in-law in the United States Navy . We`ve got to ensure that classified materials, especially those that have been alleged in this indictment, that bear upon our national security, are protected and secured. But that being... (CROSSTALK) PENCE: ... that being said, we`ve gone through years, Chuck -- we`ve gone through years of... TODD: But during the 2016 campaign, you said what Hillary Clinton did with the server and the mishandling of classified documents -- in October of 2016, you said it disqualified her to be commander in chief. Does this disqualify Donald Trump to be commander in chief again? PENCE: Well, I stand by that view. It`s one more example of a two-tier justice system that we`ve been living through for seven years. I mean, I have to tell you, after -- after seeing Hillary Clinton given a pass... TODD: By your Justice Department. PENCE: By the FBI . (CROSSTALK) TODD: It was by a -- no, no, no, wait. No, no, no, Jeff Sessions had another U.S. Attorney look into everything with Clinton... (CROSSTALK) TODD: ... and didn`t bring charges. This is a Republican... PENCE: James Comey ... TODD: This was a Republican Justice Department. PENCE: ... in the run-up to the election -- you know, Chuck... TODD: I understand that, but you guys looked at it again. PENCE: I`m not -- I`m not correcting you on history. Hillary Clinton was given a pass, and then we went two and a half years through a Russia investigation that we now know through the Durham report should have never been begun... TODD: Actually, there was an inspector general report that said there was no politics involved with this, that everything was a legitimate reason to investigate. (CROSSTALK) TODD: You`re -- again, these are all Republican appointees that have done this. PENCE: OK, Chuck, the independent counsel found that the investigation into Russia collusion should never have been initiated. And yet we lived through two and a half years of a constant barrage, on -- on your network, on the cable network associated with you and many of the other mainstream media, suggesting that there was Russian collusion. We had public officials that said there was evidence of collusion -- never happened. And then -- I thought it was disgraceful the way big media and big tech essentially colluded to suppress the story of the Hunter Biden laptop in the run-up to the 2020 campaign, when the FBI actually had the laptop and knew it was legitimate. So, look, I -- it`s hard for me to believe that politics didn`t play some role in the unprecedented decision to bring an indictment against a former president of the United States... TODD: Let me flip it on you... PENCE: But I want to be clear... TODD: I understand that you take it seriously. PENCE: ... that no one`s above the law, and the allegations are serious. TODD: You believe there`s all this politics that influenced this decision. What was the Justice Department supposed to do? Should they not have charged him because he`s an active candidate for president, even in the face of all of these serious allegations? Should they not have brought charges? PENCE: Well, as I said in the run-up to this indictment, I had hoped that the Department of Justice would see its way clear to resolve this issue short of criminal charges. TODD: Is that on the Justice Department or on the former president? PENCE: Well... TODD: I mean, he could have -- he didn`t respond to a subpoena. He didn`t respond to requests. I mean, as Bill Barr said, he brought this on himself. PENCE: Chuck, I -- I understand what`s been reported in the news. [09:10:00] We`ll -- we`ll see what comes out in evidence in the court of law. But, look, I want to say to you that I had hoped, for -- for several reasons, that the Department of Justice would have done otherwise. Because, as we have seen in the last week, this has only served to further divide our divided politics. And I have to tell you, as someone that has represented the United States on the world stage, as someone who was on the International Relations Committee for 10 years, we`re the gold standard of justice in the world. And to -- to see a former president of the United States to be subject to an indictment by the administration of the current president, that he may be running -- he may well be facing again in the future, that sends a terrible message to the wider world, where you know there are many third- world countries around the world where that pattern is very common. TODD: Flip the script. Imagine deciding that you have evidence that a former president commits a crime and you don`t charge it. That could be just as damaging to our gold standard rule of law example, could it not? PENCE: I -- I think the proper answer, right now, because we have an indictment, and I said, the allegations are serious, and the proper approach now is for equal treatment under the law. The Department of Justice, I would like to see bring equal vigor to the investigation into allegations around Hunter Biden . And we have investigations... TODD: How do you know they`re not? PENCE: ... swirling around Hunter Biden , about... TODD: How do you know that they`re not doing that right now? PENCE: Well, I -- I want to see them come forward... TODD: There`s a U.S. Attorney in Delaware... PENCE: ... with action that would... TODD: ... that`s been looking into this for quite some time. PENCE: ... reflect their commitment to equal treatment under the law. And, frankly, you know, the fact that -- that President Biden was found to have had classified documents dating all the way back not just to his years as vice president but to his years in the United States Senate , I -- I would like to see the Department of Justice moving forward... TODD: They have a special... PENCE: ... vigorously into that investigation. TODD: He appointed a special counsel. PENCE: That`s equal treatment under the law. TODD: So what -- so you approve of what Garland did by having a special counsel look into President Biden? PENCE: Well, we`ll see what happens, Chuck. I mean, the American people... TODD: Give me your definition of equal treatment... PENCE: The American people have seen so far that the former president has been subject to an indictment. TODD: But there`s a difference between equal treatment and equal outcomes. PENCE: There is a perception, Chuck... TODD: Are you looking for an equal outcome or equal treatment? Did you get my point? PENCE: I get your point, and I -- I think I`m being very clear on this. I think the American people would like to see evidence that we don`t have a two-tiered system of justice. Seven years, it appears as though -- as though Democrats get one level of treatment and -- and Republicans, especially those of us in the Trump-Pence administration, get another... TODD: But, Mr. Vice President, you bring up seven years... PENCE: The American people want to see -- want to see action by the Department of Justice that proves to them, or starts to prove to them, that that`s not the case... (CROSSTALK) TODD: Did the Sessions-Barr Justice Department politicize things in favor of the Democrats? Is that your allegation, that, in four of the seven years you`re describing, that the Justice Department that was run by Republican - - former Republican senator Jeff Sessions, two-time Republican attorney general Bill Barr, was politicizing the Justice Department in favor of Democrats? PENCE: What I`m saying to you is that we now know that the Russia collusion investigation should have never been begun, two and a half years, put the country through... TODD: The inspector general never said that, for what it`s worth. PENCE: In the days following that, under the Biden administration now, we`ve literally seen the Justice Department targeting parents going to school board meetings. We`ve seen the Justice Department targeting pro-life activists. And -- and I have to tell you, Chuck, I`m still waiting for the rash of prosecutions of people involved in the BLM riots from the summer of 2020. I mean, where -- where is the equal treatment under the law as evidenced in the fact that -- that people are being brought into court, being held for having caused billions of dollars in damage in hundreds of riots throughout the summer of 2020? Look, clearly the American people -- or not -- or I will tell you, among Republicans, a vast majority of Republicans have lost confidence in the Department of Justice. And if I`m elected president of the United States, I`ve said, on day one, we`re going to -- we`re going to clean house at the highest levels of the Department of Justice, and we`re going to find... TODD: You`ve talked about firing Christopher Wray on day one. PENCE: ... men and women of integrity... TODD: Let me ask you this. PENCE: ... who are respected on both sides of the aisle, who will restore confidence in the rule of law. TODD: Christopher Wray is a Trump appointee. What makes him so -- so -- a person that runs a politicized FBI ? I mean, this is where -- I understand the accusation. But the facts don`t feel like they fit the accusation. PENCE: All I`m telling you is the reality today -- and, look, I -- I -- I appreciate the service of everybody serving on the top floor of the Department of Justice, but they`ve lost the confidence of the majority of the American people. [09:15:11] TODD: You have been asked a few times whether you would pardon the former president if he`s convicted and if you were the president. Would you? PENCE: Well, I just think the question is -- is premature. I mean, honestly, Chuck, I`ve -- I`ve pardoned people who were found guilty of a crime... TODD: What`s your -- what is your bar... PENCE: ... when I was governor of Indiana. TODD: ... for a pardon? PENCE: Well, let me say, first and foremost, I don`t know why some of my competitors in the Republican primary presume the president will be found guilty. Look, all we know is what -- what the president has been accused of in the indictment. We don`t know what his defense is. We don`t know if this will even go to trial. It could be subject to a motion of dismiss. We don`t know what the verdict will be of the jury. We don`t know the result of an appeal. So I think, look, the president of the United States takes an oath to support and defend the Constitution of the United States. And as I said in my announcement, I -- I`ll always choose the Constitution. But the oath the president takes also requires him to see that the laws are faithfully executed. That means respecting the Article III courts in this country. I think we need to let the courts do their job and -- and let this case work its -- work its way through our judicial system. And if I have the great privilege of being president of the United States, as I did when I was a governor, we would evaluate any request for pardon for any American. TODD: If you were President Biden, would you pardon him right now? PENCE: I just think this whole matter is incredibly divisive for the country. And, look, I -- I just think, at the end of the day, it is -- it is saddening to me that we are now in this moment, for two reasons. Number one is, look, President Trump was my friend. TODD: You said it in past tense. PENCE: Well, we -- we worked together very closely for four years. I`m incredibly proud of the record of the Trump-Pence administration. Some in this primary have taken to criticizing the record of our administration. But I`m proud of everything we accomplished for the American people. We left America stronger and more prosperous than ever before. Obviously, as you and I have talked in great detail, it did not end well. As I said in my announcement speech, the American people deserve to know that, on that tragic day of January 6th, President Trump asked me to choose him over the Constitution. And I -- I chose the Constitution, and I always will. I had no right to overturn the election. TODD: Isn`t this your way of saying he`s not qualified to be president, because he did not -- because, to put it in somebody else`s words, I think it was Liz Cheney that says, "You have to choose between the Constitution and supporting him." You chose the Constitution. Is that what he`s demanding? PENCE: Well, look, President Trump was wrong then. He`s wrong now. He`s continued to say that -- that I had the right to overturn the election. I had no right to overturn the election. And Kamala Harris will have no right to overturn the election when we beat her in 2024. Ted Cruz tried this. BAKER: Yeah. Well, it was a different environment. I mean, look. We can try to go back to 2016 over and over again, and we do see a fragmented field in which Donald Trump profits like then. But I think the context is different, and you`re hearing DeSantis say not only on this issues but even immigration, He didn`t build the wall, which was of course his main argument in 2016. TODD: Before we go, one year after the landmark Supreme Court decision overturning Roe v. Wade, we here at "Meet the Press" will be examining its impact, what it means for the future of this country and your politics. You can watch our Meet the Press special on abortion this Thursday evening at 10:30 Eastern Time on NBC News Now and after that on demand on YouTube and Peacock. That is all we have for today. Thank you for watching. We`ll be back next week because if it`s Sunday, it`s "Meet the Press". Enjoy Father`s Day. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. story_text: [19:00:00] (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Tonight, the desperate surge in the North Atlantic for a missing submersible near the Titanic. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) HOLT (voiceover): The U.S. and Canadian coast guard scouring for a sub- carrying five people. Contact lost for more than 24 hours as the tourist vessel made its way toward the Titanic 12,000 feet down. Rough seas, rain, and fog hampering the surge in rescue efforts for those on board, including a billionaire businessman and explorer. Late details just in tonight. Also tonight, the high-stakes summit between China`s President Xi Jinping and Secretary of State Anthony Blinken . A chance to reset rising tensions that have only gotten worse since the U.S. shot down a spy balloon. Our one-on-one interview with the Secretary of State. The nonstop threat of tornadoes, one dead and almost two dozen injured as multiple tornadoes tear through Mississippi. The search for survivors. A weekend of mass shooting, some of them deadly. But when it happened twice last month in another country, they took quick and decisive action. Richard Engel is there. The new boom in building, not to buy, but to rent. What`s behind it in our series "PRICED OUT." On Juneteenth, celebrations across America and a field of dreams reborn as a testament to the past. (END VIDEO CLIP) ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening and welcome. Tonight, near the site of one of the 20th century`s worst ocean disasters, a new undersea drama is unfolding. Right now, the U.S. Coast Guard leading the urgent search for a group of modern-day adventurers after the submersible carrying them to the Titanic shipwreck lost contact with the surface yesterday about an hour and 45 minutes into their journey. Five people are on board the vessel which is used to carry paying passengers to see the Titanic up close. The search happening about 350 miles off the coast of Newfoundland in waters more than two miles deep. Tonight, the company that runs the deep sea charters, Ocean Gate Expeditions, saying in a statement, our entire focus is on the crew members and their families. Tom Costello has late-breaking developments for us. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): U.S. and Canadian Coast Guard ships are this hour rushing to the North Atlantic as two U.S. C-130 planes surveyed the vast ocean surface for any signs of a private submersible and the five people on board, last seen Sunday morning as it descended to survey the wreck of the Titanic. REAR ADM. JOHN MAUGER, COMMANDER, U.S. COAST GUARD FIRST DISTRICT: During the course of the dive, they lost communications and we have not had communications with the submersible since then. COSTELLO (voiceover): The 21-foot submersible named Titan, made of titanium and carbon fiber, is owned by Ocean Gate, an operator of small subs for research, film production, and tourist trips to the Titanic for $250,000. On board a pilot and four passengers, including billionaire adventurer Hamish Harding, who had taken a submersible to the Mariana Trench and flown in space on Jeff Bezos ` Blue Origin . On his Instagram account Sunday, he signed his name on the logo as he announced he`d be diving to the Titanic. His company later tweeted, 4:00 a.m. start this morning on the RMS Titanic Mission 5. The sub had a successful launch and Hamish is currently diving. Today, Ocean Gate said our entire focus is on the crew members in the submersible and their families. We are working toward the safe return of the crew members. The CEO told our Seattle KING 5 last August he caters to Titanic enthusiasts. STOCKTON RUSH , CEO, OCEAN GATE: We have a number of people who come with us, who sometimes we referred to as Titaniacs, people who have just been consumed by the Titanic. And it was just great to take them down. COSTELLO (voiceover): The Titanic rests at treacherous depths, 12,500 feet below the surface. 1,500 people died when she sank in 1912. The missing sub was only supposed to be gone for six to eight hours with 96 hours of reserve oxygen. Already, Canadian P-8 search planes have dropped sonar buoys on the rough seas, listening for the sub in a deep, vast expanse of ocean. COSTELLO: Are they listening for voices? What could they pick up? MAUGER: We`re hoping that they can pick up any unusual sounds, maybe tapping on the hull or voices or those types of things, any signs of the vassal mare in the water. And that`s why we`ve really pressed in with the capabilities that we have. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Now, Tom as I understand it, submersible are meant to dive much deeper than say, a typical Navy sub. If the Coast Guard can locate it under the surface, can they get to it? [19:05:03] COSTELLO (on camera): They can`t. That`s the problem. They don`t have the deep-sea rescue capabilities that the Navy has. So, both the U.S. and the Canadian navies are rushing those assets to the scene as well as contacting private companies who have those capabilities. But if they find this crew, it`s going to be a very, very challenging rescue operation and the clock is ticking, Lester. HOLT: All right, Tom Castello, thank you. Let`s turn out of that critical meeting in China today between President Xi Jinping and Secretary of State Antony Blinken with relations at a low point. Blinken now touting progress at an interview with Janis Mackey Frayer. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANTONY BLINKEN , U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE: Good afternoon. JANIS MACKEY FRAYER, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, a high-stakes visit to Beijing, capped by a handshake. Secretary of State Antony Blinken meeting China`s President Xi Jinping for 35 minutes to stop what officials call a downward spiral in relations. BLINKEN: Direct engagement and sustained communication at senior levels is the best way to responsibly manage our differences and ensure that competition does not veer into conflict. FRAYER (voiceover): Xi`s message to Blinken, I hope that through this visit, Mr. Secretary, you`ll make more positive contributions to stabilizing China-U.S. relations. There`s no shortage of flashpoints here, tension over Taiwan, China`s role in the fentanyl crisis, unanswered questions about the origins of COVID. Chinese officials not holding back on their grievances either, like U.S. export bans on technology. Tonight, in an interview with NBC News, Blinken said the two-day visit has stabilized ties, at least for now. BLINKEN: Both China and the United States, I think, recognized that we were in an increasingly unstable place in our relationship. I think this is the start of a process to put a little more stability into it. FRAYER (voiceover): But China refused Blinken`s request to reopen military crisis lines that were cut off by Beijing nearly a year ago. Since then some close calls, including this Chinese warship sailing within 150 yards of a U.S. destroyer in the Taiwan Strait, and this Chinese fighter jet darting in front of an American surveillance plane, something we saw for ourselves when we were on board another U.S. Navy plane intercepted by a Chinese jet. BLINKEN: We`ve seen a couple of very dangerous incidents in the last couple of weeks. FRAYER (voiceover): China says the encounters are justified to protect its sovereignty. Blinken`s first trip here was called off after that Chinese spy balloon which was shot down after it flew over the U.S. Senior U.S. officials told NBC News it collected intelligence from American military sites. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I think it was more embarrassing than it was intentionally. FRAYER: So, with Beijing, the balloon incident is over. It`s water under the bridge? BLINKEN: Well, we did what we needed to do to protect our interests. We said what we needed to say and made clear what we needed and made clear in terms of this not happening again. And so, as long as it doesn`t, that chapter should be closed. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Janis, Secretary Blinken insists the relationship is now stabilized, but was anything concrete accomplished? FRAYER: Lester, relations are at such a low point that even having the meeting is seen by both sides as a positive. Other high-level visits can now follow with President Xi potentially meeting President Biden in the U.S. before the end of the year. Lester? HOLT: All right, Janis Mackey Frayer in Beijing, thank you. In Mississippi, at least one person died and almost two dozen were injured by an overnight tornado, the latest in a wave of destructive storms. Blayne Alexander reports. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Across the South, it`s the unforgiving sound of summertime severe weather striking in the dead of night. Its latest target, Louin, Mississippi. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Oh, that was big. ALEXANDER (voiceover): Overnight, a reported tornado tore through this community an hour outside of Jackson, where people were rushed from their mangled homes on stretchers. Daylight reveals the true scope of the devastation, trees torn to shreds, homes now unrecognizable. All of it leaving more than two dozen people injured and claiming at least one life, 67-year-old Georgine Hayes. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: She`s a good person, good church person, you know. ALEXANDER (voiceover): Her cousin, Lester, lives right across the street. He helped pull her from the rubble. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Her house where a black Jeep at -- ALEXANDER: Right there. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It was right there. It`s gone. There isn`t anything there. ALEXANDER: So it`s completely gone. ALEXANDER (voiceover): It`s the latest in a deadly storm system sweeping across the South and central plains, producing at least 17 confirmed tornadoes in just four days. Among the towns hit, Perryton, Texas where the storms destroyed downtown and this mobile home community, killing three people. Oscar Hernandez lost his four businesses in a matter of minutes. He spoke to NBC`s Priscilla Thompson. [19:10:02] OSCAR HERNANDEZ, BUSINESS OWNER: It`s really hard. It`s really hard. All the lost, all the people that lost their lives. ALEXANDER (voiceover): Severe weather continues to sweep the South. Today, a confirmed tornado along the Florida Panhandle and flash flooding in Alabama, an ominous sign of what`s to come. (END VIDEOTAPE) ALEXANDER (on camera): And across the region, hundreds of thousands of people remain without power in some of the very same places that are seeing triple digit highs making cleanup like this all the more difficult with threats of more tornadoes tonight. Lester? HOLT: All right, Blayne, thank you. And we have breaking news tonight about the first named storm in the Atlantic this season. Tropical Storm Bret has formed in the central Atlantic. It`s about 1,300 miles from the lesser Antilles. It is expected to strengthen to become a category one hurricane by tomorrow night and could impact Puerto Rico by the weekend. We`ll stay on top of that one. Across America, the long weekend, a string of mass shootings. Near Chicago, 23 people were shot, one of them fatally during a Juneteenth event yesterday. In Kellogg, Idaho, four people were shot and killed. A suspect was arrested. And in San Francisco, six people were injured in a shootout involving two cars. Two were hit by stray bullets and two young girls were hit by the cars. With little agreement in Washington over to how to stop the violence, tonight, Richard Engel reports on how lawmakers in Serbia responded following two mass shootings there. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) RICHARD ENGEL, NBC NEWS CHIEF FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Serbians didn`t see it coming. On May 3rd, a 13-year-old boy stormed into a school with his father`s two guns and a hitlist and killed eight classmates. The next day, a man with a history of violence opened fire in a village, killing eight more. But then came more than thoughts and prayers. Tens of thousands demanded not just tighter gun controls, but a reorientation of society away from violence. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I think a lot of us have just had enough. ENGEL (voiceover): Zarco Svechik`s (ph) nine-year-old daughter Zora was in the school when the 13-year-old boy went on a killing spree. ENGEL: What would you say to Americans who`ve been through this and then see no change? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I would say to them, you know, safeguard your democracy if you still have it and mobilize. ENGEL (voiceover): Within weeks of the shootings here, new laws were introduced and old ones enforced. Now all sales of new guns are banned for two years. Gun owners must submit to in-person psychological and background checks. And owning an illegal gun is punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Many Serbians are turning in their guns voluntarily. ENGEL: Here`s a lot of AKs and assault rifles. ENGEL (voiceover): There are 70,000 guns in this police warehouse surrendered under a no-questions-asked amnesty. The Deputy Interior Minister says this is only the start. ENGEL: What do you think when you see all of this? ENGEL (voiceover): I see life saved, he said. Serbia is deeply divided politically, but overhauling gun laws was universally popular. Dobrica Veselinovic, is an opposition politician. ENGEL: Why is it do you think you were able to cross political divides? DOBRICA VESELINOVIC, SERBIAN POLITICIAN: We are not having these big gun lobbies and the big industry which is behind it. (END VIDEOTAPE) ENGEL (on camera): The father we spoke, to and many others now want to push further, dialing back violence in the media and in political discourse. Lester.? HOLT: All right, Richard, thank you. In 60 seconds, tracking who gets an abortion. One state tried to make sure personal data isn`t used to follow women who are driving there for the procedure. Plus, the new housing boom in rentals. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: It`s no secret there is surveillance almost everywhere we go these days. Now, one state is taking action to prevent the tracking of women who may be driving to get an abortion. Anne Thompson explains. [19:15:07] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANNE THOMPSON, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): If it feels like you are being tracked, it may be because you are, at red lights going in and out of the office on your smartphone. But what if you could be tracked seeking a legal abortion simply by your license plate? ALEXI GIANNOULIAS, SECRETARY OF STATE, ILLINOIS: I don`t think people realize how much of their personal data is collected, that their whereabouts are tracked. THOMPSON (voiceover): That`s why Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias backs what he says is a first-in-the-nation bill to outlaw sharing or selling license plate data for women seeking abortions. THOMPSON: Who has access to license plate trackers? GIANNOULIAS: A number of private and public entities have this personal sensitive data. THOMPSON (voiceover): Data he fears could be weaponized as some states try to criminalize helping someone get an abortion even in a state where it is legal. Three other states have passed laws aimed at protecting health data from such efforts. GIANNOULIAS: When they travel, whether it`s to an abortion clinic or the grocery store, we need to make sure this data is protected. THOMPSON (voiceover): Illinois Right to Life Executive Director Mary Kate Zander opposes abortion. THOMPSON: Do you think this bill is necessary? MARY KATE ZANDER, DIRECTOR, ILLINOIS RIGHT TO LIFE EXECUTIVE: I think it`s unnecessary. They`re trying to create a narrative around what the pro-life movement may or may not be doing. THOMPSON (voiceover): She says her organization is not trying to criminalize women seeking the procedure. THOMPSON: Is the right to life movement tracking license plates of women? ZANDER: No, absolutely not. THOMPSON: Has it done that in the past? ZANDER: No, absolutely not. THOMPSON: Do you see it doing that in the future? ZANDER: Absolutely not. Absolutely not. That`s just not a tactic that we would use. THOMPSON (voiceover): With a quarter of their patients now from out of state, Illinois Planned Parenthood CEO Jennifer Welch is not convinced. Patients need to know that when they come for health care, that information won`t be shared with anybody, law enforcement, activists, anybody else. THOMPSON (voiceover): Data collection and privacy, a new frontier in the nation`s fight over abortion rights. Anne Thompson, NBC News, Chicago. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Still to come here tonight, the rush to rent. Why more people are saying yes to signing lease and it`s shaking the foundation of housing in America. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: Trying to buy a home these days is a real struggle. Between high mortgage rates and low inventory, many are fighting themselves priced out. The CNBC`s Diana Olick explains, it`s fueling a boom in so-called build-to- rent properties. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DIANA OLICK, CNBC SENIOR CLIMATE AND REAL ESTATE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Single mom Robin Ashford had planned to buy a home near Columbia, South Carolina last year but mortgage rates suddenly shot sharply higher. ROBIN ASHFORD, SINGLE MOM: I found out that I was going to have as much buying power as I would have about two or three years ago. And my mortgage, my monthly mortgage payments were too much that I could handle. OLICK (voiceover): So, instead, Ashford turned to this brand new community built specifically for renters. ASHFORD: I don`t have to worry about taxes on the home. I don`t have to worry about if something breaks, you know. It`s the landlord`s responsibility. BRUCE MCNEILAGE, CO-FOUNDER, KINLOCH PARTNERS: They have large open floor plans. OLICK (voiceover): And an increasing share of the landlords are now big builders like Bruce McNeilage`s Nashville-based Kinloch Partners as more Americans decide to rent not only by necessity but by choice. MCNEILAGE: We`ve had a societal shift to people wanting to rent because they want a maintenance-free lifestyle or they want the ability to move to a city and just give the keys back to the landlord at the end of the lease. OLICK (voiceover): Builders put up 68,000 new single-family rental homes last year, a 31 percent increase over the year before, according to John Burns` research. JOHN BURNS, JOHN BURNS RESEARCH AND CONSULTING: I think it`s at the early stages of being a very, very big business, just like the apartment market is. OLICK (voiceover): Burns counted 708 build-to-rent communities coming soon across the U.S. Entire communities of single-family homes built not for sale, but specifically for rent. BURNS: The people that want a home, but have now been priced out due to rising prices and then rising mortgage rates, are saying, well, I want a home, I`m going to rent for a while. So, it`s created more demand for the rental homes. OLICK: And renters are demanding more of the builders, amenities like pools, fitness centers, dog parks, of course, on-site maintenance, and as in this community, bigger backyards. OLICK (voiceover): But all that comes at a price. The average rent here is about $2,200 a month and single-family rents across the nation are rising. ASHFORD: That`s something that I do need to think about because trying to stay for a home while paying high rent, it`s hard. OLICK (voiceover): For now, she`s enjoying the new home, even if it`s not her new home. For NBC News, Diana Olick, Blythewood, South Carolina. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: When we come back here tonight, the boys of summer back on this historic field of dreams. The remarkable story of how fans brought this baseball stadium back from the brink. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Across the country today, people mark Juneteenth with parades, festivals, and marches marking the end of slavery in the U.S. And at this beloved baseball stadium, players and fans are reclaiming a part of African-American history on their very own field of dreams. Ron Allen explains. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) RON ALLEN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): At the Jackal`s home opener against the miners in Patterson, New Jersey, a huge comeback. The grand reopening of historic Hinchliffe Stadium itself. WILLIE RANDOLPH, FORMER MLB PLAYERS MANAGER: I get goosebumps when I think about it. We need to keep this kind of venue and places like this, you know, flourishing. ALLEN (voiceover): One of the last ballparks still standing from the days of baseball`s Negro leagues and segregated sports, a hallowed venue that for the past few decades had been shut down, abandoned, and about to be demolished. ALLEN: As worse, what do you remember about this? BRIAN LOPINTO, CO-FOUNDER, FRIENDS OF HINCHLIFFE STADIUM: At its worst, what I remember are the trees growing in the stands, people living in the press box. ALLEN (voiceover): Brian LoPinto helped lead a local effort to save the stadium, now a national historic landmark that just underwent a $100 million renovation. The Minor League Jackal`s new home once home for the New York Black Yankees and New York Cubans where legends such as Patterson`s own Larry Doby, who broke baseball`s color barrier after Jackie Robinson once played. ALLEN: A lot of legends played here. Do you feel that? NILO RIJO, PLAYER, NEW JERSEY JACKALS: I can feel it. I mean, I`m grateful that I`m playing, you know, in the same place that a lot of, you know, legends played in. ANDRE SAYEGH, MAYOR, PATERSON, NEW JERSEY: This is the real field of dreams. This stadium is sacred and this stadium tells the story of the struggle for social justice, civil rights, and American integration. ALLEN (voiceover): Reopening day, a chance for fans to celebrate and enjoy sites many thought they`d never see. ALLEN: What do you think when you`re in this place now? You know, I mean, what I think is wild. ALLEN (voiceover): And the Jackals held on to win the opener 10-6. All those legends who played here, perhaps giving the home team an edge. Ron Allen, NBC News, Patterson, New Jersey. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Quite a piece of history. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Monday. Thanks for watching. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: DATELINE for September 9, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [22:00:15] LESTER HOLT, NBC DATELINE HOST: I`m Lester Holt. Tonight on Dateline, a dramatic new development in the story of a wife, a mistress, and maybe a murderer. BONNIE CONTRERAS, BILL HALL`S MISTRESS: How many more bombshells is there going to be? F. HALL: She goes, I`m having an affair with your husband. ANDREA CANNING, NBC DATELINE CORRESPONDENT: You`re getting text messages from Bonnie of the two of them having sex. CONTRERAS: She saw me and then made the U turn. I looked in my rearview mirror and it was Frances. F. HALL: I get her little finger. CANNING (on camera): The middle finger? F. HALL: Right. I start following her. CONTRERAS: I said, what the hell. F. HALL: She brakes. And I brake and I forgot to stop. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: He`s pronounced dead at the hospital. F. HALL: I lost my husband, the man that I love. TIMOTHY LOVETT, PROSECUTION COLLISION EXPERT: This is not an accident. SCOTT SIMPSON, PROSECUTOR: She doesn`t stop the vehicle. If it`s an accident, you stop your vehicle. F. HALL: I did not deliberately hurt him. CANNING (on camera): A lot of hatred and anger in this case. NICO LAHOOD, CRIMINAL DISTRICT ATTORNEY: A lot. LEIGH CUTTER, FRANCES HALL`S ATTORNEY: To see manipulation, you have all the elements. NIKKI HALL, BILL HALL`S DAUGHTER: Her story changed, I don`t know how many times. CANNING (on camera): How do we know who to believe? CONTRERAS: That`s the world`s decision. HOLT (voice-over): Here`s Andrea Canning with "Collision." CANNING (voice-over): This is the story of two intense women battling for the heart of one much loved man. It`s about sex, secrets, and lies, red hot Texas passion and a bitter feud, all leading to a final showdown on a two lane highway. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Bexar County 911. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I got a black Escalade and a Range Rover. They`re hauling ass, acting like idiots. CANNING (voice-over): A high speed chase that went horribly, horribly wrong. N. HALL: It was a nightmare. CANNING (voice-over): When the dust settled, one life would be over. Many others shattered. HANK HALL, BILL HALL`S COUSIN: We all lost here. CANNING (voice-over): And tonight, there`s a Hall new chapter. San Antonio, Texas, home of the Alamo, The Riverwalk, and the Hall family. Three generations of truckers with deep roots in the city. It was here that Bill Hall met the love of his life at the tender age of 16. Her name was Frances. (on camera): What happened the first time you laid eyes on Bill? F. HALL: I just fell in love with him. I knew this was the man I was going to marry. CANNING: At 16? F. HALL: At 16. CANNING (voice-over): They married right out of high school. A year later, daughter Nikki was born. (on camera): Where your parents in love? N. HALL: Oh yes. We definitely saw love growing up in the house. F. HALL: I love my baby. CANNING (voice-over): For years after Nikki came Justin. Bill worked hard to give his young family a better life. F. HALL: Bill used to clean airplanes. He went to college. And on the weekends if he was off, he`d go dig ditches. We made ends meet. CANNING (voice-over): But his true passion was big rigs. So one day he up and quit school started his own business, Bill Hall Jr. Trucking. F. HALL: That`s what his family did for a living so it`s in their blood. CANNING (voice-over): Bill got his first truck and went to work delivering topsoil, while Frances hit the phones to drum up new business. F. HALL: He was a dreamer. And he always said I`m going to go big vieja. Vieja is a Hispanic term, which means old lady. CANNING (voice-over): After just a few years, Bill and Frances turned that one truck into a fleet of 130. At its height, their empire was valued at more than $15 million. (on camera): All his dreaming paid off. F. HALL: And hard work. He put his life his heart and soul into it. Bill was Bill Hall Jr. Trucking. CANNING (voice-over): But for Bill, it wasn`t all work and no play. N. HALL: He was a daredevil. He loved racing. And in his later years he loved hunting. He was a man`s man. CANNING (voice-over): And also a bit of a ladies man according to Bill`s cousin Hank. H. HALL: You know beautiful women. You work hard, you play hard, and you do things, you know, that you`re not supposed to be doing. He was a great man but he was not the perfect man. CANNING (voice-over): Bill`s imperfections became painfully clear nearly 32 years into their marriage when Frances says she got a call from a mysterious woman. It was September 13th, 2013, Friday the 13th. [22:05:14] F. HALL: She goes, you don`t know me but I`m having an affair with your husband. CANNING (on camera): Wow. F. HALL: I was in shock. CANNING (voice-over): Heartbroken, furious. Frances says she confronted Bill and asked, was it true? F. HALL: By that time he is crying, and telling me that he`s sorry? That it`s true. I was devastated. CANNING (on camera): This is three decades of marriage. F. HALL: And I finally asked him, how long has this been going on? He cried again. Told me, three years. And I go, this is not an affair, this is a relationship. CANNING (voice-over): About that and only that she and the other woman agreed. (on camera): You don`t like the word mistress, do you? CONTRERAS: No, I don`t. CANNING (voice-over): This is Bonnie Contreras. (on camera): What is it about that word that bothers you? CONTRERAS: Mistress, it just sounds like I don`t want to say, yes, that I was the side person because I was more than that to him. This man was the man I wanted to marry and spend the rest of my life with. CANNING (voice-over): Bonnie was a 28-year-old single mom when they met, about 20 years younger than Bill and Frances. She said their love affair bloomed in the most unlikely of places. CONTRERAS: I met him at a Spinach Festival. CANNING (on camera): Spinach? CONTRERAS: Spinach Festival, I was helping my aunt sell chicken on a stick, believe it or not. I know it sounds kind of corny, but that`s how I met him. CANNING (voice-over): Bill happened to stroll by that chicken stand with some friends. CONTRERAS: As soon as I saw Bill, we kind of just locked eyes. CUTTER: The text messages, the calls, the taunting, those would probably make you really hate someone, but never having seen them until their drive by in your car. If that`s not sudden passion, where you are incapable of thinking clearly I don`t know what it is. CANNING (voice-over): But prosecutor Scott Simpson told jurors not to be swayed by emotions. SIMPSON: You shouldn`t for one second, feel ashamed or bad for doing what you believe to be right. CANNING (voice-over): After about three hours of deliberations, the jury was ready. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We unanimously find the defendant caused the death of Bill Hall under the immediate influence of sudden passion. We assess her punishments return for two years. CANNING (voice-over): Two years, the absolute minimum sentence. On September 7th, 2018, after serving her time, Frances walked out of prison a free woman. We thought that this was the end of the story, but we were wrong. There`s a whole new chapter. This summer Frances was indicted in a multimillion dollar fraud scheme. She`s accused of providing false payroll information to get lower insurance premiums for the company she and Bill founded. The Texas Department of Insurance said the scheme allowed the company and its owners to avoid more than $9 million in premium payments. We plan to speak with Frances in person this week, but due to COVID concerns we met via Zoom. She denies the charges and the indictment. F. HALL: I`m an honest woman. I didn`t do anything illegal. I didn`t falsified anything. I`m innocent. I don`t have anything to hide. CONTRERAS: How many more bombshells is there going to be? CANNING (voice-over): We also caught up again with Bonnie Contreras to hear her thoughts on Frances`s latest troubles. CONTRERAS: She looks like a liar. She looks like a con. She just -- she looks bad all the way around. CANNING (voice-over): Bonnie now runs some businesses of her own, including a CBD spa. She believes the new charges just might change some people`s perceptions of Frances and herself. CONTRERAS: They were constantly calling me a gold digger. So who looks like the gold digger now? Is it me? Or is it her? F. HALL: I don`t even think she knows what the word gold digger means. What I`m going through right now has nothing to do with gold digging. Now what she did on her free time with my husband, that`s gold digging. I have Bill`s kids, I have Bill`s grandkids, something she`ll never have. And I have all the memories of Bill. That`s not a gold digger. That`s a wife. So she should have maybe looked it up on the dictionary first. CANNING (voice-over): Frances told us if the new case goes to trial, she`ll take the stand. It worked for her at the sentencing hearing in Bill`s murder. But insurance fraud is a serious crime too. And there`s no sudden passion defense. If convicted. The woman who served just two years for killing her husband will face the possibility of life in prison yet again. [22:59:16] HOLT (voice-over): That`s all for this edition of Dateline. I don`t even think she knows what the word love means. CANNING (voice-over): Of course, Bonnie sees things very differently. (on camera): They`ve really gone after you with names. CONTRERAS: Of course. And I understand where the Halls are coming from. It`s a pretty big pill to swallow when your husband wants to divorce you after 32 years, you know, and of course they`re never going to say anything good about me. CANNING: Do you want to clear it up, were you an exotic dancer? CONTRERAS: I worked at a strip club. Yes. And that was way before. CANNING: As a dancer? CONTRERAS: Yes. And that was a mistake that, I mean, I regret that, no one is perfect. CANNING (voice-over): But the fake Facebook accounts stalking Frances, the abortion in exchange for breast implants. None of that ever happened, said Bonnie. CONTRERAS: For her to sit there and say that I switched a baby`s life that was going inside of me coming from a man that I love dearly for breast augmentation, ridiculousness. CANNING (voice-over): Each woman clung to her truth. The battle for Bill raged. H. HALL: He couldn`t stop Bonnie and really couldn`t stop Frances really, you know. CANNING (on camera): It sounds like two hurricanes. H. HALL: Oh, yes. CANNING (voice-over): Then about a week before Bill`s death, the hurricanes collided. Not on the road. Not yet. This war was waged via text. (on camera): You`re getting text messages from Bonnie of the two of them having sex. F. HALL: Uh-huh. HOLT (voice-over): Coming up, the case heads to court where one expert testifies that Frances deliberately rammed Bonnie. LOVETT: This is not an accident. HOLT (voice-over): While another expert provides a demonstration that seems to show the SUVs never even touched. CHARLES RUBLE, ACCIDENT RECONSTRUCTIONIST: That simple physics. [22:38:57] HOLT (voice-over): When Dateline continues. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) CANNING (voice-over): The battle over Bill Hall Jr. had gone on for weeks. And it all led up to a confrontation about a week before his death. Bill and Frances met at this hotel. She said they were trying to work things out. But then Bonnie showed up at the front desk. N. HALL: Saying she was his wife and she needed to get access to his room and my dad told them, no, she`s not my wife. My wife is here with me. CANNING (voice-over): Security asked Bonnie to leave though she insists she never claimed to be Bill`s wife. But all parties agree that night an all- out war began via text. (on camera): You`re getting text messages from Bonnie of the two of them having sex. F. HALL: Pictures of sexual positions. CANNING (voice-over): Photos with captions like, this is what he really likes you fat old woman. (on camera): Normally the mistress keeps a very low profile. F. HALL: She wanted to make sure I knew now she was in the picture. CANNING (voice-over): Did she ever? Many of the messages are too graphic to show. But you can get a good sense of them from these excerpts. Let me know if you want some good juicy pics of me and your hubby, you stupid old person, keep fixing yourself up maybe he`ll find you more attractive. (on camera): What`s the worst text message she sent you? F. HALL: The hollow bitch. CANNING: She actually called you -- F. HALL: Hollow. CANNING: Because? F. HALL: Of my hysterectomy. CANNING (voice-over): Complete with a diagram to reinforce the point. Bonnie admits she sent those nasty texts. (on camera): You have to imagine though that people are going to see this and they`re going to think that some of those text messages are cruel. CONTRERAS: I never sent her pictures of me and Bill having sexual intercourse. What I did send her pictures of was three butt pics of me. And that`s because she infuriated me because she told me that my butt looked like a broken saddlebag. It looked like a broken toilet seat. Trust me. She was going at me very hard. CANNING (voice-over): In fact, Bonnie, says it was Frances who started the text war. CONTRERAS: Plain and simple, I was defending myself. CANNING (on camera): The texts that Frances said hurt her the most was the one where you called her hollow and sent the diagram of a woman who had had a hysterectomy. CONTRERAS: That is cruel. CANNING: That would hit a woman hard. CONTRERAS: And I`m not happy about that. CANNING: Why did you do it? CONTRERAS: Because I was pissed at her. She was telling me vicious ugly thing. [22:45:00] CANNING: Did you send any back to her that were nasty as well not really, no, because it`d be hard not to engage. F. HALL: Well, yes, I started to at the hotel, but I think I did one or two. CANNING (voice-over): Had them in the palm of your hand and couldn`t keep him. Frances wrote to Bonnie, keep sending fatal attraction. Cops need all the pics. F. HALL: I mean, I couldn`t keep up, I text slow. This girl`s young. She knows technology. CANNING (voice-over): Bonnie says Frances more than held her own. Don`t flatter yourself. He`s been cheating on you with me. But says Frances, the nastier text, Bonnie, received didn`t come from her. She says Bill sent them. F. HALL: Bill grabbed the phone and he said let me take care of her. CONTRERAS: No, he didn`t. That was her. It was her sending those text messages. Bill wouldn`t have never disrespected me like that. CANNING (voice-over): But if there was any doubt that she`d been following the Halls, she seemed to confirm it herself by sending photos of their house and Frances`s car. (on camera): Why were you sending those pictures? CONTRERAS: To piss her off. To defend myself. CANNING: Why, what are you -- I mean, you`re the one -- CONTRERAS: Her telling me that bill didn`t love me, her telling me that Bill was using me. CANNING: But Bonnie, you`re the one who`s having the affair with Bill. So why are you attacking his wife? CONTRERAS: Because she was attacking me and I will defend myself. CANNING (voice-over): One week after that text message viewed came the car chase that left Bill Hall dead. Nearly three years after that, Frances Hall went on trial for murder. Prosecutors Stephanie Paulissen and Scott Simpson laid out the case for the jury. STEPHANIE PAULISSEN, PROSECUTOR: We understand why she was angry. But that`s not justification to go attempt to run down your husband`s mistress and kill him in the process. CANNING (voice-over): The star witness for the prosecution, Bonnie Contreras. CONTRERAS: I start to get hit from behind. CANNING (voice-over): Bonnie told the jury how she watched with horror as she believed Frances deliberately knocked Bill off the road. CONTRERAS: -- can fly off the motorcycle. CANNING (voice-over): Bonnie said she later discovered Frances`s daughter Nikki Hall had left a message on her voicemail during the car chase, a message that seemed to speak to Frances`s intent that evening. N. HALL: I told you to watch your back, you -- stupid slut. CONTRERAS: What does that tell you? That they were out to cause harm to somebody. LOVETT: This is not an accident. CANNING (voice-over): Tim Lovett was the state`s collision reconstruction expert. He said the evidence showed Frances chased and hit Bonnie. LOVETT: That Escalade definitely hit that Range Rover at least two maybe three times. But Frances`s defense attorneys, Leigh Cutter and Jean Brown said investigators made a big mistake when they bought into the story of Bonnie Contreras. CUTTER: Everyone got their information from one person at the scene. That`s Bonnie and Bonnie lied her ass off. CANNING (voice-over): Defense accident reconstructionist Charles Ruble said there was no physical evidence to back up Bonnie`s claims that Frances had hit her over and over again, no evidence he said the SUVs had even touched. RUBLE: Not even once. CANNING (voice-over): And remember how Bonnie said her purse flew forward off the seat when Frances hit her? RUBLE: This is her purse in her car. I get hit in the rear, where`s my purse go? It doesn`t come on the front. That`s simple physics. CANNING (voice-over): In fact, he said the purse falling forward supports Frances`s claims that Bonnie was repeatedly slamming on her brakes. RUBLE: She does a sudden break and she`s moving like this. Then the purse would go into the floorboard. Bonnie Contreras is not telling the truth. CANNING (voice-over): What`s more, both defense and prosecution agreed Bonnie was wrong about her contention that Bill`s motorcycle was struck from behind. Evidence showed the motorcycle actually collided with the side of Frances`s SUV. CUTTER: I can`t believe a damn thing she said on there. CANNING (voice-over): In closing arguments, the defense said Bill`s death was simply a terrible accident. And Frances Hall had suffered enough. CUTTER: She`s been living in hell for three years. Let her go home. Let her fell her family and let her warn her husband. CANNING (voice-over): But the prosecution told the jury, Frances must be held accountable for her actions. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Of course, the defendant hated Bonnie Contreras. We don`t blame her for that, any wife would. What we do blame her for getting in her Escalade chasing after Bonnie and then veering into Bill. There`s your felony murder. CANNING (voice-over): The jury deliberated into the night. Who would they believe? HOLT (voice-over): Coming up, the verdict. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We the jury find the defendant -- HOLT (voice-over): And then this story about death on the highway takes off in a brand new direction. [22:49:57] CONTRERAS: How many more bombshells is there going to be? (COMMERCIAL BREAK) CANNING (voice-over): The jury deciding Frances Hall`s fate deliberated into the evening hours of September 8th, 2016. And then, just before 8:45, a verdict. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We, the jury, find the defendant, Frances Hall, guilty of murder -- CANNING (voice-over): Guilty of murder and aggravated assault. Frances`s friends and family were shocked. H. HALL: It was the worst feeling in my life. It was a moment Frances herself did not seem prepared for. But things weren`t over yet for Frances, there was still a second phase of trial sentencing. Texas law allows the defendant to be sentenced by either the judge or the jury. Frances chose the jury, the same one that found her guilty. As her attorneys made the case for leniency, they found a secret weapon and the Texas criminal code. CUTTER: We said this caveat this was written for Frances Hall, if any whatever. [22:55:01] CANNING (voice-over): The law calls it sudden passion, essentially that the defendant was immediately provoked to a degree of anger that would make an ordinary person incapable of cool reflection. That offense told the jury sudden passion gripped Frances when she spotted Bill and Bonnie on the road. CUTTER: She sees this woman who has not led up and tried to ruin her life for the last month. CANNING (voice-over): The stakes were enormous. A finding of sudden passion could drastically reduce Frances`s sentence from possible life in prison to a maximum of 20 years and a minimum of just two. For the first time, the jury heard from Frances Hall directly. F. HALL: You don`t understand, I love this man hearted whole. I gave him my life. I would have never hurt him, never. CANNING (voice-over): In her final arguments, Defense Attorney Leigh Cutter insisted Frances Hall`s actions were a textbook example of sudden passion. CUTTER: The text messages, the calls, the taunting, those would probably make you really hate someone, but never having seen them until their drive by in your car. If that`s not sudden passion, where you are incapable of thinking clearly I don`t know what it is. CANNING (voice-over): But prosecutor Scott Simpson told jurors not to be swayed by emotions. SIMPSON: You shouldn`t for one second, feel ashamed or bad for doing what you believe to be right. CANNING (voice-over): After about three hours of deliberations, the jury was ready. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We unanimously find the defendant caused the death of Bill Hall under the immediate influence of sudden passion. We assess her punishments return for two years. CANNING (voice-over): Two years, the absolute minimum sentence. On September 7th, 2018, after serving her time, Frances walked out of prison a free woman. We thought that this was the end of the story, but we were wrong. There`s a whole new chapter. This summer Frances was indicted in a multimillion dollar fraud scheme. She`s accused of providing false payroll information to get lower insurance premiums for the company she and Bill founded. The Texas Department of Insurance said the scheme allowed the company and its owners to avoid more than $9 million in premium payments. We plan to speak with Frances in person this week, but due to COVID concerns we met via Zoom. She denies the charges and the indictment. F. HALL: I`m an honest woman. I didn`t do anything illegal. I didn`t falsified anything. I`m innocent. I don`t have anything to hide. CONTRERAS: How many more bombshells is there going to be? CANNING (voice-over): We also caught up again with Bonnie Contreras to hear her thoughts on Frances`s latest troubles. CONTRERAS: She looks like a liar. She looks like a con. She just -- she looks bad all the way around. CANNING (voice-over): Bonnie now runs some businesses of her own, including a CBD spa. She believes the new charges just might change some people`s perceptions of Frances and herself. CONTRERAS: They were constantly calling me a gold digger. So who looks like the gold digger now? Is it me? Or is it her? F. HALL: I don`t even think she knows what the word gold digger means. What I`m going through right now has nothing to do with gold digging. Now what she did on her free time with my husband, that`s gold digging. I have Bill`s kids, I have Bill`s grandkids, something she`ll never have. And I have all the memories of Bill. That`s not a gold digger. That`s a wife. So she should have maybe looked it up on the dictionary first. CANNING (voice-over): Frances told us if the new case goes to trial, she`ll take the stand. It worked for her at the sentencing hearing in Bill`s murder. But insurance fraud is a serious crime too. And there`s no sudden passion defense. If convicted. The woman who served just two years for killing her husband will face the possibility of life in prison yet again. [22:59:16] HOLT (voice-over): That`s all for this edition of Dateline. We`ll see you again next Friday at 9:00, 8:00 Central as we begin our 31st season with all new two our mysteries. And of course, I`ll see you each week night for NBC Nightly News.
