headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for March 6, 2023, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS HOST (on camera): Tonight, the urgent search for four Americans kidnapped at gunpoint in Mexico. (voiceover): The terrifying video appearing to show the Americans being dragged into the back of a pickup after gunmen opened fire on their minivan. Was it a case of mistaken identity? The reward the FBI is offering and what we`re learning. Also tonight, scary moments in the air. The passenger on a United plane accused of trying to open the emergency exit and stab a flight attendant. A Southwest plane making an emergency landing in Cuba. Smoke filling the cabin. And a passenger dying after severe turbulence. California slammed with even more snow. Desperate residents trapped for more than a week. And the new winter threats we`re tracking. Protesters and police clashing in Atlanta. Nearly two dozen now facing domestic terror charges. The NTSB investigating after another Norfolk Southern train derails in Ohio. Our one-on-one with transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. We asked, should the company be forced to pause operations? Jurors in the Alex Murdaugh double murder trial breaking their silence. What they say about his decision to take the stand. And he was the last original member of a legendary rock band. Remembering guitarist Gary Rossington. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT: Good evening, everyone. And thank you for joining us. Chilling images tonight appear to show four Americans kidnapped at gunpoint moments after crossing from Texas into Mexico on Friday. Tonight, the FBI asking for the public`s help, offering a $50,000 reward to help locate the Americans who were attacked by armed men after crossing from Brownsville, Texas into Matamoros riding in a minivan bearing North Carolina plates. One woman seen being dragged into a pickup truck. A U.S. official tells NBC News the attack may have been a case of mistaken identity. Authorities say a Mexican citizen was killed during the confrontation. Gabe Gutierrez reports it happened in an area that has become increasingly dangerous. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): These photos shared widely on social media appear to show the kidnapping`s aftermath. The FBI says the four Americans entered Matamoros, Mexico Friday in a white minivan with North Carolina license plates before armed gunmen opened fire and abducted them. A law enforcement official with knowledge of the matter tells NBC News this video depicts part of the kidnapping, appearing to show one woman walking on her own, forced into a white pickup truck. Armed men with bulletproof vests are then seen dragging other people into the vehicle. KARINE JEAN-PIERRE , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: We are closely following the assault and kidnapping of four U.S. citizens in Matamoros, Mexico. These sorts of attacks are unacceptable. GUTIERREZ: Authorities say a Mexican citizen was killed during the incident. A law enforcement official tells NBC News the Americans did not cross the border for any criminal purpose and that this appears to be a case of mistaken identity. Today Mexico`s president said they`d entered the country to buy medicine, although U.S. officials have not confirmed that. We visited Matamoros to report on migrant tent camps for years, but violence there has escalated. The city of about half a million people just across the border from Brownsville, Texas is home to warring factions of the gulf drug cartel. The shootouts on Friday prompted the U.S. consulate to issue another security alert. Tonight, the FBI is offering a $50,000 reward for the safe return of the Americans. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And Gabe is with me now. Do we know anything about the identities of the Americans? GUTIERREZ (on camera): Well, Lester, the FBI has not confirmed any details but I just spoke with a family member of one of those abducted and she says the group was from South Carolina but had a rental car with North Carolina plates. She says the group crossed the border for a medical procedure. A law enforcement source with knowledge of the matter tells NBC News it was cosmetic surgery. And the family is pleading for their safe return tonight, Lester. HOLT: Gabe Gutierrez, thank you. Let`s turn now to those mid-air scares. The latest, a man arrested for allegedly trying to open a plane`s emergency exit door during a flight, then stab a flight attendant. That coming after a Southwest flight was forced to land after a bird strike. Here`s Tom Costello. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): It happened on a United flight from L.A. to Boston. Federal prosecutors say 45 minutes before landing, a male passenger attempted to open an exit door between first class and coach. When flight attendants confronted the man, he allegedly tried to stab one of them in the neck with a broken spoon. Fellow passengers tackled and subdued the passenger until the plane landed in Boston. 33-year-old Francisco Torres tonight being held on federal charges. Meanwhile, smoke and panic on Southwest flight 3923 Sunday. The 737 hit by birds as it took off from Havana, Cuba headed for Fort Lauderdale. The engine exploded and on fire and on fire. Terrified passengers donned oxygen masks as the crew circled back, making an emergency landing in Havana. [19:05:28] UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Smoke started coming into the cabin, and they just said stay in your seats and we had to start breathing. COSTELLO: Bird strikes are common, but rarely cause serious damage. The miracle on the Hudson landing in 2009 came after a flock of geese took out both of the plane`s engines. Meanwhile, tragedy on board a private plane when a passenger, 55-year-old Dana Hyde of Maryland, was killed as the Bombardier Challenger plane hit severe turbulence. The plane flying from New Hampshire to Virginia making an emergency landing in Connecticut. The NTSB says the pilots were dealing with a trim issue at the time, suggesting they may have hit clear air turbulence in a jet stream moving 50 to 100 miles an hour faster than normal. JOHN COX, NBC NEWS AVIATION ANALYST: Clear air turbulence is not something that radar shows. So, pilots are unable to see it in advance. COSTELLO: Every year, passengers and crew members suffer head lacerations, broken bones and bruises in severe turbulence. SARA NELSON , INTERNATIONAL PRESIDENT, ASSOCIATION OF FLIGHT ATTENDANTS: This is exactly why we tell you to wear your seat belt because if you`re not wearing your seat belt when severe turbulence like this happens, it can actually be deadly. (END VIDEOTAPE) COSTELLO (on camera): The incidents are rare but they come as the FAA prepares for an aviation safety summit next week. Lester? HOLT: All right, Tom, thank you. Parts of Southern California remain under a state of emergency tonight with many residents still trapped after days of historic snowfall. First responders still trying to reach those stranded with some running out of food and medicine. Miguel Almaguer is there. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): As blizzard- like conditions blanket California cities already buried under feet of snow -- ROBIN UNWIN-BASSETT, RESIDENT, TWIN PEAKS, CALIFORNIA: We have neighbors who are panicking. They`re without, you know, food, power, heat, medications. ALMAGUER: For nearly two weeks now, trapped residents near Lake Arrowhead just two hours outside of Los Angeles have been pleading for help. Today, middle school teacher Steve Gaskell is a literal lifeline. His jeep loaded with meals and insulin for Marisa Kupsak`s uncle who`s stranded at home. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Thank you. It`s overwhelming because my husband can`t even come home. He`s stuck at the bottom of the hill. ALMAGUER: As the desperate ration food and medicine, mounds of snow are trapping the most vulnerable who can`t dig or plow their way out. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It`s -- it`s tough. It really is. I`m sorry. ALMAGUER: The National Guard and firefighters have been called in to help. But it`s volunteers, some walking miles through waist-deep snow, making the difference. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I think the first responders are overwhelmed with the sheer volume of calls that they`re getting. ALMAGUER: With major roads being plowed, hand crews are slowly starting to reach senior citizens like Sidney White. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I can`t see myself getting out of here without them. ALMAGUER: But with more than nine feet of snowfall, the weight of these storms was far too great for the only grocery store in the community of crestline. The parking lot now a free food distribution site for residents like the Moncriefs, who were lucky to get past road blocks. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: People want to go to their homes. Let them home. ALMAGUER: Tonight, the sense of desperation spelled out across this community as help finally arrives for some but not all. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: So, Miguel, what is the situation right now with power and water? ALMAGUER (on camera): Well, Lester, people without power and water are slowly getting it back. I want to show you a live picture from our drone overhead. It shows another major problem they`re dealing with all across this area. That heavy snowfall is collapsing roofs. Lester, the people in this area, they need help and they need it fast. Lester? HOLT: All right, Miguel, thanks. Let`s bring in Dylan Dreyer who`s tracking all this. Dylan, when will the West Coast get some relief? DYLAN DREYER, NBC NEWS METEOROLOGIST (on camera): Well, where Miguel is we`re going to get some relief, but the next storm is already making its way across central and Northern California where over the next several days we`re going to see rounds of snow. So all the way through Wednesday at least, we will see several inches of snow, and in the higher elevations of the Sierra Nevada mountain range we`ll see one to three feet of snow. Then we`ll get a bit of a break before the next big storm system makes its way on shore for Friday into Saturday. We also have a weak little system moving across Lake Erie right now. This is going to produce just enough snow to make things tricky for Tuesday morning. Heaviest amounts will be across north-central Pennsylvania. But even in New York City just north of Philly, we could end up with enough on the roads to make things slippery for tomorrow morning. HOLT: OK, Dylan, thanks very much. Alarming scenes outside Atlanta where police say they faced a coordinated attack by rioters at the site of a planned police training facility. Tonight, more than 20 people are charged with domestic terrorism. Blayne Alexander has late details. [19:10:12] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In Atlanta, a chaotic clash. Atlanta Police released this video that they say shows rioters throwing fireworks at officers and setting construction vehicles and a trailer on fire. In the end, 23 charged with domestic terrorism. DARIN SCHIERBAUM, CHIEF, ATLANTA POLICE: When you throw Molotov cocktails, large rocks, a number of items at officers, your only intent is to harm. ALEXANDER: Police call it a coordinated attack by violent agitators. Of the 23 arrested, only two are from Georgia. While protesters say it all started at a family-friendly music festival and that officials used excessive force to arrest some who were not involved. All of it centered around a planned public safety training center that opponents have dubbed cop city. The planned site is right here, 85 acres just outside of Atlanta. A training facility for both Atlanta Police and Fire. Now, officers have been stationed nearby but they say they`re going to increase their presence in the coming days. Officials tout it as a way to improve community policing. ANDRE DICKENS , MAYOR OF ATLANTA: This is where your community and neighborhood watch programs, will learn how to keep your neighborhood safe. ALEXANDER: But critics say it will do just the opposite. KAMAU FRANKLIN, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, COMMUNITY MOVEMENT BUILDERS: 90 acres of the forest are going to be destroyed right away to build cop city. So, we see this as a further militarization of the police. ALEXANDER: This is the latest flashpoint in a fight that has stretched well over a year. In January, a protester was killed. A Georgia State Patrol trooper injured. Tonight, protesters say that this is just the start of a week of demonstrations. Blayne Alexander, NBC News, Atlanta. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: We turn now to Ohio and another derailment by a Norfolk Southern train. This one just a month after that toxic explosion in East Palestine. All as there is growing outrage over the response by the rail company and the federal government. Jesse Kirsch reports. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JESSE KIRSCH, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the NTSB is investigating another Norfolk Southern crash in Ohio, the company`s fourth derailment in this state in less than five months. This Springfield train wreck caught on camera. The company says 28 cars went off the track this weekend with two crew members on board. No injuries or public health threats were reported. JENNIFER HOMENDY, CHAIR, NTSB : 212 rail cars, some of which were tank cars transporting hazardous materials. KIRSCH: Norfolk Southern says the cars with hazardous materials were not among those that derailed. Today, the company promising more investment in sensors that detect overheated wheel bearings. PETE BUTTIGIEG, U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE: Even one derailment is too many. And yet the average in recent years has been several every single day. KIRSCH: Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg says railroad standards need to change. BUTTIGIEG: But it`s really the entire industry that has been pushing hard to water down or delay safety regulations. KIRSCH: Is it now time to try figuring out a way to possibly pause Norfolk Southern `s operations until these investigations are completed? BUTTIGIEG: Well, the reality is that our economy depends on a strong freight rail network operating 24/7. We shouldn`t have to shut down the rail system in this country in order to make sure that it is safe. KIRSCH: Still, some residents here don`t fully trust what they`re hearing from officials after last month`s toxic derailment in East Palestine more than 200 miles away. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I don`t know if it`s frustrating, but it`s just kind of scary that I`m sure there`s safety protocols in place and they`re not being followed. (END VIDEOTAPE) KIRSCH (on camera): Bipartisan calls for rail safety reform growing. Meanwhile, Norfolk Southern `s trains here once again on the move. Lester? HOLT: Jesse Kirsch, thank you. In 60 seconds, jurors in the Alex Murdaugh murder trial speak out about their guilty verdict, revealing their reactions after Murdaugh took the stand. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) A lawyer for Alex Murdaugh tells NBC News he is now off suicide watch but remains in isolation in a South Carolina prison. And now we`re hearing from some of the jurors who convicted him of murdering his wife and son. Here`s Catie Beck. [19:15:12] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CATIE BECK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): After six weeks of testimony and tears -- ALEX MURDAUGH, FOUND GUILTY OF KILLING HIS WIFE AND SON: Seeing my boys lay face down -- BECK: Jurors in the Alex Murdaugh trial breaking their silence about the decision to seal his fate. JAMES MCDOWELL, JUROR, ALEX MURDAUGH MURDER TRIAL: We already know that he`s a lawyer. He`s able to be emotional with cases, he`s able to be emotional with himself, so I think we were kind of able to read right through that. BECK: Murdaugh found guilty and sentenced to life for killing his wife Maggie and son Paul. Now, a convicted murderer behind bars. Alex Murdaugh will remain at the Kirkland Correctional Center for at least 30 days to be processed and evaluated. Murdaugh was on suicide watch for the first 72 hours and is now in protective custody, locked in isolation for 23 hours a day. Jurors say Murdaugh`s fate was close to decided from the first minutes inside the jury room. AMIE WILLIAMS, JUROR, ALEX MURDAUGH MURDER TRIAL: Everyone had questions, but we were able to explain everything. BECK: Jurors say Murdaugh`s decision to take the stand in his own defense hurt his case more than it helped. MCDOWELL: I think that he believes that he`s so convincing that he felt like that was his, you know, last resort. BECK: But for several, the cell phone video from the dog kennels tipped the scales to guilty. Some jurors accept they may never understand Murdaugh`s motive but have no doubt the punishment fits the crime. GWEN GENERETTE, JUROR, ALEX MURDAUGH MURDER TRIAL: He wanted to have control of everything. Some thinking it was more like greed, him being in control. BECK: Catie Beck, NBC News, Columbia, South Carolina. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And next, as we continue tonight, our exclusive reporting on a new legal challenge to the near total abortion ban in Texas. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: Back with our NBC News exclusive. A new lawsuit being filed in Texas challenging the state`s near-total ban on abortion and seeking clarity on when doctors are allowed to intervene in dangerous pregnancies without a fear of prosecution. Here`s Yamiche Alcindor. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) YAMICHE ALCINDOR, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): When Amanda and Josh Zurawski found out they were expecting a baby girl, they were overjoyed. The name they picked for her, Willow. AMANDA ZURAWSKI, HAD AN ABORTION: I mean, it was magical. The first 17 weeks were very easy, very smooth sailing. ALCINDOR: But just before week 18, something felt wrong. Amanda`s body was preparing for labor too early. The news from her doctor was devastating. A. ZURAWSKI: She said pretty quickly, you know, all in one breath, you`re going to lose the baby. She`s not going to survive. I thought what they would do is go in and intervene immediately, but she told me that they couldn`t because the baby`s heart was still beating and I wasn`t sick. ALCINDOR: Laws in Texas ban doctors from performing abortions except when a medical emergency endangers a person`s life or major bodily function. Those who violate the law could face up to life in prison. Take me into what it was like to wait. A. ZURAWSKI: I just existed in sorrow and fear. I was really, really scared. JOSH ZURAWSKI, HUSBAND OF AMANDA: This just isn`t something that you do with any other kind of medical issue, is you have to ask am I sick enough to get treatment. It was just -- it was infuriating. ALCINDOR: Three days after the diagnosis, Amanda`s health deteriorated. Doctors performed an abortion, but serious infections led to sepsis, and Amanda spent three days in the ICU. A. ZURAWSKI: Because of the law, I very nearly died. Nothing about this is pro-life. ALCINDOR: Now, Amanda is part of a group of seven plaintiffs represented by the Center for Reproductive Rights who plan to file a lawsuit against the State of Texas tonight. A. ZURAWSKI: Until there is a legal fight, nothing`s going to change. And something has to change. story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS HOST (on camera): Tonight, the urgent search for four Americans kidnapped at gunpoint in Mexico. (voiceover): The terrifying video appearing to show the Americans being dragged into the back of a pickup after gunmen opened fire on their minivan. Was it a case of mistaken identity? The reward the FBI is offering and what we`re learning. Also tonight, scary moments in the air. The passenger on a United plane accused of trying to open the emergency exit and stab a flight attendant. A Southwest plane making an emergency landing in Cuba. Smoke filling the cabin. And a passenger dying after severe turbulence. California slammed with even more snow. Desperate residents trapped for more than a week. And the new winter threats we`re tracking. Protesters and police clashing in Atlanta. Nearly two dozen now facing domestic terror charges. The NTSB investigating after another Norfolk Southern train derails in Ohio. Our one-on-one with transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. We asked, should the company be forced to pause operations? Jurors in the Alex Murdaugh double murder trial breaking their silence. What they say about his decision to take the stand. And he was the last original member of a legendary rock band. Remembering guitarist Gary Rossington. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT: Good evening, everyone. And thank you for joining us. Chilling images tonight appear to show four Americans kidnapped at gunpoint moments after crossing from Texas into Mexico on Friday. Tonight, the FBI asking for the public`s help, offering a $50,000 reward to help locate the Americans who were attacked by armed men after crossing from Brownsville, Texas into Matamoros riding in a minivan bearing North Carolina plates. One woman seen being dragged into a pickup truck. A U.S. official tells NBC News the attack may have been a case of mistaken identity. Authorities say a Mexican citizen was killed during the confrontation. Gabe Gutierrez reports it happened in an area that has become increasingly dangerous. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): These photos shared widely on social media appear to show the kidnapping`s aftermath. The FBI says the four Americans entered Matamoros, Mexico Friday in a white minivan with North Carolina license plates before armed gunmen opened fire and abducted them. A law enforcement official with knowledge of the matter tells NBC News this video depicts part of the kidnapping, appearing to show one woman walking on her own, forced into a white pickup truck. Armed men with bulletproof vests are then seen dragging other people into the vehicle. KARINE JEAN-PIERRE , WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: We are closely following the assault and kidnapping of four U.S. citizens in Matamoros, Mexico. These sorts of attacks are unacceptable. GUTIERREZ: Authorities say a Mexican citizen was killed during the incident. A law enforcement official tells NBC News the Americans did not cross the border for any criminal purpose and that this appears to be a case of mistaken identity. Today Mexico`s president said they`d entered the country to buy medicine, although U.S. officials have not confirmed that. We visited Matamoros to report on migrant tent camps for years, but violence there has escalated. The city of about half a million people just across the border from Brownsville, Texas is home to warring factions of the gulf drug cartel. The shootouts on Friday prompted the U.S. consulate to issue another security alert. Tonight, the FBI is offering a $50,000 reward for the safe return of the Americans. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And Gabe is with me now. Do we know anything about the identities of the Americans? GUTIERREZ (on camera): Well, Lester, the FBI has not confirmed any details but I just spoke with a family member of one of those abducted and she says the group was from South Carolina but had a rental car with North Carolina plates. She says the group crossed the border for a medical procedure. A law enforcement source with knowledge of the matter tells NBC News it was cosmetic surgery. And the family is pleading for their safe return tonight, Lester. HOLT: Gabe Gutierrez, thank you. Let`s turn now to those mid-air scares. Fellow passengers tackled and subdued the passenger until the plane landed in Boston. 33-year-old Francisco Torres tonight being held on federal charges. story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:30:18] JOSE DIAZ-BALART, NBC NEWS HOST: Tonight, a historic storms slams the state of California. Millions still under life threatening flash flood alerts after a rare system dumped heavy snow, torrential rain, and caused damaging wind gusts. The daring rescues and dangerous conditions as the storm moves east. Overseas, Ukraine heads into its second year of war. The images of solidarity emerging from across the globe. What the conflict could look like six months from now? Plus today, the CDC is out in East Palestine three weeks after that toxic train derailment as residents come forward with new health concerns (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) MELISSA BLAKE (ph): They poisoned me. They shouldn`t get away with that. (END VIDEO CLIP) DIAZ-BALART: And any day now, a Texas judge could make one of the biggest rulings on abortion access since Roe v. Wade was overturned. Could a popular and FDA approved abortion pill be pulled off the shelves nationwide? Plus, what we now know about a top college basketball star being linked to a fatal shooting. And the dancing grannies hit the streets during Mardi Gras. Why it was so much more than just a celebration. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Jose Diaz-Balart. DIAZ-BALART: Good evening. We begin tonight with a rare storm that hasn`t been seen in California in decades. As we come on the air, millions are under life threatening flash flood alerts after an historic system pummeled the state. Just listen to this, a blizzard warning was issued for the first time ever in San Bernardino County, where they saw more than five feet of snow. Other parts of the state saw hurricane force winds and torrential rains. Rescue workers were raced against the clock to save stranded drivers. And now that storm system is pushing east. Our Dana Griffin is in Los Angeles with the very latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DANA GRIFFIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): Life threatening flooding in the Golden State. In Southern California`s Ventura County, multiple RVs swept into the river. Watch this dramatic rescue, one of several in the region. A driver stuck in raging floodwater flings to a rescuer. They`re both hoisted swinging in the wind before safely landing on solid ground. This morning, near Los Angeles, a dangerous light show. A live wire fell into the water, setting a car on fire. The historic winter weather walloped California with heavy snow. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Now we`re having of trouble because the snow is making it slippery. GRIFFIN: Torrential rain in some areas, nearly an entire month`s worth in 48 hours. And strong wind gusts creating blizzardlike conditions in the San Bernardino County mountains. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: First time seeing snow in a long time. GRIFFIN: With San Francisco seeing its lowest temperatures in over a century. And Los Angeles experiencing its first blizzard warning in more than 30 years. In San Diego, several water rescues today. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We just had a vehicle that was in the deep water, unable to drive out, and two occupants of the vehicle that needed to be rescued and brought back to dry land. So, we anticipate doing this a few more times. GRIFFIN: The stunning system now headed east toward Oklahoma City, Wichita and Kansas City, where 9 million are at risk for large hail and even tornadoes. In Michigan, more than 400,000 remain without power from an ice storm earlier this week. Back in Southern California, tonight, the mess the storm left behind and the dangers this system could still bring to the area. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: Dana Griffin joins us from hard hit Los Angeles. Dana, what threat remains even as the storm now moves out? GRIFFIN: While, Jose, those lingering impacts could include mudslides and additional flooding. Just take a look at the Los Angeles River, it is moving so swiftly at such a dangerous pace, and the water level is usually not this high. Jose? DIAZ-BALART: Dana Griffin in Los Angeles. Thank you. And now to the war in Ukraine. The conflict entering its second year with no end in sight. And around the world today, signs of solidarity in support of the war-torn country. Erin McLaughlin reports tonight from Kyiv. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ERIN MCLAUGHLIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): From New York to Taipei, Toronto to Tbilisi, a sea of yellow and blue. Outside the Russian embassy in Warsaw, protesters blasting the sound of air raid sirens. Ukraine is waking up under the sounds of real Russian bombs and rockets, she says. [18:35:10] A global show of support for Ukraine as the Russian assault enters its second year. The United States now pledging $2 billion more to help the Ukrainians fight. But President Biden Friday ruling out sending Ukrainian President Zelenskyy F-16 fighter jets for now. JOE BIDEN , (D) U.S. PRESIDENT: We`re sending him what our seasoned military thinks he needs now. He needs tanks, he needs artillery. MCLAUGHLIN: All things Ukrainian officials agree they need to win this war and quickly. (On camera): Where do you see this war in six months? Both men are now charged with capital murder, and investigators say Miles admits he provided the gun used in the shooting to Davis. But in a court hearing this week, police testified it was Miller who brought the handgun to his former teammate after getting text messages to pick him up and bring Miles gun. In a statement, Miller`s attorney said Brandon never touch the gun, was not involved in its exchange to Mr. Davis in any way, and never knew that illegal activity involving the gun would occur. Miller hasn`t missed a game since the investigation began. The university is stressing he`s fully cooperating with authorities and is not considered a suspect. OATS: Make decisions based on available facts, and that`s what we did here. CHESKY: Tonight, the mother of Jamea Harris upset Miller was allowed to play today, saying had there been no gun, her daughter would still be alive. DECARLA HEARD, JAMEA HARRIS` MOTHER: I haven`t stopped being angry. I haven`t stopped long enough to grieve because I`m so angry. She has a five- year-old son that`s still at home waiting on his mom to come home. And she never come home. CHESKY: Morgan Chesky, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: All right, we are back in a moment with the failure to comply, why some hospitals still are not posting prices for patients despite a law saying they have to. Plus, the deadly crash that killed two bicyclists into Arizona. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:50:49] DIAZ-BALART: We are back at the scene of a deadly crash in Arizona, where a pickup truck struck a large group of bicyclists riding across a bridge. At this time, there are two confirmed fatalities and eleven others injured. Officials say the driver stayed on the scene and police are investigating the incident. Two years ago, laws were put into place that required hospitals nationwide to post the prices of medical procedures so that patients knew how much they would have to pay for treatment in advance. But patient advocates say many hospitals still are not posting prices, and customers are being shocked by the large medical bills. Marissa Parra has more. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MARISSA PARRA, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): The pressure of paying for medical procedures has haunted Jeff King in Kansas for years. JEFF KING, SURPRISE MEDICAL BILLS VICTIM: I went back to my follow up appointment. They said, how are you doing? I said, well, your medical bill about put me into AFib again. PARRA: But it is his right to know how much a procedure costs in advance, and it has been since January of 2021, when federal price transparency became federal law. CHIQUITA BROOKS-LASURE, CENTERS FOR MEDICARE AND MEDICAID SERVICES ADMINISTRATOR: It`s so incredibly important. PARRA: Chiquita Brooks-LaSure, the Administrator for Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services , also oversees hospital transparency. In a report released last week, CMS says that of the 600 hospitals they sampled, 70% were in full compliance, up from the 27% the year before. But patient advocacy groups are dissatisfied. CYNTHIA FISHER, PATIENTRIGHTSADVOCATE.ORG FOUNDER: It is not happening fast enough. PARRA: And they`re challenging CMS`s survey results. PatientRightsAdvocate.org released their own report weeks ago, analyzing the websites of 2000 hospitals within the nation`s largest hospital systems, their findings only 25% were in full compliance. Patient Advocate Cynthia Fisher shows us what patients should see on a compliant hospital`s website. FISHER: It`s showing all of the codes. PARRA: And she showed us what she found on many instead. FISHER: Instead of prices, they put N/As in the field. PARRA: So we took it to CMS. (On camera): Would this hospital be considered compliant? BROOKS-LASURE: Yes, because N/A according to our rules means we don`t do the procedure. PARRA: Which would mean if they provide these procedures? BROOKS-LASURE: They should be telling us how much it costs. PARRA: In the two years since the law took effect, CMS has only issued two fines given as NBC was pressing the HHS secretary last summer. (On camera): The buck stops with you. You`re the secretary. (Voice-over): Brooks-LaSure says they`ve given 500 warning letters to hospitals, and now the maximum fines have been increased from $100,000 to $2 million. So we asked, what`s the biggest hold up? CMS blames the pandemic. BROOKS-LASURE: So they haven`t always had all of the staff to really focus on some of the IT system changes that need to happen. PARRA: The American Hospital Association , which represents healthcare networks and hospitals, says health systems remain, "deeply committed, despite considerable strains on the hospital workforce over the past three years." PARRA: Who hurts the most? FISHER: It`s the American people. It`s the hard-working. PARRA: In Washington, Marissa Parra, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: When we come back, the heartwarming reason these grannies are dancing through the streets of the Big Easy. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:56:45] DIAZ-BALART: There is good news tonight about the power of friendship and how love and dancing help heal the pain. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: For the famous Milwaukee Dancing Grannies, this week`s visit to New Orleans was the trip of a life. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Ladies and gentleman, the Milwaukee Dancing Grannies. DIAZ-BALART: A chance to perform in one of the city`s Mardi Gras parades. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Oh, they were amazing. DIAZ-BALART: But for Jan Kwiatkowski and the rest of the group, it was about so much more. (On camera): Jan, what was it like to be in New Orleans for Mardi Gras? JAN KWIATKOWSKI: It was the probably absolute most amazing, profound, exciting lifegiving thing that not only myself, but all of us have done. DIAZ-BALART: She says the celebration was also a time of healing. That`s because in November 2021, three of their members and a dancer`s husband were killed along with two other people during the Waukesha Christmas parade when a man driving an SUV intentionally plowed through the crowds. (On camera): In that senseless, horrible tragedy, how do you all as a group go forward? KWIATKOWSKI: The reality is you don`t heal unless you`re healing in community. DIAZ-BALART: Community they found in the New Orleans dance group called The 610 Stompers. They call themselves extraordinary men with extraordinary moves. And they invited the grannies to Mardi Gras as a sign of solidarity. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I cannot begin to tell you how much that means to all of us. (CHEERING & APPLAUSE) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Why can`t we just come together and try to heal and -- DIAZ-BALART: Stompers Chris Second (ph) and Brett Patron just knew their city would welcome them with open arms. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m going to tell you that right now. They are hard to handle. But they were so much fun. DIAZ-BALART: The two dance groups now forever friends with joyful memories they`ll never forget. KWIATKOWSKI: It`s just such a tangible way of saying you`re not alone. That meant a lot. I can`t even put into words. I`m going to cry now how much that meant. (END VIDEOTAPE) DIAZ-BALART: The Grannies hope to have The 610 Stompers join them in a parade sometime this year back in Wisconsin. That`s NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for this Saturday. Kate Snow will be here tomorrow night. I`m Jose Diaz-Balart. Thank you for the privilege of your time, and good night. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the bombshell testimony. Alex Murdaugh taking the stand at his murder trial. (voiceover): The South Carolina attorney denying he killed his wife and son, but then stunning the courtroom, admitting he lied to police about his alibi that night. The paranoid thoughts he said he thought he was having and the moment Murdaugh broke down as he described finding the bodies. Then the prosecution`s turn. The tough questions he faced under cross- examination. Also tonight, a deadly winter storm on the move. More than a million customers without power. In the Midwest, a downed power line killing a firefighter. A parking garage collapsing under snow. The new threat in the west. Rare blizzard warnings in southern California. Al Roker is here. New clues in the toxic train derailment in Ohio. The NTSB saying it was 100 percent preventable. The preliminary report finding an alarm went off just before the wreck. What investigators say about the crew`s actions and the potential cause. The shooting spree in Florida. A TV reporter and a 9-year-old girl killed. New body cam of police arresting the suspect. The new details. And the Emmy-winning star of Abbott Elementary, Sheryl Lee Ralph on the obstacles she has overcome and inspiring a new generation. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT: Good evening. For the defense, accused murderer Alex Murdaugh taking the witness stand today in South Carolina. Dramatic and at times tearful testimony from the man at the center of the country`s most closely followed criminal trial. Murdaugh under questioning from his lawyers saying I didn`t shoot my wife or son. And addressing what has appeared to be some of the prosecution`s strongest evidence. Murdaugh from the witness box admitting he lied about his whereabouts the night his wife and 22-year-old son were shot to death. Shocking at the lies to an opioid addiction and paranoia. Under cross-examination, Murdaugh, a former lawyer also admitted to stealing from clients. The prosecution has maintained the murders were part of Murdaugh`s attempt to escape accountability for financial misdeeds. We begin tonight with Catie Beck reporting from Walterboro, South Carolina. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CATIE BECK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): After nearly five weeks of testimony, a stunning surprise. ALEX MURDAUGH, ACCUSED OF KILLING HIS WIFE AND SON: I am going to testify. I want to testify. BECK: The trial`s most anticipated witness takes the stand. Alex Murdaugh testifies in his own defense. The first questions aimed at the heart of the case. JIM GRIFFIN, DEFENSE LAWYER: Did you take this gun or any gun like it and blow your son`s brains out on June 7th, or any day, or any time? MURDAUGH: No, I did not. GRIFFIN: Did you take another blackout such as this and fire it into your wife Maggie`s leg, torso, or any part of her body? MURDAUGH: No, I did not. BECK: Quick to confront what is perhaps the prosecution`s strongest evidence, the video taken by Paul Murdaugh at the dog kennels, placing Alex at the crime scene minutes before the murders. He`s told investigators he wasn`t there, but admits now he was lying. GRIFFIN: Alex, why did you lie? MURDAUGH: As my addiction evolved over time, I would get in these situations or circumstances where I would get paranoid. BECK: Murdaugh says he didn`t trust state law enforcers, and regrets the lie that led to many others. GRIFFIN: Did you continue lying after that night, did you not? MURDAUGH: Once I lied, I continued the lie, yes, sir. BECK: Emotional and crying throughout, Murdaugh`s testimony largely rewrites his timeline on the night of the murders, showering and changing clothes before dinner, and describing the moment he discovered the bodies, again saying he checked for signs of life. MURDAUGH: I know I tried to turn him over. GRIFFIN: When you say you tried to turn him over, why were you trying to turn him over? MURDAUGH: I don`t know. I don`t know. I don`t know why I tried to turn him over. My boy`s laying face-down. BECK: Later in testimony, Alex admits a long-time addiction to opioids, that he stole clients` funds, but denies being overly concerned about getting caught prior to the murders. CREIGHTON WATERS, CHIEF PROSECUTOR: What kind of cases did you normally do? BECK: On cross-examination, prosecutors began by pressing Murdaugh on the fraud cases, where he admits he stole money from his clients and lied to them. And prosecutors suggesting all the stolen money wasn`t going to fund his pill addiction. WATERS: You were generating millions of dollars in fees. That was not enough for you? Would you concede that? [19:05:08] MURDAUGH: If by concede that, you mean was I also stealing money that I shouldn`t have, yes, sir, I agree with that. I`ve said that, repeatedly. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Catie, what do we know about how the jury was taking all this in how they may have reacted? BECK (on camera): Well, Lester, the jury was captivated, so attentive to Alex Murdaugh`s testimony on the stand today. At times, Murdaugh was repositioning his body to face the jurors directly and answer the questions directly to them. At one point, when Murdaugh got extremely emotional, one juror that was sitting close to him actually slid a Kleenex box in his direction. Lester? HOLT: All right, Catie Beck, thank you. Let me bring in our Senior Legal Correspondent Laura Jarrett now. Laura, what was the defense strategy here, and how does it appear to be playing out? LAURA JARRETT, NBC NEWS SENIOR LEGAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, this is the defense team going on offense. Clearly, the goal was to try to take the sting out of the damning evidence that the prosecution would raise on cross-examination, and that`s likely why he was forced to admit that he lied to police and to his family, all while trying to plant seeds of reasonable doubt. But testifying at all, it`s a risky gamble. Already the prosecution has tried to highlight his inconsistencies and also pierce through his folksy demeanor on cross-examination to try to show this jury that he is an accomplished lawyer who knows how to cover his tracks. Lester? HOLT: All right, Laura, thank you. Now to that deadly crippling winter storm that is stretching right now across the country and a separate threat here in the West. Gabe Gutierrez is watching it all from Minneapolis. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, devastating snow, ice, and wind pummeling even more of the country. This time knocking out power to nearly a million people across the Midwest. Most of those outages in Michigan where a volunteer firefighter was killed when a tree brought down a high-voltage line. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: A volunteer just died in here for free. He gave his life for free. GUTIERREZ: In Wisconsin, authorities say snow likely caused a partial collapse of a parking garage at a shopping mall. Today, Minneapolis under a snow emergency. Over the last few hours, we`ve seen a very rapid snowfall here. The road conditions are getting worse. Snow totals not as high as predicted earlier in the week, still around a foot blanketed the twin cities over three days. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is a big one. For all coming down at once, like, yes, this is a pretty big one. GUTIERREZ: Coast-to-coast, treacherous road conditions. Portland, Oregon recording its second snowiest day on record with more than 10 inches. This 20-car pileup in Southern California injuring at least eight people. A separate system now prompting the first blizzard warnings since 1989 for the mountains near L.A. The nationwide weather whiplash is remarkable even for February. Across the Mid-Atlantic and southeastern U.S., record heat, unusually high temperatures as far north as Philadelphia. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Having a 70-degree day is just such a welcome break. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (on camera): But air travel is still dicey. More than 2,000 U.S. flights canceled just today, Lester. HOLT: All right, Gabe, thank you. And that takes us to Al Roker . Al, as one storm moves out, another moves in impacting the West Coast. AL ROKER, NBC NEWS WEATHER ANCHOR: Lester, we have six million folks out west looking at winter weather advisories, winter storm warnings, blizzard warnings, including the San Bernardino Mountains. First blizzard warning ever issued there. Record lows likely. We`re looking at morning lows in Reno in the 20s. Vegas into the 30s. Even Los Angeles into the upper 30s. Salt Lake City in the 20s. We`re looking at five to eight feet of snow back through the Sierra, but also the San Bernardino Mountains and the Santa Barbara Mountains as well. We`re also looking upwards of 10 inches of rain through Southern California. Significant roadway flooding and airport delays likely. Lester? HOLT: All right, Al Roker , thank you. And new tonight, a preliminary finding about the cause of that toxic train disaster in Ohio as the Transportation Secretary visited for the first time. Ron Allen is there. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) RON ALLEN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, with the scene being cleaned up, new details about what caused the fiery derailment. Federal investigators saying a preliminary investigation shows an overheated wheel bearing likely to blame. JENNIFER HOMENDY, CHAIR, NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION SAFETY BOARD : This was 100 percent preventible. ALLEN: The NTSB says the train passed over two detectors, which showed the bearing was heating up. By the time it hit a third detector, it was 253 degrees above air temperature, triggering an audible alarm to warn the crew, who then slowed and stopped the train. HOMENDY: This is a community that is suffering. This is not about politics. What I care about is figuring out how this happened. ALLEN: The NTSB chair says there is no evidence the crew did anything wrong. In a statement, Norfolk Southern says our highest priority is the safety of our people and the communities we serve. Adding, it will continue to support the NTSB `s investigation. While today, Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg visited for the first time after criticism from some residents that he should have come sooner, demanding the nation`s rail operators stop resisting safety measures to cut costs. [19:10:19] PETE BUTTIGIEG, U.S. SECRETARY OF TRANSPORTATION: Let`s get people from both sides of the aisle to the table and come to agreement on some steps that are needed, even if the rail industry is pushing back. ALLEN: Meanwhile, near the crash, this Figleys only comes back to the farm to check on things like their chickens. They`re part of a class action lawsuit that attorneys say includes over 500 residents. MARILYN FIGLEY, RESIDENT, EAST PALESTINE: I live out of my car and at my daughter`s house. It`s awful. I feel homeless. ALLEN: Why won`t you come back home? FIGLEY: Because I don`t know what I`m coming home to, and I`m 70 years old. ALLEN: Ron Allen, NBC News, East Palestine, Ohio. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Now to Florida, where a series of shootings left three people dead, including a young girl and a reporter. Two more are hospitalized. A suspect is under arrest. Guad Venegas is there for us. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Get on your (BLEEP) face! GUAD VENEGAS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, the Orange County Sheriff releasing bodycam footage of the arrest of Keith Moses, the 19-year-old suspect accused of a deadly shooting spree in Orlando. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Roll him on his side real quick. VENEGAS: Three victims killed, including a news reporter and a 9-year-old girl, two others critically wounded. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We`re getting multiple gunshots wound calls in the Hialeah Street area. VENEGAS: The first shooting happened Wednesday morning where authorities found 38-year-old Natacha Augustin dead from a gunshot wound. Officials say the victim was an acquaintance of the suspect. Hours later, a news crew covering that incident was ambushed in their car, deputies say. The gunfire killing 24-year-old Spectrum News 13 reporter Dylan Lyons and critically wounding cameraman Jesse Walden. I just happened to catch a bullet. But he kept shooting at me as I ducked behind the wheel of my car, and he walked forward and shot into my car and ended up striking our reporter. VENEGAS: Authorities say the suspect then fled the scene and entered a nearby home. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`ve got two more victims, 9-year-old female. VENEGAS: Deputies say he then opened fire again, killing a 9-year-old girl and critically injuring her mother. The suspect was arrested a short time later. JOHN MINA, SHERIFF, ORANGE COUNTY, FLORIDA: We recovered a Glock 40, a semiautomatic handgun from inside of his pants. That gun was still hot to the touch, meaning it had just been fired. VENEGAS: Moses is now charged with first-degree murder. (END VIDEOTAPE) VENEGAS (on camera): And tonight, officials are still investigating a motive, but they say the 19-year-old suspect had a lengthy criminal history, including eight felony and 11 misdemeanor arrests. Lester? HOLT: Guad Venegas, thank you. In 60 seconds, the battle over abortion. How an imminent court ruling about a widely used abortion drug could have an impact nationwide. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: It could be the most consequential abortion decision since Roe v. Wade was overturned. A Texas judge will soon decide whether to block access to a commonly used abortion pill nationwide. Dasha Burns reports. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CROWD: We can`t go back! DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Amarillo, Texas now at the center of America`s abortion debate. CROWD: I believe that we will win! BURNS: Here, a group of anti-abortion doctors and medical organizations are suing the FDA , challenging the approval of Mifeprex, generically known as Mifepristone, part of a two-drug regimen commonly used for abortions that has been approved by the FDA since 2000. Alliance Defending Freedom arguing the FDA didn`t adequately evaluate the drug`s safety. ERIK BAPTIST, SENIOR COUNSEL, ALLIANCE DEFENDING FREEDOM: We`re asking the court to do what is right, to follow -- and ask the FDA to follow the law by taking these dangerous drugs off the marketplace. BURNS: Presiding over the case, a conservative judge appointed by former President Trump. An injunction would set off access to Mifepristone nationwide. If the plaintiffs win this lawsuit, what will be the effects? [19:15:01] DR. SERINA FLOYD, MEDICAL DIRECTOR, PLANNED PARENTHOOD OF METROPOLITAN WASHINGTON, DC: It will be devastating. Even in places where they`ve worked very hard to secure access to abortion, states like California, New York, here in D.C. BURNS: Abortion providers like Dr. Serina Floyd say the lawsuit is based on misinformation. How dangerous is this medication? FLOYD: It`s not dangerous at all. The evidence is solid, the science is solid. The complication rate is less than one percent. BURNS: The FDA told NBC News it does not comment on ongoing litigation. But in the court filings said the claims in the lawsuit are unsupported by any evidence. Since 2000, more than five million women have taken mifepristone with 28 deaths associated with the drug reported. Millions of women have taken these drugs safely. Doesn`t that paint a contrary picture to your complaint? DR. CHRISTINA FRANCIS, AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF PRO-LIFE OBSTETRICIANS AND GYNECOLOGISTS: I`m seeing these women in my own practice. My emergency room physicians, they`re telling me how frequently they`re seeing these complications, that women come in with retained tissue, with heavy bleeding, with serious life-threatening infections. BURNS: In a court brief, the country`s leading group of OBGYN say the mifepristone is "exceedingly safe and effective, calling the lawsuit ideological and not scientific. The result if you win is that abortion access will be significantly limited. Is that the goal of this lawsuit? BAPTIST: No, the goal of this lawsuit is to protect American women and girls from dangerous chemical abortion drugs. BURNS: There is another drug, Misoprostol, that can be used for abortions, but doctors say it can be less effective on its own. Back in Amarillo, Amanda Barnes travelled from Atlanta to protest this case. AMANDA BARNES, ACTIVIST: It`s ridiculous that just because, you know, we were born with a uterus and certain body parts that we should have to be subjected to this treatment. BURNS: The next frontier in America`s abortion battle. Dasha Burns, NBC News, Amarillo, Texas. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Coming up, our exclusive report in the flow of goods into Russia, despite sanctions. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: As the war in Ukraine approaches the one-year mark, the U.S. is pushing for more sanctions against Russia. But are the ones already in place having an impact? Keir Simmons went inside neighboring Georgia to find out how Russia is getting around them. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS SENIOR INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): If you want to know how the Russian economy is surviving amid punishing western sanctions, you might come here. We`re just across the border in Georgia, and it`s lined with trucks. President Putin`s supply line. You`re going from Turkey to Russia? To Moscow? He`s carrying xerox printer ink, he says. Since Putin`s invasion and unprecedented Western sanctions, satellite images along with international trade data shows this mountain pass becoming much busier. That`s not surprising. At the outset of the war, Russia dropped most import restrictions on things like cars. The Russian border is about 25 miles that way, but police tell us they`ve closed the road because of an avalanche risk. Business has stopped, but only temporarily. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Hello! SIMMONS : Then hidden in the snow, a stunning discovery. Two brand-new American ram pickups. American cars, American trucks? It was never driven, he says. Take a look at this. Look, it`s still got the protection on the dashboard. Look, they`re brand-new. Where are they going? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: To the Moscow. SIMMONS: To Moscow, he tells me. The men tell us they`ve sold both vehicles for around $170,000 each. They say they are moving cars every week. Does it matter that there is a war on? Where is that war, he asks. It doesn`t matter for us. We have obtained one of the vehicle ID numbers and asked the manufacturer who told us it was legally sold to a private customer by an authorized distributor in Abu Dhabi, that they cannot prevent that customer from reselling it, and the company complies with all U.S. and international sanctions. And it`s not only Georgia. Satellite images also show lines of trucks on the roads to Russia from China. President Putin and China`s top diplomat meeting yesterday, pledging to strengthen ties. China already provides crucial economic help to Russia. Back in Georgia, the road reopens, and we pass a construction site where China is helping build a new tunnel through the mountain. The half-billion project was started before the Ukraine invasion. But the plan will be more trade with Russia. Clearly, not every country wants this to be the end of the road for moscow. (END VIDEOTAPE) SIMMONS (on camera): Despite all the sanctions, the IMF says Russia`s economy is actually set to grow this year, though only by 0.3 percent. Lester? HOLT: Keir Simmons tonight, thank you. Up next, our inspiring one-on-one with actress and singer Sheryl Lee Ralph. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: She is the star of a hit sitcom, an Emmy winner, and recently sang at the Super Bowl. Sheryl Lee Ralph now on the hurdles she overcame and why she is only just getting started. She spoke with Dana Griffin. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DANA GRIFFIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): With a career spanning nearly five decades in showbiz, Sheryl Lee Ralph is back in the spotlight. Do you still have pinch me moments, especially now when you see we`re sitting in the middle of Hollywood? SHERYL LEE RALPH, SINGER: Yes. I have real pinch me moments in life, because, you know, I`ve lived most of my life as a very regular normal human being. I will go to the 99 Cent Store, the Dollar Tree or whatever. I will do that. And now when I go, I`m like, what in the world are they staring at? And then, I`m like, oh my God, it`s me. GRIFFIN: The entertainment icon has had a whirlwind of recent success, inspiring a new generation. RALPH: Now, who took that picture of me? GRIFFIN: Last year, she won an Emmy for supporting comedy actress for her role in Abbott Elementary where she plays teacher Barbara Howard. What was that moment like for you? RALPH: First of all, I was -- I was listening to the whole thing, and I was like getting ready to be happy for somebody. And I realized, no, this is very real. She just called my name. GRIFFIN: And more recently, the critics choice awards where her message resonated with many. RALPH: When you look in the mirror, you better love what you see. GRIFFIN: Her Broadway, TV and film career dates back to the `70s. In 1981, she starred in the original Broadway cast of Dream Girls. Her latest performance, Super Bowl LVII, singing Lift Every Voice And Sing. But stealing the show hasn`t always been easy. RALPH: They used to say you`re too dark. Your lips are too big. Your hair is too nappy. Suppose I listened to them? GRIFFIN: But Ralph persevered. What else do you want to accomplish? RALPH: More. I want to tell stories that deserve to be told, characters whose voices were dimmed or dulled or muted just because they were Black. Now is the time to tell those stories. GRIFFIN: Dana Griffin, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And that`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Thursday. Thanks for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2023 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. I want to testify. BECK: The trial`s most anticipated witness takes the stand. Alex Murdaugh testifies in his own defense. The first questions aimed at the heart of the case. MURDAUGH: As my addiction evolved over time, I would get in these situations or circumstances where I would get paranoid. BECK: Murdaugh says he didn`t trust state law enforcers, and regrets the lie that led to many others. GRIFFIN: Did you continue lying after that night, did you not? MURDAUGH: Once I lied, I continued the lie, yes, sir. BECK: Emotional and crying throughout, Murdaugh`s testimony largely rewrites his timeline on the night of the murders, showering and changing clothes before dinner, and describing the moment he discovered the bodies, again saying he checked for signs of life. MURDAUGH: I know I tried to turn him over. GRIFFIN: When you say you tried to turn him over, why were you trying to turn him over? MURDAUGH: I don`t know. I don`t know. BAPTIST: No, the goal of this lawsuit is to protect American women and girls from dangerous chemical abortion drugs. BURNS: There is another drug, Misoprostol, that can be used for abortions, but doctors say it can be less effective on its own. AMANDA BARNES, ACTIVIST: It`s ridiculous that just because, you know, we were born with a uterus and certain body parts that we should have to be subjected to this treatment. Keir Simmons went inside neighboring Georgia to find out how Russia is getting around them. Since Putin`s invasion and unprecedented Western sanctions, satellite images along with international trade data shows this mountain pass becoming much busier. That`s not surprising. At the outset of the war, Russia dropped most import restrictions on things like cars. GRIFFIN: The entertainment icon has had a whirlwind of recent success, inspiring a new generation. RALPH: Now, who took that picture of me? GRIFFIN: Last year, she won an Emmy for supporting comedy actress for her role in Abbott Elementary where she plays teacher Barbara Howard. What was that moment like for you? RALPH: First of all, I was -- I was listening to the whole thing, and I was like getting ready to be happy for somebody. And I realized, no, this is very real. She just called my name. GRIFFIN: Her Broadway, TV and film career dates back to the `70s. In 1981, she starred in the original Broadway cast of Dream Girls. Her latest performance, Super Bowl LVII, singing Lift Every Voice And Sing. But stealing the show hasn`t always been easy. RALPH: They used to say you`re too dark. Your lips are too big. Your hair is too nappy. Suppose I listened to them? GRIFFIN: But Ralph persevered. What else do you want to accomplish? RALPH: More. I want to tell stories that deserve to be told, characters whose voices were dimmed or dulled or muted just because they were Black. Now is the time to tell those stories. GRIFFIN: Dana Griffin, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And that`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Thursday. Thanks for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. headline: Nationwide Marches On Anniversary Of Roe v. Wade
story_text: KATE SNOW: Today, the landmark abortion ruling, Roe v. Wade turns 50 years old. But the controversy surrounding last year`s reversal or Roe is heating up once again, with marches across the country. And now, more than six months after that decision, where does the battle over abortion rights stand? Marissa Para reports from Madison, Wisconsin. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We will win. I believe that we will win. MARISSA PARRA, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, on the 50th anniversary of Roe v. Wade, abortion rights activists drumming up defiance, moving their main women`s march bigger than Roe, from the capitol to the Midwest. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: This time, we move the National March to Madison in order to kick off our newfound campaign to the states, which is where battle is taking place. PARRA (on camera): So, I have the main march here in Madison, Wisconsin, that is because we are just weeks away from a primary judicial election and a state Supreme Court seat is up for grabs. And if it is filled with a pro- abortion rights candidate, then the Wisconsin abortion ban could be overturned. PARRA (voiceover): Sister marches in hundreds of cities across the country, just days after the National March for life against abortion and just seven months after Roe v. Wade was overturned in a five-four decision, sending both sides of the debate into action. The state of play, a murky patchwork. Roughly two dozen states have either a total abortion ban or are close to it. Some state laws changed immediately, like Wisconsin`s abortion ban. Some, like neighboring Illinois, later passing abortion protection. And last fall, historically red states, Kansas and Kentucky, voted down antiabortion ballot measures. Today, Vice President Kamala Harris once again calling to codify Roe. KAMALA HARRIS , U.S. VICE PRESIDENT: Congress must pass a bill that protects freedom and liberty. PARRA (voiceover): But with Republicans in control of the House, the federal abortion debate remains in a deadlock, making mobilizing on a local level more important than ever. From Madison, Wisconsin, Marissa Parra, NBC News. (END VIDEO CLIP) SNOW: Still ahead, a goodbye at Graceland, the moving tributes from celebrities and fans today for Lisa Marie Presley. How her mother remembered her. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [18:50:00] SNOW: A violent protest in Downtown Atlanta is under investigation tonight. It happened late Saturday. A group demonstrating against a new police training center got out of hand. Police say some people smashed windows and set a patrol car on fire. Others were carrying explosive devices. Six people were arrested and charged with domestic terrorism, arson, and criminal damage. A small plane made an emergency landing northwest of Houston Today. Take a look at this. The single engine aircraft reported that it lost power and it went down, crashing on top of an 18-wheeler. The plane then caught fire. The most astonishing thing about all this, the pilot and the truck driver were not injured. END Content and programming copyright 2023 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: 50 Years After Roe v. Wade, America Is An Abortion Battleground After The Supreme Court Decision Overturning It
story_text: LESTER HOLT: We have new details on the Supreme Court`s probe into the stunning leak last year, that draft opinion overturning Roe v. Wade. The Supreme Court Marshal revealed today she spoke with each justice in addition to court employees, but investigators were not able to identify the leaker. And this weekend marks 50 years since the Roe v. Wade decision. In the months since it was overturned, the U.S. has become a patchwork of laws varying from state to state. Anne Thompson with more now on the deep impact on clinics. [19:15:07] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANNE THOMPSON, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The days are nonstop at Florida`s Jacksonville Health Center. 50 years after roe versus wade and seven months after the Dobbs ruling that overturned it, demand for abortion at this Planned Parenthood Clinic hasn`t slowed says Manager Jessica Wannemacher. JESSICA WANNEMACHER, MANAGER, PLANNED PARENTHOOD CLINIC, JACKSONVILLE: It`s getting worse. THOMPSON: What do you mean? WANNEMACHER: The amount of patient load that we need to be able to see more patients. THOMPSON: Four years ago, the clinic offered abortion services once a week. Now, it`s up to five days. Dr. Shelly Tien specializes in high-risk pregnancies. Of the 63 patients you`re seeing today, how many of those are seeking abortion services? DR. SHELLY TIEN, PLANNED PARENTHOOD CLINIC: The vast majority. THOMPSON: Has it been like that since the Supreme Court decision? TIEN: It has. THOMPSON: Florida bans abortions after 15 weeks with narrow exceptions. It also requires two in-person doctor`s visits at least 24 hours apart, but the outright bans and heartbeat bills in neighboring states have more than doubled the out-of-state patients here. For opponents of abortion rights like Andrew Shervill, it is a frustrating consequence of the Supreme Court decision. ANDREW SHIRVELL, FOUNDER AND EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, FLORIDA VOICE FOR THE UNBORN: It`s extremely -- actually, it`s extremely infuriating because here Florida`s leading on so many other issues, but we should not be in this position at all. THOMPSON: So, what`s next? SHIRVELL: What`s next? Here in Florida, we`re pushing for a complete abortion ban. THOMPSON: But at the clinic Dr. Tien believes any restrictions come with dire consequences. TIEN: Women are going to die because of what has happened to reproductive rights in this country. THOMPSON: A recent Commonwealth Fund study analyzed data from 2020 and found maternal death rates were 62% higher in states that had abortion restrictions. The battle is now in states like Florida. SHIRVELL: I think the Dobbs decision properly returned the public policy fight to the states, and that for the foreseeable future is where activists on both sides are going to be engaged. THOMPSON: Should medical doctors have a role in crafting abortion law? SHIRVELL: No, I don`t believe so. THOMPSON: Dr. Tien disagrees. TIEN: It must be shared decision-making between the patient, her family and her healthcare team. THOMPSON: Do politicians have a role in this? TIEN: Absolutely not. Absolutely not. THOMPSON: Rulings may change, but the debate has no end in sight. Anne Thompson, NBC News, Jacksonville. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: All right, coming up, it may say organic, but is it food fraud? headline: 50 Years After Roe v. Wade, America Is An Abortion Battleground After The Supreme Court Decision Overturning It
story_text: LESTER HOLT: We have new details on the Supreme Court`s probe into the stunning leak last year, that draft opinion overturning Roe v. Wade. The Supreme Court Marshal revealed today she spoke with each justice in addition to court employees, but investigators were not able to identify the leaker. And this weekend marks 50 years since the Roe v. Wade decision. In the months since it was overturned, the U.S. has become a patchwork of laws varying from state to state. Anne Thompson with more now on the deep impact on clinics. [19:15:07] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) ANNE THOMPSON, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The days are nonstop at Florida`s Jacksonville Health Center. 50 years after roe versus wade and seven months after the Dobbs ruling that overturned it, demand for abortion at this Planned Parenthood Clinic hasn`t slowed says Manager Jessica Wannemacher. JESSICA WANNEMACHER, MANAGER, PLANNED PARENTHOOD CLINIC, JACKSONVILLE: It`s getting worse. THOMPSON: What do you mean? WANNEMACHER: The amount of patient load that we need to be able to see more patients. THOMPSON: Four years ago, the clinic offered abortion services once a week. Now, it`s up to five days. Dr. Shelly Tien specializes in high-risk pregnancies. Of the 63 patients you`re seeing today, how many of those are seeking abortion services? DR. SHELLY TIEN, PLANNED PARENTHOOD CLINIC: The vast majority. THOMPSON: Has it been like that since the Supreme Court decision? TIEN: It has. THOMPSON: Florida bans abortions after 15 weeks with narrow exceptions. It also requires two in-person doctor`s visits at least 24 hours apart, but the outright bans and heartbeat bills in neighboring states have more than doubled the out-of-state patients here. For opponents of abortion rights like Andrew Shervill, it is a frustrating consequence of the Supreme Court decision. ANDREW SHIRVELL, FOUNDER AND EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, FLORIDA VOICE FOR THE UNBORN: It`s extremely -- actually, it`s extremely infuriating because here Florida`s leading on so many other issues, but we should not be in this position at all. THOMPSON: So, what`s next? SHIRVELL: What`s next? Here in Florida, we`re pushing for a complete abortion ban. THOMPSON: But at the clinic Dr. Tien believes any restrictions come with dire consequences. TIEN: Women are going to die because of what has happened to reproductive rights in this country. THOMPSON: A recent Commonwealth Fund study analyzed data from 2020 and found maternal death rates were 62% higher in states that had abortion restrictions. The battle is now in states like Florida. SHIRVELL: I think the Dobbs decision properly returned the public policy fight to the states, and that for the foreseeable future is where activists on both sides are going to be engaged. THOMPSON: Should medical doctors have a role in crafting abortion law? SHIRVELL: No, I don`t believe so. THOMPSON: Dr. Tien disagrees. TIEN: It must be shared decision-making between the patient, her family and her healthcare team. THOMPSON: Do politicians have a role in this? TIEN: Absolutely not. Absolutely not. THOMPSON: Rulings may change, but the debate has no end in sight. Anne Thompson, NBC News, Jacksonville. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: All right, coming up, it may say organic, but is it food fraud?
