story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, another deadly mass shooting in America, this time at a Virginia Walmart just before Thanksgiving. (voiceover): The gunman, a store manager laughing before opening fire in the Walmart break room according to witnesses and police. At least six killed before the shooter took his own life. The horror unfolding as the store was filled with holiday shoppers. We`re on the scene. It comes just days after the massacre at an LGBTQ club in Colorado. The suspect making a first court appearance today slumped over in a wheelchair with visible facial injuries. What happened at that hearing? Also, tonight, the busiest day on the roads as nearly 55 million Americans travel for Thanksgiving. And the holiday storm threat. We`re tracking it. Russia`s new missile strikes on Ukraine. A maternity ward hit. A newborn infant killed. The first bombings in Jerusalem in years. The deadly blasts being called a terrorist attack. New details in the murders of four University of Idaho students. And now, the other unsolved stabbing case. Police are looking at it. Is there a link? The countdown to Black Friday. Where to find the best deals despite soaring inflation? And the spirit of a holiday. What kids say they`re most thankful for this year. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. We keep ending in the same place, don`t we? Morning victims who could have been any of us, scratching our heads over possible motives, and reciting the growing list. All those places where mass violence has snuffed out or threatened to take innocent lives. Tonight, just days after the Colorado Springs attack, we`re absorbing details of the latest horrific mass shooting in this country. Six people at a Chesapeake, Virginia Walmart shot to death by a long-time store employee who opened fire with a handgun. Several others were wounded. A survivor is saying the attack in an employee break room was preceded by the gunman`s laughter. The 31-year-old took his own life before police arrived. The killer described by a senior law enforcement official as a disgruntled employee. But what that means as to a specific motive is unclear. In a statement, President Biden speaking with many are thinking tonight, there are now even more tables across the country that will have empty seats this Thanksgiving. NBC`s Cal Perry is in Chesapeake with the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CAL PERRY, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tragedy in Chesapeake, Virginia. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: How many medics do we have left in the city right now? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Currently six medics available. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Go ahead and dispatch all of them. PERRY: 911 receiving its first call to the Walmart Supercenter at 10:12 p.m. Officers arriving within two minutes. We got a whole scene out here but it`s crazy out here right now. They everywhere. The 31-year-old shooter who police say worked at the store since 2010 came armed with a handgun and multiple magazines. One senior law enforcement official tells NBC News he was a disgruntled employee. BRIANA TYLER, WITNESS: I literally was frozen. I just stood there. I`d like I literally could be dead right now. It didn`t kick in until I looked at my coworker and she was bleeding out of her neck. PERRY: Six people were killed ranging in age from 16 to 70. At least four others were wounded before the shooter turned the gun on himself. MARK SOLESKY, CHIEF, CHESAPEAKE, VIRGINIA POLICE DEPARTMENT: The investigation is still ongoing, and we`ll be processing that scene for days. GOV. GLENN YOUNGKIN (R-VA): The most important thing we need to do is come around families and support them. It`s unimaginable what they`re dealing with today. PERRY: 24-year-old Jalon Jones had been working at the Walmart for about a year. He`s recovering at a nearby hospital. KIMBERLY SHUPE, MOTHER OF JALON JONES: He knew he was being shot. He made it to the front of the store. And then when he made it to the front door, he was shot again. PERRY: 28-year-old Jessie says it was just her fifth day on the job. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I saw a lot of bad thing that happened to really good people. And I didn`t understand it. And it didn`t feel real. PERRY: She says she was in the break room when the shooter came in laughing and started firing. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: He got the gun pointed at me and he looks at me and he puts it up in the air. And all he said was just to go home. I ran. I didn`t look back. I want to look back. PERRY: Do you know why he let you go, Jessie? Do you have any idea? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: No, I know. PERRY: So far, there`s no word on motive, and it`s unclear if the victims were targeted. Authorities today cordoned off this vehicle in the parking lot saying it`s a vehicle of interest. DR. JESSICA BURGESS, SENTARA NORFOLK GENERAL HOSPITAL: It`s heartbreaking. PERRY: Chesapeake, Virginia, just the latest community left grappling with yet another senseless shooting. [19:05:01] BURGESS: It was just two days ago that I was contacting one of my colleagues in Colorado Springs wishing her well and checking in to see how she was doing after she had just taken care of shooting victims. So it`s very disheartening that now I`m in the same position with my colleagues from across the country checking in on me. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Cal, what are investigators focusing on right now? PERRY (on camera): Lester, investigators are focused on any connection they can find between the victims and the shooter. For example, if any of the victims worked with the shooter, that could go a long way in finding a motive. Lester? HOLT: All right, Cal Perry tonight, thank you. In Colorado Springs today, the first court appearance by video from jail for the suspect in the killing of five people at that LGBTQ nightclub four days ago. The suspect who was subdued and beaten by club patrons was released from the hospital yesterday. The suspect, on public defenders, identify as non-binary person, was ordered held without bail and faces possible murder and hate crime charges. We have been through this so many times this year. By one count, there have been 608 mass shootings defined as four or more people shot. That`s not far from last year`s record. Here`s Tom Costello. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): On this Thanksgiving Eve, America is reckoning with the violence that is tearing up the national fabric. This afternoon, four high school students shot in Philly. Every week, nearly 13 mass shootings, so many we too often forget those that happened last week or last month. 21 children and teachers killed in Uvalde, Texas. 10 people gunned down in a Buffalo grocery store. Five and Raleigh, four in Memphis, four in Tulsa, six in Sacramento. The list is excruciatingly long. ROB BONTA, ATTORNEY GENERAL, CALIFORNIA: We know that this is America`s disease, unique in the world. COSTELLO: David Hogg, one of the high school students from Parkland, Florida where 17 people died, tweeted at 2:24 this morning, I am tired of waking up to texts about another mass shooting in America. DAVID HOGG, PARKLAND SHOOTING SURVIVOR: It`s going to continue happening. And we have to work together to actually stop this from happening. COSTELLO: Nationwide, 49 people die in gun violence every day. STEVEN DETTELBACH, DIRECTOR, ATF: My biggest fear is that somehow as a country, we become callous or to kind of accept or think that this is OK, that this is somehow part of our national story. COSTELLO: Pediatrician Emily Lieberman was with her children in Highland Park, Illinois when a gunman killed seven people on July 4. Now, she`s leading a group of doctors demanding the Senate pass more than the gun safety measures enacted after Uvalde. EMILY LIEBERMAN, PEDIATRICIAN: Now, the number one cause of death of children in this country is gun violence. It`s time to start tackling gun violence as a public health problem and listening to people like physicians who know how to solve this problem. (END VIDEOTAPE) COSTELLO (on camera): The country holding a mirror to itself with politicians expected back in D.C. next week. And the decades-old gun control debate likely to be a dinner table topic tomorrow. Lester? HOLT: Tom Costello, thank you. We`ll take a turn out of the busy Thanksgiving travel rush. Almost 55 million Americans expected to travel this year nearly hitting pre pandemic levels. And we`re also tracking storms that could bring heavy rain to the south and Gulf Coast tomorrow. Erin McLaughlin joins us now from Los Angeles. Erin, what`s the traffic like there? ERIN MCLAUGHLIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, things are looking pretty good here, Lestrer, especially for Los Angeles. Nearly 49 million Americans are expected to hit the road this Thanksgiving. That`s slightly compared to last year with the national average price of a gas, a gallon of gas, just below that $5.00 mark we saw back in June. Meanwhile, across the nation`s airports tonight, some good news for the most part. Flights have been on time thanks largely to clear skies and good weather across the country. Here in Los Angeles at LAX airport, they`re expecting some 200,000 passengers today alone. It`s the busiest they`ve been since the beginning of the pandemic. Lester? HOLT: Erin McLaughlin in Los Angeles, thank you. Two bombings in Jerusalem today killed a teenager and injured at least 18 others including two Americans. The explosions were near bus stops during the morning rush hour. Israeli police say the bombs were left at those locations and blamed Palestinians for the attacks. It`s the latest in a surge of violence between Israelis and Palestinians. And in Ukraine, Russia launching a new barrage of missile strikes. Ukrainian officials say a newborn infant was killed when a missile hit a hospital maternity ward in the southern part of the country. Much of Ukraine without power after Russians attack the energy infrastructure in Kyiv and several other cities. Tonight, new details from the police in the killings of those four college students in Idaho. Lots of leads and progress reported in the case but still no suspect identified. Gadi Schwartz has the latest. [19:10:06] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GADI SCHWARTZ, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): For the 11th day in a row, investigators saying still no suspect, no motive and the killings of four Idaho university students, but trying to assure the public they are making headway. COL. KEDRICK WILLS, IDAHO STATE POLICE: At this crime scene, we collected 103 pieces of individual evidence. SCHWARTZ: But frustration is growing among family members who fear investigators fell behind during the first crucial 48 hours of the case. WILLS: No tip is too small and we would urge anybody that has any information whatsoever to please provide that to help us solve this case. SCHWARTZ: Those who live in Moscow also asking about a recent dog mutilation that happened three miles away from the murders. Jim and Pam Colbert say about a month ago, someone grabbed their dog at 2:00 a.m. and skinned him in a field in front of their home. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Right over there. Right over -- SCHWARTZ: Took his fur but left his unbuckled collar behind. So, somebody actually had to unclasp it. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Unclasp it right here. See, that stays. And somebody had to undo it. Because if you had a knife, wouldn`t you have cut it? SCHWARTZ: But Moscow police say they don`t think that case has anything to do with the murders. Police also asked about an unsolved murder 300 miles away in Oregon, in which a masked intruder attacked a couple with a knife in their sleep. JAMES FRY, CHIEF, MOSCOW, IDAHO POLICE: Actually, I had a tip come in on that case and I`ve ordered it to our tip line. SCHWARTZ: Meanwhile, the University of Idaho giving students the option of finishing their semester remotely while families of the victims are struggling with the thought of Thanksgiving without their loved ones and praying that the killer won`t strike again. Gadi Schwartz, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Also tonight, the so-called tripledemic, RSV, the flu, and COVID, is already pushing hospitals to the brink. The U.S. facing shortages of pediatric beds, medical staff, and now even some medications. Here`s Gabe Gutierrez. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In Buffalo, some store shelves normally filled with children`s Tylenol are empty. Pharmacists say a spot shortage of the drug in Canada triggered by mounting cases of RSV is spilling over the border. DON ARTHUR, PHARMACIST: Apparently, up in Canada, the liquid forms of Tylenol are unavailable. GUTIERREZ: Johnson and Johnson , the maker of Tylenol, says there`s no overall shortage in the U.S., telling NBC News we are experiencing high consumer demand and they`re doing everything we can to make sure people have access to the products they need. Still, the FDA currently lists amoxicillin as being in short supply. And it all comes as the healthcare industry braces for a potential tripledemic this winter. RSV, flu, and COVID colliding. In New York, Ella Rose Giam (PH) is home after a week in the hospital. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It was surreal. Like, seeing your daughter on a breathing mask and she`s only three and a half. GUTIERREZ: Adding to the strain on the system, an increasingly dire staffing shortage. More than half a million people in the healthcare and social services industries quit their positions in September. Were you burnt out? Extremely. Yes, sir. Reece Brown in Louisiana is no longer a traveling nurse. REECE BROWN, NURSE: That joy which is literally being sucked out of us. We were doing everything that we could and we just -- it was never enough. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (on camera): As for COVID, the CDC says new data shows the Omicron boosters offer better protection against variants than earlier doses. Still, they are not as effective as the original COVID vaccine was against the initial virus. Lester? HOLT: All right, Gabe Gutierrez, thanks. In 60 seconds, new abortion restrictions and the agonizing decisions they are forcing some families to make. Our in-depth look at the issue coming up next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: The Georgia Supreme Court today reinstated a ban on abortions after six weeks of pregnancy while it considers an appeal. And while a few states including Georgia make exceptions when a fetus has life-threatening problems, most states with new abortion restrictions do not. Blayne Alexandre has more. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Jill Hurtle could not wait to become a mom. She still remembers the second she found out. JILL HURTLE, HAD ABORTION: I was like sobbing. I was so excited. [19:15:02] ALEXANDER: You felt like a mom. HURTLE: I felt like a mom in that -- in an instant. ALEXANDER: Her husband, Matt, dreamed of being a girl dad. They even picked out a name Ivy Grace. Every doctor`s appointment brought good news until the 18-week scan. HURTLE: And our world`s like came crashing down. She came in and she said her heart isn`t what it is supposed to look like. I think in that exact moment, my stomach dropped and I think I truly knew that it was going to be a really severe situation. ALEXANDER: It was. A condition known as hypoplastic left heart syndrome, HLHS. Doctor said her baby`s case was especially severe, and her daughter would likely not survive long after birth. HURTLE: I didn`t want her to have to go through so much pain and suffering. ALEXANDER: After more tests and more devastating news, Jill and her husband made the painful decision. HURTLE: If she were to live an hour or 10 days, I didn`t want her to just - - I didn`t want her to know nothing but pain. So, my protective instinct was to do what I knew what was best for her, which was to send her to heaven. ALEXANDER: Every year, congenital or fetal anomalies impact one in every 33 babies born in the U.S. and range from minor to life-limiting or life- threatening. Since the Supreme Court decision overturning Roe v. Wade, at least 16 states have successfully enacted laws further restricting abortion access. Only three have exceptions for lethal fetal anomalies. DR. DAVID LEVINE, NEONATOLOGIST: We`re not dealing with one size fits all. We can`t make laws for one size fits all. ALEXANDER: Dr. David Levine is a neonatologist who opposes abortion access and believes the baby should be carried to term even with a grim prognosis. LEVINE: Most families who have decided to spend time with their babies however short it might be, by and large, have benefited from it. They`ve been able to bond with their baby. ALEXANDER: Is it therefore a law to make that decision for a parent? LEVINE: There are many decisions that are taken out of our hands. Is it fair for the mother to make that decision to take a baby`s life away from him. ALEXANDER: Jill had to leave South Carolina and wait two weeks for an appointment in Washington, DC. HURTLE: Those two weeks were probably the hardest two weeks I`ve ever experienced in my life. Every time you feel her kick or move, it`s just a dagger to the heart. ALEXANDER: She believes abortion bans should have exceptions for cases like hers, giving women the chance to make a choice, however painful. HURTLE: I am a mom. I`m a mom to an angel in heaven. And I know that she`s at peace. ALEXANDER: Blayne Alexander, NBC News, Charleston, South Carolina. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, as the holiday shopping rush begins, top tips on where and how you can save in our series "RACE TO DELIVER." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: As you may have noticed, many retailers have already rolled out their Black Friday deals. So, where can you save the most? NBC`s Brian Cheung has been shopping around for our series "RACE TO DELIVER." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BRIAN CHEUNG, NBC NEWS BUSINESS AND DATA REPORTER (voiceover): Tonight, amid a growing unease in the nation`s economy, the dash for holiday deals is on. With consumer prices up 7.7 percent compared to last season and one in three households saying their finances are worse off from a year ago, shoppers are left with tighter budgets. TRAE BODGE, SMART SHOPPING EXPERT, TRUETRAE.COM: Retailers are aware of the fact that consumers only have so much to spend. CHEUNG: That`s why even before Black Friday, many retailers are already offering deep discounts vying for your holiday dollars. The most discounted items this season, everything from TVs, laptops, to home appliances, and beauty products. For electronics, consider older models for an even better deal. Many clothing retailers are also offering extra deep discounts this season in part because of excess inventory falling supply chain lock-ups last year. BODGE: We are seeing a lot of overstock still and retailers have been spending the last couple of months trying to sell through that merchandise. CHEUNG: Which could lead to even deeper discounts. BODGE: I do expect to see discounts deeper than usual in categories like casual apparel, TVs, furniture, home decor. And so, in addition to the exciting cyber weekend sales that we`ll see, we`ll also see kind of extra discounts as retailers look to clear out all those overstocks. CHEUNG: Experts say shopping with strategy will save you big bucks. Start by creating a shopping list with a spending cap. Then compare prices online and in store. And check your credit card for additional discounts and offers. (END VIDEOTAPE) CHEUNG (on camera): And don`t forget about gift cards which are always a hot item every year. Many can actually be bought at a discount. Lester? HOLT: All right, Brian, thanks. Up next, what are you thankful for? Some children will tell us right after the break. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally, a lot of news has been especially grim this week, but we thought you might be uplifted or find a smile in listening to the gratitude expressed by some New York school kids we spoke to about Thanksgiving. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) HOLT (voiceover): At Manhattan Country School, today`s lesson is all about giving thanks. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Thank you God for a mother. HOLT: And after two years of holidays overshadowed by COVID, many students told us they`re grateful for a Thanksgiving that feels a little more normal. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m thankful for like, family and friends because like, during COVID, I wasn`t able to see -- I wasn`t able to see like, a lot of my friends. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m very grateful that me and my family -- or my family and I have been healthy and happy and able to see each other. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m really thankful for the school and for my teachers and my friends. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m thankful for my dog. She`s good at comforting people especially me. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m thankful for my family because they give me comfort and I just love them. HOLT: Of course, on Thanksgiving -- UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I love cooking. HOLT: Comfort also comes in the form of turkey, stuffing, and potatoes. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We bake and we coconut we have this huge feast at the end. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We make an angel fruitcake which I really love to do with my grandma. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m definitely looking forward to eating because we do cook pretty good Thanksgiving meal. HOLT: When you`re in grade school, there`s something else to look forward to. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We get a lot of days off from school. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The first thing I think about it is wrapped up in a blanket drinking hot chocolate and watching a movie, and I just get really excited about that. HOLT: A moment of peace with the people you love, to give thanks, isn`t that what the day is all about? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: When I think about the holidays, I think about community and spending time with the people that I love and giving back to them and hopefully receiving the same. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And thank all of you for being here tonight. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS. Be sure to tune in for the Macy`s Thanksgiving Day Parade at 9:00 Eastern here on NBC and Peacock. Thank you for watching and Happy Thanksgiving, everyone. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. PERRY: So far, there`s no word on motive, and it`s unclear if the victims were targeted. Authorities today cordoned off this vehicle in the parking lot saying it`s a vehicle of interest. DR. JESSICA BURGESS, SENTARA NORFOLK GENERAL HOSPITAL: It`s heartbreaking. PERRY: Chesapeake, Virginia, just the latest community left grappling with yet another senseless shooting. PERRY (on camera): Lester, investigators are focused on any connection they can find between the victims and the shooter. For example, if any of the victims worked with the shooter, that could go a long way in finding a motive. Lester? HOLT: All right, Cal Perry tonight, thank you. In Colorado Springs today, the first court appearance by video from jail for the suspect in the killing of five people at that LGBTQ nightclub four days ago. The suspect who was subdued and beaten by club patrons was released from the hospital yesterday. The suspect, on public defenders, identify as non-binary person, was ordered held without bail and faces possible murder and hate crime charges. We have been through this so many times this year. By one count, there have been 608 mass shootings defined as four or more people shot. That`s not far from last year`s record. Here`s Tom Costello. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): On this Thanksgiving Eve, America is reckoning with the violence that is tearing up the national fabric. This afternoon, four high school students shot in Philly. Every week, nearly 13 mass shootings, so many we too often forget those that happened last week or last month. 21 children and teachers killed in Uvalde, Texas. 10 people gunned down in a Buffalo grocery store. Five and Raleigh, four in Memphis, four in Tulsa, six in Sacramento. The list is excruciatingly long. ROB BONTA, ATTORNEY GENERAL, CALIFORNIA: We know that this is America`s disease, unique in the world. COSTELLO: David Hogg, one of the high school students from Parkland, Florida where 17 people died, tweeted at 2:24 this morning, I am tired of waking up to texts about another mass shooting in America. DAVID HOGG, PARKLAND SHOOTING SURVIVOR: It`s going to continue happening. And we have to work together to actually stop this from happening. COSTELLO: Nationwide, 49 people die in gun violence every day. STEVEN DETTELBACH, DIRECTOR, ATF: My biggest fear is that somehow as a country, we become callous or to kind of accept or think that this is OK, that this is somehow part of our national story. EMILY LIEBERMAN, PEDIATRICIAN: Now, the number one cause of death of children in this country is gun violence. It`s time to start tackling gun violence as a public health problem and listening to people like physicians who know how to solve this problem. (END VIDEOTAPE) COSTELLO (on camera): The country holding a mirror to itself with politicians expected back in D.C. next week. And the decades-old gun control debate likely to be a dinner table topic tomorrow. Lester? HOLT: Tom Costello, thank you. We`ll take a turn out of the busy Thanksgiving travel rush. Almost 55 million Americans expected to travel this year nearly hitting pre pandemic levels. And we`re also tracking storms that could bring heavy rain to the south and Gulf Coast tomorrow. Erin McLaughlin joins us now from Los Angeles. Erin, what`s the traffic like there? ERIN MCLAUGHLIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, things are looking pretty good here, Lestrer, especially for Los Angeles. Nearly 49 million Americans are expected to hit the road this Thanksgiving. It`s the latest in a surge of violence between Israelis and Palestinians. And in Ukraine, Russia launching a new barrage of missile strikes. Ukrainian officials say a newborn infant was killed when a missile hit a hospital maternity ward in the southern part of the country. Much of Ukraine without power after Russians attack the energy infrastructure in Kyiv and several other cities. Tonight, new details from the police in the killings of those four college students in Idaho. Lots of leads and progress reported in the case but still no suspect identified. Gadi Schwartz has the latest. [19:10:06] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GADI SCHWARTZ, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): For the 11th day in a row, investigators saying still no suspect, no motive and the killings of four Idaho university students, but trying to assure the public they are making headway. COL. KEDRICK WILLS, IDAHO STATE POLICE: At this crime scene, we collected 103 pieces of individual evidence. SCHWARTZ: But frustration is growing among family members who fear investigators fell behind during the first crucial 48 hours of the case. WILLS: No tip is too small and we would urge anybody that has any information whatsoever to please provide that to help us solve this case. SCHWARTZ: Those who live in Moscow also asking about a recent dog mutilation that happened three miles away from the murders. Jim and Pam Colbert say about a month ago, someone grabbed their dog at 2:00 a.m. and skinned him in a field in front of their home. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Right over there. Right over -- SCHWARTZ: Took his fur but left his unbuckled collar behind. So, somebody actually had to unclasp it. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Unclasp it right here. See, that stays. And somebody had to undo it. Because if you had a knife, wouldn`t you have cut it? SCHWARTZ: But Moscow police say they don`t think that case has anything to do with the murders. Police also asked about an unsolved murder 300 miles away in Oregon, in which a masked intruder attacked a couple with a knife in their sleep. JAMES FRY, CHIEF, MOSCOW, IDAHO POLICE: Actually, I had a tip come in on that case and I`ve ordered it to our tip line. SCHWARTZ: Meanwhile, the University of Idaho giving students the option of finishing their semester remotely while families of the victims are struggling with the thought of Thanksgiving without their loved ones and praying that the killer won`t strike again. Gadi Schwartz, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Also tonight, the so-called tripledemic, RSV, the flu, and COVID, is already pushing hospitals to the brink. The U.S. facing shortages of pediatric beds, medical staff, and now even some medications. Here`s Gabe Gutierrez. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In Buffalo, some store shelves normally filled with children`s Tylenol are empty. Pharmacists say a spot shortage of the drug in Canada triggered by mounting cases of RSV is spilling over the border. DON ARTHUR, PHARMACIST: Apparently, up in Canada, the liquid forms of Tylenol are unavailable. GUTIERREZ: Johnson and Johnson , the maker of Tylenol, says there`s no overall shortage in the U.S., telling NBC News we are experiencing high consumer demand and they`re doing everything we can to make sure people have access to the products they need. Still, the FDA currently lists amoxicillin as being in short supply. And it all comes as the healthcare industry braces for a potential tripledemic this winter. RSV, flu, and COVID colliding. In New York, Ella Rose Giam (PH) is home after a week in the hospital. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It was surreal. Like, seeing your daughter on a breathing mask and she`s only three and a half. GUTIERREZ: Adding to the strain on the system, an increasingly dire staffing shortage. More than half a million people in the healthcare and social services industries quit their positions in September. Were you burnt out? Extremely. Yes, sir. Reece Brown in Louisiana is no longer a traveling nurse. REECE BROWN, NURSE: That joy which is literally being sucked out of us. We were doing everything that we could and we just -- it was never enough. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (on camera): As for COVID, the CDC says new data shows the Omicron boosters offer better protection against variants than earlier doses. Still, they are not as effective as the original COVID vaccine was against the initial virus. Lester? HOLT: All right, Gabe Gutierrez, thanks. In 60 seconds, new abortion restrictions and the agonizing decisions they are forcing some families to make. Our in-depth look at the issue coming up next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: The Georgia Supreme Court today reinstated a ban on abortions after six weeks of pregnancy while it considers an appeal. And while a few states including Georgia make exceptions when a fetus has life-threatening problems, most states with new abortion restrictions do not. Blayne Alexandre has more. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Jill Hurtle could not wait to become a mom. She still remembers the second she found out. JILL HURTLE, HAD ABORTION: I was like sobbing. I was so excited. [19:15:02] ALEXANDER: You felt like a mom. HURTLE: I felt like a mom in that -- in an instant. ALEXANDER: Her husband, Matt, dreamed of being a girl dad. They even picked out a name Ivy Grace. Every doctor`s appointment brought good news until the 18-week scan. HURTLE: And our world`s like came crashing down. She came in and she said her heart isn`t what it is supposed to look like. I think in that exact moment, my stomach dropped and I think I truly knew that it was going to be a really severe situation. ALEXANDER: It was. A condition known as hypoplastic left heart syndrome, HLHS. Doctor said her baby`s case was especially severe, and her daughter would likely not survive long after birth. HURTLE: I didn`t want her to have to go through so much pain and suffering. ALEXANDER: After more tests and more devastating news, Jill and her husband made the painful decision. HURTLE: If she were to live an hour or 10 days, I didn`t want her to just - - I didn`t want her to know nothing but pain. So, my protective instinct was to do what I knew what was best for her, which was to send her to heaven. ALEXANDER: Every year, congenital or fetal anomalies impact one in every 33 babies born in the U.S. and range from minor to life-limiting or life- threatening. Since the Supreme Court decision overturning Roe v. Wade, at least 16 states have successfully enacted laws further restricting abortion access. Only three have exceptions for lethal fetal anomalies. DR. DAVID LEVINE, NEONATOLOGIST: We`re not dealing with one size fits all. We can`t make laws for one size fits all. ALEXANDER: Dr. David Levine is a neonatologist who opposes abortion access and believes the baby should be carried to term even with a grim prognosis. LEVINE: Most families who have decided to spend time with their babies however short it might be, by and large, have benefited from it. They`ve been able to bond with their baby. ALEXANDER: Is it therefore a law to make that decision for a parent? LEVINE: There are many decisions that are taken out of our hands. Is it fair for the mother to make that decision to take a baby`s life away from him. ALEXANDER: Jill had to leave South Carolina and wait two weeks for an appointment in Washington, DC. HURTLE: Those two weeks were probably the hardest two weeks I`ve ever experienced in my life. Every time you feel her kick or move, it`s just a dagger to the heart. ALEXANDER: She believes abortion bans should have exceptions for cases like hers, giving women the chance to make a choice, however painful. HURTLE: I am a mom. I`m a mom to an angel in heaven. And I know that she`s at peace. ALEXANDER: Blayne Alexander, NBC News, Charleston, South Carolina. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, as the holiday shopping rush begins, top tips on where and how you can save in our series "RACE TO DELIVER." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: As you may have noticed, many retailers have already rolled out their Black Friday deals. So, where can you save the most? NBC`s Brian Cheung has been shopping around for our series "RACE TO DELIVER." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BRIAN CHEUNG, NBC NEWS BUSINESS AND DATA REPORTER (voiceover): Tonight, amid a growing unease in the nation`s economy, the dash for holiday deals is on. TRAE BODGE, SMART SHOPPING EXPERT, TRUETRAE.COM: Retailers are aware of the fact that consumers only have so much to spend. CHEUNG: That`s why even before Black Friday, many retailers are already offering deep discounts vying for your holiday dollars. The most discounted items this season, everything from TVs, laptops, to home appliances, and beauty products. For electronics, consider older models for an even better deal. Many clothing retailers are also offering extra deep discounts this season in part because of excess inventory falling supply chain lock-ups last year. BODGE: We are seeing a lot of overstock still and retailers have been spending the last couple of months trying to sell through that merchandise. CHEUNG: Which could lead to even deeper discounts. BODGE: I do expect to see discounts deeper than usual in categories like casual apparel, TVs, furniture, home decor. And so, in addition to the exciting cyber weekend sales that we`ll see, we`ll also see kind of extra discounts as retailers look to clear out all those overstocks. CHEUNG: Experts say shopping with strategy will save you big bucks. Start by creating a shopping list with a spending cap. Then compare prices online and in store. And check your credit card for additional discounts and offers. (END VIDEOTAPE) CHEUNG (on camera): And don`t forget about gift cards which are always a hot item every year. Many can actually be bought at a discount. Lester? HOLT: All right, Brian, thanks. Up next, what are you thankful for? Some children will tell us right after the break. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally, a lot of news has been especially grim this week, but we thought you might be uplifted or find a smile in listening to the gratitude expressed by some New York school kids we spoke to about Thanksgiving. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) HOLT (voiceover): At Manhattan Country School, today`s lesson is all about giving thanks. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Thank you God for a mother. HOLT: And after two years of holidays overshadowed by COVID, many students told us they`re grateful for a Thanksgiving that feels a little more normal. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m thankful for like, family and friends because like, during COVID, I wasn`t able to see -- I wasn`t able to see like, a lot of my friends. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m very grateful that me and my family -- or my family and I have been healthy and happy and able to see each other. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m really thankful for the school and for my teachers and my friends. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m thankful for my dog. She`s good at comforting people especially me. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m thankful for my family because they give me comfort and I just love them. HOLT: Of course, on Thanksgiving -- UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I love cooking. HOLT: Comfort also comes in the form of turkey, stuffing, and potatoes. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We bake and we coconut we have this huge feast at the end. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We make an angel fruitcake which I really love to do with my grandma. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m definitely looking forward to eating because we do cook pretty good Thanksgiving meal. HOLT: When you`re in grade school, there`s something else to look forward to. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We get a lot of days off from school. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The first thing I think about it is wrapped up in a blanket drinking hot chocolate and watching a movie, and I just get really excited about that. HOLT: A moment of peace with the people you love, to give thanks, isn`t that what the day is all about? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: When I think about the holidays, I think about community and spending time with the people that I love and giving back to them and hopefully receiving the same. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And thank all of you for being here tonight. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS. Be sure to tune in for the Macy`s Thanksgiving Day Parade at 9:00 Eastern here on NBC and Peacock. Thank you for watching and Happy Thanksgiving, everyone. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. headline: The Issue That Turned Out To Be A Game-Changer In States Red And Blue
story_text: [19:20:00] LESTER HOLT: In the wake of the Supreme Court overturning Roe v Wade, the Midterm Elections saw a record number of abortion-related measures on the ballot. And in every state where voters had a direct say, they opted against restricting access. Here`s Yamiche Alcindor. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) YAMICHE ALCINDOR, NBC NEWS WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, Democrats across the country are celebrating sweeping wins for supporters of abortion rights. JOSH SHAPIRO (D-PA), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: A woman`s right to choose one. SEN. MAGGIE HASSAN (D-NH): I will always, always keep fighting to protect a woman`s fundamental freedom. GOV. GRETCHEN WHITMER (D-MI): We will make Michigan a leader, a place where women make their own decisions. ALCINDOR: In Michigan, residents voted to enshrine abortion rights into the state constitution, an issue Governor Gretchen Whitmer and her running mate been a central part of their successful reelection campaign. WHITMER: This is a right that we are not going to go backwards on. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I`m proud of my state. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I don`t want the government in my bedroom. ALCINDOR: And abortion rights did drive people to the polls. It was the second most important issue to voters behind inflation. In addition to Michigan, voters in California and Vermont codified abortion rights into their state constitutions. And it wasn`t just blue states, voters in Kentucky and Montana shot down measures that could have restricted access. What do you make of that nationally? WHITMER: I think it`s a sign that the American public has had rights for 49 years. We`re not going to go backward. And so, whether it`s state by state we see this happen or hopefully at some point, you know, a national effort again, I think that this is where the fight is at the moment. ALCINDOR: Those against abortion rights not processing the results. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I believe abortion is first-degree murder. ALCINDOR: Eric Scheidler from the Pro-Life Action League says he`s gearing up to continue their push. ERIC SCHEIDLER, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, PRO-LIFE ACTION LEAGUE: If we`ve learned anything over the past 50 years as a movement is that we`ve got to be able to take a punch. ALCINDOR: Still, Americans in five states send a clear message about reproductive rights. Yamiche Alcindor, NBC News, Detroit. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Coming up, their new mission: training troops to become teachers in "THOSE WHO SERVE." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for November 9, 2022, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the Midterm Election cliffhanger. The battle for Congress still too close to call. (voiceover): The Senate and the House still up for grabs after the Democrats held off a red wave. President Biden at the White House today calling it a good day for democracy. In Georgia, the tight Senate race headed to a runoff. In Pennsylvania, John Fetterman defeating Mehmet Oz. And in Florida, a big reelection win for Governor Ron DeSantis setting up a possible 2024 showdown with Donald Trump . And what President Biden said today about his own 2024 plans. Our team across the country with a race is still in play. Also breaking tonight, Nicole strengthening into a hurricane and taking aim at Florida flooding on the coast. Buildings collapsing into the sea, mandatory evacuations ordered, the new track tonight. The potential major setback for Russia ordering a retreat from the key city of Kherson in southern Ukraine. Why Kyiv is skeptical. WNBA star Brittney Griner moved to a penal colony in Russia. How the U.S. is responding. Facebook `s parent company Meta laying off thousands. Why Mark Zuckerberg is slashing jobs on the heels of concept Twitter . And "THOSE WHO SERVE," the veterans answering a new call in the classroom. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening, everyone, again, tonight from our election headquarters in New York. It was a good day for democracy, President Biden`s first public reaction to yesterday`s Midterm Elections in which Democrats defied the gravity of broad voter dissatisfaction and history itself to avoid massive losses in that widely-predicted Republican wave. Let me tell you from the start tonight, much of our reporting this evening is framed by what we don`t know and that is which party will control Congress. At this hour, control of the Senate is still up for grabs with some races too close to call, while the Georgia Senate contest is headed toward a December runoff election. And the House still in play for both sides, though Republicans currently lead. But there is broad agreement that these were not the results most expected, an unpopular president faced with a bad economy managing to avoid the fate of his predecessors. The President`s message to voters tonight, I get it. Our team has fanned out again this evening watching the count and the issues that shaped the vote starting tonight with Kristen Welker at the White House. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): 24 hours after ballots were cast, tonight, control of Congress is still up for grabs. President Biden insisting it was a good night for Democrats. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: While the press and the pundits are predicting a giant red wave, it didn`t happen. WELKER: Republicans who had been hoping to take the House in a red wave now just looking for a win. The GOP still favored to take over but with a smaller margin than expected. REP. KEVIN MCCARTHY (R-CA): We will be in the majority and Nancy Pelosi will be in the minority. WELKER: Much more suspense in the Senate where Republicans still could gain the one seat they need to take control but Democrats could hang on to with NBC News projecting races that are too early to call in Nevada and in Arizona. And in Georgia, the showdown between Democratic senator Raphael Warnock and Republican Herschel Walker , NBC News Now projects will go to a runoff. SEN. RAPHAEL WARNOCK (D-GA): We always knew that this race would be close. HERSCHEL WALKER (R-GA), SENATE CANDIDATE: I`m like Ricky Bobby. I don`t come to lose. WELKER: Democrats` biggest win of the night coming in the critical Pennsylvania Senate race. Democrat John Fetterman , six months after suffering a stroke, defeating Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: We did what we needed to do. WELKER: Republicans with big victories too including Georgia Governor Brian Kemp easily defeating Democrat Stacey Abrams . And in the biggest win of the night, Florida Republican Governor Ron DeSantis winning reelection in a 19- point landslide, sweeping virtually every county in the state, including heavily Latino Miami Dade. GOV. RON DESANTIS (R-FL): We reject woke ideology. We will never ever surrender to the woke mob. Florida is where woke goes to die. WELKER: DeSantis seen as a possible 2024 presidential contender where he could face former President Trump who had a tough night. His endorsed candidates in Ohio and North Carolina won but several of Mr. Trump`s other handpick candidates in key races, including New Hampshire, Michigan, and Pennsylvania all lost. Meanwhile, President Biden was asked what he will do differently with most Americans saying they`re dissatisfied with the state of the country. [19:05:08] BIDEN: Nothing because they`re just finding out what we`re doing. The more they know about what we`re doing, the more support there is. WELKER: And we pressed him about running again. Two-thirds of Americans in exit polls say that they don`t think you should run for reelection. What is your message to them? And how does that factor into your final decision about whether or not to run for reelection? BIDEN: It doesn`t. WELKER: What`s your message to those two-thirds of Americans? BIDEN: Watch me. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Kristen, the President is likely facing divided government. Did he talk about working with Republicans how it would go? WELKER (on camera): Well, Lester, he did. The President says he`ll call top House Republican Kevin McCarthy tonight and says he`s hoping for bipartisanship on issues like Ukraine. The President also saying he`ll make his decision on running early next year. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker at the White House, thanks. That pivotal Senate race in Georgia, as we said, is neck and neck. Gabe Gutierrez is there. And Gabe, what can we expect in this coming run off? GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, this is what both campaigns and many voters did not want, another month of campaigning. But incumbent Raphael Warnock and challenger Herschel Walker are already fundraising ahead of the runoff now set for December 6. Neither managed to get 50 percent of the vote. But in the governor`s race here, Republican incumbent, Brian Kemp easily won reelection over Democrat Stacey Abrams . And that suggests some Republicans may have split their tickets in the Senate contest and voted for Warnock. Now, back in 2020, this state had to runoffs that tipped the balance of power in the Senate. And based on ad spending back then, it`s possible that we could see upwards of $200 million dollars in TV ads here over the next several weeks. Lester? HOLT: Gabe Gutierrez in Atlanta, thanks. Another key state in play. Arizona remains in flux both in the U.S. Senate race between incumbent Mark Kelly and Republican Blake Masters and in the governor`s race. Vaughn Hillyard is in Phoenix tonight. Vaughn, where do things stand right now? headline: The Governor`s Race In Georgia Too Early To Call Between Brian Kemp And Stacey Abrams
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Dozens of governors seats are also in play being driven by issues ranging from inflation to abortion. Blayne Alexander is following the key races. Blayne, what should we know? BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, Lester, when I`ve spoken to voters, both of those issues came up and more. So much of it just depends on the state. And tonight, Lester, many of those key governor`s races are very tight. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) B. ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, it`s not just control of Congress that`s at stake, also what for grabs, 36 critical Governor seats, including here in Georgia, Republican Governor Brian Kemp`s rematch against Stacey Abrams . A win would make her the first Black woman governor in U.S. history. A big focus for Kemp, his early decision to reopen Georgia during COVID. GOV. BRIAN KEMP (R-GA): She was criticizing me for just simply giving you the opportunity to go back to work or to open your business. B. ALEXANDER: Abrams, like many Democrats around the country emphasizing abortion access. STACEY ABRAMS (D-GA), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: We know for women in Georgia, this is the lethal decision. B. ALEXANDER: In Arizona, it`s a marquee matchup between Democrat Katie Hobbs and Kari Lake, a Trump-backed Republican who has repeatedly denied the 2020 election results and is already casting doubt on this election. KARI LAKE (R-AZ), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: We`re so ready for fair elections, aren`t we? I`m worried about tomorrow. KATIE HOBBS (D-AZ), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: When people like Kari Lake denied the results of the election, we stood firm. B. ALEXANDER: TWO other contests to watch feature Democratic incumbents in tight races. Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer in a tough fight against Republican Tudor Dixon and perhaps most surprising in deep blue New York where Governor Kathy Hochul is facing a serious challenge from Republican Lee Zeldin , who is focusing on rising crime. LEE ZELDIN (R-NY) GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: Voters of all walks of life, Republicans, Democrats, and Independents, they`ve had enough. (END VIDEOTAPE) B. ALEXANDER (on camera): And Georgia officials say there have been very few lines at polling places today, they point to a record 2.5 million people who cast early votes. Lester? HOLT: Blayne Alexander, thank you. I want to bring in now our political director and moderator of "MEET THE PRESS," Chuck Todd. Chuck, you`ve been digging into the exit polls. What do voters seem to be most concerned about? CHUCK TODD, NBC NEWS POLITICAL DIRECTOR (on camera): Well, it will not surprise you. The number one issue overall, inflation. What`s interesting is that there`s only a five-point difference. Abortion came in second 27 percent. And then you see the other three issues you saw a lot in TV ads, crime, gun policy, and immigration. Inflation-breaking Republican, abortion-breaking Democrat. Crime-breaking Republican. Gun, if you pick guns, you broke Democrat and immigration by Republican. Let me show you by party. As you can see here, among Democrats, the most important issue was abortion. Among Republicans, the number one issue is inflation. And here`s the tiebreaker perhaps, the difference between getting 49 percent and 51 percent in some of the Senate races. Independents picked inflation. Now, let me give you a little teaser about some of the state polls, Lester. In two of our Senate battlegrounds, abortion topped inflation, Pennsylvania and New Hampshire. Just something to keep in mind tonight as we figure out who`s going to control the Senate. HOLT: Interesting trends starting to emerge. All right, Chuck, thanks very much. And our Chief Washington Correspondent Andrea Mitchell joins us now with some concerns that figured tough numbers about our exit polls. ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Exactly. Well, as Chuck was just pointing out, the top issue was inflation. But abortion was a top concern among a lot more voters than we had expected and crime less than expected. But there`s something else that really stuck out to me. This early exit poll shows that 46 percent of voters say President Biden`s policies are hurting the country. Only 36 percent say they`re helping the country. 16 percent say his policies are not making a difference. Even some of Mr. Biden`s base voters, including Black voters and young voters, are not convinced that his policies are working. The President in the final weeks of the campaign has been saying that this election is a choice between his party and the Republicans and not a referendum on his presidency. But if voters ended up making their decision based on how they feel about his record -- his record, that`s not a good sign for Democrats. Lester? HOLT: All right, Andrea, thanks for that. Washington could look dramatically different in the days to come. How Congress have the Biden administration are strategizing for a big shift. Plus, we`ll take you inside a vote-counting center. Why it could take a while before the full picture of the elections is known. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: Herschel Walker Facing A New Allegation Of Paying For An Abortion Of A GOP Senate Candidate Is Responding Tonight
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Let me turn now to Kristen. Kristen, there`s a new headline in that tight Georgia Senate race, an anonymous allegation against Herschel Walker . What do we know? KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, that`s right. This latest allegation comes from an anonymous woman who spoke on Zoom without showing her face in a press conference arranged by Attorney Gloria Allred, an allegation Herschel Walker is strongly denying tonight. Now, the woman claims she had an affair with Walker, the football star turned Republican Senate candidate, and got pregnant nearly 30 years ago. She says Walker pressured and paid for her to have an abortion, but she did not provide any evidence to support those claims. Now, Walker fired back today calling the claims foolishness and a lie, saying his Democratic opponent Senator Raphael Warnock "lost the debate and Democrats will now say anything to win." The woman`s claim comes after another woman accused Walker of paying for her abortion which Walker also strongly denied. The Georgia race is a toss-up that could determine Senate control. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker, thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2022 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. headline: The Fallout From A High Stakes Showdown In Pennsylvania With Control Of Congress Hanging In The Ballots
story_text: [19:00:00] LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the fallout from a high stakes showdown in Pennsylvania with control of Congress hanging in the ballots. (voiceover): Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz facing off in their first and only debate. Fetterman`s health struggles in the spotlight months after he suffered a stroke. Oz under scrutiny for an answer he gave on abortion. The reaction from voters just 13 days before the Midterms. Also, tonight, Herschel Walker facing a new allegation of paying for an abortion of a GOP Senate candidate is responding tonight. The verdict in the trial of a Wisconsin man who killed six people when he plowed his SUV into a Christmas parade. The deadly school shooting in St. Louis. The warning the shooters family gave to police and they`re pleas to take a gun away from him months before the rampage. Vladimir Putin overseeing nuclear drills as Russia pushes unproven dirty bomb allegations against Ukraine. And the American fighter killed in Ukraine two months ago finally on his way back home. Hospitals filling up with children infected with RSV. What parents need to know. The critical shortage in a medication millions used to treat ADHD. And he went from homeless to shooting college hoops. The basketball star inspiring America. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. Just 13 days before the Midterm Elections, and a flood of political ads are saturating the airwaves on the heels of another marquee debate reminding just what is at stake in hard-fought congressional races, power and control of Congress. In the House, Democrats trying to defend their majority with all 435 seats of the body up for election. Dems facing the same challenge in the U.S. Senate with 35 seats are up for election. The balance of power in the Senate could be determined by a handful of tight races, including Pennsylvania where last night`s debate pitted Republican Mehmet Oz against Democrat John Fetterman sparring over abortion, fracking, and immigration. But not before Fetterman call out what he described as the elephant in the room, his health. Dasha Burns starts us off tonight with the latest. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, Pennsylvania Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz back on the campaign trail following last night`s critical one and only face-off. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: Pennsylvania deserves better than Fetterman. BURNS: His opponent, Democrat John Fetterman , not yet making any public appearances after the fierce clash. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: It`s something called the Oz rule that if he`s on TV, he`s lying. OZ: And this is the only debate I could get you to come to talk to me on and I had to beg. BURNS: A debate the Fetterman`s health front and center. Fetterman whose campaign says suffers from auditory processing challenges after a stroke six months ago, requesting these closed captioning monitors in the studio. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke. He`s never let me forget that. And I might miss some words during this debate. Mush two words together, but it knocked me down, but I`m going to keep coming back up. BURNS: Fetterman did miss some words during the hour-long showdown, at times of struggling to answer questions, including this moment. Fetterman was asked about his changing position on fracking, which he now says he supports. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: There is that 2018 interview that you said, "I don`t support fracking at all." So, how do you square the two? FETTERMAN: I do support fracking. And I don`t --I don`t -- I support fracking and I stand -- and I do support fracking. BURNS: Fetterman would not commit to releasing his full medical records. FETTERMAN: My doctor believes that I`m fit to be serving, and that`s what I believe is where I`m standing. BURNS: And in one of the biggest clashes of the night going after Dr. Oz on abortion rights. FETTERMAN: He celebrated when Roe v. Wade went down and my campaign would fight for Roe v. Wade, and if given the opportunity, to codify it into law. BURNS: And tonight, the Fetterman campaign zeroing in on this response from Oz. OZ: I want women, doctors, local political leaders letting the democracy that`s always allowed our nation to thrive to put the best ideas forward so states can decide for themselves. Local political leaders. Local political leaders. BURNS: Turning it into a campaign ad against his opponent. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Oz is too extreme for Pennsylvania. BURNS: But Oz calling Fetterman the extreme candidates throughout the night, especially on the issue of crime. OZ: We have taken away the ability of police to do their job and that son John Fetterman . BURNS: The momentous matchup coming just two weeks before Election Day. Voters with strong reactions about Dr. Oz. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: His comment about political leaders, you know, determining what a woman -- a woman can and cannot do with her body is -- was very telling. [19:05:09] BURNS: And Fetterman. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I just don`t think he`s capable at this time to be in that position. I mean, if you have somebody that can`t even handle a debate that has to, you know, read from this prompter. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And Dasha, some big names could soon be campaigning there on both sides. BURNS (on camera): Yes, Lester. Plans are coming together for both President Biden and former President Obama to campaign with Fetterman, and the Democratic candidate for governor. And former President Trump will campaign with Dr. Oz and the Republican gubernatorial candidate. Lester? HOLT: Dasha Burns, thank you. Let`s bring in Andrea Mitchell and Kristen Welker. Andrea, first to you. What are you hearing there in Pennsylvania about the impact of that debate? ANDREA MITCHELL, NBC NEWS CHIEF WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, Democrats here are telling me that they think Fetterman will be OK, given his labor support and Oz`s missteps on abortion and the minimum wage. But they acknowledge that this format did not work for Fetterman. Republicans say they`re pleased with how it went. The fact that this race is even close, though, tells you Republicans have momentum right now and it`s happening nationwide. In the Senate, enough incumbent Democrats could lose, giving Republicans several chances to take control. And in the House Democrats are in trouble in states like Oregon and New York, which are normally safe. Last night there was a debate for New York Governor where Republican Trump ally Congressman Lee Zeldin is within striking distance of Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul , which is remarkable in a solid blue state. Lester? HOLT: Andrea, thanks. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2022 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. IKEDA: That day, the school doors were locked, and seven unarmed security guards were on site. But authorities say the government managed to avoid the school`s checkpoints. Seattle Children`s tells NBC News it`s a 200 percent capacity in the ER. JOSHUA ROSS, PEDIATRIC EMERGENCY MEDICINE PHYSICIAN, UW HEALTH -KIDS: Suctioning the nose, nasal passages, staying well hydrated, using anti- fever medications usually do the trick. COSTELLO: Seek immediate help if a child is in respiratory distress, breathing fast, nose flaring, using their shoulders or pulling under their ribs to breathe, and turning blue. DR. RICK PLACE, PEDIATRIC MEDICAL DIRECTOR, INOVA L.J. MURPHY CHILDREN`S HOSPITAL: If you think your child is in danger, you need to go to the E.R. I mean that`s a flat-out message. And in doing so, what they`re doing is they`re destroying the most important institution in our nation, you know, the freedom and the right to vote. GUTIERREZ: He also says his office is investigating this incident captured on cell phone video where a woman tried to take a picture of one of their license plates and was pushed. And when people are standing around, you know, with handguns on them and sometimes tactical gear, you know, it really does scare the average person. GUTIERREZ: Law enforcement Nationwide is on alert. MERRICK GARLAND , U.S. ATTORNEY GENERAL: The Justice Department has an obligation to prevent to guarantee a free and fair vote. GUTIERREZ: Back in Arizona where early votes are already been counted, Republican election officials have called these armed drop box watchers uninformed vigilantes. As a Republican, how frustrating is it to you that some of these groups have latched on to conspiracy theories? STEPHEN RICHER, MARICOPA COUNTY RECORDER: Well, it`s been an interesting last two years. And you know, for the party of facts and logic, at times, we have fallen short from, in my estimation, on facts and logic. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (on camera): Voter rights organizations have now sued to temporarily block at least some of these groups from monitoring these ballot drop-off boxes. Lester? HOLT: All right, Gabe, thank you. Coming up, at $700 million, it`s one of the biggest Powerball jackpots in history. Could there be a winner tonight? Plus, he was homeless before he found his place on the court. "INSPIRING AMERICA" is next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Tonight`s Powerball jackpot has grown to a massive $700 million, the fifth largest in the game`s history. No one has won since August. The odds are one in 293 million. If you bought your tickets, good luck to you. And finally, the student-athlete beating formidable odds with a former NBA point guard coaching them on. Kathy Park with tonight`s "INSPIRING AMERICA." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KATHY PARK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Jeremiah Armstead picked up a basketball at 14, the same age he realized life wasn`t a game. JEREMIAH ARMSTEAD, BASKETBALL PLAYER: I felt like I wasn`t in at 14. That`s what I feel like. Because that`s when they really picked up homeless and stuff like that. ARMSTEAD: My first goal which is get my mom and my sister out to shelter that they`re in. PARK: Family first while making moves on and off the court. Kathy Park, NBC News, Nashville. headline: Missed Cases Of Breast Cancer: The Detection Delayed In Dozens Of Patients And The Hospital At The Center Of The Controversy
story_text: [19:15:00] LESTER HOLT: There`s no question that mammograms save lives were the early detection of breast cancer, but a review of cases at one hospital showed many cancers were initially missed even though they appeared on the scans. Kristen Dahlgren has our investigation. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN DAHLGREN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Jim and Pat Ratliff had a 54-year love story. JIM RATLIFF, WIFE HAD BREAST CANCER: We were attached at the hip. DAHLGREN: Through ups and downs, including Pat`s breast cancer more than a decade ago, which is why she was so diligent about screening and concern when she noticed changes in her other breast. She had imaging at a nearby hospital, part of NIH Northern Arizona Health Care. And they told her what? RATLIFF: They couldn`t find anything. DAHLGREN: Eventually, Pat saw breast surgeon Beth DuPree. DR. BETH DUPREE, BREAST SURGEON: I literally couldn`t believe what I was seeing. It was screaming cancer. DAHLGREN: Advanced breast cancer. Two years later, Pat was gone. Dr. DuPree had just moved to Sedona to develop a state-of-the-art Breast Center at NIH . Pat was just the first patient she says who came to her with a cancer missed on previous scan. DUPREE: These were misses that are not subtle. DAHLGREN: The hospital has an exclusive contract with Northern Arizona Radiology. DuPree who says she continued to flag misread mammograms push them to hire dedicated breast imagers, including Mike Ulissey who couldn`t believe some of what he says was missed. MIKE ULISSEY, BREAST IMAGER: I said my god, Beth. That`s the size of a tangerine. I don`t understand how they can call it normal. DAHLGREN: The hospital requested the radiology group have those new breast imagers review more than 6000 patients whose scans had initially been read by a particular general radiologist. Ulissey says they found cancer in an additional 25 women. CHRISTIE GALLO, HAD BREAST CANCER: The recommendation was returned to me here. DAHLGREN: Among them Christie Gallo (PH). GALLO: My question was, how can I go from normal to having three tumors in one year? That didn`t make sense to me. DAHLGREN: Dr. DuPree believes the number of patients with missed cancers was much greater than the 25 detected in the review. She made a poster with all of her patients whose diagnoses she says were delayed, hoping to show it to the hospital board. We`re only showing those who gave us permission. It must be hard to look at their faces. DUPREE: It is. DAHLGREN: NBC News obtained an email from one of the breast imagers to the radiology group sent before the review was complete, warning of the gravity of the situation. After the review, there was still concern. ULISSEY: We thought that there were a significant chance that additional patients were in harm`s way. We need to expand our investigation. DAHLGREN: But Dr. Ulissey says the radiology group did not. In his statement to NBC, NIH points out the radiology group is a separate entity and says in part, "The hospital quickly acted to address these concerns. We ensured these mammograms were reread specifically by a team of breast fellowship-trained radiologists, saying very few required any follow-up. And since this review, all mammograms are read by specialized breast radiologists." The hospital`s Chief Counsel spoke on a Zoom with community advisors. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: So, the quality process works. There was an error. We`re humans. Doctors are human. GALLO: They messed up and they don`t want to fess up to it. DAHLGREN: Northern Arizona radiology called the review results well within national standards. In a statement, it says, "All radiologists are board certified and meet all requirements, including those under the Mammography Quality Standards Act. DuPree and three out of four new breast imagers including Dr. Ulissey have now left. NBC News has learned the general radiologist who was the subject of the review is now working in another state. As for Gallo, her cancer is in remission, but she`s not sure the questions will ever go away. GALLO: Maybe if they had caught it sooner, it could have been a just a lumpectomy instead of a whole mastectomy choice, but I didn`t get that choice. DAHLGREN: Kristen Dahlgren, NBC News, Sedona, Arizona. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next for us, late news about today`s earthquake in California. Plus, top brands cut ties after antisemitic comments by music and fashion mogul Kanye West. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: Back with the new troubles for Kanye West. Adidas ended its deal today with the music mogul and designer who now goes by Ye over his recent antisemitic comments. Hours later, Gap said it is immediately removing West`s clothing line from its stores. Forbes reports that without his lucrative Adidas deal, West is no longer a billionaire. Some scary moments in Northern California today when an earthquake struck near San Jose. The quake had a preliminary magnitude of 5.1 according to the U.S. Geological Survey . Seismologists say it`s the biggest quake to hit the Bay Area in more than eight years, but there are no reports of injuries or significant damage. Up next, the dramatic rescue. Tourists trapped hundreds of feet underground at a cavern in Arizona. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. JOHN PAXTON, COCONINO COUNTY SHERIFF`S OFFICE: If you can picture a fire escape on the side of a tall building, you know, like I think -- we think of New York, and you`d have to do that for 21 floors. JIMENEZ: We`ve all agreed on this. Grateful for our family members because things could have gone way worse. When they got hoisted out, somebody could have fell. JIMENEZ: I just feel a lot of love for my family. It makes you not want to take anything for granted. ALMAGUER: After a 30-minute tour became nearly a 30-hour ordeal, tonight, everyone is back above ground after a rocky start to a deep excursion. Miguel Almaguer, NBC News. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Quite a drama and quite a rescue. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Tuesday. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. headline: The New Pledge From President Biden, If Democrats Keep Control Of Congress, He`ll Immediately Move To Pass National Abortion Rights
story_text: LESTER HOLT: 21 days before the Midterms, President Biden trying to keep abortion rights front and center, but polls show voters worrying most about the economy and soaring inflation. Peter Alexander reports on the new clashes between candidates in key battlegrounds. [19:05:09] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PETER ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): With just three weeks until the Midterms and Republicans slamming Democrats over the economy and record inflation, President Biden tonight trying to amplify the politically divisive issue of abortion rights, urging voters to keep Democrats in control of Congress. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Here`s the promise I make to you and the American people. The first bill that I will send to the Congress will be to codify Roe v. Wade. ALEXANDER: But some Democrats fear the potency of that message may be waning. Tonight, a new poll shows 44 percent of likely voters cite the economy or inflation as the number one problem facing the country while just five percent list abortion as their top issue. And now, Republicans have a four-point lead when voters are asked which party`s candidate they`d support. In Ohio, one of several crucial races that`ll determine control of the Senate. Republican candidate J.D. Vance hammered Democrat Tim Ryan over skyrocketing prices in a heated final debate. J.D. VANCE (R-OH) SENATE CANDIDATE: That rising energy price that people see at the pump, that they see in the utility bills, that was the direct result of policies enacted by Joe Biden and Nancy Pelosi and supported 100 percent by Tim Ryan . ALEXANDER: While Ryan slammed Vance for embracing former President Trump. REP. TIM RYAN (D-OH): You were calling Trump America`s Hitler. Then he kissed his ass -- VANCE: It`s not true. RYAN: It is true. And then you kissed his ass, and then he endorsed you. And you said he`s the greatest president of all time. ALEXANDER: There are critical governor`s races too in the battlegrounds of Arizona and Michigan and a rematch in Georgia between Republican Governor Brian Kemp and Democrat Stacey Abrams . Their one and only showdown last night. STACEY ABRAMS (D-GA), GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE: We live in a state of fear. And this is a governor who for the last four years has beat his chest but delivered very little for most Georgians. ALEXANDER: Kemp touting his early moves to reopen the state during the pandemic and going after Abrams. GOV. BRIAN KEMP (R-GA): Miss Abrams is going to lie out my record because she doesn`t want to talk about her own. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Peter, President Biden is going to pivot to the economy tomorrow focusing on high gas prices. ALEXANDER (on camera): Yes, Lester, that`s right. Looking to lower those prices, the President is going to announce that the administration will move forward with the release of as many as 15 million additional barrels of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It`s a controversial move that comes amid Russia`s war in Ukraine and after Saudi Arabia snub the President`s request to boost oil production. Lester? HOLT: Peter Alexander at the White House, thank you. There`s breaking news and a trial involving a murder they went unsolved for 25 years. A California man convicted late today for killing Kristin Smart, a college student who disappeared in 1996. Paul Flores, a former classmate of Smart`s wasn`t arrested for the crime until last year. Flores` father who was accused of helping move Smart`s body was found not guilty. Smart`s remains were never found. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. The new pledge from President Biden, if Democrats keep control of Congress, he`ll immediately move to pass national abortion rights. Will it be enough with polls showing voter concerns focused on the economy right now? More than 25 years after the disappearance of Kristin Smart, the verdict in the murder trial or for former college classmate. Blackouts in Ukraine after officials say Russia destroyed nearly a third of its power stations in little over a week. Growing fears for an Iranian climber after she competed without a hijab. headline: Dr. Mehmet Oz On Crime And His Campaign`s Attacks On Fetterman`s Health
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Just 25 days before the Midterms, tonight, we speak exclusively with Dr. Mehmet Oz, the Republican facing off against Democrat John Fetterman in that critical Pennsylvania Senate race. Our Dasha Burns pressing Dr. Oz on crime and his campaign`s attacks on Fetterman`s health. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Pennsylvania Republican Senate candidate and celebrity doctor, Mehmet Oz, has focused much of his campaign on crime and blasting Democrat John Fetterman on his votes as the head of the state`s Board of Pardons. He says he believes in second chances, the former president with his First Step Act, also was about giving second chances to prisoners who deserve it. Why don`t prisoners who prove good behavior, who are modeled prisoners, why don`t they deserve second chances? MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: The First Step Act had nothing to do with convicted murderers being released from prison, especially if they`ve been sentenced to life in prison. It`s a whole different game. When John Fetterman is asked, if you could wave a magic wand, what`s the one thing you would do, the one thing? And he says why get rid of life in prison? BURNS: Well, I asked him that. He actually said, it would be codifying Roe versus Wade and abolishing the Filibuster. OZ: Well, he`s answered it the way I just described in the past as well. And too often, John Fetterman seems to pay more attention to the feelings of the criminals than the innocent who were hurt. BURNS: We also asked about his campaign`s attacks on Fetterman`s health. He was off the campaign trail for months after suffering a stroke. One of your campaign staffers said that John Fetterman wouldn`t have had a stroke if he had "ever eaten a vegetable in his life." You`re a doctor. You`re a heart doctor. You of all people understand what John Fetterman is going through better than most. Why would you allow your campaign to mock him like that? OZ: I have tremendous compassion for what John Fetterman has gone through. I mean, not only do I, as a doctor, appreciate the challenges, but I know his specific ailment because it`s a specialty area of mine. BURNS: But would you ever talk to your patients like this? OZ: No. BURNS: He criticizes Fetterman for not releasing his medical records, while Fetterman accuses Dr. Oz of not being transparent on abortion rights. This is what he told us this week. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATE CANDIDATE: Dr. Oz likes to make fun of me that I might miss a word. But you know, he`s missed, you know, two words. And that is a yes or no on the national abortion ban. BURNS: So, we asked him about Republican Senator Lindsey Graham`s bill that would ban abortions after 15 weeks. If you win, you`re going to be a colleague of his. You`re going to have to vote on bills like this. So, can you tell us right now, yes or no on that bill? OZ: I`m giving you a bigger answer than yes or no. I`m telling you. I don`t want any federal rules limiting what states do with abortion. It should be up to the states. (END VIDEOTAPE) BURNS: Lester, there was more we wanted to discuss. We had to ask for the same amount of time Fetterman gave us about 30 minutes, but the campaign said they had time constraints, so we only spoke for about half that time. Lester? HOLT: Dasha Burns, thank you. END Content and programing copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2022 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc.
