headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for October 14, 2022, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the search for answers after a deadly shooting rampage in North Carolina. (voiceover): A 15-year-old suspect in custody after the mass shooting that left five people dead in Raleigh. What we`re learning about the victims. Among them an off-duty police officer and a 16-year-old boy. What was the shooter`s motive? Also, tonight, the new move in the battle of her documents seized at Mar-a- Lago. What the DOJ is asking an appeals court to do regarding the special master. And Donald Trump sending a 14-page letter to the January 6 Committee after it voted to subpoena him. What it says? And the video from the day of the attack, Nancy Pelosi saying she wanted to punch Mr. Trump out. Our NBC News exclusive with Dr. Mehmet Oz, GOP Senate candidate in Pennsylvania. Does he stand by his campaign`s attacks on the health of his Democratic rival John Fetterman ? Does he support a federal ban on abortion and his anti-crime message? The holiday shopping season, why it`s off to an early start. Where to get big bargains right now? It`s America`s fastest-growing sport with fans like Tom Brady and LeBron James. How Pickleball is going pro. And remembering the actor who brought up a beloved Harry Potter character to life. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. We are going to begin with the tragic and frightening story that was breaking in North Carolina as we came on the air here last night. We now know five people died allegedly at the hands of a teenage shooter who held a Raleigh neighborhood in fear, forcing residents to barricade themselves inside their homes. North Carolina`s Governor calling it the nightmare of every community. Authority say the alleged shooter left a two-mile trail of victims and crime scenes behind him. Tonight, the 15-year-old suspect is being held and is in critical condition after a long standoff with police. The dead include an off-duty police officer and range in age from 16 to 52. Two other people were injured. And eyewitnesses are now describing to us their own harrowing encounters with the accused shooter. Blayne Alexander is in Raleigh and has late details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The crime scene stretched more than two miles from his quiet Raleigh neighborhood to a nearby walking path, a literal trail of terror all left by one gunman who police say is just 15 years old. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Officer down. We have an officer down. ALEXANDER: The first chance came just after 5:00 p.m. as neighborhood kids were getting off the school bus. Nayesha Royle (PH) was at home and heard screams outside. NAYESHA ROYLE, RALEIGH RESIDENT: A neighbor`s kids were knocking banging on the door. I`m telling her like open the door. Something`s going on. And you hear the kids say he has a gun. He has a gun. There`s a gun. ALEXANDER: And when you open the door, what did you see? ROYLE: Chaos. Chaos. ALEXANDER: She also saw the gunman and frantically started pulling neighbors and schoolchildren into her house. ROYLE: If you could have seen a fear in their eyes -- like, the little girl was like, he pointed the gun at me. And they`re kids. They`re kids. ALEXANDER: For more than four hours, police combed the area, bringing dogs and helicopters and telling residents to stay inside. Finally, they say they found the gunman hiding nearby. He was taken into custody and to the hospital in critical condition. MARY-ANN BALDWIN, MAYOR, RALEIGH: There are several families in our community waking up this morning without their loved ones. ALEXANDER: Among those killed according to officials, 29-year-old Gabriel Torres, an off duty police officer headed to work, 16-year-old James Roger Thompson a high school junior, the Sue Karnatz who was out for a run. Her husband says that was her biggest passion outside of their three boys. Nicole Connors, a caregiver at heart dedicated to her husband and their dog Sammy. And 35-year-old Mary Marshall set to get married in just two weeks. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Blayne, none of it makes sense. Did police said anything about a possible motive? ALEXANDER (on camera): Unfortunately, not yet, Lester. In fact, police are not saying what led up to that shooting, only that the entire thing is still under investigation. But we are learning more about charges. Tonight, the DA`s office confirms that even though the suspect is only 15 years old, he will be charged as an adult. Lester? HOLT: Blayne Alexander in Raleigh tonight, thank you. This evening, former President Trump`s response after the January 6 Committee voted to subpoena him as new video from inside the Capitol on that day shows the fear and frustration of congressional leaders. Kelly O`Donnell has late details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KELLY O`DONNELL, NBC NEWS SENIOR WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Former President Trump used 14 pages to vent his anger, disappointment, and complaint at the January 6 Committee for not investigating his claims of election fraud rejected by courts. With crowd photos, he embraced rioters as hard-working American patriots, but no answer on whether he will comply with a subpoena to testify. [19:05:22] SEN. CHUCK SCHUMER (D-NY): You know, the Capitol has been totally overrun. Answer my question. O`DONNELL: NBC News obtained 42 minutes of documentary footage shot by Speaker Pelosi`s daughter. CNN obtained additional clips that show congressional leaders of both parties. SEN. MITCH MCCONNELL (R-KY): Get them there in one hell of a hurry. Do you understand? O`DONNELL: Scrambling to get guard troops sent to the Capitol. SCHUMER: We need them there now, whoever you got. O`DONNELL: In another exchange -- REP. NANCY PELOSI (D-CA): Hi, Mr. Vice President. O`DONNELL: Speaker Pelosi reaches Mike Pence . PELOSI: I worry about you being in that Capitol building. Don`t let anybody know where you are. O`DONNELL: From concern, to fury at President Trump. PELOSI: I want to punch him out and I`m going to go to jail, and I`m going to be happy. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And Kelly O`Donnell joining us now. And there are also new legal developments, Kelly, in the search of the former president`s Mar-a-Lago estate. O`DONNELL (on camera): That`s right. The Department of Justice is asking an appeals court in the Mar-a-Lago documents case to end the use of an independent reviewer of those materials seized that Mr. Trump had requested. Lester? HOLT: Kelly, thank you. HOLT: Dasha Burns, thank you. Now to the migrant crisis. The Biden administration announcing this week it will start expelling more Venezuelan migrants to Mexico. It comes as President Biden is under pressure to do more after a record number of illegal border crossings. Gabe Gutierrez reports now from Yuma, Arizona. ALEXANDER LUKASHENKO , PRESIDENT, BELARUS (through translator): If you put a person or a country in a corner, there is only one way out from there, to move forward? (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Spending by Americans remain flat in September which is bad news for retailers but it may be good news for holiday shoppers already being lured with deep discounts. So, is Black Friday a thing of the past? Here`s Miguel Almaguer with tonight`s "PRICE YOU PAY." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: This is Black Friday now. [19:15:14] KIMBERLY PALMER, PERSONAL FINANCE EXPERT, NERDWALLET : Black Friday has already started because the sales have begun, the discounts have already been launched. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: If there`s a deal, of course, I`m just going to swipe that up. ALMAGUER: As families tighten budgets amid high-interest rates, steep gas prices and rising rents, more than 40 percent of Americans say they aren`t earning enough to cover the cost of holiday gifts this year. PALMER: Basically, retailers know that consumers are really stressed out financially by spreading out those sales over a multi-week, multi-month period. It makes it easier for consumers to keep spending. ALMAGUER: The best advice say experts, do your holiday shopping now and wait for the perfect sale. Last year, 50 percent of shoppers did their holiday shopping before Thanksgiving. Lester? HOLT: All right, Miguel, thanks. Up next, they`re a pivotal group of voters changing the political map. The race to connect with Latinos in our series "POWER OF THE VOTE." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Back now with our series the power of the vote. And tonight, the battle over the all-important Latino vote. As the political landscape rapidly changes, Tom Llamas takes us to South Florida where some long- standing expectations about Latino voters are being put to the test in the Midterms. CHUCK TODD, NBC NEWS POLITICAL DIRECTOR: This Latino thing is an issue here for the Democrats. LLAMAS: Joe Biden won the presidency but Donald Trump took nearly half of the Latino vote in Florida. LLAMAS: A new NBC News Telemundo poll shows while Latinos lean Democrat and prefer Democratic control of Congress, support for the GOP is up 10 points over five midterm cycles. story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the search for answers after a deadly shooting rampage in North Carolina. (voiceover): A 15-year-old suspect in custody after the mass shooting that left five people dead in Raleigh. What we`re learning about the victims. Among them an off-duty police officer and a 16-year-old boy. What was the shooter`s motive? Also, tonight, the new move in the battle of her documents seized at Mar-a- Lago. What the DOJ is asking an appeals court to do regarding the special master. And Donald Trump sending a 14-page letter to the January 6 Committee after it voted to subpoena him. What it says? And the video from the day of the attack, Nancy Pelosi saying she wanted to punch Mr. Trump out. Our NBC News exclusive with Dr. Mehmet Oz, GOP Senate candidate in Pennsylvania. Does he stand by his campaign`s attacks on the health of his Democratic rival John Fetterman ? Does he support a federal ban on abortion and his anti-crime message? The holiday shopping season, why it`s off to an early start. Where to get big bargains right now? It`s America`s fastest-growing sport with fans like Tom Brady and LeBron James. How Pickleball is going pro. And remembering the actor who brought up a beloved Harry Potter character to life. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. We are going to begin with the tragic and frightening story that was breaking in North Carolina as we came on the air here last night. We now know five people died allegedly at the hands of a teenage shooter who held a Raleigh neighborhood in fear, forcing residents to barricade themselves inside their homes. North Carolina`s Governor calling it the nightmare of every community. Authority say the alleged shooter left a two-mile trail of victims and crime scenes behind him. Tonight, the 15-year-old suspect is being held and is in critical condition after a long standoff with police. The dead include an off-duty police officer and range in age from 16 to 52. Two other people were injured. And eyewitnesses are now describing to us their own harrowing encounters with the accused shooter. Blayne Alexander is in Raleigh and has late details. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The crime scene stretched more than two miles from his quiet Raleigh neighborhood to a nearby walking path, a literal trail of terror all left by one gunman who police say is just 15 years old. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Officer down. We have an officer down. ALEXANDER: The first chance came just after 5:00 p.m. as neighborhood kids were getting off the school bus. Nayesha Royle (PH) was at home and heard screams outside. NAYESHA ROYLE, RALEIGH RESIDENT: A neighbor`s kids were knocking banging on the door. I`m telling her like open the door. Something`s going on. And you hear the kids say he has a gun. He has a gun. There`s a gun. ALEXANDER: And when you open the door, what did you see? ROYLE: Chaos. Chaos. ALEXANDER: She also saw the gunman and frantically started pulling neighbors and schoolchildren into her house. ROYLE: If you could have seen a fear in their eyes -- like, the little girl was like, he pointed the gun at me. And they`re kids. They`re kids. ALEXANDER: For more than four hours, police combed the area, bringing dogs and helicopters and telling residents to stay inside. Finally, they say they found the gunman hiding nearby. He was taken into custody and to the hospital in critical condition. MARY-ANN BALDWIN, MAYOR, RALEIGH: There are several families in our community waking up this morning without their loved ones. ALEXANDER: Among those killed according to officials, 29-year-old Gabriel Torres, an off duty police officer headed to work, 16-year-old James Roger Thompson a high school junior, the Sue Karnatz who was out for a run. Her husband says that was her biggest passion outside of their three boys. Nicole Connors, a caregiver at heart dedicated to her husband and their dog Sammy. And 35-year-old Mary Marshall set to get married in just two weeks. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Blayne, none of it makes sense. Did police said anything about a possible motive? ALEXANDER (on camera): Unfortunately, not yet, Lester. In fact, police are not saying what led up to that shooting, only that the entire thing is still under investigation. But we are learning more about charges. Tonight, the DA`s office confirms that even though the suspect is only 15 years old, he will be charged as an adult. Lester? HOLT: Blayne Alexander in Raleigh tonight, thank you. headline: Top Republicans Traveling To Georgia To Campaign With Herschel Walker Amid His Abortion Controversy
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Just four weeks until the Midterms, today`s Senate Republican heavyweights rally behind Herschel Walker as he tries to weather the abortion controversy now overshadowing his campaign in all-important Georgia. Here`s Peter Alexander. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PETER ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, in Georgia, Republican reinforcements arriving to pollster embattled Senate nominee Herschel Walker . SEN. TOM COTTON (R-AR): It`s especially good to be here with the next United States Senator from Georgia Herschel Walker . ALEXANDER: Key senators Tom Cotton and Rick Scott standing by the former football great as he faces an allegation that he paid for an abortion for an ex-girlfriend more than a decade ago, while now campaigning on his opposition to abortion rights. Walker has strongly denied the accusation, but today for the first time publicly acknowledged he now knows who the woman is. The senators tonight insists the controversy will not cost Walker the race. SEN. RICK SCOTT (R-FL): Inflation, crime, parents not being involved in schools. That`s what people are going to vote on. ALEXANDER: Still, some state Republicans have criticized Walker. Lieutenant Governor Geoff Duncan writing, Walker has not yet earned my vote. He has four weeks left to change our minds. While, overnight, another critical clash over Ohio`s open Senate seat. In their first debate, Democratic Congressman Tim Ryan , accusing Republican J.D. Vance of lavishing praise on former President Trump. REP. TIM RYAN (D-OH): Ohio needs an ass-kicker, not an ass-kisser. ALEXANDER: While Vance attacked Ryan for voting 100 percent of the time with President Biden who remains unpopular with Ohio voters. J.D. VANCE (R-OH), SENATE CANDIDATE: We`re getting close to Halloween and Tim Ryan is put on a costume where he pretends to be a reasonable moderate. (END VIDEOTAPE) [19:10:07] ALEXANDER (on camera): Tim Ryan also tried to distance himself from President Biden saying he does not believe the President should run for reelection in 2024. Lester? HOLT: Peter, thank you. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Transcription Copyright 2022 VIQ Media Transcription, Inc. Now to the disaster in Florida and is still-rising death toll from Hurricane Ian. Many people remain desperate for help more than a week after the storm hit. Sam Brock is there for us. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) SAM BROCK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Eight days in, and the havoc wreaked by Hurricane Ian is still hard to comprehend. Sheriff`s deputies canvassing this trailer park in Lee County with mailboxes but no residence. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: What we need right now is some kind of housing temporary. [19:10:o6] BROCK: The death toll now sits at more than 130, the highest from any Florida storm since 1935, more than five times the U.S. death toll from Hurricane Andrew, a category five 30 years ago. Ian`s rapid storm intensification residents remaining behind, and massive population growth in southwest Florida, all likely playing a role. 49-year-old Liz Maguire was among those lost. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: There`s going to be a huge hole. BROCK: Her mom, Susan, says she was a foundation of love for her family. BROCK: Has it sunk in yet? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes. We`re sitting here in her house and she`ll never be here again. I`m looking at her things. Yes, it sunk in. BROCK: Liz was a mother and a grandmother. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: She just enjoyed everything. BROCK: She suffered a medical emergency during the storm and called for help. But first responders couldn`t reach her. She was found with her cell phone in her hand. Susan last spoke with her daughter that afternoon. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: She always ended every conversation with I love you. I love you, mom. I love you too, sweetie. If you can pick anything to be the last thing you say to a person, that would be it. (END VIDEOTAPE) BROCK (on camera): Back where Susan lives, on hard-hit Pine Island, supplies are still being brought in by helicopter. And the conditions are only expected to get more challenging. Many of the bridges that serve as a lifeline for Southwest Florida are unusable. On a typical day, some 80 truckloads worth of materials and supplies would pass right through here. But now, that won`t happen for months. Lester? HOLT: All right, Sam Brock, thank you. In Thailand, the deadliest mass killing ever in that country. A former police officer with a gun and a knife attack a daycare center, killing 34 people, 24 of them children. Then he fatally shot himself at his home where his wife and son were also found dead. Authorities say he was fired previously for drug possession. Now to the war in Ukraine. In the extraordinary lengths, some Russians are taking to avoid President Vladimir Putin is draft. Two Russian citizens sailing hundreds of miles to U.S. soil to request asylum. And inside Ukraine, our NBC News exclusive tonight with a top official leading the U.S. effort to help rebuild. We get more now from Cal Perry. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CAL PERRY, NBC NEWS INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, more Russians fleeing Putin`s war. Following that crush of traffic along Russia`s borders, now two Russian men arriving in Alaska by boat requesting asylum saying they too are fleeing military service. On the battlefield, Ukrainian troops press their offensive while Russia lashes back once again targeting civilians. Ukraine saying a rocket attack killing at least three people in a residential building in Zaporizhzhia. While in Kyiv, USAID Administrator Samantha Power here to spearhead the effort to rebuild. The challenges must be immense to rebuild a country while it`s fighting a war. SAMANTHA POWER, ADMINISTRATOR, USAID : Yes, and I hear a lot of build back better. It`s interesting. You start to see this government, and really they`ve done this from the beginning but increasingly walking and chewing gum at the same time. PERRY: Even during our interview, the sounds of war break through. POWER: We have provided now more than $25 billion in a combination of military and security assistance. PERRY: All of it coming after that startling report in The New York Times about this deadly car bomb attack in Russia back in August. The victim Darya Dugina, the daughter of a prominent Russian nationalist. According to the report, U.S. intelligence agencies believe parts of the Ukrainian government authorized her assassination and fear it could widen the war. (END VIDEO CLIP) PERRY (on camera): NBC News has not confirmed the Times` report. And tonight, a top Ukrainian official suggesting that Russia was behind the attack. Lester? HOLT: All right, Cal Perry, thank you. In 60 seconds, soaring crime and understaffed police departments, a controversial plan to have civilians pick up the slack in one major city next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:15:00] HOLT: Tonight, investigators are poring over a grisly crime scene. Four members of a family, including an 8-month-old baby were killed after being kidnapped. Miguel Almaguer is following this. Miguel, what do we know about this? MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, Lester, authorities have not officially released a motive but say it`s possible the suspect may have known the family and that the family`s ATM card was used after the heinous crime. On Monday, investigators say Jesus Salgado forced two brothers out of their business office at gunpoint in the city of Merced , zip tie in their hands behind their back before returning for a young mother and her 8-month-old daughter. The family was then driven away in a truck. All of their bodies were found two days later in a central California orchard. Investigators have not said how the family was killed, but the suspect is talking to police. The sheriff says the suspect has a long criminal history and deserves the death penalty. Lester? HOLT: Just an awful crime. All right, Miguel, thank you. New Orleans is one of many cities seeing a dramatic rise in murders is now taking a controversial approach to combating its shortage of police officers, hiring civilians. Gabe Gutierrez is there. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Seventh grader Byron Kelly was just 13 years old when he was shot and killed in New Orleans earlier this year. CARLA THOMAS, MOTHER OF BYRON KELLY: I just been praying. And I keep telling myself, don`t cry, don`t cry. GUTIERREZ: His mother, Karla Thomas, says it`s been hard to get a hold of the police officers working the unsolved case. THOMAS: I have called them, I have sent them text messages. I have like, none, nothing. GUTIERREZ: Police did not respond to our interview requests. The homicide rate in New Orleans is soaring, up 40 percent just this year. Now, the Big Easy is taking drastic measures hiring civilians to help with policing, including detective work like going to crime scenes to gather evidence. SHAUN FERGUSON, SUPERINTENDENT, NEW ORLEANS POLICE: This is also to reduce some of the workload currently placed on our patrol and district personnel. GUTIERREZ: Good idea? MIKE GLASSER, PRESIDENT, POLICE ASSOCIATION OF NEW ORLEANS: No, not really. GUTIERREZ: Mike Glasser, who heads up one of the city`s police unions blames plummeting morale for a crushing shortage of about 600 officers from Seattle to St. Louis, Atlanta, to Philadelphia. Major cities across the country are also reporting a cop staffing crisis. GLASSER: If we`re going to send civilians in there that are unarmed, inexperienced, untrained for what it turns into, that`s dangerous for them and it`s dangerous for the public. GUTIERREZ: Highlighting the crime problem, during our brief interview today, someone broke into a car in the Police Union`s own parking lot. Is the city safe? LATOYA CANTRELL, MAYOR OF NEW ORLEANS: So, the city of New Orleans is one that is grappling with violent crime like many other cities throughout the country, GUTIERREZ: Democratic mayor Latoya Cantrell blames the pandemic slowing down the court system as well as progressive prosecutors for the spike in crime. But her critics also blame her and are mounting a recall effort. CANTRELL: Well, the recall organizers in my view are absolutely unfair but are demonstrating their democratic rights. I have led on key issues that no other mayor has. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (on camera): The mayor recently suggested that the officer shortage could impact Mardi Gras. She has since walked that back, Lester. HOLT: Gabe Gutierrez in New Orleans, thanks. Next, retailers overstock a much, much different picture from last year. How you can save this holiday season. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: It is not even Halloween but the holiday shopping season is already here and it`s far different from last year when just about everything seemed in short supply. Here`s Emilie Ikeda. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) EMILIE IKEDA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): As we enter the holiday shopping season, a new story is emerging at America`s ports as companies worldwide experienced economic whiplash. With sky-high inflation cutting into shoppers buying power, some shipping companies are now canceling trips. U.S. shippers say they`re seeing a 20 percent drop in ocean freight orders. A sharp contrast to last year when big retailers hired private vessels to transport goods. LORI ANN LAROCCO, CNBC SENIOR EDITOR: Based on the items on the water right now and what is being processed in, retailers are anticipating a customer that is not going to be spending quite as much. IKEDA: This week, the WTO warning global trade is losing momentum. NGOZI OKONJO-IWEALA, DIRECTOR-GENERAL, WORLD TRADE ORGANIZATION: The picture for 2023 has darkened considerably. IKEDA: Still, there`s room for the consumer to benefit this holiday season. Major retailers are now trying to clear their shelves that this year are overstocked. Nike says its North America inventories up 65 percent compared to last year. That means steep discounts for bargain hunters. Everyone is looking for a deal right now. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We`re trying to stretch our money as far as we can possibly stretch it. IKEDA: To luring cautious customers, retailers including Kohl`s and Target jumpstarted their holiday deals today. And for the first time, Amazon will hold a second prime day-like event within one year. So, when sorting through the savings, shopping experts say, compare prices online. Look for retailers who offer price matching and use a cashback credit card to stretch your dollar the furthest as inflation curbs the power of your paycheck. Emily Ikeda, NBC News New York. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, the 100-year-old Marathon Man inspiring America. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Finally, we want to introduce you to a 100-year-old who has truly gone the distance and shows no sign of slowing down. Maggie Vespa with "INSPIRING AMERICA." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MAGGIE VESPA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Runners often strive to outpace time. MIKE FREMONT, 100-YEAR-OLD RUNNER: The nice thing about running at this age -- VESPA: Mike Fremont defies it. FREMONT: -- is that there`s very little competition. VESPA: At 100, the retired Cincinnati engineer and great grandfather of four logs five to 10 miles three times a week. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You are so sweet. VESPA: His 14-minute mile pace only slowed by starstruck fans. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You`re an inspiration to a lot of people. VESPA: Does that feel weird to hear that you`re a celebrity? FREMONT: Absolutely embarrassing. VESPA: With 60 marathons under his feet, Mike boasts four world records, fastest marathons for his age at 80 and 90. Fastest half marathons at 90 and 91. Running started his therapy in his 30s after the loss of his first wife. FREMONT: So, starting to run and it worked. VESPA: Decades later, after battling cancer, Mike went vegan and with the encouragement of his second wife, Marilyn, ran marathon after marathon. What do you think is fueling it? MARILYN WALL, WIFE OF MIKE FREMONT: I think he can`t quit. VESPA: Proving her point, his other hobby, canoeing. Of course, racing goes to. For people who think at 100, a person should be slowing down. What do you say to that? FREMONT: I think they ought to be speeding up. VESPA: Proof no matter your age, your best time may still lie ahead. Maggie Vespa, NBC News, Cincinnati. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And he just keeps going. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Thursday. Thank you for watching. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Goodnight, everyone. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. But tonight, President Biden declaring it`s time to right the wrongs of what he called a failed approach to marijuana, announcing he is pardoning all prior federal offenses of simple possession of marijuana, and asking states where most pot convictions take place to do the same, potentially impacting thousands. It`s an effort to end what the President sees as unfairness in simple marijuana possession cases where he says Black and Brown people are more likely to be prosecuted. And he also wants a hard look taken and how the government classifies pot, which for now is regarded as more serious than fentanyl. Kelly O`Donnell has details. KELLY O`DONNELL, NBC NEWS SENIOR WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Today, President Biden changed the lives of thousands of Americans 33 days before the Midterm Elections. JOE BIDEN , PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: No one should be in jail just for using or possessing marijuana. O`DONNELL: The President granted a full pardon for simple possession of marijuana as a federal crime. Weldon Angelo has been advocating for this clemency. WELDON ANGELOS, MUSIC PRODUCER: Having this pardon is going to allow these individuals to move on with their lives. O`DONNELL: But there had been no outward sign this dramatic move was coming. The president held unrelated events in New York State. Aboard Air Force One, he used his pen to wipe out these prior federal convictions. An estimated 6500 people convicted from 1992 to 2021, and thousands more who live in the District of Columbia. Angelos previously had his own drug convictions pardoned and met with Biden officials on this policy. ANGELOS: The society has determined that cannabis is not a crime. And so, the federal government needs to catch up with the rest of the nation. O`DONNELL: Advocates say these convictions lead to real-world barriers in jobs and housing that have been a greater burden in minority communities. Candidate Biden in 2020 promised to take action on marijuana convictions BIDEN: -- of a marijuana conviction. Automatically, that should be expunged, so when you get asked a question, have you ever been convicted, you can honestly say no, because you have to put it down now on a job application. O`DONNELL: Laws and attitudes have changed. 19 states and the District of Columbia permit marijuana use for adults. Medical marijuana use is legal in 38 states and DC. The President is urging governors to grant similar pardons. And his administration will review whether marijuana should still be classified with drugs like LSD under federal law. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And Kelly joins me live now. Kelly, the President is not decriminalizing marijuana possession with these pardons, right? O`DONNELL: That`s right. He doesn`t have that power. Congress would have to change federal law on marijuana possession. And the President is clear that there must still be strict laws on trafficking, marketing, and selling marijuana to underage users. Lester? HOLT: Kelly O`Donnell, thank you. A prominent member of the Proud Boys pleaded guilty to seditious conspiracy today for his role in plotting the January 6 attack. Jeremy Bertino was the first Proud Boys member to plead guilty to that charge. Officials say Bertino has agreed to cooperate with the Justice Department`s investigation. [19:05:15] With a little over A month until the Midterms, a growing firestorm in Georgia of a Republican Senate candidate Herschel Walker . the woman who says Walker paid for her abortion is now making a new allegation which Walker is strongly denying. Yamiche Alcindor is there. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) YAMICHE ALCINDOR, NBC NEWS WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): After a campaign event in Georgia, tonight Herschel Walker defiant. HERSCHEL WALKER (R-GA), SENATE CANDIDATE: And I`m not going to back down. The stakes are way, way too high. ALCINDOR: Following the latest twist and the controversy surrounding the Republican Senate candidate and former football star. The Daily Beast reporting the unnamed woman who the legend Walker paid for her abortion more than a decade ago says she`s also the mother of one of his children. Previously, she provided the news outlet with a receipt from an abortion clinic as well as a check and a get-well card she says are from Walker. She has not revealed her name citing privacy concerns, and NBC News has not verified her story nor the documents. Walker, an abortion rights opponent, again strongly denying the accusation. WALKER: I know this is untrue. I know nothing about any woman having an abortion. ALCINDOR: But Walker`s son, Christian, has fiercely criticized his father. CHRISTIAN WALKER, SON OF HERSCHEL WALKER : Don`t lie on the lives you`ve destroyed and act like you`re some moral family man. Y`all should care about that, conservatives. ALCINDOR: Today, we pressed Walker. What`s your reaction to people so close to you, your son, a mother of your -- someone who says that she`s the mother of your kid saying that you`re lying. What`s your reaction to people so close to you saying don`t trust you? WALKER: Just like what I just said. Democrats are desperate for this seat. This seat is important. ALCINDOR: They`re your family. WALKER: They`re very desperate for to seat. I love my family. I always love my family. I`m going to win this race. ALCINDOR: The Daily Beast says the anonymous woman, a registered Democrat, who says she`d had a years-long relationship with Walker thinks his denials are quote ridiculous. Many National Republican standing by Walker slamming it, and said it`s Democratic distraction from issues like inflation and crime. SEN. TED CRUZ (R-TX): Herschel Walker is going to win that race. This is an effort from Democrats to hold on to power. ALCINDOR: But some state Republican starting to voice their unease. LT. GOV. GEOFF DUNCAN (R-GA): Even the most staunch Republicans I think are rattled at the continued flow of information. ALCINDOR: Meanwhile, voters in Georgia sounding off. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It`s 100 percent true right now, but we don`t know a whole story. I`m voting for Herschel. I mean, he made a mistake. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: The only reason Herschel Walker is on his ballot right now is because he supports Trump. If you support Trump, you can have any kind of morals in this country. (END VIDEOTAPE) ALCINDOR: Today, Walker`s opponent, Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock called these allegations, "disturbing." And he`s reiterated his support for abortion rights. Next week, both men are scheduled to face off in a debate. Lester? HOLT: All right, Yamiche, thank you. Now, to new reporting that Hunter Biden could potentially face federal criminal charges. Ken Dilanian explains. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEN DILANIAN, NBC NEWS JUSTICE AND INTELLIGENCE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, new signs Hunter Biden could face criminal charges. The Washington Post reporting federal agents believe they have a plausible case to charge the president son with tax crimes, and also with lying on a gun application when he said he wasn`t using illegal drugs citing people familiar with the case. The final decision about whether to file charges rests with the top federal prosecutor in Delaware who was appointed by President Trump. The Justice Department declined comment. NBC News has not confirmed the report. Biden`s lawyer saying prosecutors, in this case, are diligently and thoroughly weighing not just evidence provided by agents but also all the other witnesses. Hunter Biden`s business dealings have repeatedly come under fire including taking a lucrative position on a Ukrainian energy companies board while his father was vice president. An NBC News analysis of information on his laptop showed he and his firms were paid $11 million from 2013 to 2018 including by Chinese and Ukrainian firm. Last year, Hunter Biden insisted he did nothing wrong. HUNTER BIDEN , SON OF PRESIDENT JOE BIDEN : I will be cleared of any wrongdoing. DILANIAN: His lawyer said he paid a $2 million tax debt. (END VIDEOTAPE) DILANIAN (on camera): President Biden has repeatedly said he was not involved in his son`s business dealings. The White House tonight is declining comment. Lester? HOLT: Ken Dilanian in our Washington newsroom, thank you. Terrifying moments today along the Las Vegas strip where police say an attacker went on a stabbing rampage with a large kitchen knife in front of a Wynn Casino. At least two people were killed, six others injured, three in critical condition tonight. A suspect is in custody. Police say the motive is under investigation but it appears, they say, unprovoked. Now to the disaster in Florida and is still-rising death toll from Hurricane Ian. Many people remain desperate for help more than a week after the storm hit. Sam Brock is there for us. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) SAM BROCK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Eight days in, and the havoc wreaked by Hurricane Ian is still hard to comprehend. Sheriff`s deputies canvassing this trailer park in Lee County with mailboxes but no residence. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: What we need right now is some kind of housing temporary. [19:10:o6] BROCK: The death toll now sits at more than 130, the highest from any Florida storm since 1935, more than five times the U.S. death toll from Hurricane Andrew, a category five 30 years ago. Ian`s rapid storm intensification residents remaining behind, and massive population growth in southwest Florida, all likely playing a role. 49-year-old Liz Maguire was among those lost. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: There`s going to be a huge hole. BROCK: Her mom, Susan, says she was a foundation of love for her family. BROCK: Has it sunk in yet? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes. We`re sitting here in her house and she`ll never be here again. I`m looking at her things. Yes, it sunk in. BROCK: Liz was a mother and a grandmother. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: She just enjoyed everything. BROCK: She suffered a medical emergency during the storm and called for help. But first responders couldn`t reach her. She was found with her cell phone in her hand. Susan last spoke with her daughter that afternoon. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: She always ended every conversation with I love you. I love you, mom. I love you too, sweetie. If you can pick anything to be the last thing you say to a person, that would be it. (END VIDEOTAPE) BROCK (on camera): Back where Susan lives, on hard-hit Pine Island, supplies are still being brought in by helicopter. And the conditions are only expected to get more challenging. Many of the bridges that serve as a lifeline for Southwest Florida are unusable. On a typical day, some 80 truckloads worth of materials and supplies would pass right through here. But now, that won`t happen for months. Lester? HOLT: All right, Sam Brock, thank you. In Thailand, the deadliest mass killing ever in that country. A former police officer with a gun and a knife attack a daycare center, killing 34 people, 24 of them children. Then he fatally shot himself at his home where his wife and son were also found dead. Authorities say he was fired previously for drug possession. Now to the war in Ukraine. In the extraordinary lengths, some Russians are taking to avoid President Vladimir Putin is draft. Two Russian citizens sailing hundreds of miles to U.S. soil to request asylum. And inside Ukraine, our NBC News exclusive tonight with a top official leading the U.S. effort to help rebuild. We get more now from Cal Perry. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) CAL PERRY, NBC NEWS INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, more Russians fleeing Putin`s war. Following that crush of traffic along Russia`s borders, now two Russian men arriving in Alaska by boat requesting asylum saying they too are fleeing military service. On the battlefield, Ukrainian troops press their offensive while Russia lashes back once again targeting civilians. Ukraine saying a rocket attack killing at least three people in a residential building in Zaporizhzhia. While in Kyiv, USAID Administrator Samantha Power here to spearhead the effort to rebuild. The challenges must be immense to rebuild a country while it`s fighting a war. SAMANTHA POWER, ADMINISTRATOR, USAID : Yes, and I hear a lot of build back better. It`s interesting. You start to see this government, and really they`ve done this from the beginning but increasingly walking and chewing gum at the same time. PERRY: Even during our interview, the sounds of war break through. POWER: We have provided now more than $25 billion in a combination of military and security assistance. PERRY: All of it coming after that startling report in The New York Times about this deadly car bomb attack in Russia back in August. The victim Darya Dugina, the daughter of a prominent Russian nationalist. According to the report, U.S. intelligence agencies believe parts of the Ukrainian government authorized her assassination and fear it could widen the war. (END VIDEO CLIP) PERRY (on camera): NBC News has not confirmed the Times` report. And tonight, a top Ukrainian official suggesting that Russia was behind the attack. Lester? HOLT: All right, Cal Perry, thank you. In 60 seconds, soaring crime and understaffed police departments, a controversial plan to have civilians pick up the slack in one major city next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:15:00] HOLT: Tonight, investigators are poring over a grisly crime scene. Four members of a family, including an 8-month-old baby were killed after being kidnapped. Miguel Almaguer is following this. Miguel, what do we know about this? MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Well, Lester, authorities have not officially released a motive but say it`s possible the suspect may have known the family and that the family`s ATM card was used after the heinous crime. On Monday, investigators say Jesus Salgado forced two brothers out of their business office at gunpoint in the city of Merced , zip tie in their hands behind their back before returning for a young mother and her 8-month-old daughter. The family was then driven away in a truck. All of their bodies were found two days later in a central California orchard. Investigators have not said how the family was killed, but the suspect is talking to police. The sheriff says the suspect has a long criminal history and deserves the death penalty. Lester? HOLT: Just an awful crime. All right, Miguel, thank you. New Orleans is one of many cities seeing a dramatic rise in murders is now taking a controversial approach to combating its shortage of police officers, hiring civilians. Gabe Gutierrez is there. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Seventh grader Byron Kelly was just 13 years old when he was shot and killed in New Orleans earlier this year. CARLA THOMAS, MOTHER OF BYRON KELLY: I just been praying. And I keep telling myself, don`t cry, don`t cry. GUTIERREZ: His mother, Karla Thomas, says it`s been hard to get a hold of the police officers working the unsolved case. THOMAS: I have called them, I have sent them text messages. I have like, none, nothing. GUTIERREZ: Police did not respond to our interview requests. The homicide rate in New Orleans is soaring, up 40 percent just this year. Now, the Big Easy is taking drastic measures hiring civilians to help with policing, including detective work like going to crime scenes to gather evidence. SHAUN FERGUSON, SUPERINTENDENT, NEW ORLEANS POLICE: This is also to reduce some of the workload currently placed on our patrol and district personnel. GUTIERREZ: Good idea? MIKE GLASSER, PRESIDENT, POLICE ASSOCIATION OF NEW ORLEANS: No, not really. GUTIERREZ: Mike Glasser, who heads up one of the city`s police unions blames plummeting morale for a crushing shortage of about 600 officers from Seattle to St. Louis, Atlanta, to Philadelphia. Major cities across the country are also reporting a cop staffing crisis. GLASSER: If we`re going to send civilians in there that are unarmed, inexperienced, untrained for what it turns into, that`s dangerous for them and it`s dangerous for the public. GUTIERREZ: Highlighting the crime problem, during our brief interview today, someone broke into a car in the Police Union`s own parking lot. Is the city safe? LATOYA CANTRELL, MAYOR OF NEW ORLEANS: So, the city of New Orleans is one that is grappling with violent crime like many other cities throughout the country, GUTIERREZ: Democratic mayor Latoya Cantrell blames the pandemic slowing down the court system as well as progressive prosecutors for the spike in crime. But her critics also blame her and are mounting a recall effort. CANTRELL: Well, the recall organizers in my view are absolutely unfair but are demonstrating their democratic rights. I have led on key issues that no other mayor has. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (on camera): The mayor recently suggested that the officer shortage could impact Mardi Gras. She has since walked that back, Lester. HOLT: Gabe Gutierrez in New Orleans, thanks. Next, retailers overstock a much, much different picture from last year. How you can save this holiday season. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: It is not even Halloween but the holiday shopping season is already here and it`s far different from last year when just about everything seemed in short supply. Here`s Emilie Ikeda. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) EMILIE IKEDA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): As we enter the holiday shopping season, a new story is emerging at America`s ports as companies worldwide experienced economic whiplash. With sky-high inflation cutting into shoppers buying power, some shipping companies are now canceling trips. U.S. shippers say they`re seeing a 20 percent drop in ocean freight orders. A sharp contrast to last year when big retailers hired private vessels to transport goods. LORI ANN LAROCCO, CNBC SENIOR EDITOR: Based on the items on the water right now and what is being processed in, retailers are anticipating a customer that is not going to be spending quite as much. IKEDA: This week, the WTO warning global trade is losing momentum. NGOZI OKONJO-IWEALA, DIRECTOR-GENERAL, WORLD TRADE ORGANIZATION: The picture for 2023 has darkened considerably. IKEDA: Still, there`s room for the consumer to benefit this holiday season. Major retailers are now trying to clear their shelves that this year are overstocked. Nike says its North America inventories up 65 percent compared to last year. That means steep discounts for bargain hunters. Everyone is looking for a deal right now. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We`re trying to stretch our money as far as we can possibly stretch it. IKEDA: To luring cautious customers, retailers including Kohl`s and Target jumpstarted their holiday deals today. And for the first time, Amazon will hold a second prime day-like event within one year. So, when sorting through the savings, shopping experts say, compare prices online. Look for retailers who offer price matching and use a cashback credit card to stretch your dollar the furthest as inflation curbs the power of your paycheck. Emily Ikeda, NBC News New York. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, the 100-year-old Marathon Man inspiring America. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Finally, we want to introduce you to a 100-year-old who has truly gone the distance and shows no sign of slowing down. Maggie Vespa with "INSPIRING AMERICA." (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MAGGIE VESPA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Runners often strive to outpace time. MIKE FREMONT, 100-YEAR-OLD RUNNER: The nice thing about running at this age -- VESPA: Mike Fremont defies it. FREMONT: -- is that there`s very little competition. VESPA: At 100, the retired Cincinnati engineer and great grandfather of four logs five to 10 miles three times a week. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You are so sweet. VESPA: His 14-minute mile pace only slowed by starstruck fans. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: You`re an inspiration to a lot of people. VESPA: Does that feel weird to hear that you`re a celebrity? FREMONT: Absolutely embarrassing. VESPA: With 60 marathons under his feet, Mike boasts four world records, fastest marathons for his age at 80 and 90. Fastest half marathons at 90 and 91. Running started his therapy in his 30s after the loss of his first wife. FREMONT: So, starting to run and it worked. VESPA: Decades later, after battling cancer, Mike went vegan and with the encouragement of his second wife, Marilyn, ran marathon after marathon. What do you think is fueling it? MARILYN WALL, WIFE OF MIKE FREMONT: I think he can`t quit. VESPA: Proving her point, his other hobby, canoeing. Of course, racing goes to. For people who think at 100, a person should be slowing down. What do you say to that? FREMONT: I think they ought to be speeding up. VESPA: Proof no matter your age, your best time may still lie ahead. Maggie Vespa, NBC News, Cincinnati. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And he just keeps going. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Thursday. Thank you for watching. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Goodnight, everyone. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. headline: Herschel Walker , The GOP Candidate Who Has Called For A Ban On Abortion, Denying That He Paid For An Ex-Girlfriend`s Abortion More Than A Decade Ago
story_text: LESTER HOLT: Just 35 days before the Midterms, a new allegation is rocking that very tight Senate race in Georgia. Republican Herschel Walker strongly denying an accusation that he paid for a former girlfriend abortion. Here`s Kristen Welker. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, Republican candidate and former football star Herschel Walker forcefully denying an allegation that`s rocking the critical Georgia Senate race. A new accusation that Walker who supports an abortion ban after 15 weeks without any exceptions, paid for his then-girlfriend to have an abortion in 2009. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Do you know the woman that is making this allegation? HERSCHEL WALKER (R-GA), SENATE CANDIDATE: I have no -- I had no idea but it is a flat-out lie. WELKER: The explosive report appearing in The Daily Beast which did not name the woman citing privacy concerns. She says she and Walker agreed she would have the abortion. The Daily Beast publishing a photo of a get-well card she says this from Walker. The news outlet also says she gave them a receipt from an abortion clinic and an image of a $700 check she says his from Walker. NBC News has not seen nor independently verified any of the documents. WALKER: I never asked anyone to get an abortion. I never pay for an abortion and that`s a lie. WELKER: But tonight, Walker is facing fierce criticism from his 23-year-old son Christian saying Walker`s family urged him not to run because we all knew some of his past. CHRISTIAN WALKER, SON OF HERSCHEL WALKER : Don`t lie about your life at the expense of me, my mom, and all of the people that you`ve affected throughout your life. You don`t get to pretend you`re some moral family guy. WELKER: Herschel Walker tweeting I love my son no matter what. And blasting the allegations as a last-minute distraction by Democrats. WALKER: There`s inflation, the border wide open, crime. They don`t want to talk about that. So, they`re making up lies now because they need this Georgia seat. WELKER: Now, top national Republicans are rallying around him from former President Trump to Senator Rick Scott tonight saying Democrats know that Herschel Walker is winning so they have cranked up this smear machine. (END VIDEOTAPE) WELKER: Incumbent Democrat Senator Raphael Warnock not weighing in on the controversy, but saying he`s been a consistent abortion rights supporter. Lester? HOLT: Kristen Welker, thanks. It appears that Elon Musk`s plan to buy Twitter is back on tonight. A lawyer for the billionaire tells federal regulators that Musk is willing to go forward with a $44 billion deal if a Delaware court ends Twitter `s lawsuit against Musk. Twitter file that soon after Musk put the deal on hold last spring. END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: NBC NIGHTLY NEWS for October 4, 2022, NBC
story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight, the desperate search in Florida as the death toll from Hurricane Ian rises even higher. (voiceover): The race against time. Rescuers going door to door looking for survivors nearly a week after Ian hit as a powerful category four storm. The death toll climbing to at least 108. Our team on the ground tonight. Also, this evening, the new move by former President Donald Trump and his battle over classified documents seized from Mar-a-Lago. His emergency request to the Supreme Court. The explosive report of the Georgia Senate race. Herschel Walker , the GOP candidate who has called for a ban on abortion, denying that he paid for an ex-girlfriend`s abortion more than a decade ago. Walker`s son lashing out calling his father a liar. How Republicans are reacting. Elon Musk`s about-face reviving his $44 billion bid to buy Twitter . What the company is saying. The major new provocation from North Korea launching a ballistic missile over Japan for the first time in five years. How the U.S. responded with a show of force. NBC News investigates how did a driver busted with a record amount of fentanyl escaped from the feds. And from coal miner`s daughter to the Queen of Country Music. Remembering the iconic Loretta Lynn. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. HOLT (on camera): Good evening. Now, six days after Hurricane Ian`s devastating impact in Florida, a grim acceptance is setting in about the fates of those yet to be found. Rescuers know the most critical hours to find the trapped or injured alive have passed. But still tonight, the search goes on and the death toll ticks upward now more than 100 in the U.S. almost all in Florida which took Ian`s mightiest blow. Power there is being restored. The number of homes and businesses in the dark now dropping below 400,000. But for many who survived the storm and are now left with nothing, these are harrowing and trying days of another kind. In some communities, there was a growing sense of neglect. Help they say has arrived for so many in southwest Florida, but not for them. Kerry Sanders continues our reporting tonight from the disaster zone. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Search and rescue. KERRY SANDERS, NBC NEWS SENIOR NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Today`s search teams move door to door again and again. The death toll climbed. More than 100 people killed by Hurricane Ian, about half of them in Lee County. The search and rescue now shifting to mostly recovery. CARMINE MARCENO, SHERIFF, LEE COUNTY, FLORIDA: More towards the second and third phase. SANDERS: Which is -- MARCENO: It`s possible there are still people out there, possible, but most likely we`re on recovery now. And you know that`s very difficult. SANDERS: FEMA has been on the ground but miles from the coast in predominantly Black and Hispanic neighborhoods, some say Help has not arrived. Do you feel ignored here? RUBY WILLIAMS, HURRICANE IAN SURVIVOR: Yes, very much. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: No Red Cross, no FEMA, no nothing. SANDERS: Though the damage here is not as dramatically visible, Ruby Williams says her community was also hit hard. WILLIAMS: We have water up to here. I say look, it looked like the Gulf of Mexico in front of her house just that quick. SANDERS: Williams used an extension cord, all she could find in that moment, to tie herself to her niece so they wouldn`t get swept away. WILLIAMS: It was the grace of God we survived. SANDERS: Now they`re concerned they won`t get the aid they need. A recent study shows communities with large populations of Black, Hispanic, or Native American residents often receive less money from FEMA than mostly white communities. GOSK (on camera): There`s no way to know for sure if the drugs were headed here to South Bend but we decided to come and see if the fentanyl problem was an issue. And like so many cities and towns in this country, fentanyl is killing people. How bad is the problem right now? ROBIN VIDA, DIRECTOR OF HEALTH OUTREACH, PROMOTION AND EDUCATION, ST. JOSEPH COUNTY HEALTH DEPARTMENT: How bad is it? It`s everywhere. GOSK (voiceover): Recently, seven overdose deaths in a single week all suspected to be from fentanyl. VIDA: All of a sudden in July of 2021, I began to notice almost all of my death certificates had some form of fentanyl listed on it. GOSK: Robin Vida works for the County`s Department of Health. If there was a big bust, if someone was arrested who was dealing fentanyl in the city, would it help you guys? VIDA: Yes, hands down. We need to stop dangerous drugs from entering into our community. GOSK: The DEA says fentanyl is their top priority. Letting a suspect like David Maldonado slip away isn`t going to help. Stephanie Gosk, NBC News, South Bend, Indiana. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: In 60 seconds, how inflation is driving millions to change holiday travel plans. When to buy your tickets next. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:15:00] HOLT: After more than two years of pandemic-related stress and a surge in unruly passengers, the FAA has announced a new rule guaranteeing flight attendants more rest. We get more from Tom Costello. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): They`re on the front lines in the nation`s skies dealing with safety, in-flight emergencies, and bad behavior. For years flight attendants have complained that they`re overworked and overstressed as federal rules allowed them to work 14-hour days with nine hours of rest between shifts. Today, the FAA order flight attendants must get a minimum of 10 hours rest. BILLY NOLEN, ADMINISTRATOR, FAA : They need just as much rest because flight attendants are the foundation of aviation safety`s culture starting with cabin safety. COSTELLO: It comes after airlines asked all crew members to work extra shifts during the summer travel surge. It`s not just the full flights and the overtime. Flight attendants continue to deal with this increase in unruly, sometimes even violent behavior onboard their planes. SARA NELSON , PRESIDENT, ASSOCIATION OF FLIGHT ATTENDANTS INTERNATIONAL: This has been the most challenging time in the history of our aviation. COSTELLO: While some airlines have already adopted the new rest rules, they must all comply after the new year. Meanwhile, 43 percent of Americans are planning to pay more to travel this holiday season. But a new Bankrate survey finds nearly eight out of 10 are changing their plans due to inflation. Roughly a quarter say they`ll travel fewer days and shorter distances, drive instead of fly, and select less expensive destinations or hotels. A third say how will they travel plans will strain their budgets. TED ROSSMAN, SENIOR INDUSTRY ANALYST, BANKRATE: They still want to travel. They still want to have the big holiday meal and all the gifts under the tree. But they`re going to try to cut some corners and do it differently. COSTELLO: The time to buy airline tickets say travel pros is now. Tom Costello, NBC News, Washington. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next for us tonight, fighting a crime wave. One city makes it easier for police to use private video surveillance. We`ll tell you about the controversy tonight. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: And now, our look at a controversial move by San Francisco on fighting crime. The city is now giving the police power to monitor private surveillance video as part of a new pilot program. Jake Ward explains. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JAKE WARD, NBC NEWS TECHNOLOGY CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Soon after Michael Su opened his San Francisco shoe store, it was robbed. MICHAEL SU, STORE OWNER: The perpetrator used the blowtorch to get in to bypass our alarm system. WARD: Thieves have hit the store three times. SU: When somebody breaks in, it`s like somebody`s breaking into your home. WARD: Now, a San Francisco ordinance gives police access to live private footage like Su`s. They need the owner`s permission, but they do not need a warrant. SU: I want to be the first one in line to give them access to my camera. WARD: San Francisco has seen a surge in retail thefts, including by this 2021 group that evaded police while robbing downtown stores. LONDON BREED, MAYOR, SAN FRANCISCO: Some of that potentially could have been avoided if they were able to watch the situation in real-time. And when those video footages are already readily available to our law enforcement and yet we still cannot deliver safety results, where does this lead us? WARD: Michael Su says he`ll hand over access but within limits. SU: Obviously, they wouldn`t need to really see the inventory room. Cameras, I`m willing to share whatever it`s needed, you know, for the police to do their job. WARD: Jake Ward, NBC News, San Francisco. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, we`ll remember the queen of country music. Loretta Lynn was born in 1932 in Butcher Hollow, Kentucky, one of eight children with a hardscrabble upbringing that later fueled her music. LORETTA LYNN, SINGER: I write about my life. LYNN: I`d give anything in the world if he would have been here when I recorded the Coal Miner`s Daughter. But I think he hears me. And one day, I will sing it to him.
