story_text: [19:00:00] (COMMERCIAL BREAK) LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR (on camera): Tonight the emotional outpouring of Scotland bids farewell to Queen Elizabeth. (voiceover): The Queen`s children, King Charles and his three siblings leading the solemn procession as crowds lining the streets of Scotland`s capital. The moving service. The 500-year-old crown of Scotland placed on the Queen`s casket. Thousands lining up for hours to pay tribute as the Queen lies in rest for 24 hours before her final journey to London. And Prince Harry breaking his silence. His powerful tribute to the woman he called granny. Also tonight, Ukraine saying its lightning advance has retaken more than 1000 square miles from Russia. In just 48 hours Russia retaliated by striking Ukraine`s power grid. Is the war at a turning point? Donald Trump`s legal team objecting to the DOJ`s special master candidates to review the classified documents ceased from Mar-a-Lago. What they are asking the judge to do? Extreme weather in the West. Heavy rain triggering mudslides. More than 50 people rescued as dozens of wildfires rage in the region. Caught on camera, Jeff Bezos ` unmanned Blue Origin rocket bursting into flames after liftoff. And the tributes for the Queen and what officials are now asking mourners to stop leaving behind. ANNOUNCER: This is NBC NIGHTLY NEWS with Lester Holt. Good evening. The coffin of Queen Elizabeth II lies at rest tonight in Edinburgh, Scotland where thousands have lined up to pay their respects. Tonight, the Queen`s daughter and three sons led by Charles holding a vigil for their mother at St. Giles cathedral. It was a day filled with powerful and poignant images including a quiet stately procession of the Queen`s coffin down the cobblestone streets of Edinburgh`s Royal Mile to the Cathedral. The crown of Scotland placed atop her coffin. Her children walking behind the hearse, as it slowly made its way past a silent crowd gathered to say goodbye. Scotland, a country adored by the Queen and in fact the place she died on Thursday. The newly crowned king meantime making several appearances today including addressing parliament as he both grieves and consoles the nation. Keir Simmons starts our reporting tonight from London. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS SENIOR INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): It was a powerful tribute. The Queen`s daughter and sons including King Charles walking slowly behind her cortage. Thousands lining Edinburgh`s famous Royal Mile. Crowd so quiet, you could hear the hooves of the horses on the cobbled streets of Scotland`s capital. Queen Elizabeth loves this country. The silence speaking volumes about their respect for her. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I can`t find my words. It`s -- I`m so sorry. SIMMONS: The Queen helps plan every detail of today`s service and the many days of remembrance ahead. From the pageantry, like the precise military choreography, carrying her coffin inside the 12th-century Cathedral, to the intensely personal. In church, the Queen`s children looking on as the nearly 500-year-old Scottish crown is laid on her oak casket, taking its place alongside a wreath of flowers, including some of her favorites picked from her Balmoral garden, all on top of Scotland`s Royal Standard. CHARLES III, KING, UNITED KINGDOM: The tangible connections to my darling late mother, we see all around us. SIMMONS: Earlier, King Charles speaking to the British Parliament . CHARLES III: She set an example of selfless duty which, with God`s help and your counsels, I am resolved faithfully to follow. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Andrew, you`re a sick (BLEEP). SIMMONS: Not everything was scripted today. One person protesting Prince Andrew was quickly removed from the crowd. Today`s events in Edinburgh capping off that solemn weekend journey that carried the Queen through 180 miles of stunning Scottish countryside after leaving her beloved Balmoral Castle. People on horseback paying respects along the road. These tractors a tribute to her from local farmers. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We`re proud to be Scottish and we`re proud to be British. And it`s nice to say goodbye. SIMMONS: And another poignant moment in this long goodbye. The Queen`s children mounting a vigil standing on all sides of her casket heads bowed. Even as many thousands of mourners kept coming, each given just a few minutes to say goodbye to a queen who gave them her life. (END VIDEOTAPE) [19:05:10] HOLT: Keir, it was quite a day. I know tomorrow, the focus of the solemn ceremonies will turn to London. SIMMONS (on camera): That`s right, Lester. The Queen`s body will be brought here to Buckingham palace tomorrow. Then, on Wednesday, move to Westminster for four days where hundreds of thousands are expected to wait in line. And then, a week today, that historic State Funeral. Lester? HOLT: Keir Simmons, thank you. And NBC is Tom Llamas has been on the ground for us in Edinburgh, the last few days. And Tom, you walk the Royal Mile today. TOM LLAMAS, NBC NEWS SENIOR NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (on camera): Lester, that`s right. The scene down there was remarkable because of the size of the crowd. It was double, if not triple what we experienced when the Queen`s hearse first pulled into Edinburgh on Sunday. But tonight, that solemn procession uphill through the medieval street with the king and the Queen`s children marching along through a sea of people so many onlookers were pouring over staircases on some corners. But the impact of Queen Elizabeth`s reign, it hit us afterwards, Lester, it`s what many didn`t see, the line nine hours long in some cases to see the Queen`s casket up close. I spoke to several people in the crowd, some who said they wanted to witness history but so many other saying the Queen earned that devotion with her 70 years on the throne. Two female veterans told me they were waiting all that time to personally salut the coffin. And tonight, Lester, this is a live image of the scene outside St. Giles Cathedral. The sun has gone down. It is chilly here. It`s very late. People are tired and yet they still wait to say goodbye. If you have any doubt of how the Queen touched people, look at that right there, Lester. HOLT: Yes, remarkable but not surprising outpouring tonight. Tom, thanks. And one of the more striking scenes as these events unfolded, King Charles ` sons William and Harry emerging together with their wives over the weekend in a rare reunion. Here`s Molly Hunter. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MOLLY HUNTER, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): It was a welcome reunion that took the country by surprise. Getting out of the same car, the new Prince and Princess of Wales, William and Kate, alongside Harry and Meghan. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We didn`t imagine all four of them to be together, but I think that was the Queen`s last wish. HUNTER: We now know it was Prince William, who reportedly offered the olive branch reaching out to Harry and Meghan inviting them to greet the crowds at Windsor, a suggestion perhaps coming from the new king before such a critical week. DAISY MCANDREW, NBC NEW ROYAL COMMENTATOR: I firmly believe it was Charles who tried to metaphorically bang their heads together and say please, for me, for the future of the monarchy for your father, can you put on a brave face and go out and give us a sign of unity? HUNTER: And unity, at least for that brief hour, was seen and felt by the lucky thousands. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: That was really special, actually. I was really surprised all four of them were together. And yes, that`s quite emotional, I think, being a Brit seeing them, the two brothers side by side. HUNTER: Since Harry and Meghan famously left behind their Royal duties, fueling the brotherly rift, Prince William has moved into the role he was born for assuming his father`s former title. As the heir apparent, his official state responsibilities now a world away from Harry`s new life and California. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Growing up Princess Diana famously really wanted Harry and William to be equally important. Even though William`s destiny was very different, he was always going to be the monarch, she didn`t want Harry to feel less important, less significant. HUNTER: In a new tribute to granny, Harry says he`s forever grateful for my earliest childhood memories to meeting you for the first time as my commander-in-chief. But the brothers strike different notes. While Harry pledges to honor his father`s new role, William says he`ll be supporting my father the king in every way I can as the next in line. And now it`s William and Kate, the new Princess of Wales, Princess Diana`s former title, who are the most popular members of the Royal Family, stepping into the spotlight, shouldering the responsibility of modernizing this monarchy. (END VIDEOTAPE) HUNTER: Now, looking ahead, there are a number of opportunities where we might see the two brothers together again. What`s clear, though, is they don`t want it to distract from the critical week ahead for the Royal Family. Lester? HOLT: Molly, thank you. The Queen has been mourned well beyond Great Britain. She was also the official head of state and 14 other nations, including some that carry memories of a painful past. Kerry Sanders reports tonight from Jamaica. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) KERRY SANDERS, NBC NEWS SENIOR NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In former British colonies around the world, flags at half-staff including in India, once part of the sprawling British Empire. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I remember her in such a way that she`s that`s like our mother`s figure. SANDERS: The Queen often visited Britain`s colonies and former colonies. Today, there are 14 Commonwealth realms where the king is still recognized as the head of state including here in Jamaica. Are you mourning the Queen`s death? CLIFF HUGHES, JAMAICA HISTORIAN: No. SANDERS: No. HUGHES: Because her passing is regrettable but she`s not that close to us for us to be mourning. [19:10:10] SANDERS: Jamaica historian Cliff Hughes says this country`s beautiful shores hold an ugly past, slavery. The enslaved forced to the West Indies by the Royal-African company. They harvested sugar known as green gold. FAE ELLINGTON, RESIDENT, KINGSTON, JAMAICA: It built England. It built the streets. It built the big businesses. SANDERS: That`s the value of sugar at the time. ELLINGTON: Yes. SANDERS: The New King, Charles III, now inherits that legacy. HUGHES: When slavery was finally abolished, those who were the enslavers were paid 20 million pounds, which was 40 percent of Britain`s annual budget. SANDERS: And how much were the slaves themselves who were now free given? HUGHES: Not one cent. SANDERS: Which is why reparations remained a hot topic. When the now-Prince and Princess of Wales visited Jamaica in March, there were protests and demand for an official apology. Some now hope that comes from the new King. (END VIDEOTAPE) SANDERS (on camera): Under the court system here which mirrors England`s, if there were an official apology, that could well open the door to reparations. Lester? HOLT: All right, Kerry Sanders tonight in Jamaica, thank you. We`ll turn now to another major story, the lightning advance by Ukraine`s military reclaiming more ground against Russian forces in the northeast as Russia retaliates by striking Ukraine`s power grid. Our Megan Fitzgerald is in Kyiv. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MEGAN FITZGERALD, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): In a fast and furious reaction, Russia launching missiles and Ukraine`s east, striking critical infrastructure plunging millions into the dark. The strike seen as retaliation as Ukraine sweeps through the Russian front line in a shocking advance. Ukraine now claims in the last 12 days, they`ve taken back 2300 square miles of Russian-held territory in the northeastern Kharkiv region. Ukraine putting out this video, an incredible scene as the Ukrainian flag is raised in a village east of Kharkiv, as many residents overcome with emotion thanking the Ukrainian soldiers for liberating them. Ukraine releasing images showing Russian artillery and tanks left behind, as they say Russian soldiers were forced to withdraw. Ukraine`s President Zelenskyy thanking his troops, saying the world is impressed and the enemy is panicking. UK`s ministry of defense describes the territory Ukraine says it took back as twice the size of London, though Russia still controls the south and the east. Russia`s President Putin not commenting on Ukraine`s counter- offensive so far. A spokesperson only saying the Russian military operation is ongoing and will achieve its objective. But the question tonight, is this a turning point in the war. (END VIDEOTAPE) FITZGERALD (on camera): And tonight, Ukraine is claiming that it`s not just Russian equipment they`ve captured, it`s also Russian soldiers, saying they have so many POWs they`re running out of room. Lester? HOLT: OK, Megan Fitzgerald in Ukraine, thank you. Back home now to the battle over the FBI search at Mar-a-Lago. Attorneys for former President Trump objecting to the candidates the Justice Department proposed to serve as special master to review the classified documents seized by the FBI . Mr. Trump`s team disputing the documents classified status and asking the judge to reject the DOJ -- the DOJ`s request to continue reviewing the files. In 60 seconds, parts of the West can`t catch a break. The threat of more extreme weather after dozens are rescued in mudslides and wildfires raged on. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) HOLT: Back now with the extreme weather in the West. Flood watches in effect after mudslides forced dozens of rescues on the heels of record heat. Here`s Miguel Almaguer. [19:15:07] (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) MIGUEL ALMAGUER, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Tonight, a year of extremes in just a matter of days, historic heat fires, floods, and now mudslides. The volatile Western weather creating havoc for first responders and dangerous conditions for those suddenly in harm`s way. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: All these vehicles are stuck in about two feet of -- 20 mile an hour debris flow. ALMAGUER: Outside Los Angeles, firefighters rescued more than 50, including young families who suddenly became trapped and caked in debris as a mudslide covered a canyon road. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It was terrifying. ALMAGUER: On the heels of record-shattering heat, the remnants of Tropical Storm Kay brought flash flooding that`s soaked the region. Downed trees, swamp neighborhoods, and sidewalk rescues. From floods to fires, there`s been little relief. Across the West, more than 90 large wildfires are burning in a region mired in drought. Some 800,000 acres scorched from active fires as crews battle to gain the upper hand. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: The flames are 300 feet in the air, the trees were exploding. ALMAGUER: With entire communities under evacuations, in recent days, four have been killed trying to escape the flames. And now, after this crash, three firefighting personnel nearly lost their lives also trying to battle them. Tonight, the West can`t catch a break from a sudden season of extremes. Miguel Almaguer, NBC news. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: A spectacular rocket failure today for Blue Origin , a company owned by Jeff Bezos . It happened about a minute into the launch, flame scene shooting out of the rocket. Luckily, there were no people on board. The capsule was able to separate and parachute to Earth. This is the same type of rocket that sends paying customers to the edge of space but the capsule is different. Up next tonight, after Roe, abortion is rewriting November ballots. Ahead, one swing state`s looming battle in our series power of the vote. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:20:00] HOLT: We`re back now with our series power of the vote. With less than two months until Election Day, in Michigan, voters will decide if abortion rights should be protected by the state constitution. Here`s Yamiche Alcindor. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) YAMICHE ALCINDOR, NBC NEWS WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): Lifelong Republican Jessica Leech was devastated when the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. JESSICA LEECH, LIFELONG REPUBLICAN: I cried for weeks. I cried for my daughter. I always considered myself pro-life. ALCINDOR: Now, she changed her mind and her party. Jessica got pregnant at 19 and visited an abortion clinic to weigh her options. She decided to have her son who`s now 17 and says being able to make that choice is something every woman deserves. What do you say to people who think your story is an example of why abortion shouldn`t be an option? LEECH: I would tell those people that until recently, it was always a hypothetical. I would beg them to understand that having these options paved the way for me to be a good mother. ALCINDOR: In Michigan, residents will vote on a ballot referendum in November that would enshrine abortion rights into the state constitution. GOV. GRETCHEN WHITMER (D-MI): You`re a doctor. ALCINDOR: Incumbent Democratic Governor Gretchen Whitmer is also up for reelection. What is at stake in this election and in the ballot referendum? WHITMER: Well, abortion and the right to be a full American citizen with agency of your body is on this ballot. ALCINDOR: Her views are also shaped by her experiences. WHITMER: In college, in the days after I was raped, it dawned on me. Oh, my God, I might be pregnant. And the only thing that gave me a little bit of relief is knowing that I could make a decision that was right for me if that happened. ALCINDOR: Her opponent, Republican Tudor Dixon, supports banning abortion with no exception for rape or incest. I wonder if you could just talk a bit more about your own views and talk to people who are worried about your views being too extreme. I have shared my own pro-life story. I lost a baby 18 weeks. When I lost the baby and the doctor said this baby probably died in the womb at 16 weeks, I held a beautiful baby girl. ALCINDOR: Dixon also does not believe abortion is a top issue for voters. DIXON: They`re concerned with how to get their kids back on track after they were kept out of school. And if you look at our crime rates in the past couple of years, it`s just continued to rise. And why our businesses are being crushed by the government? ALCINDOR: Both supporters and opponents of the referendum are mobilizing like anti-abortion rights activist Christen Polo, now working overtime after voters in Kansas recently voted to keep abortion protections in its state constitution. CHRISTEN POLO, ACTIVIST: I`m very concerned. Frankly, the policies that are being put forth in this abortion amendment here in Michigan are some of the most extremist policies we`ve seen in the entire country. ALCINDOR: Meantime, Jessica hopes sharing her story helps keep abortion legal in Michigan. Her son Cameron sent her a text on the day of our interview. Your life experiences, our relationship, after you decided to keep me and change your life around me, and now your perspective of life is what the world needs most. ALCINDOR: Yamiche Alcindor, NBC News, Michigan. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: And up next, the tributes from everyday people honoring the Queen. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [19:25:00] HOLT: Finally, beyond the formal tributes, the tokens people have left to honor the Queen, small gestures adding up to a powerful message. Here`s Kelly Cobiella. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) KELLY COBIELLA, NBC NEWS FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT (voiceover): The ordinary, the extraordinary, messages and memories. Many shedding a tear for the Queen leaving a token. A small way just to say thank you for a life of service. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: She means a lot to all the people here and she`s done so much for everyone. So, we kind of need to honor her. COBIELLA: And a way to say goodbye, drawings cards, notes. Thank you for being the best Queen ever, one read. Another, with her beloved Corgi. Tributes for mourners around the world marking Queen Elizabeth`s extraordinary life. Katarina Mostova (PH) and her family fled the war in Ukraine and brought her country`s national flower, the sunflower, for the queen. Why did you come? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Because we want to make honor to Queen. This is so important for us. COBIELLA: Mountains of flowers and marmalade sandwiches, a nod to the Queen`s surprise skit with the children`s character Paddington Bear in June. Now, so many sandwiches and stuffed bears, they`re begging the public just to bring flowers. Members of the royal family are deeply touched. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Have you seen the messages? WILLIAM, PRINCE OF WALES: Yes, amazing. It`s the little 7-year-olds and 11- year-olds messages get straight through every time. COBIELLA: Notes from children have only been alive for a fraction of the Queen`s long reign like this one: "Thank you for showing the world how strong a woman can be." Kelly Cobiella, NBC News, Edinburgh Scotland. (END VIDEOTAPE) HOLT: Messages from the heart. That`s NIGHTLY NEWS for this Monday. Thank you for watching, everyone. I`m Lester Holt. Please take care of yourself and each other. Good night. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) END Content and programming copyright 2022 NBCUniversal. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. headline: The Cancer Survivor`s Journey To Starting A Family That Is Giving New Hope To Other Couples
story_text: SHEINELLE JONES: Back at 8:43 this morning on Your Health. One woman`s journey that`s giving hope to others facing breast cancer while also wanting to have children. CARSON DALY: NBC senior national correspondent Kate Snow joins us with that story. Kate, good morning. KATE SNOW, NBC SENIOR NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Hey. Good morning Carson. Good morning, guys. For many younger women diagnosed with cancer, the toxic treatment can take away their fertility. But new innovations and increased awareness have given some women the chance to preserve their fertility and build a family even after surviving cancer. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SHELLY BATTISTA, CANCER SURVIVOR: Hi. SNOW: Which one is Nina? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: This is Nina. SNOW: Nina? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes, she came first. SNOW: Hi, Nina. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And then this is little Margot. SNOW (voice-over): These days, life is a bit different for Shelly and Robert Battista. They grew from a family of three to five. While the Chicago couples days are now filled with dirty diapers, crying and lots of laundry, they wouldn`t have it any other way. Three years ago, Shelly was diagnosed with an aggressive form of breast cancer and learn she has a genetic mutation that raises her risk for ovarian cancer too. (on camera): How frightening is all of that? S. BATTISTA: Yes, it was terrifying. You know, we had a six-month-old baby at home. We felt like we were just starting our life together and we get this shocking news. SNOW (voice-over): Shelly needed to start treatment immediately, but the couple had their heart set on a big family and the chemotherapy would destroy her fertility. S. BATTISTA: We were so blessed to have Emilia prior to this breast cancer diagnosis. But, you know, you still have dreams of having more children. SNOW (voice-over): Dr. Kara Goldman specializes in fertility preservation at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago. [08:45:04] KARA GOLDMAN, PHYSICIAN: Chemotherapy that is used in young patients with triple negative breast cancer is very toxic to the ovaries. This is a tremendous blow for a young woman who a day prior was healthy and had no medical diagnosis. JONES: But Dr. Goldman told the couple there was hope. Before starting chemotherapy, Shelly and Robert could create frozen embryos. GOLDMAN: We have to do it quickly. We started her fertility preservation journey two days later. She started medications and two weeks later, she had eight frozen embryos. SNOW (voice-over): Shelly had 12 rounds of chemotherapy, a double mastectomy and had her ovaries and fallopian tubes removed. A year after treatment, she was healthy enough to get pregnant even without ovaries. GOLDMAN: The ovaries and the uterus function very independently of each other. So in Shelly`s case, because she did not have ovaries producing hormones, we were able to provide her the hormones necessary for pregnancy. SNOW (voice-over): The first two trials were unsuccessful, they tried a third embryo. And eight days later, Dr. Goldman called them with the news Shelly was pregnant. S. BATTISTA: She called me herself, personally, we were both static and crying, and yelling. ROBERT BATTISTA, SHELLY`S HUSBAND: And this was just kind of like the cherry on top. It was awesome. We`re going to have another kid. Shelly`s healthy, like everything was just like behind us at that point. SNOW (voice-over): But the surprises weren`t over yet. At their first ultrasound, the technician saw something. S. BATTISTA: She was like, oh, there`s two of them. And I was like -- we both were kind of like two of what? Like -- she`s like, there`s two babies. SNOW: You didn`t implant two embryos. S. BATTISTA: We implanted one embryo and the embryo split. And so they are identical twins. SNOW (voice-over): The chance of that happening, just 1%. Nine months later, two healthy little girls were born., Margot and Nina, born on the two year anniversary of Shelly being declared cancer free. R. BATTISTA: I think it`s like the best celebration of Shelly`s cancer journey. It`s like you`ve beaten cancer and now here`s this extra, like love you get on top of it. S. BATTISTA: It`s loud, it`s tiring. We have lots of laughs, lots of cries, lots of laundry. It`s chaotic but it is -- that`s perfect. (END VIDEO CLIP) SNOW: It`s perfect. Having a baby after cancer treatment is becoming a lot more common thanks to better technology and awareness. Also important to note, guys, the Battistas live in one of just a handful of states that require insurance to cover fertility after cancer. Most states don`t do that, so they live in Chicago, they had an Illinois law. JONES: This is going to grab the attention of so many of voice because there are so many families who are dealing with this exact same challenge. MELVIN: By the way, while you`re here, folks, in addition to being our senior national correspondent, we got to talk about this exciting personal project that Kate Snow has taken on. It`s been on your bucket list for years. We`ve talked about this but I want folks to take a look. SNOW: I`m not, I`m not. So that was Nashville Tennessee. I`m in a vocal tracking booth there. You heard the backing band. I met with a whole bunch of great amazing musicians in Nashville through friends of friends. I`ve been a singer my whole life. Carson think it`s funny. JONES: Well because we didn`t know. DALY: I did not see this coming. SNOW: I know. Nobody -- MELVIN: But you`re putting out songs, like music. SNOW: I have three songs out now, so that was one of them that you just heard. SOBOROFF: Just wait till they turn the chairs for you on "The Voice", Kate. JONES: Kate, I love you. DALY: Are they all covers or do you write? SNOW: They all covers. DALY: OK. SNOW: So "Nothing Compares to You" is what you just heard, "Because the Night" and "Can`t Find My Way Home." DALY: Oh my God, amazing. SNOW: Three of my favorite songs. JONES: I love it, Kate. Did you just feel like you know what it`s time to - - SNOW: It was -- yes, total (inaudible) like why not? What am I waiting for? JONES: Absolutely. SNOW: And so, kind of made it happen. DALY: How can people hear the music? It`s all -- the three of them are up on any place you stream music, Spotify , YouTube -- SOBOROFF: That is amazing, just hearing that. This is a tremendous blow for a young woman who a day prior was healthy and had no medical diagnosis. JONES: But Dr. Goldman told the couple there was hope. Before starting chemotherapy, Shelly and Robert could create frozen embryos. GOLDMAN: We have to do it quickly. We started her fertility preservation journey two days later. She started medications and two weeks later, she had eight frozen embryos. SNOW (voice-over): Shelly had 12 rounds of chemotherapy, a double mastectomy and had her ovaries and fallopian tubes removed. A year after treatment, she was healthy enough to get pregnant even without ovaries. GOLDMAN: The ovaries and the uterus function very independently of each other. So in Shelly`s case, because she did not have ovaries producing hormones, we were able to provide her the hormones necessary for pregnancy. SNOW (voice-over): The first two trials were unsuccessful, they tried a third embryo. And eight days later, Dr. Goldman called them with the news Shelly was pregnant. S. BATTISTA: She called me herself, personally, we were both static and crying, and yelling. ROBERT BATTISTA, SHELLY`S HUSBAND: And this was just kind of like the cherry on top. It was awesome. We`re going to have another kid. Shelly`s healthy, like everything was just like behind us at that point. SNOW (voice-over): But the surprises weren`t over yet. At their first ultrasound, the technician saw something. S. BATTISTA: She was like, oh, there`s two of them. And I was like -- we both were kind of like two of what? Like -- she`s like, there`s two babies. SNOW: You didn`t implant two embryos. S. BATTISTA: We implanted one embryo and the embryo split. And so they are identical twins. SNOW (voice-over): The chance of that happening, just 1%. Nine months later, two healthy little girls were born., Margot and Nina, born on the two year anniversary of Shelly being declared cancer free. R. BATTISTA: I think it`s like the best celebration of Shelly`s cancer journey. It`s like you`ve beaten cancer and now here`s this extra, like love you get on top of it. S. BATTISTA: It`s loud, it`s tiring. We have lots of laughs, lots of cries, lots of laundry. It`s chaotic but it is -- that`s perfect. (END VIDEO CLIP) SNOW: It`s perfect. Having a baby after cancer treatment is becoming a lot more common thanks to better technology and awareness. Also important to note, guys, the Battistas live in one of just a handful of states that require insurance to cover fertility after cancer. Most states don`t do that, so they live in Chicago, they had an Illinois law. story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:00:00] CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: It`s 8:00 on "TODAY." Coming up, bracing for a decision. All eyes on the grand jury in the criminal case against Donald Trump, as witnesses take the stand over allegations of hush money payments. The former president says he will be arrested tomorrow. We`ll have the latest on where the case goes from here. Plus, on air scare. A meteorologist recovering this morning after suddenly collapsing during a live broadcast. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) RACHEL KIM, KCAL NEWS WEEKEND ANCHOR: Oh. NICHELLE MEDINA, CBS NEWS LA ANCHOR: You know, we`re going to go ahead and go to break right now. KIM: Yes. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: Just ahead, how she`s feeling and her message for viewers. Then, coming to America. Why a growing number of royal families from all over the world are packing up their bags to move to the states. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: These are jet-setting, successful families. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: So, who`s making the trip and where are they headed? That story is coming up. And special celebration. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Hip, hip. CROWD: Hooray. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: Bruce Willis` family coming together for a special milestone as his wife speaks out amid the star`s battle with dementia. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) EMMA HEMING WILLIS, BRUCE WILLIS` WIFE: As much as I do it for myself I do it for you because I know how much you love my husband. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: Today, Monday, March 20, 2023. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CROWD: Starting off the week. CROWD: From Cabot, Arkansas. CROWD: Tamarac, Florida. CROWD: Houston, Texas. CROWD: And Springfield, Illinois. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Shout out to my dad and my brother. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Watching in Atlanta. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: From Michigan. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Ohio. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And Minnesota. CROWD: We`re on a girl`s trip. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Celebrating my 40th birthday. CROWD: From Raleigh, North Carolina. CROWD: From Ashland, Kentucky. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: And first time in New York City. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: And welcome to New York City. Look at all those smiling faces. JACOB SOBOROFF, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Hello. MELVIN: Girls trips and birthdays and anniversaries. That`s a good Monday crowd. SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS 3RD HOUR OF TODAY, CO-HOST: It`s spring break time. MELVIN: That`s right. JONES: It`s all around the country, folks. It`s freezing a little bit. MELVIN: We`re going to get outside in just moment. We`ve got Sheinelle with us. We`ve got Jacob with us. With Savannah on assignment today. Hoda enjoying time off this week. Good to have you back. SOBOROFF: You know what first day of spring means? JONES: What? MELVIN: What`s that? SOBOROFF: Summer is almost here. MELVIN: There you go. JONES: Almost here. Almost here. MELVIN: That`s right. We`ll have more on the spring from Mr. Rocker in just a moment. But let`s get right your news at 8:00. In the new and unexpected witness set to testify before grand jury in the Donald Trump hush money investigation. Over the weekend the former president himself predicting he would be arrested as soon as tomorrow. NBC`s Garrett Haake is at the district attorneys` office here in Manhattan. Garrett, good morning. GARRETT HAAKE, NBC NEWS SENIOR CAPITOL HILL CORRESPONDENT: Hey, Craig. Good morning. And yes, this courthouse behind me is going to be the center of the political world later today when grand jurors are expected to hear from what could be the final witness in what`s been a yearslong probe into those alleged hush money payments from Donald Trump going all the way back to 2016. Now, Donald Trump made clear over the weekend, he believes this investigation is going to end with his arrest. He said it would come on Tuesday. Now, to be clear, there has been no formal word from the district attorney that any indictment is coming, but law enforcement officials here in New York City have been planning for that possibility and planning for the possibility that folks could listen to Mr. Trump`s call for protests if and when that happens. Now, while we wait for the legal fallout, the political fallout is already happening. We`ve heard from speaker of the house over the weekend calling for folks not to protest any decision that may come out of here. And we`ve heard from some of Donald Trump`s political rivals rallying to his defense, calling any prosecution purely political. Now, about that witness today, Robert Costello is his name. He was a legal adviser to the prosecution`s star witness in this case, but he has been called by Donald Trump`s attorneys, according to a source directly familiar. We`ll be watching very closely throw see what comes out of that grand jury room today and what decisions are made in court and on the presidential playing field here as it relates to this over the next couple of days. Craig. MELVIN: All right. Garrett Haake, for us there. Garrett, thank you. JONES: Now, to some frightening moments for a New York lawmaker and pilot forced to make an emergency landing on a Long Island Beach. Take a look at this. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: New York state assemblyman Clyde Vanel says, he was practicing some maneuvers when suddenly his engine went out. So, he had no choice but to land his plane -- MELVIN: Wow. JONES: -- right there on the beach. MELVIN: Geez. JONES: Thankfully, both Vanel and his passenger walked away with only a few cuts and bruises. SOBOROFF: Out in L.A., a meteorologist is recovering after a frightening on air moment. She suffered a medical emergency in the middle of a broadcast, leaving her co-anchors and viewers completely stunned. NBC`s Emilie Ikeda is here with that story. Emilie, good morning. [08:05:00] EMILIE IKEDA, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Jacob, good morning. It was around this time, Saturday morning, when a local CBS Meteorologist Alissa Carlson, collapsed on live TV. We`re told she`s on the mend and she`s thanking everyone for their support. A warning to viewers, some of these images may be hard to watch. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) NICHELLE MEDINA, CBS NEWS LA ANCHOR: Let`s start off with a check of your next weather. IKEDA (voiceover): An on-air scare in Los Angeles. MEDINA: She joins us live in the studio, Alissa -- IKEDA (voiceover): Local CBS Meteorologist Alissa Carlson`s eyes appearing to roll back right before she slowly leans forward and then suddenly collapses to the floor. KCAL`s co-anchors quickly tossing to commercials after realizing something was very wrong. RACHEL KIM, KCAL NEWS WEEKEND ANCHOR: Oh. MEDINA: You know, we`re going to go ahead and go to break right now. KIM: Yes. IKEDA (voiceover): According to the station, the team took immediate action to comfort Alissa and call 9-1-1. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: 78-Immediate dispatch on 4200 Radford Avenue. IKEDA (voiceover): After she was taken to the hospital, Carlson sharing a message of reassurance on Facebook . Posting, thanks for all the text, calls, and well wishes. I`m going to be OK. This isn`t the first time she has suffered a health scare during a broadcast. Back in 2014, she got sick working as the chief meteorologist for NBC`s affiliate KGET. ALISSA CARLSON, CBS METEOROLOGIST: All of a sudden, during the newscast, I threw up in the weather center. IKEDA (voiceover): Carlson later learned she had a leaky heart valve, a diagnosis that inspired her to embrace a healthier lifestyle and advocate for the American Heart Association . And later, after giving birth to her daughter, a miraculous surprise. CARLSON: The stem cells from my baby had started to heal my heart. IKEDA (voiceover): It`s not clear why Carlson fainted in this latest incident, but she told us her heart is fine. She`s not the only TV news personality to suffer an on-air medical emergency. Just last year, Julie Chin experienced what was believed to be the beginning of a stroke while anchoring for our Tulsa, Oklahoma, affiliate. JULIE CHIN, NEWS ANCHOR, TULSA NBC AFFILIATE KJRH: -- today at the -- at the -- at the event. The event features live -- I`m sorry. Something is going on with me. IKEDA (voiceover): Chin lost partial vision while her hand and arm went numb. She was unable to read the teleprompter but managed to toss back to her co-workers on live TV. Chin later reflecting on that harrowing incident on "TODAY." CHIN: And of course, I mean, I want to know what caused it. So, you know, maybe we can prevent it from happening again. (END VIDEO CLIP) IKEDA (on camera): OK. So, the good news is, Alissa Carlson tells us she is out of the hospital and even enjoying some pizza. You can tell she`s incredibly grateful for the support of her co-workers and the thoughts and prayers from viewers. She says, she is recovering from a head injury suffered in the fall and understandably is not sure when she will be back on air. But, of course, we`re rooting for her. JONES: Absolutely. SOBOROFF: I was going to say. JONES: A quick recovery. SOBOROFF: Oh, man. So scary, but glad she`s OK. IKEDA: Absolutely. SOBOROFF: Emilie, thank you. JONES: Thank you, Emilie. MELVIN: Thanks, Emilie. JONES: All right. That`s it for the news. Do you want to give us a "Boost"? MELVIN: Hoda`s not here, JONES: OK. MELVIN: But I`ll do my best. This morning, a sweet reunion between a little girl and her dog named Leo. It turns out Leo got lost back in January. But last week, their family finally got that phone call they had been waiting for. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: Oh, so sweet. MELVIN: Oh. You can see the little girl there, overcome with emotion after seeing Leo for the first time in months. JONES: Awe. MELVIN: Thankfully another family was apparently taking good care of him until they were finally able to connect with his owners and she could not wait to give little Leo a big hug. JONES: Leo was happy to see her too. MELVIN: Oh, yes. SOBOROFF: Yes, Leo was. And shout out to that family for taking care of Leo. MELVIN: Right. JONES: That was sweet. SOBOROFF: How nice is that. MELVIN: Right. JONES: That was good. SOBOROFF: That was a go ahead one. All right. Ladies and gentlemen, just ahead, Adam Sandler honored overnight with one of the most prestigious awards in all of comedy. Carson`s is going to have that story and more coming up on "POP Start." JONES: But first, Vicky is here to kick off our brand-new series, "Money- Saving Mondays". VICKY NGUYEN, NBC NEWS SENIOR CONSUMER INVESTIGATIVE CORRESPONDENT: Hey, good morning, guys. With food costs continuing to rise, how best to preserve your produce from the ideal fridge tempts to which fruits you should be hanging. I`ll have all the food hacks to help you leave no food behind. That`s next, right here on "TODAY." (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:10:00] MELVIN: We are back. 8:14 now with our new series, "Money-Saving Mondays". We`re going to start with your food budget. NGUYEN: Yes. [08:15:00] JONES: I like it. I can eat the props. Prices at the supermarket have increased more than 11 percent in just a year. So, of course, you want those groceries to last. Here with tips to make our food stay fresh longer, we have NBC`s Senior Consumer Investigative Correspondent Vicky Nguyen. Hey, Vicky. NGUYEN: Hello, good morning. JONES: All right. So, let`s take it here. NGUYEN: Yes. OK. JONES: You say the easy thing we can do right now, first of all, check your refrigerators. NGUYEN: Yes, exactly. JONES: What are we looking for? NGUYEN: First step, you want to check the fridge temp. JONES: OK. NGUYEN: So, the USDA -- JONES: Oh, the temperature. OK. NGUYEN: -- says 40 degrees is what they recommend but a lot of food experts say, keep it even lower, between 35 and 38 degrees. And how would you know? Well, if you don`t have one of those built in thermometers -- JONES: Yes. NGUYEN: -- you can get one. And what I would say is, check it every day and see it in different regions so you know, is the top of my fridge cooler, is the bottom. But 35 to 38, it will help inhibit the growth of bacteria like salmonella, E. Coli, listeria, and it will keep your food fresher. The other this is make sure your fridge is not too crowded and that it`s not too empty -- JONES: That`s a good advice. NGUYEN: -- because that will make it not as efficient. JONES: And then the freezer? NGUYEN: Freezer is zero degrees. JONES: Zero. NGUYEN: And one sign there is if you have too much frost buildup, that means your fridge or your freezer is too cold. JONES: Really? NGUYEN: Yes. And if you keep it too cold, you`re going to lose moisture and flavor. So, zero degrees is the recommendation. JONES: OK. All right. You have a few tricks to prevent some of the food we have in the fridge from spoiling. NGUYEN: Yes. JONES: Let`s start with greens. NGUYEN: Moisture is the enemy of your greens. MELVIN: Oh. NGUYEN: That`s what causes it to wilt. So, after you bring your greens home, you want to store them in an air tight container and just throw a paper towel in there. JONES: I do this. NGUYEN: This is -- JONES: It really works. NGUYEN: Yes, it keeps them fresh longer. JONES: And I will admit, like, even in the bag salad -- NGUYEN: Yes. JONES: -- you just stick a paper towel in there. NGUYEN: Stick it in there. Perfect. JONES: That`s good. NGUYEN: Very good. JONES: All right. What about mushrooms? NGUYEN: Mushrooms, OK. So, they sell them with plastic. JONES: Yes. NGUYEN: You want to rip that plastic off right away. You can either keep it in a cardboard box or if you want to keep it in a little paper bag. JONES: Really? NGUYEN: This will keep your mushrooms fresh longer. You can actually even keep them out of the fridge if you want, in just a cool, dry, dark place. JONES: Really? NGUYEN: Yes, but don`t keep the moisture in. That is what will cause your mushrooms to rot. JONES: Oh, so that`s -- and I`ve done that. NGUYEN: But they`re sold in plastic -- JONES: And then I`ll -- won`t get to use them. NGUYEN: -- so it`s confusing. Yes. JONES: They`re, like, mushy by the time I get to them. NGUYEN: Exactly. JONES: All right. Last but not least, let`s do butter. NGUYEN: Yes. OK. So, this is really interesting. NGUYEN: And other key is to wrap your cheese in wax paper before you put it into an air tight bag. Look, we`re using Ziplocs, but I like to use those resealable, reusable silicon bags. JONES: Yes, yes. NGUYEN: Those are fine too. The key is just keeping the air out of everything. JONES: Is that what butter does to the end of the -- NGUYEN: The butter will just keep the cheese fresher, longer on the cut end. JONES: Wow. OK. MELVIN: So, Vick, these are two items that you actually -- I`ve never thought about freezing nuts or herbs. But you maintain that`s the way to make them last longer. NGUYEN: Craig, you`re going to hear it here first. MELVIN: Yes. NGUYEN: Freeze your nuts. MELVIN: Freeze your nuts. NGUYEN: Never would think to do that, but yes, nuts have a very high oil content. They can go rancid within two to four weeks and they`re expensive. So, that`s the key when you think it, but freeze your nuts. This may be my last time on TV with you, Craig. The other thing is -- AL ROKER, NBC TODAY WEATHER ANCHOR: Yay, Vicky. NGUYEN: -- chop up your herbs, this is another thing, a lot of other people don`t think about it. Fresh herbs are so expensive. MELVIN: Yes. NGUYEN: So, you chop them up after you`ve washed them, pat them dry, chop them up, and pre-portion them, spread them on a cookie sheet, put them in the freezer, then you can dump them all into a bag. So, you`ve got here parsley, rosemary, sage. It works with all kinds of herbs. MELVIN: Frozen herbs, frozen nuts. NGUYEN: Yes. MELVIN: Let`s come over here to -- so, these are items that you maintain that you can actually keep keep on the counter -- NGUYEN: Yes. MELVIN: -- or somewhere room temperature. NGUYEN: Yes, absolutely. So, with tomatoes, I never knew this. But if you keep your tomatoes stem side down, that actually helps them ripen in the right way -- MELVIN: Oh. JONES: Oh. NGUYEN: -- and then the bottoms don`t get mushy from the weight of the tomatoes -- MELVIN: OK. NGUYEN: -- so they don`t go bad as long. And also keep them out room temperature, cool dark place. The only time you put tomatoes in the fridge is after you`ve cut them and you wrap them in plastic or put them in a container so that you prevent the growth of bacteria. MELVIN: OK. NGUYEN: OK. And then when it comes to fruit, so, check your fruit often. See, this, like, little old guy here. MELVIN: The pear doesn`t look good. NGUYEN: Yes. MELVIN: That`s a bad looking pear. NGUYEN: This will cause everything else to slowly go bad. MELVIN: Oh, I didn`t know that. SOBOROFF: Yes. NGUYEN: Check your fruit bowl, you know, fairly -- MELVIN: So, spoiled fruits can spread? NGUYEN: Absolutely. MELVIN: Didn`t know it. NGUYEN: Because it`s releasing all this gas and it will spread to everything else. I didn`t know this either. MELVIN: You`re blowing our minds, Vicky. NGUYEN: Yes. SOBOROFF: Speaking of onions, Vicky. NGUYEN: Yes. SOBOROFF: We appear to have onions in a pair of pantyhose. NGUYEN: Yes. OK. NGUYEN: I know, because pantyhose is not that cheap, actually. But if you -- SOBOROFF: I was going to say, yes, I don`t know about that. NGUYEN: -- if you want your onions to last months and months and months, people swear by this tech teak. So, you get a pair of pantyhose, and you separate them with a knot. SOBOROFF: With a knot, yes. NGUYEN: This helps to keeps them dry. SOBOROFF: OK. NGUYEN: It helps to keep the air circulating, and it helps to keep your onions around for a long time. So, I don`t know where you find the space to do it. But if -- let`s say you harvest your onions and you -- MELVIN: There is not a single person in America. NGUYEN: There you go. SOBOROFF: With all that space you have, by the way -- MELVIN: Not one person. SOBOROFF: -- to hang your onions with pantyhose, you should also be hanging other things, right -- NGUYEN: Listen, it works. SOBOROFF: -- like bananas? NGUYEN: It works. JONES: Maybe. SOBOROFF: Bananas. NGUYEN: OK. So, Jacob, Craig`s freezing his nuts, you`re going to hang your bananas. OK. SOBOROFF: OK. NGUYEN: Hanging your bananas, it keeps them from bruising. OK. SOBOROFF: Vicky, you are an angel. OK. So, what else do we have here? So, herbs. NGUYEN: The other thing you want to hang are your herbs. SOBOROFF: So, they don`t dry out. NGUYEN: Yes -- well, actually, they will dry out, but that`s OK. SOBOROFF: OK. Arid, fine. And finally, deli meats. NGUYEN: Yes. SOBOROFF: And we`ve got pieces of raw salmon here. What do we do with these? NGUYEN: Oh, my gosh. The key with meats is just to remember to keep them max three to five days in an airtight container, whether you get them fresh from the deli or you get them prepackaged. So, that is the key. SOBOROFF: Vicky Nguyen with the greatest segment of all time. JONES: I mean, really. MELVIN: You had a good run here at the Peacock, Vick. NGUYEN: Thank you. SOBOROFF: Thank you. (LOCAL NEWS) ROKER: All right. Best time of the morning. MELVIN: Yes, it is. ROKER: Let`s start the week of my friend. CARSON DALY, NBC NEWS HOST: I don`t know. headline: Clearing Up Some Common Nutrition Myths With The Registered Dietitian
story_text: SAVANNAH JONES: Welcome back this morning on Your Health. Common myths and maybe misguiding your diet decisions. Nora Minno is a registered dietician and she`s here to clear these things up once and for all. Nora, good morning to you. NORA MINNO, REGISTERED DIETICIAN: Good morning, Sheinelle. JONES: So we have five nutrition myths that we`re going to debunk. I should say there are three of us here because congratulations. MINNO: Yes, thank you. JONES: She was so worried as nutritionist people are going to be like, oh, she`s got little (inaudible). No, no, there`s a little baby in there. MINNO: Exactly. JONES: We are girl, we don`t know, OK. First things first, I should avoid all carbs. This is a big one. MINNO: Yes. JONES: I know so many people who just -- they feel like if they touch a carb, they explode. MINNO: I agree. And I have good news for all you carb lovers. I`m pretty sure as everybody body, right? Carbs are your friend. In fact, there are a really important part of a healthy balanced diet. They do a lot for us. They are our body`s preferred source of fuel, same with our brain. They help our digestion and they actually just make us feel good. JONES: So then, what are we doing wrong then? Because a lot of people, you know, I guess obviously probably shouldn`t have carbs before bed, but where are we going wrong? MINNO: Exactly. So really, when it comes to carbs, it is just about the quality of carbs that you`re picking and the quantity that you`re consuming. That`s really where a lot of people go wrong over consuming things like refined carbs, sweets, white breads, things like that. But if you focus on portions, choose more complex carbs. JONES: What`s a good carb? Give me a couple of example. MINNO: Fruits, vegetables, whole grains, oatmeal, things like that, you should be in the clear. JONES: All right. So myth number two, fresh produce is healthier than frozen or canned. What would you say? MINNO: No. This is not true at all. In fact, sometimes your frozen or canned options can be actually more nutritious. There was a study done that found that vegetables can lose 15% to 55% of their vitamin C by the time they`re picked, by the time they make it to your grocery shelf. So frozen, they typically flash freeze right on the spot. So you`re packing a lot more nutrients. And they`re actually a little bit better for your wallet too. JONES: I was just about to say there`s a cost benefit as well. MINNO: Exactly. Less food waste, oftentimes they are more budget friendly. And then you just have some good things on hand if you want to make a smoothie, a salad, things like that. JONES: Absolutely. OK, our next myth, this is a good one. Plant milk is healthier than dairy milk. What say ye? MINNO: All right. Well, this is not always the case. This one really comes down just to preference because you know, now it just seems like there`s a million different plant milks out there. There are options galore, which is great, but cow`s milk is still a really great option. One cup of skim milk packs in 10 grams of protein and a quarter of your daily calcium needs. Whereas plant milk like an almond milk has one gram of protein per serving. JONES: You know what it is, I guess also just depends on, you know, whether you`re lactose intolerant, you know, if you have a dietary issue. MINNO: Exactly. So this one -- one is not better than the other, it`s just going to come down to choice. And if you are picking a plant milk, you want to pick varieties that have low or no added sugar, and ones that are more fortified with things like calcium, vitamin D that you might not be getting if you`re picking that -- JONES: I will admit that the plant milks, I didn`t realize some of them do have a lot of sugar. MINNO: Some do. JONES: I just didn`t realize that. MINNO: Some do. So be a savvy reader. JONES: All right. Let`s talk about fat there. Remember for a while everything was low fat this, low fat that. MINNO: Yes. MINNO: So the nutrition or the myth number four all fat is bad. Obviously it`s not. [08:45:05] MINNO: It`s not. And thank goodness that low fat craze in the `90s and thereafter is over because we know now that fats, most importantly, mono and polyunsaturated fats are really good for us. It is still American Heart Month, and we want to get those fats in from things like avocados, nuts, seeds, olive oils, and even our fatty fish to help protect our heart boost that HDL, which is our good cholesterol, and lower LDL, which is our bad cholesterol. JONES: Sounds good. And I think sometimes when you`re eating, you just don`t know which one is right. MINNO: Exactly. So we do want to avoid certain fats, there are facts called saturated fats, that the American Heart Association says we should stay at or below 13 grams a day -- JONES: Oh wait, that`s good advice. MINNO: -- for a hearth healthy diet. JONES: All right. Si when you get a package is something flipped over the back. MINNO: Yes. JONES: And if you see saturated fats, how many grams did you say it should be layered? MINNO: 13, approximately around 13 per day. JONES: Per day. MINNO: So if you have four ounces of kind of lean ground beef, you`re already at that 13 mark. So you want to be a real savvy label reader. JONES: OK, all right. Myth number five soy, I`m actually interested in what you`re going to say. Soy increases risk for breast cancer. MINNO: Yes. You know, I hear this one all the time. JONES: Me too. MINNO: And it`s still very common and abundant. So this myth really stems from the fact that soy contains something called phytoestrogens. And we know that estrogen can sometimes be linked to an increase in breast cancer. JONES: Right. MINNO: But the estrogens in soy are very different than mammalian estrogens, ones that we have in our body, and they act differently. And in fact, they can be protective against things like breast cancer, because what we`ve seen in Asian countries where they consume more soy, is that breast cancer risk is actually much lower. JONES: Does it depend on the product or what kind of soy you`re consuming? No? MINNO: Not really. And again, the American Heart Association said 25 grams of soy protein per day can actually be heart protective. So you can get your tofu, your (inaudible), your soy milk, your edamame at a sushi restaurant, right? Lots of really great options to pack some good soy protein. JONES: There you go. So you don`t have to avoid it. Nora, thank you. MINNO: That`s OK. Thank you, Sheinelle. JONES: All right. headline: The Today Show for February 20, 2023, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:00:00] SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS 3RD HOUR OF TODAY, CO-HOST: It is 8:00 on "TODAY." Coming up, surprise visit. Overnight, President Biden making history arriving in Ukraine. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , U.S. PRESIDENT: I`m here to show our unwavering support for the nation`s independence, and sovereignty, and territorial integrity. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: A major sign of support from the U.S. as the war in Ukraine approaches its one-year anniversary. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BIDEN: That`s how long we`re going to be with you, Mr. President, for as long as it takes. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: We`re live with the latest. Then, holiday sales. Hoping to save some money this long weekend. We have a look at all the best Presidents` Day deals, everything from furniture to appliances, electronics, and cars. Plus, the three questions you should ask yourself before making a purchase. And royal treatment. The Prince and Princess of Wales joining stars from around the world for the so-called British Oscars. We`re highlighting all the best moments including an emotional tribute to Queen Elizabeth. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) HELEN MIRREN, ACTRESS: Cinema at its best does what her majesty did effortlessly, bring us together and unite us in a story. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: So, what films took home the night`s biggest awards? All that and more. Today, Monday, February 20, 2023. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Spending Presidents` Day. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: On the plaza. CROWD: From Fort Worth, Texas. CROWD: Murrysville (ph), Pennsylvania. CROWD: Huntsville, Alabama. CROWD: St. John, Indiana. CROWD: And New Lenox, Illinois. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Celebrating milestone birthdays. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: My 30th. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: And my 60th. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: From Jacksonville, Florida. CROWD: Lea`s (ph) turning 18. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Shout out to our NBC family. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: At KOMU 8 News. CROWD: In Columbia, Missouri. CROWD: Happy Presidents` Day. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: Welcome back to "TODAY." We certainly appreciate you being with us on this Monday morning. And take a look at all of these folks. We are happy to see this happy holiday crowd. This is on -- in our corner of the woods here at Rockefeller Plaza. TOM LLAMAS, NBC NEWS SENIOR NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Yes, they came from all over the country. We always love that. JONES: Uh-huh. LLAMAS: A lot of states represented. Savannah and Hoda, you know them, will be back tomorrow, of course, and it will be a big morning here in Studio 1A. JONES: That is right. Grammy winning superstar Pink will be here. She`s coming out with a new album and heading on tour. So, a lot to talk about. Plus, she`ll treat us to a live performance when she joins us for our 8:00, 9:00, and 10:00 hours. So, join us tomorrow. JACOB SOBOROFF, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: I am not going anywhere. LLAMAS: Yes. JONES: Right SOBOROFF: I`m going to stick around for that. JONES: It`s going to be a party. LLAMAS: She always brings it. Like, live -- JONES: She does. LLAMAS: -- Pink live is always amazing. JONES: She does. And we`ll get back outside and say hi to all those folks coming up in just a bit. Meantime, it is a busy morning. So, let`s get to your news at 8:00. In an unprecedented show of support for Ukraine, President Biden took a high stakes trip to the war zone overnight. His surprise journey to Kyiv coming just days before the first anniversary of the Russian invasion. NBC`s Erin McLaughlin is in the Ukrainian capital with more on this historic visit. Erin, good morning. ERIN MCLAUGHLIN, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Good morning, Sheinelle. President Zelenskyy calling the visit historic, timely, and brave. The visit began here in the capital at the presidential palace. President Biden was greeted by President Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena. He signed a guest book and announced a $500 million military aid package and delivered this message. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JOE BIDEN , U.S. PRESIDENT: One year later, Kyiv stands and Ukraine stands, democracy stands. America stands with you and the world stands with you. (END VIDEO CLIP) MCLAUGHLIN: From the palace, they made their way to St. Michael`s Cathedral. I watched as air raid sirens echoing in the distance. The two presidents walked out this way and paid tribute to the thousands of fallen Ukrainian soldiers in the memorial behind me. From there, President Biden made his way to the U.S. embassy where he met with staff before departing the capital. In Russia, this visit is being seen as a provocation. But here in Ukraine, it is being seen as a remarkable show of support and solidarity by America. Back to you. JONES: All right. Erin, thank you. LLAMAS: And as we just saw there, the president`s secret trip showing his unwavering support for Ukraine, even as some in NATO and in Congress are questioning the ongoing commitment. NBC`s Chief White House Correspondent and Weekend TODAY co-anchor Kristen Welker joins us now live from Poland where the president will be marking this week`s first anniversary of the war. Kristen, good morning. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT AND "SATURDAY TODAY" ANCHOR: Hi, Tom. Good morning to you. That`s right. [08:05:00] This trip was so secret because of the dangers that it posed, that only a handful of the president`s inner staff was aware that he was actually traveling to Kyiv. And that keen message just adding to what Erin said, the president saying, we`re not leaving. But executing on that is going to be more challenging to keep the global community on board and Congress, with some Republicans, already saying they are not going to write a blank check to Ukraine. So, what happens now? Well, he travels here to Poland. He`s going to be meeting with the president of Poland. He will be meeting with leaders of the critical eastern flank and then he`s going to deliver his capstone address in the same location where he spoke in Warsaw when he visited when the war was just a month old. And I am told in talking to top officials, that part of his message is going to be a condemnation of Vladimir Putin building on what we heard from the vice president over the weekend, that Putin has committed crimes against humanity and should be held accountable. Now, this all comes amid new concerns about China, it`s believed that China is providing nonlethal aid to Russia. The secretary of state, over the weekend, saying that they believe China is considering providing lethal aid as well. The secretary of state warning that would be met with serious consequences, all as this war enters a pivotal new phase. Tom. LLAMAS: All right. Kristen Welker with a lot of new developments there. Kristen, thank you. SOBOROFF: Breaking overnight, North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles towards Japan today, it`s second weapons test in the last three days. The missiles landing in the waters off the west coast of Japan. The test prompting Tokyo to call for an emergency meeting of the United Nations Security Council . Over the weekend North Korea also launched an intercontinental ballistic missile, and in response, the U.S. military yesterday held bilateral air drills with South Korea and Japan. JONES: All right. We`ve covered the news. Now, are you ready for a "Morning Boost"? LLAMAS: Yes. SOBOROFF: Yes, please. JONES: All right. This is a good one. A young Australian basketball fan was in tears after watching his team, the Tasmanian Jackjumpers get knocked out of the playoffs during a game in New Zealand. While on his way back to the locker room the Australian captain noticed the heartbroken fan and knew that he had traveled a long way to come see the game. So, he walked over to comfort him and even gave him a pair of sneakers. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: How is that, mate? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Amazing. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Wow. CLINT STEINDL, TASMANIA JACKJUMPERS BASKETBALL TEAM CAPTAIN: As much as I try to put a smile on his face, he still had the tears. But maybe puts them up in his bedroom or something, gives him something to aspire to. And that`s what we`re trying to do in Tasian (ph), you know, I just try to help the little fella out. (END VIDEO CLIP) JONES: Oh, that`s sweet. A little classy move. Keeping in mind that the player has got to be hurting too from that season ending loss. Listen, there are fans young and old, and it hurts when you lose, you know. LLAMAS: Yes, that`s -- SOBOROFF: Shout out to the Jackjumpers. JONES: There you go. LLAMAS: Tasmanian Jackjumpers. I like those jerseys too. SOBOROFF: Nice. JONES: Learn something everything. LLAMAS: Those are pretty cool. All right. Coming up, the Prince and Princess of Wales rubbing elbows with the stars of Hollywood. We`re going to take you live to London for an inside look at the big night at the British version of the Oscars. JONES: But first, expert tips you need to hear to make the most of today`s holiday sales. We`ll get to that in a moment right after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:10:00] JONES: Welcome back this morning on "TODAY`s Consumer". We are focusing on those Presidents` Day sales. LLAMAS: Yes, inflation is putting a strain on your budget, it could be a great day to find a few deals, but, of course, there are things you need to consider. JONES: Joining us now is CNBC`s Senior Personal Finance Correspondent Sharon Epperson. Sharon, good morning to you. SHARON EPPERSON, CNBC`S SENIOR PERSONAL FINANCE CORRESPONDENT: Good morning. JONES: All right. Before we get into it, you say, before we get to the deals, you have three questions you want people to ask themselves. EPPERSON: Very important questions to ask. JONES: OK. EPPERSON: First of all, do you need it? JONES: Fair. EPPERSON: Do you love it? And can you pay it off immediately? JONES: Fair enough. EPPERSON: And so, it`s not just can you afford it. Because you`re probably going to put it on a credit card. JONES: Yes. EPPERSON: You don`t want to carry that interest on the credit card. You want to pay that off immediately or that savings is really something you`re going to be paying for, for months and months in interest. JONES: So, can you pay it within the month before you get that bill? EPPERSON: Exactly. JONES: All right. Fair enough. LLAMAS: I feel that`s a good life lesson -- JONES: It is. LLAMAS: -- not just for Presidents` Day. JONES: It is. I know. That is good. LLAMAS: Speaking of Presidents` Day, talk about some of the deals. EPPERSON: Well, there are a lot of different deals. A lot of people look at mattresses for Presidents` Day, furniture, maybe electronics. You may think about home appliances, large ones or little gadgets for your kitchen. LLAMAS: Uh-huh. EPPERSON: Maybe even a new car. So, there are a lot of different deals out there. I think I seem to be getting messages all the time about this deal or that deal for Presidents` Day doesn`t necessarily mean it`s something that I need. JONES: Right, right. EPPERSON: So, I kind of delete that message. LLAMAS: OK. All right. JONES: So, you were saying -- what about like kitchen or -- the kitchen appliances, are we talking like coffee pots or like refrigerators, like big ticket items? EPPERSON: There are some big ticket items too that are -- that you can get. One of the things to keep in mind when you`re talking about appliances, whether they`re large or small, as you`re often sold a or asked to purchase a warranty, an extended warranty -- JONES: OK. EPPERSON: -- or sometime service agreement. JONES: OK. EPPERSON: Important thing to check out there is to make sure that you actually really need that because it`s not going to be lasting that long. And that you could use that money, perhaps, to put into a savings account to buy a new one. What`s the replacement cost of that? JONES: That`s right. EPPERSON: Do you need to buy the extended warranty or the service agreement. JONES: The service agreement. LLAMAS: All right. Let`s dig a little deeper here. I know a family shopping around for a TV. Is it -- are electronics good right now? Is it a day to shop for electronics? EPPERSON: Well, there are large electronics. And this morning a young married couple making waves in the restaurant industry here in New York. JONES: Kevol and Ria Graham have a remarkable story when it comes to their Caribbean-inspired restaurant. They opened Kokomo in July of 2020, four months into the COVID locked down, and right before their second child. Can you imagine? [08:50:06] Now, it is one of the hottest restaurants in Brooklyn and I paid a visit to find out their recipe for success. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JONES (voice-over): Kevol and Ria Graham are living a life they never could have imagined. KEVOL GRAHAM, KOKOMO OWNER: I love hospitality. I never thought that I would have my own restaurant. But as we look back, we kind of see that every step that we took was actually leading us to this moment. JONES (voice-over): Today, they are the parents of three young children and will celebrate five years of marriage. But it`s their journey to this point running Kokomo, a popular pan-Caribbean restaurant with Indian and Asian flavors that combines their passion for food and hospitality. (on camera): Clearly, you both had some kind of restaurant background -- K. GRAHAM: (Inaudible) on nightlife and then became our roving chefs. The guys that I grew up with. RIA GRAHAM, KOKOMO OWNER: At the time, I was a marketing manager for a Caribbean restaurant as well. JONES (voice-over): They were soon married and hesitantly decided their next move together would be a restaurant. So they took the social media documenting everything about acquiring and opening a restaurant. As they were just about to open, the pandemic hit. Against all odds, they officially opened in the summer of 2020. (on camera): How challenging was it? R. GRAHAM: I would say it was like mental warfare, because you really did not know what to expect. But I think because we were so open about our feelings to our social media, people wanted to genuinely support. K. GRAHAM: Something that`s very inspirational, because Ria was a part of every step during pregnancy that motivated me to even work harder. JONES (voice-over): The couple describes the menu as elevated Caribbean fare, served up in an atmosphere that feels like the Caribbean. R. GRAHAM: I would say if you`re looking for a vibe, come here. K. GRAHAM: To represent all different parts of the Caribbean. We definitely appeal to all ethnicities, you know, whether it`s Afro Caribbean, Latin Caribbean, you know, Asian Caribbean. JONES: Did you get inspiration for different recipes? I mean, how did you do it? K. GRAHAM: We were very passionate about like bringing out things that we grew up on, you know, tapping into our Caribbean heritage. JONES: Do you feel like you are blazing a trail? R. GRAHAM: Real trailblazers for us are the grandmas, man, because there`s nothing like a Caribbean grandma in that kitchen showing her stuff. And now we`re just trying to modernize it and just make it into something fresh and new. JONES (voice-over): Some of their hottest Caribbean dishes are on flatbread. K. GRAHAM: (Inaudible) flatbread or any given day, because it`s a -- it`s something that we reinvented because I think everybody comes in and like they can get that anywhere. It serve with shrimp, foxtail, chicken. R. GRAHAM: Once we saw that brick oven, we knew we had to do O to Brooklyn by having a brick oven pizza crust, and then we`d have on top of it a tomato (inaudible) sauteed shrimp with ackee, which is the national food of Jamaica. JONES (voice-over): I had to give the food a try. K. GRAHAM: So this is our Rasta balls. JONES: OK. K. GRAHAM: Crockett fry Italian Alfredo sauce that we infuse with some jerk seasoning. Aioli only on top. JONES: Can I try it? K. GRAHAM: Of course. The flavors bursting in your mouth. JONES: Oh my gosh. This alone would have me coming back. (voice-over): As they embrace this family run business, they reflect on this moment in time. R. GRAHAM: Everything that you need to succeed is within you. K. GRAHAM: We come from very humble beginnings. Our parents struggled, I know how hard, excuse me. I know how hard they worked to leave a path for myself. In heart, we as parents worked for us to be where we are. I take nothing for granted. And you can achieve anything you want if only you believe in yourself. (END VIDEOTAPE) JONES: They are two of my new favorite people. So I`ll be texting you guys and you`ll be sick of me. (INAUDIBLE) K. GRAHAM: Can I come? JONES: Sunday (inaudible) things. So Kev and Ria say their parents also helped them run the restaurant. In the spring, they`re opening up another restaurant nearby. They`re calling it Ox Kale (ph) specializing in innovative Caribbean cuisine that`s healthy. Isn`t that -- I`m telling you, I told them, I`m like if you can make it healthy and yummy -- DREYER: Is that (inaudible) speaks for the rest of the menu? JONES (voice-over): Yes. DREYER: This is -- JONES: So, they also make their own in house coconut rum. LLAMAS: Wow, OK. JONES (voice-over): Merry Christmas. LLAMAS: Cheers. (Inaudible) JONES: So there you go. Cheers. What did you just say? SOBOROFF: Chill. I will talk about during the break. JONES (voice-over): OK. Coming up on Hoda and Jenna, actress Rosario Dawson plus a manicures to the stars which will be sharing three hot new nail trends. DREYER: But first in our 3rd Hour, a couple doing the impossible making bagels even better. JONES: Yum. LLAMAS: See, I told you. DREYER: The most delicious food you`ve ever had.
