story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. It`s Thursday. Big developments overnight in two key races that kind of decides who`s in charge in Washington. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: With just 12 days to go until the midterms, we`re going to break it all down for you. It is October 27th. This is Today. New accusations, another woman comes forward claiming Herschel Walker urged her to have an abortion. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I do not believe that Herschel is morally fit to be a U.S. senator. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: While in Pennsylvania, John Fetterman addresses his debate performance. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LT. GOV. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA), SENATOR CANDIDATE: During that debate wasn`t exactly easy. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: We got it all covered. Crisis mode, hospitals nationwide being forced to take drastic measures to handle the tripledemic surge of flu, COVID, and RSV. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Not only are there a lot of sick kids right now, there`s no place for them to go. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Just ahead, the new message from health officials all families need to hear. Breaking overnight, a new wave of protests in Iran, despite authorities intensifying a brutal crackdown, this morning the powerful scenes playing out across the country. Under pressure, Tesla reportedly facing a criminal investigation over its autopilot claims after a string of high profile crashes. So has the popular automaker misled consumers about how safe their cars really are? Those stories, plus, members only. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Contrary to popular belief, you can be any age to join AARP. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: From AARP to AAA, the surprising clubs you can sign up for to save big. And feeling lucky. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Here are tonight`s winning numbers. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: With no winner overnight, the Powerball jackpot jumps to a whopping $800 million, one of the largest prizes ever now up for grabs. Today, Thursday, October 27th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Well, good morning. It is so good to see you, happy that you`re here joining us. It is a Thursday morning. GUTHRIE: Well, you got it lined up if you want to get those Powerball tickets. The drawing is this weekend so you have time to get your tickets but jackpots up to 800 million. KOTB: It is. We`re going to have a lot more on jackpot fever coming up. But we`re going to start with another big countdown. We`re talking about the one to the midterm. GUTHRIE: Yes, 12 days to go now, and the spotlight is intensifying on two major races in Georgia and Pennsylvania. What happens there could impact the lives of every American. KOTB: Here`s what`s at stake, the balance of power in the Senate and the direction of key issues from the economy to abortion rights to rising crime rates, NBC`s senior Washington correspondent Hallie Jackson has the very latest for us. Hey, Hallie, good morning. HALLIE JACKSON, NBC NEWS SENIOR WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT: Hey Hoda, hey Savannah. You have laid out the stakes and it is crunch time now, right, for candidates in these really important really close races with big guns like former presidents in both parties set to hit the campaign trail in the coming days. And the focus today turning to Georgia, where there`s a new abortion allegations surfacing, and one of the country`s most closely watched matchups. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JACKSON (voice-over): With less than two weeks to go this morning, the future of the Senate could hang on to key states with neck and neck races in Pennsylvania and Georgia, where there`s now another twist, Republican Herschel Walker who`s campaigned on an anti-abortion platform now denying a new allegation from a second woman who says Walker pressured her to have an abortion in the early 90s. HERSCHEL WALKER (R-GA), SENATOR CANDIDATE: What I`m saying, this is a lie and I`ve said it once and I`ve moved on my campaign. JACKSON (voice-over): The anonymous woman sharing her voice only came forward in a Zoom press conference arranged by Attorney Gloria Allred. The accuser saying after she became pregnant in 1993, Walker encouraged her to have an abortion, adding she first couldn`t go through with the procedure, but that Walker encouraged her to go back driving her to a Dallas clinic where she had the abortion. The woman explaining why she`s speaking up now. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I am a registered Independent and I voted for Donald Trump in both elections. I do not believe that Herschel is morally fit to be a U.S. senator. JACKSON (voice-over): NBC News has not verified her allegations and the woman did not provide evidence Walker was involved in her abortion. WALKER: I`m done with this foolishness. JACKSON (voice-over): The Republican candidate and former football star also denied allegations earlier this month from another former girlfriend who says Walker paid for her abortion in 2009. In a statement the campaign for Walker`s opponent, Senator Raphael Warnock says Walker has a problem with the truth, a problem answering questions, and a problem taking responsibility for his actions. That match up, very close with recent polling showing Warnock leading by just five points. And in another closely watched race in Pennsylvania a tossup with polls ranking Democratic Lieutenant Governor John Fetterman and Republican candidate Dr. Mehmet Oz within the margin of error. [07:05:11] FETTERMAN: During that debate wasn`t exactly easy, you know, I knew it wasn`t going to be easy after, you know, having a stroke after five months. JACKSON (voice-over): Fetterman appearing at a campaign rally in Pittsburgh after raising $2 million, his team says, in the hours after his one and only debate against Republican Mehmet Oz. Fetterman facing questions about his at times halting debate performance with lingering auditory processing issues after a stroke five months ago. Oz also on the campaign trail hammering the issue of crime and on defense against a new Democratic ad highlighting his debate comments on abortion. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This is who Dr. Oz wants in charge of women`s health care decisions. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATOR CANDIDATE: I want women, doctors, local political leaders, local political leaders. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTHRIE: Meanwhile, Hallie, the President hitting the campaign trail today, what do you expect? JACKSON: He is all about the economy, Savannah, in this kind of closing argument here trying to highlight his administration`s record on something we know that voters care about the economy plus cost of living. The top issue that voters say matters to them come Election Day. The President is going to be at Upstate New York to argue that Democrats economic policies are better than Republicans, even as many GOP candidates have pointed to high inflation in their midterm campaigns. You`ve also got the president`s cabinet fanning out across the country too. All of it is part of this full core press ahead of Election Day. Savannah? GUTHRIE: Twelve days to go. Hallie Jackson, thank you. And we turn now to growing concerns over the dangerous tripledemic of viruses nationwide flu, COVID, and the respiratory illness, RSV. With cases surging, some hospitals even in areas of warmer weather, are running out of beds. NBC national correspondent Gabe Gutierrez is inside Phoenix Children`s Hospital this morning with more. Gabe, good morning. GABE GUTIERREZ, NBC NEWS NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Savannah, good morning. It`s only October but doctors here and across the country are dealing with patient numbers that they usually don`t see until much later in winter. And overnight we met one mother who barely heard of RSV until she ended up here with her newborn son. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ (voice-over): This morning, the latest wave of child respiratory illnesses is spreading prompting more concerns of a tripledemic this winter. In Arizona, RSV cases are up 344 percent over a typical season. CHEYENNE SHIELDER`S (ph), SON DIAGNOSED WITH RSV: Terrifying, this is serious illness. You know, with him being this young. He doesn`t have an immune system to fight it off. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): Cheyenne Shielder`s (ph) two-month-old son Ryder (ph) was in the hospital overnight. (on camera): What would you tell other parents? SHIELDER: Look up the symptoms of RSV and trust her gut to because I was on the border about coming or not to the hospital. And I feel like I probably should have come a little bit sooner. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): Last year and now this year, Phoenix Children`s Hospital has been dealing with an unusually high number of RSV cases, though the facility is not at capacity, it`s bracing for a rough winter DR. WASSIM BALLAN, PHOENIX CHILDREN`S HOSPITAL CHIEF OF INFECTIOUS DISEASES: COVID-19 combined with a potentially bad influenza season and now we`re seeing RSV going up at the same time, that obviously makes us concerned that we might get into this triple pandemic situation. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): This year, even western and southern states with warmer temperatures are seeing a significant rise in RSV and flu cases. In Arizona, 87 percent of pediatric hospital beds are occupied, in Texas 91 percent, Seattle Children`s tells NBC News it`s at 200 percent capacity in the ER. DR. ASHISH JHA, WHITE HOUSE COVID-19 RESPONSE COORDINATOR: Under normal circumstances, about 90 percent of kids end up getting RSV at least once, by the time there are two. Because of the pandemic, some of the kind of standard patterns have been disrupted so we`re seeing a lot of RSV at once. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): Parents now worried sick across the country from San Diego where Fernanda Costanarez (ph) is caring for baby Alejandra (ph). FERNANDA COSTANAREZ (ph), DAUGHTER DIAGNOSED WITH RSV: She was struggling to breathe. She was struggling breathing. And we got scared because she had no color at all on her skin. GUTIERREZ (voice-over): To Washington, D.C. where three-year-old Izzy Banki (ph) is recovering. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Nobody wants to like hold their kid down and hold a mask on their face. And so she`s screaming and trying and trying to rip the breathing tubes out. And that breaks your heart as a parent. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTIERREZ: And while COVID cases are trending downward nationwide, right now, there are concerns about new strains this winter. And of course, Savannah, concerns about that flu season that is already hitting many states hard around the country. Savannah? GUTHRIE: All right, Gabe Gutierrez, thank you. KOTB: Meantime, new unrest is rocking Iran with massive protests across the country more than a month after a young woman`s death while being held by the nation`s morality police. Some of those demonstrations turned deadly, emitted ongoing crackdown and that`s led to new sanctions from the United States, NBC`s chief international correspondent Keir Simmons has been following this story for us. Hey Keir, good morning. [07:10:00] KEIR SIMMONS, NBC NEWS CHIEF INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Hoda, good morning to you. story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. It`s Thursday. Big developments overnight in two key races that kind of decides who`s in charge in Washington. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: With just 12 days to go until the midterms, we`re going to break it all down for you. It is October 27th. This is Today. New accusations, another woman comes forward claiming Herschel Walker urged her to have an abortion. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I do not believe that Herschel is morally fit to be a U.S. senator. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Just ahead, the new message from health officials all families need to hear. Breaking overnight, a new wave of protests in Iran, despite authorities intensifying a brutal crackdown, this morning the powerful scenes playing out across the country. Under pressure, Tesla reportedly facing a criminal investigation over its autopilot claims after a string of high profile crashes. So has the popular automaker misled consumers about how safe their cars really are? Those stories, plus, members only. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Contrary to popular belief, you can be any age to join AARP. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: From AARP to AAA, the surprising clubs you can sign up for to save big. It is so good to see you, happy that you`re here joining us. It is a Thursday morning. GUTHRIE: Well, you got it lined up if you want to get those Powerball tickets. The drawing is this weekend so you have time to get your tickets but jackpots up to 800 million. KOTB: It is. We`re going to have a lot more on jackpot fever coming up. But we`re going to start with another big countdown. We`re talking about the one to the midterm. GUTHRIE: Yes, 12 days to go now, and the spotlight is intensifying on two major races in Georgia and Pennsylvania. What happens there could impact the lives of every American. KOTB: Here`s what`s at stake, the balance of power in the Senate and the direction of key issues from the economy to abortion rights to rising crime rates, NBC`s senior Washington correspondent Hallie Jackson has the very latest for us. Hey, Hallie, good morning. HALLIE JACKSON, NBC NEWS SENIOR WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT: Hey Hoda, hey Savannah. story_text: [07:00:17] HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. It`s Wednesday, all eyes were on Pennsylvania overnight. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes. The first and only Senate debate there with control of Congress hanging in the balance. It is October 26th, this is Today. MEHMET OZ (R), PENNSYLVANIA SENATE CANDIDATE: John Fetterman picks everything to an extreme and those extreme positions hurt us all. GUTHRIE: And ongoing concerns over Fetterman`s fitness to serve. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke, he`s never let me forget that. GUTHRIE: This morning the candidates in their own words and the takeaways in one of the nation`s most important midterm contests. Inside the Rampage, new details on the gunman behind that deadly school shooting in St. Louis, with a letter found in his car is revealing about a possible motive, and the stories of bravery now emerging. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I really credit my students a lot because even with the gunshots that close, they did not scream. GUTHRIE: That harrowing firsthand account just ahead. Cooling Off, housing prices falling fast after soaring to record highs. So is now the best time to buy, and what does it mean if you`re in the market to sell. We`ll break it down. The organization`s president now suspended and an investigation underway. The very latest straight ahead. And breaking news, what scientists are now saying about whether you really need to rake those leaves and it could make your weekend a lot more enjoyable. Today, Wednesday, October 26, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is TODAY with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. GUTHRIE: Good morning, everybody. Welcome back to TODAY. It is Wednesday morning, nice to have you along with us. This raking story, you want to get back those hours of your childhood raking leaves, don`t you? KOTB: Can you imagine -- you go remember all the time your parents said you got to go out and rake the leaves and stuff them into hefty bags. Who knew that we didn`t have to do that? GUTHRIE: Science is saying something different this morning. We`ll get to that. KOTB: Yes. We got a busy morning a lot to get to including we`ve got some rare good news. It`s tied to the economy at least if you`re planning to buy a house. GUTHRIE: Yes. Prices are now going down at a record rate. Tom Costello is going to have everything we need to know. KOTB: Of course, we will begin with last night`s big debate in Pennsylvania. GUTHRIE: This was highly anticipated not only because of questions concerning Democrat John Fetterman`s health after his stroke six months ago, but also because this race could decide which party controls the Senate. And that will affect every single American come next year. We`ll show you how it all played out. Let`s start this morning with NBC`s Dasha Burns in Harrisburg. Dasha, good morning. DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Savannah, good morning. This debate was highly anticipated not just by voters here in Pennsylvania but people across the country. It`s an extremely tight race, just a couple of points separating these candidates in the polls. And in a battle against one of the most familiar faces on American television, many tuned in to see how Fetterman would fare after suffering a stroke earlier this year, and the stakes could not have been higher. FETTERMAN: I`m running to serve Pennsylvania. He`s running to use Pennsylvania. OZ: John Fetterman picks everything to an extreme and those extreme positions hurt us all. Let`s discuss it and let`s predicate this by saying I don`t rake my leaves anymore. I have when you landscaping engineers to do that. MELVIN: There you go. GUTHRIE: I like that. KOTB: Carson, did you rake when you were a kid? DALY: Yes. KOTB: Did your parents make you? DALY: Yes. MELVIN: Of course. KOTB: Did your parents make you? ROKER: Absolutely. And in fact, I did -- when I was in high school, I did a whole thing. A whole research project to convince my father that we did not have to rake leaves. And that we just take the leaf catcher, that lawnmower, and mulch it (inaudible). And I`ve talked to the Queens` cooperative extension guy. He said it`s fine. I was -- oh -- GUTHRIE: You were ahead of your time. Did you rake leaves? KOTB: We raked, that was a definite chore. GUTHRIE: I grew up in the desert, we didn`t have leaves. (CROSSTALK) DALY: Yes. But would you leave -- they`re saying you should leave all the leaves on the lawn, it`s good for it. They break down, it`s natural -- GUTHRIE: Is this a great show for people because, first, kids find out that the video games are good for them. Now they don`t have to rake leaves anymore. MELVIN: Keep watching kids. GUTHRIE: It`s like no school, candy for breakfast, what`s next? MELVIN: Did you`re dad but it? ROKER: Yes, yes, he did. Because he wasn`t doing it, you know -- GUTHRIE: OK. ROKER: -- for a while DALY: But I love it after the leaves have been raked, and then just a few kind of scattered on the green lawn, how beautiful that looks. KOTB: Yes, it`s cool. DALY: I`m more likely to compost. MELVIN: You`re welcome kids. You`re welcome. DALY: How long can you hold your breath for? headline: The Today Show for October 26, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:00:00] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS TODAY, CO-ANCHOR: It`s 8:00 on "TODAY." Coming up, center stage. Inside the Pennsylvania Senate race, Democrat John Fetterman facing off against Republican Mehmet Oz sparring over the issues. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LT. GOV. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA): I`m running to serve Pennsylvania. He is running to use Pennsylvania. DR. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATE NOMINEE: John Fetterman takes everything to an extreme. And those extreme positions hurt us all. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: And John Fetterman`s health. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) FETTERMAN: I had a stroke but it knocked me down. And I`m going to keep coming back up. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: Why this race could help decide the balance of power in Congress. Then tripling down. New warnings about that oncoming tripledemic, COVID, flu and RSV. What experts are saying this morning about keeping you and your loved ones safe. Plus, all in the family. Jenna sits down with the Queen Consort Camilla`s nephew Luke Parker Bowles. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) LUKE PARKER BOWLES, QUEEN CONSORT CAMILLA`S NEPHEW: I have this name. And if I use it for something that helps people, then all the better. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: What brought him to the United States and what he hopes to accomplish here. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JENNA BUSH HAGER, HODA & JENNA HOST: If somebody had told you when you were 18, you are going to be in New Jersey when you get older, what would you say? PARKER BOWLES: I`d say what`s New Jersey? (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: Today, Wednesday, October 26, 2022. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From Vernon, Texas. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Celebrating our golden anniversary. CROWD: Friends for 35 years. CROWD: Visiting from Irvine, California. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Girls trip. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: From Philadelphia. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: To the "TODAY" show. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Shout out to my daughter. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: In Merrimac, Virginia. CROWD: From Lake Charles, Louisiana. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Because today. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I`m turning 70. (END VIDEO CLIP) CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Aw. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS TODAY, CO-ANCHOR: Aw. GUTHRIE: Aw. Hello. Good morning. Welcome back to "TODAY." What a great crowd out there. A beautiful fall morning. Relax. You don`t have to rake your leaves today. KOTB: Yes. Exactly. GUTHRIE: That`s what we`ve learned this morning. MELVIN: So, far. Yes. KOTB: Happy birthday, Lake Charles. Cool. GUTHRIE: Let`s get to the news, 8:00 on a Wednesday morning. With control of the U.S. Senate at stake, all eyes on that Pennsylvania rates last night. And the only debate, hitting Democrat John Fetterman against Republican Dr. Mehmet Oz. And it comes amid questions concerning Fetterman`s health after his stroke six months ago. NBC`s Dasha Burns joins us with some of the key moments last night. Hi, Dasha. Good morning. DASHA BURNS, NBC NEWS REPORTER: Hey, Savannah. Good morning. This debate was highly anticipated, not just by voters here in Pennsylvania, but across the country. This is an extremely tight race. Just a couple of points separating these candidates. And in the battle against one of the most familiar faces on American television, many tuned in to see how Fetterman would fair after suffering a stroke earlier this year and the stakes could not have been higher. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BURNS (voiceover): In a race that could help decide the balance of power in Congress, Pennsylvania Democrat John Fetterman and Republican Mehmet Oz neck-and-neck in the polls finally face to face on the debate stage. LT. GOV. JOHN FETTERMAN (D-PA): I`m running to serve Pennsylvania. He is running to use Pennsylvania. DR. MEHMET OZ (R-PA), SENATE NOMINEE: John Fetterman takes everything to an extreme. And those extreme positions hurt us all. BURNS (voiceover): Fetterman acknowledging what he called the elephant in the room. The stroke that nearly killed him five months ago. FETTERMAN: I had a stroke. He`s never let me forget that. And I might miss some words during this debate, mush two words together. I am also fighting for any forgotten community all across Pennsylvania that ever got knocked down that had to be made -- to get back up and I have made my entire career dedicating to those kinds of pursuits. BURNS (voiceover): Fetterman using closed captioning to assist with auditory processing, battling Dr. Oz. FETTERMAN: It`s about supporting and helping, you know, young earners, excuse me, young -- young, uh -- young, you know, students to give them a break. BURNS (voiceover): But experiencing some stumbles throughout the debate, particularly during an exchange over fracking, challenged by the moderators for past contradictory comments. FETTERMAN: I do support fracking and I don`t -- I don`t -- I support fracking and I stand -- and I do support fracking. BURNS (voiceover): Fetterman says he is fit to serve, citing a letter from his doctor. But he would not commit to releasing his full medical records. FETTERMAN: I believe if my doctor believes that I`m fit to serve and that`s what I believe is appropriate. BURNS (voiceover): The celebrity TV doctor never directly addressing Fetterman`s health, but saying this during an exchange on education. OZ: I visited vocational schools. I have an answer. But, John, because you -- obviously, I wasn`t clear enough for you to understand this. BURNS (voiceover): One point where Oz has not been clear, how he would vote on an abortion ban introduced by Republican Senator Lindsey Graham . OZ: I want women, doctors, local political leaders leading the democracy that`s always allowed our nation to thrive to put the best ideas forward so states can decide for themselves. BURNS (voiceover): A clear difference from his opponent. [08:05:00] FETTERMAN: My campaign would fight for Roe V. Wade. And if given the opportunity to codify it into law. (END VIDEO CLIP) BURNS (on camera): And, Savannah, and speaking to media after the debate, the Fetterman spokesperson said the campaign was thrilled with the Democrat`s performance saying he won, "Multiple exchanges against Oz." We also asked the Oz spokesperson about that line you just heard there where Oz said that decisions about abortion should be made between, "A woman, her doctor, and local political leaders." The campaign said that Oz is, "Pro- life with exceptions for rape, incest and the life of the mother." Savannah. GUTHRIE: All right. Dasha Burns, thank you very much. KOTB: With fears of a winter tripledemic growing, President Biden is urging Americans to get their flu and their COVID boosters as soon as they can. The president, who tested positive for COVID twice this summer, got his updated COVID shot yesterday. He noted that the virus is constantly changing but said that nearly all COVID deaths can now be prevented if enough people get vaccinated. Meantime, three quarters of all pediatric hospital beds around the country are now full because of an outbreak of RSV among children. MELVIN: Clorox is recalling eight of its Pine-Sol disinfecting cleaning products because they could contain harmful bacteria. The recall covers 37 million containers of Pine-Sol cleaners. They were made at a plant in Georgia. The CDC says the bacteria can cause blood and lung infections in people with compromised immune systems. For more information on the recall, go to our website, today.com. GUTHRIE: The International Space Station had to do defensive driving this week to avoid a potential collision with a piece of Russian satellite debris. NASA says the ISS had to fire its thrusters for more than five minutes on Monday. That raised its altitude a bit and allowed it to dodge the space junk. MELVIN: Wow. GUTHRIE: That maneuver did not affect normal operations. The debris was created by Russia`s test-firing of a missile last year that destroyed one of its old out of commission satellites. MELVIN: Space is really getting crowded. GUTHRIE: Yes. MELVIN: Really getting crowded. KOTB: All right. Guys, we got the news covered. Now, how about a boost? MELVIN: Yes. KOTB: All right. So, a UPS driver in South Dakota is the hero of the neighborhood because he made one incredible shot after he made a delivery. So, he dropped off a package, heads back to his truck, he`s walking past a driveway basketball game. The ball rolls towards the street, picks it up, and he fires off a one-handed shot. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: No way. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: No way. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: No way. MELVIN: Oh. KOTB: Oh, my gosh. After a brief celebration, the delivery man just climbs back in the truck, off he goes. MELVIN: Wow. KOTB: What a nice moment. MELVIN: That`s impressive. KOTB: That`s cool. GUTHRIE: So happy about the ring cameras sometimes. KOTB: I know. MELVIN: Yes. GUTHRIE: I mean, otherwise, they`d be like, no. But, seriously, I was away. KOTB: He did it. GUTHRIE: I did it. MELVIN: We got lots more ahead on a Wednesday morning, including our first look at a holiday special from the Marvel Universe. I can hear Al Roker screaming now. We`re going to show you the beloved star who is going to make a great cameo. GUTHRIE: But first, Jenna`s one-on-one with an extended member of the royal family, the queen consort`s nephew who lives right here in the northeast, New Jersey. Sharing his story for the first time. And Jenna, we`re looking forward to that conversation. Right after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [08:10:00] MELVIN: And welcome back. Welcome back. In the wake of Queen Elizabeth`s death, the eyes on the world are on the new monarch, King Charles and Queen Consort Camilla. GUTHRIE: Well, I learned something new today. One of their biggest supporters lives right here in the U.S., very close to us. Camilla`s nephew Luke Parker Bowles. KOTB: And Jenna met up with him to hear his intriguing story. Who knew he lived in Jersey. JENNA BUSH HAGER, HODA & JENNA HOST: I mean, he -- you would have thought you had to go across the pond. KOTB: Yes. BUSH HAGER: I just had to go in the hole and tunnel. After growing up of Parker Bowles, he`s began a new life right here in New Jersey. He is smart, charming, lovely. And now he is sharing his story for the first time. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) BUSH HAGER (voiceover): It`s an unlikely story, an unofficial British ambassador for the royal family living among the rolling hills of picturesque Montclair, New Jersey. LUKE PARKER BOWLES, QUEEN CONSORT CAMILLA`S NEPHEW: This town is so much about film and culture. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): I met with up with Luke Parker Bowles, nephew of queen consort Camilla, while he was busy promoting the Montclair Film Festival. BUSH HAGER (on camera): I never really thought I`d find a little slice of England in New Jersey. But tell me how you came here. PARKER BOWLES: I came to America, I met a beautiful woman who is now my wife. And I was in England making movies there. One of Hugh Grant`s films, "Love Actually" and everything, and I moved over here and started doing independent film. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): The father of three has lived in the United States for more than a decade. Lured away from the U.K. by the bright shiny lights of Hollywood and big dreams of an acting career. PARKER BOWLES: And after a while I -- it would -- it became very clear that I did not have the skill set, but I loved film more than anything. And so, I realized I wanted to be behind the camera. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): Far different from his life in London. He grew up the nephew of Camilla Parker Bowles, by her first marriage to Andrew Parker Bowles. His last name often casting a large and dramatic shadow as his aunt was in the spotlight. BUSH HAGER (on camera): I read that when you were younger, you were actually sometimes bullied. PARKER BOWLES: It was a rough time. It was not a great time to be a Parker Bowles. But it hasn`t scarred me. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): His family focused on using its name for good. PARKER BOWLES: All of us, I think. My cousins, my brother, and myself, we`ve always have been involved in charity. It`s much more important to be doing charitable things, not to be holier than thou, just because it gives you a focus. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): One of the charities close to his heart is the Queen Elizabeth II Garden in Lower Manhattan which pays tribute to his countrymen lost on 9/11. PARKER BOWLES: His majesty, very kindly become our trustee and helped us get this garden going, and then her late majesty allowed us to name it after her. And it`s a place for people to go down and reflect and remember. BUSH HAGER (on camera): Your heart is here. Your kids are here. Your wife is here. Your job is here. Part of you is still there. And by giving back here, you are keeping that part of you alive. PARKER BOWLES: I think my shrink would say there is some guilt involved, maybe, that I`m not over there. It goes back to the fact that I have this name. And if I can use it for something that helps people, then all the better. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): He says, it`s an example set from the very top. He admired Queen Elizabeth and her dedication to service, working for the British people up until the very end. BUSH HAGER (on camera): Watching the outpouring of love -- PARKER BOWLES: Yes. BUSH HAGER (on camera): -- for her majesty, Queen Elizabeth, we were in Scotland. So, to get to see little girls lining the street with hand- colored papers for her. PARKER BOWLES: I think, for the most part, she left this world feeling that everything was in its right place. BUSH HAGER (on camera): And she was such an example -- PARKER BOWLES: Oh, yes. BUSH HAGER (on camera): -- of service. PARKER BOWLES: Oh, yes. BUSH HAGER (on camera): -- and dedication. PARKER BOWLES: Yes. BUSH HAGER: I mean -- PARKER BOWLES: And flinchingly and never seeking thanks or approval. It was her job and she took it very seriously. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): Now, with the next generation leading the monarchy into a new area, Parker Bowles says he is optimistic and excited for the future. PARKER BOWLES: It`s been a big change for the U.K. of late. You know, we are in a lot of trouble with our financial situation, with our political situation. [08:15:00] And I think that it`s no surprise that the one ray of light, at the moment, is -- I have to get used to the queen. BUSH HAGER (on camera): Yes. PARKER BOWLES: Is his majesty and my aunt, and also Kate and William. BUSH HAGER (on camera): Yes. PARKER BOWLES: You know. I think that the queen, before she died was very smart about making sure that the four of them were front and center to the public and were showing that they actually are working. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): Parker Bowles now focuses on his business called Cinema Lab, restoring old movie theaters in the U.S. PARKER BOWLES: And it was really spurned on by seeing my daughter and her friends and my friends` daughters and sons, all hanging out at CVS car parks, or whatever it may be. BUSH HAGER (on camera): There was no movie theater for them to go? PARKER BOWLES: There`s no center. We want to bring back the community. BUSH HAGER (voiceover): That need of community and a place to come together is universal, whether it`s in London or across the pond in a small town in New Jersey. BUSH HAGER (on camera): If somebody had told you when you were 18, you are going to live in New Jersey when you get older, what would you have said? PARKER BOWLES: I`d say, what`s New Jersey, probably? Truly. But I -- it`s the best decision I ever made. (END VIDEO CLIP) BUSH HAGER: Don`t you love that, what`s New Jersey? KOTB: Wow. BUSH HAGER: It just shows you never know where life is going to take you. MELVIN: Yes. BUSH HAGER: But he talked about how important giving back was to his family. That his dad had three rules. One of them was to be kind. One was to not get caught, what he said, that one that we couldn`t break. And the other one was to do service. And I think that those were good rules to take back to our kids. But do not get caught. MELVIN: CARSON DALY, NBC NEWS HOST: Two out of three ain`t bad. GUTHRIE: Yes. BUSH HAGER: Yes, two out of three is pretty good. But he is a very charming, funny guy. And he said that Camilla is the same way, the queen consort. KOTB: Yes. BUSH HAGER: Is that same way -- has that funny -- KOTB: Wit. BUSH HAGER: -- not humor which -- you know -- KOTB: You -- GUTHRIE: Yes. KOTB: Yes, I was going to say I know someone who loves that kind of humor. GUTHRIE: People say she is fun to -- she`s the one you want to sit next to at a dinner party. KOTB: Yes. BUSH HAGER: Yes. GUTHRIE: That was the word up there in London. KOTB: Cool. GUTHRIE: Cool. KOTB: That was cool. KOTB: Thanks, Jen. MELVIN: Thanks, Jenna. KOTB: That was great. BUSH HAGER: Thank you. KOTB: All right. Mr. Roker, how about a check of the weather? AL ROKER, NBC TODAY WEATHER ANCHOR: All right. Let`s show you what we`ve got. In New Jersey and the other 49 states, we`re looking at some wet weather around the Great Lakes stretching all the way down into Northern Florida. We have also got some snow in the Rockies and up into the Western Plains. For today, temperatures, awfully chili. Alaska 20s and 30s. 80s down in Hawaii. 50s as you make your way into the Pacific Northwest. 80s in Southern Texas on into the southeast. We are looking for plenty of sunshine as you get down mid-Atlantic states down to the Gulf Coast on into the Plains up into the Great Lakes. Some mountain snows out west. Heavy rain for our friends in parts of eastern New England. That`s what`s going on around the country. Here`s what`s happening in your neck of the woods. (LOCAL NEWS) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) ROKER: And that`s your latest weather. Best time of the morning. DALY: I don`t know about that. Let`s go over some of it. ROKER: I think so. MELVIN: No. It`s -- it is. DALY: "POP Start", looking pretty solid today. We`re going to start with "Guardians of the Galaxy". Marvel`s gang of misfits is back together for a holiday special. In the trailer, Mantis and Drax are trying to cheer up their buddy Star-Lord with an extra special Christmas gift. And it leads to one heck of a celebrity cameo. Take a look. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) POM KLEMENTIEFF, ACTRESS: Maybe if we go to Earth for a really wonderful Christmas gift, it would make him happy. Something special he will never forget. DAVE BAUTISTA, ACTOR: What about someone special. KLEMENTIEFF: We are looking for the legendary Kevin Bacon. BAUTISTA: We`re looking for the legendary Kevin Bacon. KLEMENTIEFF: I just said that, Drax. BAUTISTA: But your voice is small and mousy. I think, maybe he didn`t hear you. You`re coming with us, as a Christmas present. (END VIDEO CLIP) DALY: That`s a good present. Have a new year with Kevin Bacon. KOTB: Oh, that`s cool. DALY: It makes perfect sense. ROKER: Fantastic. DALY: "The Guardians of the Galaxy" holiday special is going to start streaming November 25th on Disney Plus. MELVIN: That`s fantastic. DALY: Next up, Sir Elton John. It`s been almost 50 years since the "Rocket Man" launched into his superstardom with that legendary performance at Dodger Stadium. Next month, it`ll be a full circle moment when Elton makes that same venue his final stop in the north American farewell tour. KOTB: Wow. DALY: The Grammy is going to return for the show that`s set to live stream on Disney Plus. MELVIN: Wow. [08:20:00] DALY: The three-hour broadcast is going to pay tribute to the singer and his iconic 1975 Dodger Stadium concert. In a statement, Elton sharing his excitement for the upcoming show, calling it truly extra special. And you can catch that on November 20th. KOTB: Wow. DALY: That`ll be great. MELVIN: All right. DALY: Next up -- you owe me $5. Taylor Swift, made it in "POP Start", three for three this week. MELVIN: Every day. DALY: Seems like "Midnights" is everywhere. Swift`s new album has been showing up also in some pretty unexpected places, including one city`s local traffic report. You might remember Sheila Watko from our Philadelphia station. Over the summer, Sheila worked in more than a dozen Beyonce songs, like, titles of the songs in her live report to celebrate the release of "Renaissance". Well, she`s back. MELVIN: Uh-oh. DALY: She went full Swifty with another amazing music themed segment. Take a look. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) SHEILA WATKO, NBC10 PHILADELPHIA ENTERTAINMENT REPORTER AND TRAFFIC ANCHOR: The avenue -- this is not a glitch, Lucy. Looking great out there. Sweet nothing in both directions. This is our karma for dealing with that earlier construction on 95 in Delco. We`re dealing with an earlier vehicle fire. And if we take a wide look at the area, you`re going to see most of the map is actually bejeweled with these green roads. (END VIDEO CLIP) DALY: But Sheila -- KOTB: Go girl. ROKER: Impressive. DALY: -- Sheila got in all 20 tracks. MELVIN: Wow. GUTHRIE: That`s impressive. ROKER: Impressive. DALY: That`s impressive. MELVIN: Wow. GUTHRIE: She`s very clever. ROKER: Yes. DALY: All 20 tracks from "Midnights". MELVIN: Way to go Sheila. KOTB: Cool. DALY: There you go. Next up, People`s Choice Awards. We have a "POP Start" exclusive announcement this morning. The scoop on who is going to be hosting this year`s big show. Uncle al, drum roll please. It is our buddy Kenan Thompson. MELVIN: Yes. DALY: Emmys -- ROKER: He is on fire. DALY: -- just last month. Yes. I think he did the SPs this month -- ROKER: Yes. DALY: -- this year, too? Kenan back to host the PCAs for the second year in a row. Also, he`s nominated comedy TV star category for his work on "SNL". In a statement, Kenan said, I`m so grateful to be nominated. Shoutout to the fans and congrats to all the nominees. Get ready for round two. You can catch Kenan and the 2022 People`s Choice Awards, of course, here on NBC and E!, that`s Tuesday, December 6th. And finally, "Avatar: The Way of the Water". Fans have been excited for this sequel. It`s more than a decade in the making. James Cameron`s epic sci-fi flick is coming. And ahead of its December release in theaters, the cast now opening up about a surprising skill set that they had to learn onset. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JIMMY FALLON, "THE TONIGHT SHOW STARRING JIMMY FALLON" HOST: So, you had to learn how to, like, hold your breath for a long time. SIGOURNEY WEAVER, ACTRESS: We did. FALLON: Because a lot of it is under water. WEAVER: Yes, we had to learn free dive. And the first thing -- and we had this amazing teacher named Kirk Krack who teaches the Navy SEALs. You know, I actually got up to six and a half minutes. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: Minutes? DALY: Six and a half minutes underwater. ROKER: Wow. DALY: In an interview with " The New York Times ," James Cameron said that he didn`t want to use CGI for the underwater sequences -- MELVIN: Wow. DALY: -- because he wanted it to look real. GUTHRIE: Wow. DALY: Which I guess is the Tom Cruise , "Top Gun: Maverick" approach to filmmaking now. ROKER: Yes. DALY: Making Miles Teller and actors actually go to flight schools so those camera shots are getting, geez, it looks real. So, Zoe Saldana -- Sigourney Weaver`s co-star said she got to almost five minutes underwater. ROKER: What? KOTB: Geez. DALY: And Kate Winslet was able to hold her breath a full seven minutes while shooting "Avatar". ROKER: That`s amazing. KOTB: Wait. What? DALY: I can`t wait to see those scenes and how they turned out. "Avatar: The Way of the Way" is going to hit theaters on December 16. MELVIN: I`d just be dead. DALY: Yes. ROKER: Yes. GUTHRIE: Wow. KOTB: Wow. DALY: 45 seconds. Cut. ROKER: That`s true. DALY: I`ll be in my trailer. ROKER: I`d be floating on top. GUTHRIE: Guys, we have our special series, countdown to Halloween, exploring the "Spookiest Houses in America". MELVIN: Yes, this has been a lot of fun. So, far this week we`ve been to New York, we`ve been to Ohio. This morning, we`re going to head out west to meet the so-called Halloween queen herself. KOTB: Yes. Let`s say hello to Amanda Wilkens and her festive home in Kingsburg, California. She`s there with us alongside Caroline Collins, she`s from our local affiliate KSEE. Ladies, that`s a big -- wow. I love it. It`s nighttime there. We can actually see it. MELVIN: Yes. CAROLINE COLLINS, KSEE24 SUNRISE NEWS ANCHOR: It is, Hoda. It just adds to the spooky feeling of this house. Amanda, you are, like they said, known as the Halloween queen because of all the trips you make to your local hardware store. What goes into putting on something on like this? AMANDA WILKENS, "SPOOKIEST HOUSE IN AMERICA" HOMEOWNER: It has been a fun and exciting year of planning all of this. And we go bigger and bigger every single year. And I can`t wait to keep going. COLLINS: There is so much to it. One of the main focal points are these giant skeletons that you have outside. What do you do with the skeletons when it`s not spooky season? WILKENS: They actually stay up. And I dress them for every holiday. The kids around us love it. They gave him a name, Mr. Bones. They will put me on blast if I do not dress him accordingly or if he is not dressed in time for the next holiday. COLLINS: Oh, wow. Well, what do the neighbors think of all of this? WILKENS: The positivity has been phenomenal. I cannot thank them enough. Being from a small farm town, this right here is what makes it for us, my husband and I. That`s the time to go because they don`t celebrate over there, great prices. If you want to go this month, Hoda, October, San Diego is your destination. KOTB: Oh is it? NGUYEN: All kinds of deals on restaurants, attractions, hotels for kids. You (inaudible) the kids out. GUTHRIE: I love San Diego. It`s a good city. OK, cool. KOTB: Thank you, Vic. This was late September last year. You can see how lush it is. This year, October of 2020, look at how dry it is. And that is continuing. And in fact we are looking at record low river levels. Memphis reaching its lowest river level since 1954. And the big problem is the drought. When this is an economic lifeline, the Mississippi River, $13 billion in shipping, a 35,000 related jobs. It accounts -- get this, 92% of our nation`s agricultural exports. So it is a lifeline literally, and the big problem has been the extensive drought in the western half of the Mississippi River basin. Problem is going into the winter, doesn`t look like we`re going to get much relief, so going to continue to have problems along the Mighty Mississippi. For Today, we`re looking at sunshine returning through the southeast into the gulf, plenty of sun from Texas on up into the plains, some mountain snows where they`re going to use that for those great ski resorts and we`re looking at sunshine from San Diego, some showers in Seattle. That`s what`s going on around the country. Here`s what`s happening in your neck of the woods. (LOCAL WEATHER) ROKER: And that is your latest weather. Guys? GUTHRIE: Thank you, Al. CARSON DALY, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: There`s got to be a reason for that. That means fall is here. Pesky task of raking leaves but that chore might be a thing of the past. headline: Today for October 20, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good Thursday morning from Washington and New York. Our top story, all eyes once again on Ukraine. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Tension there building after new attacks and new threats. It is October 20th. This is Today. Leave immediately, this morning, thousands of residents in southern Ukraine being forced to flee their own homes. Mass evacuations underway after a warning of imminent attacks and martial law declared by Vladimir Putin . And this morning, mounting concern over power outages ahead of a harsh winter, we`ll have the very latest and a live report straight ahead. On the road, President Biden hits the campaign trail today in the closely watched battleground of Pennsylvania. Can he move the needle for the undecided voters with less than three weeks to go? Feeling the freeze, another day of bitter cold across much of the country, parts of the south waking up two record lows, but Al says, hang in there, a big warm ups on the way. They`ll have your full forecast. Consumer alert, the new warning from police after a string of robberies in cities across the country tied to popular online marketplaces. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CMDR. RODNEY G. HILL, CHICAGO POLICE DEPARTMENT ENGLEWOOD DISTRICT: Nine times out of 10, if you see a deal that is too good to be true, it is. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: This morning what you need to know before you click. Those stories, plus, "The Crown" and the controversy. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It is with regret, the Prince and Princess of Wales are separating. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: The growing backlash against the hit show`s upcoming storyline. Why an Oscar winner wants it to come with a disclaimer and how "The Crown`s" creator is responding. And smash hit. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: At the wall looking up, see you later. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: The Astros defeat the Yankees in game one of the ALCS while the Padres rally to tie up their series with the Phillies in a game for the record books. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Aaron Nola against Austin Nola, little brother against big brother. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: The battle of the brothers going down in history, today, Thursday, October 20th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie live from Washington, D.C. and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Well good morning. Good to see you. So happy you`re joining us on a Thursday morning. Savannah is joining us in D.C. And SG, can you imagine being the mom and dad you`re like, I`m cheering for both my sons. You go, no you go. It`s got to be a tough one. GUTHRIE: I know. Yes, moms are always like, no, I don`t have a favorite. No really, I don`t. Well, a lot more of those highlights in just a bit. Plus nearly two thirds of the country waking up to another morning of bitter cold, I know you`re feeling it there in New York, here Washington too. Record low temps expected in the south today. Al is tracking it and he has some good news on when it`ll feel a little more like fall. KOTB: But we are going to start this morning in Ukraine where new evacuations are being ordered. It comes as residents are being told to charge their devices after drone strikes knocked out key power stations, rolling blackouts now common. And this is just as the brutal Ukraine winter is approaching. NBC`s Cal Perry is in Ukraine for us. Cal, good morning. Give us the latest. CAL PERRY, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Hey, good morning to you, Hoda. Fresh strikes overnight, the target once again that vital energy infrastructure of Ukraine. It is what has prompted the mayor here to tell people turn off your electricity, save power. All the while as you mentioned, the bitter cold from the winter has arrived, the temperatures plunging overnight, all the while the strikes continue across Ukrainian cities. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) PERRY (voice-over): This morning, the people of Kherson are caught in the middle. Thousands in the port city that has been under Russian occupation for months, now being ordered to evacuate by Russian installed leaders. Some getting text messages that read, dear residents, evacuate immediately. There will be shelling of residential areas by the armed forces of Ukraine. The evacuations and apparent reaction to Ukraine`s counter offensive in the region, recapturing villages and farmland in recent weeks, Ukrainian officials accusing Russia of trying to create hysteria. It comes on the same day Russian`s President Putin declared martial law in the four Ukrainian regions currently occupied by Russia. I have signed a decree, he said, introducing martial law into these four entities of the Russian Federation. Under the order Russia can, it says, legally seize Ukrainian homes and property, move civilian populations and create local militias, meaning Moscow may try to force Ukrainians to fight against their own country. JOE BIDEN, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: It seems his only tool available to him is to brutalize individual citizens in Ukraine. PERRY (voice-over): From Mykolaiv and the south to Kyiv and the north, the Russian bombardment continues. In just over a month, at least 239 drones have been shot down by air defenses, according to the Ukrainian military. The ones that make it past those air defenses are frequently striking infrastructure targets, 30 percent of power plants have been destroyed. [07:05:17] Other times, civilians pay the price. Here in the capital of Kyiv, eight dead in 24 hours, all the while the threat of a nuclear attack looms. Children drill in a nearby school here in Kyiv. And while bulletproof vests are necessary on the battle front, swim caps and goggles must do here on the home front. (END VIDEOTAPE) PERRY: Now Ukraine is asking countries around the world to help with its air defense system. Israel the latest to offer hands saying it will help provide that very important early alert system. But holding back on the ammunition needed to actually shoot down the drones. Officials here are hoping to get that from the United States. Hoda? KOTB: We`re counting those young kids with swim caps and goggles, it`s just -- it`s also unsettling. Thank you so much. We appreciate your report there. Let`s move on back here at home. We`ve got another morning of cold temperatures and a lot of the country, record setting in parts of the South. Let`s bring in Mr. Roker to get a first check of the forecast. Good morning, Al. AL ROKER, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: All right, good morning, Hoda. Good morning, everybody. The good news is if you are one of the 76 million people under these frost advisory, freeze warnings, we`ve got some relief coming for you, so hold on. For this morning though, Memphis 39 degrees, Tallahassee right now 32, Orlando 55 degrees, Norfolk 39. But we are going to see a little bit of a change. For today though, it is going to stay cold but we are going to see a little relief. But for today, about 12 degrees below average in Buffalo behind where the Jetstream dips to the south. We`re looking at Pier 75 degrees, that`s 15 degrees above normal, Boise, Idaho 77. For tomorrow, those temperatures still a little on the chilly side from New York, Charlotte on into Jacksonville. But the warmth is coming, Little Rock 81, San Antonio 86, Dallas, it`s going to be 88 degrees. And as we get into early next week, temperatures moderate, look at this, we`ll be in the 60s in New York right on into early next week, 70s in Raleigh and in Cincinnati, Chicago as well. And hot springs Arkansas into the 80s. We have that record warmth out west, record cold in the east. However, it`s because of this jet stream that`s really been amplified. The good news is if you`re here in the east, we`re going to see a flip, cooler air with rain and snow, which is good news for Seattle and Portland. They have right now the worst air quality in the world because of all the heat and the wildfires. They`re going to see temperatures drop 10 to 25 degrees below normal here in the East, much warmer as we get into next week with temperatures 10 to 20 degrees above normal. So Savannah, we`re all getting some good news back to you. GUTHRIE: All right, I like that Al. Thank you. Well, this morning, new data is out. And it reveals more about the effects of inflation on families all across this country, and the Federal Reserve`s efforts to get it under control. This is some top business leaders are voicing big concerns about the months ahead. NBC`s Tom Costello here with us in Washington tracking it again. Not good news that we`re hearing from business leaders. TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Not good news. And we`ve been talking for months about persistent sky high inflation. And now, the head of one of the country`s biggest banks, Goldman Sachs is warning about a possible volatile period as we head into 2023. Listen, when Goldman talks, people listen, for the average family, there`s less concern right now about whether we are entering a recession or already there, but rather, when will things improve and how do we cope right now. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) COSTELLO (voice-over): From Main Street, USA to Wall Street, Americans are still staring down red hot inflation that shows no signs of cooling off. Now some top executives are warning of potentially tough times in the months ahead. DAVID SOLOMON , GOLDMAN SACHS CEO: I think it`s a time to be cautious. That doesn`t mean for sure that we have a really difficult economic scenario. But in the distribution of outcomes, there`s good chance we could have a recession. COSTELLO (voice-over): And Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos , also issuing a warning earlier this week tweeting, the probabilities in this economy tell you to batten down the hatches. With less than three weeks before the midterm elections, President Biden denies that the move to continue tapping into the nation`s emergency oil supply is politically motivated, calling on oil companies to increase production and their refining operations. BIDEN: You still make a significant profit. Your shareholders will still do very well. And the American people catch a break they deserve and get a fair price at the pump as well. COSTELLO (voice-over): But gas is just one part of the global inflation picture. In the U.K. inflation is running even hotter, above 10 percent. Food up a staggering 14.6 percent while the average American family now spends nearly $450 more per month to buy the same goods as last year. The head of the country`s largest retailer, Walmart , tell Savannah it`s hitting people in different ways. [07:10:00] GUTHRIE: Do you feel like consumers are hitting that point where they`re done paying those high prices? JOHN FURNER , WALMART U.S. CEO: I think it depends on the personal situation that consumers are in, really different depending on where you are around the country. COSTELLO (voice-over): For Stephanie Lane`s (ph) family of six living off a single income in Pennsylvania, it`s meant cutting back across the board. STEPHANIE LANE (ph), PENNSYLVANIA RESIDENT: It`s a hard pill to swallow when you have to really change everything you`ve done. And do it everything differently because you can`t afford it. COSTELLO (voice-over): Despite the challenging times, Stephanie (ph) says she and her family are looking forward. LANE (ph): We don`t know when it`s going to get better. But I do know it will. I have faith that it will. (END VIDEOTAPE) GUTHRIE: Tom, we`ve been talking so much about the Fed`s interest rates hikes and how it`s going into effect. And sometimes it takes time to see if they`re working. We`re already seeing some leading indicators right now turning up and affect in the economy. COSTELLO: Last week, you and I talked about a lagging indicator. The unemployment rate is a lagging indicator of what the economy is like right now. We have a new leading indicator, this is concerning. New home building fell 8 percent last month, the lowest since the earliest days of the pandemic, that`s a concern. Mortgage rates, of course, now up to 7.2 percent on a 30 year, that`s double in a year. As a result, existing home sales, we expect are going to be sliding dramatically when we get that data in and price is expected to fall dramatically. All of that is not good for the economy. GUTHRIE: All right, Tom, thank you so much. And, of course, another big focus here in Washington, the midterm elections, which is 19 days to go. Early voting already underway, President Biden is hitting the campaign trail in the battleground of Pennsylvania today. And that brings us over here to Kristen Welker, who`s been covering politics, of course. Well, let`s start here with gas prices. We talked to Tom about the economy, gas prices, is a leading indicator, both economically and politically for the White House. KRISTEN WELKER, NBC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: That`s absolutely right. And there`s no doubt that there`s a lot of concern about gas prices, which have ticked up a bit over the past month. They`re down significantly, though, from their high in the summer over $5 a gallon. Yesterday, President Biden announced they`re releasing another 15 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. But look, this is really the tail end of an announcement that was made several months ago to release 180 million barrels. And Savannah, it`s not clear it`s going to have a big impact on gas prices. What it does is it allows the President to make the case that he is working on this issue, which 44 percent of Americans say is their top issue right now heading into these midterms. I talked to the White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain , what`s the first thing he does every morning? Check gas prices. And it underscores, Savannah, the fact that what happens in November could very much be determined by the price of the pump. GUTHRIE: Yes, because it`s something that absolutely everyone feels and it creates a ripple through the economy. Let`s talk about the issue of abortion. Democrats thought they had a lot of momentum with that issue right on the heels of the Dobbs decision in June. Now, it doesn`t seem that it`s having as much of a sway with independent voters. WELKER: That`s right. And you look at the swing that we`re seeing among independent women in particular, who said that they favored Democrats in September. Now, huge swing over to Republicans, you saw abortion as an energizing factor in races in Kansas in special election in New York in the primaries, but I think Democrats are concerned that they need to be having a broader appeal. You saw President Biden talking about the issue of abortion earlier this week. He said remember, basically the outrage that you felt on the day that Roe v. Wade was overturned, trying to turn back the clock in essence, Savannah, but there`s a real awareness and I think a message from the White House. Yes, we need to talk about abortion. But we need to talk about issues including the economy and crime that voters care about in this election cycle, too. So that`s why the President is going to be in Pennsylvania talking about infrastructure today, for example. GUTHRIE: Yes, the polls have shown that the Republicans appeared to have some momentum going into these midterms. The control of the Senate, control of the House is on the table, Pennsylvania, where the President will be today is a key Senate race and it`s tight. WELKER: It`s very tight. It`s basically a statistical dead heat, Savannah. And what`s notable about the President stop in Pennsylvania today, he`s going to be talking about infrastructure. And here you can see these polls between John Fetterman and Dr. Oz. He`s going to talk about infrastructure and then hold a fundraising event with John Fetterman . So not the typical rally that you would usually see a President hold in these closing weeks of a campaign. Why? Well, his approval ratings are low. And I think a lot of Democrats are concerned that he will hurt, he will hinder them instead of helping them. And so that`s why I think you`re not seeing these traditional rallies. But I spoke to an administration official who said, look, the bottom line is, we think it`s more effective to have him out talking about things like infrastructure, talking about things like abortion, gas prices, the things that he has worked on, instead of basically shouting at a crowd. They point to Obama, they point to Trump, they say, look, they had big losses in their midterms as well. So they don`t necessarily see that as an effective strategy. They`re also saying he will be holding typical events getting closer. GUTHRIE: All right, Kristen Welker here in Washington with me. Thank you so much. Hoda to 14 minutes after the hour, I`ll send it over to you. [07:15:01] KOTB: All right, thank you SG. Now to the rising health concern for families across the country just as flu season is getting underway, doctors are seeing an alarming rise in cases of RSV. Now that`s a common respiratory illness that`s left some children in need of hospitalization. So the surge, so severe one Children`s Hospital in Connecticut is now using temporary units to handle their patients and is considering asking for national help. So what is going on? What`s causing it? Why now? NBC News medical contributor Dr. Natalie Azar is here with everything we need to know. Well, first of all, that sounds scary what`s happening in Connecticut. Let`s break it down. Tell us about RSV. And why is it exploding in this moment? DR. NATALIE AZAR, NBC NEWS MEDICAL CONTRIBUTOR: Right, so Hoda, so RSV is a typical seasonal respiratory virus, right? It is, by the time children are two years old, most of them will have been infected with RSV. But it does and it can cause a close to 60,000 hospitalizations every year in children. And the majority of people, it causes a mild cold like illness. So we`re talking runny nose, a low grade fever, a cough, sneezing. KOTB: How long does it last? AZAR: Usually lasts about one to two weeks, sometimes the symptoms can peak at day five. KOTB: OK. AZAR: But in certain individuals, when it goes from the upper respiratory tract into the lungs, it can actually cause more severe disease. And I think it`s very important, especially for caregivers out there of young ones who can`t communicate, the symptoms of more severe disease would be things like poor feeding, irritability, wheezing, or shortness of breath. Those are the kinds of symptoms and signs that you`d want to reach out to your pediatrician immediately. KOTB: So sometimes you wouldn`t know if your child has a cold or has this but either way, like, how do you treat it? What do you suppose to give them? AZAR: Well, that`s the thing. And so you mentioned a very good point, it`s actually indistinguishable, you know, from cold or flu or things like a COVID, you would actually need to get tested. You have to get tested, though in the doctor`s office, there are no home tests for this. In terms of treatment for the majority of people, the treatment is supportive. So that means rehydrating, managing the airway. There is a treatment, however, for people who are at risk, and that group includes premature infants, kids under the age of six months, heart lung problems, weakened immune systems, older folks. It`s a monthly injection that can actually prevent severe disease. KOTB: Just a last quick thing. There was a headline in -- here in New York that said COVID cases in some pockets of New York were up 20 percent. Is that a bellwether? Are we expecting like this big bounce in numbers? AZAR: Right, Hoda. So we`re talking about new strains, and they are descendants of the Omicron strain. This is not unexpected. This is what we expect the virus to do. At this point, it doesn`t appear that it`s causing more severe disease. But remember, more infections could lead to more hospitalizations, and then the convergence of flu. We worry about hospital capacity and of course, cases of lung COVID. So we`re certainly keeping an eye on it. KOTB: And that 20 percent is pretty alarming even in -- AZAR: It`s a pretty significant doubling time. That`s what`s making experts concerned. KOTB: All right, Dr. Azar, thank you. We appreciate it. It is 17 minutes after the hour. Hello, Craig. CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Hello, good morning, Hoda. Good morning Dr. Natalie as well and good morning to you. October best part of the year for baseball fans, major league baseball playoffs underway right now. The Houston Astros came out swinging in game one of the ALCS. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Drive into right, well hit, Judge on the run, and Chas McCormick, opposite field home run. (END VIDEO CLIP) MELVIN: And there you have it. Chas McCormick with Houston second home run of the inning there, they would go on to beat the Yankees four to two. Game two is tonight. Over to the National League now, the San Diego Padres scoring five runs in the fifth inning to take the lead there. They would hold on to that lead to win it, eight to five. That series all tied up at one game apiece. There was some history made in that game as noted at the top of the show here, Phillies pitcher Aaron Nola is facing his brother Austin Nola, who is a catcher for San Diego. You see their parents looking on there to the farm, right. It`s the first time in MLB postseason history that a pitcher faced his brother at the plate. Austin Nola getting the big RBI single there. That was smart the Padres in the fifth inning. And I heard you and SG in the top of the show about which, you know, as a parent watch. KOTB: -- you do, you know, who -- MELVIN: I`ll tell you who`s the favorite child, it`s Austin, the oldest child is always the favorite. KOTB: But, you know, I was just -- I was thinking of Peyton and Eli Manning`s mom and dad. How many times have they watch their two kids and there were one point they were in the Super Bowl together. It`s like, oh my, oh my, oh my. GUTHRIE: And guys, I was like either they put the split screen up of the parents so it`s like the brothers and the parents have to keep the neutral face, like game face. Yes, we like everyone. KOTB: Look at them, I can`t the jerseys, I see a Phillies Jersey maybe the mom`s got a Padres on. MELVIN: But if you look at the Phillies jersey, it looks like he`s got a Padres jersey on underneath and a Padres hat. KOTB: OK. All right, fair enough. Let`s go guys, time for the weather. Mr. Rocker we`re talking about some brutal cold. [07:20:01] ROKER: Although, Craig, I hope Sibby is not watching. MELVIN: I hope she`s not either. That`s just -- ROKER: -- you said the older is the favorite. MELVIN: Not in my house. Not in my house. ROKER: Nice clarification. I`ll do what I can to help you. MELVIN: Thank you. Anyway, for today, we do have that fire risk continuing in the western plains. So we`re watching that sunny and warm out west. It`s going to be another gorgeous day. They do really need the rain. We`re going to look at that in the next half hour and easing chill coming into the East. So that`s good news there. We`re going to get to your local forecast in the next 30 seconds. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (LOCAL NEWS) ROKER: And that`s your latest weather. You know it`s cold when we got the hand warmers out. KOTB: SG, I got hand warmers in here, girl. GUTHRIE: Oh my gosh. But you know who`s happy Craig Melvin, he likes it when that thermostat is breezing cold. KOTB: Exactly. MELVIN: Fall and winter in 1A. KOTB: All right, coming up, it`s a big hit. But Kelly Cobiella, we got some controversy surrounding the upcoming season of "The Crown ." Tell us about it. KELLY COBIELLA, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: That`s right, Hoda. In fact Oscar winner Dame Judi Dench is now joining a chorus of critics calling some depictions in the new season, cruelly unjust. We`ll take a look at what all the controversy is about and also what the show`s creator is saying coming up. GUTHRIE: Well, that`s a good one. We`ll find out about that. Also, guys, if you buy or sell stuff online don`t want to miss this story, especially as we`re heading into the holidays, the new warning about criminals using popular sites to find their next victims. We`re going to break down the red flags to look for and give you advice for staying safe. But first, this is Today on NBC. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) MELVIN: Still ahead, the inspiring high school football player making sports history with her touchdown. [07:24:41] KOTB: Indeed. But first, your local news. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (LOCAL NEWS) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (LOCAL NEWS) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) [07:30:18] UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Let`s please welcome the 2022 Caregiver Champion, it is not a better word to describe her, Savannah Guthrie. GUTHRIE: Thank you hidden heroes for this beautiful honor. And thank you most of all to caregivers for the privilege of knowing you. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: We are back. Boy, that was beautiful. I have even seen the whole speech and I`m in. This is the reason Savannah is in D.C. She was honored with this year`s Caregiver Champion Award. And as Tom Hanks said, there`s no better descriptor than that. That was at the Elizabeth Dole Foundation`s heroes and history makers gala. Savannah, what a night, man, I mean, that looks beautiful. The powerful new message that pop star Christina Aguilera is sending to young girls, with a new take on one of her biggest hits. Authorities say criminals are most likely to target high end items like designer purses, all-terrain vehicles, scooters, Apple iPads, and watches. To stay safe, officials they always use safe exchange locations, including in some cities inside the lobby of a police station. (on camera): And the police are OK with that? HILL: That`s what we want them to do. Especially now, the holidays are quickly approaching, we don`t want anyone to trade their safety for a great deal. Common red flags include the seller refusing to meet in person or let you see the item before purchase. Facebook says it takes the threat of scams seriously and has specialized detection tools and trained enforcement and review teams working to remove bad actors from the platform. Facebook also allows users to set up a meeting plan within the app that can be shared with a group of trusted friends, all to ensure your hunt for deals doesn`t put you in danger. NGUYEN: Yes, Hoda, when it comes to buying anything online, if you are going to use a payment method, always use your credit card because that offers another layer of fraud protection and of course, if you`re seeing a deal that is way below market, that`s your first red flag. And when you`re doing this in person, police say, anytime you feel something is off, trust your gut, leave, get out of that situation. KOTB: Right. They can tell you, meet around the corner then you should not. All right, thank you Vic. MELVIN: Thank you, Vic. Mr. Roker, it looks like a relatively quiet day in the weather. ROKER: It really is.
