headline: Conversation With Clea Shearer, About Her Breast Cancer Journey
story_text: [08:10:00] CRAIG MELVIN: We are back. 8:12 with "Pink Power TODAY". Our special series for breast cancer awareness month. And this morning, this morning we`re checking in with our friend Clear Shearer. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE: Yes, "The Home Edit" co-founder was diagnosed with breast cancer earlier this year and she has decided to share every step in her journey, including her recent milestone of finishing chemo. HODA KOTB: Yes, throughout it all, though guys, there`s been a group of women she`s been leaning on. They talk every day but they had never met face to face until two days ago. They`re amazing women. They all came together from all across the country for a very special conversation. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) CLEA SHEARER, "THE HOME EDIT" CO-FOUNDER: Look, all of your toys are so accessible. KOTB (voiceover): Clea Shearer finds joy in being a helper. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Will you guys help me? JOANNA TEPLIN, "THE HOME EDIT" CO-FOUNDER: I can`t get up there fast enough. SHEARER: Yes. TEPLIN: Like, show us the closets. SHEARER: Yes. KOTB (voiceover): She`s created a career out of it. Taking on clutter and organizing people`s lives as one half of "The Home Edit" team. SHEARER: Hey, guys. So, by now you probably read or heard that I have breast cancer. KOTB (voiceover): But after she shared her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year, Clea found herself asking for help from those who personally knew the fight she was facing. SHEARER: As you`re going through something so brutal, like chemo, everyone in your life wants to help, but there`s nothing quite like someone who`s actually been through it or going through it at the same time. KOTB (voiceover): A friend connected her to Maria Boschetti, a three-time breast cancer survivor who lives in California with her husband. The 42- year-old, who works in public relations, was first diagnosed when she was just 25. SHEARER: She`s taken so many copious notes. So, if I just say -- if I whip out any side effects she`s like, boop, boop, boop -- KOTB (on camera): Got it. SHEARER: -- page eight. She`s like, you`ll get over that real soon. KOTB (voiceover): Amy Jethway was 42 years old when she found a lump while on vacation with her boyfriend. The biotech sales account manager diagnosed with breast cancer just weeks after Clea. Their mutual friend passed along Clea`s number to Amy who lived hundreds of miles away in New Jersey. KOTB (on camera): These are strangers? People you`ve never met. SHEARER: I`ve never met them. KOTB (on camera): Just on text. Hey, girl? SHEARER: Well -- yes, literally. And I -- there are some of, you know, these women I talk to every day. If not every day, every week, and, you know, just to check in. They`re like my dear close friends. KOT (voiceover): A community connected through tough times. Dear friends who have never met. Meeting up in person for the first time. KOTB (on camera): Well, I think it`s a good time to meet them because it`s fun to text, but it`s more fun to see people in person. [08:15:00] SHEARER: Oh. Oh, my God. AMY JETHWAY, BREAST CANCER SURVIVOR: I can`t believe we get to see you. You`re real. You`re real. Oh, my God. SHEARER: It`s so good to see you. JETHWAY: I`m going to cry. Oh, my gosh. You`re so tall. KOTB (on camera): This is so cool in this moment to be sitting here. SHEARER: I can`t believe. KOTB (on camera): First of all, you haven`t met in person yet you -- SHEARER: No. Oh, my God. KOTB (on camera): -- but you know each other intimately. What did you think, Maria, when you first started connecting with Clea? MARIA BOSCHETTI, BREAST CANCER SURVIVOR: I was shocked she was so positive, right? Because it`s a terrifying time in your life. You were wanting to talk about it. You had questions but also you were -- wanting to help others. KOTB (voiceover): Others like Amy. JETHWAY: I reached out to you during your fourth AC -- SHEARER: Yes. JETHWAY: -- when you felt really horrible. SHEARER: Yes. JETHWAY: And she was so available to me. Like, that was really overwhelming to me because I was about to start my chemo journey. KOTB (voiceover): Did that make you scared or did that make you prepared? JETHWAY: I was so grateful for how open you were and how honest you were about things because if this is what`s going to happen to me, then this is going to happen. I wound up having a very different reaction with my fourth. SHEARER: I know. I was, like, so sorry. I scared you. KOTB (on camera): Oh, you were like, I`m cool. SHEARER: She was like, fine. JETHWAY: Yes. SHEARER: Meanwhile, this whole time I was, like, guys brace yourselves. It`s going to be awful. JETHWAY: Like, it aches everywhere. KOTB (voiceover): Clea`s openness about her hair loss empowering Amy as she started to lose her own. JETHWAY: I told my boyfriend, I`m going to shave this. Like, we`re -- we can do this. We can take this head on. And kind of, whatever parts of the journey you can own, you now, that`s something I got from you. KOTB (on camera): That`s important -- that`s something you got from Clea? JETHWAY: Yes. KOTB (on camera): What is that? JETHWAY: Like, owning what you can in the journey. KOTB (on camera): Were you reluctant, Clear, because there are parts that you want to share and then there are parts you want to keep. But it sounds like you were very -- SHEARER: Oh, I don`t keep much to myself. KOTB (on camera): You don`t? SHEARER: No. Hoda, you know me. I am a barrier soul kind of girl. KOTB (on camera): Yes. SHEARER: Not only did I tell everything pretty much to these ladies but, I mean, I would also tell our Instagram followers what was going on. And it made me feel understood, you know. And it`s also nice not to feel like an anomaly. KOTB (on camera): When you`re having a crummy day, you need someone who gets it. How important has that been, Maria, to have that? BOSCHETTI: It`s so important. I -- you know, I was so young the first time I was diagnosed. And I didn`t have anybody to talk to. You don`t process those emotions when you don`t have someone to talk to or ask question and that friendship. And now, you know, I was just texting Clea last night. I feel like you are this light of sunshine that`s even bringing the last eight years back in me. SHEARER: I`m sorry about that. KOTB (on camera): By the way -- BOSCHETTI: Don`t make me cry. I`m not a pretty crier. KOTB (on camera): But that`s so beautiful. That`s a really important point. BOSCHETTI: Yes, yes. KOTB (on camera): It like -- sometimes feelings lay dormant. SHEARER: Yes. JETHWAY: Yes. BOSCHETTI: Yes. KOTB (on camera): Until someone says, let`s unearth those. KOTB (voiceover): Clea, Maria, and Amy finding strength in each other and finding peace in the small things. KOTB (on camera): Everybody has their spot where they go to when they want to just, like, cleanse and clear and you all are walking in mine. This is Central Park. What`s your place, Clea? Where do you -- SHEARER: My back porch. KOTB (on camera): Your back porch? SHEARER: I have a chair. I read there. I listen to the rain there. I greet my kids after school there. KOTB (on camera): Uh-huh. SHEARER: I just -- it makes me so peaceful. KOTB (on camera): What about for you, Amy? JETHWAY: I have my one bench right on the Hudson -- SHEARER: Oh, that`s so nice. KOTB (on camera): Yes. JETHWAY: -- and that just go out. KOTB (on camera): Doing meditation, Maria, or anything that like -- BOSCHETTI: Yes. KOTB (on camera): You`re a meditator? BOSCHETTI: Yes, meditation and beach. KOTB (on camera): Meditation and beach? BOSCHETTI: Yes. KOTB (on camera): All right. So, this is a sisterhood. SHEARER: Yes. KOTB (on camera): This is something that you believe, Clea, is not for this moment. SHEARER: Uh-huh. It`s for life. KOTB (on camera): How do you know? SHEARER: You go through life and certain people enter it for a reason. I consider you one of those people, too, Hoda. Because I don`t lose friends. I only make them. headline: How To Identify Your Personal Breast Cancer Risks And The Steps You Can Take To Reduce It
story_text: [09:10:00] SHEINELLE JONES: We are back with our "Pink Power" series to mark the start of Breast Cancer Awareness Month. And this morning, we have a checklist of important information all women need to know from risk factors to screening and more. So, joining us now is Dr. Marisa Weiss , director of breast radiation oncology at Lankenau Medical Center in Pennsylvania. And Dr. Weiss is a breast cancer survivor herself. So, she certainly knows of what she speaks. Good morning to you. DR. MARISA WEISS, CHIEF MEDICAL OFFICER AND FOUNDER OF BREASTCANCER.ORG: Good morning. JONES: So, you and I we were just talking, it was 12 years ago. DR. WEISS: Yes. 12 years ago. JONES: That you were diagnosed? DR. WEISS: Yes. I am very grateful. I benefitted from early detection. And I am here today to share important information to help save other lives. JONES: I love that. So, with that, let`s dig in and get right to it. How do women assess their personal risk for breast cancer? I am hearing about women who have no family history getting breast cancer. DR. WEISS: Exactly. So, breast cancer is the most common cancer to affect women and 75 percent of the time, there is no family history. JONES: 76 percent? DR. WEISS: Yes. No inherited gene abnormality. But if you do have in your family breast cancer, ovarian cancer, prostate, melanoma in your family, you could be at higher risk of breast cancer because of an inherited gene. JONES: OK. DR. WEISS: So, that`s why it`s so important to share that information with your doctor, to assess your risk, you know, to take and make a plan to lower your risk. JONES: Absolutely. What do you mean by background? DR. WEISS: And consider genetic testing. JONES: OK. DR. WEISS: Background, well, you heard from Katie Couric about dense breast tissue? JONES: Yes. DR. WEISS: Putting you at higher risk, you might need extra test to find it. Also, black women are more likely to get breast cancer at younger ages at more advanced stages and have a more serious type of breast cancer. Jewish women are more likely to inherit an abnormal breast cancer gene. And age, our risk goes up as we grow older. But keep in mind, 20 percent of breast cancers happen before the age of 50. JONES: My goodness, which is why screening is so important. DR. WEISS: So important. Absolutely. MARTIN-BROOKS: Speaking of that, Dr. Weiss, earlier detection. DR. WEISS: Absolutely. MARTIN-BROOKS: And we talked a little bit about this in the green room. So, I have a history in my family. DR. WEISS: Yes. MARTIN-BROOKS: They told me 45 you start, this was five years ago. Now, is it 40? When should you start for these yearly mammograms? DR. WEISS: Yes. I say, please, everyone, get your yearly mammograms starting at age 40. And if you have -- MARTIN-BROOKS: Even if you don`t have family history? [09:15:00] DR. WEISS: If you don`t have family history, that`s right. And if you let things slip and slide because of the pandemic, call today to schedule your appointment. You also want to make sure that you get a comprehensive breast exam by your doctor or nurse practitioner once yearly and then, examine yourself on a regular basis just to make sure that you know what`s normal, what may have changed. And if you are at extra risk because of a strong family history, an inherited gene, or many you have dense breast, you might need extra tests like adding an ultrasound to your mammogram, then getting an MRI six months later and then, repeating that overtime. MARTIN-BROOKS: It`s really important information. DR. WEISS: It really is. Hey, Al. ROKER: So, Dr. Weiss, what should women be looking for, you know, when you talk about self-exams, things like that? DR. WEISS: Yes. Well, as it turns out, most breast cancers don`t produce signs or symptoms. They are found by mammography. But people regularly feel things or see things like a lump or an area of thickening in the breast or the armpit, area of swelling or a bulge or the skin might be dimpled or retracted, you might notice a nipple discharge or you might have, let`s say, pain or discomfort in the breast. If you have any of those symptoms that are new and persist, check them out. Call your doctor. Don`t wait. You want to find breast cancer as early as possible when it`s most treatable. ROKER: OK. DR. WEISS: Thank you. MELVIN: Dr. Weiss, what are some things that folks who are watching or listening can do to reduce the risk? DR. WEISS: Yes. Well, the good news is the same steps that reduce your risk of breast cancer improve your overall health. MELVIN: OK. DR. WEISS: Like getting to and sticking to a healthy weight, exercising regularly, even 10 minutes a day makes a big difference. You want to eat mostly a vegetarian-based diet with like meat, chicken, fish more as a sideshow. And then, reduce your alcohol use, since the more you drink, the higher the risk. And stop smoking because it increases the risk for all kinds of things. I say start with one step, then go to a next step. And before you know it, you will be in a healthier place. MELVIN: So, let`s just say you go to the doctor, you get the diagnosis. You get the dreaded C word. DR. WEISS: Yes. MELVIN: You hear it. DR. WEISS: Yes. MELVIN: Life is not over. How do you manage that part? DR. WEISS: It can really make -- I mean, I have been there. I am a doctor and a patient as it were. Well, it`s so important to get answers to your medical questions to reduce uncertainty and to know what to expect. Put your questions and concerns on a list and put the most important ones on the top and call, e-mail or text your doctor to get answers to your questions. Hey, don`t try to do it all. We women carry the weight of the world on our shoulders, right? So, delegate and reach out for help with like childcare, grocery shopping, you know, housework, all the things that don`t matter as much. Save your precious energy for your treatment. MELVIN: Lean on your friends and family. DR. WEISS: Absolutely. MELVIN: I want to ask you, you mentioned something a few moments ago, I want to follow up on. DR. WEISS: Yes. MELVIN: Genetic testing. Who should consider that? DR. WEISS: Anyone who`s got breast cancer who is -- can be -- can get genetic testing. But if you`re diagnosed at age 50 or younger, if you have a history of ovarian cancer in the family, there are men in the family with breast cancer, there`s a history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic cancer, melanoma, you should ask to get genetic testing. MELVIN: OK. DR. WEISS: If you`re of Jewish background, you should ask for genetic testing. MELVIN: OK. ROKER: And you mentioned men, doctor. DR. WEISS: Exactly. If you are a man who gets breast cancer, you are more likely to have an inherited genetic mutation, like BRCA1 and BRCA2. And you want to make sure, if there are any men in the family -- because men get breast cancer just as -- not as often as women, like about 1 percent of the time, but that goes along with higher risk of an inherited gene abnormality. ROKER: All right. MELVIN: Thank you. JONES: It`s important that we`re talking about it.; MELVIN: Thank you so much. DR. WEISS: Thank you. JONES: Dr. Weiss, thank you. DR. WEISS: You`re welcome. JONES: And for more information on breast cancer awareness, we put so much on our website. Just go to today.com/health. MELVIN: When we come back, former ambassador to the United Nations and governor of the greatest state in the country, South Carolina, Nikki Haley is here like. We`re going to talk about leadership, we`re going to talk about powerful women and of course, we`ll also talk about 2024. ROKER: Well, she lives in New York State, which is -- anyway. Then multi- talented actor and producer Kate Del Castillo is joining us in studio to talk about bringing back her international hit series. "3rd Hour of TODAY" will be right back live from New York State. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:20:00] JONES: We are back on this Monday morning. And we are reminded of a famous quote, this is from Margaret Thatcher . She said, if you want something said, ask a man. If you want something done, ask a woman. MELVIN: Former South Carolina governor, former ambassador to the United Nations under President Donald Trump , Nikki Haley took that advice to heart. In fact, it`s the basis of her new book. There`s the title, "If You Want Something Done...: Leader Lessons from BOLD WOMEN." In the book, she profiles that obstacles and accomplishments of 10 powerful women throughout history and weaves them in with her own story. And the former ambassador joins us this morning. Good to see you again. JONES: Good morning. NIKKI HALEY, FORMER SOUTH CAROLINA GOVERNOR, FORMER AMBASSADOR TO THE UNITED NATIONS UNDER DONALD TRUMP AND AUTHOR: Great to be with both of you. MELVIN: Welcome back. Welcome back. I just told you in the green room, I started reading the book this weekend. It`s a fantastic concept. We`re going to dig into the book in just a moment. But let`s start with -- because, I mean, the reality as you write this book about accomplished women and there has been some talk, perhaps you have heard, 2024, that maybe this accomplished woman would for president of the United States. I know you have said you haven`t made a decision. How are you going to decide? What factors will you consider and what`s your timetable? HALEY: Well, I mean, I think, first of all, our focus is November. You know, everybody`s looking at the November elections and I have been all over the country working on that. And then, after, you know, the first of the year, Michael and I will sit down. We`ll figure out if there is a place for me. If there is a place for me, I`ve never lost a race, I am not going to start now. We will put 1,000 percent in and we will finish it. If there`s not a place for me, I have fought for this country as long as I can remember and I will do it until my last breath. MELVIN: And you -- I think you said last spring that if your former boss, Former President Trump, if he does decide to run, that you will sit this one out, you won`t run. Is that still the case? And if so, why? HALEY: I mean, we`ll see if he runs. You know, we`ll see if he runs. He hasn`t said that he is going to run. And so, you know, we will make a decision after the first of next year and figure it out. MELVIN: Would you ever run against him? HALEY: It`s not something I think about. I was proud to serve with him in the administration. It`s something that, you know, I can tell you that I`m thrilled with the accomplishments we did together. We had a great working relationship. But right now, we will see what he does. JONES: You have been very involved in the midterm elections this year. As you know, some Republicans, you know, the candidates running have denied the results of the election. Do you think that`s a disqualifier? HALEY: Well, I mean, I think that the candidates I`m helping, they are really focused on the economy. They are very focused on crime. They are focused on education. Those are the things people are talking about. [09:25:00] I mean, do I think that the elections were real? Yes. Do I think that Joe Biden is the president? Yes. Unfortunately, I am not happy with that, but that is what it is. And the candidates that we`re talking about, real people, they are talking about the fact that it cost more money to go to the gas station, and that`s how they go to work. It cost more money at the grocery store, and that`s how they feed their family. JONES: So, they deny those election results though, you don`t think that`s a disqualifier? HALEY: I don`t know that I`ve talked to anyone that`s denied the election results. Everybody that I`m helping acknowledges the fact that the elections, you know, were real. MELVIN: Let`s talk about the book. What was the impetus? How did it come about? HALEY: You know, it`s -- this is a book about ordinary women that did extraordinary things. And if you are a parent, you know that if you raise strong women, they become strong -- if you raise strong girls, they become strong women and strong women become strong leaders. And so, I was a fan of Margaret Thatcher . And loved how she was very confident in herself. She believed in Britain but believed had herself. And then, when I went to the United Nations, I learned more about Jeane Kirkpatrick, who was my predecessor. And she was someone who was unapologetic about loving America. But then, I met people like Nadia Murad, who was in Iraq. She was part of the Yazidi community. They were overtaken by ISIS. She was gang raped. She was -- her family died and she came out, won the Nobel Peace Prize, fought for her community. Or people like Cindy Warmbier, where, you kno, her son, Otto Warmbier, we know was tortured in North Korea. But you find these stories that are just fantastic of women who had sheer will and knew that they were meant for great things, and they deserve to be in the room. And I hope that this is a reminder to every parent who has a child that we want those kids to know they deserve to be in the room. If you are someone who has had a female mentor or a leader, give them this as a thank you and say, thank you for believing in me. And these are inspirational stories. I hope it will inspire a lot of women. MELVIN: One of the things I found interesting in the book is this idea -- and I never knew this -- you, throughout the course of your career, you send notes to women who inspire you. Who have you sent notes to? HALEY: I mean, you know, any time I see a woman make a leap. You know, I think I sent one to the head of the New York Stock Exchange. I send it to the first female head of city. You know, I just sent it to the new female anchor at Fox News. You know, any time I see a woman do something, I think we have to give that and push them and say, go get them. You know, because women second guess themselves. And any time we can go and just push them a little further and say, you`ve got this, it`s important. MELVIN: Yes. JONES: And finally, listen, we just -- you just heard us talking about breast cancer awareness, we were talking so much about health and wellness for women. I was just reading that you`re running now. Did you just finish a half marathon? HALEY: I finished a half marathon in December. MELVIN: Wow. HALEY: Last I told you, I picked up running. MELVIN: Yes. HALEY: I finished a half marathon in December. JONES: What did (INAUDIBLE) finally? HALEY: You know, it`s a great way to tune out the noise. Like, a lot of people don`t realize I don`t live in the politics. MELVIN: Yes. HALEY: I have a regular life. But when you get out and run, it`s a great way to just kind of center your mind. You can take God with you and you just plan your day out and you can kind of figure out what really matters. It`s a great way to kind of forget the world for a while. So, it`s -- JONES: So, you`re just going to keep running? Marathon next? HALEY: I ran seven miles yesterday. I`m going to keep on going. MELVIN: Wow. JONES: OK. MELVIN: Tell Michael hello. Is he running with you? HALEY: Yes, he is. MELVIN: Love it. JONES: Good deal. MELVIN: All right. Thank you for your time this morning. JONES: Thank you. HALEY: Great to be with you. MELVIN: Congratulations again on the book. Again, it`s called, If You Want Something Done...: Leadership Lessons from BOLD WOMEN." It`s out tomorrow. JONES: Thank you. All right. Coming up, Kate Del Castillo joins us live. We`re going to find out about the highly anticipated return of her hit show. STEPHANIE MANSOUR, TODAY FITNESS CONTRIBUTOR: All right. So, for our October workout plan, we are including strength training. headline: How To Identify Your Personal Breast Cancer Risks And The Steps You Can Take To Reduce It
story_text: [09:10:00] SHEINELLE JONES: We are back with our "Pink Power" series to mark the start of Breast Cancer Awareness Month. And this morning, we have a checklist of important information all women need to know from risk factors to screening and more. So, joining us now is Dr. Marisa Weiss , director of breast radiation oncology at Lankenau Medical Center in Pennsylvania. And Dr. Weiss is a breast cancer survivor herself. So, she certainly knows of what she speaks. Good morning to you. DR. MARISA WEISS, CHIEF MEDICAL OFFICER AND FOUNDER OF BREASTCANCER.ORG: Good morning. JONES: So, you and I we were just talking, it was 12 years ago. DR. WEISS: Yes. 12 years ago. JONES: That you were diagnosed? DR. WEISS: Yes. I am very grateful. I benefitted from early detection. And I am here today to share important information to help save other lives. JONES: I love that. So, with that, let`s dig in and get right to it. How do women assess their personal risk for breast cancer? I am hearing about women who have no family history getting breast cancer. DR. WEISS: Exactly. So, breast cancer is the most common cancer to affect women and 75 percent of the time, there is no family history. JONES: 76 percent? DR. WEISS: Yes. No inherited gene abnormality. But if you do have in your family breast cancer, ovarian cancer, prostate, melanoma in your family, you could be at higher risk of breast cancer because of an inherited gene. JONES: OK. DR. WEISS: So, that`s why it`s so important to share that information with your doctor, to assess your risk, you know, to take and make a plan to lower your risk. JONES: Absolutely. What do you mean by background? DR. WEISS: And consider genetic testing. JONES: OK. DR. WEISS: Background, well, you heard from Katie Couric about dense breast tissue? JONES: Yes. DR. WEISS: Putting you at higher risk, you might need extra test to find it. Also, black women are more likely to get breast cancer at younger ages at more advanced stages and have a more serious type of breast cancer. Jewish women are more likely to inherit an abnormal breast cancer gene. And age, our risk goes up as we grow older. But keep in mind, 20 percent of breast cancers happen before the age of 50. JONES: My goodness, which is why screening is so important. DR. WEISS: So important. Absolutely. MARTIN-BROOKS: Speaking of that, Dr. Weiss, earlier detection. DR. WEISS: Absolutely. MARTIN-BROOKS: And we talked a little bit about this in the green room. So, I have a history in my family. DR. WEISS: Yes. MARTIN-BROOKS: They told me 45 you start, this was five years ago. Now, is it 40? When should you start for these yearly mammograms? DR. WEISS: Yes. I say, please, everyone, get your yearly mammograms starting at age 40. And if you have -- MARTIN-BROOKS: Even if you don`t have family history? [09:15:00] DR. WEISS: If you don`t have family history, that`s right. And if you let things slip and slide because of the pandemic, call today to schedule your appointment. You also want to make sure that you get a comprehensive breast exam by your doctor or nurse practitioner once yearly and then, examine yourself on a regular basis just to make sure that you know what`s normal, what may have changed. And if you are at extra risk because of a strong family history, an inherited gene, or many you have dense breast, you might need extra tests like adding an ultrasound to your mammogram, then getting an MRI six months later and then, repeating that overtime. MARTIN-BROOKS: It`s really important information. DR. WEISS: It really is. Hey, Al. ROKER: So, Dr. Weiss, what should women be looking for, you know, when you talk about self-exams, things like that? DR. WEISS: Yes. Well, as it turns out, most breast cancers don`t produce signs or symptoms. They are found by mammography. But people regularly feel things or see things like a lump or an area of thickening in the breast or the armpit, area of swelling or a bulge or the skin might be dimpled or retracted, you might notice a nipple discharge or you might have, let`s say, pain or discomfort in the breast. If you have any of those symptoms that are new and persist, check them out. Call your doctor. Don`t wait. You want to find breast cancer as early as possible when it`s most treatable. ROKER: OK. DR. WEISS: Thank you. MELVIN: Dr. Weiss, what are some things that folks who are watching or listening can do to reduce the risk? DR. WEISS: Yes. Well, the good news is the same steps that reduce your risk of breast cancer improve your overall health. MELVIN: OK. DR. WEISS: Like getting to and sticking to a healthy weight, exercising regularly, even 10 minutes a day makes a big difference. You want to eat mostly a vegetarian-based diet with like meat, chicken, fish more as a sideshow. And then, reduce your alcohol use, since the more you drink, the higher the risk. And stop smoking because it increases the risk for all kinds of things. I say start with one step, then go to a next step. And before you know it, you will be in a healthier place. MELVIN: So, let`s just say you go to the doctor, you get the diagnosis. You get the dreaded C word. DR. WEISS: Yes. MELVIN: You hear it. DR. WEISS: Yes. MELVIN: Life is not over. How do you manage that part? DR. WEISS: It can really make -- I mean, I have been there. I am a doctor and a patient as it were. Well, it`s so important to get answers to your medical questions to reduce uncertainty and to know what to expect. Put your questions and concerns on a list and put the most important ones on the top and call, e-mail or text your doctor to get answers to your questions. Hey, don`t try to do it all. We women carry the weight of the world on our shoulders, right? So, delegate and reach out for help with like childcare, grocery shopping, you know, housework, all the things that don`t matter as much. Save your precious energy for your treatment. MELVIN: Lean on your friends and family. DR. WEISS: Absolutely. MELVIN: I want to ask you, you mentioned something a few moments ago, I want to follow up on. DR. WEISS: Yes. MELVIN: Genetic testing. Who should consider that? DR. WEISS: Anyone who`s got breast cancer who is -- can be -- can get genetic testing. But if you`re diagnosed at age 50 or younger, if you have a history of ovarian cancer in the family, there are men in the family with breast cancer, there`s a history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic cancer, melanoma, you should ask to get genetic testing. MELVIN: OK. DR. WEISS: If you`re of Jewish background, you should ask for genetic testing. MELVIN: OK. ROKER: And you mentioned men, doctor. DR. WEISS: Exactly. If you are a man who gets breast cancer, you are more likely to have an inherited genetic mutation, like BRCA1 and BRCA2. And you want to make sure, if there are any men in the family -- because men get breast cancer just as -- not as often as women, like about 1 percent of the time, but that goes along with higher risk of an inherited gene abnormality. ROKER: All right. MELVIN: Thank you. JONES: It`s important that we`re talking about it.; MELVIN: Thank you so much. DR. WEISS: Thank you. JONES: Dr. Weiss, thank you. DR. WEISS: You`re welcome. JONES: And for more information on breast cancer awareness, we put so much on our website. Just go to today.com/health. MELVIN: When we come back, former ambassador to the United Nations and governor of the greatest state in the country, South Carolina, Nikki Haley is here like. We`re going to talk about leadership, we`re going to talk about powerful women and of course, we`ll also talk about 2024. ROKER: Well, she lives in New York State, which is -- anyway. Then multi- talented actor and producer Kate Del Castillo is joining us in studio to talk about bringing back her international hit series. "3rd Hour of TODAY" will be right back live from New York State. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [09:20:00] JONES: We are back on this Monday morning. And we are reminded of a famous quote, this is from Margaret Thatcher . She said, if you want something said, ask a man. If you want something done, ask a woman. MELVIN: Former South Carolina governor, former ambassador to the United Nations under President Donald Trump , Nikki Haley took that advice to heart. In fact, it`s the basis of her new book. There`s the title, "If You Want Something Done...: Leader Lessons from BOLD WOMEN." In the book, she profiles that obstacles and accomplishments of 10 powerful women throughout history and weaves them in with her own story. And the former ambassador joins us this morning. Good to see you again. JONES: Good morning. NIKKI HALEY, FORMER SOUTH CAROLINA GOVERNOR, FORMER AMBASSADOR TO THE UNITED NATIONS UNDER DONALD TRUMP AND AUTHOR: Great to be with both of you. MELVIN: Welcome back. Welcome back. I just told you in the green room, I started reading the book this weekend. It`s a fantastic concept. We`re going to dig into the book in just a moment. But let`s start with -- because, I mean, the reality as you write this book about accomplished women and there has been some talk, perhaps you have heard, 2024, that maybe this accomplished woman would for president of the United States. I know you have said you haven`t made a decision. How are you going to decide? What factors will you consider and what`s your timetable? HALEY: Well, I mean, I think, first of all, our focus is November. You know, everybody`s looking at the November elections and I have been all over the country working on that. And then, after, you know, the first of the year, Michael and I will sit down. We`ll figure out if there is a place for me. If there is a place for me, I`ve never lost a race, I am not going to start now. We will put 1,000 percent in and we will finish it. If there`s not a place for me, I have fought for this country as long as I can remember and I will do it until my last breath. MELVIN: And you -- I think you said last spring that if your former boss, Former President Trump, if he does decide to run, that you will sit this one out, you won`t run. Is that still the case? And if so, why? HALEY: I mean, we`ll see if he runs. You know, we`ll see if he runs. He hasn`t said that he is going to run. And so, you know, we will make a decision after the first of next year and figure it out. MELVIN: Would you ever run against him? HALEY: It`s not something I think about. I was proud to serve with him in the administration. It`s something that, you know, I can tell you that I`m thrilled with the accomplishments we did together. We had a great working relationship. But right now, we will see what he does. JONES: You have been very involved in the midterm elections this year. As you know, some Republicans, you know, the candidates running have denied the results of the election. Do you think that`s a disqualifier? HALEY: Well, I mean, I think that the candidates I`m helping, they are really focused on the economy. They are very focused on crime. They are focused on education. Those are the things people are talking about. [09:25:00] I mean, do I think that the elections were real? Yes. Do I think that Joe Biden is the president? Yes. Unfortunately, I am not happy with that, but that is what it is. And the candidates that we`re talking about, real people, they are talking about the fact that it cost more money to go to the gas station, and that`s how they go to work. It cost more money at the grocery store, and that`s how they feed their family. JONES: So, they deny those election results though, you don`t think that`s a disqualifier? HALEY: I don`t know that I`ve talked to anyone that`s denied the election results. Everybody that I`m helping acknowledges the fact that the elections, you know, were real. MELVIN: Let`s talk about the book. What was the impetus? How did it come about? HALEY: You know, it`s -- this is a book about ordinary women that did extraordinary things. And if you are a parent, you know that if you raise strong women, they become strong -- if you raise strong girls, they become strong women and strong women become strong leaders. And so, I was a fan of Margaret Thatcher . And loved how she was very confident in herself. She believed in Britain but believed had herself. And then, when I went to the United Nations, I learned more about Jeane Kirkpatrick, who was my predecessor. And she was someone who was unapologetic about loving America. But then, I met people like Nadia Murad, who was in Iraq. She was part of the Yazidi community. They were overtaken by ISIS. She was gang raped. headline: Katie Couric`s Message On The Importance Of Those Yearly Mammograms As She Reveals Her Own Breast Cancer Diagnosis
story_text: [07:41:32] CRAIG MELVIN: We are back. It is 7:41. We`re back with In-Depth Today. And this morning, an important story that`s really close to our hearts. HODA KOTB: Yes, every two minutes, a woman in this country is diagnosed with breast cancer and yesterday, our friend and our former colleague Katie Couric revealed she is now one of them. SAVANNAH GUTHRIE: And of course Katie has been on the frontlines of cancer awareness for decades, she lost her husband to cancer. And she`s using her story now to urge all women to get checked and to advocate for themselves. Sheinelle is here with more on that. Hi, good morning. SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. As she battles breast cancer, Katie is turning her story into a cautionary tale in hopes of saving lives. She wants to educate women not only on the importance of screening but also about something called dense breast tissue. It affects nearly half of women in this country including Katie. And doctors say knowing you have it and how to ask for proper screenings could be lifesaving. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) JONES (voice-over): Former today anchor Katie Couric has revealed that for the past several months, she has been privately battling cancer. COURIC: Thank you all for your support. JONES (voice-over): In an essay titled "Why Not Me?" the 65-year-old journalist says she was stunned by a stage one breast cancer diagnosis in June after missing her annual mammogram. I`m normally vigilant, bordering on neurotic, about taking care of my health. COURIC: I want to make sure that you all don`t put off your mammograms. JONES (voice-over): Katie is among nearly half of women over 40 in the U.S. who have dense breast tissue, which makes it more difficult to detect abnormalities on a mammogram and also increases your risk of breast cancer. Armed with this knowledge, her mammogram was followed by additional screening using an ultrasound, doctors biopsied a mass. The next day, Katie received the shocking results. It`s cancer. You`re going to be fine, but we need to make a plan. I felt sick and the room started to spin. What does this mean? What will the next weeks, months, even years look like? This isn`t the first time cancer has touched her life. Katie has long been an advocate for cancer awareness and screenings ever since her husband, Jay, was diagnosed with colon cancer and died of the disease at the age of 42. COURIC: Words of course will never describe how devastating this loss has been. JONES (voice-over): She famously underwent an on air colonoscopy on Today to encourage others to get checked. As a result, screenings went up by 20 percent, some dubbing it the Couric effect. COURIC: I have a pretty little colon. JONES (voice-over): She also lost her sister, Emily, to pancreatic cancer and 2001. The deaths of her loved ones prompting Katie to co found Stand Up to Cancer. COURIC: And I just realized I had to do something about this. JONES (voice-over): But with no family history of breast cancer, her own diagnosis came as a particular shock. Katie`s surgeon Dr. Lisa Newman. DR. LISA NEWMAN, KATIE COURIC`S SURGEON: More than three quarters of the breast cancers that we diagnose occur in women that do not have any established risk factors for breast cancer. JONES (voice-over): Katie`s cancer was caught early. She underwent a lumpectomy along with radiation and says she`ll need to take medication for the next five years. NEWMAN: It is wonderful that Katie has gone public with her experience and early detection of breast cancers will save millions of lives. JONES (voice-over): Now as she`s done before, Katie is determined to shine a light once again, on the importance of screening for cancer. Please get your annual mammogram. I was six months late this time. I shudder to think what might have happened if I had put it off longer. (END VIDEOTAPE) [07:45:08] JONES: Just six months late, here`s what we know for sure. When we do stories like this, our hope is that a woman watching or maybe a family member, that we give you a little nudge to go ahead and get that checkup. That`s what`s most important. KOTB: Six months is nothing, I mean especially with COVID and people not going in for a checkups. GUTHRIE: Yes, and you know, you kind of think, when I feel something -- KOTB: I did that. She thought she did it. She`s like, oh, it`s been that long. GUTHRIE: Really, for a mammogram or any of those screening, I actually made an appointment yesterday for a yearly physical I need. And it`s like because you remember, like, oh, yes, you know what, I`m going to do it. I`m not going to put it off another day. JONES: These kinds of stories save lives. MELVIN: We`re going to hear from Katie too, right? GUTHRIE: Yes, she`s going to join us on Monday. It`ll be her first live interview since sharing her diagnosis. It`ll be good to see Katie and give her a hug. And obviously she`s got a really important message to share. KOTB: We look forward to that. We`re going to get another check of the weather from Bill Karins. He`s in for Al. And some people have been wondering during the storm, where is Al, Al happen to test positive for COVID. We`re happy to say he`s feeling fine, just mild symptoms. He`s home. KARINS: He`s been sending us notes like he`s, you know, he wants to be here, he feels well. I can only imagine a step count in his house just like going back before, just like, you know, it`s like, yes. GUTHRIE: Disengage. KARINS: But Al has help us build an incredible weather team here at NBC News. And, you know, we`re getting you through this storm. And Al we`ll see you back here very soon. So concerns for today, the one thing I`m going to be watching is the storm surge. We have a storm surge warning still in effect for areas of northeast Florida. We`re not done yet. Irma really surprised us with the storm surge in the Jacksonville area. And here`s what we`re going to watch, the St. Johns River is one of the few rivers in our country that actually flows from south to north so that water that`s now falling in Orlando is going to trickle northwards up through the river at the same time. We`re going to see the storm surge coming in this afternoon at high tide about noon. This is all going to meet near Jacksonville. So we`re going to watch that area closely for the possibility of the four to six feet of storm surge. Right now they`ve already got a surge of about two feet. That`s look at your national weather. Now here`s a look at the weather outside your window. (LOCAL NEWS) KARINS: And that`s your Thursday forecast. MELVIN: All right. Thank you, Bill. Up next, he did it. Homerun history overnight, and we`re going to hear from Yankee`s superstar Aaron Judge after belting that 61st of the season to officially join baseball royalty. But first, these messages. headline: Today for September 29, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Hi everybody. It`s Thursday. Millions in Florida waking up to catastrophic damage from Ian. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes, the full impact being revealed as the sunrises this morning. It is September 29th. This is Today. Path of destruction, massive flooding and power outages as Ian barrels across Florida crashing ashore as one of the strongest hurricanes to ever hit the state. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: All the sudden I felt something and then heard like a train coming right to the house. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Nearly 3 million people in the dark, the devastating storm surge leaving entire neighborhoods underwater, homes and cars floating down streets. This hospital swapped from above and below, losing part of its roof, its ground floor flooded, crews still carrying out emergency rescues on land and at sea. We`re live across the state with complete coverage and what millions need to know as the threat moves up the East Coast. Get out, the urgent security alert for all Americans in Russia to leave the country immediately. And the new warning that anyone there with dual citizenship couldn`t be drafted into the Ukraine war, we`ll have the very latest. Breast cancer battle, well wishes pouring in for Katie Couric this morning after she revealed her diagnosis. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) KATIE COURIC, AMERICAN JOURNALIST: Thank you all for your support. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Just ahead, her decision to speak out and what she wants all women to know. Those stories, plus, historic blast. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Judge keep the left field. This could be it. See you. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Yankee`s superstar Aaron Judge crushes his record tying 61st homerun of the season, cementing his place among baseball royalty. Today, Thursday, September 29th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Good Thursday morning. So happy you`re joining us today. Good to see you. GUTHRIE: Yes. The sun is coming up in Florida and we`re getting a closer look now at the widespread devastation left behind by Ian. KOTB: Yes, there are two major concerns right now there, the flooding of course and the power outages. Nearly 3 million people across the state woke up this morning and could not turn the lights on, no electricity. GUTHRIE: Ian made landfall yesterday as a major category four packing 150 mile an hour winds and causing massive storm surges across Florida`s Gulf Coast. KOTB: So right now, Ian is making its way east toward the eastern side of Florida. We have a live look at some of the conditions going on. This is Orlando. And while the storm did weakened overnight, it still remains a serious threat. GUTHRIE: Yes, it`s a rain story there. And then once Ian heads away from Florida, it is expected to then curve back toward the Georgia, South Carolina coastlines impacting millions across the South in the coming days. KOTB: Yes, we got it all covered for you this morning. We`re going to start off with NBC`s Sam Brock. He is in Venice, Florida. That`s just north of where Ian made landfall. Hi, Sam, what`s the assessment this morning? SAM BROCK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Yes, Hoda, Savannah, good morning. It is terrifying to think what we`re going to see in the light of day. I was just talking to a police officer here in Venice. They resume search and rescue operations at 2 o`clock this morning looking for critically injured people. But he said look, I got to warn you, block to block, there`s dead wire, there`s live wire. As you look behind me right now, you`ll see splintered signs and power lines down all through here. Now when East Naples guys, there were 30 rescue missions yesterday as the urgent efforts right now are underway to find those imperiled by Ian. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BROCK (voice-over): It`s devastation that was predicted with the grim reality of this storm`s warped power defies imagination. Ian now with tropical storm hit the coast as a fierce hurricane shredding homes apart and Placida, Florida, tearing off roofs and splintering trees. While in the Tampa area, extremely causing this tree to crash through a home. In one of the hardest hit areas, Fort Myers, there were storm surges nearly seven feet high, nearly double the previous record more than 20 years ago. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Oh my God. BROCK (voice-over): The massive surge of water leaving entire communities completely underwater. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Do you want me to come out? BROCK (voice-over): Roads looking more like the ocean for block after block. Ian packed catastrophic 150 mile an hour winds knocking out power to more than 2 million customers. GOV. RON DESANTIS (R-FL): We have seen life threatening storm surge as was predicted. We`ve also seen major flooding, but that`s going to rank as one of the top five hurricanes to ever hit the Florida peninsula. BROCK (voice-over): This team of emergency responders unable to respond, a massive wall of water swamping their fire truck. [07:05:06] UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Now we have a truck issue and the guys are pushing the truck out of the bay. BROCK (voice-over): In Port Charlotte, hospital staff working through the storm to protect patients. Other first responders struggling to help those in need, unable to start rescues until after life threatening conditions subsided. Despite repeated warnings to leave, some people did not or could not evacuate. They found themselves stranded by a 12 foot storm surge. Mark and Elizabeth living in an apartment in Venice Island, Florida but at the last minute, grab their air mattresses and hunker down in this Sarasota office when her boss offered it to them. (on camera): Here you are with air mattresses in an office space. Your home is 50 or 100 miles away. But you consider yourself lucky. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We are. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes. BROCK: Is that because you`re saved from the storm? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes, yes, because somebody helped us. BROCK (voice-over): Others stayed behind in the flood zone, trying to help those who were unable to leave. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I want to help the people in here because they`re good people here in paradise. BROCK (voice-over): This morning, the destruction left behind by this massive blow from Mother Nature is just starting to come into focus. (END VIDEOTAPE) KOTB: Well, hats off to those first responders, all those helpers out there, Sam. There were some viral images in Tampa that were just shocking. It was actually Tampa Bay, and it looked dry. It looked like you could walk on it. People were taking video and pictures of it. What`s the after effects there? BROCK: Yes, so here`s the deal, Hoda, you`re seeing all this water being really sucked out. It`s called negative storm surge. And the reason behind it, you have counterclockwise winds and hurricanes. So on the northern edge of the eye wall, the water was being pulled out of Tampa Bay, into the Gulf of Mexico. The problem with this, Hoda, is the fact that it can then refill when wind directionality change. And it can happen in a matter of minutes. So if you see this, it might be tempting to go out there on the sand and check it out. Don`t do it for your own safety. Hoda? KOTB: All right, Sam Brock for us there in Venice, Sam, thanks. GUTHRIE: Yes. These conditions can change in a split second, the water has finally stopped rising in Fort Myers. But this morning, the impact of the catastrophic flooding there is being felt across the city. And joining us now Fort Myers Mayor Kevin Anderson. Mr. Mayor, good morning. We`re glad to have you on the phone with us this morning. Have you been able to assess damage? I know it`s still early there. What`s your sense of how bad it was? MAYOR KEVIN ANDERSON, FORT MYERS, FL: We haven`t had a full assessment obviously with the sun just coming up, but it is pretty bad. I`m standing on a floating concrete dock. I`m down in the River District of downtown. The problem is the dock is in the middle of an intersection, a block, two blocks away from the water. This is about a piece of concrete that weighs a ton. And it was moved this far away. It shows you how powerful the waters were last night. KOTB: I know one of the things, that`s most concerning in a moment like this is what happened to the people who decided to stay or who were left behind. Have you guys been able to conduct rescues? Do you know how many people are still out there and in need of your help? ANDERSON: We would estimate several dozen people who stayed behind were in need of some assistance. Our teams have been working on that. I`m happy to report at this time. I`ve been not -- I haven`t been told of any loss of life in the city. Now keep in mind, we have a metropolitan area and there may be some outside, but inside the city there`s been no reports to my knowledge. GUTHRIE: Fort Myers more or less took a direct hit, Mr. Mayor, what`s your sense of how this compares to other storms that Fort Myers has experienced? ANDERSON: I came here in the mid 70s. I was on the police department for almost 25 years, so a lot of storms here. This is by far the worst storm I have ever witnessed. They`re watching the water from my condo in the heart of downtown, watching that water rise and just flat out all the stories on the first floor. It was heartbreaking. KOTB: Boy, for -- Mayor for you who`s been there all those years and seen so many storms come and go to take a direct hit. So what is the plan now, like walk us through what will happen this morning and the days ahead? ANDERSON: So the first thing we need to do is make sure the roads are passable. And they`re safe. We do have a curfew in place for next 48 hours until we get a handle on everything. Once we get the roads cleared, you know, FPL will start working on the electricity. Our teams will be out there going through the neighborhoods trying to make sure people are safe, getting assistance, anyone who needs it.
