headline: Today for September 29, 2022, NBC
story_text: (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:00:16] SAVANNAH GUTHRIE, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Hi everybody. It`s Thursday. Millions in Florida waking up to catastrophic damage from Ian. HODA KOTB, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Yes, the full impact being revealed as the sunrises this morning. It is September 29th. This is Today. Path of destruction, massive flooding and power outages as Ian barrels across Florida crashing ashore as one of the strongest hurricanes to ever hit the state. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: All the sudden I felt something and then heard like a train coming right to the house. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Nearly 3 million people in the dark, the devastating storm surge leaving entire neighborhoods underwater, homes and cars floating down streets. This hospital swapped from above and below, losing part of its roof, its ground floor flooded, crews still carrying out emergency rescues on land and at sea. We`re live across the state with complete coverage and what millions need to know as the threat moves up the East Coast. Get out, the urgent security alert for all Americans in Russia to leave the country immediately. And the new warning that anyone there with dual citizenship couldn`t be drafted into the Ukraine war, we`ll have the very latest. Breast cancer battle, well wishes pouring in for Katie Couric this morning after she revealed her diagnosis. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) KATIE COURIC, AMERICAN JOURNALIST: Thank you all for your support. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Just ahead, her decision to speak out and what she wants all women to know. Those stories, plus, historic blast. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Judge keep the left field. This could be it. See you. (END VIDEO CLIP) KOTB: Yankee`s superstar Aaron Judge crushes his record tying 61st homerun of the season, cementing his place among baseball royalty. Today, Thursday, September 29th, 2022. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: From NBC News, this is Today with Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb live from Studio 1A in Rockefeller Plaza. KOTB: Good Thursday morning. So happy you`re joining us today. Good to see you. GUTHRIE: Yes. The sun is coming up in Florida and we`re getting a closer look now at the widespread devastation left behind by Ian. KOTB: Yes, there are two major concerns right now there, the flooding of course and the power outages. Nearly 3 million people across the state woke up this morning and could not turn the lights on, no electricity. GUTHRIE: Ian made landfall yesterday as a major category four packing 150 mile an hour winds and causing massive storm surges across Florida`s Gulf Coast. KOTB: So right now, Ian is making its way east toward the eastern side of Florida. We have a live look at some of the conditions going on. This is Orlando. And while the storm did weakened overnight, it still remains a serious threat. GUTHRIE: Yes, it`s a rain story there. And then once Ian heads away from Florida, it is expected to then curve back toward the Georgia, South Carolina coastlines impacting millions across the South in the coming days. KOTB: Yes, we got it all covered for you this morning. We`re going to start off with NBC`s Sam Brock. He is in Venice, Florida. That`s just north of where Ian made landfall. Hi, Sam, what`s the assessment this morning? SAM BROCK, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Yes, Hoda, Savannah, good morning. It is terrifying to think what we`re going to see in the light of day. I was just talking to a police officer here in Venice. They resume search and rescue operations at 2 o`clock this morning looking for critically injured people. But he said look, I got to warn you, block to block, there`s dead wire, there`s live wire. As you look behind me right now, you`ll see splintered signs and power lines down all through here. Now when East Naples guys, there were 30 rescue missions yesterday as the urgent efforts right now are underway to find those imperiled by Ian. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) BROCK (voice-over): It`s devastation that was predicted with the grim reality of this storm`s warped power defies imagination. Ian now with tropical storm hit the coast as a fierce hurricane shredding homes apart and Placida, Florida, tearing off roofs and splintering trees. While in the Tampa area, extremely causing this tree to crash through a home. In one of the hardest hit areas, Fort Myers, there were storm surges nearly seven feet high, nearly double the previous record more than 20 years ago. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Oh my God. BROCK (voice-over): The massive surge of water leaving entire communities completely underwater. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Do you want me to come out? BROCK (voice-over): Roads looking more like the ocean for block after block. Ian packed catastrophic 150 mile an hour winds knocking out power to more than 2 million customers. GOV. RON DESANTIS (R-FL): We have seen life threatening storm surge as was predicted. We`ve also seen major flooding, but that`s going to rank as one of the top five hurricanes to ever hit the Florida peninsula. BROCK (voice-over): This team of emergency responders unable to respond, a massive wall of water swamping their fire truck. [07:05:06] UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Now we have a truck issue and the guys are pushing the truck out of the bay. BROCK (voice-over): In Port Charlotte, hospital staff working through the storm to protect patients. Other first responders struggling to help those in need, unable to start rescues until after life threatening conditions subsided. Despite repeated warnings to leave, some people did not or could not evacuate. They found themselves stranded by a 12 foot storm surge. Mark and Elizabeth living in an apartment in Venice Island, Florida but at the last minute, grab their air mattresses and hunker down in this Sarasota office when her boss offered it to them. (on camera): Here you are with air mattresses in an office space. Your home is 50 or 100 miles away. But you consider yourself lucky. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We are. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes. BROCK: Is that because you`re saved from the storm? UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes, yes, because somebody helped us. BROCK (voice-over): Others stayed behind in the flood zone, trying to help those who were unable to leave. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I want to help the people in here because they`re good people here in paradise. BROCK (voice-over): This morning, the destruction left behind by this massive blow from Mother Nature is just starting to come into focus. (END VIDEOTAPE) KOTB: Well, hats off to those first responders, all those helpers out there, Sam. There were some viral images in Tampa that were just shocking. It was actually Tampa Bay, and it looked dry. It looked like you could walk on it. People were taking video and pictures of it. What`s the after effects there? BROCK: Yes, so here`s the deal, Hoda, you`re seeing all this water being really sucked out. It`s called negative storm surge. And the reason behind it, you have counterclockwise winds and hurricanes. So on the northern edge of the eye wall, the water was being pulled out of Tampa Bay, into the Gulf of Mexico. The problem with this, Hoda, is the fact that it can then refill when wind directionality change. And it can happen in a matter of minutes. So if you see this, it might be tempting to go out there on the sand and check it out. Don`t do it for your own safety. Hoda? KOTB: All right, Sam Brock for us there in Venice, Sam, thanks. GUTHRIE: Yes. These conditions can change in a split second, the water has finally stopped rising in Fort Myers. But this morning, the impact of the catastrophic flooding there is being felt across the city. And joining us now Fort Myers Mayor Kevin Anderson. Mr. Mayor, good morning. We`re glad to have you on the phone with us this morning. Have you been able to assess damage? I know it`s still early there. What`s your sense of how bad it was? MAYOR KEVIN ANDERSON, FORT MYERS, FL: We haven`t had a full assessment obviously with the sun just coming up, but it is pretty bad. I`m standing on a floating concrete dock. I`m down in the River District of downtown. The problem is the dock is in the middle of an intersection, a block, two blocks away from the water. This is about a piece of concrete that weighs a ton. And it was moved this far away. It shows you how powerful the waters were last night. KOTB: I know one of the things, that`s most concerning in a moment like this is what happened to the people who decided to stay or who were left behind. Have you guys been able to conduct rescues? Do you know how many people are still out there and in need of your help? ANDERSON: We would estimate several dozen people who stayed behind were in need of some assistance. Our teams have been working on that. I`m happy to report at this time. I`ve been not -- I haven`t been told of any loss of life in the city. Now keep in mind, we have a metropolitan area and there may be some outside, but inside the city there`s been no reports to my knowledge. GUTHRIE: Fort Myers more or less took a direct hit, Mr. Mayor, what`s your sense of how this compares to other storms that Fort Myers has experienced? ANDERSON: I came here in the mid 70s. I was on the police department for almost 25 years, so a lot of storms here. This is by far the worst storm I have ever witnessed. They`re watching the water from my condo in the heart of downtown, watching that water rise and just flat out all the stories on the first floor. It was heartbreaking. KOTB: Boy, for -- Mayor for you who`s been there all those years and seen so many storms come and go to take a direct hit. So what is the plan now, like walk us through what will happen this morning and the days ahead? ANDERSON: So the first thing we need to do is make sure the roads are passable. And they`re safe. We do have a curfew in place for next 48 hours until we get a handle on everything. Once we get the roads cleared, you know, FPL will start working on the electricity. Our teams will be out there going through the neighborhoods trying to make sure people are safe, getting assistance, anyone who needs it. We`ll start working on getting the other utilities up and functioning getting cleaned up. We`ve gotten some great support pledge by the President and the governor. So I think I`m optimistic it`s going to be a long recovery but nonetheless we`re going to recover because Floridians are very resilient. [07:10:13] GUTHRIE: They are indeed. Mr. Mayor, thank you so much. Kevin Anderson of Fort Myers, you know, it`s going to be a busy day, so we thank you for your time. KOTB: All right, let`s -- ANDERSON: Thank you. KOTB: Thank you. Let`s turn now to Bill Karins. He`s been tracking the path of destruction where it`s heading and what it`s left behind, hey. BILL KARINS, NBC NEWS METEOROLOGIST: Yes, good morning. So we`ve been showing you where all the worst has been as far as the storm surge went, that was the Fort Myers area, Bonita Springs all the way down to Naples. Overnight, we`ve still had a lot of heavy rain. Our NBC affiliate in Orlando and meteorologists were saying in Kissimmee, there`s been houses with homes with one to two feet of water in them. The little McIver River in Seminole County located right about here is one foot over record flood stage. So again, there`s still problems and still water going into homes right now because of this situation. And look at Daytona Beach. A wind gust of 69 miles per hour, so this is down to a tropical storm, but it is not a pleasant morning in Volusia County, Flagler County heading up there to Jacksonville. That`s where the storm surge is going to be coming in during the day today. So even though it`s a weekend storm, there still could be some significant problems. And then it may actually intensify a little bit on its way up tomorrow in between Savannah and Charleston here to South Carolina, we may actually get landfall that either a strong tropical storm or as a hurricane tomorrow afternoon. And of course, we`re going to get heavy rain in this area, winds could gust possibly up to 70 miles per hour. And that way we could be dealing with some more power outages, guys, in this area too. And storm surge problems, which we`ll explain more about during the show today. GUTHRIE: All right, Bill, thank you. And as we`ve come on the air President Biden has officially declared the state of Florida, a major disaster. So that opens up funding and a lot of help hopefully today. NBC Nightly News anchor Lester Holt rode out the storm overnight in Bradenton just south of Tampa Bay. Homes there flooded, the area`s airport badly damage too. Lester, good morning, the view from where you sit. LESTER HOLT, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Well, Savannah, I went out to with my trusty flashlight a little while ago surveying the immediate area around us. There appears to be no major damage here. We spoke when heard from the mayor of Sarasota a while ago. He was venturing outside his home for the first time, saw plenty of damage. He`s not aware of anything catastrophic. But certainly during the night, we can hear this thing howling, ultimately dying down now. The rain has stopped and we`re feeling relative breezes after what we saw and went through yesterday. But we`re all OK. KOTB: Yes, difficult night for a lot of people. Lester, a lot of people spent the night in shelters. I`m sure they have tons of concerns about their homes. What are you hearing from them? HOLT: Yes, we went to a shelter a few hours before the eye wall came ashore and talked to people who made that choice. They`d heard the predictions. A lot of them thought it was a no brainer, immediately went into shelters. We talked to officials there who were very concerned that while they did have a number of people, they didn`t have nearly as many as they expected. And that`s why there`s a bit of trepidation this morning as the sun comes up here. You heard from one of the other mayors the sense of what they`re going to find now in the light of day in some of these neighborhoods. One couple of we talked to said they lived in a trailer home, very worried obviously about their neighborhood, the vulnerability. They decided to get out but so many of their neighbors did not. So that will be the big focus today, trying to get to those folks who rode it out and make sure they`re OK. GUTHRIE: All right, Lester, thank you. And of course, we`ll see you tonight on nightly news from Florida. I mean, bears (ph) repeating this is in the top five of strongest storms ever to hit the U.S. KOTB: Yes, that`s an incredible statistic. And as Bill mentioned, the worst of Ian now passing through Central Florida, seeing some heavy rain, strong winds, hitting Orlando, Blayne Alexander, is there, Blayne, good morning, what are you seeing? BLAYNE ALEXANDER, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Well, Hoda, you can see just here in our live shot, just how powerful these winds are. In fact, we just spoke with an officer who said, not too far away from here, there was a tree that came down into a motel. But by far the real concern here is the rain and of course, the concerns over flooding. Just here in the Orlando area, we saw about a foot, more than a foot of rain overnight. Now to put that into perspective, that`s more than double the amount that this area typically sees in the entire month of September. And that`s what`s leading to incredible images like these. I think we can show you this. We`ve got a video from one of our affiliates, our local reporter, Tony Atkins with our affiliate WESH 2, actually rescued a woman who was stranded in her car in floodwaters. She told our affiliate that she was a nurse trying to drive to work. She was swept away by the flood. Unbelievable pictures of him actually carrying her on his back to safety. And officials believe that as this rain is expected to continue here, it`s only going to see, we`re only going to see more pictures like that. In fact, just north of where we are, we`re already getting more reports of rescues having to occur with people stranded in cars on an on ramp to a highway. We`re also getting reports of water coming into some businesses here in the Orlando area. Now the other wrinkle really that a lot of officials are watching is of course Orlando is known for its theme parks, it`s known for Disney , some for SeaWorld , Universal , all of those parks have been shut down at least through the end of today. But there were a number of people who already came into town, hoping to kind of take advantage of some of the clearer days toward the beginning of the week. [07:15:20] Well, now they`re being told to shelter in place in their hotels, as the storm has continued -- continuing to blow through. Guys, we`re expecting to see rain at this same speed and the same intensity of wind until at least noon if not later, guys. KOTB: All right, Blayne, thank you. I mean, hats off to that WESH reporter for helping that nurse. But hats off to that nurse who was getting in her car and driving to work to help people, so, wow. GUTHRIE: Incredible sight. KOTB: Yes. GUTHRIE: -- puts her on his back, I mean just incredible. KOTB: Wow. MELVIN: Thanks for helping the helper. KOTB: Yes. All right, let`s welcome in Craig. CRAIG MELVIN, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Hey, Hoda, Savannah, good morning. Good morning to you as well. Obviously the storm has brought air travel across much of Florida to a total standstill. This morning, that is having a ripple effect for passengers all over the country. NBC`s Tom Costello is at Reagan National Airport with that part of the story. Tom, good morning. TOM COSTELLO, NBC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: Good morning, Craig. I just checked 2,000 flight cancelations right now nationwide, but the vast majority are flights going into or out of Florida as you would expect. And as Ian continues to move up the east coast, we expect flight cancelations and airports to close in Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, as the storm tracks north. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) COSTELLO (voice-over): Nothing brings travel to a standstill like a hurricane. In a time lapse, Flight Radar 24 capturing the mostly empty skies over Florida with only a handful of commercial flights staying out of harm`s way hugging the east coast into and out of Miami. The FAA status map showing closed runways and airports from Key West to Naples, Sarasota to Tampa to Orlando and Melbourne and Daytona Beach, leaving behind the few travelers who didn`t get out in time. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: In here you want to go over to the middle of the food court area because the airport is closing now. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Yes. UNIDENTIFIED MALE: And we`re not set up as a shelter. COSTELLO (voice-over): In Orlando, Brittany and Paul Inglesby (ph) and their baby unable to get home to Rochester. BRITTANY INGLESBY (ph), TRAVELER: If you have a little kid with you, he takes up priority. So when he starts running low on stuff, that`s when it gets kind of terrifying. COSTELLO (voice-over): Tampa International tweeting video of the last flight out before closing down, Wednesday, leaving behind some British tourists who were unable to catch an early flight home. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Had a lovely holiday. But then we were evacuated from the beach area. So we`re here at least until Friday. All the hotels are full. COSTELLO (voice-over): On Wednesday more than 2,100 flights canceled nationwide with most airlines waiving change or cancelation fees at least through Friday. This morning, Tampa International remains empty, managers plan to assess the condition of the runways and terminal then set a reopening timeline. CEO Joe Lopano . (on camera): I know you`ve got to do a full evaluation today of the condition of the airport on the runways. How soon do you think you might open? JOE LOPANO , CEO, TAMPA INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT: There`s a lot that has to take place once we assess the airfield. So we think the earliest we could open is Friday. (END VIDEOTAPE) COSTELLO: OK, so that`s Tampa, keep in mind, Tampa was really spared in the storm. We`re watching Orlando closely to see how they are impacted by the incredible amounts of water. I just checked by the way, Jacksonville technically is open despite that storm. But about 90 percent of flights canceled so just because technically they`re open nothing is going into Jacksonville. Atlanta is also experiencing flight cancelations, Charlotte too. Guys, back to you. MELVIN: All right, Tom Costello for us there at Reagan National. Tom, thank you. As that storm moves up the coast, we also got to wonder as it hits Georgia, South Carolina, the ripple effect it`s going to have on travel there as well. KOTB: Yes, let`s bring in Bill Karins. Bill, you said this thing was going to hit hard, it did. And now it`s kind of on the way out a tropical storm now. KARINS: Yes, and it may back up to a hurricane. I mean, we still have some issues and rain will be the issue up until the mid-Atlantic and into areas of the southeast. So here`s the storm exiting the Space Coast across, it took about 16 hours across the Florida peninsula. But look at these rainfall totals anywhere from South Carolina all of North Carolina much of Virginia. This is four to eight inches of rain isolated totals up to a foot so additional flash flooding in the next two days as we watch Ian as a tropical storm heading for the Carolinas in the coming days. That`s look at your national forecast. We`ll get your local forecast in the next 30 seconds. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (LOCAL NEWS) [07:20:35] KARINS: And still to come next half hour, we`re going to talk about the storm surge threat in the Jacksonville area. It`s going to be an interesting explainer about the river and the storm surge and stay tuned. KOTB: All right, we look forward to that. Thank you, Bill. And again we`ll have more on Ian`s wrath just ahead including the heroes and the helpers. They`re stepping up in a big way to help people cope and recover from this storm. GUTHRIE: Yes, we need the helpers right now. And then our friend Katie Couric revealing she has been privately battling breast cancer for months. But she`s sharing her diagnosis now, talking about her treatment. And she has a really important message she wants every woman to hear. But first this is Today on NBC. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) GUTHRIE: Coming up, our What Works Today series focusing on good stories across the country. MELVIN: We`re going to shed a light this morning on a little known national initiative giving women a chance, a better chance to raise healthy children who are ready to succeed. We`re going to hear from one new mom who says it actually saved her life after local news. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:26:20] (LOCAL NEWS) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (LOCAL NEWS) (COMMERCIAL BREAK) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) [07:30:29] UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Please tell me you are recording. You were? UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Yes. UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: Oh, my gosh. (END VIDEO CLIP) GUTHRIE: Yes, just what a moment. That was in Jacksonville overnight. And you can see a local reporter was right there when the winds so intense cause that shopping center signed to come crashing down. She was getting ready to go live. They got the shot, but it really demonstrates the power of this storm. KOTB: That`s exactly right. Yes. MELVIN: You know, one of the things that`s always striking is when storms like this hit as you talk about all the time, the helpers really show up in mass this time even before Ian made landfall, people have stepped up to help. GUTHRIE: Yes, and this morning, we are seeing these remarkable stories play out that just neighbors helping neighbors, NBC`s Kerry Sanders is right there in hard hit Punta Gorda. Hey, Kerry, good morning. KERRY SANDERS, NBC NEWS SENIOR NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Well, good morning. You know over my shoulder here you can see the incredible power of Hurricane Ian. But now comes as we`ve already seen the selfless power of people. (BEGIN VIDEOTAPE) SANDERS (voice-over): Slamming into Florida overnight, Hurricane Ian left communities like Sanibel Island, underwater, damaged, and in the dark. Florida`s Gulf coastline bearing the brunt of the storm, the wind and rain so dangerous and Punta Gorda, I had to grab onto the street sign just to stay on my feet. Cape Coral also severely impacted by Ian, making it difficult for emergency crews to reach those who did not evacuate. ROB HERNANDEZ, CITY MANAGER FOR CAPE CORAL, FL: The minute that the winds subside to below 45 miles an hour, our crews are going to be responding out there, clearing the roads to make sure that our first responders can get to those individuals that are trapped in their homes and in their vehicles. SANDERS (voice-over): Through all of the uncertainty -- UNIDENTIFIED MALE: We`re going to keep moving in all the affected areas. SANDERS (voice-over): Neighbors, friends, even complete strangers, doing whatever they can to help. Rescues on shore and on land, some even crossing state lines to pitch in. DESANTIS: We had all these power workers, these line workers from all these different states. I saw them from Texas, Louisiana. SANDERS (voice-over): New York`s National Guard sending two heavy lift helicopters and a contingent of soldiers to assist with rescue efforts, the Coast Guard assembling a small armada of ships for offshore rescue missions. In hard hit Naples, firefighters helping a woman escaped floodwaters. But the fire department also thanking local jet skiers for helping out writing, sometimes we need a ride to the rescue ourselves. In Bonita Beach, one good Samaritan braving the elements to save a cat trapped outside on an air conditioner. In St. Petersburg, staff at a botanical gardens hunkering down with flamingos to see them through the storm. (END VIDEOTAPE) SANDERS: As we`re standing here on this street, just a short distance from where I am, you can see from this drone video as the light is beginning to show, we can take a look at some of the damage in the neighborhood here. This is just off U.S. 41 along a street called Easy Street. So this has not been easy for anybody and the proof of that is to show those who work through the storm. This is at one of the local hospitals here in Charlotte County. This is a doctor wading through the water that filled portions of the hallways there and then you can see in this other image at the fossil hospital what it was really like, I think the message there head on a swivel. Guys, there`s going to be a lot of efforts with cleaning up but really it is the first daylight for people to assess how bad this was and where the worst damage is. And of course, whether those who are out there volunteers, neighbors, et cetera whether they can safely help those who need the help right now on top of what the emergency officials are doing, guys. KOTB: Yes, Kerry, thank you. That drone footage I think was the first time we`ve actually seen what a neighborhood looks like after the storm went through, roofs ripped off, real difficult times for folks there. GUTHRIE: And we do think about those first responders, they have families too but here they are showing up to the hospital to the firehouse and doing what needs to be done. Speaking of, we`ve got Chief Pete DiMaria, he`s the head of the Naples Fire Department with us. And Chief, we know you have had a long 24 hours. First of all, you know as we have been saying the sun is just coming up. But are you able to assess the damage the situation there and Naples? CHIEF PETE DIMARIA, NAPLES, FL FIRE DEPARTMENT: We were actually out last night doing assessment to see how bad it was and we still have a lot of floodwaters on the streets, a lot of horticultural debris down and a lot of vehicles and boats that need to be tended to. There still all over the streets right now. And so we have a lot of work here in Naples to take care of the, what we need to. [07:35:17] KOTB: Chief, just -- there was an image of you and your team at the firehouse, literally waiting waist deep through water, you did an interview standing there in the water. And I watched some of your guys trying to get the trucks up and running. And there have already been rescues underway. Can you just tell us about a couple of those? DIMARIA: Well, we made a couple of rescues where we had to actually walk from the fire station about two blocks to rescue a couple that was stuck in their house that was flooding rapidly. And our personnel, we were actually trapped in our station because the floodwaters came up so quickly. We have a great station here, but the bays are set low. And so they flooded our apparatus and the bay floors. And so our personnel took off on foot and they went over and made the rescue and brought the people back to our station and they`re still sheltering here waiting to get to a safe place. MELVIN: Chief, the flooding and the power outages obviously going to be a major concern over the next few days. What are you looking for over the next 24 or 48 hours? What are you most concerned about? DIMARIA: Well, we`re really concerned about trying to serve our community and get back out on the streets and take care of everyone that needs our help. We had some calls waiting last night as we were trying to get out of the station and we just could not get to some of the places because they`re still flooded. So we`re hoping today brings a daylight, bring some positive news that we`re able to get through the streets and get out and start checking all of our neighborhoods, making sure our community is safe. And serving our community we always have and, you know, if I could just give a message to tell people to hold tight in their communities and try to be safe. Don`t explore on the waters yet. Let`s get us over there and we`ll do our best to get there as quick as possible. GUTHRIE: Yes, good message to end on. Help them -- help, you guys get out there and doing that hard work. You need all the help you can get from the community too. Naples Fire Chief Pete DiMaria, thank you very much for your time this morning, sir. DIMARIA: Thank you. KOTB: Yes, Naples is one of the most beautiful places on earth. I used to live there. And when you look at it like that, and you think of that fire chief and those guys just trying to save their city, it`s really heroic efforts. GUTHRIE: And the water come rushing in, you know what, I`m sure there will be a lot of people who want to get out there, you want to see OK, what happened but they`re saying sit tight, let us do our jobs. KOTB: Yes, indeed. MELVIN: When we come back this morning, we`re going to have everything that you need to know ahead of what could be a very bad flu season. We got the newest guidance on shots to protect your family. And what about that COVID booster, should you get it at the same time? It`s a question a lot of folks are asking. KOTB: All right, but first, Katie Couric has got a message on the importance of those yearly mammograms as our friend reveals her own breast cancer diagnosis, a very personal story she`s now sharing right after this. (COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:41:32] MELVIN: We are back. It is 7:41. We`re back with In-Depth Today. And this morning, an important story that`s really close to our hearts. KOTB: Yes, every two minutes, a woman in this country is diagnosed with breast cancer and yesterday, our friend and our former colleague Katie Couric revealed she is now one of them. GUTHRIE: And of course Katie has been on the frontlines of cancer awareness for decades, she lost her husband to cancer. And she`s using her story now to urge all women to get checked and to advocate for themselves. Sheinelle is here with more on that. Hi, good morning. SHEINELLE JONES, NBC NEWS ANCHOR: Good morning. As she battles breast cancer, Katie is turning her story into a cautionary tale in hopes of saving lives.
